stories.title: Canadian received Bell Canada text saying 'Welcome to Palestine' while visiting Jerusalem
stories.summary: Bell Canada told National Post that its "roaming notifications are automated by an external vendor’s platform."
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
A Canadian traveller who received a text from Bell Canada welcoming him to “Palestine” while he was in Israel says he is shocked and disappointed.

The Ottawa resident — who only wanted to be identified by his first name, Charles, out of concerns for his safety amid rising antisemitism — told National Post he decided to take a trip to Israel and landed there last week. He was at the Holocaust memorial and museum Yad Vashem in Jerusalem when a text from the telecommunications company popped up on his phone.

“Welcome to Palestine,” it said, followed by information about his account’s travel plan. He said he was nauseated because he was standing in a place that showed the result of the Nazis’ obsession to eradicate the Jewish people. “And I get, from Bell Canada, a welcome to a non-existent country, whose aspirational goal…is to, again, eliminate the Jewish people,” he said.

Hamas, the terrorist group that murdered 1,200 people in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, the deadliest day for the Jewish community since the Holocaust, refers to the “struggle against the Jews” as “very great and very serious” in its 1988 charter . It calls Jewish people the enemy and says they should be “vanquished.” While there are Palestinians who have denounced the terror group, it has remained in power since taking over Gaza in 2007.

Several European countries, as well as Canada and Australia, recognized the State of Palestine in 2025. Prime Minister Mark Carney said his recognition was conditional, and would be based on whether Hamas would “fully disarm, and play no role in the future governance of Palestine.” Hamas remains in Gaza, using a decentralized system of governance to maintain and expand influence, according to research published by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Despite the promise of hosting democratic elections this year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas said they would be postponed until September 2027. There have been no legislative or presidential elections held since 2006.

Charles said it feels like there is a “concerted effort” around the world to erase Israel from existence. But receiving the text from a Canadian company while travelling abroad was especially “outrageous.”

“For them to say to me, a Canadian citizen and a longtime client, ‘Welcome to Palestine’ — to me, that’s making a political statement and it’s inappropriate,” he said.

A spokesperson from Bell Canada told National Post over email that international roaming welcome messages are “automatically triggered when a mobile device connects to a network tower in a new region.”

“Because of the close proximity of network towers in the region, some customers flying into Israel or traveling nearby have occasionally received notifications for roaming in Palestinian territories,” the statement said. “Like those of other global carriers, Bell’s roaming notifications are automated by an external vendor’s platform. This platform retrieves all location terminology directly from an independent, international industry-standard database, and Bell does not determine the language used.”

stories.title: Former MN-S CEO sues for wrongful termination and breach of contract
stories.summary: Métis Nation - Saskatchewan (MN-S) and former CEO Richard Quintal have entered a legal dispute over the former employee’s claims of wrongful termination and breach of contract.
stories.author: Grace Miller
stories.content:
Métis Nation – Saskatchewan (MN-S) and former CEO Richard Quintal have entered a legal dispute over the former employee’s claims of wrongful termination and breach of contract.

Quintal filed his suit on his belief he was let go after an employment contract extension due to political pressures from the Provincial Métis Council (PMC). He alleges he did not receive the compensation he says he is owed.

“On or about April 23, 2026, and as a result of what appeared to be political pressure, the President verbally notified the Plaintiff that the Defendants were going in a different direction and that the Plaintiffs employment with the Defendants was going to be terminated without cause,” reads Quintal’s claim.

He claims after several extensions, he was contracted to work in his position until July 31, 2030, at the time of the termination notice. His claim states PMC confirmed he would be let go effective as of May 15, 2026.

Quintal says he was invited to give an exit speech to PMC and MN-S President Glen McCallum made a public statement and video announcing Quintal’s termination

“The Plaintiff (Quintal) received notice that an emergency meeting of the PMC would be happening on May 11, 2026. The meeting took the entire day, and the President notified the Plaintiff in the evening that a new resolution had been passed, which rescinded his termination without cause and placed him on Suspension,” states the claim.

Quintal says he thinks he was put on suspension to evade the cost of firing him. He says the contract stipulated after being fired without cause he would receive the remainder of the Annual Base Salary which would have been payable over the term of the Agreement.

On June 11, Quintal says he received a letter from MN-S stating that an investigation was going to be launched to review the extension of his contract. He says as of Aug, 24, the investigation was continuing.

Quintal is seeking severance payment in the amount he says he is contractually allocated as well as damages.

MN-S has responded to the court action with an intention to defend the allegations.

By Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press

“I know everyone has been working extremely hard during this inquest. Unfortunately, I will be adjourning the inquest until further notice,” said Dr. David Cameron, the coroner presiding over the inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet.

“The reason for this is that we have some quite unanticipated investigation that needs to be done before we can continue.”

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

The coroner gave no details on the nature or focus of the investigation but said jurors and the public would be informed when the inquest was ready to resume.

The inquest finished hearing evidence on Wednesday and was set to reconvene Thursday afternoon so that lawyers for about a dozen parties could make their closing remarks and suggest recommendations to the jury.

Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old woman of Afro-Indigenous and Ukrainian descent, died on May 27, 2020 after police were called to the west-end apartment she shared with relatives.

The inquest was temporarily thrown off course after her mother, Claudette Beals, made a new allegation against police, who were cleared of wrongdoing by a watchdog agency.

Beals alleged officers pushed her daughter toward the balcony, causing the inquest to go on an extended break so that lawyers could figure out a way forward.

Two officers who were in the apartment had previously testified that Korchinski-Paquet was allowed into the apartment to use the bathroom, then introduced to a paramedic. Korchinski-Paquet moved quickly to the balcony, knocking over an air conditioning unit in the process, they said.

The Special Investigations Unit, one of Ontario’s police watchdog organizations, found she died while trying to move from her apartment’s balcony to the one next door. The SIU did not participate in the inquest, and its investigation is outside the scope of the proceedings.

Jurors in coroner’s inquests do not assign blame or legal responsibility, but they may make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future.

The inquest has focused largely on Korchinski-Paquet’s history of seizures from epilepsy as well as education and training around epilepsy and postictal delirium or psychosis, mental states that can occur after seizures and lead to uncharacteristic behaviour.

Korchinski-Paquet had experienced two seizures earlier in the day, hours before police were called over a fight involving knives. Korchinski-Paquet, her mother and her brother each called 911 and mentioned her diagnosis and seizures to the call taker, jurors heard.

stories.title: Cause under investigation after large dairy barn fire near Listowel
stories.summary: Firefighters from several Perth County-area departments battled a large barn fire near Listowel on Wednesday night
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Firefighters from several Perth County-area departments battled a large barn fire near Listowel on Wednesday night that affected dozens of cattle.

North Perth Fire Department crews from the Listowel, Atwood and Monkton stations were dispatched to a working structure fire at a dairy barn on Line 88 at about 9:05 p.m.

Mutual aid assistance was provided by fire departments from Minto, Mapleton and Howick as crews worked to contain the blaze.

Heavy equipment was brought to the scene at approximately 11:15 p.m. to assist firefighters.

Officials said 88 cattle were involved in the fire, although it remains unclear how many animals were possibly lost.

No injuries to firefighters or anyone else at the scene were reported.

The cause of the fire has not yet been determined and the investigation remains ongoing.

As of Thursday morning, one Listowel fire crew remained at the scene.

stories.title: Toronto traffic agent dead after being hit by a truck in East York
stories.summary: Mayor Olivia Chow said in a statement the agent was on duty at the time of the collision, which happened near Millwood Road and Overlea Boulevard.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A City of Toronto traffic agent is dead after being hit by a truck in East York Thursday morning.

Mayor Olivia Chow said in a statement the agent was on duty at the time of the collision, which happened near Millwood Road and Overlea Boulevard.

Police said officers were called to the area at 9:02 a.m. on Thursday and that the victim was pronounced dead on scene.

The driver of the truck remained at the scene, police added.

Chow said she was “heartbroken” to learn the news.

“Traffic agents do some of the most demanding work in our city. They work in live traffic, in all weather conditions, to keep people moving and protect pedestrians, cyclists and drivers,” she said.

“Every shift, they help us get where we’re going safely. We are deeply thankful for that service, and this loss is a painful reminder of the risks they take on our behalf.”

An investigation is underway.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Ottawa buys stake in Cohere as AI firm raises money at $35.7-billion valuation
stories.summary: Financing is the largest ever by a Canadian startup and would make Cohere the country’s most valuable privately held tech company
stories.author: Murad Hemmadi, Joe Castaldo
stories.content:
Cohere Inc. has secured most of a planned $7-billion financing, including backing from the federal government, in a deal that would value the Toronto-based AI company at $35.7-billion.

The financing is the largest by a Canadian startup in history, and once completed, would make Cohere the country’s most valuable privately held technology company.

The round was led by German retail giant Schwarz Group and includes funding from Bell Canada’s venture arm and Luxembourg-based Bullhound Capital, Cohere said in a news release on Thursday.

The Canadian government is putting $1.6-billion into the deal and taking an equity stake in the firm – a direct investment of unprecedented size in a technology company that’s part of Ottawa’s strategy to build out and secure the country’s AI strengths and economic sovereignty.

Returning backers that have committed to the financing include chip giant Nvidia Corp., Montreal’s Inovia Capital, and Prosperity7 Ventures, an arm of Saudi Aramco.

Cohere chief financial officer Francois Chadwick said in an interview that the financing is necessary for the company to invest in compute infrastructure, develop its AI models and expand globally. He added that Cohere has made a number of commitments related to hiring and investing in Canada as part of the government’s investment.

“Canada needs to be there at the forefront,” Mr. Chadwick said. “Instead of having two global leaders – China and the U.S. – Canada becomes a global leader in the AI world.”

The Globe and Mail first reported last month that Cohere had told investors it was in advanced talks to raise as much as US$3-billion, including financing from the Canadian and German governments, at a valuation of US$20-billion.

“Under this agreement, Cohere will stay Candian,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a press conference announcing the investment on Thursday, calling the new round a “vote of confidence” in both Cohere and Canada.

stories.title: Toronto dad and two daughters shot in violent Bridle Path home invasion: police
stories.summary: Three of four residents of a house in an affluent Toronto neighbourhood were shot during a violent home invasion early Thursday morning.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Canada

Police say the man and one of his adult daughters suffered life-threatening gunshot wounds from three suspects who fired 'multiple times'

Three of four residents of a house in an affluent Toronto neighbourhood were shot during a violent home invasion early Thursday morning.Ernest Doroszuk/Toronto Sun

A Toronto father and his adult daughter are fighting for their lives in hospital after being shot during a violent home invasion in their affluent neighbourhood early Thursday morning.

Two other members, the man’s wife and other daughter, are also in hospital with what Toronto Police Service said are non-life-threatening injuries suffered as a result of the incident in the Bridle Path area.

In a Thursday morning news conference, holdup squad Insp. Kristy Smith said officers were dispatched to the home on Bayview Avenue and Lawrence Avenue East around 4 a.m., where three masked suspects armed with handguns forced their way in through a rear door. One also carried a hammer, but Smith said it’s unclear if it was used to break into the home.

“Once inside, they confronted the family,” Smith said.

“A struggle ensued during this altercation, in which the suspects fired their guns multiple times, and one victim was struck with a hammer.”

It was the mother who was hit with the tool, while her other daughter was shot, a police spokesperson earlier confirmed to CBC.

At this time, police don’t believe the victims returned fire.

The suspects, for whom there is no description, fled in an SUV after the attack,Toronto Police Operations posted on X.

Shooting: (Update) Bayview Ave & Lawrence Ave E 3:43am - two people are suffering from life-threatening injuries - other two individuals have non-life-threatening injuries - anyone with information, contact police @ 416-808-2222#GO2281709 ^se — Toronto Police Operations (@TPSOperations) October 29, 2026

Smith said it was too early to determine if the home was targeted or the suspect’s motive, though she did imply it could be another case of a home invasion for the purpose of stealing a high-end vehicle, incidents of which she said are on the rise.

“Typically in an affluent neighbourhood come nice things, and there’s always people out there that want to acquire nice things. And carjackings used to be a way that criminals would acquire cars. That seems to have transitioned into breaking into a home to steal a vehicle,” she said, noting the homeowner’s vehicle was not stolen.

Smith went on to say citizens “can’t go around always being paranoid about having nice things,” but they should “be ultra aware” of whether they are being followed and contact 911 if they feel like they are.

About 30 minutes after the incident, police also responded to a shooting in the area of The Queensway and Parkside Drive, at the opposite end of the city, where one adult male arrived at a hospital with a non-life-threatening gunshot wound. It’s unknown where the incident took place, and there’s no information about a suspect.

Shooting: The Queensway & Parkside Dr 4:19am - adult male attended hospital with gun-shot wound - injuries are non-life-threatening - unknown where the incident took place - no suspect information - anyone with information, contact police @ 416-808-2222#GO2281778 ^se pic.twitter.com/PaInpmvE8P — Toronto Police Operations (@TPSOperations) October 29, 2026

“We are aware of that incident, and I can’t say whether it’s connected or not,” Smith said, “but it’s definitely something that we’re going to investigate so that we can draw that connection if there is one.”

Bridle Path residents can expect an increased police presence in the days ahead as police investigate and step up patrols.

“We recognize how frightening and disturbing an incident like this is not only for the victims, but also for the residents and the entire community, including the loved ones of the extended family. People should be able to feel safe in their homes. I want to assure residents that us as the Toronto Police Service will do everything that we can to identify, locate, and bring these suspects to criminal justice.”

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Frontier AI one of greatest threats to Canadians as Ottawa releases national security strategy
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney's government released the first national security strategy in over two decades on Thursday.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Frontier AI models are one of the greatest current threats to Canadians, say federal officials as the government released a national security strategy aiming to steel the country against growing risks and even war.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government released the first national security strategy in over two decades on Thursday. At more than 13 pages, it provides a high-level view on how Ottawa aims to protect the country against wide-ranging threats such as war, artificial intelligence, hackers, espionage, sabotage and foreign interference.

It also focuses on protecting Canada’s economic interests and growing its autonomy in eight key sectors: Emerging technologies, critical minerals, defence, energy, transportation, pharmaceuticals and biotech, food security and “payments, settlements and investments”.

“Once distant threats are now proximate and immediate. The global order that long protected our sovereignty has ruptured,” reads Thursday’s document, titled The Plan for a Stronger Canada.

During a background briefing for reporters Thursday morning, senior officials laid out the threat landscape bluntly.

“The threats facing Canada and Canadians have become so complex and interrelated, from climate change to terrorism, crime, opioids, and pandemics, cyber attacks to frontier AI to the increasing possibility of a major war,” said one senior official.

To do so, the strategy states Canada is looking to boost its intelligence and security apparatus, promising to build more intelligence, counterintelligence and cyber-defence capabilities and likely grant them more legal powers in the near future.

Notably, the document promises new intelligence and national security legislation within the next year to “modernize” the existing regime. Such reforms have been infrequent and irregular throughout the last decades, leading to a national security apparatus frequently complaining of being hamstrung by outdated laws.

The document and officials also said the government will undertake a review of “our entire national security enterprise,” including oversight and review bodies, within four years.

The document also promises five more strategies specific to foreign policy, defence policy, public safety, intelligence and economic security in the coming weeks and months.

During the briefing, the officials said there would be costs to the new expected measures but declined to provide further detail ahead of next week’s federal budget announcement.

The senior officials also strongly hinted at a desire to create a new foreign human intelligence capacity that could one day lead to Canada having its own service like the U.S.’s CIA or the U.K.’s MI6.

“I don’t think we’re on the verge of announcing a separate agency that would be akin to the CIA or MI6, but at the same time we’re looking at the capabilities that our intelligence agencies have and making sure that they are fit for purpose and for the challenges that that we face today,” said one official.

“If we need to do more of something, we May look at legislative change. We May look at new authorities, and yes, maybe somewhere down the road we May look at the creation of a new body,” he added.

But one of the biggest threats to Canadians currently is frontier AI, said the officials.

Such models have exponentially boosted the speed and ability for cyber criminals to find vulnerabilities in all sorts of software and exploit them before a fix is found. The models are also infamously breaking into other companies’ systems in order to complete tasks, unbeknownst to their creators.

“AI models that are escaping and doing things that their designers did not intend them to do, and that could go in a really terrible direction,” said one official.

“Frontier AI… May be one of the greatest threats facing Canadians today,” he added.

The statement came the same day Carney is expected to make an announcement about artificial intelligence in Montreal.

The officials also acknowledged that many Canadians are wary of giving police and intelligence agencies more power — particularly when it impacts people’s privacy — and promised to be far better at communicating about the threat landscape and what the government is doing about it.

“I think through this transparency and through this awareness, the hope is that it will increase the public discourse, and hopefully better inform, and then allow us to make better policy recommendations and decisions,” said one official.

stories.title: Poll says long wait times led half of Canadians to avoid going to the hospital
stories.summary: Montreal - A new poll says long wait times lead half of Canadians to avoid seeing a doctor or going to the hospital.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The poll was conducted by Léger and commissioned by right-leaning think-tanks the Montreal Economic Institute, SecondStreet.org, and Canadian Constitution Foundation.

The percentage of respondents who say they avoid consulting doctors because of wait times is highest among women, people over 55 and Quebecers.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

Image 9Image 10Image 11

The survey numbers do not indicate whether the people who avoided seeing a doctor had seen a nurse or turned to other services like pharmacists.

It is also unclear whether respondents started avoiding hospitals because of wait times over the past year or at another point in their lives.

Just over a quarter of poll respondents say they have paid for private health care to avoid wait times or unsatisfactory service.

The survey also indicates that 61 per cent of Canadians support being able to pay out of pocket or use insurance to access private care if they cannot get timely care in the public system. However, a quarter of respondents say they oppose the coexistence of public and private health care systems.

Asked if they believe the health care system in their area needs change, 84 per cent of respondents said yes.

The poll ran from Oct. 16 to 19, 2026, among an online panel of 1,510 Canadians.

The polling industry’s professional body, the Canadian Research Insights Council, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population.

stories.title: London Police Hate Crimes Unit investigating video showing racist incident at Western
stories.summary: The London Police Service (LPS) has confirmed its Hate Crime Unit is investigating an alleged hate related incident that took place on the Western University campus Tuesday, much of which was captured on cell phone video.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content The London Police Service (LPS) has confirmed its Hate Crime Unit is investigating an alleged hate related incident that took place on the Western University campus Tuesday, much of which was captured on cell phone video.

The video appears to show a verbal altercation between a man and a group of women. The video was shared with CTV News. The sender claims there were children present when it took place. A man can be seen in a car marked with business logos arguing with a woman taking the video.

The following is a partial transcript of the altercation: Woman: He’s saying that I should take off my hijab. He’s saying that Muslims don’t belong here. Man: You don’t belong here. Woman: Why don’t we belong here. Man: Because you’re not indicative to Western culture.

Man: A woman is not supposed to wear that. Woman: A woman is not supposed to wear what? Man: The hijab. Woman: Why can’t I wear the hijab? Man: Christian values. Woman: Why can’t I wear the hijab? It’s my choice. Man: It’s not Christian values.

This is my country. The altercation continues with two other women coming to the defence of the woman taking the video Woman 2: I was born here. I know what I’m talking about. Man: You weren’t born here. You’re Pakistani.

Woman: How do you know she’s Pakistani? How do you know her? Man: I don’t give a (expletive) how I know her. Look at her. I didn’t ask for you (expletive) to be here. CTV News tracked the man down. He identified himself only as Tom.

He said the incident started when the woman flipped him the middle finger. “I consider myself a nationalist. And the fact that this country was built by the Irish, the Scottish, and basically all the Western cultures. This culture was built up on Christian values.

And I don’t see those Christian values being put forth in regards to what’s going on in today’s culture at this point in time,” he said. Muslim faith leader Abd Alfatah Twakkal, chair of the Council of London Imams, said he’s disturbed by the video.

“The contents were quite vile, racist, Islamophobic, disturbing on many different levels. And the fact that this was taking place against a visible member of our community, a woman wearing a hijab, in front of her children.

This is what makes it more egregious,” he said. The National Council of Canadian Muslims said provincial and federal governments need to take action against Islamophobia. “It’s time for elected officials to sit down with us and to build some kind of reaction or a national strategy on combatting this kind of Islamophobia,” said Nccm spokesperson Steven Zhou.

Western University issued a statement in response to the video. “Western does not tolerate hate or discrimination and is committed to using all available tools to address it,” the school said. “We are dedicated to providing a safe, respectful and supportive environment for all members of our campus community.” Western also said it’s working with all levels of government and London police “to address concerns and combat hate and discrimination in all its forms.” “We encourage anyone who has concerns with respect to hate or discrimination on campus to report such concerns directly to the Western Special Constable Service and/or the Human Rights Office.” Suspect apologizes after learning of investigation The altercation continued, with the video lasting a total of two minutes and 45 seconds.

Man: You and you’re little leftist, socialist, propogandist, little … Woman: You’re racist. Man: Yeah, I’m racist. (Expletive) right I’m racist. In the meantime, after learning from CTV News the incident is being investigated by the LPS Hate Crimes Unit, Tom said he apologized for his behaviour.

“I did do a nasty thing. I admit it. I’m trying to reconcile the difference,” he said. He was then asked if he is turning himself in. “I will probably. I’m going to give them a call definitely and make it easier for them.

And, again, I’ll have to pay for the consequences, but again this is a free country,” he said. The women in the video did not want to be identified and declined our request for an interview.

stories.title: North Perth teen charged with two counts of murder in fatal 2025 crash
stories.summary: A North Perth teenager has been charged with two counts of second-degree murder in connection with a two-vehicle crash that killed two people in the Municipality of North Perth last year.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A North Perth teenager has been charged with two counts of second-degree murder in connection with a two-vehicle crash that killed two people in the Municipality of North Perth last year.

Perth County OPP, paramedics and firefighters responded to a crash involving a passenger vehicle and a pickup truck on Perth Line 86 at about 8:30 p.m. on Oct. 4, 2025.

Police said a 72-year-old and a 75-year-old who were travelling in the passenger vehicle died from injuries suffered in the collision.

The driver of the pickup truck was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries and was later released.

Following a year-long investigation, an 18-year-old from North Perth was arrested Wednesday and charged with two counts of second-degree murder.

The accused was released from custody and is scheduled to appear in a Stratford courtroom at a later date.

Police said the accused was a youth at the time of the collision and cannot be identified under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

stories.title: Budget 2026 title and theme focus on Canada’s sovereignty, minister reveals
stories.summary: The federal government has released the title and theme for its upcoming budget set to be tabled on Nov. 5, which the finance minister's office says reflects a period of "change."
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The federal government has released the title and theme for its upcoming budget set to be tabled on Nov. 5 , which the finance minister’s office says reflects a period of “profound change and uncertainty.”

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne posted on social media Thursday morning revealing the title “Masters OF OUR Destiny: Budget 2026,” with the cover of the budget document, showing power lines suspended over a forested valley landscape.

Champagne’s office also released a statement explaining the significance of the chosen theme and title.

It was inspired by the 1962 Quebec electoral campaign of then-premier Jean Lesage, where the slogan was “Maîtres chez Nous,” loosely translated to “Masters of Our Own House.”

The note from Champagne’s office says the slogan at the time was “a defining expression during a moment of profound change and uncertainty,” as the Lesage government was planning to build up hydroelectric resources and institutions that would support the economy.

“Today, Canada faces a moment of profound change. Trade relationships are redefined. Old alliances are being tested. The forces reshaping the world are challenging our economy, our sovereignty and our sense of who we are,” the note said.

“Through Budget 2026, we reinforce that we are masters of our destiny. That we build our economic strength. That we are there for Canadians. That we defend what makes us Canadians.”

It added: “That is the ambition at the heart of Budget 2026: Maîtres chez nous. Masters of our destiny.”

Ottawa’s latest budget comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney ‘s government has been focused for over a year on rewiring Canada’s economy and trade relationships in order to reduce reliance on a more volatile United States.

U.S. tariffs and trade tensions continue to impact Canada’s economy and job market, while geopolitical conflicts lead to rising oil and gas prices and pose a risk that inflation could continue to rise as a result.

stories.title: Federal government doubles funding to $10 million for Next Gen athletes program
stories.summary: Toronto - The federal government is doubling its annual investment in the Next Gen athlete program to $10 million, money that will be matched dollar-for-dollar by private-sector donors beginning this year.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - The federal government is doubling its annual investment in the Next Gen athlete program to $10 million, money that will be matched dollar-for-dollar by private-sector donors beginning this year.

JMC[](http://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/federal-government-doubles-funding-to-10-million-for-next-gen-athletes-program/article_9e9672b3-087a-587b-b90e-04ff329020db.html)

By The Canadian Press

The announcement, made Thursday by the federal government, the Canadian Olympic Committee and the Canadian Paralympic Committee, brings total annual public-private investment in the program to more than $20 million.

Launched in 2017, Next Gen supports emerging high-performance athletes on the path to future Olympic and Paralympic Games, providing access to coaching, training environments, competition opportunities and sport science expertise.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

Of the athletes who came through the Next Gen program, the COC says 401 have gone on to the Olympic Games and 134 to the Paralympic Games.

The governing body says 62 per cent of Canada’s Olympians at the Milan Cortina Games benefited from Next Gen support, including 15 of the country’s 21 medallists.

On the Paralympic side, 65 per cent of the team received help from the program, accounting for 16 of Canada’s 30 medallists.

“Canada’s top athletes are a great source of pride for our entire country, and our government is committed to investing in their success on the world stage,” said Adam van Koeverden, Secretary of State for Sport, in a statement. “Through this innovative partnership with the private sector, we’re bringing new investment into Canadian sport to support the next generation of Team Canada athletes.”

Thursday’s announcement comes as the federal government continues to ramp up its investment in a national sport system that has been described as chronically underfunded.

In April’s spring economic update, Ottawa injected $755 million over five years, with another $118 million each year after, to help host international sporting events, support athletes and boost participation in sport.

The government also announced last week that more than 60 national sports organizations will share $60 million in additional federal funding.

Ottawa, through the Build Communities Strong Fund, also committed $26 million toward Calgary’s Olympic Oval in July and $76 million to build a new national basketball centre in Toronto in September.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ottawa quietly abandoned promise to end thermal coal exports after industry lobbying, A-G says
stories.summary: Environment and Climate Change Canada stopped its work without ever notifying the public and without any record of being directed to do so
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
Environment and Climate Change Canada abandoned its work on ending thermal coal exports without ever notifying the public and without any record of being directed to do so.

An auditor-general report tabled Thursday criticized the move and pointed out Canada is co-chair of an international alliance meant to help countries transition away from coal.

Burning coal is one of the most polluting forms of electricity generation. In 2021, Canada committed to banning thermal coal exports by 2030.

The audit found that while Environment Canada worked for three years to find a way to enforce the ban, that work stopped altogether in November, 2024 after lobbying from the coal industry.

“The department did not produce evidence of an official direction to discontinue work on the ban in 2024,” the report says.

The decision to stop the work wasn’t formalized until August, 2025, when the federal government was looking for cost-saving measures.

“However, we also found no clear records to show that the department had provided the minister with an assessment of the implications of stopping all work on the export ban,” the report reads.

“While the commitment had been announced internationally and noted in multiple federal strategies, the work on the ban was stopped with no public announcement.”

Thermal coal exports were higher in 2025 than they were in 2021, the auditor general said.

The auditor-general’s report criticized the government’s secrecy on the file.

“The lack of public information and updates on the government’s current approach is concerning,” the report said.

“Transparency in decision making provides certainty and enables interested parties, such as provincial and territorial governments, coal mining companies, transportation authorities, shipping terminals, and the labour force to contribute to a just transition.”

stories.title: Middlesex County Council Meeting Highlights – October 27, 2026
stories.summary: Council Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by Middlesex County Council or Committee of the Whole at business meetings. The Council Highlights are not an official record of County Council proceedings. To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Council Meetings and Minutes.
stories.content:
Council Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by Middlesex County Council or Committee of the Whole at business meetings. The Council Highlights are not an official record of County Council proceedings. To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Council Meetings and Minutes .

Economic Development and Tourism Shows Strong Results in Q3

The Committee of the Whole received the Q3 Economic Development and Tourism Performance Report showing strong growth in business engagement, investment attraction, workforce development, and tourism promotion throughout the third quarter of 2026.

The Economic Development department supported more than 1,100 investment inquiries, helped advance 14 business expansion opportunities, and continued advocacy efforts with organizations such as the Southwestern Ontario Marketing Alliance, Ontario Food Cluster, and the provincial and federal governments. Several significant investments were announced, including expansions by Dairy Lane Systems and Armo-Tool Limited, as well as the opening of Blue Lakes Premium Meats’ new $30 million processing facility in North Middlesex.

Tourism initiatives also gained momentum through the Find It Here in Middlesex County campaign, which showcased more than 75 local businesses and attractions. The campaign generated strong digital engagement and supported nearly 190 tourism events and initiatives across the county.

Workforce development efforts continued to connect residents with employment opportunities through the new Workforce Navigator program, which has seen 36 referrals, surpassing its initial goal. The Work in Middlesex online job portal saw growing usage from job seekers and employers alike with over 1500 job seekers registered.

Read the Economic Development & Tourism - Q3-2026 Performance Report for more information.

Updated Procedure By-Law

County Council passed the updated Procedure By-law, which provides consistency in how Council conducts business and enhances public accessibility.

The changes reflect current best practices and align with the County’s broader governance framework. Updates include revisions to inaugural meeting procedures, changes to the agenda structure, new provisions for alternate members of County Council, and the clarification of rules related to reconsidering decisions from previous terms of Council.

Under the By-law, members of the public can register to speak on items appearing on a published agenda up until noon on the day before a meeting, creating a clearer and more accessible process for public participation. It also expands and clarifies circumstances where delegations would not be permitted, helping ensure the process supports fair and effective decision-making.

For more information, see By-Law No. 7439 .

Updated Human Resources Policy Handbook

The Committee of the Whole approved an updated Human Resources Policy Handbook, the first full review of the framework in a decade. The modernization initiative streamlined and consolidated existing policies into a more user-friendly structure, organized around employment, benefits, workplace expectations, and health and safety.

The updated handbook strengthens consistency, supports legislative compliance, reduces duplication, and provides clearer guidance for employees and management. It also aligns Human Resources policies with current organizational practices and digital systems. Implementation will include modernization and standardization of the supporting forms, templates, and administrative tools associated with the policies. The policies will continue to be reviewed in response to legislative and regulatory amendments, collective agreement changes, and evolving operational practices and circumstances.

Read the Middlesex County Human Resources Policy Handbook report for more details.

Inaugural Meeting for new Council term set for November 26, 2026

County Council received details for the 2026 Inaugural Meeting, which will take place on November 26, 2026, marking the start of the new term of County Council. The event will begin with a performance by the Medway Madrigal Choir, followed by the formal inaugural meeting and reception.

The inaugural ceremony provides an opportunity to welcome the new Council and recognize the beginning of the term. Key parts of the Inaugural Meeting include swearing in members of the 2026-2030 County Council and electing Middlesex County’s next Warden, who will serve as part of Council’s leadership team for the next year.

For more information, read the 2026 Inaugural Meeting of Council report .

Recommendations made by the Committee of the Whole at the October 27, 2026, meeting will be considered by County Council at its next regular meeting on December 8, 2026 . The Legislative Services Department maintains the official record for all County government proceedings.

For more information please contact: @email

Library Board Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by the Middlesex Library Board at business meetings. The Library Board Highlights are not an official record of Board proceedings.To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Middlesex Meetings and Minutes.

2027 Draft Library Board Budget

The Middlesex County Library Board reviewed its draft 2027 operating and capital budget, which supports the continued delivery of library and EarlyON services across the county. The proposed net budget totals $7.4 million, representing an increase of $106,091 (1.5%) over 2026. The draft budget focuses on creating exceptional experiences for patrons, expanding the Library’s reach, and supporting lifelong learning.

Key investments supporting the Library’s strategic priorities include staffing adjustments, expanded branch and Indigenous-led programming, collection development, and meeting the rising costs of digital resources, subscriptions, and material processing.

The capital budget includes technology replacements such as new public and staff computers, iPads, and network infrastructure, and renovations at the Ilderton and Dorchester branches.

The EarlyON budget maintains provincial funding levels while preserving enhanced programming hours introduced in 2026 through continued Middlesex County support. The draft budget will be presented to Middlesex County’s Budget Committee in December.

See the2027 Draft Library Board Budget report") for more information.

Busy fall for Middlesex County Library

The latest Library Activity Report showcases a busy fall season at the Library. Programming highlights include PD Day Firefighter Visits at the Dorchester and Glencoe Branches on October 26, a jigsaw puzzle swap at the Lucan branch from October 26 to 31, Halloween Storytime at the Strathroy Branch on October 30, and Poppy making at the Dorchester branch on November 2.

Library staff are currently reviewing the draft Facility Master Plan, which will guide the future of library services and facility improvements. On November 3, all branches will be closed to the public while staff take part in the annual Staff Development Day, which will focus on collection management, emerging technologies, and health and safety.

For more information, read theLibrary Activities Report").

Summer Reading Program Sees Strong Growth Across Middlesex County

Middlesex County Library’s 2026 Summer at the Library program attracted more than 3000 participants across all age groups, helping residents to stay engaged with reading throughout the summer. Registration increased among children, teens, and adults, with more than 2,100 children taking part in the annual reading challenge.

New program elements helped drive participation, including collectible “reading buddies” for children and Library Quest, a Dungeons & Dragons-inspired reading challenge for teens. Adult participation also continued to grow through a summer reading contest and prize draw.

The reading program was complemented by a wide range of activities and events at library branches, including arts and crafts workshops, wildlife presentations, active games, author visits, and opportunities to connect with local camps and community groups. Programming highlights include natural lip balm making, polymer jewelry workshops, and Croc charm creation at the Dorchester branch, while the Glencoe branch offered citrus-print tea towels and a jellyfish paint night. Participants in Mount Brydges created DIY stickers, and Ilderton explored miniature coastal scenes through shoebox seascapes.

Library Board Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by the Middlesex Library Board at business meetings. The Library Board Highlights are not an official record of Board proceedings.To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Middlesex Meetings and Minutes.
2027 Draft Library Board Budget

The Middlesex County Library Board reviewed its draft 2027 operating and capital budget, which supports the continued delivery of library and EarlyON services across the county. The proposed net budget totals $7.4 million, representing an increase of $106,091 (1.5%) over 2026. The draft budget focuses on creating exceptional experiences for patrons, expanding the Library’s reach, and supporting lifelong learning.

Key investments supporting the Library’s strategic priorities include staffing adjustments, expanded branch and Indigenous-led programming, collection development, and meeting the rising costs of digital resources, subscriptions, and material processing.
The capital budget includes technology replacements such as new public and staff computers, iPads, and network infrastructure, and renovations at the Ilderton and Dorchester branches.

The EarlyON budget maintains provincial funding levels while preserving enhanced programming hours introduced in 2026 through continued Middlesex County support. The draft budget will be presented to Middlesex County’s Budget Committee in December.
See the2027 Draft Library Board Budget report") for more information.
Busy fall for Middlesex County Library

The latest Library Activity Report showcases a busy fall season at the Library. Programming highlights include PD Day Firefighter Visits at the Dorchester and Glencoe Branches on October 26, a jigsaw puzzle swap at the Lucan branch from October 26 to 31, Halloween Storytime at the Strathroy Branch on October 30, and Poppy making at the Dorchester branch on November 2.

Library staff are currently reviewing the draft Facility Master Plan, which will guide the future of library services and facility improvements. On November 3, all branches will be closed to the public while staff take part in the annual Staff Development Day, which will focus on collection management, emerging technologies, and health and safety.
For more information, read theLibrary Activities Report").
Summer Reading Program Sees Strong Growth Across Middlesex County

Middlesex County Library’s 2026 Summer at the Library program attracted more than 3000 participants across all age groups, helping residents to stay engaged with reading throughout the summer. Registration increased among children, teens, and adults, with more than 2,100 children taking part in the annual reading challenge.

New program elements helped drive participation, including collectible “reading buddies” for children and Library Quest, a Dungeons & Dragons-inspired reading challenge for teens. Adult participation also continued to grow through a summer reading contest and prize draw.

The reading program was complemented by a wide range of activities and events at library branches, including arts and crafts workshops, wildlife presentations, active games, author visits, and opportunities to connect with local camps and community groups. Programming highlights include natural lip balm making, polymer jewelry workshops, and Croc charm creation at the Dorchester branch, while the Glencoe branch offered citrus-print tea towels and a jellyfish paint night. Participants in Mount Brydges created DIY stickers, and Ilderton explored miniature coastal scenes through shoebox seascapes.
The successful summer program highlights the Library’s ongoing commitment to literacy, lifelong learning, and creating engaging experiences for residents of all ages.
Read theSummer at the Library 2026 report") for more information.

stories.title: Financial intelligence watchdog plagued by delays, auditor general finds
stories.summary: Ottawa - The auditor general says Canada's financial intelligence watchdog is moving at a snail's pace when it comes to providing law enforcement with information to support criminal investigations.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The auditor general says Canada’s financial intelligence watchdog is moving at a snail’s pace when it comes to providing law enforcement with information to support criminal investigations.

Oct. 29, 2026

Updated 11 mins ago

By Kyle Duggan The Canadian Press

The Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre plays a key role in Canada’s anti-money laundering and anti-terrorist financing regime.

But a new audit released today says it takes the agency an average of about four months to pass on intelligence to law enforcement — and that half the time, the information arrives too late to be useful to investigations.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

That’s just one of several damning conclusions in nine federal audits the office of Auditor General Karen Hogan tabled in Parliament today.

Another report reveals Environment Canada stopped its work in 2024 on banning thermal coal exports — and didn’t bother to tell the public, even though Canada’s commitment to banning thermal coal exports by 2030 remained firmly in place.

Another audit says Health Canada went more than a billion dollars over budget on implementing the new Canadian Dental Plan in the first two years of the program, and struggled to track whether it was improving oral health.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Stelco must recall laid off workers ‘immediately,’ Joly says in new letter
stories.summary: In a letter dated Oct. 29 addressed to Stelco’s president, Paul Simon, Joly said she expects a 'concrete and credible plan for re-engagement with these workers.'
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said she is prepared to sit down with Stelco representatives on the basis that the laid off workers are “recalled immediately.”

In a letter dated Oct. 29 obtained by Global News and addressed to Stelco’s president, Paul Simon, Joly said she expects a “concrete and credible plan for re-engagement with these workers.”

Stelco began issuing layoff notices to about 500 employees at the beginning of October following an announcement of its plans to pull back on operations at its Hamilton plant.

The company has said the employees laid off in Hamilton will be offered jobs at their Lake Erie facility but the union representing Stelco workers told Global News only 40 jobs have been offered to the impacted employees.

In a letter sent last week, Joly warned Stelco that if they do not reverse the layoffs within 15 days, the federal government will start legal action against the company that could ultimately lead to the parent company Cleveland-Cliffs being forced to divest of the Canadian steel firm.

Joly said she reviewed an interim compliance report that was provided by Stelco on Oct. 26 but said the report was “far from satisfactory.”

“It does not alter my belief that Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs are not in compliance with their undertakings under the Investment Canada Act as set out in my October 22 section 39 demand,” she said in the most recent letter.

The industry minister said she expects Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs to address her demands “fully and directly” and “provide the underlying data, documents and other evidence necessary to support their assertions.”

With files from Global News’ Mackenzie Gray.

stories.title: Audit finds military using only half of ammunition purchases
stories.summary: The AG has found that the CAF is vastly overestimating how much ammunition it needs for regular use in training and international missions.
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal auditor general has found that the Canadian Armed Forces is vastly overestimating how much ammunition it needs for regular use in training and international missions, and it says part of the problem can be chalked up to a lack of usable military equipment and an ongoing shortfall of uniformed personnel.

The audit also found that while the Department of National Defence has started to replenish the military’s strategic ammunition stockpile — the lethal ammunition needed for emergencies and combat operations — critical gaps remain.

Canada has identified a lack of available ammunition and stockpiled ammunition as a reason why it is not meeting the readiness level required of Nato members.

The five Canadian Armed Forces groups that account for 87 per cent of its regular ammunition use — the Army, Navy and Air Force along with the special operations forces command and Canadian joint operations command — are only using 56 per cent of what’s assigned to them, ON average.

The reasons for that were not well tracked. The audit noted that key equipment like tanks and ships are often out of service and unavailable for use in training and exercises, and that a lack of personnel and poor environmental conditions might prevent training from happening.

The audit said that because National Defence doesn’t track the reasons it’s not using its regular ammunition supplies, it has difficulty determining how much it will need each year. Ammunition that’s not used is expensive to store, and risks degrading or expiring on the shelf.

The report comes as the federal government is pouring billions of dollars into national defence in an effort to meet Canada’s Nato commitment to spend the equivalent of two per cent of GDP per year on defence.

In 2024-25, the government awarded some $800 million in contracts to procure ammunition. That number rose to $3 billion in 2025-26.

The audit looked at 15 of those contracts and found it took an average of 19 months between signing a deal and receiving the ammunition. In many cases, the ammunition was delivered late and contracts were extended.

In 2024, the government set aside $9.2 billion over 13 years to restore the strategic ammunition stockpile.

The audit noted that after decades of depleting that stockpile for things like training exercises, National Defence limited access to it in 2021 and tried to establish an inventory baseline. Five years later, the stockpile lacked “required types and quantities of ammunition necessary to meet targeted operational requirements,” the audit found.

The auditor general’s office is calling on the department to establish a formal, regular and documented process for supplying the stockpile.

Also in 2021, National Defence issued a directive to create an ammunition and explosives program meant to address supply and demand gaps and do a comprehensive review of existing processes. The five Canadian Armed Forces groups that account for 87 per cent of its regular ammunition use — the Army, Navy and Air Force along with the special operations forces command and Canadian joint operations command — are only using 56 per cent of what’s assigned to them, ON average.

stories.title: Studio Red Live is back to showcase Fanshawe College music students
stories.summary: A popular student-fueled Fanshawe TV show is back, as part of a collaboration between the college's TV Film, M...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
A popular student-fueled Fanshawe TV show is back, as part of a collaboration between the college’s TV Film, Musical Industry Arts (MIA) and Multimedia Journalism programs.

Fanshawe TV control room (Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM)

Fanshawe’s Studio Red Live aired Tuesday, featuring Fanshawe MIA band You Might Be Sleeping and hosted by journalism student Owen Schuller. The last episode aired nearly a year ago, in November 2025.

“It came up from one of our bosses saying, ‘this show was great. Let’s bring it back,'” said TV Production professor Scott Navarro.

Student camera operator Riley Seferiades said the show provides students an opportunity to get hands-on experience operating and moving heavy broadcast equipment.

“I love music and I’ve done music broadcast in the past, but this is more professional and a great learning experience,” said Seferiades.

This is the first year journalism students have joined the production.

Set up for Studio Red Live. Nico Valeriote, Attila Fay, Toby Rossi, Owen Schuller (Credit: FanshaweTV /YouTube)

“I’m excited to host a live show and watch the music they’re going to perform. I think it’s a great way to collaborate with the different programs,” Schuller said.

You Might Be Sleeping is an indie-rock band that has been together for almost six years, since the members were in high school.

“Our manager Nick McCarthy and coordinator got in contact with each other talking about the show and he recommended us which was awesome,” said bassist, Toby Rossi.

The band also consists if drummer, Attila Fay, and Nico Valeriote, who said the band gets some inspiration from popular 90s music.

Nico Valeriote (Credit: FanshaweTV /YouTube)

“Seeing my dad play guitar inspired me and singing came from guys like Curt Cobain (of Nirvana). I always like guys who play and sing,” Valeriote said.

Studio Red Live is already available on YouTube, and will soon be available on Rogers.

The next live episode airs next Tuesday Nov. 3, 2026 at 6 p.m.

stories.title: Shooting near Toronto’s Bridle Path neighbourhood injures four
stories.summary: Police say they received reports of three people who were shot inside a residence near Bayview Avenue and Lawrence Avenue East at around 3:43 a.m.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
Toronto police say two people are in critical condition and two others were injured following a shooting inside a home near the Bridle Path neighbourhood.

Police say they received reports of three people who were shot inside a residence near Bayview Avenue and Lawrence Avenue East at around 3:43 a.m.

Police say four people were transported to the hospital, two in life-threatening condition and two with non-life-threatening injuries.

Investigators say three suspects fled in an SUV.

No descriptions of the suspects were provided.

Investigators are asking anyone with more information to contact the police.

stories.title: Western alumni and students win top honours in Global Undergraduate Awards
stories.summary: Western ranks third worldwide for undergraduate research recognized through international competition
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
On the morning of her first day of graduate school, Michelle-Lynn Balderston opened an email with some unexpected news: a paper she had written during her final year at Western had been named the best in the world in its category.

Balderston, BA’26, was named Global Winner in the global communication category for the 2026 Global Undergraduate Awards – an international academic competition celebrating exceptional undergraduate research and creative work.

“I was completely shocked,” she said. Receiving the news that morning “definitely provided me with a good dose of motivation and confidence to tackle the new school year.”

Balderston is one of 12 Western students recognized in this year’s awards, which drew 2,373 submissions from 327 universities in 112 countries. For the second consecutive year, Western ranked first in the Americas and second globally for ‘highly commended’ entries. The university also ranked third worldwide and second in the Americas overall.

Balderston’s paper explored how two anti-Apartheid organizations in the Netherlands used posters and collective memories in their activism against South Africa’s apartheid system, bringing together her interests in activism and her Dutch heritage. Read more about Balderston’s research.

Among all the Western winners, research spanned eight of the competition’s 25 award categories, from health and life sciences to the humanities and social sciences.

DiLosa’s research explored whether a bacterial enzyme could be used as a tool to help scientists study an important lipid found in cell membranes. She also modified the enzyme to see whether she could improve its activity.

“When I realized I was a regional winner, I couldn’t believe it. It felt validating to have my hard work recognized globally,” she said. Read more about DiLosa’s research.

Torres Escandon’s fourth-year thesis explored how inflammation is regulated in the brain, research that could help scientists better understand inflammation associated with neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s.

“It felt like the hours I put into my thesis had come full circle, and like the perfect way to end my undergraduate degree at Western,” she said. Read more about Torres Escandon’s research.

Agakishiev’s research examined why workplace violence against nurses remains prevalent in Canadian health care settings despite existing legal protections. She explores gaps between legal safeguards and their implementation, identifying underreporting, inconsistent enforcement, limited employer accountability, and institutional cultures that normalize violence as key barriers.

“This experience showed me you don’t have to be free of doubt to take a chance on yourself,” she said. Read more about Agakishiev’s research.

Eight Western students also earned ‘highly commended’ honours across a range of disciplines.

The recipients were Jamal al-Ghaziri (literature); Ananya Kalra (psychology); Isaac McKeown and Justin Donovan (medical sciences); Aranya Thavakumar (nursing, midwifery and allied health care); Anum Qaiser and Yi Qu (sociology and social policy); and Ebunoluwa Esomojumi (anthropology and cultural studies), who received the recognition for two separate submissions.

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

stories.title: Ottawa launches telecom roadmap to improve competition, consumer choice
stories.summary: The federal government says it is launching a roadmap to boost competition and choice within Canada's telecommunications sector.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Minister of Industry Melanie Joly rises during Question Period in the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Justin Tang

By Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

Posted October 29, 2026 9:19 am.

Last Updated October 29, 2026 9:58 am.

The federal government says it is launching a roadmap to boost competition and choice within Canada’s telecommunications sector.

The plan, announced late Wednesday by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, is meant to break down regional barriers and promote cross-Canada competition in the internet and mobile services sector.

Ottawa says it will take action to give consumers more choices and make it easier for providers to access existing networks, or expand the infrastructure they own.

It also wants to help consumers take advantage of more affordable plans, noting cellular plan prices are down 49 per cent compared with 2019, and says the government “will spotlight” competitive offers on the market.

The government says it will help companies deploy the latest fibre-optic networks, experiment with new technologies and strengthen access to connectivity in northern, rural and Indigenous communities.

It plans to monitor progress through indicators such as prices, switching behaviour, network speeds, coverage and consumer complaints.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Two people charged after human remains found in Calgary home: police
stories.summary: Calgary police said its officers were called around 8:15 a.m. Tuesday to a home in the 200 block of Skyview Ranch Road N.E. for a welfare check.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Two people are facing charges after Calgary police reportedly found human remains inside a home.

Calgary police said its officers were called around 8:15 a.m. Tuesday to a home in the 200 block of Skyview Ranch Road N.E. for a welfare check.

The remains were found during a search of the home, police said. A 49-year-old man and a 50-year-old woman have each been charged with indignity to a dead body.

Police are in the process confirming the identity of the remains and how they died.

An autopsy is scheduled for Thursday, and the victim’s name will be released once officially identified by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

The investigation is ongoing.

Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Auditor general reports to detail greenhouse gases, coal and pesticides
stories.summary: The federal spending watchdog plans to issue report cards today tracking government agencies' progress on reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The federal spending watchdog plans to issue report cards today tracking government agencies’ progress on reducing greenhouse gas emissions and working toward a ban on the export of thermal coal.

The latest batch of reports from Auditor General Karen Hogan will also evaluate efforts to reduce health and environmental risks from pesticides, manage the Canadian Dental Care Plan and oversee the national emergency stockpile.

Other audits will examine the activities of Canada’s anti-money laundering centre, the Canadian Armed Forces’ management of ammunition and the federal border agency’s collection of customs duties and taxes.

Another report will assess whether several agencies managed procurement and contracts of selected call centre systems with regard to economy, efficiency and effectiveness.

Hogan plans to hold a media conference to discuss the reports after they are tabled in the House of Commons.

Liberal cabinet ministers and opposition MPs are also expected to comment on the auditor’s findings.

stories.title: National security strategy release expected to focus on economic safegaurds
stories.summary: The Liberal government plans to release a national security strategy today that maps out plans to safeguard Canada's economy.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Liberal government plans to release a national security strategy today that maps out plans to safeguard Canada’s economy.

The long-awaited strategy is also expected to discuss the handling of traditional security threats, including espionage, foreign interference and terrorism.

David Morrison, diplomatic and international affairs adviser to Prime Minister Mark Carney, recently told a House of Commons committee the strategy looks to bolster Canada’s defences against an array of security threats.

Privy Council Office spokesperson Mélany Gauvin said recently the strategy would increase Canada’s focus on economic security.

In 2004, the Liberal government led by Paul Martin released Securing an Open Society, the most recent overarching national security policy.

The new policy is likely to address shifting global alliances, Arctic security and Canada’s intelligence needs in a volatile world.

stories.title: OPP lay murder charge following death in Norfolk County
stories.summary: Norfolk County OPP officers were called to a property on Brantford Road 4 in Vanessa shortly after 9:30 a.m. on Wednesday for a report of an altercation involving two people.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 36-year-old man has been charged with second-degree murder following a fatal altercation in Norfolk County, provincial police say.

Norfolk County OPP officers were called to a property on Brantford Road 4 in Vanessa shortly after 9:30 a.m. on Wednesday for a report of an altercation involving two people.

Police said officers found one person suffering from life-threatening injuries. The victim was taken to hospital, where they were later pronounced dead.

A second person was taken into custody at the scene and transported to hospital with minor injuries.

As a result of the investigation, a 36 year old from Saint Catherine, Jamaica, has been charged with second-degree murder.

The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to appear in court in Simcoe on Nov. 3.

Police have not released the identity of the victim.

Anyone with information that May assist investigators is asked to contact Norfolk County OPP at 1-888-310-1122.

stories.title: Half of Canadians have avoided hospitals because of wait times: poll
stories.summary: Most Canadians believe the health-care system needs to change and 61% are willing to pay for surgery at private clinics, the poll suggests.
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
long waits and more than 25 per cent said they have turned to the private system for care, according to a new poll.

Most Canadians say health services where they live need to change — 58 per cent believe the system needs to change in a major way — and 61 per cent are open to allowing people to pay for surgery at private clinics if the public system can’t deliver timely care, the survey found.

“Canadians are very OK with the idea of more private health services being used,” said Renaud Brossard, vice-president of communications at the Montreal Economic Institute, or MEI.

“They see it as a safety valve” rather than simply being added to months-long waiting lists for publicly funded care, he said.

The new Leger poll, jointly commissioned by the MEI, SecondStreet.org and the Canadian Constitution Foundation, found many Canadians are avoiding seeking medical attention because of wait times.

“When people avoid seeking medical attention for a health issue, it doesn’t just magically go away,” SecondStreet.org president Colin Craig said in a news release.

Only 10 per cent of those polled believe the health-care system doesn’t need to change and “just needs more public funding.”

By contrast, 84 per cent said health services where they live require some degree of change: 58 per cent said major change and 26 per cent said minor.

The poll didn’t ask what people specifically believed needed changing. However, “people recognize it’s not just a matter of funding,” Brossard said.

“What we typically hear is, ‘If we were just able to properly fund the health system, everything would be OK.’ It’s what we’ve been hearing for 40, 50 years,” he said.

“The result has still been very long wait times to get surgery, long wait times at the emergency room and patients without family doctors. That has remained a constant for the past 40 or 50 years.

“People recognize that something is not working. It’s not just a lack of money,” Brossard said.

When asked, “Do you ever avoid going to a hospital or a doctor because you don’t believe you will receive timely treatment,” 50 per cent of those polled responded yes; 47 per cent said they haven’t avoided hospitals or doctors. The remainder were unsure.

Women (59 per cent), the under-55s (55 per cent) and people living in Quebec (56 per cent) were more likely to have avoided visiting a hospital or doctor.

Some six million Canadians don’t have a family doctor and even many of those who do face long waits to be seen. Untreated problems can grow worse, ultimately requiring a higher, and more expensive level of care than what they would have needed otherwise, Brossard said.

But surveys have found only 36.9 per cent of adults with a family doctor or clinic can get same- or next-day urgent care. Meanwhile, emergency departments are reporting historic wait times, with one in 10 people spending 14 hours or more in emergency in 2024-25, the Canadian Institute for Health Information reported this summer.

“There are a lot of people who might have an ailment that actually needs (medical attention), but they ask themselves, ‘Can I afford to wait four hours, six hours, eight hours until I see a doctor?’” Brossard said.

In 2024-25, 1.2 million emergency visits — about eight per cent of all emergency visits — involved someone leaving the emergency room before being assessed by a doctor, according to Cihi. Pre-pandemic, it was 5.4 per cent, or roughly 800,000 visits.

People who leave emergency without being seen have a 14 per cent higher risk of death or hospitalization within seven days, Canadian researchers have reported.

According to the Leger poll, 27 per cent of Canadians have paid for private health care to avoid long wait times and “unsatisfactory services in the public system.” Most sought it within their own province, while some (four per cent) went outside their province, or outside the country (four per cent). Nearly half of Quebec residents (46 per cent) said they’ve used their own money or extended health insurance to pay for private care.

“Canadians recognize that our ‘everything-by-the state’ approach just isn’t working in getting everybody the treatment they need,” Brossard said.

“Universal access is something we can do with a mixture of both public and private facilities.”

“They see it as a safety valve” rather than simply being added to months-long waiting lists for publicly funded care, he said.
The new Leger poll, jointly commissioned by the MEI, SecondStreet.org and the Canadian Constitution Foundation, found many Canadians are avoiding seeking medical attention because of wait times.
“When people avoid seeking medical attention for a health issue, it doesn’t just magically go away,” SecondStreet.org president Colin Craig said in a news release.
Only 10 per cent of those polled believe the health-care system doesn’t need to change and “just needs more public funding.”
By contrast, 84 per cent said health services where they live require some degree of change: 58 per cent said major change and 26 per cent said minor.
The poll didn’t ask what people specifically believed needed changing. However, “people recognize it’s not just a matter of funding,” Brossard said.
“What we typically hear is, ‘If we were just able to properly fund the health system, everything would be OK.’ It’s what we’ve been hearing for 40, 50 years,” he said.
“The result has still been very long wait times to get surgery, long wait times at the emergency room and patients without family doctors. That has remained a constant for the past 40 or 50 years.
“People recognize that something is not working. It’s not just a lack of money,” Brossard said.

When asked, “Do you ever avoid going to a hospital or a doctor because you don’t believe you will receive timely treatment,” 50 per cent of those polled responded yes; 47 per cent said they haven’t avoided hospitals or doctors. The remainder were unsure.
Women (59 per cent), the under-55s (55 per cent) and people living in Quebec (56 per cent) were more likely to have avoided visiting a hospital or doctor.

Some six million Canadians don’t have a family doctor and even many of those who do face long waits to be seen. Untreated problems can grow worse, ultimately requiring a higher, and more expensive level of care than what they would have needed otherwise, Brossard said.

But surveys have found only 36.9 per cent of adults with a family doctor or clinic can get same- or next-day urgent care. Meanwhile, emergency departments are reporting historic wait times, with one in 10 people spending 14 hours or more in emergency in 2024-25, the Canadian Institute for Health Information reported this summer.

“There are a lot of people who might have an ailment that actually needs (medical attention), but they ask themselves, ‘Can I afford to wait four hours, six hours, eight hours until I see a doctor?’” Brossard said.

In 2024-25, 1.2 million emergency visits — about eight per cent of all emergency visits — involved someone leaving the emergency room before being assessed by a doctor, according to Cihi. Pre-pandemic, it was 5.4 per cent, or roughly 800,000 visits.

“Canadians recognize that our ‘everything-by-the state’ approach just isn’t working in getting everybody the treatment they need,” Brossard said.
“Universal access is something we can do with a mixture of both public and private facilities.”

Many health agencies disagree, worrying that wait times in the public system will worsen with more private care and create a two-tier system that will give people access to care based on their ability to pay, not medical need.
The Canadian Medical Association has called for a federal review of Alberta’s “dual-practice” model that allows some doctors working in public hospitals to also offer private care.
The poll’s results suggest “there is a lag in terms of where Canadians are, and where the public debate needs to be,” Brossard said.

stories.title: Four people sent to hospital after shooting in Bridle Path home: Toronto police
stories.summary: Toronto police said its officers were called to the home on Hyde Park Cricle, near Bayview and Lawrence avenues, around 3:43 a.m. for reports of a shooting.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Four people were taken to hospital early Thursday morning after a shooting inside a Bridle Path home.

Toronto police said its officers were called to the home on Hyde Park Circle, near Bayview and Lawrence avenues, around 3:43 a.m. Oct. 29.

It had reports that three people were shot inside a home; three suspects fled in an SUV, but police did not have descriptions to provide.

Four people were taken to hospital, police said. Two people had life-threatening injuries, while the others had non-life-threatening injuries.

An investigation is underway.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

Montreal police explain why it took a day to dismantle unit accused of misconduct

Russ Wyatt voted out of Winnipeg city council, Lora Meseman to represent Transcona
