stories.title: Ontario calls for new investors in Niagara casinos, slashes tax rate for operators
stories.summary: The announcement is party of Ford’s plan to boost Niagara’s profile as a prime tourist attraction
stories.author: Laura Stone, Andrew Willis
stories.content:
The Ontario government is slashing the tax rate for gambling operators in Niagara as it issues a call for new investors, part of Premier Doug Ford’s plan to attract big-name casinos to the region.

The government, along with the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corp., which manages gambling in the province, issued a “call for investment” on Wednesday, with the goal of raising $3-billion in direct investment from the sector, as well as an additional $600-million from the private sector over the next 20 years.

The announcement is part of Mr. Ford’s multibillion-dollar Destination Niagara strategy, a plan to boost the region’s profile as a prime tourist attraction, which the government says will lead to billions of dollars in growth for the provincial economy, as well as tens of thousands of jobs.

But it has also raised questions about the government’s priorities and added to more general concerns around the proliferation of online gambling, as well as the need for community consultation.

Ontario is asking “world-class gaming operators” to express interest in the region, which includes Niagara Falls and borders New York State, by Dec. 3. The government said it will then shortlist proponents who will be able to enter a competitive process to submit detailed proposals for new casino developments.

As part of the pitch, the province said it will introduce a standardized gambling tax rate of 9.75 per cent for Niagara operators, which is considered highly competitive with other jurisdictions in North America. The current tax rates, which vary by individual casinos, are not public, but two industry sources put them upward of 40 per cent. The Globe and Mail is not naming the sources as they are not authorized to speak publicly about internal matters.

“New gaming investment will bring exciting attractions and experiences to the region, helping drive tourism, create good-paying jobs and support Niagara’s future as a world-class, year-round destination,” said Zee Hamid, Ontario’s Minister of Tourism, Culture and Gaming.

The government said the new market will be open to a maximum of three new operators, who will be required to make a minimum investment of $1.5-billion, with potential for further expansion after a 10-year fixed term.

In addition, each new casino operator will have to pay a $100-million entrance fee. The fee is intended to offset provincial revenue losses after the government ended MGE Niagara Entertainment Inc.’s exclusivity rights to operate casinos in the area earlier this summer.

MGE is a division of Mohegan Tribal Gaming Authority, a company based in Uncasville, Conn., that operates two Ontario properties, Casino Niagara and the Fallsview Casino. In the nine months ending June 30, the two casinos reported revenues of US$199-million.

In August, Mohegan chief operating officer Joseph Hasson said on a conference call that in exchange for giving up its exclusive rights in Niagara Falls, OLG pledged to make up any decrease in revenue at Mohegan’s Ontario properties caused by the opening of new casinos. Mr. Hasson declined to comment on how much the company could receive, but told analysts: “We are comfortable that our new commercial arrangement leaves us better off under all scenarios.”

Mohegan has operated the two Niagara Falls properties since 2019 under a 21-year contract with OLG.

NDP MPP Wayne Gates, who represents Niagara Falls in the legislature, said he’ll always support investment that creates good-paying jobs in the region.

“But I’ll be honest with you, I have serious questions about this announcement, and I believe the residents do too,” he said in an interview.

Mr. Gates said the government must consult residents about its plans and cited the need for protections for casino workers. He also said the proliferation of online gambling is hurting bricks-and-mortar casinos, costing jobs.

Ontario Liberal MPP Rob Cerjanec, the party’s critic for tourism, sport and culture, said the government should answer some basic questions about its proposal, noting declining revenue and foot traffic for casinos.

“The government has never released a business case for new casinos, and it should,” he said in a statement.

Mr. Hamid’s spokesman, Scott Clark, said the process is open to qualified proponents capable of making substantial long-term investments and enhancing Niagara’s tourism, entertainment and gambling offerings.

Mr. Clark also said the government is committed to promoting safer gambling and connecting people across Ontario to the prevention, treatment and recovery supports they need.

Mr. Ford has made no secret of his desire to transform Niagara into a premier tourist destination.

Last December, the Premier announced plans to double the number of visitors to the region, with visions of multiple new casinos, a theme park, an expanded airport and more.

Niagara’s existing casinos attract more than five million visitors annually and generate more than $500-million a year for the province in gambling revenue. Mr. Ford said he wants to see more in order to provide additional jobs and spur growth in the tourism sector.

“All the big casinos in Las Vegas – we’re serious,” he said in Niagara Falls then.

“It’s happening. Get on board. Come and put a proposal in. Come and tell us how you’re going to build a billion-dollar hotel with attractions, with cinemas inside, with live theatre. That’s what we’re looking for.”

As part of its Destination Niagara strategy, the government aims to attract 25 million annual visitors and double the region’s tourism to generate an additional $3-billion for Ontario’s GDP each year.
paragraphs: The Ontario government is slashing the tax rate for gambling operators in Niagara as it issues a call for new investors, part of Premier Doug Ford’s plan to attract big-name casinos to the region.

The government, along with the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corp., which manages gambling in the province, issued a “call for investment” on Wednesday, with the goal of raising $3-billion in direct investment from the sector, as well as an additional $600-million from the private sector over the next 20 years.

The announcement is part of Mr. Ford’s multibillion-dollar Destination Niagara strategy, a plan to boost the region’s profile as a prime tourist attraction, which the government says will lead to billions of dollars in growth for the provincial economy, as well as tens of thousands of jobs.
But it has also raised questions about the government’s priorities and added to more general concerns around the proliferation of online gambling, as well as the need for community consultation.

Ontario is asking “world-class gaming operators” to express interest in the region, which includes Niagara Falls and borders New York State, by Dec. 3. The government said it will then shortlist proponents who will be able to enter a competitive process to submit detailed proposals for new casino developments.

As part of the pitch, the province said it will introduce a standardized gambling tax rate of 9.75 per cent for Niagara operators, which is considered highly competitive with other jurisdictions in North America. The current tax rates, which vary by individual casinos, are not public, but two industry sources put them upward of 40 per cent. The Globe and Mail is not naming the sources as they are not authorized to speak publicly about internal matters.

“New gaming investment will bring exciting attractions and experiences to the region, helping drive tourism, create good-paying jobs and support Niagara’s future as a world-class, year-round destination,” said Zee Hamid, Ontario’s Minister of Tourism, Culture and Gaming.

The government said the new market will be open to a maximum of three new operators, who will be required to make a minimum investment of $1.5-billion, with potential for further expansion after a 10-year fixed term.

In addition, each new casino operator will have to pay a $100-million entrance fee. The fee is intended to offset provincial revenue losses after the government ended MGE Niagara Entertainment Inc.’s exclusivity rights to operate casinos in the area earlier this summer.

MGE is a division of Mohegan Tribal Gaming Authority, a company based in Uncasville, Conn., that operates two Ontario properties, Casino Niagara and the Fallsview Casino. In the nine months ending June 30, the two casinos reported revenues of US$199-million.

In August, Mohegan chief operating officer Joseph Hasson said on a conference call that in exchange for giving up its exclusive rights in Niagara Falls, OLG pledged to make up any decrease in revenue at Mohegan’s Ontario properties caused by the opening of new casinos. Mr. Hasson declined to comment on how much the company could receive, but told analysts: “We are comfortable that our new commercial arrangement leaves us better off under all scenarios.”
Mohegan has operated the two Niagara Falls properties since 2019 under a 21-year contract with OLG.
NDP MPP Wayne Gates, who represents Niagara Falls in the legislature, said he’ll always support investment that creates good-paying jobs in the region.
“But I’ll be honest with you, I have serious questions about this announcement, and I believe the residents do too,” he said in an interview.

Mr. Gates said the government must consult residents about its plans and cited the need for protections for casino workers. He also said the proliferation of online gambling is hurting bricks-and-mortar casinos, costing jobs.

Ontario Liberal MPP Rob Cerjanec, the party’s critic for tourism, sport and culture, said the government should answer some basic questions about its proposal, noting declining revenue and foot traffic for casinos.
“The government has never released a business case for new casinos, and it should,” he said in a statement.

Mr. Hamid’s spokesman, Scott Clark, said the process is open to qualified proponents capable of making substantial long-term investments and enhancing Niagara’s tourism, entertainment and gambling offerings.
Mr. Clark also said the government is committed to promoting safer gambling and connecting people across Ontario to the prevention, treatment and recovery supports they need.
Mr. Ford has made no secret of his desire to transform Niagara into a premier tourist destination.
Last December, the Premier announced plans to double the number of visitors to the region, with visions of multiple new casinos, a theme park, an expanded airport and more.

Niagara’s existing casinos attract more than five million visitors annually and generate more than $500-million a year for the province in gambling revenue. Mr. Ford said he wants to see more in order to provide additional jobs and spur growth in the tourism sector.
“All the big casinos in Las Vegas – we’re serious,” he said in Niagara Falls then.

“It’s happening. Get on board. Come and put a proposal in. Come and tell us how you’re going to build a billion-dollar hotel with attractions, with cinemas inside, with live theatre. That’s what we’re looking for.”

As part of its Destination Niagara strategy, the government aims to attract 25 million annual visitors and double the region’s tourism to generate an additional $3-billion for Ontario’s GDP each year.

stories.title: Fired metal shredder worker argued that her alcoholism is a disability
stories.summary: Arbitrator found that a more likely explanation is the worker was ‘caught in her misconduct’ and tried to hide behind the Human Rights Code.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A woman who worked near a shredder that grinds up old cars and other large, discarded metal objects at a Whitby, Ont., recycling facility who was fired from a “safety sensitive position” for drinking on company property, has failed to convince an arbitrator that her alcoholism is a disability and she should get her job back.

Zoe Stanley, whose former job is described in the arbitrator’s recent decision as an “air traffic controller” directing loaded dump trucks and cranes to the shredder at Gerdau Long Metal North America’s Whitby recycling plant, was finishing up a night shift on Feb. 1, 2024, when a fellow employee reported to management that she “appeared to be under the influence of alcohol and was about to drive home.”

After a manager tracked Stanley down in the parking lot and convinced her to come to the office, she was quizzed about the “overwhelming ‘smell’ of alcohol on her (also on her breath) — noticeable immediately on entering the room.”

At first, Stanley denied that she had consumed alcohol on Gerdau premises.

Stanley explained the “strong smell of alcohol on her work clothes” was because she and her husband make moonshine at home “as a hobby,” arbitrator Bernard Fishbein wrote in his Oct. 27 decision.

“She also did mention that she had been drinking heavily at home as a possibility, but it was not really made clear why that would affect her ‘work clothes’ and the strong smell of alcohol on them.”

More than four hours after her shift ended, Stanley “tested positive, 0.040 per cent on the first test and 0.035 per cent on the second test.”

Gerdau’s policy was that anything over 0.02 per cent was considered being “under the influence,” said the arbitrator.

Stanley, who had worked at the plant since 2017, was sent home pending further investigation.

At a meeting the next month with company officials, Stanley “reiterated that she had not been drinking while working,” said the decision.

“However, now, for the first time, although steadfastly denying that she had ever been drinking while working or during the shift, she admitted that she just happened to have alcohol in her bag that day and had taken ‘a sip’ (or maybe two) after the conclusion of her shift at her locker and before going to her vehicle.”

When asked about what had prompted her to take the drink, Stanley “indicated that she had ‘personal things’ going on at that time which had been exacerbated recently. Ultimately, she went further and admitted she had a problem with alcohol but had not gotten help in the past because she did not know where to get help.”

Stanley later revealed that she had increasingly been “drinking heavily at home virtually daily (but never at work) for some time” due to financial difficulties that resulted in the loss of her family home.

Stanley was a member of the International Union of Operating Engineers, Local 793.

Without a ‘disability there is obviously no duty to accommodate’

Her union “raised the possibility of some return to work under some form of ‘last chance agreement,’ but the discussion did not go far,” said the decision.

Then, at a March 12, 2024, meeting, Gerdau “advised that their investigation was pretty much concluded and that there had been a serious violation of its drug and alcohol policy which were grounds for termination.”

But since Stanley “for the first time had indicated she had an alcohol problem, Gerdau was prepared to consider some form of last chance agreement” that would allow her “to eventually return to work” if she completed a credible residential alcohol treatment program and agreed to random testing.

Stanley “almost immediately strongly objected” to any residential treatment as she had small children at home.

Gerdau “indicated it would consider other options if they provided effective relief.”

Nearly six weeks after she was suspended, Gerdau indicated Stanley needs to “start a program soon and try to come to an agreement on terms, otherwise we May need to proceed with our original position that this incident warrants termination.”

By March 26, 2024, “Gerdau was losing patience,” said the decision.

Stanley testified that she had visited a clinic, but an intake interview would take some time to arrange.

Believing that Stanley “was not ‘holding up her end of the bargain’ and not co-operating in attempts to afford her accommodation,” Gerdau prepared her termination letter.

When she “was asked if there was anything she had done in the last two months to deal with her problem,” Stanley indicated she had gone to two counselling sessions, “but had stopped because Gerdau’s position as she allegedly understood it from the union was that was not good enough.”

After a meeting with company officials where Stanley refused to take any medication, shouted and slammed a door, Gerdau fired her.

Stanley’s family doctor and a social worker and psychotherapist who had counselling sessions with Stanley produced records to substantiate Stanley’s “claim of a disability (alcoholism) and any treatment of it” and her ability to safely return to work, said the decision.

“Strangely none of the reports explicitly state a diagnosis or conclusion of alcoholism—that (Stanley) was an alcoholic.”

Stanley’s union asked the arbitrator to “substitute a lesser penalty,” given her seven years of discipline-free work at the recycling plant. Fishbein concluded that he should not.

“Equally, the union’s arguments that this was an isolated incident and spur of the moment and not premeditated incident, I find hardly persuasive when the union also argues that the grievor is an alcoholic,” said the arbitrator.

“More significantly, this is a safety sensitive position in a sensitive safety workplace — which not only did the grievor appreciate but stressed herself as why she would never drink while actually performing her work.”

The arbitrator was unable to find that Stanley or her union established that she suffers from the disability of alcoholism.

“I find the better characterization of the events is the one Gerdau makes — the grievor caught in her misconduct, unable to deny or evade it at first, seeks to hide behind the (Human Rights Code) and an alleged disability.”

Without a “disability there is obviously no duty to accommodate,” Fishbein said. “If I am wrong about the existence of a disability here, then I conclude that Gerdau has fulfilled its duty to accommodate here.”

Gerdau “indicated it would consider other options if they provided effective relief.”

Nearly six weeks after she was suspended, Gerdau indicated Stanley needs to “start a program soon and try to come to an agreement on terms, otherwise we May need to proceed with our original position that this incident warrants termination.”
By March 26, 2024, “Gerdau was losing patience,” said the decision.
Stanley testified that she had visited a clinic, but an intake interview would take some time to arrange.
Believing that Stanley “was not ‘holding up her end of the bargain’ and not co-operating in attempts to afford her accommodation,” Gerdau prepared her termination letter.

When she “was asked if there was anything she had done in the last two months to deal with her problem,” Stanley indicated she had gone to two counselling sessions, “but had stopped because Gerdau’s position as she allegedly understood it from the union was that was not good enough.”
After a meeting with company officials where Stanley refused to take any medication, shouted and slammed a door, Gerdau fired her.

Stanley’s family doctor and a social worker and psychotherapist who had counselling sessions with Stanley produced records to substantiate Stanley’s “claim of a disability (alcoholism) and any treatment of it” and her ability to safely return to work, said the decision.
“Strangely none of the reports explicitly state a diagnosis or conclusion of alcoholism—that (Stanley) was an alcoholic.”
Stanley’s union asked the arbitrator to “substitute a lesser penalty,” given her seven years of discipline-free work at the recycling plant. Fishbein concluded that he should not.

“Equally, the union’s arguments that this was an isolated incident and spur of the moment and not premeditated incident, I find hardly persuasive when the union also argues that the grievor is an alcoholic,” said the arbitrator.

“More significantly, this is a safety sensitive position in a sensitive safety workplace — which not only did the grievor appreciate but stressed herself as why she would never drink while actually performing her work.”
The arbitrator was unable to find that Stanley or her union established that she suffers from the disability of alcoholism.

“I find the better characterization of the events is the one Gerdau makes — the grievor caught in her misconduct, unable to deny or evade it at first, seeks to hide behind the (Human Rights Code) and an alleged disability.”

Without a “disability there is obviously no duty to accommodate,” Fishbein said. “If I am wrong about the existence of a disability here, then I conclude that Gerdau has fulfilled its duty to accommodate here.”

stories.title: Dead whale with tail severed is spotted in Howe Sound near BC Ferries collision site
stories.summary: Vancouver - A federal department has confirmed a dead humpback whale was spotted floating in Howe Sound, B.C., about a week after a BC Ferries vessel collided with a whale in the same region.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A federal department has confirmed a dead humpback whale was spotted floating in Howe Sound, B.C., about a week after a BC Ferries vessel collided with a whale in the same region.

The Fisheries Department said in a statement that two whales were seen near the ferry on Oct. 18 as it sailed between Grace Point and Keats Island in Howe Sound, and one of the whales was struck after it surfaced in front of the vessel.

stories.title: As B.C. scraps time change, experts have a warning about the risks
stories.summary: Vancouver Coastal Health has released a warning that the morning commute will be darker than usual and could discourage walking or biking to school or work.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
For the first time in more than a century, B.C. won’t change its clocks back this fall and experts warn it could have wide-ranging effects on people.

Vancouver Coastal Health has released a warning that the morning commute will be darker than usual and could discourage walking or biking to school or work.

They recommend improving visibility by wearing bright colours, reflective gear and making eye contact with drivers.

Drivers are warned that they should slow down and drive for the conditions.

Vancouver Coastal Health also says that morning light plays an important part in setting the body’s internal clock, which helps to support healthy sleep patterns.

“Humans are dependent on the morning light,” Ralph Mistlberger, a psychology professor at Simon Fraser University, told Global News.

He co-authored a report in the Canadian Medical Association Journal on the potential dangers of adopting year-round daylight saving time.

“When you move the morning light later, the clock moves later, so what does that mean?” Mistlberger asked.

“It’s easier to stay up later and it’s harder to wake up early. It’s easier to sleep in longer, so your whole sleep-wake cycle shifts. But if your social calendar, your social schedule, your social clock doesn’t shift… then you generate a misalignment.”

Patrick Baylis with the University of British Columbia’s School of Economics said it will also affect work schedules.

“The rule of thumb is the less flexible your work hours are and the closer that start is to when sunrise would have been, the more effective you are going to be,” he said.

“So whereas you know, if you’re just required to be at work at eight, this matters a lot because you’re now going from a few weeks where the sunrise was going to be after the time where you were supposed to be at work, to a few months.”

British Columbians should also expect to encounter a disconnect with parts of the Pacific Northwest that have historically been on the same time as B.C.

For example, after Nov. 1, B.C. will be one hour ahead of Washington State and residents should remember that when crossing the border.

Alberta and Manitoba have also announced they are ending the practice of changing the clocks this year. On Wednesday, Quebec’s government announced it also plans to scrap the time change .

Saskatchewan has not changed its time since 1966, while Yukon ended the practice in 2020.

stories.title: Shoppers scoop up popular costumes as Halloween nears
stories.summary: As children across Canada prepare for Halloween, costume stores including The Glow Halloween Store in Halifax are seeing an increase in demand for trendy costumes.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax- As children across Canada prepare to celebrate Halloween this weekend, costume stores including The Glow Halloween Store in Halifax are seeing an increase in demand for trendy costumes.

Store supervisor Melissa Landry says despite selling hundreds of costumes there are three items that are the hot sellers this Halloween season.

“Toy Story is one of the big ones because there was a new movie out, and Harry Potter because it is the 25th anniversary this year for the movie,” said Landry. “And Super Mario because there is a new movie out for that too.”

Yearly, without fail, Landry said shoppers typically wait until the final few days before Halloween to buy their costumes, which means the store is now getting busier by the hour.

“It has now picked up increasingly through the day, and the nighttime are super slammed for us right now,” said Landry.

Choosing a costume

12-year-old Jordan Peterson, while on lunch break from school, tried on several costumes before deciding on what to wear on Halloween.

“I am being Bonnie from Five Nights at Freddy’s,” Peterson said, describing the characters from the indie media franchise. “My older friend is going to be Springtrap, which is yellow, so he is being the yellow one, and I am being the purple one.”

“It is one of my favourite holidays, just after Christmas,” Peterson said.

Young shopper Annabelle Laing went to the store with more than just Halloween to celebrate.

“Today is my birthday, and I am 11,” she said. “I want to dress up as deer for Halloween.”

School bus driver Chris Peterson has rules of the road to abide by as a driver, but he eventually chose a simple costume that the students hopefully would appreciate.

“You are limited to what you can wear if it doesn’t affect your driving,” he said. “So, I’m going with the vampire fangs.”

Halloween generates business

According to retail analyst Bruce Winder, from a commercial standpoint, Halloween has grown to appeal to people of all ages and because of that, it generates a lot of business in Canada, creating more than $1 billion in retail sales.

“It has morphed into more than just a children’s event now to adults going to lavish parties and spending several hundred dollars and buying or renting outfits for these parties,” said Winder.

The Glow Halloween Store in Halifax is a seasonal pop-up that will close in November after Halloween. Its large sales floor is packed with costumes and decorations, and Landry said she expects many of those items to sell over the next several days as the pre-Halloween rush continues.

stories.title: London Police Hate Crimes Unit investigating video showing alleged racist incident at Western
stories.summary: The London Police Service (LPS) has confirmed its Hate Crime Unit is investigating an alleged hate related incident that took place on the Western University campus Tuesday, much of which was captured on cell phone video.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
The London Police Service (LPS) has confirmed its Hate Crime Unit is investigating an alleged hate related incident that took place on the Western University campus Tuesday, much of which was captured on cell phone video.

The video appears to show a verbal altercation between a man and a group of women. The video was shared with CTV News. The sender claims there were children present when it took place. A man can be seen in a car marked with business logos arguing with a woman taking the video.

The following is a partial transcript of the altercation: Woman: He’s saying that I should take off my hijab. He’s saying that Muslims don’t belong here. Man: You don’t belong here. Woman: Why don’t we belong here. Man: Because you’re not indicative to Western culture.

Man: A woman is not supposed to wear that. Woman: A woman is not supposed to wear what? Man: The hijab. Woman: Why can’t I wear the hijab? Man: Christian values. Woman: Why can’t I wear the hijab? It’s my choice. Man: It’s not Christian values.

This is my country. The altercation continues with two other women coming to the defence of the woman taking the video Woman 2: I was born here. I know what I’m talking about. Man: You weren’t born here. You’re Pakistani.

Woman: How do you know she’s Pakistani? How do you know her? Man: I don’t give a (expletive) how I know her. Look at her. I didn’t ask for you (expletive) to be here. CTV News tracked the man down. He identified himself only as Tom.

He says the incident started when the woman flipped him the middle finger. “I consider myself a nationalist. And the fact that this country was built by the Irish, the Scottish, and basically all the Western cultures. This culture was built up on Christian values.

And I don’t see those Christian values being put forth in regards to what’s going on in today’s culture at this point in time,” he said. Muslim faith leader Abd Alfatah Twakkal, chair of the Council of London Imams, says he’s disturbed by the video.

“The contents were quite vile, racist, Islamophobic, disturbing on many different levels. And the fact that this was taking place against a visible member of our community, a woman wearing a hijab, in front of her children.

This is what makes it more egregious,” he said. The National Council of Canadian Muslims says provincial and federal governments need to take action against Islamophobia. “It’s time for elected officials to sit down with us and to build some kind of reaction or a national strategy on combatting this kind of Islamophobia,” said Nccm spokesperson Steven Zhou.

Western University issued the following statement in response to the video: “Western does not tolerate hate or discrimination and is committed to using all available tools to address it. We are dedicated to providing a safe, respectful and supportive environment for all members of our campus community.

We’re also committed to working in partnership with all levels of government and the London Police Service to address concerns and combat hate and discrimination in all its forms. We encourage anyone who has concerns with respect to hate or discrimination on campus to report such concerns directly to the Western Special Constable Service and/or the Human Rights Office.

This matter is an active police investigation and all questions should be directed to London Police Service.” The altercation continued, with the video lasting a total of two minutes and 45 seconds. Man: You and you’re little leftist, socialist, propogandist, little … Woman: You’re racist.

Man: Yeah, I’m racist. (Expletive) right I’m racist. In the meantime, after learning from CTV News the incident is being investigated by the LPS Hate Crimes Unit, Tom said he apologizes for his behaviour. “I did do a nasty thing.

I admit it. I’m trying to reconcile the difference,” he said. He was then asked if he is turning himself in. “I will probably. I’m going to give them a call definitely and make it easier for them. And, again, I’ll have to pay for the consequences, but again this is a free country,” he said.

The women in the video did not want to be identified and declined our request for an interview.

Man: A woman is not supposed to wear that. Woman: A woman is not supposed to wear what? Man: The hijab. Woman: Why can’t I wear the hijab? Man: Christian values. Woman: Why can’t I wear the hijab? It’s my choice. Man: It’s not Christian values.

This is my country. The altercation continues with two other women coming to the defence of the woman taking the video Woman 2: I was born here. I know what I’m talking about. Man: You weren’t born here. You’re Pakistani.

Woman: How do you know she’s Pakistani? How do you know her? Man: I don’t give a (expletive) how I know her. Look at her. I didn’t ask for you (expletive) to be here. CTV News tracked the man down. He identified himself only as Tom.

He says the incident started when the woman flipped him the middle finger. “I consider myself a nationalist. And the fact that this country was built by the Irish, the Scottish, and basically all the Western cultures. This culture was built up on Christian values.

And I don’t see those Christian values being put forth in regards to what’s going on in today’s culture at this point in time,” he said. Muslim faith leader Abd Alfatah Twakkal, chair of the Council of London Imams, says he’s disturbed by the video.

“The contents were quite vile, racist, Islamophobic, disturbing on many different levels. And the fact that this was taking place against a visible member of our community, a woman wearing a hijab, in front of her children.

This is what makes it more egregious,” he said. The National Council of Canadian Muslims says provincial and federal governments need to take action against Islamophobia. “It’s time for elected officials to sit down with us and to build some kind of reaction or a national strategy on combatting this kind of Islamophobia,” said Nccm spokesperson Steven Zhou.

Western University issued the following statement in response to the video: “Western does not tolerate hate or discrimination and is committed to using all available tools to address it. We are dedicated to providing a safe, respectful and supportive environment for all members of our campus community.

We’re also committed to working in partnership with all levels of government and the London Police Service to address concerns and combat hate and discrimination in all its forms. We encourage anyone who has concerns with respect to hate or discrimination on campus to report such concerns directly to the Western Special Constable Service and/or the Human Rights Office.

This matter is an active police investigation and all questions should be directed to London Police Service.” The altercation continued, with the video lasting a total of two minutes and 45 seconds. Man: You and you’re little leftist, socialist, propogandist, little … Woman: You’re racist.

Man: Yeah, I’m racist. (Expletive) right I’m racist. In the meantime, after learning from CTV News the incident is being investigated by the LPS Hate Crimes Unit, Tom said he apologizes for his behaviour. “I did do a nasty thing.

I admit it. I’m trying to reconcile the difference,” he said. He was then asked if he is turning himself in. “I will probably. I’m going to give them a call definitely and make it easier for them. And, again, I’ll have to pay for the consequences, but again this is a free country,” he said.
The women in the video did not want to be identified and declined our request for an interview.

stories.title: B.C. soldier burned in CFB Wainwright fire remains in Edmonton ICU
stories.summary: The family of Pte. Trevor Flegel says he is still in hospital more than 10 days after the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright.
stories.author: Sarah Ryan
stories.content:
The family of Pte. Trevor Flegel says he is still in hospital more than 10 days after the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright.

Pte. Flegel suffered severe burns to half of his body. The 26-year-old has been in the military since 2024, having enlisted “to challenge himself physically and mentally, discover what he was capable of, and experience life beyond his small hometown of Kitimat, BC,” his family said in a statement.

They describe him as quiet, independent, strong-willed and determined, adding: “Trevor approaches life on his own terms. His time in the military challenged him in ways he’d never experienced before, helped him grow as a person, while creating lifelong friendships with his military brothers.”

Outside of work, Pte. Flegel loves riding dirt bikes and being outdoors.

His family says his burns mean he has a long road to recovery ahead. As a result, they have started a GoFundMe campaign.

“We are incredibly grateful for all the love and support our family has received from our friends, community and people across Canada. We’re also deeply thankful for the incredible medical team caring for Trevor and the compassion they’ve shown our family.”

stories.title: Montreal’s ‘raccoon guy’ collected over $110,000 in cryptocurrency fees
stories.summary: The "Pepper" coin was launched on Oct. 10 by an online trader using the name "Hiruzen," who said he named it after Louka Berman's raccoon.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
A Montreal man who has come to be known as the “raccoon guy” says he has made over $110,000 in transaction fees from an obscure cryptocurrency named after his adopted pet.

The “Pepper” coin was launched on Oct. 10 by an online trader using the name “Hiruzen,” who said he named it after Louka Berman’s raccoon.

The new cryptocurrency has allowed Berman to cash in on his new-found online popularity after months of taking care of the mammal, which he said he decided to adopt after finding it injured at a construction site last May.

The currency is listed on a platform called Pump.fun, which is on a warning list from Quebec’s financial market regulator as a site that investors should avoid due to high risks.

Berman said Hiruzen contacted him and offered to partner with the raccoon owner to allow him to collect the transaction fees.

Berman’s income from the cryptocurrency on Pump.fun is visible by adding up the transactions listed on his personal profile, which indicates he is receiving “creator rewards.”

He said he hadn’t thought a lot about the financial risk for investors who are powering his new source of income.

“I didn’t know how it worked,” he said. “I don’t want to be on the side of someone profiting from something that, in the end, will mean there are some people suffering.”

He confirmed he has used about $20,000 of this money for personal expenses and to pay off debt. He said he is planning to use the rest of the money to build an animal sanctuary and that he has started the process of applying for permits to get the project off the ground, which he estimates would cost $400,000.

He said he has additional income through compensation he is getting from a previous workplace injury.

Berman said he had never expected something like this to happen and that he was grateful for the support the cryptocurrency got.

“The feeling of relief … it’s pretty intense,” he said, adding that this money had been “life-changing.”

Quebec’s financial market regulator added the investment platform Pump.fun to its “Investor warnings” list on Sept. 25. The platform is not registered with the authority and is not allowed to solicit investors in the province, said spokesperson Sylvain Théberge.

Théberge said the ease at which some platforms allow users to create cryptocurrency coins increases risks of financial loss.

“(Investors) are venturing into extremely dangerous terrain with a company that is not registered in our country, with a business that does not meet the legal criteria to operate in Quebec. And, of course, if this leads to a financial loss for the investor on this platform, then you will not have any recourse,” he said.

The financial market authority can investigate these platforms if they receive a complaint of suspected fraud, and even shut them down if they find these platforms are breaking the law. But Théberge said the trading platforms often reappear under a new name.

Pump.fun did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment.

The Pepper coin had a peak value of around $2.8 million between Oct. 14 and 15.

On Wednesday, the currency’s value had fallen to around $240,000 on Pump. Fun.

“It has clearly lost a lot of value over the past days,” said Katrin Tinn, professor at the McGill University’s management faculty.

“It’s very similar to other cryptocurrencies which don’t have something backing them — it really depends on the interest of other people to buy it for speculative purposes,” she added.

When asked about people who May have lost money, Berman said if they hadn’t invested in the Pepper coin, they might have lost money on another cryptocurrency such as Dogecoin, the Trump cryptocurrency or “something that wouldn’t have gone to a project to help wild animals.”

The Dogecoin was openly created as a joke but continues to sell, with a market value of around $15 billion, according to cryptocurrency tracker CoinGecko.

“You’re buying, effectively, a hope to sell it to somebody else later on in the future,” Tinn said.

She added she worries the Pepper coin might mislead people into thinking they are supporting Berman directly when only a fraction of their investment is going to help the raccoon.

“People might be thinking that if they are sending $100 to this token, they are giving $100 dollars to the raccoon, which is clearly not happening,” she said.

If the goal is to raise money, she said crowdfunding would be more straightforward and transparent.

But Berman said the Pepper coin has allowed him to reach a new community that now seems deeply invested in his story. Compared to the tens of thousands he said he has made with the coin, an online fundraiser on the platform GoFundMe, which a user started for Berman on Oct. 15, had raised close to $3,500 as of Wednesday.

The Canadian Press contacted the creator of the cryptocurrency using an email address they had used to communicate with Berman.

They agreed to an interview and defended the creation of the currency, but declined to give their real name.

stories.title: University Health Network gets $35-million donation for transplant institute
stories.summary: Ajmera family has now given a total of $62-million to UHN
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
The University Health Network says a landmark $35-million donation from a prominent Toronto family will help advance organ transplantation in Canada through the creation of a specialized institute.

With this latest donation, the Ajmera family – which founded FGF Brands, one of North America’s largest industrial baking and food-processing companies – has cumulatively given $62-million to UHN. The total amount is the largest known donation in Canada to support transplant care by a single family.

The gift will lead to the development of the Ajmera Transplant Institute, which UHN said will be a global hub for organ transplants, research and education.

Sam Ajmera, who was born in India and co-founded FGF Brands, said in a statement that he wanted to build a better life for his family when he immigrated to Canada at age 26, and now he wants to continue to give back to the country that allowed him to do just that.

“My hope is that the Ajmera Transplant Institute will turn the discoveries of today into the treatments that save lives tomorrow – improving the lives of patients and families for generations to come,” Mr. Ajmera said.

The institute will build off the work already done at the Ajmera Transplant Centre, the country’s largest and most comprehensive transplant program. Located at Toronto General Hospital within the UHN, it is also named after the Ajmera family in recognition of a previous donation.

The team at the centre have been at the forefront of organ donation. Their successes include creating the world’s first centre for living organ donation, performing a rare five-organ transplant and using living-donor liver transplantation to treat people with otherwise incurable metastatic tumours.

Deepali Kumar, medical director of the Ajmera Transplant Centre, said in an interview that there are not enough organs available for everyone who needs one.

Each year, more than 250 Canadians die waiting for a life-saving organ, according to Canadian Blood Services. Hundreds more face rejection or other complications related to transplantation.

The new institute, Dr. Kumar said, will help the team identify new ways to either generate organs or make better use of the organs available.

“The institute will be all things transplant, so it will include the clinical care, including all the organs we transplant. It will include research. It will include education. We will be able to recruit the best and brightest people from around the planet.”

She said investments will be made in artificial intelligence to improve organ transplantation, and in ex vivo technologies, which manipulate living cells, tissues or organs outside of a body.

A section of the institute will focus on diabetes, specifically pancreas and islet transplantation, which are therapies to restore insulin production, she added.

“The gift marks a defining moment for UHN and for the future of transplantation,” Dr. Kumar said in a subsequent statement. “With it, we will have the opportunity to reimagine what is possible for those facing organ failure, reduce wait times and improve outcomes, and advance the next generation of transplant therapies.”

The UHN said in a statement that challenges in transplant care require a new collaborative model between experts in clinical care, engineering, immunology, regenerative medicine, cell therapy and data science. The Ajmera Transplant Institute, it said, will meet that need.

stories.title: Exclusive: London still negotiating Development Charge reduction to lower new home prices as other cities announce deals
stories.summary: As communities across Ontario announce agreements to cut municipal Development Charges (DCs) on residential construction, London is still negotiating the terms of its participation.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
As communities across Ontario announce agreements to cut municipal Development Charges (DCs) on residential construction, London is still negotiating the terms of its participation in an $8.8 billion joint federal-provincial program aimed at lowering the cost of new homes.

Ontario’s Development Charge Reduction Program (Odcrp) would reduce DCs by at least 30 to 50 per cent for a minimum of three years.

Last week, Mayor Josh Morgan said city hall recently had to resubmit part of its application.

“We’ve gotten some feedback,” Morgan explained. “We need to do a resubmission of some part of [the application]. I can’t talk about the details because that’s a confidential discussion with the [provincial] government, but we’re ready to participate in the program. We’ve just got to work out the terms.”

Based on a philosophy that growth should pay for growth, DCs are fees applied to new construction that offset the cost of growth-related infrastructure, including new roads, sewers, library branches, and fire halls.

Within London’s Urban Growth Boundary, development charges range from $22,364 per unit in a small apartment building, $34,195 for a townhouse, and $50,564 for a single-detached home.

The Odcrp offers senior government funding to offset certain growth-related infrastructure projects currently slated to be paid through DCs, and in return participating municipalities agree to temporarily reduce their development charges.

At a hastily summoned Council meeting in June, city staff were directed to apply to the Odcrp even before the list of local growth-related infrastructure projects had been completed.

At the time, Morgan assured council colleagues that a final decision to accept or decline the funding would be in front of them for a decision in August.

However, negotiations with the province are ongoing.

He told CTV News, “We’ll participate in a program to lower DCs, as long as it’s not going to involve putting property taxpayer money into the program. We’re looking to offset the cost of those projects with government dollars.”

Jared Zaifman, CEO of the London Home Builders’ Association (Ldba), said builders are eager for a reduction that could help bring new homebuyers off the sidelines.

“It’s hugely important,” Zaifman explained to CTV News at the same event attended by Morgan. “It’s something our industry [and] our members are asking about on a weekly basis, wondering when is the Development Charge reduction program going to happen in London? We were obviously very supportive of the city putting forward a submission to that program and we are constantly trying to speak with both the province and the city to say, where’s this at?”

Former Coun. Sandy Levin suspects the list of projects included in the City of London’s application to the province has been changed behind closed doors.

“The hard thing to figure out is what’s on the table? This was presented [confidentially] in-camera, which was really interesting because the original proposal was very public,” Levin suggested. “So it seems likely that London didn’t get what it asked for, and that has required some additional negotiations.”

He warns there are potentially massive financial consequences to signing a deal if it contributes to an infrastructure funding gap in the future, “The city is stuck with it for three years, and that means if there’s a gap in what the revenue was forecasted to be, then there’s only two ways to deal with that, either you delay projects that include growth funding, or you ask the taxpayer to fund it.”

St. Thomas, Windsor, Hamilton, Barrie, Guelph, and Sudbury are among the communities that have recently announced agreements to reduce their development charges for at least three years.

Morgan said London is not falling behind, “Although announcements have been made across this province, there is not yet, TPA (Transfer Payment Agreement) signed with any municipality. So, we’re working towards signing them at the same time as others do.”

stories.title: ‘Every vote is going to matter’: Manitobans head to the polls, amid signs of higher voter engagement across the country
stories.summary: Manitobans across the province head to the polls, amid record advance voting in Winnipeg and signs of increased voter engagement in elections across Canada.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Winnipeg – Manitobans across the province are heading to the polls amid record advance voting in Winnipeg and signs of increased voter engagement in elections across Canada.

More than 130 municipalities across Manitoba are holding municipal elections Wednesday, with voters choosing mayors, reeves, councillors and school trustees.

A record number of voters cast their ballots in advance of Winnipeg’s municipal election, with a total of 50,767 votes cast. That is a 21.2 per cent increase from 2022, when the previous advance voting record was set in the city.

“I think every vote is going to matter in this one. With so many options, I think that you might see a little bit more of a dispersion in the results that come in,” said Winnipeg voter Alexander Hryndzio.

Twelve candidates are vying for Winnipeg’s mayoral seat, including incumbent Scott Gillingham and former city councillor Kevin Klein. Voters will also elect representatives to 15 city council wards and choose school trustees across the city’s school divisions.

Public safety, housing, affordability, homelessness and public transit have emerged as key issues during the campaign.

‘Every election is important’

“For me, it’s important to get out and vote to make sure that I have a voice (in) what I feel I want to happen with the city,” said Cory Gergulich, who voted Wednesday morning.

“I live in downtown and I care about the city.”

Other voters feel this election in Winnipeg could turn out to be a pivotal one.

“Every election is important, but this one seems to have a higher degree of importance,” said Andrea Kohuch.

“There’s a lot of issues in the city that need to be addressed, and I think needs to be taken care of, so I think voting for a mayor in the city is by far one of the most important votes,” said Desiree Tessier, who voted on Wednesday.

The elections in Winnipeg and across Manitoba come amid signs of increased voter participation in other parts of the country.

Toronto’s civic election earlier this week had a 45 per cent voter turnout, following the historically low 2022 election, when voter turnout failed to reach 30 per cent.

Quebec’s provincial election earlier this month saw a slight increase in voter turnout from the previous election four years ago, with 66.93 per cent of eligible voters casting their ballots.

B.C. is the exception, as its snap election saw a record-low turnout .

“I think fluctuation is normal,” said political expert Lori Turnbull. “I think that, you know, we’ll see higher turnout in some cases, and lower turnout in others.”

Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University in Halifax, says the numbers May reflect a growing appetite for change among voters.

“In some cases, there’s a real change momentum, in the sense that the voters want to see change; they want to come out and make sure that they are heard,” she said.

“The potential impact, if the other side wins, will propel people to come out and vote.”

stories.title: Feds open to supporting elements of Divorce Act amendments, but fate unclear
stories.summary: Bill C-223, introduced by Liberal MP Lisa Hepfner, would amend the Divorce Act to curb parental alienation claims, among other changes.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Justice Minister Sean Fraser indicated Wednesday the government is open to supporting elements of a private member’s bill to amend the Divorce Act , though it’s not clear what the bill will ultimately look like.

Women’s groups warned last week that it appeared the Liberal government had changed its mind and the bill, currently before a House of Commons committee, could be killed.

Bill C-223, introduced by Liberal MP Lisa Hepfner, would amend the Divorce Act to curb parental alienation claims, among other changes.

It would also impose new requirements on lawyers to screen for signs of family violence during divorce cases, give judges new tools to identify the existence and impact of coercive control on children, and ensure that — in some circumstances — children can express their preferences to a judge in a custody dispute.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the government wants to see the committee make some amendments.

“We want to ensure that we protect the discretion of the court to consider all evidence that’s in the best interest of the child, but I’m optimistic that we can work with the sponsor to ensure we deliver important protections, but at the same time protect against the concerns that we had around judicial discretion,” Fraser said.

Hepfner told reporters there are elements of the bill that are more controversial than others, but declined to say which elements could be removed.

“If we can pass a version of the bill that everyone agrees, including the (Canadian) Bar Association … would make the family court system safer for kids, then I think we should go ahead,” she said.

Hepfner has said she proposed the legislation after hearing horrifying stories from Suzanne Zaccour, director of legal affairs at the National Association of Women and the Law.

Zaccour said in an interview Wednesday it’s important to know what amendments Fraser has in mind.

“There’s some things that I think everyone should be able to agree on, and I hope that the minister will be prepared to support,” she said.

She said there should be nothing controversial about changing the law to ensure that, in cases where there is “a finding of family violence, that the parent who was abusive should not be able to blame the other parent for their strained relationship with the child.”

A report from the National Association of Women and the Law released in September that looked into the deaths of eight children said the concept of parental alienation is frequently invoked in Canada’s courts.

The report said it’s used by parties in child custody cases to explain why a child resists seeing a parent, and to cast doubt on allegations of domestic violence.

Hepfner said in an interview she can’t say with certainty what the bill will look like at the end of the process.

“But I’m working my hardest to try and just get some substantial changes moving now, and then some certainty or some assurances that the government will continue to look at this issue and address some of the problems that have been raised with my bill,” she said.

stories.title: How the latest interest rate hike could affect everyday Canadians
stories.summary: While Wednesday's hike is less significant than those that followed the pandemic, experts say people who are already struggling to make ends meet will feel the burden first.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
The Bank of Canada raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in more than three years on Wednesday as it tries to get ahead of looming price hikes.

Already plagued by the rising costs of gas and groceries, consumers will feel the hit.

“A consumer who holds about $200,000 in a variable rate mortgage or a variable-rate home equity line of credit, they will feel about $500 worth of interest cost annually as relates to this,” Lara Stilin, chief financial officer at Your Neighbourhood Credit Union (Yncu), told Global News.

While Wednesday’s hike is less significant than the series of increases issued following the COVID-19 pandemic, experts say people who are already struggling to make ends meet with rising inflation will feel the burden first.

Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent in September, which the Bank of Canada has largely attributed to high gas prices.

The central bank now expects annual inflation will hit 3.5 per cent at the end of this year before gradually easing to around two per cent by mid-2028.

Food inflation is expected to average around four per cent in 2027, up about a half a percentage point from this year.

“I’m more worried about households that have already stopped eating out, put off big purchases and dipped into their savings, and are still coming up short. For them, another increase doesn’t mean finding one more thing to cut. It means deciding which bill gets paid this month and which one waits until next month,” Kristy Rachkowski, chief member experience officer at Yncu, said in a statement.

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said Wednesday inflation is likely to be “more persistent.”

“And I think when you look at it through that risk lens, that also tilted in favour of raising the policy rate now,” he said.

What experts say is more concerning for Canadians, is if they can expect more hikes to follow.

“Is this the first of many, or is this first of a few, or is this the first and last, which is still I’d say, unclear right now as the economic situation evolves,” Stilin said.

Macklem said the central bank will take its upcoming rate decisions “one meeting at a time” but also suggested future hikes are still in the cards.

“There could be a need to raise the policy rate further, but given the uncertainties, we will proceed carefully,” he said.

Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union, said in a note to clients that he expects the central bank will deliver back-to-back hikes to end the year with a policy rate of 2.75 per cent.

He said only a weakening economy or softer than expected inflation will prevent a future hike.

Stilin said the majority of Canadians May not need to worry just yet, but said it is prime time to make sure you understand your own budget and the flux space you have within it.

“If you are already feeling the pinch with rising fuel prices, rising grocery prices, now is the time to act,” she said.

stories.title: Alberta tables bill to protect consumers when buying cars, show tickets
stories.summary: Under the bill, consumers could get some power to fight back when they purchase defective vehicles that cannot be properly repaired.
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Alberta’s government is proposing new rules to give consumers more protection when buying vehicles, tickets, electronics and more.

Service Alberta Minister Dale Nally has introduced a bill that, if passed, would create a so-called lemon law to give consumers some power to fight back when they purchase defective vehicles that cannot be properly repaired.

The bill would also create a so-called right-to-repair framework to give consumers more freedom to get products fixed rather than having to rely on manufacturers.

The government is also considering limits on markups for ticket resellers as well as an overall price cap.

The government says most of the details of the new protections will be determined later through regulations.

There is no timeline on implementation for right-to-repair or ticket reselling rules.

stories.title: Six Canadians injured, one ‘unaccounted for’ in fatal Spanish train crash
stories.summary: Spanish officials reported at least 68 people killed, and another 58 were receiving treatment at local hospitals
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
Six Canadians are among the injured and a seventh remained unaccounted for following a high-speed rail crash in central Spain Wednesday morning.

The deadly accident occurred just before 9 a.m. local time, when one train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks. Spanish officials reported at least 68 people killed, and another 58 were receiving treatment at local hospitals.

Global Affairs Canada spokesperson Thida Ith said Wednesday the department had confirmation six Canadians injured in the crash, and one more was still unaccounted for by Wednesday evening. Ith said Canadian officials are providing consular assistance and are in contact with local authorities to gather more information.

“Our thoughts are with their families and loved ones as well as all of those affected,” said Ith.

Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed Canada’s solidarity with victims and family members and indicated Ottawa would help as needed. Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said on social media he had reached out to his Spanish counterpart.

“I also thank the emergency responders and medical teams working around the clock to help those impacted by this tragedy,” McKinnon said.

Spain’s rail system operator Adif said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. It involved two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain.

A train operated by the state-owned Renfe company struck the rear of another train operated by private company Iryo that was stopped. The collision derailed two carriages on the tail of the Iryo train and the front of the Renfe train.

Authorities said 397 passengers were in the Renfe train and 147 passengers in the Iryo train.

Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Spain’s Transport Minister Oscar Puente said the crash was caused by what he called an “inexplicable” order from a central command centre for Spain’s trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.

Puente said at 8:30 a.m., local time, the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometres stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the Renfe train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped Iryo train at 8:53 a.m.

Puente said the train never should have been told to start moving again, since there was still a “stop signal” active on that line, and that it should at least have been told to go at a reduced speed.

Authorities were still trying to determine Wednesday how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph for that stretch of the track, Puente said.

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yebenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Until this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain’s dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992. Now there have been two in just 10 months.

In January, 46 people died in southern Spain when an Iryo train jumped the track and hit an oncoming Renfe train.

“Today all of Spain is grieving,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.

Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.

“It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.

stories.title: Halton police officer charged in 2025 pursuit that left one person injured: SIU
stories.summary: A Halton regional police officer who was involved in a vehicle chase that left one person seriously injured in Mississauga last year has been charged.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A Halton regional police officer who was involved in a vehicle chase that left one person seriously injured in Mississauga last year has been charged.

Ontario’s police watchdog says it has reasonable grounds to lay a criminal charge against Sgt. David Joseph after the pursuit of a stolen vehicle that collided with a tractor trailer.

stories.title: Did the B.C. Conservatives’ election win run against the federal tide, or with it?
stories.summary: They jettisoned extremism and federally the Liberal Party has shifted to the centre
stories.author: Andrew Coyne
stories.content:
Some days it feels as if Canadian democracy is a complete farce. Provincial governments elected with near majorities on the strength of 28 per cent of the vote – the same 28 per cent that in another province is worth just two seats. Referendum ballots with 10 loaded questions, none of them binding.

Party leaders elected by children, non-citizens, and tens of thousands of instant members, signed up in a frenzy with who knows what checks against fraud or foreign interference. Party caucuses expected to offer unquestioning obedience to leaders they had no say in choosing.

Premiers and prime ministers winning elections on a solemn promise to do one thing, then doing the precise opposite thing to the one they promised. Turnout percentages that run to the 60s federally, the 40s and 50s provincially, as low as the 20s municipally. And so on.

But every now and then we get a glimpse of the democracy that might be. However broken our institutions, however venal our political class, they are occasionally forced into contact with the final guardrail, the ultimate reality check: the voters. The Alberta referendum, in which 75 per cent of the electorate voted to send the secessionists packing, was one such moment. The B.C. election was another.

We can’t know what combination of desperation and cynicism led the NDP Premier, David Eby, to call a snap election, just two years after the last, and two days after the leader of the B.C. Conservative Party, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, had been forced out . But it’s a safe bet that he and his advisers thought they would get away with it.

Though the move, calling an election while the opposition was without a permanent leader, was without precedent in Canada’s history – and though snap elections were supposed to have ended with the province’s fixed-election-date law – they must have calculated any outrage would prove fleeting. “Two-day story,” they told themselves. The media will fuss, but after a while people will get over it.

But there were a few things they didn’t reckon with. One was the basic decency of the voters, who know a bit of dirty pool when they see it. A second was the depths of public dissatisfaction with the party, which had been papered over by the bizarre shenanigans on the opposition benches during Ms. Findlay’s chaotic tenure, including the departure of 13 caucus members.

And a third, which perhaps escaped their notice as they were plotting their brilliant manoeuvre: Ms. Findlay’s decommission wasn’t the only thing going on in the Conservative Party. The normies in the party (mostly former BC Liberals) were staging a palace coup. The craziest members of caucus had already decamped. The remainder rallied around an interim leader, an unassuming former publisher and rodeo rider by the name of Lorne Doerkson, whose first act was to readmit the mainstream caucus members who had either left or been expelled by Ms. Findlay.

Mr. Doerkson’s reassuring, grandfatherly presence, coupled with the party’s disciplined, economy-focused campaign, proved to be enough to persuade swing voters, who had been preparing to hold their nose and vote NDP, that it was safe to vote Conservative. Couple that with the many disaffected New Democrats who stayed home, and you had the ingredients for a remarkable victory (though the turnout, at less than 50 per cent, takes some of the shine off).

There’s a lesson in this, besides “don’t call snap elections when your opponents are leaderless,” and that is for the federal Conservatives. Lately the party has been having a debate between those who argue the party can only win by moderating its policies and moving to the middle, and those arguing for a no-prisoners, culture-war approach, using the state to shape society in much the same way as progressives do, only to conservative ends.

The B.C. Conservative win is an example of neither of these. The party platform was robustly conservative, complete with personal income tax cuts, business tax relief, deregulation, and faster approvals for resource projects. Yes, there were some culture-war planks, like abolishing Dripa, legislation encoding the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples into provincial law. But much the greater emphasis was on the economy: traditional smaller-government, lower taxes conservatism.

More important, the tone was relentlessly moderate. This is the kind of moderation most voters are looking for: moderation of temperament, more than of ideology. Once they’ve concluded that you’re a reasonable person with sound judgment, they’re more willing to give you the benefit of the doubt in policy terms. The B.C. Conservatives, like many successful parties, didn’t move to the middle. They moved the middle to them.

But maybe the result was foreordained. After all, the federal Liberals are in power in Ottawa. And isn’t it often said that Canadian voters like to “ balance ” off a Liberal government federally with a provincial Conservative government, and (less often) a Conservative federal government with a Liberal or NDP provincial government, rather like American voters in a midterm?

Sure enough, there are currently seven Conservative or at least conservative provincial governments, to just one Liberal (and one NDP).

But it’s far from clear that this is the product of any conscious attempt at balancing. Rather, the same trends that explain the rise or fall of one or another party at the federal level May also be observable at the provincial level, but with a lag.

Before the Liberals came to power federally, there was a swing to progressive governments in the provinces: at one point in the latter years of the Harper government there was only one large-c Conservative provincial government in the country (though Brad Wall’s Saskatchewan Party government was certainly conservative and Christy Clark’s BC Liberal government was a coalition of federal Liberals and Conservatives).

As the Trudeau Liberals fell deep into public odium, the pendulum began to shift, with the results we are now seeing. But with the rise of the Carney Liberals, the pendulum May begin to shift back again. The Saskatchewan NDP is within a few points of the governing Saskatchewan Party, while the NDP and the United Conservative Party are neck and neck in Alberta .

In Ontario , the Liberals are now just six points back of the Conservatives, even without a leader. The Liberals finished just four points behind the Parti Québécois in the recent Quebec election , up from fourth in the popular vote the last time.

Still, it’s a striking contrast, between the Liberals’ relative weakness at the provincial level – in the four Western provinces they barely register a pulse – and their strength federally, where they now lead the Conservatives by an average of 15 points.

What’s most remarkable about it is its breadth. It is not surprising to see the federal Liberals do well in Ontario , where they lead by 18 points; in Quebec , where they lead by 19; or in Atlantic Canada , where they lead by 25. It is extraordinary to see them leading in the West.

Yes, leading: across the West, the Liberals now stand at an average of about 40 per cent support in the polls, to 39 per cent for the Conservatives. That’s largely on the strength of the 14-point lead they enjoy in B.C., but even in Manitoba and Saskatchewan they trail the Conservatives by only six points.

More extraordinary still, they are now at an average of 35 per cent support in Alberta . Several pollsters have them at 40 per cent or more, including Liaison Strategies, Leger, and Ekos. How extraordinary is this? The last time the Liberals won more than 40 per cent of the vote in Alberta was in 1908. The last time they won even 36 per cent of the vote was in 1940.

The most recent 338Canada.com projection has them winning a majority of the seats in the West – that hasn’t happened since 1949 – including 13 seats in Alberta. Not only has that not happened since 1940: in the 26 elections since then the party has averaged a little over one seat in Alberta. In 13 of those elections they won zero.

Whether the Liberals can maintain these levels of support at the next election, of course, remains to be seen. It will depend, in part, ON when the next election is. But the temptation to call one soon will be strong. This has the makings of a historic realignment.

Conservatives can console themselves that much of the Liberals’ current popularity is owing to their abrupt – some might say shameless – shift to the right under Mark Carney. So in a sense the current mood of conservatism in provincial politics is mirrored, rather than contrasted, federally.

But the federal Liberals are only able to play that shape-shifting role because of the persistence of three-, four- and five-party politics at the federal level. In provincial politics, Duverger’s Law – the tendency of first past the post electoral systems to drive out smaller parties in favour of two dominant parties – is more apparent. (Though see Quebec, where five parties now have at least 10 per cent support.)

Federal politics, ON the other hand, is harder to break down into a simple left-right dichotomy, whether because of the national unity question, traditionally the Liberals’ trump card, or lately because of the threat from the United States. So a middle party like the Liberals is less likely to be caught in the sort of polarizing squeeze that is so common elsewhere.

At any rate, it’s not at all clear the Carney Liberals would be terribly displeased by the B.C. election result. Between the party of Kerry-Lynne Findlay and the party of Justin Trudeau there would have been an unbridgeable chasm. But between Mr. Doerkson and Mr. Carney? Not so much – less, arguably, than between Mr. Carney and Mr. Eby.

Mr. Doerkson’s Conservatives moved the middle to them. Mr. Carney’s Liberals moved to the middle. But in the end the result is much the same.

stories.title: Liberals keep B.C. oil tanker ban in place, vote down Conservative bill
stories.summary: The Conservatives have argued the law is undermining Canada's prosperity by limiting the potential for oil exports from B.C.'s northern coast to international markets.
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
The Liberal government has voted to keep the B.C. oil tanker ban place, defeating a Conservative bill that would have repealed it.

MPs voted along party lines during second reading in the House of Commons today, with only the Conservatives voting to move the bill forward to the committee stage.

Prime Minister Mark Carney , who made a rare appearance after question period to vote in person on several bills today, struck a deal with the B.C. government earlier this summer to keep the ban in place.

The existing law, the Oil Tanker Moratorium Act, prohibits tankers from carrying more than 12,500 metric tonnes of crude oil in areas along the northern coast of British Columbia.

The Conservatives have argued the law is undermining Canada’s prosperity by limiting the potential for oil exports from B.C.’s northern coast to international markets.

Alberta originally envisioned that the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline would export from the northern coast, but the route was revised this summer to go south to respect the ban.
