stories.title: Ontario pauses some skills training funding for unemployed people
stories.summary: There has been no communication from the government about the status of the program that aims to get people off social assistance and into the work force
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
In addition to freezing Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all private postsecondary institutions, the province has paused at least some funding through Better Jobs Ontario, which helps unemployed people get skills training.

But the government won’t explicitly say so.

There has been no public communication from the government about the status of the program that aims to get people off social assistance and into the work force, but people who were depending on the program and the institutions that were set to train them are taking note.

Reece Daniel was hoping to begin an Hvac program in London, Ont., ON Oct. 19. The government had initially scheduled a meeting for Oct. 13 to give him information about the funding agreement, but a few days before that they cancelled and said applications were under review.

The next intake for the Hvac program is in May, 2027.

“This course was something that was going to get me jumped back on my feet,” Daniel said.

“I’m still probably going to be presented with the opportunity to go to school next year, but the significant delays ... waiting for so long, putting off work for so long, it’s a little bit disappointing and frustrating.”

Pathways Employment Help Centre had been assisting Daniel in his application, and is seeing other clients experiencing the same delays and uncertainty with their Better Jobs Ontario funding decisions, the CEO said.

“Despite our agency’s repeated efforts to obtain clarification, the absence of a definitive decision prevented Reece and other clients from proceeding with their planned training as scheduled,” Ben Cecil said.

Career Colleges Ontario said the association has heard from member schools that Better Jobs Ontario funding for students at career colleges has been paused, but it has not received any formal communication from the government.

“We are concerned about any disruption to funding for students attending compliant institutions,” it wrote in a statement.

“As with Osap, we are urging the government to restore access to funding for students attending institutions where there are no identified compliance concerns. We continue to advocate for a targeted approach that allows students to access the support they need while maintaining strong accountability across the sector.”

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced earlier this month that Osap payments are paused for students at all private postsecondary institutions, after preliminary audit findings raised serious concerns about financial aid usage at some career colleges.

Trillium College has suspended classes due to the Osap pause, and wrote in a letter to students that it is a temporary measure due to the uncertainty caused by that freeze and “the separate funding interruption affecting Better Jobs Ontario-funded students at Trillium College.”

When asked recently if Better Jobs Ontario funding was also paused, Quinn’s spokesperson said little.

“Preliminary audit findings point to serious, systemic concerns about Osap usage at private postsecondary institutions,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote.

“Osap payments to students at these institutions are paused, and other streams of provincial funding to private institutions past and present are under review.”

Giacoboni refused to list those other streams of funding.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said if the government is taking action against another source of funding they should come out and say it.

“It’s happening,” he said. “They know it’s happening and I don’t know why they’re afraid to say it.”

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the government is ducking accountability.

“This government is terrified of facing the music,” she wrote in a statement.

“They won’t even do the bare minimum of explaining themselves. They’re leaving thousands of people who rely on this program to build a better future and find good jobs without any certainty or support. This is not how you protect Ontario in the face of growing job losses.”

stories.title: Three people dead following multi-vehicle crash near Windsor: OPP
stories.summary: Three people are dead following a multi-vehicle crash early Wednesday morning in a town just outside of Windsor, Ontario Provincial Police say.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Three people are dead following a multi-vehicle crash early Wednesday morning in a town just outside of Windsor.

Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) said its officers responded to the crash on County Road 22 in Lakeshore around 6:07 a.m.

The drivers of two vehicles involved in the crash were pronounced dead on scene; a passenger was taken to hospital where they were pronounced dead.

Police are assessing others for injuries. The OPP did not specify the amount of people or vehicles involved in the crash.

The cause of the crash is not known.

An investigation is underway.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Bank of Canada interest rate announcement nears as economists expect a hike
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada is expected to make an interest rate announcement Wednesday, with many economists predicting a hike for the first time in three years.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The Bank of Canada is expected to make an interest rate announcement Wednesday, with many economists predicting a hike for the first time in three years.

The central bank is facing pressure to raise interest rates as the Iran war and other geopolitical conflicts result in higher prices for oil and gas, which is expected to lead to higher prices for goods and services beyond the gas pump.

Financial markets and a Reuters poll of economists are betting that the central bank will deliver a quarter-point hike to its policy rate, the first increase in the key lending rate since July 2023.

The floor for borrowing rates set by the Bank of Canada has been 2.25 per cent since October 2025, when rates were cut from 2.5 per cent.

Alongside the rate decision, the Bank of Canada will also release updated forecasts for inflation and economic growth.

– with a file from The Canadian Press

More to come.

stories.title: Finalists for Governor General’s Literary Awards include Miriam Toews, Hannah Moscovitch
stories.summary: The Canada Council for the Arts named 69 finalists across seven categories in English and French and winners will be announced on Nov. 12
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
The Globe and Mail’s Greg Mercer is a finalist for this year’s Governor General’s Literary Awards for his non-fiction book The Lobster Trap , joining authors including Miriam Toews, Hannah Moscovitch and Kim Fu.

Toews’ memoir A Truce That Is Not Peace is one of five books up for the English-language non-fiction prize. Toews explores the question, “why do you write?” in the book while reflecting on the suicides of her sister and father. The Toronto-based writer previously won the Governor General’s fiction prize for her 2004 novel A Complicated Kindness .

The Canada Council for the Arts named 69 finalists across seven categories in English and French on Wednesday. The 14 winners, who each receive $25,00, will be announced on Nov. 12.

Moscovitch is nominated in the drama category for her play Red Like Fruit , which follows a journalist covering a high-profile domestic violence case while a sense of unease pervades her thoughts. The Halifax playwright, who is also a writer for the AMC television series, Interview with the Vampire , previously won the Governor General’s drama prize in 2021 for Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes .

Fu is among the five finalists for the English-language fiction prize for her novel The Valley of Vengeful Ghosts about a woman unravelling in the aftermath of her mother’s death. The Vancouver-born writer was previously a finalist for the Giller Prize in 2022 for her short story collection Lesser Known Monsters of the 21st Century .

Also nominated in the fiction category is Sharon Bala for her novel Good Guys about the dark side of philanthropy and Sara Peters for her novel Mother of God about a woman with psychic powers who returns home to see her estranged mother. Rounding out the fiction finalists is Nina Dunic for Suddenly Light and Kate Cayley for Property .

The Governor General’s Literary Awards, which celebrates homegrown literature, will also hand out honours for poetry, writing and illustration in young people’s literature, as well as French-to-English translation. There are separate French-language categories for francophone writing.

stories.title: Pork producer Canada Packers reports third-quarter loss as market turns
stories.summary: Sales totalled $420.7-million in the quarter, down from $481.80-million a year ago
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A confluence of unusual headwinds from weaker demand to plummeting hog prices weighed on pork producer Canada Packers Inc.’s Cpkr-T third-quarter results.

Chief executive Dennis Organ said the company’s losses extended into the third quarter as it contended with “the combination of softer U.S. demand, slower exports and high year-over-year U.S. inventories at a time of steady supply.”

But Organ said the downturn is “cyclical.”

“The reason I consider it cyclical, one, is: I’ve seen it before multiple times. Two, it’s the relationship between demand and supply, which happens in all businesses,” he told analysts during an earnings call on Wednesday.

While Organ said he remains confident on a recovery, he said he has “no idea” when the market will return to normal.

The pork producer, based in Mississauga, Ont., reported a loss of $28.1-million or 94 cents per diluted share in the quarter ended Sept. 26 compared with a profit of $25.6-million or 86 cents per diluted share a year earlier.

The results included a $47.6-million non-cash decrease in fair value of biological assets compared with $4.9-million in the same quarter last year. On an adjusted basis, it earned 23 cents per share in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted profit of $1.13 per share a year earlier.

RBC analyst Irene Nattel said Canada Packers’ soft earnings were in line with expectations, reflecting a “sharp deterioration in market conditions and the absence of typical seasonal profitability dynamics, driving margin compression.”

Lower pork cut-out, which estimates the value of a hog based on the prices for each individual cut of meat from the animal, also weighed on overall sales, the company said.

“Cut-out values declined approximately 15 per cent from a year ago, and the weakness we experienced in the second quarter continued through the third quarter,” Organ said.

Wholesale commodity prices for hogs have plunged to a five-year low to roughly US$62 per pound, which also added volatility to the company’s financial results.

“While we can’t control commodity markets, our attention remains squarely on how we operate,” Organ said.

Sales in the quarter totalled $420.7-million, down from $481.8-million a year ago, when they included operations not acquired in its spinoff from Maple Leaf Foods Inc.

stories.title: Edmonton experiences first major snowfall — just days before Halloween
stories.summary: The ghosts, ghouls and goblins on some of Edmonton's front lawns were made even spookier by the chilling sight of Old Man Winter.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
The ghosts, ghouls and goblins on some of Edmonton’s front lawns were made even spookier by the chilling sight of Old Man Winter.

The city, days before Halloween, woke up on Wednesday to its first significant snowfall.

Environment Canada forecasters said upwards of 15 centimetres of snow could fall through parts of central Alberta by Thursday morning.

The weather office has issued a number of special weather statements for the city and surrounding communities.

The snow was expected to have a significant effect on rush-hour traffic.

Officials have urged drivers to allow for extra travel time and prepare for fast-changing road conditions.

stories.title: Warmth returns to southern Ontario
stories.summary: Our sunny stretch continues into Wednesday as a warm front moves into the region.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Our sunny stretch continues into Wednesday as a warm front moves into the region.

“Temperatures are headed up so a bit of cloud cover overnight will make way for lots of sunshine heading into the afternoon,” said CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison. “Warm temperatures will hold as we head into your Thursday.”

However, a cold front is on its way that could bring a few showers to midwestern Ontario come Thursday night.

“As that frontal boundary comes through, temperatures will be dipping down as we head into Friday,” said Atchison.

Looking ahead to the weekend, Atchison says Halloween is looking mainly cloudy, but dry.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast

Wednesday: Clearing in the morning. High 20. UV index 3 or moderate.

Wednesday night: Clear. Low 10.

Thursday: A mix of sun and cloud with 30 per cent chance of showers. High 20.

Friday: Sunny. High 16.

Saturday: Cloudy. High 14.

Sunday: Cloudy with 30 per cent chance of showers. High 14.

stories.title: Ontario pauses some skills training funding for unemployed people: career colleges
stories.summary: The Ford government is pausing at least some funding through Better Jobs Ontario, which helps unemployed people get skills training.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
In addition to freezing Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all private post-secondary institutions, the province has paused at least some funding through Better Jobs Ontario, which helps unemployed people get skills training.

But the government won’t explicitly say so.

There has been no public communication from the government about the status of the program that aims to get people off social assistance and into the workforce, but people who were depending on the program and the institutions that were set to train them are taking note.

Reece Daniel was hoping to begin an Hvac program in London, Ont., ON Oct. 19. The government had initially scheduled a meeting for Oct. 13 to give him information about the funding agreement, but a few days before that they cancelled and said applications were under review.

The next intake for the Hvac program is in May 2027.

“This course was something that was going to get me jumped back on my feet,” Daniel said.

“I’m still probably going to be presented with the opportunity to go to school next year, but the significant delays … waiting for so long, putting off work for so long, it’s a little bit disappointing and frustrating.”

Pathways Employment Help Centre had been assisting Daniel in his application, and is seeing other clients experiencing the same delays and uncertainty with their Better Jobs Ontario funding decisions, the CEO said.

“Despite our agency’s repeated efforts to obtain clarification, the absence of a definitive decision prevented Reece and other clients from proceeding with their planned training as scheduled,” Ben Cecil said.

Career Colleges Ontario said the association has heard from member schools that Better Jobs Ontario funding for students at career colleges has been paused, but it has not received any formal communication from the government.

“We are concerned about any disruption to funding for students attending compliant institutions,” it wrote in a statement.

“As with Osap, we are urging the government to restore access to funding for students attending institutions where there are no identified compliance concerns. We continue to advocate for a targeted approach that allows students to access the support they need while maintaining strong accountability across the sector.”

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced earlier this month that Osap payments are paused for students at all private post-secondary institutions, after preliminary audit findings raised serious concerns about financial aid usage at some career colleges.

Trillium College has suspended classes due to the Osap pause, and wrote in a letter to students that it is a temporary measure due to the uncertainty caused by that freeze and “the separate funding interruption affecting Better Jobs Ontario-funded students at Trillium College.”

When asked recently if Better Jobs Ontario funding was also paused, Quinn’s spokesperson said little.

“Preliminary audit findings point to serious, systemic concerns about Osap usage at private postsecondary institutions,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote.

“Osap payments to students at these institutions are paused, and other streams of provincial funding to private institutions past and present are under review.”

Giacoboni refused to list those other streams of funding.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said if the government is taking action against another source of funding they should come out and say it.

“It’s happening,” he said. “They know it’s happening and I don’t know why they’re afraid to say it.”

There has been no public communication from the government about the status of the program that aims to get people off social assistance and into the workforce, but people who were depending on the program and the institutions that were set to train them are taking note.

Reece Daniel was hoping to begin an Hvac program in London, Ont., ON Oct. 19. The government had initially scheduled a meeting for Oct. 13 to give him information about the funding agreement, but a few days before that they cancelled and said applications were under review.
The next intake for the Hvac program is in May 2027.
“This course was something that was going to get me jumped back on my feet,” Daniel said.

“I’m still probably going to be presented with the opportunity to go to school next year, but the significant delays … waiting for so long, putting off work for so long, it’s a little bit disappointing and frustrating.”

Pathways Employment Help Centre had been assisting Daniel in his application, and is seeing other clients experiencing the same delays and uncertainty with their Better Jobs Ontario funding decisions, the CEO said.

“Despite our agency’s repeated efforts to obtain clarification, the absence of a definitive decision prevented Reece and other clients from proceeding with their planned training as scheduled,” Ben Cecil said.

Career Colleges Ontario said the association has heard from member schools that Better Jobs Ontario funding for students at career colleges has been paused, but it has not received any formal communication from the government.
“We are concerned about any disruption to funding for students attending compliant institutions,” it wrote in a statement.

“As with Osap, we are urging the government to restore access to funding for students attending institutions where there are no identified compliance concerns. We continue to advocate for a targeted approach that allows students to access the support they need while maintaining strong accountability across the sector.”

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced earlier this month that Osap payments are paused for students at all private post-secondary institutions, after preliminary audit findings raised serious concerns about financial aid usage at some career colleges.

Trillium College has suspended classes due to the Osap pause, and wrote in a letter to students that it is a temporary measure due to the uncertainty caused by that freeze and “the separate funding interruption affecting Better Jobs Ontario-funded students at Trillium College.”
When asked recently if Better Jobs Ontario funding was also paused, Quinn’s spokesperson said little.
“Preliminary audit findings point to serious, systemic concerns about Osap usage at private postsecondary institutions,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote.
“Osap payments to students at these institutions are paused, and other streams of provincial funding to private institutions past and present are under review.”
Giacoboni refused to list those other streams of funding.
Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said if the government is taking action against another source of funding they should come out and say it.
“It’s happening,” he said. “They know it’s happening and I don’t know why they’re afraid to say it.”

stories.title: Gloom settles over the Canadian housing market
stories.summary: ‘There are no fundamentals for a rebound,’ says Cpac chief economist
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
A plateau in Canada’s housing market appears to be crumbling towards a steeper slide, cautions David-Alexandre Brassard, chief economist with Chartered Professional Accountants of Canada, who says that rising borrowing costs are threatening to put downward pressure on buyer demand heading into the final months of the year.

“There are no fundamentals for a rebound,” Mr. Brassard said in an interview.

He points to the U.S.-Canada trade war, weaker labour markets and slower economic growth as some of the other factors making buyers jittery in cities across the country.

The Canadian Real Estate Association (Crea) also acknowledged the gloomy outlook recently when the organization downgraded its 2026 forecast for sales and prices for the third time this year.

Crea points to a recent rise in rates for fixed-term mortgages and uncertainty surrounding the Bank of Canada’s next moves – which set the direction of variable rates – as steep global energy prices spark worries about broader inflation.

National home sales fell 2.3 per cent in September from August on a seasonally adjusted basis, while new listings declined 1.8 per cent in the same period.

Crea’s National Composite Home Price Index slipped 0.4 per cent in September from August as the average price dropped in heavyweight Toronto and price growth in other cities moderated.

The national average home price dipped 1.6 per cent in September compared with the same month last year to stand at $666,538.

With the sharp deterioration in September, Crea now expects national sales this year to come in 5.2 per cent below the 2025 level.

Mr. Brassard stresses that the country does not have one housing market, but many – and the factors shaping consumers’ decisions to forge ahead or hold off vary by city.

One development that surprised economists was the recent revision to data on the size of Canada’s population , Mr. Brassard notes.

The adjustment is particularly relevant in the Toronto and Vancouver metropolitan areas, he adds, as those cities draw a higher proportion of temporary residents.

Statistics Canada now estimates that the country’s population expanded by 0.5 per cent as of July 1 instead of shrinking by 0.5 per cent from the same time last year.

The stronger-than-expected demographics indicate that faltering sales in the Greater Toronto Area are the result of factors other than population decline, Mr. Brassard notes.

Sales in the GTA fell 5.3 per cent in September from August on a seasonally adjusted basis to mark a second consecutive monthly decrease.

Consumers in Toronto and Vancouver are more likely to be influenced by rising rates, Mr. Brassard points out, because the high prices in those cities already hinder aspiring buyers.

Andre Kutyan, broker with Harvey Kalles Real Estate, says sales in Toronto are subdued.

“The fall has been stalled,” he says.

Mr. Kutyan attracted 12 offers after he listed an older four-bedroom house in Forest Hill with an asking price of $1.695-million and a deadline for reviewing offers.

Many high-priced listings in the tony neighbourhood are sitting, he says, but he figured there would be good appetite for the entry-level property at 617 Lonsdale Rd.

On offer night, the top contenders entered a second round of bidding when – out of nowhere – the fourth-place offer vaulted ahead and the contest went to a third round, Mr. Kutyan says.

The house sold for $2.235-million.

“It’s only certain pockets and certain price ranges,” Mr. Kutyan says of the properties that spark competition.

In the Bayview Avenue and Eglinton Avenue East area, 30 Walder Ave. was listed with an asking price of $2.349-million in July before Mr. Kutyan cut the asking price to $2.249-million in August.

In September the house sold for $2.197-million.

Mr. Kutyan says buyers are nervous about committing.

“There are people paralyzed by indecision, that’s for sure.”

He points to the example of clients with a budget around the $3-million mark who found an attractive four-bedroom house in midtown with an asking price of $3.2-million.

When the price dropped below $3-million, Mr. Kutyan’s clients submitted an offer during the Thanksgiving long weekend.

The two sides haggled until they were $50,000 apart, then the sellers walked away and the deal died, Mr. Kutyan says.

The sellers reconsidered and – four days later – contacted Mr. Kutyan to say they would accept the amount of the buyers’ last bid.

But by then the buyers had cooled off, says Mr. Kutyan.

“They didn’t even want to agree to what they offered a few days earlier,” he says as they wonder, “‘is there going to be something better or something cheaper?’”

In many cities across Canada, buyers are slowing down.

Sales in September dropped in Edmonton, Calgary, Winnipeg, Ottawa and Hamilton.

Ariane Curtis, senior North America economist with Capital Economics, says growth in Canada’s economy appears to have lost momentum in the third quarter.

She predicts that headwinds from new tariffs and ongoing trade uncertainty will weigh on economic activity over the next few quarters.

In Montreal, a market shift is leading to rising supply as demand weakens, and Quebec City’s torrid price growth has moderated.

Ontario and Quebec are particularly vulnerable to tariffs and the impact on manufacturing, autos, steel and aluminum, Mr. Brassard notes.

The economist is pessimistic about the chances of a market rebound, but a decline in prices is not a negative outcome, in his view.

Slumping sales are a greater concern because that trend has implications for the economy: unemployed people who cannot sell their house, for example, lack the mobility to find work elsewhere.

If inflated prices lose some air, Mr. Brassard points out, people currently priced out of the market would have an opportunity to buy.

The economist owns a home in Quebec, he says, but overall Canadians plow too much of their income and investment into housing, in his opinion.

“I think homeowner wealth is an illusion in the sense that it only materializes when you sell.”

People less burdened by home ownership can put their cash towards other things and diversify their assets.

“They’d have more money to invest elsewhere, and that could be in the economy.”

As an example, Mr. Brassard points to his recent business trip to Toronto. He noted that the city’s restaurants reside in real estate worth millions of dollars, and restaurateurs inevitably pass on that expense to diners.

He estimates dining out in his home city costs half as much as it does in Toronto in many cases.

“The food is much greater in Quebec City – and a lot less expensive,” he quips.

stories.title: Home designed for builder’s family sells over asking in two days
stories.summary: Four-bedroom house goes for $2-million
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
263 Windermere Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $1,899,000 (September, 2026)

Selling price: $2-million (October, 2026)

Previous selling price: Not applicable

Taxes: $9,522 (2026)

Days on the market: Two

Listing agent: Nutan Brown, Royal LePage Terrequity Realty

The seller of this four-bedroom house had planned to open it for visitors for one week this fall before considering offers. But a couple of eager house hunters actively shopping for homes in the area west of High Park took two tours of the space and made an offer within 48 hours that was $101,000 over the asking price. The seller quickly accepted.

“We only had about six to eight people going through,” said agent Nutan Brown.

“[The owner] had a certain price in mind and when she saw that, she said it was enough, and she was done.”

Ms. Brown believes the process unfolded quickly due to the size and design of the roughly 25-year-old home.

“Because the owner’s father was a reputable and renowned builder in the community, he built above and beyond what most people had at that time,” Ms. Brown said.

“On the second floor, there are four bedrooms and three full bathrooms, which is unheard of.”

This two-storey house has about 1,840 square feet of living space, including living and dining areas separated by a three-sided gas fireplace.

There are five bathrooms and a kitchen with double doors to a deck.

Upstairs, the primary bedroom has a walk-in closet, cathedral ceilings, a Juliet balcony and a three-piece bathroom.

stories.title: Older Baby Point house needing work sells $124,000 below list price
stories.summary: Two-storey house has 1,580 square feet of living space, a den and a traditional living room with a wood-burning fireplace
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
87 Riverview Gardens, Toronto

Asking price: $1,799,000 (September, 2026)

Selling price: $1,675,000 (September, 2026)

Previous selling price: not available

Taxes: $8,778 (2026)

Days on the market: eight

Listing agents: Luke and Daiva Dalinda, Royal LePage Real Estate Services Ltd.

That this three-bedroom house has aging mechanics and finishes from the 1920s was taken into account in its listing price under $1.8-million. It opened its doors to visitors before the Labour Day long weekend, and about a dozen visitors considered how they might modernize the home near Étienne Brûle Park and the Humber River. Adjacent properties had traded in the $2.3-million range and others in the enclave approached $10-million, noted agent Luke Dalinda.

“The price sits below renovated neighbours because the home is still in original condition – not because demand is soft,” said Mr. Dalinda.

“That makes this an outstanding chance to buy into one of Toronto’s most coveted pockets and create value through renovation.”

Within eight days, one buyer determined the detached home on a 30-by 94-foot lot was worth $1,675,000.

“Properties in this exclusive pocket sell very rapidly, regardless of condition,” Mr. Dalinda said.

“The setting is spectacular. It is situated on a secluded, Old Mill cul-de-sac overlooking the Humber River, with the added privacy of having homes on only one side of the street. It feels like a quiet sanctuary right in the city.”

This two-storey house has 1,580 square feet of living space, including a den and a traditional living room with a wood-burning fireplace and stained-glass windows.

There is a formal dining room next to the eat-in kitchen.

A heated sunroom, three bedrooms, and an updated bathroom are upstairs.

A recreation area and a powder room are in the basement.

A side entrance exits to a private driveway, garage and backyard.

“While the property sits on a peaceful, secluded cul-de-sac, it is actually just a five-minute walk from the vibrant energy of Bloor West Village, top-tier local schools, and Jane subway station,” Mr. Dalinda said.

stories.title: Builders are finding new ways to get shovels in the ground
stories.summary: Disappearance of investor-buyers in the apartment market means builders have to cater to end users
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
With the demand for newly built homes subdued, developers and builders are searching for alternative ideas on how to fund and bring their products to market.

There has been an almost total freeze on new projects in the multi-family space, whether it’s rental apartments or condominiums. The type of ultra-dense high-rise buildings that had boomed in the first half of the last decade are no longer contemplated. But there’s still a need for new apartments, and funding models that are either novel or not in the mainstream of the Toronto or Vancouver markets could offer some possible paths forward.

One of the bright stars in the Greater Toronto Area market is townhouses. Year-over-year, new condominium townhouse sales have tripled in the third quarter of 2026, according to Zonda Home’s vice-president of market research, Pauline Lierman.

Since the implementation of the provincial-federal HST rebate on April 1, there have been 3,381 condo townhouses sold – that’s 67 per cent of the yearly total of 5,032 so far. That has led to a surge in new launches; 16 sites had opened by September, and another 22 should be launched by November, according to Ms. Lierman.

There was a time when townhouses were the ugly duckling of the condo space, comprising only a small share of the total in 2021 when more than 30,000 preconstruction condos were sold. According to Ms. Lierman, in this quarter, apartment sales were just 12 per cent (226 of 1,745) of all condos sold in the region.

The disappearance of investor-buyers in the apartment market – those who had no intention of living in the condos they purchased, hoping to either flip them to someone else or rent out the units – has meant that builders have to cater to so-called end users, or someone who wants to move into the apartment themselves.

In Guelph, Ont., London-based builder Tricar attracts end users with a development method almost unheard of in recent decades in the Toronto region: it started construction of its apartment building “on spec,” or in other words, not pre-sold.

“It was a little bit out of necessity; there wasn’t a real robust local presale market,” said Adam Carapella, a vice president at Tricar, which started out building rental apartments 20 years ago in London, Ont. In Toronto and Vancouver, the lenders financing huge condominium building projects typically required builders to show they had buyers already signed up before breaking ground. Sometimes 60 to 80 per cent of the planned units needed deposits and sales contracts for banks to approve a construction loan. After starting as a rental builder, where capital tends to be more patient, Tricar had backers that didn’t require all those presales.

The benefits of that model are that rather than waiting an average of five to seven years between signing a preconstruction contract and moving in, buyers with Tricar can see a building that is already taking shape and May take less than a year to complete construction. Flexibility is a key consideration for a downsizer who is selling their home to buy a new condo. Tricar even agrees to sell apartments with contracts that are conditional on the sale of the buyer’s home (another strategy unthinkable in the Toronto market).

“Our product is going to end users 95 per cent of the time,” Mr. Carapella said. Even in the current slow market, the company has sold 100 preconstruction condo apartments this year in the third phase of a nearly-complete 180-unit building on the southern edge of Guelph. The size of the apartments is also enticing to buyers: about 70 per cent of the building is two-bedrooms or larger. “Even the one-bedrooms are fairly livable; 790-830 square feet,” he said, with the larger suites between 1,110 and 1,600 square feet.

Price matters, too: Tricar’s Gordon Square project costs about $600 per square foot, which is even cheaper than big-money bulk-condo buyers are getting in tough negotiations to buy unsold inventory in Toronto. According to a recent report from analysts at Urbanation Inc., Toronto-area bulk sales averaged $763 per square foot, or a 40-per-cent discount from other sold prices in the same buildings.

There are also new ideas in the works in the affordable rental market, with Ottawa’s Nesting Ground recently announcing it had raised $20-million from a variety of philanthropic donors for a fund that would serve as the financial backstop for non-profit housing partners with limited balance sheets that need support to get projects from the planning stage to construction.

According to Graeme Hussey, president of Nesting Ground, the idea behind the Affordable Housing Guarantee Pool (Ahgp) is not to raise the construction funds necessary to build out all the projects, but to have hard cash that can serve as collateral for larger loans.

“The analogy is that of a parent guaranteeing their child’s mortgage,” said Mr. Hussey, meaning the cash in the Ahgp fund can be leveraged into multiples with lenders willing to extend construction funds. For example, one of the fund’s first projects in Ottawa is with Windmill Developments, proposing two mid-rise buildings with about 200 apartments: each building will likely cost about $150-million to build.

Mr. Hussey previously worked at Cahdco, a building and development company founded by the non-profit Centretown Citizens Ottawa Corporation. In his experience, the lack of solid financial backing killed more good project ideas than any lack of expertise or willingness in the non-profit space. He hopes the fund will help unlock affordable housing that has been stuck at the starting line.

“Right now Nesting Ground has about 12 projects and 2,500 units that we’re hoping all begin construction in the next three years and will be built in the next five,” he said.

stories.title: Saving No. 97 from the flippers in Toronto’s Little Portugal
stories.summary: Three-storey home ‘untouched since the sixties’ was gutted by builders before neighbours bought it
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
“They were planning on, I think, putting stucco on the whole front,” begins Philippe Blanchard, interim dean of Ocad University’s faculty of art. “And then a mirrored glass [from the] ground floor to third floor, like, along the bay windows.”

“A real shopping mall vibe,” Katie McCormack, partner and co-owner of Bridgeable, says with a laugh.

“We saved this house, I’m not joking,” says designer Jessica Nakanishi of Msds Studio.

Mr. Blanchard, Ms. McCormack and their three boys, you see, had front-row seats. Living in a similar, but smaller, bay-and-gable across the street (they prefer not to mention the street name) in Toronto’s Little Portugal, they watched as No. 97 went up for sale. Thinking about purchasing a second property, they considered it. However, since it was “untouched since the sixties” and would require a great deal of renovation, they passed and instead purchased the house immediately next door, No. 90, which had the same owner.

As they were busy with that renovation, they watched as No. 97 sold, and a builder/flipper gutted it. They watched as a band of bricks – in the wrong colour – were added to the top in order to raise the ceiling height of the third floor.

“For a while, there was no roof on the house,” says Mr. Blanchard.

Once the new roof went on, they watched No. 97 sit on the market. Real estate photos showed a raw interior with roughed-in plumbing and illustrations of the “dream” interior that would be built. Actually, say the couple, there were a few options for interiors, one just as tacky as the next. A few years passed. Finally, with two of their three boys approaching teenhood and about to “take up a lot of room,” the couple sold their two properties and purchased No. 97. Not only was it larger, but that clean slate meant they could tailor the design to their specific needs.

But, as with all things real estate-related, timing was tight. Would it be possible to find a firm that could deliver a finished interior within four to six months?

“Jessica was wonderfully understanding and flexible,” says Ms. McCormack about the designer. And although most of what the couple has seen of Msds Studio was commercial – an office for Shopify, House of Anansi Press and a delightful ping-pong bar called Spin Toronto – it was their “use of colour” that resonated with Ms. McCormack. After the pandemic, however, Msds had taken on some residential projects, so Ms. Nakanishi and her life/business partner, furniture designer Jonathan Sabine, were able to show the couple that their mojo worked just as well in that regard.

So, it went from completely raw to completely fabulous on all four floors – basement apartment, main floor, second-floor “boys’ wing” and a third-floor parental suite. And despite the rush in getting it done, there was no surge pricing.

“When you hire a designer, you hire their Rolodex, right?” Ms. Nakanishi says with a smile.

That means, in the kitchen, the acres and acres of sapele cabinetry (which looks like mahogany) with incredible bevelling and detailing were fabricated by a furniture maker rather than a millworker. “He doesn’t do this too often because it’s too much for him, but for some of our projects he works with us,” says Ms. Nakanishi. That work carries over to a sideboard/bookshelf in the living room.

It means, too, that when one quote for the new staircase metalwork (there were only construction stairs) came in at $90,000, Msds was able to spin their well-thumbed address wheel to find a company that could do the work for $19,000.

It’s why, says Ms. McCormack, the total came in at around $600,000: “I think it could have been much more if we hadn’t had Jessica’s support; just getting to a decision quickly, having drawings in place to communicate, and [to] work well with everyone we pulled into the process.”

Walking through the house, thoughts of valuations vanish and are replaced by the oohs and ahhs generated by good tradecraft, thoughtful design, abundant texture, and the warmth of lighting and art (much of it prints by Mr. Blanchard).

While the first floor is open concept, there is a hidden powder room, paths to walk, partial obstructions to offer “what’s around the corner” surprises, and places to pause and linger. On the second floor, each boy has his own space, there’s a small office for Mr. Blanchard, and the laundry pair, conveniently, is located inside a hallway closet – which means the corridor becomes the “room” when it’s wash day.

The pièce de résistance is the adult floor ensuite. Standing in Ms. McCormack’s home office, a tantalizing peek of a sculptural tub tucked into a gable offers the first clue to washroom divinity. Through the threshold, one discovers compartments for different functions: there, the water closet, here a shower, and what’s that? A woodsy, welcoming sauna! And speaking of surrounding oneself with wood, wrapping the walls and ceiling around the tub wasn’t easy, says Ms. Nakanishi: “Nothing was aligned. … They came, they put up whatever they had to put up on top of the frame, it was just this ugly corner that we had to deal with.”

Now beautiful – like the rest of No. 97 – this corner has become “one of my favourite spots,” Ms. McCormack says with a laugh. “You presented this vision … and we trusted you implicitly; it’s such a cozy space.”

It’s not easy to create cozy. It’s a delicate balance of scale, different types of lighting, tactility, busy spots versus restful spots and a hundred other intangibles the builder-flipper never considers (this writer knows he’s stumbled into a builder-flipper house when he spots 100 pot lights where a half-dozen would’ve sufficed).

So, thank you, Msds, your Rolodex, and your very thoughtful clients, for saving No. 97. And, more importantly, the neighbourhood thanks you, too.

stories.title: Walkerton woman dies in Brockton crash involving commercial vehicle
stories.summary: Emergency crews, including South Bruce OPP, Bruce County Paramedic Services and the Brockton Fire Department, were called to the intersection of Bruce Road 19 and Concession 8 at about 7:33 p.m. on Oct. 27.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 44-year-old Walkerton woman has died following a collision involving a commercial vehicle and a passenger vehicle in Brockton on Tuesday evening.

Emergency crews, including South Bruce OPP, Bruce County Paramedic Services and the Brockton Fire Department, were called to the intersection of Bruce Road 19 and Concession 8 at about 7:33 p.m. on Oct. 27.

Police said the crash involved a passenger vehicle and a commercial motor vehicle. The driver of the commercial vehicle, a 44-year-old woman from Walkerton, was pronounced dead at the scene.

The driver of the passenger vehicle was taken to hospital with injuries. Police did not immediately release the extent of those injuries.

Road closures remain in place as investigators examine the scene. Bruce Road 19 is closed between Concession 10 and Concession 6 East, while Concession 8 is closed between Sideroad 20 and Sideroad 10 South.

Police are asking anyone who witnessed the collision, or who May have dash camera footage from the area at the time of the crash, to contact the South Bruce OPP.

No further information has been released. The investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Calgary city council approves stiff hikes to water rates over the next 4 years
stories.summary: The Calgary Chamber of Commerce called the rate hikes "egregious" and warned the costs will impact business competitiveness and stretch bottom lines.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Calgarians and local businesses are set to pay more for water over the next four years after city council approved a slew of fee increases proposed by city administration Tuesday.

Those increases are set to amount to nearly 20 per cent for drinking water, 15.2 per cent for wastewater and 5.8 per cent for stormwater annually between 2027 and 2030.

Water rates for the average household are set to increase from $119 monthly this year, to $134 per month in 2027, eventually increasing by $90 to $206 monthly by 2030.

Mayor Jeromy Farkas called the hikes an “accountability moment” after what he said was more than 10 years of underinvestment in the city’s water system.

“Us as a council, we’re taking charge, we’re committing to Calgarians that we are addressing this and we are not going to tolerate failure of the fundamental responsibility of a municipality, which is safe and clean drinking water,” Farkas told reporters.

The increases are set to help pay for a $6.5 billion capital invesment over the next four years to renew critical infrastructure, expand drinking water, wastewater and stormwater capacity, reduce water loss and improve emergency readiness.

Challenges with the city’s water system have been highlighted by two catastrophic breaks along the Bearspaw feeder main, one of the city’s most critical water lines that carries more than 60 per cent of Calgary’s drinking water.

“This is not a one-off, this is a sign the entire system needs investment and needs work,” said Michael Thompson, chief operating officer of the city’s water utility.

According to Thompson, the city tried to keep water rates “low and affordable” over the last 10 years.

“I think what happened over that last decade was we focused on rates and not on the infrastructure as well,” he told council.

A report from administration warned of “major risks” within the city’s water system and delaying investment could leak to an increase service disruptions, emergency repairs and long-term costs.

“This isn’t all of what is needed, but it does scratch the surface,” Farkas said. “This is the bare minimum that we need to avoid the literal ‘crap-pocolypse’ of our stormwater, wastewater and water system failing again.”

City council voted 9-6 in favour of the new water rates, which will be included in the upcoming four-year budget deliberations in November. Councillors Landon Johnston, Rob Ward, Kim Tyers, Mike Jamieson, Jennifer Wyness and Dan McLean opposed.

McLean told reporters he hoped city administration would look at alternate funding mechanisms for water infrastructure, like municipal bonds, to help offset the impact on Calgarians’ water bills.

“I understand the need for this but I don’t think we’ve looked at every other option,” McLean told reporters. “This is too much on top of what we’re looking at for a proposed municipal property tax, so I just could not support it at this time.”

City administration said any funding the city receives from other orders of government could reduce rates in the future.

Although Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot included an amendment to review the rates next year instead of halfway through the budget in 2028, there were no attempts from city council to reduce the hikes from administration.

“I was hoping that my fellow colleagues would see the cries from Calgarians, from small businesses, from large businesses… saying please slow this down,” Tyers told reporters. “During the budget, there’s definitely room for us to revisit this.”

Businesses are also facing an “egregious” rate hike, according to the Calgary Chamber of Commerce.

A medium sized business using 400 cubic metres of water monthly could see its bills increase from $1,661.33 per month this year to $3,093.19 monthly in 2030.

“It really renders our businesses very uncompetitive, it will squeeze their bottom lines significantly,” said Chamber of Commerce president Deborah Yedlin. “When you think about the fact that 95 per cent of Calgary’s businesses are small and medium sized enterprises, this is a huge concern.”

When pressed on the increases facing businesses, Farkas suggested using less water to reduce the costs.

“For us to give, say, a big break to our largest industrial users and redistribute that burden to the local residential class, that doesn’t make sense to me,” he said.

stories.title: Miriam Toews, Hannah Moscovitch finalists for Governor General's Literary Awards
stories.summary: Toronto - Works by Miriam Toews, Hannah Moscovitch and Kim Fu are among the finalists for this year's Governor General's Literary Awards.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Works by Miriam Toews, Hannah Moscovitch and Kim Fu are among the finalists for this year’s Governor General’s Literary Awards.

Toews’ memoir “A Truce That Is Not Peace” is one of five books up for the English-language non-fiction prize. Toews explores the question, “why do you write?” in the book while reflecting on the suicides of her sister and father. The Toronto-based writer previously won the Governor General’s fiction prize for her 2004 novel “A Complicated Kindness.”

The Canada Council for the Arts named 69 finalists across seven categories in English and French on Wednesday. The 14 winners, who each receive $25,00, will be announced on Nov. 12.

Moscovitch is nominated in the drama category for her play “Red Like Fruit,” which follows a journalist covering a high-profile domestic violence case while a sense of unease pervades her thoughts. The Halifax playwright, who is also a writer for the AMC television series, “Interview with the Vampire,” previously won the Governor General’s drama prize in 2021 for “Sexual Misconduct of the Middle Classes.”

Fu is among the five finalists for the English-language fiction prize for her novel “The Valley of Vengeful Ghosts” about a woman unraveling in the aftermath of her mother’s death. The Vancouver-born writer was previously a finalist for the Giller Prize in 2022 for her short story collection “Lesser Known Monsters of the 21st Century.”

Also nominated in the fiction category is Sharon Bala for her novel “Good Guys” about the dark side of philanthropy and Sara Peters for her novel “Mother of God” about a woman with psychic powers who returns home to see her estranged mother. Rounding out the fiction finalists is Nina Dunic for “Suddenly Light” and Kate Cayley for “Property.”

The Governor General’s Literary Awards, which celebrates homegrown literature, will also hand out honours for poetry, writing and illustration in young people’s literature, as well as French-to-English translation. There are separate French-language categories for francophone writing.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

Daylight saving time (DST) traditionally ends on Nov. 1 in Canada, but this year some provinces and territories are preparing to leave seasonal time changes behind.

For years, Canadians have called for an end to the twice-yearly clock change, with public consultations in several provinces prompting some governments to move toward making DST permanent.

While some jurisdictions have changed their clocks for the final time, others are sticking to the status quo, meaning things are about to get confusing. Here’s a breakdown of which provinces are doing what with their time zones come November.

Alberta, B.C., Manitoba, Saskatchewan, the Northwest Territories and Yukon have all made the decision to stop switching between daylight and standard time. Therefore, clocks in these provinces won’t fall back an hour on Nov. 1.

Saskatchewan was the first province to abandon the practice in 1966, and Yukon made the change in 2020.

Alberta, B.C. and the Northwest Territories all decided to stay on DST over the past year, and Manitoba made the decision last month.

To make things even more complicated, the Ontario government announced on Oct. 13 that northwestern parts of the province that have usually kept their clocks in sync with neighbouring Manitoba will also be making DST permanent.

The remaining provinces, which includes most of Ontario, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Newfoundland and Labrador, will see their clocks fall back an hour on Nov. 1, returning to standard time.

But Ontario isn’t the only province with multiple time zones. Quebec’s northern region of Nunavik made the decision to stay permanently on DST in the past year, but the rest of the province will change its clocks next month.

Nunavut spans three time zones, all of which change their clocks on Nov. 1, except for Southampton Island, which remains on Eastern Standard Time all year long.

Elsewhere, the East Kootenay region in southeast B.C. will keep time in line with Alberta, which will stay on permanent Alberta Time (previously called Mountain Daylight Time).

B.C., Yukon and Western parts of Nunavut will all have the same time this winter, which is seven hours behind Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Now that B.C. has made DST permanent, its time difference with Ontario and Quebec will shrink from three hours to two during winter.

Ontario announces permanent daylight saving time for northwestern parts of the province

U.S. House of Representatives votes to move America to permanent daylight savings time. Will Canada follow suit?

Alberta and the Northwest Territories, meanwhile, will be just one hour behind Ontario and Quebec, and Manitoba will be on the same time as them during the winter.

Saskatchewan will now be on the same time as Alberta and the Northwest Territories year-round, and one hour ahead of B.C.

Most of Atlantic Canada will be three hours ahead of B.C., two hours ahead of Alberta and one hour ahead of Ontario and Quebec.

Announcing Manitoba’s decision to remain on DST on Sept. 17, the provincial government referenced a public engagement campaign from May, which found that 92 per cent of Manitobans surveyed wanted to see an end to seasonal time changes. A majority of Manitobans (58 per cent) preferred to stay on permanent DST.

“Permanent daylight saving time is good for Manitoba businesses,” said Loren Remillard, president and CEO of the Winnipeg Chamber of Commerce, in a statement at the time. “More daylight in the evening means more opportunity for restaurants, retailers, farmers, and communities across our province to make the most of the day.”

Meanwhile, an analysis by Manitoba Health, Seniors and Long-Term Care concluded that eliminating time changes would be better for population health than maintaining the status quo.

A few weeks later, the Ontario government said it intends to make DST permanent in Kenora and the northwestern regions of the province. It said in the announcement : “Maintaining alignment with Manitoba would help businesses operate more efficiently across provincial boundaries, while making it easier for residents and service providers to coordinate activities such as health-care appointments and travel.”

The Northwest Territories said it was ending seasonal time changes due to feedback gathered in 2022 , while B.C. conducted a public engagement on time observance in 2019, which saw 93 per cent support for adopting year-round DST . In Yukon, 93 per cent wanted seasonal time changes to stop . Of those, 70 per cent were in favour of permanent DST.

Alberta said it was adopting permanent Alberta Time to reduce disruption, improve predictability, align Alberta with neighbouring jurisdictions and reduce confusion for those who live, work, or do business across borders.

Standard time runs from November to March in the provinces that haven’t decided to put an end to clock changes. On the second Sunday in March, clocks in these provinces will go forward an hour, switching to DST.

DST was originally adopted to better match hours of daylight to the times of the day when most people are awake, and to conserve the amount of energy people use lighting their homes. It results in an extra hour of daylight in the evening, but darker mornings.

In 2020, Ontario passed a law saying it would also end the practice of changing times twice per year, but only if Quebec and New York followed suit. While Nunavik will remain on DST, Quebec as a whole hasn’t put an end to seasonal time changes — yet.

Elsewhere, the Nunavut government is reportedly exploring the possibility of ending seasonal time changes, with Cambridge Bay MLA Fred Pedersen recently telling CBC he wants to table a resolution to end the time change at the next sitting of the legislative assembly.

stories.title: Kevin Pillar, Andre Reed, Serge Savard, Joe Bowen among celebrities confirmed for St. Thomas Sports Spectacular
stories.summary: Beloved former Toronto Blue Jay Kevin Pillar, NFL Hall of Famer Andre Reed, NHL Hall of Famer Serge Savard, and the former “voice of” the Toronto Maple Leafs Joe Bowen have confirmed their attendance at the St. Thomas Sports Spectacular.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
Beloved former Toronto Blue Jay Kevin Pillar, NFL Hall of Famer Andre Reed, NHL Hall of Famer Serge Savard, and the former “voice of” the Toronto Maple Leafs Joe Bowen have confirmed their attendance at the St. Thomas Sports Spectacular on Jan. 21, 2027.

Nine sports stars have been locked in for the annual event in support of St. Thomas Special Olympics at the St. Anne’s Centre.

Pillar played 13 seasons in Major League Baseball, seven of those with the Toronto Blue Jays. Known as “Superman,” he was an elite defensive outfielder who was a starter during the playoff runs in 2015 and 2016.

Reed was part of the Buffalo Bills dynasty in the early 1990s. The NFL Hall of Famer went to seven Pro Bowls and has the third most receptions in Superbowl history.

Bowen was “the voice” of the Toronto Maple Leafs for over 3,000 games for the organization.

With his catchphrase “Holy Mackinaw,” Bowen started calling games in 1982, and retired at the end of last season.

Savard won nine Stanley Cup championships, seven as a player and two more as a general manager, all with the Montreal Canadiens.

Toronto Star podcaster and columnist Mike Wilner will return as emcee, a role he’s held since 2015.

Tickets will be available online starting Nov. 3, 2026.

In 1978, Father Patrick Costello, pastor of St. Anne’s Parish, had the dream to invite celebrities from the world of sport to our community.

Since its inception, the volunteer-run event has raised more than $1 million to support a variety of projects for local Special Olympics, Community Living Elgin, and adults with disabilities. With a great cause, the event has been able to draw superstars from the sports world to a small Southwestern Ontario city.

Confirmed Head Table guests for 2027:

Kevin Pillar- Former Toronto Blue Jays Outfielder

Andre Reed- NFL Hall of Fame, 4 AFC titles with Buffalo Bills

Joe Bowen- Former Toronto Maple Leafs’ broadcaster

Serge Savard- NHL Hof’er, 9x Stanley Cup champion

James Edwards- 3x NBA Champion with Detroit and Chicago

Sarah Wilkes- Olympic Bronze Medal Curler

Joe Siddall- Former MLB Catcher/ Blue Jays analyst

Madison Shipman- Blue Jays Central analyst

D’Lo Brown- 4x WWE title holder

stories.title: Donations for 24 Sussex renovation reach 11% of the $50 million goal
stories.summary: The Rideau Hall Foundation also said its campaign has achieved a "significant milestone" by topping 4,000 donors.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — The foundation running the government’s efforts to raise money to renovate the prime minister’s official residence says donations are up sevenfold since early August, while also announcing that a council has been created to add fuel to the campaign.

In a news release to be released Wednesday, the Rideau Hall Foundation also said its campaign has achieved a “significant milestone” by topping 4,000 donors who have contributed a total of $5.7 million. That’s 11.4 per cent of the $50-million target that was established in June, when Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled a process to restore the 35-room stone mansion.

Less than three months ago, the foundation had raised just $735,000 to help make 24 Sussex Dr. habitable.

That government’s reno process includes making the foundation responsible for raising private donations for the restoration project and holding an open competition for bids to renovate the historic home, which has been vacant for 11 years.

The update also announced the new Council for 24 Sussex, a group of “distinguished” supporters of the project who will add their voices, expertise and access to networks, while helping raise awareness and encourage contributions. The council will include at least 23 members from across the country.

Although the campaign remains far from its target, the foundation said Canadians have shown broad support for a project “rooted in the idea that important national institutions are worthy of renewal.”

The contributions reflect “a growing community of Canadians coming together, at all levels, around a shared national project,” the news release says.

The prime minister’s residence in downtown Ottawa has been vacant for more than a decade. It had been plagued by criticisms from former prime ministers who lived there and an array of problems: heating and cooling, outdated wiring, asbestos, water damage, mould, rats, and more practical problems such as insufficient space for offices and events.

While most of the problems have been dealt with, Carney and Justin Trudeau, his predecessor as prime minister, have lived across the road at Rideau Cottage on the grounds of the Governor General’s residence at Rideau Hall.

Built in the late 1860s by a lumber baron and MP, the home has been the prime minister’s official residence since 1951 and home to 10 Canadian leaders.

Heritage advocates cheered the government’s announcement earlier this year that the historic building would finally be fully renovated and possibly expanded, but questions were also raised that the appeal for donations could create possible conflicts of interest.

The big remaining question is whether decision makers opt for a modest renovation that makes the property functional for future prime ministers, or whether a more elaborate proposal will be chosen. A construction budget has not yet been announced, but the government expects to announce a winning design proposal and its plan by July 1.
paragraphs: Ottawa — The foundation running the government’s efforts to raise money to renovate the prime minister’s official residence says donations are up sevenfold since early August, while also announcing that a council has been created to add fuel to the campaign.

In a news release to be released Wednesday, the Rideau Hall Foundation also said its campaign has achieved a “significant milestone” by topping 4,000 donors who have contributed a total of $5.7 million. That’s 11.4 per cent of the $50-million target that was established in June, when Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled a process to restore the 35-room stone mansion.
Less than three months ago, the foundation had raised just $735,000 to help make 24 Sussex Dr. habitable.

That government’s reno process includes making the foundation responsible for raising private donations for the restoration project and holding an open competition for bids to renovate the historic home, which has been vacant for 11 years.

The update also announced the new Council for 24 Sussex, a group of “distinguished” supporters of the project who will add their voices, expertise and access to networks, while helping raise awareness and encourage contributions. The council will include at least 23 members from across the country.

Although the campaign remains far from its target, the foundation said Canadians have shown broad support for a project “rooted in the idea that important national institutions are worthy of renewal.”

stories.title: Nearly 75% of Canadians think PM Carney is on the right track seeking closer ties with Europe: poll
stories.summary: The poll finds Prime Minister Carney's approach has nation-wide approval, with the strongest support in British Columbia.
stories.author: Michael Talbot
stories.content:
Canadians widely approve of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s move to seek closer ties with Europe amid an unpredictable trading relationship with the United States, a new Canada Pulse Insights polls reveals.

Seventy-three per cent believe Carney is on the right track in seeking a closer economic and security alliance with the European Union, with 27 per cent saying it’s the wrong track and won’t be enough to offset the loss of trade with the United States.

The poll finds Carney’s approach has nation-wide approval, with the strongest support in British Columbia (81 per cent), followed by Atlantic Canada (79 per cent), Québec (75 per cent), Ontario (72 per cent), Saskatchewan/Manitoba (64 per cent) and Alberta (62 per cent).

Support rises with age and education, and is lower among Canadians in households earning under $50,000.

There is one group, however, that stands in opposition to the PM’s approach.

“Current Conservative supporters are the only political group reported in which a majority say wrong direction: 58 per cent take that position, while 42 per cent say right track,” a release states.

Carney will host European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa at the Canada-EU Summit in Montreal on Oct. 29 and Oct. 30.

Methodology: The survey was conducted with 1,531 Canadian adults (18+) as part of a Canada Pulse Insights national omnibus survey, fielded from Oct. 1–8, 2026. A random sample of Canadian adult respondents was invited to complete the survey through an online panel platform. The margin of error for a comparable probability-based random sample of the same size is ±2.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: Warm, sunny stretch continues across region
stories.summary: Our sunny stretch continues into Wednesday as a warm front moves into the region.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Our sunny stretch continues into Wednesday as a warm front moves into the region.

“Temperatures are headed up so a bit of cloud cover overnight will make way for lots of sunshine heading into the afternoon,” said CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison. “Warm temperatures will hold as we head into your Thursday.”

However, a cold front is on its way that could bring a few showers to midwestern Ontario come Thursday night.

“As that frontal boundary comes through, temperatures will be dipping down as we head into Friday,” said Atchison.

Looking ahead to the weekend, Atchison says Halloween is looking mainly cloudy, but dry.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast

Wednesday: Clearing in the morning. High 20. UV index 3 or moderate.

Wednesday night: Clear. Low 10.

Thursday: A mix of sun and cloud with 30 per cent chance of showers. High 20.

Friday: Sunny. High 16.

Saturday: Cloudy. High 14.

Sunday: Cloudy with 30 per cent chance of showers. High 14.
