stories.title: Osap freeze alarms private colleges as minister feels the heat
stories.summary: Opposition MPPs called on Premier to fire Nolan Quinn over policy that’s left for-profit schools on shaky financial footing
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
On a recent afternoon at the Southern Ontario Dental College, worries about paying the bills were as common as the mouth mirrors and polishing wands the future hygienists used to clean their clients’ teeth.

Katerina Athanasopoulos, a 35-year-old mother of three who commutes two hours each way from Sarnia for her classes at the school in Ancaster, a community in Hamilton, worried about having to pick up extra shifts at her part-time job as a dental assistant, on top of the 40 hours a week she spends in dental hygiene school.

Konika Bhalwal, 31, worried about making rent and having to ask her boyfriend to help pay for her groceries.

Isabella Quenneville, 27, worried about being forced to quit for financial reasons in the middle of the program, having already taken on student debt to pay for her first year of hygienist training.

All three women and their classmates are feeling vulnerable because of the Ontario government’s decision earlier this month to pause Ontario Student Assistance Program loan payments to tens of thousands of students attending private postsecondary institutions, including Southern Ontario Dental College – even though there is no suggestion the students or their school did anything wrong.

“We’re all very scared,” Ms. Quenneville said. “We’ve been trying to keep each other very positive because we’ve heard nothing, and it’s so easy to spiral out of control and feel helpless because we are helpless right now.”

The sudden freeze, which the Progressive Conservatives say they imposed to safeguard the financial aid program after explosive growth in OSAP applications and allegations of wrongdoing in online-only programming at fewer than 10 private career colleges, has put the entire for-profit educational sector in Ontario on shaky financial footing. At least one vocational school with multiple campuses, Trillium College, has already suspended academic programming because it can’t get by without OSAP.

As Ontario politicians returned to the legislature Tuesday for the first time since June, Opposition MPPs called on Premier Doug Ford to fire Nolan Quinn, the Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, who they accused of punishing hundreds of blameless private colleges for the alleged sins of a few.

The Liberals and NDP noted that the PC government had been warned as far back as January of 2023 by Career Colleges Ontario – the association that represents schools now imperilled by the pause – of massive spikes in OSAP applications at some career colleges that smacked of “suspicious activity.” Mr. Quinn “looked the other way” and “dragged his feet” on inspecting private colleges he now accuses of defrauding OSAP, said Peggy Sattler, the NDP critic for colleges and universities. “Clearly, he has failed to do his job.”

The Premier defended Mr. Quinn, who told the legislature he had no choice but to halt loans to all career college students while a third-party auditor and the Ontario Provincial Police investigate. “We need to hold the bad actors accountable,” Mr. Quinn said. “If what we have found proves to be what we think it is, then it is nothing short of criminal.”

Hundreds of pages of court documents, first reported on by The Canadian Press, shed light on what the Ministry’s OSAP Inspection and Compliance Unit allegedly discovered when it inspected three Greater Toronto Area campuses of a private career college called Academy of Learning in 2025.

The schools were among six notified in May that their OSAP eligibility wouldn’t be renewed for the coming academic year.

Ministry inspectors allege they found red flags with online-only programs at Academy of Learning campuses in Brampton, North York and downtown Toronto, including dozens of students accessing coursework from the same IP addresses, often located outside North America.

They found evidence that students completed entire asynchronous online courses in a day or two and finished exams in less than five minutes. And when inspectors contacted apparent students, some couldn’t “name the institution, program or courses they completed” or “communicate independently in English,” according to inspection reports.

None of the allegations have been proven in court.

Owners of the three Academy of Learning franchises deny wrongdoing. They responded to concerns raised by inspectors with detailed corrective action plans, and say they were working in good faith with a ministry-approved compliance monitor when they learned their OSAP status wouldn’t be renewed.

Before loan payments were paused across the sector, there were 242 private postsecondary institutions in Ontario whose students were eligible for OSAP. Although the freeze applies to private universities, chiropractic and naturopathic medicine colleges and even Canada’s National Ballet School, most of the institutions affected are private career colleges.

Private career colleges offer short, skill-specific training programs for jobs such as hairdressers, personal support workers, medical office assistants and early childhood educators. They tend to attract new Canadians, recent high school graduates from working-class backgrounds, and parents looking to upskill.

They also tend to charge higher fees than most public colleges and universities because they aren’t subsidized by taxpayers. Tuition for Southern Ontario Dental College’s 22-month hygienist program, for instance, is $51,997, an amount that covers everything from scrubs to textbooks to dental equipment.

It’s no surprise, then, that low-income students taking expensive courses would rely on financial aid. At Southern Ontario Dental College, more than 90 per cent do. Their OSAP disbursements for this academic year had already been approved. Most were expecting lump sums of a few thousand dollars or more in September to defray living costs while they attend school full-time.

The dental college itself was expecting about $2-million in tuition payments from OSAP, its chief source of revenue. Although classes are carrying on as usual for now, “the hard reality is, we can’t survive if we don’t have the money,” said Alysse Estrabillo, the college’s chief operating officer. She and her husband, dentist Roland Estrabillo, have owned the college for 22 years. They have about 70 staff and 282 students to think of.

“I’m a big mama bear,” Ms. Estrabillo said, “and I just feel sick to my stomach.”

Alysse Estrabillo and her husband, Roland, own the Southern Ontario Dental College, established in 2004. More than 90 per cent of students here rely on financial aid. Nick Iwanyshyn/The Globe and Mail

The college is also a working clinic for dental cleanings, X-rays and other services. One second-year student, Crystal Au, gives a patient tips on proper flossing; another, Kiera Donohue, works on an assignment with clinical instructor Sava Pijanovic. Nick Iwanyshyn/The Globe and Mail

That ill feeling has been spreading through the private postsecondary sector ever since Mr. Quinn announced the OSAP loan pause on Oct. 6.

By that point, the provincial government had already suspended OSAP eligibility for six private colleges in the Greater Toronto Area, including the three Academy of Learning sites. When, in August, the PCs brought in third-party auditor KPMG to examine OSAP use in the private postsecondary sector more broadly, enough “serious concerns” emerged that the government notified the Auditor-General and referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police.

Mr. Quinn later confirmed that OSAP payments to private postsecondary students wouldn’t resume until January at the earliest, after the government passes legislation to strengthen oversight, including placing caps on OSAP-funded enrolment and excluding predominantly online-only programs.

Five of the private college campuses accused of wrongdoing are suing the Ontario government for cutting off their OSAP eligibility. Owners of three Academy of Learning campuses in Brampton, North York and downtown Toronto and two Citi College campuses in Mississauga and Toronto say in separate applications for judicial review filed over the summer that the decision should be quashed because it’s unreasonable and procedurally unfair. (The sixth school is another Academy of Learning franchise that hasn’t taken legal action against the government.)

A huge increase in financial aid applications from students attending a relatively small number of private Ontario career colleges has had ramifications beyond Ontario, and beyond private colleges. The federal government cited the spike when it announced , in last November’s budget, that the Canada Student Grant for Full-time Students would no longer be available to people studying at private, for-profit postsecondary institutions across the country (with exemptions for some health and child-care programs, including dental hygiene.)

Ontario followed suit last February, ending OSAP grants to private college students as of the 2026-2027 academic year. From then on, career college students would have access only to repayable loans.

At the same time – and more controversially – the Ontario government overhauled OSAP for students at publicly funded colleges and universities. Under the new formula, a maximum of 25 per cent of a student’s OSAP would be given as nonrepayable grants, down from the old ceiling of 85 per cent. The rest would be disbursed as loans, saddling the next generation of low-income learners with a heavy debt burden.

Premier Doug Ford, perhaps straying off script, suggested at the time that the change was necessary because he’d heard “nightmare stories” about students “buying fancy watches and cologne” with financial aid. But the official line from Mr. Quinn’s office was that Ontario had to bring its ratio of grants to loans more in line with other provinces because OSAP was hurtling towards financial unsustainability.

Indeed, spending on OSAP grants ballooned to about $3.4-billion in 2024-2025, a 32-per-cent increase from three years earlier, according to data obtained through a freedom-of-information request.

But the entire increase in grant outlays could be laid at the feet of students attending private colleges. Spending on OSAP grants for students attending public institutions actually fell slightly over that period, the data show.

Furthermore, as The Canadian Press reported using data from a separate freedom-of-information request, much of the increase in OSAP grant spending could be attributed to just seven private career colleges in the GTA that saw explosive growth in online-only classes, including the Academy of Learning franchises now suing the province.

“The government justified pulling the rug out from students who were relying on OSAP grants by saying the program was unsustainable,” Ms. Sattler of the NDP said in an interview before the legislature returned. “But they knew all along why it was unsustainable – or they should have known all along why it was unsustainable.”

Caitlyn Elton, Lucy Tran and Preet Powar are among 282 students at Southern Ontario Dental College, which has a staff of about 70. Alysse Estrabillo, the chief operating officer, says she’s worried what the loss of OSAP will mean for them. Nick Iwanyshyn/The Globe and Mail

It was an association of career colleges that alerted the province to the problems in the sector. Career Colleges Ontario first raised the issue in January of 2023, according to a Feb. 26, 2026, letter to the co-ordinator of the Ministry’s OSAP Inspection and Compliance Unit filed as part of the Academy of Learning court case.

Officials from the private college association met with the province’s inspection and compliance unit in January, May and twice in November of 2023. By April of 2024, the association was urging ministry inspectors to call the police on a career college whose name is redacted in the court documents.

“We were advised that the Ministry did make contact with police, and that police indicated they would need to conduct their own investigation in order to proceed,” the letter says.

Career Colleges Ontario knew about the suspicious enrolment spikes because it processes financial aid applications in co-operation with the province for much of the sector.

In a separate letter to ministry inspectors sent Jan. 15, 2025, the association practically begged for help. OSAP applications at eight schools had grown by more than 500 per cent in two years. Another two grew by more than 200 per cent.

One member school whose name is blacked out in an accompanying chart had grown from 107 OSAP-funded students in 2022 to 2,992 in 2024 – an increase of nearly 3,000 per cent.

Two of the Academy of Learning campuses involved in the court case appear in the same chart. One campus grew from 775 OSAP submissions in 2022 to 1,612 in 2023 and then to 5,748 in 2024.

“These anomalies are concerning, and we find ourselves with limited ability to audit and justify these increases,” Kate Bartz, the executive director of Career Colleges Ontario wrote. “We are writing to you as we want to protect the integrity of OSAP. Our goal is to maintain public trust, safeguard taxpayer dollars, and ensure access to quality career education for eligible students … I want to reiterate that our concern is limited to 10 school locations and not the sector as a whole.”

Three months before the private college association sent that letter, in October of 2024, Ministry inspectors started a routine inspection of the Academy of Learning franchises in Brampton and on Bay Street. But they postponed their work until the following summer, according to documents filed in court. “I apologize for the delay, which was due to transitions in roles and the implementation of new inspection procedures,” a ministry official wrote in an e-mail to Academy of Learning on Aug. 12, 2025, four days after the schools received their annual OSAP approval for the coming academic year.

The Bay location received a failing grade on its inspection in September of 2025, while the Brampton and North York locations were notified of their failures in March of 2026.

Meanwhile, in Ottawa, officials had also noticed ballooning financial aid use from students at some Ontario career colleges. (Although provinces administer student loan and grant programs, some of the aid they distribute comes from federal coffers.) Mr. Quinn has said publicly that the federal government notified Ontario of its concerns in May of 2025.

Then, on Sept. 18, 2025, Academy of Learning officials received two notices from Economic and Social Development Canada warning that federal student aid could be suspended for students at the Bay and Brampton East campuses. The letters, which are similar, flag high growth in the number of new federal student financial assistance recipients – including an increase of 1,617 per cent over three years at the Brampton East location – and a surge in students from “certain demographic categories who may not be eligible for student financial assistance.”

When the department selected 241 students for an “enhanced validation process,” 42 per cent couldn’t be confirmed as qualifying students, the federal letter to Brampton East says.

In response, Academy of Learning officials wrote a long response “respectfully” submitting “that institutional growth should not be viewed as an inherent risk indicator. Rather, it represents a reflection of program relevance, responsiveness to work force needs, and public confidence in the institution’s delivery of quality education.”

But Academy of Learning said its students with those SIN numbers were legitimate refugees or other federally protected groups, who are eligible for government financial aid.

There were balloons and a cake and smiling group photos.

Mr. Sandhu, in a news release marking the occasion, trumpeted the college as a beacon of hope. “I know that Academy of Learning has been playing a vital, very important role in providing career-focused, more flexible, accessible education, to thousands of learners right here in Brampton.”

(The offices of Mr. Sarkaria and Mr. Sandhu referred questions about their attendance at the event to Mr. Quinn’s office, which provided a one-line statement: “The referenced institutions are part of the six that had their OSAP suspended as part of corrective action taken as a result of non-compliance before the sector-wide OSAP pause was implemented to protect the integrity of the postsecondary sector.”)

And dental offices are always calling, looking for qualified assistants and hygienists, especially now that the federally funded dental plan has expanded access to oral health care.

paragraphs: On a recent afternoon at the Southern Ontario Dental College, worries about paying the bills were as common as the mouth mirrors and polishing wands the future hygienists used to clean their clients’ teeth.

Katerina Athanasopoulos, a 35-year-old mother of three who commutes two hours each way from Sarnia for her classes at the school in Ancaster, a community in Hamilton, worried about having to pick up extra shifts at her part-time job as a dental assistant, on top of the 40 hours a week she spends in dental hygiene school.
Konika Bhalwal, 31, worried about making rent and having to ask her boyfriend to help pay for her groceries.
Isabella Quenneville, 27, worried about being forced to quit for financial reasons in the middle of the program, having already taken on student debt to pay for her first year of hygienist training.

All three women and their classmates are feeling vulnerable because of the Ontario government’s decision earlier this month to pause Ontario Student Assistance Program loan payments to tens of thousands of students attending private postsecondary institutions, including Southern Ontario Dental College – even though there is no suggestion the students or their school did anything wrong.

“We’re all very scared,” Ms. Quenneville said. “We’ve been trying to keep each other very positive because we’ve heard nothing, and it’s so easy to spiral out of control and feel helpless because we are helpless right now.”

The sudden freeze, which the Progressive Conservatives say they imposed to safeguard the financial aid program after explosive growth in OSAP applications and allegations of wrongdoing in online-only programming at fewer than 10 private career colleges, has put the entire for-profit educational sector in Ontario on shaky financial footing. At least one vocational school with multiple campuses, Trillium College, has already suspended academic programming because it can’t get by without OSAP.

As Ontario politicians returned to the legislature Tuesday for the first time since June, Opposition MPPs called on Premier Doug Ford to fire Nolan Quinn, the Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, who they accused of punishing hundreds of blameless private colleges for the alleged sins of a few.

The Liberals and NDP noted that the PC government had been warned as far back as January of 2023 by Career Colleges Ontario – the association that represents schools now imperilled by the pause – of massive spikes in OSAP applications at some career colleges that smacked of “suspicious activity.” Mr. Quinn “looked the other way” and “dragged his feet” on inspecting private colleges he now accuses of defrauding OSAP, said Peggy Sattler, the NDP critic for colleges and universities. “Clearly, he has failed to do his job.”

The Premier defended Mr. Quinn, who told the legislature he had no choice but to halt loans to all career college students while a third-party auditor and the Ontario Provincial Police investigate. “We need to hold the bad actors accountable,” Mr. Quinn said. “If what we have found proves to be what we think it is, then it is nothing short of criminal.”

Hundreds of pages of court documents, first reported on by The Canadian Press, shed light on what the Ministry’s OSAP Inspection and Compliance Unit allegedly discovered when it inspected three Greater Toronto Area campuses of a private career college called Academy of Learning in 2025.
The schools were among six notified in May that their OSAP eligibility wouldn’t be renewed for the coming academic year.

Ministry inspectors allege they found red flags with online-only programs at Academy of Learning campuses in Brampton, North York and downtown Toronto, including dozens of students accessing coursework from the same IP addresses, often located outside North America.

They found evidence that students completed entire asynchronous online courses in a day or two and finished exams in less than five minutes. And when inspectors contacted apparent students, some couldn’t “name the institution, program or courses they completed” or “communicate independently in English,” according to inspection reports.
None of the allegations have been proven in court.

Owners of the three Academy of Learning franchises deny wrongdoing. They responded to concerns raised by inspectors with detailed corrective action plans, and say they were working in good faith with a ministry-approved compliance monitor when they learned their OSAP status wouldn’t be renewed.

Before loan payments were paused across the sector, there were 242 private postsecondary institutions in Ontario whose students were eligible for OSAP. Although the freeze applies to private universities, chiropractic and naturopathic medicine colleges and even Canada’s National Ballet School, most of the institutions affected are private career colleges.

Private career colleges offer short, skill-specific training programs for jobs such as hairdressers, personal support workers, medical office assistants and early childhood educators. They tend to attract new Canadians, recent high school graduates from working-class backgrounds, and parents looking to upskill.

They also tend to charge higher fees than most public colleges and universities because they aren’t subsidized by taxpayers. Tuition for Southern Ontario Dental College’s 22-month hygienist program, for instance, is $51,997, an amount that covers everything from scrubs to textbooks to dental equipment.

It’s no surprise, then, that low-income students taking expensive courses would rely on financial aid. At Southern Ontario Dental College, more than 90 per cent do. Their OSAP disbursements for this academic year had already been approved. Most were expecting lump sums of a few thousand dollars or more in September to defray living costs while they attend school full-time.

The dental college itself was expecting about $2-million in tuition payments from OSAP, its chief source of revenue. Although classes are carrying on as usual for now, “the hard reality is, we can’t survive if we don’t have the money,” said Alysse Estrabillo, the college’s chief operating officer. She and her husband, dentist Roland Estrabillo, have owned the college for 22 years. They have about 70 staff and 282 students to think of.
“I’m a big mama bear,” Ms. Estrabillo said, “and I just feel sick to my stomach.”

Alysse Estrabillo and her husband, Roland, own the Southern Ontario Dental College, established in 2004. More than 90 per cent of students here rely on financial aid. Nick Iwanyshyn/The Globe and Mail

The college is also a working clinic for dental cleanings, X-rays and other services. One second-year student, Crystal Au, gives a patient tips on proper flossing; another, Kiera Donohue, works on an assignment with clinical instructor Sava Pijanovic. Nick Iwanyshyn/The Globe and Mail
That ill feeling has been spreading through the private postsecondary sector ever since Mr. Quinn announced the OSAP loan pause on Oct. 6.

Two of the Academy of Learning campuses involved in the court case appear in the same chart. One campus grew from 775 OSAP submissions in 2022 to 1,612 in 2023 and then to 5,748 in 2024.

stories.title: B.C.’s next premier must jump-start plans to combat money laundering through shell companies
stories.summary: The province was once at the forefront of the battle and the country needs its leadership for a pan-Canadian initiative
stories.author: Rita Trichur
stories.content:
British Columbia’s next premier has a laundry list of political priorities.

Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson won a majority government in a come-from-behind victory in Saturday’s provincial election. Observing that B.C. voters “ chose change ,” he outlined goals such as collaborating on the proposed Pacific Link pipeline project and eliminating barriers to labour mobility and internal trade.

Mr. Doerkson appears focused on strengthening B.C.’s role in the Canadian federation. That’s encouraging because there is a pressing matter that he must add to his political agenda to safeguard the country’s economic sovereignty: Jump-starting his province’s stalled plans to unmask the owners of shell companies through a publicly-accessible corporate registry.

The long-promised creation of a provincial database that would reveal the owners of secret companies dates back to the Commission of Inquiry into Money Laundering in British Columbia’s final report in June, 2022. Those plans for a so-called beneficial ownership registry fell victim to outgoing Premier David Eby ’s procrastination and prioritization of an early election.

Mr. Doerkson, who vowed in his election platform to provide police and prosecutors with the resources to combat money laundering and other crimes, has an opportunity to finally realize that goal for the betterment of B.C. and Canada as a whole.

Although the “Vancouver model” of money laundering has gained infamy in recent years, illicit financial flows aren’t just washing up in B.C. casinos .

The abuse of anonymous shell companies and other corporate structures by money launderers and other financial criminals is also a festering problem in B.C. overall and other parts of Canada. It is known as “ snow-washing .”

Shell corporations are businesses that exist purely on paper since they lack operations. Although they do have legitimate uses, criminals routinely exploit these corporate entities to launder illicit profits because they can be used to access the banking system while hiding their true owners.

The failure to stop the flow of dirty money into the economy has implications for trade diversification, national security, and even Canada’s sovereign credit rating.

Some 70 per cent of all money-laundering cases in Canada involve the abuse of corporate entities, according to federal data. But the vast majority of shell corporations, at least 85 per cent, are incorporated at the provincial level.

For those reasons, Prime Minister Mark Carney ’s government is urging provinces and territories to join a pan-Canadian corporate registry to enhance beneficial-ownership transparency. Indeed, Ottawa’s goal is to “ safeguard Canada’s economic security .”

Quebec is the only province with an operational corporate registry to date. Others, including Ontario and B.C., previously considered a provincial leader in this effort, are working on their own databases.

B.C.’s money laundering inquiry commissioner Austin Cullen, a former associate chief justice of the B.C. Supreme Court, originally recommended that B.C. work with its federal, provincial and territorial partners to ensure a pan-Canadian corporate beneficial ownership registry would be in place before the end of 2023.

“There is a near consensus that a beneficial ownership registry is needed in British Columbia; the question is no longer whether the Province should implement such a registry, but how it should be done,” Mr. Cullen stated in his final report.

B.C. must regain its momentum on corporate transparency because it is home to a large proportion of private companies.

The Financial Action Task Force (Fatf), a global body that sets standards to combat money laundering and terrorist financing, recently rated Canada’s beneficial ownership efforts as moderate because of provincial disparities.

“Corporations can be formed quickly, cheaply and remotely from abroad, with or without the assistance of professional intermediaries and undertake business globally, including with individuals and entities operating in high-risk foreign jurisdictions,” the Fatf stated in its September report.

Meanwhile, the End Snow-Washing Coalition, a Canadian umbrella group formed in 2017 that advocates for corporate transparency, has argued that provincial fragmentation on ownership disclosure is dangerous. paragraphs: British Columbia’s next premier has a laundry list of political priorities.

Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson won a majority government in a come-from-behind victory in Saturday’s provincial election. Observing that B.C. voters “ chose change ,” he outlined goals such as collaborating on the proposed Pacific Link pipeline project and eliminating barriers to labour mobility and internal trade.

Mr. Doerkson appears focused on strengthening B.C.’s role in the Canadian federation. That’s encouraging because there is a pressing matter that he must add to his political agenda to safeguard the country’s economic sovereignty: Jump-starting his province’s stalled plans to unmask the owners of shell companies through a publicly-accessible corporate registry.

The long-promised creation of a provincial database that would reveal the owners of secret companies dates back to the Commission of Inquiry into Money Laundering in British Columbia’s final report in June, 2022. Those plans for a so-called beneficial ownership registry fell victim to outgoing Premier David Eby ’s procrastination and prioritization of an early election.

Mr. Doerkson, who vowed in his election platform to provide police and prosecutors with the resources to combat money laundering and other crimes, has an opportunity to finally realize that goal for the betterment of B.C. and Canada as a whole.
Although the “Vancouver model” of money laundering has gained infamy in recent years, illicit financial flows aren’t just washing up in B.C. casinos .

The abuse of anonymous shell companies and other corporate structures by money launderers and other financial criminals is also a festering problem in B.C. overall and other parts of Canada. It is known as “ snow-washing .”

Shell corporations are businesses that exist purely on paper since they lack operations. Although they do have legitimate uses, criminals routinely exploit these corporate entities to launder illicit profits because they can be used to access the banking system while hiding their true owners.
The failure to stop the flow of dirty money into the economy has implications for trade diversification, national security, and even Canada’s sovereign credit rating.

Some 70 per cent of all money-laundering cases in Canada involve the abuse of corporate entities, according to federal data. But the vast majority of shell corporations, at least 85 per cent, are incorporated at the provincial level.

For those reasons, Prime Minister Mark Carney ’s government is urging provinces and territories to join a pan-Canadian corporate registry to enhance beneficial-ownership transparency. Indeed, Ottawa’s goal is to “ safeguard Canada’s economic security .”

Quebec is the only province with an operational corporate registry to date. Others, including Ontario and B.C., previously considered a provincial leader in this effort, are working on their own databases.

B.C.’s money laundering inquiry commissioner Austin Cullen, a former associate chief justice of the B.C. Supreme Court, originally recommended that B.C. work with its federal, provincial and territorial partners to ensure a pan-Canadian corporate beneficial ownership registry would be in place before the end of 2023.

“There is a near consensus that a beneficial ownership registry is needed in British Columbia; the question is no longer whether the Province should implement such a registry, but how it should be done,” Mr. Cullen stated in his final report.
B.C. must regain its momentum on corporate transparency because it is home to a large proportion of private companies.

The Financial Action Task Force (Fatf), a global body that sets standards to combat money laundering and terrorist financing, recently rated Canada’s beneficial ownership efforts as moderate because of provincial disparities.

“Corporations can be formed quickly, cheaply and remotely from abroad, with or without the assistance of professional intermediaries and undertake business globally, including with individuals and entities operating in high-risk foreign jurisdictions,” the Fatf stated in its September report.

That brings us back to B.C.’s premier-designate, who has also promised to modernize the province’s business registry services. A database that reveals who owns and controls shell companies would dovetail with that goal.

Given its size and economic importance, B.C. must be at the forefront of the fight against snow-washing. Canada’s future prosperity is at stake. It’s not just British Columbians who are counting on Mr. Doerkson.

stories.title: At least 64 dead in high-speed train crash in central Spain, 5 Canadians ‘affected”
stories.summary: The crash occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes in Spain.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Iain Sullivan and Joseph Wilson, The Associated Press,

Posted October 28, 2026 4:55 am.

Last Updated October 28, 2026 11:44 am.

A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 64 people on Wednesday in central Spain, authorities said.

The central government’s office for Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll had risen.

The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, had said at least 80 people were injured as rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies.

Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed that at least two Canadians were injured in the crash. “Our thoughts are with their families, the victims and their loved ones in the days and weeks ahead. If there is any assistance we can give, we will provide,” said Carney.

Anita Anand, Minister of Foreign Affairs, later said that five Canadians “are affected” by the train crash.

It was the second major train accident in Spain this year.

Deeply saddened by the tragic train accident in the province of Toledo, Spain. My heartfelt condolences go to all those affected by this terrible event and to the people of Spain. I also thank the first responders working tirelessly on the difficult rescue efforts. To our… — Anita Anand (@AnitaAnandMP) October 28, 2026

Spain’s rail system operator Adif said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. The accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain, according to Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region.

One ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.

Padilla said that the cause of the crash was not known. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.

“It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy,” García said.

The accident involved a train from Spain’s state-owned Renfe company and the private rail company Iryo. It appeared the Renfe train rammed the Iryo train, Spanish media reported. García-Page said 24 died in the Renfe train, and six in the Iryo one.

Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the Renfe train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the Iryo.

“We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact,” he said. “The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook.”

Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the Renfe train and 147 passengers in the Iryo train.

Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.

Iryo, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has “activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities.”

The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, said that that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to injured passengers.

A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police. Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez canceled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was “dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo.”

“Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers,” wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. “All my thoughts are with the victims and their families.”

Spain’s King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were following news of the accident.

“We are deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident in Urda (Toledo),” the royal couple said. “We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected.”

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said “My heart goes out to the victims’ families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you.”

Spain’s soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.

Spain already suffered a devastating train crash this year

The wreckage of Wednesday’s crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when a Iryo train jumped the track and hit an oncoming Renfe train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.

That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.

The January incident shook confidence in the European country’s extensive high-speed rail service.

Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country’s railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.

Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.

Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against Renfe. Iryo started operating in Spain in 2022.

A spokesperson for Spain’s train workers’ union, Joan Rodríguez, said that the increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.

“We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodríguez told TVE. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”

stories.title: To fix a toxic culture, Csis is trying to build trust in a world where no one trusts anyone
stories.summary: Csis has a morale issue. It has a red tape problem. It's strained from under-resourcing. It also has a serious leadership trust issues.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — When Csis director Dan Rogers meets staff at one of the spy agency’s offices across the country, there comes a time when he asks the bosses to leave the room.

Then, he asks spy agency staff how thing are really going.

There’s good reason for the head of the spy agency — who marked two years on the job earlier this month — to want to put his ear directly to the ground.

Csis has a morale issue. It has a red tape problem. It’s strained from years of under-resourcing. And above all, it has a serious leadership trust issues.

In an interview alongside Csis’s deputy director Vanessa Lloyd and human resources head Jesse Schwartz, Rogers candidly acknowledges those problems. In fact, he’s brutally honest in his assessment of the service.

The agency is full of passionate people who are extremely dedicated to their mission of keeping Canada safe. But it’s also struggling.

“Csis is strained,” he told National Post.

“We have an organization that is extremely overtaxed in an extraordinarily complex environment, and people do hard work in stressful environments every day.”

Rogers May lead one of the most mysterious and shadowy agencies in the country, but he spends a lot of his time thinking not about spy stuff… but about culture change.

That’s because the same year he was appointed, the government released the 2024 edition of the Public Service Employment Survey (Pses) that showed deeply concerning results for Csis workers.

The poll suggested only half (51 per cent) of Csis respondents believed senior managers “lead by example in ethical behaviour.” Far fewer (40 per cent) said they had confidence in top management, whereas barely 29 per cent believed senior management makes “effective and timely decisions.”

Just over half (56 per cent) said they had the tools, technology and equipment to do their job.

Nearly one in five (17 per cent) of respondents said they’d been harassed in the previous 12 months.

In all those cases, Csis’s results were both consistent or worse than previous surveys and below the average across the federal public service.

That’s on top of repeat allegations of racism , sexism, a “macho” environment and even sexual assault over the last decade within the secretive service. Notably, in 2017, then- Director David Vigneault issued a statement acknowledging “serious concerns surrounding retribution, favouritism, bullying and other inappropriate behaviour” in the service’s Toronto office.

Issues with trust and ethics are of particular concern at Csis because the spy agency has tremendous and invasive investigative power. With the proper ministerial authorization, agents can even break the law to advance an investigation.

The agency is also required to act quickly to detect and respond to imminent national security threats. Red tape and overly complex internal processes are likely to complicate that mission.

Last year, National Post revealed that Rogers sent a memo to staff in June 2025 acknowledging the “disappointing and unacceptable” Pses results. Culture change would become his and management’s “overriding priority,” he wrote, because the current environment was hampering Csis’s ability to deliver on its critical national security role.

The director and his colleagues are well aware that changing a culture — particularly one that has been allowed to fester slowly for so long — is not an overnight experience.

“Habits are hard to change,” said Schwartz in the recent interview in which she, Rogers and Lloyd listed a number of changes they were implementing following his memo.

One is improving communication by having senior executives speak more directly to their staff and vice-versa. Executives need to speak more directly to their reports, and employees are encouraged to write directly to a senior leader, and even the director himself.

“You can make all the right decisions as a senior manager, but if people never know who you are, they don’t know your values, and they don’t hear the context about why you made the decision that you made, and they don’t feel like you’re being earnest with them, and you’re just this nameless, faceless thing that exists and communicates them through an email or a very corporate speak message, they might assume the worst,” Rogers said.

A second is making it clear to executives that their priority over the next year was to focus on “key elements of our workforce”, such as creating a better team environment. It’s now part of their performance reviews and directly impacts their bonus.

Another is hiring more, faster and addressing critical staffing gaps.

For Schwartz, the head of HR, much time has been spent speeding up recruitment and the infamously slow enhanced top secret security clearance process. There is no lack of applicants to the spy agency, she said, but getting them through the door has not always been easy.

She said she’s worked to cut down on hiring “bottlenecks”, speed up the clearance process such as by hiring more polygraph operators, and avoiding redundancies in the process.

“So this year we have (hiring) targets. Next year, we have more ambitious targets because we know that this year we’re going to take a bit of time to build the capacity because we hadn’t been doing it for a while. I expect that that trajectory gets better,” Rogers explained.

He also said the service has “really fundamentally adjusted the way that we do training, the way that we classify people in positions” in the name of efficiency.

There’s also recognition. Because of Csis’s secret mandate, much of the work done to protect Canada’s national security like foiling a terrorist plot or preventing sabotage on Canadian infrastructure goes unrecognized. It’s a longstanding frustration by employees at the service .

So if a team has a “great operational success,” instead of sending them an email, why not bring them a box of donuts, say thank you and ask them how they did it, Rogers said. Simple stuff that simply wasn’t being done consistently.

But in an organization where so many employees are spies who are trained to lie, deceive and conceal their true identity professionally, how does Rogers ensure executives are actually making the changes he demands?

On the same day National Post sat down with Rogers, former intelligence officer Diana Bayko published an account of her time at Csis in which she explained how her then-boss had advised her to handle conflict with her colleagues.

“Handle my co-workers like sources. Meaning: assess their reliability, spot vulnerabilities and exploit them if need be, and trust sparingly,” wrote Bayko.

So, how does Rogers make sure he isn’t being lied to?

“That’s a great question,” Rogers said. “There are ways we can try and figure that out and try and mitigate against the risk of inaction where we expect action.”

For example, he ordered multi-rater assessments (also know as 360-degree review tests) for every single executive in the organization. The comprehensive (and generally expensive) test gathers feedback from not only the executive’s subordinates, but their colleagues and their bosses through a questionnaire of hundreds of questions. It’s a lot of work.

The point, he said, is to get a holistic assessment of an executive’s work seen by a coterie of other people. Then, you can compare it to what they should be doing.

Another example is his meetings with staff both at headquarters and regional offices without the bosses around.

“When I’ll go to visit a region, I’ll have a meeting with management. I’ll also have a meeting without management in the room, and I’ll ask questions, and I’ll say, ‘You can email me directly’,” Rogers said.

“And people will email me directly, and they will say, ‘I do not want you to share this with my management, but here’s something I think you should know’,” he continued.

“It’s not an irregular occurrence that people will email. Now, to be candid, sometimes I wish they didn’t have to. They’re emailing because they feel like they don’t have another resort.”

Rogers wouldn’t say if any executives been fired, demoted or sanctioned for not living up to expectations, citing privacy rules. But he noted that it was crucial for him to set expectations for culture change before holding people to account.

“We are going to have to get there,” he said of identifying executives and staff who aren’t performing as expected.

Asked how the situation got so bad, Csis leadership demurs, unwilling to blame any particular previous leader or policy.

“I’m not going to cast blame. Having come in, I saw a lot of people trying to resolve these issues,” Rogers said.

“I know this is hard, and I’m pretty forgiving about the fact that some people May not have been able to create exactly the culture that we would want.”

But now, Canada’s spy chief spends much of his time cleaning up the mess.

National Post cnardi@postmedia.com

“You can make all the right decisions as a senior manager, but if people never know who you are, they don’t know your values, and they don’t hear the context about why you made the decision that you made, and they don’t feel like you’re being earnest with them, and you’re just this nameless, faceless thing that exists and communicates them through an email or a very corporate speak message, they might assume the worst,” Rogers said.

A second is making it clear to executives that their priority over the next year was to focus on “key elements of our workforce”, such as creating a better team environment. It’s now part of their performance reviews and directly impacts their bonus.
Another is hiring more, faster and addressing critical staffing gaps.

For Schwartz, the head of HR, much time has been spent speeding up recruitment and the infamously slow enhanced top secret security clearance process. There is no lack of applicants to the spy agency, she said, but getting them through the door has not always been easy.
She said she’s worked to cut down on hiring “bottlenecks”, speed up the clearance process such as by hiring more polygraph operators, and avoiding redundancies in the process.

“So this year we have (hiring) targets. Next year, we have more ambitious targets because we know that this year we’re going to take a bit of time to build the capacity because we hadn’t been doing it for a while. I expect that that trajectory gets better,” Rogers explained.
He also said the service has “really fundamentally adjusted the way that we do training, the way that we classify people in positions” in the name of efficiency.

There’s also recognition. Because of Csis’s secret mandate, much of the work done to protect Canada’s national security like foiling a terrorist plot or preventing sabotage on Canadian infrastructure goes unrecognized. It’s a longstanding frustration by employees at the service .
content_blocks.html: There’s also recognition. Because of CSIS’s secret mandate, much of the work done to protect Canada’s national security like foiling a terrorist plot or preventing sabotage on Canadian infrastructure goes unrecognized. It’s a longstanding frustration by employees at the service.

content_blocks.text: So if a team has a “great operational success,” instead of sending them an email, why not bring them a box of donuts, say thank you and ask them how they did it, Rogers said. Simple stuff that simply wasn’t being done consistently.

But in an organization where so many employees are spies who are trained to lie, deceive and conceal their true identity professionally, how does Rogers ensure executives are actually making the changes he demands?

On the same day National Post sat down with Rogers, former intelligence officer Diana Bayko published an account of her time at Csis in which she explained how her then-boss had advised her to handle conflict with her colleagues.
content_blocks.html: On the same day National Post sat down with Rogers, former intelligence officer Diana Bayko published an account of her time at CSIS in which she explained how her then-boss had advised her to handle conflict with her colleagues.

content_blocks.text: “Handle my co-workers like sources. Meaning: assess their reliability, spot vulnerabilities and exploit them if need be, and trust sparingly,” wrote Bayko.
So, how does Rogers make sure he isn’t being lied to?
“That’s a great question,” Rogers said. “There are ways we can try and figure that out and try and mitigate against the risk of inaction where we expect action.”

For example, he ordered multi-rater assessments (also know as 360-degree review tests) for every single executive in the organization. The comprehensive (and generally expensive) test gathers feedback from not only the executive’s subordinates, but their colleagues and their bosses through a questionnaire of hundreds of questions. It’s a lot of work.
The point, he said, is to get a holistic assessment of an executive’s work seen by a coterie of other people. Then, you can compare it to what they should be doing.
Another example is his meetings with staff both at headquarters and regional offices without the bosses around.

“When I’ll go to visit a region, I’ll have a meeting with management. I’ll also have a meeting without management in the room, and I’ll ask questions, and I’ll say, ‘You can email me directly’,” Rogers said.
“And people will email me directly, and they will say, ‘I do not want you to share this with my management, but here’s something I think you should know’,” he continued.
“It’s not an irregular occurrence that people will email. Now, to be candid, sometimes I wish they didn’t have to. They’re emailing because they feel like they don’t have another resort.”

Rogers wouldn’t say if any executives been fired, demoted or sanctioned for not living up to expectations, citing privacy rules. But he noted that it was crucial for him to set expectations for culture change before holding people to account.
“We are going to have to get there,” he said of identifying executives and staff who aren’t performing as expected.
Asked how the situation got so bad, Csis leadership demurs, unwilling to blame any particular previous leader or policy.
“I’m not going to cast blame. Having come in, I saw a lot of people trying to resolve these issues,” Rogers said.
“I know this is hard, and I’m pretty forgiving about the fact that some people May not have been able to create exactly the culture that we would want.”
But now, Canada’s spy chief spends much of his time cleaning up the mess.

stories.title: Quebec is bracing for a big battle with U.S. streamers on ‘discoverability’ of French content
stories.summary: “Our culture is at stake. We will... negotiate directly until our Quebec culture can once again flourish and shine,” the premier said.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon May have received congratulations from U.S. President Donald Trump on his election win, but that won’t deter him from his goal to force big U.S. streamers to showcase more French content on their platforms.

In unveiling his cabinet last week, St-Pierre Plamondon named his most experienced member of caucus, Pascal Bérubé, to become his minister of culture. He described him as a man “who knows how to stay on course when the wind is blowing hard.”

In a speech, the premier said Bérubé will have the mandate to negotiate a 30-per-cent quota of French content on large U.S. online platforms such as Netflix and Spotify.

“From now on, Quebec will represent itself in this regard. Because we cannot rely on the federal government — that has been demonstrated so many times,” he said.

“Our culture is at stake. We will mobilize all available resources and negotiate directly until our Quebec culture can once again flourish and shine,” he added.

Bérubé told reporters after the fact he did not intend to sit idly by in his new role.

“Just watch us go — we are very determined. He didn’t send me to the culture portfolio for nothing; he’s sending his most experienced elected official. We have big plans, and it won’t be long now. My first actions will be taken very quickly,” he said.

Bérubé was not made available for an interview to describe his new mandate, which arrives at a critical time for trade talks between Canada and the United States.

Experts and political insiders consulted by National Post have questions about the leverage a single province would have in these negotiations, what these talks would achieve exactly and how they could affect Canada’s efforts in alleviating U.S. tariffs.

“The United States will take a tougher stance toward Canada. Is that their goal?” openly wondered a Canadian diplomatic source speaking in Washington D.C.

The Trump administration has already listed Quebec’s Bill 109, which seeks to promote cultural sovereignty and increase the discoverability of French cultural content for streaming services, as a potential trade barrier in a report issued earlier this year.

The former Coalition Avenir Québec government adopted Bill 109 in December 2025, but the legislation has yet to be in effect with regulations that will determine, among other things, the level needed of French content on these platforms.

As one source close to the file put it, the new Parti Québécois government already has all the legislative tools in place and simply has to enforce the law with regulations.

“They want to negotiate… but what is there to negotiate exactly?”

Michèle Rioux, a professor in the department of political science at UQÀM and director of a research laboratory focused on discoverability and the transformation of cultural industries, said Quebec’s leverage against U.S. streaming giants is “zero.”

However, she said the task at hand for Bérubé May be to instead raise awareness among the platforms about the importance of ensuring the discoverability of French cultural products that are consistently sidelined in favour of English content.

Peter Menzies, a Macdonald-Laurier Institute senior fellow and former vice-chair of the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission, said Quebec going at it alone would create “an absolutely chaotic situation” for everyone involved.

“As far as the federal government is concerned, broadcasting and telecommunications are federal jurisdiction,” he said, noting that since the passage of the Online Streaming Act in 2023, online video and audio platforms were brought under federal jurisdiction.

But he noted that Ottawa probably does not want to get into a fight on that issue.

The office of the Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture, Marc Miller, cited “cooperative federalism” when asked to comment on Quebec’s intentions.

“We will continue to work constructively with Quebec’s new government to support French-language culture and ensure it can thrive,” said press secretary Hermine Landry in an email.

Then, there is the issue of whether those streamers could realistically get to 30-per-cent of French content — which is the stated goal of the Quebec government.

“Should they be designing a different Netflix for instance for Quebec than for the rest of Canada? Should Spotify have to play different music in Quebec, and how do you manage that jurisdictionally, legally and practically?” Menzies asked.

Bill 109 mentions “cultural content originally expressed in the French language.”

That could mean that platforms could use original francophone content from France, Algeria, Tunisia and other French-speaking countries, Menzies noted. Or, if that is not possible, he said there is a risk some smaller platforms simply pull out of Quebec.

“How is BritBox going to do 30-per-cent original French language content?” he asked of the subscription streaming service focused on British television.

Another unfortunate scenario for consumers could see streamers pulling out some of their English content in Quebec to satisfy the government criteria, according to a source that worked closely on the file and who thinks 30-per-cent is simply too high.

However, those percentages are in line with current European regulations on cultural discoverability which require that at least 30-per-cent of each service’s catalogue be titles from the European Union and that these titles must be made prominent.

France requires at least 60-per-cent EU titles and 40-per-cent titles in French.

Gilbert Gagné, a professor at Bishop’s University who studies cultural trade, said the government of Quebec had little choice but to step in to protect its culture at a time when the federal government has “yielded” to U.S. pressure to avoid trade retaliation.

“I feel the government of Quebec is doing the job that Ottawa should have done months ago,” he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has recently said he will not change his mind about his decisions to eliminate the digital services tax and Canadian content contributions which were put in place by the government of his predecessor Justin Trudeau.

But Miller’s office said the federal government has taken concrete action to make Canadian content easier to discover with more than $1.5 billion invested in arts and culture over the past year.

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet said he believes Quebec has what it takes to go it alone to improve discoverability of French cultural content.

Ultimately, he said the full weight to make these decisions come with independence.

stories.title: Cut tax, reduce deficit, grow economy. Can B.C. Conservatives do it all at once?
stories.summary: Victoria - With two-thirds of the seats in the next legislature, the B.C. Conservatives May have a resounding mandate to follow through on their election promises to cut taxes, reduce the deficit and grow the economy at 3.2 per cent — but some economists say the challenge will be doing it all at once.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VICTORIA - With two-thirds of the seats in the next legislature, the B.C. Conservatives may have a resounding mandate to follow through on their election promises to cut taxes, reduce the deficit and grow the economy at 3.2 per cent — but some economists say the challenge will be doing it all at once.

Cutting tax and simultaneously fixing the budget “are contradictory,” said Werner Antweiler, a professor at the University of British Columbia.

And the surge in government spending behind the record $14-billion projected deficit is conversely a contributor to economic growth, said Marc Lee, senior economist with the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives.

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has promised the appointment of a panel to conduct a “core review” of the books before presenting his government’s first budget.

But instead of easy solutions, tough choices await about what to cut, said Jairo Yunis, policy director with the Business Council of B.C.

Yunis said public sector employment had grown by over 45 per cent since 2019 under the NDP, while private sector employment in the same time was up only about three per cent.

He said public sector cuts need to be a “big part of the conversation” in an extensive review of government spending, which should take lessons from former federal Liberal prime minister Jean Chrétien and his governments.

The review should question whether the province still needs certain programs, whether there is duplication and if they can be delivered differently.

“My point is to make choices based on priorities and outcomes,” he said.

He said the deficit could be halved as a result of the review, more discipline around the use of contingencies, economic growth and lower regulatory burdens. But it won’t be easy, he said.

“That is going to entail a lot of hard choices,” Yunis said.

And the Conservatives have signalled that not every ministry will be coming under scrutiny — the party says its “core review” will exclude health, education and child care, social development, children and family development, the Attorney General and public safety.

‘SHRINK WE MUST’

The Conservatives promised to raise B.C.’s basic personal income tax exemption to $32,000, amounting to a $1,000 tax cut for most individual workers. As for the deficit, their platform pledged to bring it down with the help of growth it forecast to reach 3.2 per cent, well in excess of most predictions.

The party’s platform notably omitted detail on what might be cut to help make ends meet.

Antweiler agreed the Conservatives would need to shrink the public workforce.

But the government would also need to raise more revenue and it cannot cut taxes and fix the budget at the same time, he said.

Antweiler said voters have given Doerkson a mandate, but plans may need revising after the financial assessment, and nothing should be ruled out.

“There are things we cannot do right away, that may have to wait later until economic conditions improve actually enable us to do that,” he said. “There needs to be a small dose of austerity to fix what is quite obviously broken.”

He said the public service accounts for a “huge chunk of the expenditures,” but shrinking it can be tricky because it is heavily unionized, and Doerkson’s government can’t cut back on health care, education or public safety without compromising quality.

“Provincial governments have a limit how far they can go, because many of these expenditures are written in stone,” he said.

Shrinking the public service would have to be balanced in ways that make a difference in the budget, without triggering labour unrest, he said. “But shrink we must, because I don’t think there is any other avenue,” he said.

The Conservative platform foresees economic growth increasing to 3.2 per cent in 2029, raising an additional $2.62 billion without raising taxes.

Antweiler said the growth forecast was “lofty” and not realistic.

Lee at the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives said that while history showed the provincial economy could sometimes improve quickly, there was plenty of uncertainty.

“We don’t even know what is going to happen next week after the U.S. election,” he said. “If there is a major stock market crash, which seems incredibly likely in the next six months, that’s going to change the situation.”

Lee said the provincial economy ran on trade, housing and immigration, and government spending. But the trade engine was sputtering because of the trade war and the housing engine was completely dead, because of changes in immigration, he said.

“The B.C. budget has been contributing to B.C.‘s economic growth,” Lee said. “If we didn’t have that budget deficit, we would probably be in a recession.”

He said that to reduce the deficit “you are going to need to increase tax or cut spending.”

Antweiler said he favoured an all-of-the-above approach, combining cuts with higher revenues from economic growth and more indirect forms of taxation.

He said the NDP government of outgoing Premier David Eby made a mistake by getting rid of the carbon tax, which blew a $2-billion hole in the budget.

He said the next finance minister should look at all options, including raising resource royalties, shifting taxation from income to consumption, and encouraging investment.

The Conservatives may need to “jump over their shadow” and break their tax promises, he said.

Yunis said B.C. has more of a spending problem than a revenue problem.

And British Columbia, he said, needed to improve its tax-competitiveness.

All three economists agreed that the new finance minister faced a difficult file.

“A new chapter needs to be turned now,” Antweiler said. “It’s not too late to turn the wheel around.”

stories.title: 'A stab in the back': How it feels to be barred from accessing Maid for mental illness
stories.summary: Toronto - For Lisa Marr, the government's decision to ban people from accessing medical assistance in dying for mental illness feels like "a stab in the back."
stories.author: Hannah Alberga The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - For Lisa Marr, the government’s decision to ban people from accessing medical assistance in dying for mental illness feels like “a stab in the back.”

“They’re not thinking about those people who have lived with it their entire life and have treatment-resistant conditions,” Marr said from her bedroom in Eastern Passage, N.S.

“Like myself,” she added.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser introduced a bill Tuesday that, if passed, will stop a scheduled expansion of Maid access to those suffering solely from a mental illness.

Fraser told reporters there is a lack of consensus about the irremediable nature of mental illnesses within the medical community. Irremediability is a criteria for Maid that requires a person have an incurable illness, be in an advanced state of irreversible decline, and intolerable suffering in order to be considered eligible. The justice minister said he also worried the lack of access to mental health care could cause people to turn to Maid.

In Quebec, a person with a ‘serious and incurable illness leading to incapacity’ can request Maid years or months in advance.

Marr responded to Fraser’s reasoning by writing him a letter about her more than five decades of mental illness, beginning from the age of five. She said she told him about her treatment resistant depression, suicidal ideation, generalized anxiety disorder, bipolar II disorder, and the complex post-traumatic stress disorder that has gripped her since retiring as a paramedic in 2017.

“I believe that it should be an option for those that cannot get better no matter how much therapy, medications, and other treatments one endures for years and years. I have had 20-plus psychiatrists and have been seeing a psychologist weekly for the last 10 years,” she wrote.

“Fighting with every ounce of strength you can muster just to get out of bed each day is not quality of life.”

The irremediability of a mental illness has been debated by health-care providers and politicians for years, ever since the government asked a group of experts in 2021 to study safeguards to safely introduce mental illness to Canada’s Maid regime. That expansion was repeatedly delayed, until Fraser announced that it wouldn’t happen at all.

Based on the evidence to date, the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health’s chief medical officer Dr. Sanjeev Sockalingam said studies show mental health diagnoses can change, as can prognoses for people believed to be treatment resistant.

“It is very difficult for Maid assessors and individuals assessing people living with mental illness for Maid to truly appreciate and prognosticate or predict if someone is going to recover from their mental illness,” Sockalingam said.

Testifying at a parliamentary committee hearing in April, Sockalingam described the circumstances he believes need to be in place in order to offer Maid to people whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness.

“Only when we have evidence-informed, consensus-based criteria for determining the irremediability of a person’s mental illness and for distinguishing between a request for Maid and suicide intent — and only when such criteria can be introduced into a well-resourced mental health system,” he said.

Dr. Tim Holland, who has been providing Maid since it became legal in Canada, said “irremediability, incurable, irreversible,” are always hard to define in medicine, whether that’s in relation to mental or physical health.

It can be more challenging to determine irremediability in depression versus metastatic lung cancer, but there are also people who will disagree on when a metastatic cancer is considered incurable, he said.

“It’s not like we don’t have any understanding of these conditions. We do have a very robust understanding of mental health and what responds to certain treatments,” said Holland, who is also the head of the bioethics department at Dalhousie University.

“It’s a challenge in both and it’s doable in both,” he said. “To say that Maid assessors can’t do it is false.”

Psychiatrist Dr. Mona Gupta said the yearslong policy debate about Maid has unfolded as though the exclusion of people with mental disorders comes with no negative consequences for those who planned to apply.

“As a society, we have chosen to pretend that people with severe, chronic, treatment-refractory mental disorders simply do not exist.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.
