stories.title: Being my daughter’s sous-chef for a week was exactly what I needed
stories.summary: Watching her in her element, I was able to see the capable and resilient woman she had become
stories.author: Ann Diehl
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

It wasn’t the Vancouver Island getaway I had planned – or anything close to it.

My husband and I were looking forward to staying in our daughter Sarah’s new condo just before she left to work as a chef at a wilderness lodge.

Not long after we arrived, her phone rang. Sarah’s sous-chef couldn’t make the trip.

Ten guests were arriving from New York, expecting three gourmet meals a day, everything fresh and made from scratch.

“There’s no way I can do this alone,” Sarah said. “I’ll have to cancel.”

Sarah had spent years working as a professional chef around the world. Now halfway through a master’s degree and changing careers, she accepted only a few summer cooking jobs to help pay her tuition.

Knowing how important this one was, the next morning, I found myself on a boat with Sarah, surrounded by boxes and coolers stuffed with $5,000 worth of fine foods. I marvelled at the sights as we navigated the channels between the many small islands scattered along the coast.

After 90 minutes, Sarah pointed out the lodge, perched on a small hill among the trees. We were welcomed by staff who carried our supplies up to the lodge.

With guests arriving by float plane in a few hours, Sarah quickly sprang into action. We unpacked boxes, finding places for the food in the large pantry and industrial fridge and freezer. Sarah started preparing dinner and I was assigned the task of making five different salad dressings. After an hour of chopping and mixing, I proudly set the tall bottles on the counter, suggesting they needed labels.

“Don’t bother,” Sarah said, stirring a pot of crème brulee. “We don’t have time. Just taste them before you use them.”

This offended my organizational sensibilities. I spent far too long hunting for masking tape and a felt marker and carefully labelling each bottle. As I put them into the fridge, I thought it was clear that there were still a few things my daughter could learn from me.

And so began a week of chopping, peeling, mixing, stirring and scrubbing. My job was to work under the chef, carry out instructions quickly and efficiently. I was also to keep what I May have thought were good suggestions to myself.

This is not always easy when the chef is your daughter. When Sarah was young, I had been the one overseeing kitchen tasks, insisting things be done my way. Now she was looking over my shoulder, asking me to pick up the pace, make the charcuterie platter more attractive, suggesting I be extra careful when plating dessert.

After many hours on my feet and too little sleep, I sometimes couldn’t help but make a few snappish comments. Once, when Sarah told me to make another pot of rice because mine wasn’t light and fluffy enough, I found myself close to tears.

But as we settled into the daily routine, I started really watching what Sarah was doing. She could have five pots bubbling on the stove and several pans in the oven while decorating 10 plates with sauces, herbs and flowers. She knew exactly when to pull crab from a huge pot of boiling water and how long to sear fresh ling cod. She was calm, exacting and completely in charge.

Even when I burned a pan of pine nuts, she remained calm. Another test arose after I had prepared a beautiful Mediterranean salad with olives, feta, grape tomatoes and fresh herbs. I took my carefully labelled balsamic dressing from the fridge, gave the salad a generous coating and handed it to Sarah.

She popped a tomato into her mouth and frowned.

“You used the Asian dressing.”

Somehow, in my determination to label everything properly, I had mixed up the labels.

The guests were already seated. There was no time to start again. Sarah smiled, picked up the plates and carried them to the dining room. Miraculously, there were no complaints. After that, I tasted everything.

At the end of each day, guided by moonlight, Sarah and I made our way up to our little cabin in the trees. We would pour a glass of wine and talk about the day – the things that went wrong, the things that went right, the antics of the guest, sometimes laughing until we cried. Usually, after only a few sips, we crawled into bed, exhausted.

Eventually Sarah found a young sous-chef to take my place. She carried my bag down the boat and gave me a hug.

“You were great, Mom,” she said. “Are you sure you don’t want to stay?”

“I’m lucky I made it through the week,” I laughed.

As the boat pulled away, I waved at my daughter standing on the dock, amazed that she could keep up this pace for another two weeks.

I had gone to the island because I thought Sarah needed me. It turned out I needed the week, too – to step out of my familiar role as her mother. There hadn’t been any time to explore the island, swim in the bay, watch for whales. Instead, there were precious hours with my daughter, a unique opportunity to work side-by-side, to see the capable and resilient woman she had become.

Ann Diehl lives in Kamloops, B.C.

stories.title: Canada’s Eurovision finalists include Rêve, Tyler Shaw
stories.summary: The public will be invited to vote for Canada’s Eurovision entrant from the five finalists, with the winner set to be announced by December.
stories.author: Alex Nino Gheciu
stories.content:
The five finalists vying to represent Canada at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest have been announced.

They are Montreal dance-pop artist Rêve, Quebec vocalist William Cloutier, Ottawa pop-rocker Talk, New Brunswick singer-songwriter Josiane and B.C. pop crooner Tyler Shaw.

CBC/Radio-Canada revealed the competitors Tuesday at a splashy media event in Toronto.

The public broadcaster says 325 artists from across Canada applied earlier this year for a chance to become the country’s inaugural representative at the international music competition.

The public will be invited to vote for Canada’s Eurovision entrant, with the winner set to be announced by December.

Canada will make its official debut at the 71st Eurovision Song Contest, set to take place next May in Burgas, Bulgaria. It will be the first new country to join the competition since Australia in 2015.

CBC/Radio-Canada said its music team sifted through applications to make initial selections before a seven-member jury chose the finalists at an Oct. 8 meeting in Toronto.

The panel included Montreal International Jazz Festival programming director Maurin Auxéméry, choreographer and director Sam Chouinard, television composer and musical director Orin Isaacs, social media strategist and Eurovision specialist Shawn Myers, and soprano Élisabeth St-Gelais.

Rounding out the jury were Radio-Canada executive vice-president Dany Meloul and CBC executive vice-president Douglas Smith.

CBC/Radio-Canada said the winning artist will then work with leading music-industry talent to develop Canada’s Eurovision song and performance.

Eurovision is considered one of the world’s largest live music spectacles.

Organizers say more than 130 million viewers across 35 markets watched this year’s edition. The event also drew unprecedented social engagement, including more than a billion views on Instagram alone.

The competition has helped propel several major artists to international fame.

Céline Dion’s 1988 win for Switzerland, with the Swiss-written song “Ne partez pas sans moi,” launched her to international stardom.

The contest also helped turn Abba from a Swedish touring band into global superstars, while Italy’s Måneskin achieved international success following their 2021 win.

The competition has also faced controversy. Israel’s participation amid the conflict in Gaza prompted five public service broadcasters — from Ireland, the Netherlands, Spain, Slovenia and Iceland — to boycott this year’s event.

Ireland’s public broadcaster RTÉ has confirmed a second consecutive boycott of both participating in and broadcasting next year’s Eurovision Song Contest.

In contrast, the Netherlands is making a complicated return; while its entertainment broadcaster Avrotros continues its boycott, the umbrella public broadcaster NPO has stepped in to ensure the country competes in Burgas.

In 2022, the European Broadcasting Union banned Russia from participating in the contest following its invasion of Ukraine.

stories.title: Lots of sunshine despite slightly cooler temperatures
stories.summary: There’s lots of sunshine through southern Ontario, despite temperatures cooling slightly Tuesday.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
There’s lots of sunshine through southern Ontario, despite temperatures cooling slightly Tuesday.

CTV Meteorologist Julie Atchison says temperatures are in the low to mid-teens, between 9 and 11 C throughout Huron-Perth and Grey-Bruce and are expected to rise a couple of degrees throughout the afternoon.

“High pressure will continue to drift into south and central Quebec and I’m tracking a warm front that will arrive as we head into tomorrow,” Atchison said.

“That means a push of warmth across the area and overnight temperatures are set to climb. So, some nice warm air moving in for your Wednesday.”

Overnight, temperatures will fall to 7 C.

Here’s a full look at your forecast:

Tuesday night: Partly cloudy. Low 7 C.

Wednesday: A mix of sun and cloud. High 18 C.

Wednesday night: Clear. Low 9 C.

Thursday: A mix of sun and cloud with a 30 per cent chance of showers. High 20 C.

Friday: Sunny. High 16 C.

stories.title: Former Ontario cabinet minister who resigned over expenses scandal defends promotion
stories.summary: A former member of Ontario Premier Doug Ford's cabinet who resigned his post over an expenses scandal is defending his recent promotion.
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
A former member of Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s cabinet who resigned his post over an expenses scandal is defending his recent promotion.

Stan Cho resigned as tourism, culture and gaming minister in July after expensing $16,000 in Toronto hotel stays despite living in the city.

Cho says he made a mistake and has repaid the debt to taxpayers.

Ford recently promoted Cho to parliamentary assistant to Education Minister Paul Calandra, which comes with a $22,000 pay bump.

Publicly available expense records show that some of Ford’s cabinet ministers and other caucus members who live in and near Toronto had been using a so-called special circumstances rule on Toronto hotel expenses since about 2023.

Opposition parties have called for Cho to resign his seat in the legislature and say a promotion is outrageous.

stories.title: After election victory, Chow to face budget pressure and new deal with Ontario
stories.summary: Negotiations with the province to help relieve Toronto's budget pressures loomed over Olivia Chow's election victory, as she vowed to be the "mayor for everyone."
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
Negotiations with the province to help relieve Toronto’s budget pressures loomed over Olivia Chow’s election victory, as she vowed to be the “mayor for everyone.”

Chow fended off challenger Brad Bradford and convinced voters to back her progressive agenda for a second term headlined by free school lunches and a weekly transit fare cap.

She reiterated today her promise to keep property taxes at or around the rate of inflation while fielding questions about negotiations for new budget help from the province.

Chow, who negotiated a 2023 deal set to expire this year for $1.2 billion in operating cash from the province, is facing down a 2027 budget shortfall the city has put at roughly $1.1 billion.

Fresh off Monday’s win, she also deflected questions about whether this would be her last term, saying she intends to spend “every moment” of the next four years “working hard for the people of Toronto”.

Premier Doug Ford congratulated Chow on the victory and says he will “work with anyone to drive the economy to make sure we protect communities and companies and people” from U.S. tariffs.

stories.title: Galloway success disappeared 'almost overnight' following assault claims: publisher
stories.summary: Vancouver - An executive publisher for Steven Galloway's books says the author became persona non grata in the literary community, with sales potential disappearing "almost overnight," following unproven allegations of sexual assault against him in 2015.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A publisher for Steven Galloway’s books has testified that the author became persona non grata in the literary community, with speaking engagements and sales potential disappearing “almost overnight,” following unproven allegations of sexual assault.

“It was extraordinary and I had not seen that before ever,” said Louise Dennys, a high-profile figure in the publishing industry who served as executive vice-president at Penguin Random House Canada and helped edit and promote Galloway’s work.

Her testimony via video conference on Tuesday came midway through the hearing of Galloway’s defamation lawsuit against his accuser, a former student at the University of British Columbia, and other defendants in a Vancouver B.C. Supreme Court.

Dennys said Galloway’s third book, “The Cellist of Sarajevo,” was met with “spectacular” success in Canada and internationally, and while his subsequent book, “The Confabulist,” didn’t initially reach those heights, the assault allegations forced the publisher to shelve the marketing campaign for its paperback run.

Galloway, the former chair of creative writing at the university in Vancouver, denies the allegations, which emerged in late 2015.

He is suing his accuser, known as A.B., whose assault claims were found unsubstantiated by a former judge, and other defendants, alleging they defamed him by publishing the unproven allegations online and elsewhere.

The court has previously heard from Galloway’s literary agent, Henry Dunow, who testified the allegations resulted in the cancellation of a $100,000 contract for a three-novel series Galloway pitched about a ventriloquist detective.

Dennys said Tuesday the publisher had signed the contract after Mary Ellen Boyd, the retired judged hired by the university to look into the allegations against Galloway, completed her probe and found the assault claims unsubstantiated.

Boyd’s report, which wasn’t made public, gave the publisher “the hope that the thing would die away completely now, because (Boyd) had indicated that there were no grounds for substantiating a rape,” Dennys said.

But the allegations didn’t cease, she said.

“We held in for two years waiting for things to pass, but in 2018, we eventually put it on hold, the (detective) series, because Steven indicated to us that he simply did not, trauma had been so great, that he certainly didn’t have the ability to write.”

Dennys said it was “one of the most heartbreaking things” she’d heard as a publisher.

Under cross-examination, Sydney Gomez, counsel for A.B., showed Dennys a chart that she said showed declining sales of “The Cellist of Sarajevo” predating the allegations.

But there was confusion over the way the figures were laid out, and Dennys said they didn’t match her recollection of the book that sold more than 130,000 copies in Canada.

Dennys also disagreed with the assertion from Gomez that the publisher expected “The Confabulist” to perform as well as its predecessor, saying it was common for successful authors to explore new creative possibilities.

Several people originally named as defendants in the lawsuit filed in 2018 have settled with Galloway and offered public apologies.

The court learned earlier this month that A.B. was no longer asserting in her defence that Galloway assaulted her, rather that she reported he had done so.

paragraphs: Vancouver - A publisher for Steven Galloway’s books has testified that the author became persona non grata in the literary community, with speaking engagements and sales potential disappearing “almost overnight,” following unproven allegations of sexual assault.

“It was extraordinary and I had not seen that before ever,” said Louise Dennys, a high-profile figure in the publishing industry who served as executive vice-president at Penguin Random House Canada and helped edit and promote Galloway’s work.

Her testimony via video conference on Tuesday came midway through the hearing of Galloway’s defamation lawsuit against his accuser, a former student at the University of British Columbia, and other defendants in a Vancouver B.C. Supreme Court.

Dennys said Galloway’s third book, “The Cellist of Sarajevo,” was met with “spectacular” success in Canada and internationally, and while his subsequent book, “The Confabulist,” didn’t initially reach those heights, the assault allegations forced the publisher to shelve the marketing campaign for its paperback run.
Galloway, the former chair of creative writing at the university in Vancouver, denies the allegations, which emerged in late 2015.

He is suing his accuser, known as A.B., whose assault claims were found unsubstantiated by a former judge, and other defendants, alleging they defamed him by publishing the unproven allegations online and elsewhere.

The court has previously heard from Galloway’s literary agent, Henry Dunow, who testified the allegations resulted in the cancellation of a $100,000 contract for a three-novel series Galloway pitched about a ventriloquist detective.

Dennys said Tuesday the publisher had signed the contract after Mary Ellen Boyd, the retired judged hired by the university to look into the allegations against Galloway, completed her probe and found the assault claims unsubstantiated.

Boyd’s report, which wasn’t made public, gave the publisher “the hope that the thing would die away completely now, because (Boyd) had indicated that there were no grounds for substantiating a rape,” Dennys said.
But the allegations didn’t cease, she said.

“We held in for two years waiting for things to pass, but in 2018, we eventually put it on hold, the (detective) series, because Steven indicated to us that he simply did not, trauma had been so great, that he certainly didn’t have the ability to write.”

stories.title: Unclaimed $40M Lotto Max ticket expires Wednesday, OLG says
stories.summary: An unclaimed Lotto Max ticket worth $40 million will expire Wednesday, the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation says.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
An unclaimed Lotto Max ticket worth $40 million will expire Wednesday, the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG) says.

The winning ticket from the Oct. 28, 2025, Lotto Max draw was bought at an authorized retailer somewhere in Grey County, the OLG said in a news release Tuesday.

It will expire Wednesday – one year since the draw was held.

With only hours remaining, the OLG is urging anyone who purchased a Lotto Max ticket in Grey County, or anyone who visited the area around the time of the draw, to check their tickets immediately.

Grey County is made up of communities like Owen Sound, Meaford, The Blue Mountains, Flesherton, Markdale, Durham and Hanover.

“Because Grey County is a popular destination for tourists, cottagers and day-trippers, there is possibility that the winning ticket May not belong to a local resident,” the OLG said.

“Someone visiting the area could have purchased the ticket, tucked it away and never realized they were holding a $40 million jackpot winner.”

The winning numbers for the Oct. 28, 2025, Lotto Max draw are 6, 14, 17, 19, 26, 43, 45, with 27 being the bonus number.

stories.title: Trump slaps tariffs on Canadian 'trash trucks.' How much garbage is being sent to the U.S.?
stories.summary: Donald Trump has added tariffs to 100 more Candian imports, one of which is municipal waste, meaning garbage from households and businesses.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
On Friday, U.S. President Donald Trump removed 50 per cent tariffs on 22 Canadian goods. But he added tariffs to 100 more, including municipal waste — meaning garbage from households and businesses.

The move has been backed by Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who has spent decades raising his concerns about Canadian garbage imports. Speaking on stage with Trump at a rally in Port Huron on Sunday, Rogers accused Canada of sending “truck after truck after truck loaded with their trash into our state.”

But how much Canadian garbage actually crosses the border into the U.S., and why is it being sent there?

Canada is the largest source of waste imports to Michigan, accounting for 14 per cent of all waste disposed of in Michigan landfills in fiscal year 2025, according to a March report by the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (Egle).

Michigan’s proximity to Canada, combined with its relatively low landfill tipping fees (just 36 cents per tonne), makes it an appealing option for organizations in Canada responsible for disposing of waste.

Solid waste imports from Canada reached almost 3.2 million tonnes, down 8 per cent from FY 2024, when 3.5 million tonnes of solid waste was imported to Michigan from Canada.

Meanwhile, other U.S. states made up less than 4 per cent of waste disposed of in Michigan landfills in 2025. Waste that originated in Michigan made up 82 per cent.

Canada doesn’t track its own waste exports, according to a 2024 report from Environment and Climate Change Canada .

However, Waste to Resource Ontario (W2RO), which represents organizations in the waste, recycling, and resource management sector in the province, reports that, in 2024, 27 per cent (3.44 million tonnes) of waste that was generated in Ontario and sent to landfills was exported to the U.S.

The exported waste was sent primarily to Michigan, New York and Ohio.

Like Canada, the U.S. doesn’t consistently track shipments of municipal waste on a national level. However, a 2003 Canadian government report on imports and exports of non-hazardous waste suggests that far less garbage enters Canada from the U.S. than in the opposite direction.

It estimated that Canada imported approximately 35,000 tonnes of non-hazardous waste from the U.S. for landfill disposal in 2003, compared to the 3 million tonnes exported from Canada to the U.S. in the same year.

According to the WR2O report, Ontario is running out of landfill capacity. It says that if the borders close to Ontario’s waste, the province will run out of landfill capacity by 2034. And even while maintaining exports to U.S. landfills, it predicts that the average remaining capacity will be depleted by 2037.

Meanwhile, Michigan’s landfill tipping fees are relatively low. Last year, Michigan’s Governor Gretchen Whitmer recommended increasing fees from the solid waste surcharge from 36 cents per tonne to US$5 per ton in the 2026 fiscal budget proposal .

The proposal said this would bring Michigan in line with the average Midwest tipping fee as well as “directly addressing the volume of out-of-state waste.”

Municipal and clinical waste are among the new items that will be subject to 50 per cent tariffs from Oct. 30, under an amendment issued by the White House on Friday.

Trump said he was providing a tariff exemption for some agricultural goods that are “consistent with the interest of the United States,” allowing 22 products previously subject to 50 per cent tariffs to cross the border duty free, while 100 new products were added under Section 338.

Items subject to exemption include refrigeration and freezing equipment, agricultural machinery and packing equipment, while other new items that will be subject to tariffs include cocoa powder, carpets and shampoo.

Rogers has been raising the issue of Canadian waste imports for decades. In a floor speech in the U.S. House in 2002 , he said that Canada sent 4.2 million cubic yards of waste to Michigan in the year 2000, and expressed concerns about the environmental impact on Michigan.

In 2003, Rogers backed a Bill that would have amended the Solid Waste Disposal Act to allow states to enact laws prohibiting or limiting the receipt of waste from other countries, but it never made it past the committee stage.

On Friday, Rogers called the new tariffs on waste coming from Canada “huge progress” in a video posted on social media, adding Canada’s “trash trucks” have been “a huge problem” for Michigan.

“I called the secretary’s office a few days ago and said, ‘Listen, we need some relief on Canadian tariffs. But if you’re going to tariff anything, tariff those trash trucks,'” he said.

But the Michigan Senate hopeful hasn’t always been so emphatic in his support of Trump’s trade war, having previously broken ranks in a campaign video shared on social media.

“Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now. As Michigan senator, I’ll bring both parties together to lower your prices,” he said in the clip.

Meanwhile, Michigan has become a key battleground for the upcoming U.S. midterms and is currently considered a toss-up for the Senate race by The Cook Political Report .

The Democrats need to gain four more seats to win back the Senate majority in the upcoming mid-term elections on Nov. 3.

content_blocks.text: On Friday, U.S. President Donald Trump removed 50 per cent tariffs on 22 Canadian goods. But he added tariffs to 100 more, including municipal waste — meaning garbage from households and businesses.

The move has been backed by Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who has spent decades raising his concerns about Canadian garbage imports. Speaking on stage with Trump at a rally in Port Huron on Sunday, Rogers accused Canada of sending “truck after truck after truck loaded with their trash into our state.”
But how much Canadian garbage actually crosses the border into the U.S., and why is it being sent there?
How much garbage does Canada send to Michigan?

Canada is the largest source of waste imports to Michigan, accounting for 14 per cent of all waste disposed of in Michigan landfills in fiscal year 2025, according to a March report by the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (Egle).
content_blocks.html: Canada is the largest source of waste imports to Michigan, accounting for 14 per cent of all waste disposed of in Michigan landfills in fiscal year 2025, according to a March report by the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE).

content_blocks.text: Michigan’s proximity to Canada, combined with its relatively low landfill tipping fees (just 36 cents per tonne), makes it an appealing option for organizations in Canada responsible for disposing of waste.
Solid waste imports from Canada reached almost 3.2 million tonnes, down 8 per cent from FY 2024, when 3.5 million tonnes of solid waste was imported to Michigan from Canada.
Meanwhile, other U.S. states made up less than 4 per cent of waste disposed of in Michigan landfills in 2025. Waste that originated in Michigan made up 82 per cent.
How much garbage does Canada send to the U.S.?
Canada doesn’t track its own waste exports, according to a 2024 report from Environment and Climate Change Canada .
content_blocks.html: Canada doesn’t track its own waste exports, according to a 2024 report from Environment and Climate Change Canada.

content_blocks.text: However, Waste to Resource Ontario (W2RO), which represents organizations in the waste, recycling, and resource management sector in the province, reports that, in 2024, 27 per cent (3.44 million tonnes) of waste that was generated in Ontario and sent to landfills was exported to the U.S.

content_blocks.text: The exported waste was sent primarily to Michigan, New York and Ohio.

Like Canada, the U.S. doesn’t consistently track shipments of municipal waste on a national level. However, a 2003 Canadian government report on imports and exports of non-hazardous waste suggests that far less garbage enters Canada from the U.S. than in the opposite direction.

However, a 2003 Canadian government report on imports and exports of non-hazardous waste suggests that far less garbage enters Canada from the U.S. than in the opposite direction.

content_blocks.text: It estimated that Canada imported approximately 35,000 tonnes of non-hazardous waste from the U.S. for landfill disposal in 2003, compared to the 3 million tonnes exported from Canada to the U.S. in the same year.

content_blocks.text: Why does Ontario send its garbage to Michigan?

According to the WR2O report, Ontario is running out of landfill capacity. It says that if the borders close to Ontario’s waste, the province will run out of landfill capacity by 2034. And even while maintaining exports to U.S. landfills, it predicts that the average remaining capacity will be depleted by 2037.

Meanwhile, Michigan’s landfill tipping fees are relatively low. Last year, Michigan’s Governor Gretchen Whitmer recommended increasing fees from the solid waste surcharge from 36 cents per tonne to US$5 per ton in the 2026 fiscal budget proposal .
content_blocks.html: Meanwhile, Michigan’s landfill tipping fees are relatively low. Last year, Michigan’s Governor Gretchen Whitmer recommended increasing fees from the solid waste surcharge from 36 cents per tonne to US$5 per ton in the 2026 fiscal budget proposal.

content_blocks.text: The proposal said this would bring Michigan in line with the average Midwest tipping fee as well as “directly addressing the volume of out-of-state waste.”
Will Canada’s waste shipments be affected by U.S. tariffs?
Municipal and clinical waste are among the new items that will be subject to 50 per cent tariffs from Oct. 30, under an amendment issued by the White House on Friday.

Trump said he was providing a tariff exemption for some agricultural goods that are “consistent with the interest of the United States,” allowing 22 products previously subject to 50 per cent tariffs to cross the border duty free, while 100 new products were added under Section 338.

Items subject to exemption include refrigeration and freezing equipment, agricultural machinery and packing equipment, while other new items that will be subject to tariffs include cocoa powder, carpets and shampoo.
What has Mike Rogers said?

Rogers has been raising the issue of Canadian waste imports for decades. In a floor speech in the U.S. House in 2002 , he said that Canada sent 4.2 million cubic yards of waste to Michigan in the year 2000, and expressed concerns about the environmental impact on Michigan.

“I called the secretary’s office a few days ago and said, ‘Listen, we need some relief on Canadian tariffs. But if you’re going to tariff anything, tariff those trash trucks,'” he said.

stories.title: Chow turns to new Ontario deal after fending off Bradford in mayoral election
stories.summary: Chow reiterated her promise to keep property taxes in check while fielding questions about negotiations for new budget help
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
Negotiations with the province to help relieve Toronto’s budget pressures loomed over Olivia Chow’s election victory on Tuesday, as she vowed to be the “mayor for everyone.”

Chow took her first question from reporters hours after she held off challenger Brad Bradford in Monday’s election and convinced voters to back a second term of her progressive agenda.

“There’s a firm belief that we are stronger together. And the majority of the people of Toronto spoke out so loudly, with such enthusiasm,” she said.

“They know that we can take better care of each other.”

Her peacemaking political style earned her approving words from Premier Doug Ford during the campaign, who stopped just short of endorsing her in the contest.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow says it doesn't matter who voted for her, she'll be mayor for everyone in Toronto, and will work with the new council and other levels of government to addr…

Now, Chow will likely look to summon that goodwill as she looks to negotiations with Ford on a new Toronto-Ontario fiscal deal. The city has projected a 2027 budget hole of around $1.1-billion. Transit ridership continues to lag behind pre-pandemic levels while a softening real estate market is expected to squeeze the municipal land transfer tax.

Chow inherited a $1.8-billion shortfall when she was first elected in 2023. She sought to plug the hole with two sizable property tax increases and a major deal with Ford’s government. Ontario assumed maintenance of the city’s expressways and provided $1.2-billion in operating dollars for transit and shelters, while Chow dropped the city’s opposition to the Ontario Place redevelopment.

That deal is now set to expire at the same time as Chow has campaigned on a promise to keep property taxes at or below the rate of inflation. She reiterated that tax pledge on Tuesday while highlighting that the city had secured its first credit-rating upgrade in more than two decades during her first term.

“I do know the budget very well. I just hope that there is no surprises from outside the City of Toronto, but I don’t expect any,” she said.

Asked on Tuesday how quickly she planned to hash out a new deal with the province, Chow said she had exchanged texts with the premier earlier that morning.

“And no matter which level of government, whether it’s a federal or provincial government, they want to work together and they want do the best they can for the residents of Toronto.”

Chow managed to stave off her challenger on a night where several incumbents were toppled in Ontario’s municipal elections, including Mississauga’s Carolyn Parrish, Hamilton’s Andrea Horwath and Windsor’s Drew Dilkens.

Premier Doug Ford congratulated Chow on the victory and says he will “work with anyone to drive the economy to make sure we protect communities and companies and people” from U.S. tariffs.

Chow will preside over a council with a boosted progressive bloc as she seeks to make good on other campaign promises to cap weekly transit fares, introduce free school lunches and strengthen renter protections.

The departure of rival Bradford from council heralded the political resurrection of former Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith, who aligned himself with Chow in his successful run in Beaches East-York after a failed pivot to provincial politics. Chiara Padovani, a tenant organizer, defeated Toronto’s longest-serving councillor Frances Nunziata in York South-Weston.

Voter turnout was around 46 per cent, the highest it’s been since 2014. Chow’s 13 percentage point victory over Bradford would mark the narrowest win by a sitting mayor since the city’s amalgamation.

The dust barely had time to settle on Monday night’s election before Chow, 69, was asked about her long-term political future. As she stood outside city hall, she brushed off a question Tuesday about whether this would be her last run for mayor.

“I’m going to spend every moment of today and the next four years working hard for the people of Toronto,” she said. “As to the future, let us take one day, one week, one month, one year at a time.”

stories.title: EU representative praises closer work with Canada on vaccines as U.S. pulls back
stories.summary: Ottawa - The European Union is working more closely with Canada on creating, stockpiling and researching vaccines as the United States pulls back, says a senior official from Brussels.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson and Émilie Bergeron The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The European Union is working more closely with Canada on creating, stockpiling and researching vaccines as the United States pulls back, says a senior official from Brussels.

“Our production, research and development capabilities, and how we communicate about our existing (vaccine) stock, are extremely sensitive matters,” European Crisis Management Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said in a French-language interview Monday in Ottawa.

“Canada is the only country outside the European Union with which we do this.”

Lahbib said her visit was scheduled before plans were made for the EU-Canada summit that starts Thursday in Montreal. She said the health sector is one of many fields where the bloc wants to work closely with Canada.

“This shows the level of closeness we have today, and of trust. And so, we are now going to begin this work in the health sector, boosting research, in life sciences … to be stronger together,” she said.

The goal, she said, is to “truly secure our supply chain (and) not depend on actors who are becoming less and less loyal, or let’s say less and less predictable, in order to be able to confront all the dangers we face today.”

Alexandre Bergeron, a spokesperson for the Office of the Minister of Health, said in an email that the lessons from recent global health emergencies have shown that preparedness begins long before a crisis occurs.

“Through our strengthened partnership with the European Union, Canada is building a stronger health system by advancing research, innovation, and supply chain resilience to ensure critical medical countermeasures are available when needed,” said Bergeron.

In fall 2024, Ottawa launched Health Emergency Readiness Canada, an agency the government said is “dedicated to protecting Canadians against future pandemics and delivering on Canada’s life sciences and medical countermeasures readiness objectives.”

The agency has had little public visibility and has an interim chair.

In June 2025, the agency’s EU equivalent signed an agreement with Health Emergency Readiness Canada to co-ordinate on cross-border public health threats.

Lahbib said that work includes sharing information on chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear threats linked to anything from terrorism to laboratory mishaps to pandemics.

Health Emergency Readiness Canada’s agreement could see Europe and Canada work closer together on securing raw ingredients for vaccines and share information on vaccine shortages. Canada and Europe could also link up their supply chains to ensure adequate supplies of masks and other protective gear in a future pandemic.

The two jurisdictions are already co-ordinating research in fields like vaccine development through partnerships such as the Horizon Europe grant program, Lahbib said.

That research might be deployed against future threats emerging from climate change, including viruses trapped in permafrost that could be unleashed for the first time in centuries.

“It truly spans every sector. The efforts are aligned so that, at a technical level, we continue to work together and share the workload,” she said. “It’s extremely unique.”

Lahbib, who is Belgian, noted that the first COVID-19 vaccines to reach Canada came from a Pfizer lab in her home country. Now, a Moderna plant in Montreal is helping European efforts to invent vaccines to combat the Ebola strain ravaging parts of Congo.

“If we work directly hand-in-hand with Canada, it will go faster,” she said.

She said both jurisdictions are also planning “stress tests” to assess how well they can respond to major threats.

Lahbib contrasted this approach to border-crossing disease outbreaks to that of the United States under President Donald Trump.

Trump’s administration has promoted vaccine skeptics and made it harder to secure COVID-19 shots and childhood immunizations. It has drastically cut back funding for medical research on ideological grounds.

“There have been policy changes in the United States, including in vaccine research, even against measles, with increasingly frequent cases of measles because there is a certain skepticism that has taken hold. It is by no means impossible that we could see cases of measles in Europe as a result,” Lahbib said.

“We also have pharmaceutical companies whose research is under threat, and has almost ground to a halt, because of a policy change in the United States. So, where do we welcome them? In Canada? In Europe?

“In any case, we believe in science. We trust scientific research, we share the same values and we believe in multilateralism, too.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

The two jurisdictions are already co-ordinating research in fields like vaccine development through partnerships such as the Horizon Europe grant program, Lahbib said.
That research might be deployed against future threats emerging from climate change, including viruses trapped in permafrost that could be unleashed for the first time in centuries.
“It truly spans every sector. The efforts are aligned so that, at a technical level, we continue to work together and share the workload,” she said. “It’s extremely unique.”

Lahbib, who is Belgian, noted that the first COVID-19 vaccines to reach Canada came from a Pfizer lab in her home country. Now, a Moderna plant in Montreal is helping European efforts to invent vaccines to combat the Ebola strain ravaging parts of Congo.
“If we work directly hand-in-hand with Canada, it will go faster,” she said.
She said both jurisdictions are also planning “stress tests” to assess how well they can respond to major threats.
Lahbib contrasted this approach to border-crossing disease outbreaks to that of the United States under President Donald Trump.

Trump’s administration has promoted vaccine skeptics and made it harder to secure COVID-19 shots and childhood immunizations. It has drastically cut back funding for medical research on ideological grounds.

“There have been policy changes in the United States, including in vaccine research, even against measles, with increasingly frequent cases of measles because there is a certain skepticism that has taken hold. It is by no means impossible that we could see cases of measles in Europe as a result,” Lahbib said.

“We also have pharmaceutical companies whose research is under threat, and has almost ground to a halt, because of a policy change in the United States. So, where do we welcome them? In Canada? In Europe?
“In any case, we believe in science. We trust scientific research, we share the same values and we believe in multilateralism, too.”

stories.title: ‘$40 million is a lot of money!’: Lotto ticket bought in Grey County unclaimed with 24 hours until deadline
stories.summary: Tony Bitonti has the cheque already made up, he just needs to fill in the name of the ticket holder of a $40 million LottoMax prize, that could expire if not claimed soon.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Tony Bitonti has the cheque already made up, he just needs to fill in the name of the ticket holder of a $40 million LottoMax prize, that could expire if not claimed soon.

“We’ve been waiting. Almost a year. It’s going to be a year in a little less than 24 hours that we’ve been waiting for this $40 million ticket holder to come forward,” said Bitonti, Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation’s Media Relations Coordinator.

“And what I can tell you, and this is the sad part, is that this ticket has not even been checked yet. Not been checked on our OLG app, not at our retailer.”

The $40 million ticket was bought somewhere in Grey County for the Oct. 28, 2025, draw. The winning numbers are 06, 14, 17, 19, 26, 43, 43, with bonus number 27.

“So, OLG has every piece of information about this ticket, except one critical piece of information. Exactly who the owner is, Bitonti added.

“But we know exactly where it was purchased. When it was purchased, what else it was purchased with. Was there an encore? Did they also buy a 6/49 ticket or a Pro Line ticket? We have all that information. We just need the ticket holder to come forward. And even if they’ve lost the ticket, to come forward with that information and we’ll do some due diligence, we’ll make sure that they are the rightful owner and then hopefully we can pay them $40 million.”

60 people have already claimed they have the winning ticket, but Bitonti says all the information hasn’t added up yet, so they are still searching. If the winner doesn’t come forward before midnight on Oct. 28, the $40 million goes back into the prize pool.

“Listen, $40 million is a lot of money. That’s life-changing amounts of money. And it’s not our money. It’s not Olg’s money,” Bitonti said.

“It is somebody that paid five or $10 for a ticket at a $40 million jackpot, and won the jackpot and hasn’t come forward to claim it. So where is this person? That’s the $40 million question, and I hope to fill in the name on this cheque, very soon.”

If you believe you purchased this winning Lotto MAX ticket, you can go to the OLG.CA Unclaimed Tickets page to fill in your information to start the claim or contact OLG at 1-800-387-0098.

stories.title: Ontario modernizes hydro utilities to drive economic growth, cites London Hydro success
stories.summary: The Ontario government is rolling out significant changes aimed at strengthening the province’s hydro utilities, improving competitiveness, protecting consumers, and bolstering the economy.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
The Ontario government is rolling out significant changes aimed at strengthening the province’s hydro utilities, improving competitiveness, protecting consumers, and bolstering the economy. Citing the need to meet escalating energy demands and modernize aging infrastructure, the province is looking to models like London Hydro for effective leadership.

During a news conference at Queen’s Park on Tuesday morning, Minister of Energy and Mines Stephen Lecce announced a suite of legislative and regulatory reforms designed to prepare Ontario’s electricity distribution sector for future challenges.

The province projects that energy demand will increase by the equivalent of the City of Toronto’s entire consumption every six years. A key focus of the proposed reforms is strengthening the governance of municipally owned Local Distribution Companies (LDCs).

The province intends to elevate standards, following the precedent set by municipalities including London, Oakville, and Oshawa, by encouraging the adoption of skills-based boards to enhance transparency, expertise, and good governance practices.

London Hydro was specifically highlighted for its proactive approach. Minister Lecce pointed to the utility’s adoption of a skills-based board as an example of effective leadership, with Lecce stating, “London Hydro. They’ve taken action.

They’ve led the way. They’ve been able to move to embrace this concept of a skills-based board.” Lecce also noted London Hydro’s instrumental role in attracting a $500 million Hitachi transformer insulation plant announced earlier this month.

Ysni Semsedini, CEO of London Hydro, emphasized the critical role utilities play in economic development. “We have never faced a greater challenge in building our system to meet the demands of a growing community,” Semsedini said.

“Over the next decade, we plan to invest more in our infrastructure than we have in the last century. It’s a remarkable undertaking and reinforces why utilities need the right tools to plan for and finance the grid of tomorrow.” The government’s plan also includes new authorities to drive joint and local procurement initiatives, promoting “Buy Ontario” and “Buy Canada” policies to improve efficiency and scale.

Enabling greater use of shared services is also a strategy to help utilities reduce costs. To ensure long-term planning, utilities will be required to develop 10-year plans that encompass condition assessments, financing strategies, and workforce development.

These measures come as the Electricity Distributors Association forecasts up to $120 billion in distribution investments over the next two decades to meet growing demand and replace aging infrastructure. The reforms also aim to enhance consumer protection, particularly for residents in condominiums, apartments, and multi-unit residential buildings served by unit sub-metre providers.

This includes a ban on winter disconnections and increased transparency for ratepayers.

stories.title: Regis Korchinski-Paquet's mother questions purpose of coroner's inquest
stories.summary: Toronto - Regis Korchinski-Paquet's mother questioned Tuesday the purpose of a coroner's inquest examining the circumstances of her daughter's death as she was pressed to clarify what she saw that day.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s mother questioned the purpose of a coroner’s inquest examining the circumstances of her daughter’s death as well as the video and audio evidence presented in it, as lawyers for several police officers pressed her Tuesday to clarify what she saw that day.

Claudette Beals was again shown excerpts of a video combining security footage from the hallway outside the apartment with audio from a police microphone as she resumed her testimony at the inquest.

Last week, Beals testified she saw police push her daughter toward the balcony, causing the inquest to halt for several hours as counsel for the parties figured out how to move forward.

A lawyer representing one of the officers who was in the apartment when Korchinski-Paquet went over the balcony cross-examined her Tuesday, suggesting Beals was only inside the apartment for about a minute and also didn’t understand what was happening at the time.

Gary Clewley played a portion of the video where someone can be heard asking, “What is she doing?”

Last week, Beals agreed it was her and that she was talking about her daughter, but at one point Tuesday, she said she was actually asking what police were doing, drawing further questions.

“That’s you, isn’t it?” Clewley asked after pausing the clip.

“That’s me because I couldn’t hear Regis’s voice anymore and I wanted to know what was going on,” Beals said.

As the exchange went on, Beals voiced her frustration with the inquest process.

“I thought this was for change. I didn’t really know that I’m going through a court case and we’re here to make the police look better,” she said, a sentiment she later repeated. “I didn’t know that the inquest was about this.”

Moments later, she asked to take a break and the inquest paused for lunch.

The nearly 50-minute video, which in some parts includes audio from five 911 calls, has previously been played in its entirety.

Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman, fell to her death from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in the home on May 27, 2020.

The inquest has largely focused on her history of seizures from epilepsy and the episodes of confusion and aggressive behaviour that often followed, as well as police procedures and training.

A neurologist who did not treat her but examined her records testified that she’d shown symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium on several occasions in the years before her death. Postictal delirium is an altered mental state that can occur after seizures.

Korchinski-Paquet had experienced two seizures that day, one in the early morning and one in the early afternoon, her mother testified. Beals was one of three people to call 911, and she said she was hoping police would take her daughter to Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health.

On Tuesday, Beals said she felt police escalated the situation. She repeated her allegation that police pushed her daughter toward the balcony and added another: that they’d pushed Korchinski-Paquet in the hallway.

She said the incident was captured on video but agreed it wasn’t in the stretch played for her Tuesday, which began with the officers’ arrival at the building and continued past the point when Korchinski-Paquet went into the apartment with two officers.

A lawyer representing the Toronto Police Association asked Beals about the interview she gave to a police watchdog shortly after her daughter’s death.

At the time, Beals told the Special Investigations Unit that she had heard from her son that officers were “grabbing” Korchinski-Paquet in the hallway but hadn’t seen it herself, Peter Ketcheson said.

Beals said Tuesday she didn’t recall everything during the interview but now remembered officers pushing her daughter in the hallway.

Ketcheson noted Beals made several comments during her testimony calling into question the video and audio evidence shown at the inquest. “Because you don’t trust the video, correct?” he said.

“I don’t trust the police, that’s the problem, not a video — video can’t do nothing by itself, but somebody can alter it,” she said.

“So if I showed you a video that shows something different, you wouldn’t care because you know what you saw,” Ketcheson asked shortly afterward.

“I know what I saw and ... your videos could be altered,” she replied. Her testimony wrapped Tuesday afternoon.

The inquest also heard Tuesday from Korchinski-Paquet’s brother, Reece Korchinski, who testified that he also called 911 that day but had hesitations about the police response based on his previous interactions with police officers.

Korchinski said that once police arrived, they assumed an “aggressive” tone toward his sister.

“I remember their body language, the way they were communicating. They weren’t treating her like a citizen. They were treating her more like a suspect,” he said.

Korchinski said he felt threatened by what appeared to be a shotgun in one of the officer’s hands, but he didn’t know at the time it was a less-lethal weapon used by police. He said it seemed “unnecessary to have that many police officers crowding (Korchinski-Paquet) in such a small space, all carrying firearms.”

As Clewley cross-examined Korchinski while showing portions of the video from the apartment building hallway, the brother agreed that he did not see Korchinski-Paquet in the moments leading up to her death, but said he saw officers “moving aggressively” toward the balcony.

“You did not see the police do anything to your sister in that apartment, correct?” Clewley asked.

“No, all I’ve seen was police moving aggressively towards the balcony,” Korchinski replied before that line of questioning grew tense and the inquest adjourned for the day.

The SIU has cleared the officers of any wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death. The agency found she fell as she was trying to move from her apartment’s balcony to the neighbouring one.

Last Friday, the Toronto Police Association posted on social media that its lawyers would “vociferously cross-examine” Beals about her allegation against police.

Jurors in a coroner’s inquest do not assign blame or legal responsibility but can issue recommendations meant to prevent similar deaths in the future. Those recommendations are not binding, however.

paragraphs: Toronto - Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s mother questioned the purpose of a coroner’s inquest examining the circumstances of her daughter’s death as well as the video and audio evidence presented in it, as lawyers for several police officers pressed her Tuesday to clarify what she saw that day.
Claudette Beals was again shown excerpts of a video combining security footage from the hallway outside the apartment with audio from a police microphone as she resumed her testimony at the inquest.
Last week, Beals testified she saw police push her daughter toward the balcony, causing the inquest to halt for several hours as counsel for the parties figured out how to move forward.

A lawyer representing one of the officers who was in the apartment when Korchinski-Paquet went over the balcony cross-examined her Tuesday, suggesting Beals was only inside the apartment for about a minute and also didn’t understand what was happening at the time.
Gary Clewley played a portion of the video where someone can be heard asking, “What is she doing?”
Last week, Beals agreed it was her and that she was talking about her daughter, but at one point Tuesday, she said she was actually asking what police were doing, drawing further questions.
“That’s you, isn’t it?” Clewley asked after pausing the clip.
“That’s me because I couldn’t hear Regis’s voice anymore and I wanted to know what was going on,” Beals said.
As the exchange went on, Beals voiced her frustration with the inquest process.

“I thought this was for change. I didn’t really know that I’m going through a court case and we’re here to make the police look better,” she said, a sentiment she later repeated. “I didn’t know that the inquest was about this.”
Moments later, she asked to take a break and the inquest paused for lunch.
The nearly 50-minute video, which in some parts includes audio from five 911 calls, has previously been played in its entirety.
Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman, fell to her death from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in the home on May 27, 2020.
The inquest has largely focused on her history of seizures from epilepsy and the episodes of confusion and aggressive behaviour that often followed, as well as police procedures and training.

A neurologist who did not treat her but examined her records testified that she’d shown symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium on several occasions in the years before her death. Postictal delirium is an altered mental state that can occur after seizures.

Korchinski-Paquet had experienced two seizures that day, one in the early morning and one in the early afternoon, her mother testified. Beals was one of three people to call 911, and she said she was hoping police would take her daughter to Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health.

On Tuesday, Beals said she felt police escalated the situation. She repeated her allegation that police pushed her daughter toward the balcony and added another: that they’d pushed Korchinski-Paquet in the hallway.

She said the incident was captured on video but agreed it wasn’t in the stretch played for her Tuesday, which began with the officers’ arrival at the building and continued past the point when Korchinski-Paquet went into the apartment with two officers.
A lawyer representing the Toronto Police Association asked Beals about the interview she gave to a police watchdog shortly after her daughter’s death.

At the time, Beals told the Special Investigations Unit that she had heard from her son that officers were “grabbing” Korchinski-Paquet in the hallway but hadn’t seen it herself, Peter Ketcheson said.
Beals said Tuesday she didn’t recall everything during the interview but now remembered officers pushing her daughter in the hallway.
Ketcheson noted Beals made several comments during her testimony calling into question the video and audio evidence shown at the inquest. “Because you don’t trust the video, correct?” he said.
“I don’t trust the police, that’s the problem, not a video — video can’t do nothing by itself, but somebody can alter it,” she said.
“So if I showed you a video that shows something different, you wouldn’t care because you know what you saw,” Ketcheson asked shortly afterward.
“I know what I saw and ... your videos could be altered,” she replied. Her testimony wrapped Tuesday afternoon.

The inquest also heard Tuesday from Korchinski-Paquet’s brother, Reece Korchinski, who testified that he also called 911 that day but had hesitations about the police response based on his previous interactions with police officers.
Korchinski said that once police arrived, they assumed an “aggressive” tone toward his sister.
“I remember their body language, the way they were communicating. They weren’t treating her like a citizen. They were treating her more like a suspect,” he said.

Korchinski said he felt threatened by what appeared to be a shotgun in one of the officer’s hands, but he didn’t know at the time it was a less-lethal weapon used by police. He said it seemed “unnecessary to have that many police officers crowding (Korchinski-Paquet) in such a small space, all carrying firearms.”

As Clewley cross-examined Korchinski while showing portions of the video from the apartment building hallway, the brother agreed that he did not see Korchinski-Paquet in the moments leading up to her death, but said he saw officers “moving aggressively” toward the balcony.
“You did not see the police do anything to your sister in that apartment, correct?” Clewley asked.
“No, all I’ve seen was police moving aggressively towards the balcony,” Korchinski replied before that line of questioning grew tense and the inquest adjourned for the day.
The SIU has cleared the officers of any wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death. The agency found she fell as she was trying to move from her apartment’s balcony to the neighbouring one.
Last Friday, the Toronto Police Association posted on social media that its lawyers would “vociferously cross-examine” Beals about her allegation against police.
Jurors in a coroner’s inquest do not assign blame or legal responsibility but can issue recommendations meant to prevent similar deaths in the future. Those recommendations are not binding, however.

stories.title: Who is Keanin Loomis, Hamilton's new American-born mayor?
stories.summary: Hamilton has a new mayor in Keanin Loomis, a 51-year-old former lawyer and business professional originally born in the U.S.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Four years after narrowly losing Hamilton’s mayoral election, Keanin Loomis completed his political comeback Monday night.

“Hamilton loves a comeback. It’s a comeback city,” the mayor-elect told CP24 as he celebrated an apparent decisive win over opponents Rob Cooper and incumbent Andrea Horwath.

“It’s poised for a comeback as well, because tonight is the night that we change and we’re headed in a different direction.”

While results are still unofficial, Loomis, 51, came away with nearly 42 per cent of the vote. Cooper, a Hamilton councillor and businessman, finished second (32 per cent) and Horwath, the former Ontario NDP leader who edged Loomis by 1,663 votes in the 2022 municipal election, finished a distant third (14.5 per cent).

Here’s what to know about Loomis, the American-born business leader who became prominent in Steeltown’s economic development community before pursuing public office.

Loomis was born in Oswego, New York, ON the shores of Lake Ontario, in 1974. He was raised in poverty by his mother after his father, whose name he carries, left when he was too young to remember, according to the Hamilton Spectator.

At 12, his mother married a Canadian man with whom she’d been in a long-distance relationship and relocated the family to London, Ont.

He studied political science at the nearby University of Waterloo, where he met his future wife, Hamilton native Trish Loomis, mother to their three children. He then obtained a law degree from the College of William & Mary in Virginia and practised private law in Washington D.C. for almost a decade — getting married and having two kids during this time.

“I didn’t want to give the pound of flesh required to climb in D.C.,” he told the Spectator, noting U.S. politics had lost its sheen for him.

“It’s when I realized that I think I’m actually Canadian.”

When the 2008 economic crisis resulted in a contract buyout from his law firm, he and the family moved back to Hamilton, briefly living in his in-law’s basement.

At the time, he was intent to use Hamilton as a launching point for wider efforts in neighbouring Toronto, according to a pre-election interview with The Public Record , but he “ended up falling in love with this community because of the potential.”

In 2010, Loomis became the founding CEO of the not-for-profit business accelerator Innovation Factory, leaving in 2013 to become president and CEO of the Hamilton Chamber of Commerce.

Upon his departure to run for mayor in 2022, Ontario Chamber of Commerce (OCC) president & CEO Rocco Rossi call Loomis “a brilliant, values-driven, tireless leader” who created a “remarkable legacy” locally, provincially and nationally.

After his failed bid for the mayoralty, he became a vice-president of the OCC.

In June 2024, Loomis was appointed president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, a position he left for this election.

The future for Hamilton’s youngest residents, including his own, was another driving factor in deciding to run again.

“I’m doing this not for power, a paycheque or a pension. I’m doing this for my kids. I’m doing this for the other kids across this great community,” he told the Record.

Loomis is the second American-born mayor in Hamilton’s history, according to the Independent.

The first was New Hampshire-born John Fisher, who moved to the city in 1835 and opened what is believed to be its first foundry. He was the city’s fourth mayor, serving a single year in 1850.

Loomis wasn’t the only American-born mayor elected in an Ontario city on Monday.

Marianne Meed Ward won her third consecutive term as the mayor of Burlington according to unofficial results. The 60-year-old former Miss Canada and journalist was born to a Canadian father and American mother in Greeley, Colorado, spent her earliest years in California, where her father was a park ranger at famed Yosemite , and moved to Kingston, Ont. before Kindergarten.

Oakville incumbent mayor Rob Burton, who grew up bouncing around the U.S. with his military family before relocating to Canada, was defeated Monday night, finishing third according to unofficial results.

Another currently sitting mayor with U.S. roots is Halifax’s Andy Fillmore, who was born in Bloomington, Indiana, to Atlantic Canadian parents studying abroad, his profile on the city website reads . The family returned to Canada when he was four, but Fillmore studied and worked in Boston before returning to Canada and eventually becoming an MP in Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government.

Another notable modern-day Canadian mayor born in the U.S. was Toronto’s David Miller , a native of San Francisco who came to Canada with his mother in 1967.

Loomis told the Spectator he doesn’t think the city “is dangerous” but doesn’t disregard people’s apprehension about the downtown core.

The first pillar in the Smart plan he campaigned on is safety and features three main components.

Safe Public Spaces Hamilton would establish city-wide safety standards, set response times for hazards and publicly track the city’s performance. Loomis also vows to revive a partnership with the Hamilton Anchor Institution Leadership (Hail) to better coordinate resources. The third tranche is a downtown safety and economic plan that works for all stakeholders — residents, business owners and visitors.

He also promises to sit on the Hamilton Police Services Board, a seat Horwath resigned last September due to schedule conflicts, The Bay Observer reported.

“The Mayor gets the opportunity to sit on that board if they so choose, and I will be doing so for my entire term. That is how you exercise leadership,” Loomis told the Record earlier.

Statistics Canada reported earlier this year that Hamilton’s crime severity index — a statistical measure of the number of police-reported crimes relative to the population — was down seven per cent last year compared to 2024, below both the national and provincial averages.

At the same time, Hamilton Police Service’s 2025 annual report shows a 10 per cent jump in violent crimes over the year prior, a 39.4 per cent increase in weapons violations and drug offences up 196 per cent.

Another 2025 police report showed a 12.2 per cent year-over-year increase in the number of violent crimes involving youth aged 12 to 17, led by assault with a weapon, up 38.1 per cent.

Along those lines, weapon possession offences by youth were up 256.2 percent over 2024, police reported.

Hamilton also experienced a 12 per cent increase in hate/bias incidents in 2025, the majority of which were racially motivated.

In addition to safety, Loomis’s Smart plan is also focused on mobility, accountability, responsive government and taxpayer respect.

On the latter, Loomis has promised to determine “a number that can be absorbed by taxpayers” using “zero-based budgeting” — where total revenue minus total expenses equals zero each year.

“We are far too often going to the taxpayers and businesses in this community every single time we need more revenue. We have to recognize that it’s far too much, that there’s an affordability crisis out there, and we need to keep tax increases as low as possible,” he told the Record.

“Folks do want lower taxes, but they also don’t want cuts to their services, so we have to figure out how we’re going to do it.”

Loomis’s economic strategy for Hamilton is to attract investment, create jobs and expand the city’s commercial and industrial tax base to reduce pressure on residential taxpayers.

His platform called for preventative road maintenance, better coordination of construction projects to reduce disruptions and improved transit connections. He also wants to modernize housing approvals and reduce red tape to make home construction easier.

On housing, Loomis has pledged to work toward delivering up to 5,000 affordable housing units in this four-year term.

In 2010, Loomis became the founding CEO of the not-for-profit business accelerator Innovation Factory, leaving in 2013 to become president and CEO of the Hamilton Chamber of Commerce.

Upon his departure to run for mayor in 2022, Ontario Chamber of Commerce (OCC) president & CEO Rocco Rossi call Loomis “a brilliant, values-driven, tireless leader” who created a “remarkable legacy” locally, provincially and nationally.
After his failed bid for the mayoralty, he became a vice-president of the OCC.
In June 2024, Loomis was appointed president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, a position he left for this election.
The future for Hamilton’s youngest residents, including his own, was another driving factor in deciding to run again.
“I’m doing this not for power, a paycheque or a pension. I’m doing this for my kids. I’m doing this for the other kids across this great community,” he told the Record.
Loomis is the second American-born mayor in Hamilton’s history, according to the Independent.
The first was New Hampshire-born John Fisher, who moved to the city in 1835 and opened what is believed to be its first foundry. He was the city’s fourth mayor, serving a single year in 1850.
Loomis wasn’t the only American-born mayor elected in an Ontario city on Monday.

Marianne Meed Ward won her third consecutive term as the mayor of Burlington according to unofficial results. The 60-year-old former Miss Canada and journalist was born to a Canadian father and American mother in Greeley, Colorado, spent her earliest years in California, where her father was a park ranger at famed Yosemite , and moved to Kingston, Ont. before Kindergarten.

Oakville incumbent mayor Rob Burton, who grew up bouncing around the U.S. with his military family before relocating to Canada, was defeated Monday night, finishing third according to unofficial results.

Another currently sitting mayor with U.S. roots is Halifax’s Andy Fillmore, who was born in Bloomington, Indiana, to Atlantic Canadian parents studying abroad, his profile on the city website reads . The family returned to Canada when he was four, but Fillmore studied and worked in Boston before returning to Canada and eventually becoming an MP in Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government.
Another notable modern-day Canadian mayor born in the U.S. was Toronto’s David Miller , a native of San Francisco who came to Canada with his mother in 1967.
Loomis told the Spectator he doesn’t think the city “is dangerous” but doesn’t disregard people’s apprehension about the downtown core.
The first pillar in the Smart plan he campaigned on is safety and features three main components.

Safe Public Spaces Hamilton would establish city-wide safety standards, set response times for hazards and publicly track the city’s performance. Loomis also vows to revive a partnership with the Hamilton Anchor Institution Leadership (Hail) to better coordinate resources. The third tranche is a downtown safety and economic plan that works for all stakeholders — residents, business owners and visitors.
He also promises to sit on the Hamilton Police Services Board, a seat Horwath resigned last September due to schedule conflicts, The Bay Observer reported.
“The Mayor gets the opportunity to sit on that board if they so choose, and I will be doing so for my entire term. That is how you exercise leadership,” Loomis told the Record earlier.

Statistics Canada reported earlier this year that Hamilton’s crime severity index — a statistical measure of the number of police-reported crimes relative to the population — was down seven per cent last year compared to 2024, below both the national and provincial averages.

At the same time, Hamilton Police Service’s 2025 annual report shows a 10 per cent jump in violent crimes over the year prior, a 39.4 per cent increase in weapons violations and drug offences up 196 per cent.
Another 2025 police report showed a 12.2 per cent year-over-year increase in the number of violent crimes involving youth aged 12 to 17, led by assault with a weapon, up 38.1 per cent.
Along those lines, weapon possession offences by youth were up 256.2 percent over 2024, police reported.
Hamilton also experienced a 12 per cent increase in hate/bias incidents in 2025, the majority of which were racially motivated.
In addition to safety, Loomis’s Smart plan is also focused on mobility, accountability, responsive government and taxpayer respect.
On the latter, Loomis has promised to determine “a number that can be absorbed by taxpayers” using “zero-based budgeting” — where total revenue minus total expenses equals zero each year.

“We are far too often going to the taxpayers and businesses in this community every single time we need more revenue. We have to recognize that it’s far too much, that there’s an affordability crisis out there, and we need to keep tax increases as low as possible,” he told the Record.
“Folks do want lower taxes, but they also don’t want cuts to their services, so we have to figure out how we’re going to do it.”
Loomis’s economic strategy for Hamilton is to attract investment, create jobs and expand the city’s commercial and industrial tax base to reduce pressure on residential taxpayers.

His platform called for preventative road maintenance, better coordination of construction projects to reduce disruptions and improved transit connections. He also wants to modernize housing approvals and reduce red tape to make home construction easier.
On housing, Loomis has pledged to work toward delivering up to 5,000 affordable housing units in this four-year term.

stories.title: Donald Trump congratulates Quebec's new premier, 22 days after election
stories.summary: American President Donald Trump congratulated Quebec's new premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, ON social media on Tuesday morning.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The post comes 22 days after the sovereigntist Parti Québécois won enough seats in the Oct. 5 provincial election to form a minority government.

Trump attached a news article by the Irish Times, titled Separatists win Quebec provincial election in blow to Mark Carney, to his post.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

The trade war and the American president’s influence loomed over the electoral campaign.

Outgoing premier Christine Fréchette had warned the U.S. could be interfering in the election, before she backtracked.

St-Pierre Plamondon repeatedly criticized his opponents, saying they were trying to capitalize on the fear and instability sowed by the American president and his tariffs.

A few days before the electoral campaign began, St-Pierre Plamondon said he would not hold his promised referendum on Quebec independence until after Trump left the White House in 2029.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: An Anonymous $6M Gift to Establish Canada’s First National Myeloma Research Biobank in London
stories.summary: $6M Gift to Further Cancer Research in London London will have its own national research biobank of Canada for...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
$6M Gift to Further Cancer Research in London London will have its own national research biobank of Canada for multiple myeloma, which is one kind of blood cancer.

An anonymous person who himself/herself is suffering from multiple myeloma has donated $6 million to create the Canadian Myeloma Research Biobank at London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute.

The biobank will allow researchers in Canada to access patients’ samples to gain knowledge of the disease and discover further treatments.

Martha Louzada, who is a myeloma researcher at LHSC, stressed the need for research funding.

“Funding from the Walk of Champions is vital to advancing myeloma research. It enables us to explore new therapeutic strategies tailored to our patients, improving outcomes and quality of life for those living with this challenging disease.”

The name of the donor has not been revealed. The biobank is anticipated to become functional in 2027.

Source: London Health Sciences Foundation and LHSC Research Institute.

stories.title: Quebec premier accuses Ottawa of censoring him at EU Summit
stories.summary: The premier wrote on social media that Ottawa is seeking to impose economic decisions on Quebec without allowing the province a seat at the negotiation table.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is accusing Ottawa of muzzling him at the upcoming Canada-European Union summit in Montreal.

The federal government has assured the premier that he is invited to dinner with EU representatives , but the premier will not speak at the summit taking place Thursday and Friday.

The premier wrote on social media that Ottawa is seeking to impose economic decisions on Quebec without allowing the province a seat at the negotiation table.

Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in Ottawa that geopolitics, including the summit, fall under federal jurisdiction.

The Parti Québécois government also says Ottawa denied Quebec’s request to host a reception on the sidelines of the summit, which was submitted by former premier Christine Fréchette in September.

A spokesperson for the party says the EU routinely holds a forum for economic leaders during such summits, which the province could have hosted or co-hosted.

The PQ insists that there is precedent to include Quebec at the summit, as provincial representatives participated in negotiations for the Canada-European Union Free Trade Agreement.

The tension around the summit comes after St-Pierre Plamondon did not participate in a meeting on Monday between the federal government, provincial premiers and First Nations.

The Quebec premier also spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday.
