stories.title: Business leaders and Emirati officials on guest list for Carney’s dinner with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince
stories.summary: A guest list of nearly 120 names shows many in Canada’s corporate elite were invited to dine with Sheikh Khaled and senior members of the ruling circle
stories.author: Steven Chase
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is courting wealthy Gulf investors, hosted a dinner in Ottawa on Monday for Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, the oil-rich heart of the United Arab Emirates.

A guest list of nearly 120 names obtained by The Globe and Mail shows many in Canada’s corporate elite were invited to dine with Sheikh Khaled and senior members of Abu Dhabi’s ruling circle.

The dinner capped the first day of a two-day visit to Canada by the Crown Prince, whose father is the president of the UAE.

The blossoming relationship between Canada and the UAE has included the inking of a free trade agreement in July and an investment protection treaty that went into force in May. Mr. Carney came back from a visit to the country last fall touting a UAE commitment to invest $70-billion in Canada.

Ottawa is deepening ties with the UAE and other foreign trade partners as part of a push by the Prime Minister to lessen Canada’s economic reliance on the United States.

One of the most prominent invitees to the dinner was former prime minister Stephen Harper. The list leaned toward companies and investors with stakes in defence and security, energy, critical minerals, infrastructure, international development, space, advanced communications, quantum computing and artificial intelligence – all areas in which the Prime Minister’s Office has said the two countries will expand relations.

The invitees also included lawyers, consultants and lobbyists representing business interests in Ottawa, as well as provincial representatives, hospital and university leaders, museum administrators and representatives of Indigenous communities.

Members of the Desmarais family, long synonymous with Power Corporation of Canada, were on the list. André Desmarais, deputy chairman of Power Corporation of Canada, and Paul Desmarais III, a senior vice-president, were both listed, along with executives from Power Sustainable, a Power Corp. investment arm.

Also among the invitees were representatives of several large industrial companies, including Gregory Ebel, chief executive of Enbridge Inc.; Ian Edwards of engineering firm AtkinsRéalis; Alexandre L’Heureux of WSP Global; Kieran Hawe of construction company EllisDon; Bruce Power’s chief operating officer, James Scongack; and Eric Desaulniers, head of graphite developer Nouveau Monde Graphite.

Victor Dodig, recently appointed chief executive of Telus Corp., was also listed, as was Éric Martel, chief executive of Bombardier Inc.

Members of the tech industry were invited, including Joelle Pineau, chief AI officer at Cohere, and Valérie Pisano, chief executive of Mila.

Big investors and lenders were also on the list, including Deborah Orida, chief executive of PSP Investments; Alison Nankivell of Export Development Canada; and Geneviève Bouthillier, an executive vice-president at BDC Capital. So were government-relations heads from Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, Hoopp and Sun Life, and venture investor Chris Arsenault of Inovia. Gurinder Grewal, named chief executive of Invest in Canada on Aug. 31, was also on the list.

Many members of Mr. Carney’s inner circle were listed, including Marc-André Blanchard, his chief of staff; Michael Sabia, Clerk of the Privy Council; David Morrison, a senior diplomatic adviser; Scott Gilmore, principal secretary; and Jennifer MacIntyre, a deputy chief of staff. The ambassadors to the United States and the UAE, Mark Wiseman and Angad Dhillon, were also on the list. So was Sébastien Carrière, Global Affairs Canada’s chief of protocol.

Many of the Emiratis who were invited work for the Abu Dhabi Crown Prince’s Court. Sheikh Khalifa bin Tahnoon Al Nahyan, the court’s chairman, and Saif Ghobash, chairman of the Crown Prince’s Office and secretary-general of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council, were listed, as was Sultan Al Jaber, who is both the Uae’s minister of industry and advanced technology and chief executive of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.

Among the rest of the Emirati contingent on the list were representatives of DP World, a Dubai-based port operator that on Monday announced a memorandum of understanding with the owner of Manitoba’s Port of Churchill to explore further development of an expanded northern shipping corridor. Douglas Smith, chief executive officer of the company’s operations in Canada, was invited, as was Sultan bin Saeed Al Mansoori, chairman of Dubai Chambers, who also sits on DP World’s board.

content_blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is courting wealthy Gulf investors, hosted a dinner in Ottawa on Monday for Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, the oil-rich heart of the United Arab Emirates.
content_blocks.html: Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is courting wealthy Gulf investors, hosted a dinner in Ottawa on Monday for Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, the oil-rich heart of the United Arab Emirates.

content_blocks.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney hosts Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi at a state dinner in Ottawa on Monday. Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: A guest list of nearly 120 names obtained by The Globe and Mail shows many in Canada’s corporate elite were invited to dine with Sheikh Khaled and senior members of Abu Dhabi’s ruling circle.
content_blocks.html: A guest list of nearly 120 names obtained by The Globe and Mail shows many in Canada’s corporate elite were invited to dine with Sheikh Khaled and senior members of Abu Dhabi’s ruling circle.

content_blocks.text: The dinner capped the first day of a two-day visit to Canada by the Crown Prince, whose father is the president of the UAE.
content_blocks.html: The dinner capped the first day of a two-day visit to Canada by the Crown Prince, whose father is the president of the UAE.

content_blocks.text: The blossoming relationship between Canada and the UAE has included the inking of a free trade agreement in July and an investment protection treaty that went into force in May. Mr. Carney came back from a visit to the country last fall touting a UAE commitment to invest $70-billion in Canada.

stories.title: CPP and OAS payments land in bank accounts tomorrow. Here’s what you need to know
stories.summary: Canadians over the age of 60 can apply to receive hundreds of dollars in monthly benefits.
stories.author: Megan Mills Devoe
stories.content:
Benefits from the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and the Old Age Security (OAS) program will be arriving in eligible Canadians’ bank accounts on Wednesday.

These plans offer monthly payments to millions of Canadians above the age of 60. Whether you are already receiving these benefits, or curious about your eligibility, this is the guide for you.

Here’s what you need to know.

The amount you receive monthly from the CPP retirement pension is based on your age, your contributions to the CPP and your average earnings when you were working. Your OAS payment is dependent on your age, net income and the number of years you’ve lived in Canada as an adult.

This year, the maximum monthly payment for the retirement pension is $1,507.65, and the average for new beneficiaries is $858.34.

Maximum monthly payments for seniors receiving OAS range from $762.50 to $838.75, depending on your age.

Starting your CPP pension later in life will result in higher payments per month. Starting before the age of 65 will result in payments decreasing by a small percentage each month. Starting after 65 will result in payments increasing by a small percentage each month. The maximum monthly payment is reached at age 70 and will not increase past then.

OAS payments work similarly.

You can calculate your approximate OAS payment using the Benefits Estimator tool on the Canadian government’s website. You can use your My Service Canada Account (Msca) in order to see your CPP contributions and calculate your approximate monthly CPP benefits.

Payment amounts for OAS benefits are reassessed quarterly in order to reflect the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Notably, payments will only increase if the CPI goes up, payments will never decrease if the CPI goes down.

The Canada Revenue Agency has said that based on changes in the CPI, OAS benefits increased by 1.4 per cent for the October to December 2026 quarter, for an increase of three per cent over the past year, from October 2025 to October 2026.

If you have lived in Canada for 10-40 years after the age of 18, you are only eligible for a partial OAS pension. Using the Benefits Estimator tool can help you figure out the payments to expect.

In order to qualify for CPP payments, you must be 60 or above and have made at least one valid contribution to the plan. Contributions to the CPP are automatically deducted from your paycheque. If you are self employed, you contribute when you file your taxes.

You do not need to be retired to qualify for the CPP retirement pension, working will not reduce the amount you are paid or impact your eligibility.

If you are a Canadian citizen or legal resident aged 65 or above you May qualify for the OAS benefit. If you have lived in Canada for less than 20 years as an adult, your eligibility May be impacted.

The OAS benefit is not contingent on your current or previous working status, however, there is a maximum income threshold.

People aged 65 to 74 must have an annual net income less than $152,062 to qualify. If you are 75 or above, your income must be less than $157,923.

You must submit your tax return each year in order to receive CPP and OAS benefits.

The CPP primarily provides benefits to Canadians outside of Quebec. However, if you have lived or worked in Quebec, you May still be eligible for CPP benefits. If you are unsure of your eligibility, check with Retraite Québec .

If you have lived or worked outside of Canada, you May be eligible to receive CPP pension and a pension from the other country.

Even if you are eligible, you will not be automatically registered for CPP payments, you must apply. You have the option to apply online through your Msca or apply by mail using a paper form.

Those who apply online can expect to receive a decision within 28 days, whereas applications by mail May take up to 120 days to receive a decision. If you would like the decision you received to be reconsidered, you will have 90 days to submit a request for reconsideration .

Most people will be eligible to apply online, but there are some exceptions. Before applying online, be sure to check if you qualify . If you apply online, you will be able to track the status of your application using your Msca.

Beyond retirement benefits, the CPP also provides disability benefits, benefits for children of CPP contributors and benefits for surviving dependants of deceased CPP contributors.

Most eligible Canadians over the age of 65 will be automatically enrolled in OAS and receive a confirmation letter from Service Canada. If you are eligible, but Service Canada is lacking necessary information to register you for the program, you May need to apply.

The final two dates for 2026 pension benefits will be Nov. 26 and Dec. 22.

stories.title: Stolen vehicle spotted in drive-thru
stories.summary: London, ON (October 27, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service arrested two after a stolen vehicle was spotted in a drive-thru near the downtown core yesterday morning.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (October 27, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service arrested two after a stolen vehicle was spotted in a drive-thru near the downtown core yesterday morning.

On Monday, October 26, 2026, at approximately 3:45 a.m., a vehicle entered a drive-thru in the area of Oxford Street West and Wharncliffe Road North followed by an officer in an unmarked cruiser.

While in the drive-thru, the officer learned that the vehicle was stolen. The officer followed the vehicle, requested additional resources, and the vehicle was stopped in a nearby laneway. Both suspects were taken into custody without incident.

As a result of the investigation, Ryan Robert Mercer, 46, and Amber Leigh Cottrelle, 37, both of London, have been charged jointly with possession of property obtained by crime over $5,000.

Amber Leigh Cottrelle has additionally been charged with fail to comply with release order and possession of a Schedule 1 substance.

Both of the accused have upcoming court dates.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Premier Doug Ford said there will be "zero tolerance" for any fraud in the Osap system
stories.summary: Questions about the government’s handling of the student aid controversy dominated the first day back at Queen’s Park.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford said there will be “zero tolerance” for any fraud in the OSAP system — but that he feels sorry for students at private career colleges caught up in the temporary ban on student aid .

Questions about the government’s handling of the student aid controversy dominated the first day back at the legislature after a 21-week break , with opposition critics asking the government why it didn’t act sooner, and why students at all private colleges are being penalized for what, so far, is a handful of rogue institutions.

“For more than three years, this government has been shovelling hundreds of millions of OSAP grant funding to a handful of private career colleges without any oversight, monitoring or accountability,” said New Democrat MPP Peggy Sattler, her party’s post-secondary critic. “That’s why OSAP costs were rising.

“This government’s failure to act earlier has protected bad-actor institutions and you are attacking students instead,” she said in the legislature Tuesday.

Earlier this month, Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced that his ministry notified the Ontario Provincial Police after a third-party audit uncovered irregularities in the OSAP system around a number of private career colleges, and that he was banning all career colleges from the aid system until the new year when a new, more stringent process will be rolled out.

Quinn has also permanently removed online-only programs at private colleges from OSAP eligibility.

The loss of access to OSAP grants, and now loans, amid fraud allegations at 8 schools is sparking fears for the future.

He had previously changed the OSAP system that was heavy on non-repayable grants to loans, citing ballooning costs. However, The Canadian Press later revealed that much of that increase was because of seven private career colleges, which received $385 million in 2024-25, the same amount that all public colleges received that same year.

The third-party audit continues, and police say they are still reviewing the referral from ministry.

In the meantime, Ford said it is “heartbreaking” for students but that the government had to act on the alleged fraud.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he feels "terrible" for honest students caught up in a career college system where financial aid is now unavailable. Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn paused Ontario Student Assistance Program payments at all private post-secondary institutions earlier this month after he says preliminary findings of a KPMG audit turned up significant concerns. (Oct. 27, 2026)

“That’s who I feel sorry for,” the premier said when asked about those who have not received previously approved funds to pay their tuition.

While not wanting to “paint a broad brush against all colleges — because there are really good private career colleges — but there’s some really bad, bad people and we’re auditing the system right across the board,” Ford said, adding “there will be zero tolerance for any fraud. They’re going to jail. We’re going to hold them accountable, simple as that.”

Opposition critics accused the government of ignoring the problem for years, even after an auditor report in 2021, and Career Colleges Ontario reaching out with its concerns in 2023.

Minister Nolan Quinn asks Ontario Provincial Police to investigate “criminal allegations.”

Speaking to reporters at the legislature, Quinn said the government brought in the third-party auditor after his ministry’s own investigations, “recognizing that we saw some similarities across the inspections that we have done.”

He said he has sympathy for students, “but we have to remember these are serious criminal allegations. These are bad actors, and they’ve had to act to protect taxpayer dollars.”

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said “here’s the story for thousands and thousands of students receiving OSAP: They’re approved, they’re enrolled and then they’re abandoned in a period of seven weeks.”

The province has promised it will work with financial institutions to help facilitate loans in the meantime, but no further details have been released.

Some of the 242 colleges that had been eligible for OSAP have allowed students to continue classes in the interim .

With files from Robert Benzie

stories.title: Althia Raj: What B.C.‘s Conservative win and Alberta’s referenda should teach Pierre Poilievre
stories.summary: Hanging on to the Conservative party’s most extreme members comes at a long-term cost, Althia Raj suggests.
stories.author: Althia Raj
stories.content:
As Conservative MPs gather for their weekly caucus meetings, some are attempting to read the tea leaves from last week’s Alberta referenda and British Columbia’s big Conservative win.

Saturday, David Eby’s early election gamble — two years into his NDP government’s mandate — failed spectacularly . B.C. interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson won a majority after running a disciplined campaign and uniting his party — and the conservative movement — around his leadership.

On X, federal B.C. Conservative MP Aaron Gunn posted that Doerkson and his team had articulated a compelling vision for the province “and did so Without abandoning key conservative priorities or principles, including Dripa (the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act ), Sogi (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity) and ending safe supply. “Those trying to use this victory to argue the federal Conservative Party needs to abandon its conservative principles in order to win an election are doing so either disingenuously or ignorantly,” he wrote.

Despite his rodeo announcer background, Doerkson did not create a stampede to the polls . Only 48 per cent of the B.C. electorate showed up to vote. The Conservatives obtained fewer votes than they did in 2024 — 862,688 to 911,153.

What led to the party’s large majority is that 273,768 NDP voters from 2024 failed to show up for their party.

Some likely voted Green, others Conservative, but many simply stayed home.

That is a success of the Conservative campaign.

And it isn’t because Doerkson and his team flexed on controversial issues, like Sogi — it’s precisely because they didn’t.

Since Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from “a bad deal” with the U.S. in August, his popularity has reached new heights. This makes the

What the B.C. Conservatives presented, through careful messaging, was a Conservative leader that British Columbians did not need to fear. Doerkson seemed like a nice positive guy, talking about running a competent government and lowering taxes. He was a blank slate. With not much of a record to defend, his campaign successfully stripped centrists and progressive voters of a reason to mobilize. And the NDP failed to make a compelling case otherwise.

Depressing an opponent’s turnout can be as important as turning out your own voters.

While the NDP made a series of own goals, from calling an election they were ill-equipped to fight, to having no clear message, to Eby’s subsidized child-care revelation , the Conservatives amplified the setbacks. NDP voters were left unmotivated.

Gunn May believe that Dripa and Sogi policies led British Columbia to turn blue and that the same strategy will pay off for Poilievre. But not only does the data suggest that is not true — Research Co.’s exit poll found fewer than 30 per cent of respondents said those were vote drivers — Poilievre is no Doerkson. Voters have already made up their minds about Poilievre, and poll after poll suggests they don’t like him. Recent figures from Abacus Data suggest 45 per cent of the country does not like him; Liaison suggests the number is 55 per cent; an Ekos survey this month pegs it at 70 per cent .

This isn’t because voters can’t see beyond admiration for Prime Minister Mark Carney . According to Liaison, NDP Leader Avi Lewis’s negatives are dropping. But Lewis is just becoming known; Poilievre is a known quantity.

During the 2025 federal election, a major vote driver was U.S. President Donald Trump and his 51 st state threats, but dislike for Poilievre also sent voters to the Liberal camp.

Trump May not be there to help the Grits during the next election, but it’s difficult to see how Poilievre can help Conservatives. He remains a drag on his party, notably in vote-rich Ontario. Funnily enough, Carney and Poilievre might both be hoping the Conservatives win the upcoming byelection in Brantford—Brant South, otherwise a potential leadership review could throw both their plans out the window.

The Alberta result offers a different but related lesson.

With almost all votes counted, referendum results show all of her proposed constitutional

Premier Danielle Smith must not only contend with the fallout of a plebiscite she thought she’d easily win that instead leaves her with no mandate to seek financial compensation to opt out of federal programs, or to fight for the supremacy of provincial laws over federal laws. She must also face the challenge of trying to steer her party to where the voters are, rather than where her party’s base is.

Do federal Conservatives also want their party driven by the voices of Western separatists, anti-vaxxers, and those focused on gender identity messages? Hanging on to the party’s most extreme members might keep the floor from dropping in public opinion polls, but increasingly MPs are aware it comes at a long-term cost.

Those voices are defining the party’s agenda to one that a majority of swing voters cannot support — voters that the Conservatives need without a stronger NDP splitting the Liberals’ base of support.

Those lessons are fresh on the minds of some Conservatives this week.

stories.title: Daylight savings will end on Sunday. Here’s what you should know
stories.summary: While most Ontarians will turn their clocks back an hour this weekend, some communities in the province will no longer have to make the switch.
stories.author: Megan Mills Devoe; Samm Mohibuddin
stories.content:
Most Ontarians will get an extra hour of sleep this weekend as daylight saving time comes to an end, but for some residents in the province, changing the clock could soon be a thing of the past.

Daylight saving time will end at 2 a.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1 , when clocks will be turned back one hour to 1 a.m.

The change means brighter mornings but earlier sunsets as Ontario returns to standard time.

Most smartphones, computers and other internet-connected devices will adjust automatically, although clocks on appliances, watches and other devices May need to be changed manually.

Daylight saving time began this year on March 8, when clocks moved forward by one hour.

The debate around daylight saving time is nothing new, but recent changes have brought the conversation back into the forefront.

Earlier this month, Kenora and other northwestern regions of Ontario decided to adopt permanent DST in order to be better aligned with neighbouring areas in Manitoba. Manitoba is one of the six provinces and territories that do not turn clocks back and forward.

The decision follows Manitoba’s announcement in September that it would stop changing its clocks twice a year beginning Nov. 1

Ontario has since filed a regulation allowing communities west of the 90th meridian to remain on the same time year-round.

The move is intended to keep communities along the provincial border aligned, making it easier for residents and businesses to co-ordinate travel, health-care appointments and other services.

In Kenora, more than 93 per cent of respondents to a municipal survey supported permanent daylight saving time, and city council subsequently voted unanimously in favour of the change.

Why hasn’t Ontario ended daylight saving time altogether?

Ontario passed legislation in 2020 that would allow the province to adopt permanent daylight saving time.

However, the legislation has not been brought into force across the province.

The provincial government has previously said it wants to co-ordinate the change with neighbouring jurisdictions, particularly Quebec and New York, because of their economic ties to Ontario.

For Toronto and much of the province, that means the twice-yearly clock changes will continue.

Why do we change our clocks?

Daylight saving time is intended to make better use of daylight during the warmer months by shifting an hour of sunlight from morning to evening.

Clocks move forward in the spring, giving people more daylight later in the day, before moving to standard time in the fall.

How does the time change affect your health?

An extra hour of sleep might sound appealing, but changing the clocks can still disrupt the body’s internal schedule.

The body’s circadian rhythm , which regulates sleep and wakefulness, is influenced by natural light. Changes in the timing of sunrise and sunset can affect when people feel tired or alert.

According to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, seasonal clock changes can disrupt sleep and affect mood, although the health risks associated with the spring transitions are generally more pronounced.

How can you prepare for the time change?

Maintaining a consistent sleep schedule in the days leading up to the change can help make the transition easier.

Getting natural light in the morning can also help regulate the body’s internal clock, while keeping regular bedtimes and wake-up times May reduce disruptions to sleep.

People particularly sensitive to changes in their sleep schedules May benefit from gradually adjusting their routines before Sunday.

Daylight saving time will end at 2 a.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1 , when clocks will be turned back one hour to 1 a.m.
The change means brighter mornings but earlier sunsets as Ontario returns to standard time.
Most smartphones, computers and other internet-connected devices will adjust automatically, although clocks on appliances, watches and other devices May need to be changed manually.
Daylight saving time began this year on March 8, when clocks moved forward by one hour.
The debate around daylight saving time is nothing new, but recent changes have brought the conversation back into the forefront.

Earlier this month, Kenora and other northwestern regions of Ontario decided to adopt permanent DST in order to be better aligned with neighbouring areas in Manitoba. Manitoba is one of the six provinces and territories that do not turn clocks back and forward.
The decision follows Manitoba’s announcement in September that it would stop changing its clocks twice a year beginning Nov. 1

Daylight saving time is intended to make better use of daylight during the warmer months by shifting an hour of sunlight from morning to evening.

stories.title: Horwath among incumbents ousted across Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area
stories.summary: Several mayoral incumbents in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area have lost their jobs while others are heading back to city hall.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Election night in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (Gtha) delivered some upsets, with several incumbent mayors losing their bids for re-election.

Former Ontario NDP leader Andrea Horwath , who became Hamilton’s mayor in 2022 after her party’s provincial defeat, was in a distant third place at 14 per cent with 177 of 207 polls reporting as of 11:24 p.m.

Horwath trailed city councillor Rob Cooper who had 32 per cent of the vote and Canadian Institute of Steel Production CEO Keanin Loomis, who had 41 per cent of the vote.

Loomis claimed victory in a speech shortly before 11 p.m., saying he was “at a loss for words.”

“Tonight is about more than winning an election, it’s about hope, it’s about change, and it’s about believing again in what this city can be,” Loomis said.

It’s a reversal from 2022 when Horwath beat Loomis by just under 1,700 votes. Loomis noted that loss, saying he listened to what residents had to say before coming back to win in 2026, calling it a “true Hamilton story.”

Canada’s longest-serving mayor has lost his job after 15 consecutive terms.

Milton’s Gord Krantz was first elected as mayor in 1980, after previously serving as a councillor from 1965 until 1980.

But with all polls reporting Monday night, Krantz trailed Coun. George Minakakis by a 20-point margin.

Krantz isn’t the only long-time mayor poised to lose his seat.

In Oakville, five-term incumbent mayor Rob Burton finished in third place, having received only 20 per cent of the vote. Long-time councillor Jeff Knoll, who has served since 2000, has 36 per cent of the vote and is the mayor-elect, according to unofficial results.

The night started, though, with incumbent Mississauga mayor Carolyn Parrish losing her re-election bid after about two years in office.

Rookie city councillor Alvin Tedjo soared past her and former mayor Bonnie Crombie to win the election, receiving roughly 74,000 votes with all polls reporting as of 11:24 p.m.

“This wasn’t a normal election. We haven’t had a normal two-and-a-half years. These are tough times that we’re living in,” Parrish said in her concession speech.

While some incumbents in the Gtha have lost re-election, others are returning with relatively sizeable outcomes of more than half of the vote.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow won re-election with about 54 per cent of the vote, besting councillor Brad Bradford who received roughly 41 per cent.

Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown also saw victory Monday night, being re-elected to his third term in office with about 54 per cent of the vote.

But some Gtha mayors saw even larger margins of victory on election night, with former Ontario Liberal leader and Vaughan Mayor Steven Del Duca winning 81.5 per cent of the vote with 71 of 71 polls reporting.

Richmond Hill Mayor David West is also heading back to city hall after getting 83 per cent of the vote with all polls reporting.

Markham city council will also see Mayor Frank Scarpitti back at the helm for another term, after taking 72 per cent of the vote.

stories.title: Olivia Chow’s mayoral win was not a vote for Toronto’s status quo
stories.summary: The former city councillor and NDP MP should be more ambitious in her second term as mayor
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
A wind of change is blowing in Canadian politics.

In British Columbia, the mayor of Vancouver and then the premier of the province were toppled in spectacular fashion, the first beaten by a Green Party upstart, the second by the leader of a party, the Conservatives, that had been in complete disarray. In Quebec, the separatist Parti Québécois returned to power after a dozen years in the wilderness, reducing the ruling Coalition Avenir Québec to precisely zero seats in the National Assembly.

Olivia Chow managed to buck the trend on Monday evening, beating back a serious challenge from an energetic city councillor, Brad Bradford, and winning a second term as mayor of Toronto. It was quite an achievement for the former city councillor and NDP MP, who turns 70 next year. She arrived in Canada from Hong Kong with her parents at the age of 13, moving into a sprawling public housing complex. She won election to the school board at just 28, beginning a political career that has spanned four decades.

That career seemed to be over in 2015, after she lost a bid for mayor, then a by-election that would have given her back a seat in the House of Commons. But when former mayor John Tory resigned amid a personal scandal in 2023, Ms. Chow took another stab and won the mayor’s chair in a special by-election. If all goes well, she will hold it until 2030.

In this moment of triumph, she is bound to see a vindication of the record she has established at city hall and the program she had laid out for the future. She is entitled to that view.

Unlike most government leaders, mayors are elected directly. With parties prohibited at the city level, voters mark their ballots for the candidate alone. Armed with that legitimacy – along with the “strong mayor” powers the provincial government has granted to cities – Ms. Chow has a solid mandate and considerable power.

In her first term, she managed to create a school snack program, open all libraries seven days a week and strike a cost-sharing deal with Premier Doug Ford worth billions of dollars to the city. In this term, she plans to fight for tenants’ rights, create more affordable rental housing, keep transit fares frozen and invest in youth programs.

But it would be a mistake to interpret Monday’s vote as a rubber stamp for the status quo. Mr. Bradford gave Ms. Chow a real run for her money. He told voters that Toronto was crying out for change, and that message clearly struck a chord, bringing him close to even with a well-known sitting mayor in late-campaign opinion polls.

Voters will not be content with a steady-as-she-goes approach to governing Canada’s leading metropolis. Traffic congestion is a genuine problem, frustrating to locals and mind-boggling for visitors. It costs Torontonians countless hours of wasted time and the city many billions of dollars in lost productivity.

Though Toronto is safe by North American standards, with crime rates down in several categories, the plague of mental illness, drug addiction and homelessness that afflicts so many cities is painfully visible. Ms. Chow managed to get most of the tent encampments out of municipal parks, but city dwellers continue to witness scenes of disorder and despair on sidewalks and in transit stations.

The general state of Toronto’s parks, roads and many of its transit stations is not what it should be. Ms. Chow has put lots of resources into making sure Toronto’s most disadvantaged residents get the help they deserve, but little into making sure that the city’s economic engine keeps humming.

Rather than coast on her victory, Ms. Chow would be well advised to reach out to Toronto’s business community about how to feed the goose that lays the golden eggs, and focus more on issues of simple urban maintenance such as cleanliness and conduct in public spaces.

Toronto is a thriving city, more stuck than broken, as Mr. Bradford put it. Most of its problems, like high housing costs and crowded roads, are problems of success. But looking around at other cities of its size, it is hard to avoid the feeling that it is falling behind. Its transit network is nowhere near as good as you would find in many major European or East Asian cities. Its cultural assets are below par.

While she is hard working, decent and sincere, Ms. Chow sometimes seems to lack the ambition that the leader of a dynamic city like Toronto needs.

The wind of change is blowing in Toronto, too. Ms. Chow would be unwise to ignore it.

content_blocks.text: In British Columbia, the mayor of Vancouver and then the premier of the province were toppled in spectacular fashion, the first beaten by a Green Party upstart, the second by the leader of a party, the Conservatives, that had been in complete disarray. In Quebec, the separatist Parti Québécois returned to power after a dozen years in the wilderness, reducing the ruling Coalition Avenir Québec to precisely zero seats in the National Assembly.

content_blocks.text: Olivia Chow managed to buck the trend on Monday evening, beating back a serious challenge from an energetic city councillor, Brad Bradford, and winning a second term as mayor of Toronto. It was quite an achievement for the former city councillor and NDP MP, who turns 70 next year. She arrived in Canada from Hong Kong with her parents at the age of 13, moving into a sprawling public housing complex. She won election to the school board at just 28, beginning a political career that has spanned four decades.

But when former mayor John Tory resigned amid a personal scandal in 2023, Ms. Chow took another stab and won the mayor’s chair in a special by-election. If all goes well, she will hold it until 2030.

stories.title: Nearly 89% of Ontarians now have primary care, province says
stories.summary: A calculation from the latest numbers shows that 1.8 million people remain without a health care provider
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Ontario is making progress in connecting its residents with primary care services, with more than half a million additional people attached to a health care setting since January, 2025, the province reported on Monday.

The numbers were released two years after the provincial government appointed former federal health minister Jane Philpott to lead a drive to improve access to family doctors and other primary care providers.

There has been a net increase of 511,000 people connected to primary care since January, 2025, when the government launched its Primary Care Action Plan.

A total of 14,259,000 Ontarians, or 88.7 per cent of the population, now have a primary care provider, the province reported.

Officials wouldn’t confirm how many people are still without a doctor, but a calculation from the latest numbers shows that 1.8 million Ontarians remain without a health care provider.

The government said it has cleared 470,000 names from the HealthCare Connect list, although there are still more than 24,000 registrants who have waited more than six months for a referral.

“I am incredibly proud of the progress we’ve made,” Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones said at a press conference.

Dr. Philpott said the province is on pace to meet its goal to connect every Ontarian to primary care by 2029.

Adil Shamji, health critic for the Ontario Liberals and a physician, cautioned that the improved numbers don’t reflect factors such as retiring doctors, population increase or the difficulties in retaining health care professionals.

“It’s great to finally see some action getting taken on this and some attention being paid to this issue, but a lot of the announcements today, I just don’t find credible,” he said.

Dr. Shamji said Ministry of Health data indicate that more than 2,100 Ontario family doctors with three million patients are over 60, and could be expected to retire in coming years.

The Ontario Medical Association released the results of an online survey last December, showing that half of the province’s doctors are planning to retire or considering that option in the next five years.

“This government prioritizes health care recruitment, but not health care worker retention, and so I am very concerned that this government will not be able to deliver on the promises that it is making,” Dr. Shamji said.

Dr. Philpott said the new 88.7-per-cent access rate cannot be compared to metrics from the Canadian Institute for Health Information, which tracks countrywide medical data. The institute’s numbers show that in 2024, Ontario was the province with the highest proportion of adults with a primary care provider, at 88.5 per cent.

The institute’s number is based on a survey sample, Dr. Philpott said, whereas Ontario’s Ministry of Health has developed a more accurate methodology in the last two years. “We can actually tell almost down to a person who is and isn’t connected to ongoing primary care rather than a survey sample,” she said.

Most of Ontario’s newly attached patients were put in touch with a family doctor, though in a minority of cases, the connection could have been made with a community health centre, an Indigenous primary health care organization, or a clinic led by nurse practitioners

When the province first launched the Primary Care Action Plan in January, 2025, it said it intended to connect approximately two million more people to primary care.

The province historically already had among the highest attachment rates in the country.

In Quebec, former premier François Legault pledged in 2018 that every Quebecker would have a family doctor. In British Columbia, outgoing Premier David Eby, whose NDP government was defeated on Saturday, promised that every resident who wanted a family doctor or nurse practitioner would be connected by the end of 2025.

Neither premier was successful: Primary care access in both provinces remained under 80 per cent, as per the most recent estimates available.

stories.title: Canada’s natural gas producers thrive off B.C. election, but oversupply threatens their riches
stories.summary: Long-term potential of industry is strong, in part because of the Montney region in B.C. and Alberta
stories.author: Tim Kiladze
stories.content:
The shock outcome of British Columbia’s provincial election positions natural gas producers in Northern B.C. and Alberta to thrive, with the new BC Conservative premier-designate Lorne Doerkson vowing to triple exports of liquefied natural gas by 2035.

Yet the industry’s producers, which include Calgary-based Tourmaline Oil Corp. TOU-T and Denver-based Ovintiv Inc. OVV-T , will have to be patient. Substantial increases to LNG exports are years away, and natural gas in Western Canada remains in oversupply.

Because there aren’t enough ways to export the region’s abundance of natural gas, the local price, known as the Aeco (Alberta Energy Company Ltd.) price, is depressed and currently hovers around US$1.40 per million BTU – roughly half the price of U.S. natural gas on the Gulf Coast, and a fraction of global prices.

Owing to the export bottleneck, natural gas producers risk pouncing on the premier-designate’s vision and boosting production too soon. If they do, the oversupply May worsen, hurting their profit margins. It could also discourage investors from buying back into the sector. Lately, they have been deterred by the supply glut, and they are also enamoured by the profit surge in Canadian oil.

However, the long-term potential of Canadian natural gas is real, particularly because wells in the Montney region in northern B.C. and Alberta are often filled with byproduct liquids such as condensate.

On Monday, Ovintiv – formerly Encana – bought Logan Energy for $890-million, adding natural gas and liquids assets in the area. The deal is Ovintiv’s fourth purchase in the Montney over the past couple of years. Previous transactions include the purchase of NuVista Energy Corp., as well as assets from Paramount Resources Ltd. and Advantage Energy Ltd.

The Montney region is known not only for its sizeable reserves, but also for the quality of its wells, which rival those in the prolific Permian Basin that straddles Texas and New Mexico. It is also affordable by comparison. The Permian has become an expensive place to purchase new land or assets, so producers are turning to the Montney instead.

“The two places that we really saw the potential for our company to deliver differentiated returns were the Permian and the Montney,” Ovintiv chief executive officer Brendan McCracken said in an interview.

He is particularly enthused about all the condensate found in the Montney natural gas wells. The product is used as a diluent that helps to move heavy oil through pipelines, and Mr. McCracken believes it is the best resource product in Canada – “the only one that attracts a global premium price.”

The Montney acquisition activity dovetails with B.C.’s new strategy. On the campaign trail, Mr. Doerkson repeatedly touted his “B.C. Energy Superpower Plan” to double LNG production by 2032 in the province, and triple it by 2035.

“We will deliver this by cutting red tape, faster permitting, faster approvals,” he said during a campaign announcement in September.

B.C. is already well on its way to achieving this after Shell Canada announced in late September that it will greenlight phase two of its recently built LNG facility in Kitimat, B.C., enabling the company to double its production capacity.

The expansion follows Shell’s $19-billion acquisition of Arc Resources Ltd. in September, significantly boosting its natural gas reserves in the Montney region. Future production will be used to feed the export plant.

As for Ovintiv, Mr. McCracken acknowledged that expanded LNG exports will take years to materialize, but he said there are other opportunities and the company has found a way to sell 80 per cent of its Montney production to a diversified mix of buyers, so its not held captive by the Aeco price in Alberta.

In fact, the Montney’s appeal is so strong that Ovintiv has retooled its corporate strategy to expand there.

Nearly two decades ago, Ovintiv – then Encana – was one of the first companies to bet on natural gas, and even sold off its oil sands assets into a new company called Cenovus Energy Inc. But the strategy backfired. When the oil sands assets were sold, the price of Aeco gas was around US$11 per million BTU. By 2012, it had dropped to US$2 because new drilling technology unlocked vast quantities of so-called shale oil and gas in the U.S.

To pivot, Encana bet on U.S. shale oil and gas, moved its headquarters to Denver and renamed itself.

But now that Canadian energy has grown more popular – spurred in part by more favourable government policies – the company is happy to reinvest in the Montney again. And it is possible more rivals will buy Montney assets, too.

In a note to clients last week, BMO Nesbitt Burns analyst Jeremy McCrea wrote that Montney assets are attractive not just for their discount prices relative to the Permian, but the region also has a “high number of undrilled locations.” Companies with assets there often stress that less than 10 per cent of the Montney’s reserves have been produced.
paragraphs: The shock outcome of British Columbia’s provincial election positions natural gas producers in Northern B.C. and Alberta to thrive, with the new BC Conservative premier-designate Lorne Doerkson vowing to triple exports of liquefied natural gas by 2035.

Yet the industry’s producers, which include Calgary-based Tourmaline Oil Corp. TOU-T and Denver-based Ovintiv Inc. OVV-T , will have to be patient. Substantial increases to LNG exports are years away, and natural gas in Western Canada remains in oversupply.

Because there aren’t enough ways to export the region’s abundance of natural gas, the local price, known as the Aeco (Alberta Energy Company Ltd.) price, is depressed and currently hovers around US$1.40 per million BTU – roughly half the price of U.S. natural gas on the Gulf Coast, and a fraction of global prices.

Owing to the export bottleneck, natural gas producers risk pouncing on the premier-designate’s vision and boosting production too soon. If they do, the oversupply May worsen, hurting their profit margins. It could also discourage investors from buying back into the sector. Lately, they have been deterred by the supply glut, and they are also enamoured by the profit surge in Canadian oil.

However, the long-term potential of Canadian natural gas is real, particularly because wells in the Montney region in northern B.C. and Alberta are often filled with byproduct liquids such as condensate.

On Monday, Ovintiv – formerly Encana – bought Logan Energy for $890-million, adding natural gas and liquids assets in the area. The deal is Ovintiv’s fourth purchase in the Montney over the past couple of years. Previous transactions include the purchase of NuVista Energy Corp., as well as assets from Paramount Resources Ltd. and Advantage Energy Ltd.

stories.title: Cleveland-Cliffs says it is in compliance with commitments to Ottawa, seeks meeting with Joly
stories.summary: Joly has repeatedly said that Cliffs hasn’t lived up to its promises, could face legal action or be forced to divest Stelco
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
U.S. steel maker Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. is reiterating it is in compliance with its Investment Canada Act undertakings and has requested a meeting with Industry Minister Mélanie Joly to discuss ways to potentially reverse its recent layoffs at its subsidiary Stelco.

After the markets closed, Ohio-based Cliffs said in a statement that it had performed an “exhaustive review” of its compliance in its 34 undertakings, referring to commitments it made when acquiring Stelco in 2024. It also said it had submitted a letter to Ms. Joly on Monday confirming it is in “full compliance.”

On Sept. 28, Stelco announced that it was laying off up to 500 workers at its plants in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont.

The federal government has said that by proceeding with the layoffs, Cliffs is in breach of its undertaking to maintain at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada for five years.

Cliffs on Monday said that for the current reporting period, it expects Stelco’s average annual employment to be at least 1,879 for its unionized employees, which is 113 above the required level of 1,766. For salaried employment at Stelco, the number is expected to average at least 627, above the required level of 603, the company said.

Ms. Joly has repeatedly said that Cliffs hasn’t lived up to its ICA commitments and warned the company could face legal action or be forced to divest Stelco.

In her latest letter sent to the company on Thursday, Ms. Joly said that by advocating for U.S. President Donald Trump’s steel tariffs , Cliffs chief executive Lourenco Goncalves had violated a promise to be “a strong advocate for policies that benefit both the U.S. and Canadian steel industries.”

But Cliffs said in its Monday statement that it is complying with the undertaking regarding advocacy for trade policy.

In the Monday statement, Mr. Goncalves reiterated his support for U.S. tariffs.

“We remain strong advocates for the U.S. Section 232 policy, and believe a Fortress North America solution would be in the best interest of the United States and Canada,” he said.

Cliffs said it reached out to Ms. Joly on Friday to schedule a meeting “to discuss a path toward resuming full employment of the 175 workers in Hamilton who have been temporarily laid off.”

stories.title: Three GTA law firms put into receivership after accusations of mishandling millions in real estate funds
stories.summary: A rash of similar cases where lawyers allegedly violated their client’s trust and misappropriated their money have ignited a debate in the legal profession
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
Three law firms in the Greater Toronto Area have been put into receivership after being accused of mishandling millions in client funds during real estate transactions – allegations that an Ontario Superior Court justice warned could be just “the tip of an iceberg.”

Justice Sean Dunphy issued an order last week appointing accounting firm Doane Grant Thornton LLP as the receiver to take control of Simran Law Professional Corp. of Brampton, Ont., and JP Mann Law Firm Professional Corp. of Mississauga.

In his ruling, Justice Dunphy said the mishandling of legal trust accounts during real estate transactions has been occurring “with distressing regularity,” and that “if left unaddressed, represents an exceptionally grave attack on the profession of law at large and the integrity of our civil legal system.”

In a separate ruling on Friday, Justice Dunphy also issued an order to put RSG Law – the firm founded by former Liberal MP Rajvinder Grewal – under the control of receiver AlixPartners Advisory Inc. The firm has been facing mounting civil lawsuits alleging it was at the centre of a series of frauds against its own clients and their lenders.

Mr. Grewal or RSG Law are named in more than 30 civil cases, many involving allegations of trust-account manipulation or mortgage fraud.

“I shall refrain from using more superlatives to describe the shocking scope of the fraud that has been laid in front of me in relation to the operation of that firm’s trust account,” Justice Dunphy wrote in Friday’s court order. The allegations of fraud have not been proven in court.

Mr. Grewal has not been suspended from working, but has agreed not to practice law while he awaits a disciplinary hearing at Ontario’s Law Society Tribunal.

A rash of similar cases where lawyers allegedly violated their client’s trust and misappropriated their money have ignited a debate in the legal profession about how to ensure clients and the public are protected.

“Lawyers themselves need to raise the bar, that’s why we’re self-regulated,” said Joseph Berljawsky, managing partner of Property Law Firm CB LLP, one of the largest real estate law firms in the country.

In his decision involving Simran Law, Justice Dunphy said there were 25 occasions since February where lawyer Simranjyot Kaur represented sellers in a real estate deal, while lawyer Jagpal Mann of JP Mann Law Firm acted for the purchasers. More than $18-million in mortgage funds from a variety of smaller lenders were paid into the lawyers’ trust accounts, intended for paying out mortgages held by some of the country’s largest banks.

Instead, the money went missing.

“This is NOT a ‘one off’ case of records having been inadequately maintained or sloppy ledger-keeping,” Justice Dunphy wrote. “Not one of the mortgages was in fact discharged with the mortgage advance proceeds. Solicitors’ undertakings to discharge the mortgages were not honoured … None of the funds have been returned or accounted for.”

The application for a receiver to be appointed was brought by the title insurer in each of the transactions, FCT Insurance Company Ltd.

FCT was also the title insurer in three civil cases where lenders sought to recover mishandled trust funds from Brampton lawyer Anil K. Sharma. In an Oct. 14 court order on those matters, Justice Dunphy issued a sharp rebuke to the Law Society of Ontario’s handling of real estate fraud by lawyers.

In Mr. Sharma’s cases, almost $5-million was allegedly misappropriated in a similar manner to other recent cases: Mortgage funds were taken into his legal trust fund, but were not remitted to the intended recipients.

In his order for Mr. Sharma’s case, Justice Dunphy wrote he was “shouting into the wind” about the seriousness of recent alleged frauds and the need for swifter action from the law society’s regulators or from any authority.

The law society hasn’t made any public announcements about professional sanctions against Mr. Sharma, Ms. Kaur or Mr. Mann. None of those lawyers responded to requests for comment.

Mr. Grewal’s lawyer, Simon Bieber of Adair Goldblatt Bieber LLP, said his client “sold his shares in RSG Law in 2023 and has not been in control of the trust account since then.”

In a statement, the law society said it had obtained a court order freezing Mr. Sharma’s trust account and could not comment on its investigations. However, the society said it “has been involved in the receivership applications and as part of the receiverships is taking steps to safeguard the solicitor-client privilege of all clients.”

Mr. Berljawsky has been pushing a series of reforms at the law society that would make trust-account abuse and mortgage fraud more difficult to commit – or at least would lead to speedier discovery.

Requiring a second professional’s signature (though not in the case of sole practitioners) for any trust-account transaction is a start, according to Mr. Berljawsky. But he said a more meaningful and pro-active step would be to make law firms send monthly reconciliation reports of their trust funds to the law society that could be checked against their bank account balances.

In his view, the current system places too much trust in lawyers to make the right decisions, effectively creating an honour system and not a regulatory one. Mr. Berljawsky is warning that lawyers could find themselves cut out of the lucrative real estate market entirely if reforms can’t restore the trust of the public and of financial institutions.

“We need to come together ... to make sure residential conveyancing is safer and better, or rightfully, we will lose our role in the process,” he said.

“I shall refrain from using more superlatives to describe the shocking scope of the fraud that has been laid in front of me in relation to the operation of that firm’s trust account,” Justice Dunphy wrote in Friday’s court order. The allegations of fraud have not been proven in court.
Mr. Grewal has not been suspended from working, but has agreed not to practice law while he awaits a disciplinary hearing at Ontario’s Law Society Tribunal.

A rash of similar cases where lawyers allegedly violated their client’s trust and misappropriated their money have ignited a debate in the legal profession about how to ensure clients and the public are protected.

“Lawyers themselves need to raise the bar, that’s why we’re self-regulated,” said Joseph Berljawsky, managing partner of Property Law Firm CB LLP, one of the largest real estate law firms in the country.

In his decision involving Simran Law, Justice Dunphy said there were 25 occasions since February where lawyer Simranjyot Kaur represented sellers in a real estate deal, while lawyer Jagpal Mann of JP Mann Law Firm acted for the purchasers. More than $18-million in mortgage funds from a variety of smaller lenders were paid into the lawyers’ trust accounts, intended for paying out mortgages held by some of the country’s largest banks.
Instead, the money went missing.

“This is NOT a ‘one off’ case of records having been inadequately maintained or sloppy ledger-keeping,” Justice Dunphy wrote. “Not one of the mortgages was in fact discharged with the mortgage advance proceeds. Solicitors’ undertakings to discharge the mortgages were not honoured … None of the funds have been returned or accounted for.”
The application for a receiver to be appointed was brought by the title insurer in each of the transactions, FCT Insurance Company Ltd.

FCT was also the title insurer in three civil cases where lenders sought to recover mishandled trust funds from Brampton lawyer Anil K. Sharma. In an Oct. 14 court order on those matters, Justice Dunphy issued a sharp rebuke to the Law Society of Ontario’s handling of real estate fraud by lawyers.

In Mr. Sharma’s cases, almost $5-million was allegedly misappropriated in a similar manner to other recent cases: Mortgage funds were taken into his legal trust fund, but were not remitted to the intended recipients.

In his order for Mr. Sharma’s case, Justice Dunphy wrote he was “shouting into the wind” about the seriousness of recent alleged frauds and the need for swifter action from the law society’s regulators or from any authority.
The law society hasn’t made any public announcements about professional sanctions against Mr. Sharma, Ms. Kaur or Mr. Mann. None of those lawyers responded to requests for comment.
Mr. Grewal’s lawyer, Simon Bieber of Adair Goldblatt Bieber LLP, said his client “sold his shares in RSG Law in 2023 and has not been in control of the trust account since then.”

In a statement, the law society said it had obtained a court order freezing Mr. Sharma’s trust account and could not comment on its investigations. However, the society said it “has been involved in the receivership applications and as part of the receiverships is taking steps to safeguard the solicitor-client privilege of all clients.”
Mr. Berljawsky has been pushing a series of reforms at the law society that would make trust-account abuse and mortgage fraud more difficult to commit – or at least would lead to speedier discovery.

Requiring a second professional’s signature (though not in the case of sole practitioners) for any trust-account transaction is a start, according to Mr. Berljawsky. But he said a more meaningful and pro-active step would be to make law firms send monthly reconciliation reports of their trust funds to the law society that could be checked against their bank account balances.

In his view, the current system places too much trust in lawyers to make the right decisions, effectively creating an honour system and not a regulatory one. Mr. Berljawsky is warning that lawyers could find themselves cut out of the lucrative real estate market entirely if reforms can’t restore the trust of the public and of financial institutions.
“We need to come together ... to make sure residential conveyancing is safer and better, or rightfully, we will lose our role in the process,” he said.

stories.title: Toronto awaits results after polls close in municipal election
stories.summary: Incumbent Oliva Chow and challenger Brad Bradford are vying for the mayoralty in a race that is expected to be close
stories.author: Patrick White, Jeff Gray, Laura Stone
stories.content:
Olivia Chow, the long-time NDP stalwart who campaigned on capping transit fares and expanding a school meal program, was re-elected as mayor of Toronto on Monday, staving off a stiff challenge from east-end councillor Brad Bradford.

Her victory stands as an endorsement of a conciliatory leadership style that managed to charm the likes of Premier Doug Ford, who once declared that a Chow mayoralty would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city. Three years into her term, the conservative Premier couldn’t help but gush about his relationship with Ms. Chow, stopping just short of a full-throated endorsement.

That unlikely support helped her rebuff the Bradford campaign’s withering critiques of her time in office, which focused mainly on crime and the rising cost of living.

According to unofficial results provided by the city, Ms. Chow had 54 per cent of the vote, compared with Mr. Bradford’s 41 per cent, as of late Monday evening with almost all votes counted.

Ms. Chow addressed cheering supporters at the Great Hall in the city’s west end and thanked Mr. Bradford for his spirited run.

“I know we share a love for Toronto and a belief in its future,” she said. “We can disagree on how we get there, or what it looks like, but I do not doubt we both want what is best for our city.”

She was joined on stage by friends, family and a range of union leaders, including the incoming head of the Toronto Police Association.

Her victory speech focused on healing the differences that emerged during a bruising campaign.

“Whatever your background, whatever you believe, whoever you love, wherever you live, I will listen to you,” she said. “I will stand up for you.”

Speaking in a ballroom at the Fairmont Royal York hotel in downtown Toronto, Mr. Bradford told supporters he spoke with Ms. Chow and congratulated her on her re-election, and that her win is indisputable.

“I want her to succeed. And my supporters and the nearly 400,000 people that cast a vote for us tonight, they want her to succeed too,” he said.

“We all love this city. We know it can be better.”

Mr. Bradford acknowledged that a lot of people said his campaign faced long odds. “An incumbent has never been defeated in Toronto’s history. They said it was challenging. You know, maybe they were right,” he said to laughter.

It was a bad night for incumbents in other nearby cities.

In neighbouring Mississauga, councillor Alvin Tedjo defeated both incumbent mayor Carolyn Parrish and former Ontario Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie, who had left the mayor’s chair for her provincial bid and was seeking to return.

In Hamilton, incumbent mayor Andrea Horwath, a former Ontario NDP leader, lost to local business advocate Keanin Loomis.

The Toronto campaign was a study in political contrasts. Ms. Chow, the 69-year-old incumbent, has been a progressive political fixture in the city since 1985, when she was first elected as a Toronto school board trustee.

Despite a political résumé that includes stints as a councillor and MP, she came across as reserved in public appearances, leaning on a reputation for getting things done behind the scenes rather than in front of the cameras.

The 40-year-old Mr. Bradford, by comparison, is a relative newcomer, a truculent political showman first elected to council in 2018.

He ran in the 2023 mayoral by-election, prompted by then-mayor John Tory’s resignation over an affair with a staffer, and finished in eighth place with just 1.28 per cent of the vote. But Mr. Bradford emerged undaunted about his future political prospects.

For the next three years, Mr. Bradford effectively remained in campaign mode.

He tacked right on council, taking positions against certain bike lanes, the renaming of Yonge-Dundas Square to Sankofa Square, the creation of bus lanes and cuts to police funding – all policies he’d earlier supported.

He held campaign-style news events across the city well before the campaign period opened.

He declared that city crime had become so bad he slept with a baseball bat next to his bed.

The pre-emptive electioneering succeeded on two fronts. His citywide popularity grew in polling, and he established himself early as the leading conservative to take on Ms. Chow, deterring other potential right-leaning candidates from entering the race.

In March, Mr. Tory, who is also a former leader of the provincial Progressive Conservative Party, announced he would not run, clearing Mr. Bradford’s path to court the anti-Chow vote.

His campaign focused on portraying Toronto as a city of high crime, excessive spending, poor transit and congested streets that had become “stuck” under Ms. Chow’s leadership.

With hate crimes rising, he also allied himself with Toronto’s Jewish community while highlighting Ms. Chow’s absence from a debate on antisemitism.

He pledged to hire 1,000 police officers, commission a line-by-line review of city finances and eliminate the city’s land-transfer tax on home sales under $1.1-million.

Over the waning days of the campaign, most public opinion polls showed a statistical dead heat between the front-runners.

Ms. Chow struggled to counter her opponent’s gloomy portrayal of the city, despite a host of indicators in her favour. Under her watch, the number of homicides, shootings and homeless encampments all declined, while traffic congestion and homelessness rates improved.

In office, she patched up an inherited $1.8-billion budget hole with two large property-tax hikes and a “new deal” with Mr. Ford, which included $1.2-billion in operating cash over three years and the transfer of the expensive-to-maintain Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway to the province. The moves were among the reasons the city won a credit-rating upgrade to AA-plus from S&P Global Ratings.

Ms. Chow’s campaign focused on reducing fares for frequent TTC riders and providing free school lunches, while maintaining future property-tax hikes “in and around” the rate of inflation.

Much of the final days of campaigning centred around a core city function that generally flies under the political radar: water.

A municipal department that reports to city council and bills residents independently of city taxes, Toronto Water maintains a self-sustaining capital program that pays for projects through user fees rather than debt.

Mr. Bradford put forward a plan to spin off the water department as a public utility corporation. Rates would be set by an independent board with Toronto as the sole shareholder. The new structure could shave $300 off the average household water bill by funding capital projects through debt, according to Mr. Bradford.

The Chow campaign seized on the idea, saying it would open the door to privatization, and ran digital ads in the closing days of the race featuring the likes of environmentalist David Suzuki.

The salvo forced Mr. Bradford, for several days in a row, to reiterate that his water scheme would keep the utility in public hands and that current provincial legislation does not allow private ownership.

The results in several key council races also appeared to go Ms. Chow’s way, with progressives or likely allies winning in all four open wards, including her stepson – son of the late former federal NDP leader Jack Layton – in University-Rosedale. Former Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith, a failed candidate for the Ontario Liberal leadership, won easily in Mr. Bradford’s former ward of Beaches-East York.

The election also saw the defeat in York South-Weston of longtime city hall fixture Frances Nunziata, who spent 16 years as speaker of council, presiding over its debates, and whose career in local politics stretches back to the 1980s.

stories.title: Montreal police officer under investigation after allegedly urinating on homeless person
stories.summary: Quebec’s newly appointed Domestic Security Minister Guy Jr. Lapointe, a former police officer, has triggered new investigations into allegations of a Montreal police officer urinating on a homeless person.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Montreal- Quebec’s newly appointed Domestic Security Minister Guy Jr. Lapointe, a former police officer, has triggered new investigations into allegations of a Montreal police officer urinating on a homeless person.

Advocates welcome the move but want more action to protect vulnerable people.

Alex Berthelot, an administrator with “Le Rapsim”, an organization defending the rights of homeless Montrealers, said independent inquiries are the bare minimum of what needs to be done.

“I think we are really in a kind of extreme situation,” said Berthelot. “For me, the litmus test is going to be when and if we see that police officer arraigned in front of a court of justice, because urinating on somebody else is a criminal offence.”

Montreal daily newspaper La Presse reported earlier this month that over the span of a year, an officer had allegedly filmed himself humiliating homeless people, and that on at least one occasion, he had urinated on a person sleeping on the streets.

The officer was on patrol in District 21, a downtown area with a significant homeless population.

An internal investigation was triggered and the officer was suspended with pay.

Lapointe said the newly announced investigations by the province’s police watchdog, known as the BEI, and the ethics commissioner were neither a vote of non-confidence in the Spvm (Montreal police), nor a way to question the quality of the force’s investigation.

“It’s clear to me that in this case, the investigation must be conducted by an external entity to preserve public confidence,” Lapointe said in a statement.

Newly elected Quebec Liberal Member of the National Assembly James Hughes welcomed the new inquiries. Before he became a member of the Opposition, Hughes was the president-director general of the Old Brewery Mission, a non-profit dedicated to supporting adults experiencing, or at risk of experiencing homelessness in Montreal. He has been involved in the fight to end homelessness for decades.

“Our hearts got out to this gentleman who was abused in this way, treated in such an inhumane fashion,” Hughes said in an interview with CTV News. “It just boggles the mind to think that anyone could do this, let alone a police officer.”

Hughes said he is particularly concerned because he had noted improvement in the last decade in the way police officers from downtown Montreal police station interact with the homeless population.

“They need to be treated with humanity and dignity and thoughtfulness at all times,” said Hughes. “As a general rule, the people have been so much better than we have seen in the past. There are obvious exceptions from time to time, but when you hear a story like this, it just makes you stop and go ‘how much progress have we really made?’”

He considered this an exceptional case that needs to be treated in an exceptional way.

“It’s got civil dimensions, potentially criminal dimensions to it,” said Hughes. “So, I think it’s quite right that it be analyzed by independent parties the way the minister has indicated.”

He hopes all parties in Quebec, at all levels of government, can lock arms and find solutions.

But some advocates say the allegations against police are evidence that a fundamental change in public discourse is desperately needed. Berthelot said there has been a dehumanization of homeless people over the last five or six years.

“We are seeing them as a nuisance to public order instead of people who need help and people who are living through difficult situations. This has led us to where we are now.”

Quebec’s new government plans to hold a summit on homelessness next year and has promised to cut the number of people experiencing homelessness in half by 2030.

stories.title: Canadian man freed after being imprisoned, tortured in Ethiopia
stories.summary: Accused of supporting rebels in the Amhara region, Esubalew Birhanie was imprisoned without trial
stories.author: Geoffrey York
stories.content:
An Ethiopian judge has ordered the release of a Canadian man who suffered torture and beatings from police during a year of imprisonment in the country.

Thirty-nine-year-old Esubalew Birhanie was arrested at Ethiopia’s main airport last year when he tried to return home to Toronto after a month-long visit to his relatives. Accused of supporting rebels in the Amhara region, he was imprisoned without trial.

Mr. Birhanie had worked as a ground technician at Toronto Pearson Airport for more than two years when he was arrested in Ethiopia. He was finally freed this month when police failed to provide evidence to the judge to support their allegations.

Now he is struggling to rebuild his life. “I’ve lost everything,” he said after returning to Toronto last week. “I lost my apartment, I lost my job, I lost my health – everything.”

Mr. Birhanie said he was tortured by police who wanted him to confess to “inciting terrorism” by supporting rebels. They handcuffed him, forced him face down on the prison floor and stomped on his neck until he fainted, he said. When he awoke, they were beating him on the back with clubs and batons, he said.

A nine-page report by the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission, obtained by The Globe and Mail last March, confirmed his story. The report said the commission had investigated the case and concluded that the Canadian man was “beaten by officers, resulting in significant physical injuries.”

The commission called for a full criminal investigation of the police who had perpetrated the abuse. It also recommended compensation be paid to Mr. Birhanie for the “physical and psychological trauma” he suffered.

Instead, he was kept in prison for a further six months, until the judge decided there was no evidence against him.

Mr. Birhanie said the police made two allegations against him. The first was that he had incited opinion against the government at a public meeting in Toronto in 2020 when he spoke about the plight of Amhara people who had been killed or displaced. But the judge ruled that he was entitled to express his opinions, he said.

The second allegation was that he had posted anti-government statements on Facebook. But this was based on a fake Facebook account that the police had installed on his phone after his arrest, Mr. Birhanie said. When the judge requested proof of the posts, the police were unable to provide any because they had deleted the fake account to conceal the date when it was created, he said.

The Ethiopian government has often used anti-terrorism laws as a pretext to prosecute dissidents and journalists, according to several reports by human-rights groups.

Corruption is another factor in some arrests. When he was first detained, the police offered to release him in exchange for a bribe, the equivalent of about $23,000, he said.

Mr. Birhanie said he was finally released from prison on Oct. 8. But when he arrived at the airport to return to Toronto, he was told he was prohibited from leaving the country. He went into hiding for two weeks, fearing another arrest, while he tried to get a court order to lift the travel ban.

The restrictions were eventually lifted, and he flew back to Toronto on Friday. “I am incredibly relieved and excited to have finally left Ethiopia,” he told The Globe. “What I went through there was horrible and deeply traumatic.”

Now he is searching for a new job, a new apartment and specialized medical treatment for his back. He is taking painkillers but says he still feels pain when he sits or sleeps. He plans to launch legal action to seek justice and compensation from the Ethiopian government.
