stories.title: Sask. First Nations leaders raise land rights, policing concerns at historic Ottawa meeting
stories.summary: Federal government heard reasoning behind amending Indian status legislation and setting up First Nations policing from Saskatchewan chiefs.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
First Nations leaders from Saskatchewan who attended a long-awaited first ministers meeting say they raised several concerns affecting their people.

Speaking to reporters afterward, Lac La Ronge Indian Band Chief Tammy Cook-Searson said she was given three minutes to speak. She used them to advocate for a proposed change to the Indian Act that would allow any person with at least one status parent to inherit federal Indian status.

“We have children, grandchildren, members of our communities that are not part of our nation because of this discriminatory policy of the federal government,” Cook-Searson told reporters Monday.

Cook-Searson, acting as Saskatchewan’s regional representative, said she did not hear any commitments from the federal government on the issue but will “continue to push forward.” The bill, known as S-2, has passed the Senate and awaits action from the House of Commons Standing Committee on Indigenous and Northern Affairs.

She also asked Ottawa to consider adding survivors of the Timber Bay Children’s Home, near Lac La Ronge, Sask., to the residential school settlement agreement.

She says she has pushed for this since she first became chief more than two decades ago. At one point, Ottawa was at the table, but the province was not.

Now, Cook-Searson says Premier Scott Moe has “given us his word” that Saskatchewan will return to the negotiations.

“Now we need the feds to come back to the table, so if we can get the two together, the province and the feds. Then we will be able to settle this injustice with the Timber Bay Children’s Home survivors and their families.”

Premier Scott Moe was among the premiers at the meeting but did not make himself available for media comment Monday.

Cook-Searson was joined by several other chiefs represented by the Prince Albert Grand Council, who each raised their top concerns in hopes Ottawa would take note.

For Chief Kirby Constant of James Smith Cree Nation, policing remains top of mind four years after a mass stabbing attack that killed 11 people and wounded 17 others on the First Nation. He wants to see support for First Nations policing to improve public safety in the region.

“Without First Nation Policing, we’re feeling that the RCMP is not fulfilling their requirements to keep our community safe,” Constant told reporters, adding that the service would allow people with similar cultural backgrounds and traditional knowledge to serve their communities.

As the meeting was underway, members of the Onion Lake Cree Nation, located approximately 50 kilometres north of Lloydminster, Sask., took to the streets of Ottawa to protest the event.

“No organization or government has the authority to speak for Onion Lake Cree Nation, negotiate our rights, or make commitments on our behalf without our consent,” Onion Lake Cree Nation Chief Pete Chief told Global News in an interview Monday.

Onion Lake formally withdrew from the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) three years ago, after an internal referendum ended its membership.

Chief said his First Nation has no problem with Prime Minister Mark Carney’s development agenda but wants meaningful consultation that goes beyond a closed-door meeting where not everyone is present.

“Come to our lands, come and develop that relationship with us and so that we also can be a part of the development, a part of whatever the project May be,” he said. Carry the Kettle First Nation also opposed the meeting. In a letter posted on social media, the nation said it has not consented to being represented by the Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations (Fsin) or the AFN.

“In the absence of our consent and any rights at law, we request that Fsin and AFN expressly exclude our Nation from any representation today at the Prime Minister and First Ministers,” wrote Carry the Kettle Chief Dwayne (Cliff) Thomson.

Before the meeting, the AFN said regional representatives would attend. Fsin Chief Bobby Cameron is Saskatchewan’s regional representative, but it is unclear whether he was there, since Cook-Searson presented herself as his proxy.

Global News has asked the Fsin to confirm Cameron’s attendance and has not yet heard back.

Earlier this month, the Fsin announced it would take the federal government to court after Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) served it a final repayment notice for $12.4 million, following a forensic audit in the fall of 2025. ISC later said it would file a statement of claim to recover the money.

The last time Indigenous leaders met with the premiers and the prime minister of Canada was during the Kelowna Accord talks in 2005, which were centred on socioeconomic gaps in Indigenous communities and were led by then-prime minister Paul Martin.

Carney said Monday it’s “sobering” to consider that this is the first meeting to bring together federal, provincial and First Nations leaders in two decades.

“Our task is twofold. First is to work together to create opportunities for all our peoples, while building a country that is stronger, more sovereign and more independent,” he said.

The meeting May not be the last. Cook-Searson said representatives received “a commitment” from some premiers to meet annually.

Representatives of Saskatchewan’s Métis people were also absent, but the president of Métis Nation-Saskatchewan says talks with the federal government are ongoing.

“We just did our lobbying not very long ago last week and it went very well with the speaker and the speaker’s lounge and got to meet all parties and begin this conversation in regards to the importance of having the Metis be involved,” he said.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alvin Tedjo projected to win Mississauga mayoral race, defeating Parrish and Crombie
stories.summary: Alvin Tedjo had served one term as city councillor before deciding to enter the mayoral race, beating incumbent Carolyn Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
One-term Mississauga city councillor Alvin Tedjo will become mayor after a race against the incumbent and her predecessor, Global News projects.

Unofficial results posted by the city show Tedjo leading the race with 63,508 votes as of 8:45 p.m. Monday. Incumbent Mayor Carolyn Parrish has received 45,178 votes, while former Mississauga mayor and Ontario Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie received 37,477 votes. About 89 per cent of polls were reporting.

Tedjo’s victory comes after weeks of campaigning that saw the rookie councillor pick up steam as it went on.

Speaking to supporters Monday, Crombie said she had called Tedjo to congratulate him on his victory.

“Alvin, your energy, your enthusiasm and the joy you bring to politics matter,” Crombie said in her concession speech. “You’ve inspired people to get involved and to believe that they can help shape the city’s future. That is something to be proud of.”

She added that a “new generation” was taking the reins and would cheer for the city to succeed under Tedjo’s leadership.

Only a few days before election day, Tedjo was shown by a Liaison Strategies poll on Oct. 22 with 31 per cent support, just behind Crombie.

Tedjo has sought the mayor’s position before, having run for it during the 2024 byelection. He came in second with 25 per cent, behind Parrish’s 31 per cent.

Crombie and Parrish sparred at a debate earlier this month with the incumbent saying staff was “terrified that the blonde bombshell is coming back.” Crombie appeared to criticize how Parrish governed, saying “sometimes you have to leave your office, go meet people” and convince investors to come to Mississauga.

That discourse May have led to Tedjo’s ability to surge up the middle and end up with a resounding lead over the two other frontrunners.

During his time on council, Tedjo served on multiple committees and on the Region of Peel Council.

stories.title: Cowichan Tribes to bring forward private property protection solution, lawyer says
stories.summary: B.C. First Nations groups say they are ready to work with the new provincial government to advance reconciliation and uphold rights and title
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
The lawyer for the Cowichan Tribes said they will make a proposal in January that protects private property rights in the landmark Aboriginal title case that the B.C. Conservatives have said calls into question who controls British Columbia.

Lawyer David Rosenberg said that if it has “the right attitude,” the incoming Conservative government will find it easier to resolve the Cowichan case than to repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, known as Dripa.

The 2025 Cowichan ruling on a portion of Crown, city and private land in Richmond, B.C., found that Aboriginal title is a “senior interest” compared with fee-simple title, and sections of B.C.’s Land Title Act that establish fee-simple title as “indefeasible” do not apply to Aboriginal title.

It has triggered concerns about the impact on private property rights and values, but Rosenberg said the tribes will go to court in the new year with a solution to respect and protect private property and its value, as well as Cowichan Aboriginal title.

“That is what negotiations are supposed to be leading to,” he said.

He said the case has nothing to do with the repeal of Dripa, which premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has said is his top priority after Saturday’s election victory.

Rosenberg said Doerkson’s election could be seen as a fresh start in resolving the Cowichan case.

“That a new government could come to the issue with a positive attitude, and show some leadership, and take the high road, and say, ‘We’re going to recognize Aboriginal title and we’re going to protect property interests,’” he said.

While Rosenberg said it could be easier to resolve the Cowichan case, former B.C. Conservative leader John Rustad said Dripa can be repealed quickly, while the Cowichan Tribes case could drag on for years.

Rustad, who didn’t seek re-election, said last year that “Indigenous rights and private property cannot co-exist,” and called on the Supreme Court of Canada to resolve the conflict as soon as possible.

He said in an interview on Monday that the case cannot be allowed to drag on because of the uncertainty it has created around private property rights.

Rustad said the incoming government must argue in its appeal for the extinguishment of Aboriginal title, something the previous government did not do in the original case.

“Private property is the foundation of society,” he said. “If you are going to take private property rights, which the court is now in the process of doing, you completely undermine society,” he said.

Extinguishment, however, does not rule out some agreement that would compensate First Nations, said Rustad, who was the Aboriginal relations minister under the former B.C. Liberal government.

But Rosenberg said neither British Columbia nor the federal government could extinguish existing Aboriginal title, unless the Constitution were amended, and he warned against conflating Dripa with the Cowichan Tribes case. He added that the City of Richmond had argued for extinguishment, and was unsuccessful.

“I don’t believe the repeal of Dripa would in substance affect what the court ordered,” he said, referring to the ruling that British Columbia must negotiate in good faith how to reconcile fee-simple interests with Cowichan Aboriginal title.

Rosenberg said the tribes’ proposal on private property will be filed when the court hears requests for the Cowichan judgment to be stayed pending appeal.

The Conservatives’ resounding election win, in which they secured a two-thirds majority, has raised concern among First Nations leaders.

The First Nations Leadership Council said Monday that B.C. is at a crossroads with the incoming government that could result in either a “battleground” or reconciliation.

Doerkson said at a postelection news conference on Sunday that he is “completely committed to working with First Nations” but would stick with his election promise to repeal Dripa.

He said the declaration act brought in by the New Democrat government had caused more problems.

“So, I am committed with working on a great path forward of respect, partnership, friendship and conversation.”

Rustad said the situation facing the new government is how to reconcile private property rights with outstanding Indigenous rights.

“The Indigenous question is the elephant in the room,” Rustad said. “You cannot get your economy going without finding a path forward, working with First Nations, which means you can’t do all these other things that you want to do.”

The leadership council, made up of executives from three main First Nations groups in B.C., said in a statement that it was ready to work with the government to advance reconciliation and uphold rights and title.

Grand Chief Stewart Phillip of the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs said outgoing Premier David Eby’s loss on Saturday was “hugely disappointing.”

“We are at a historical crossroads: Battleground B.C. or reconciliation through the principles and road map of the Declaration Act,” he said.

B.C. Assembly of First Nations Regional Chief Terry Teegee said in the statement that some provincial politicians in the recent past have campaigned on anti-Indigenous racism.

“We call on premier-designate Doerksen to uphold a zero-tolerance policy for racism, discrimination or hatred in his caucus, including holding his members accountable for some of the reprehensible statements made during the election,” he said.

First Nations Summit Chief Shana Thomas said no economic projects in the province could happen without involvement of First Nations.

A statement from the office of the clerk of the legislative assembly said swearing-in ceremonies can’t take place until the election results are certified and provided by the chief electoral officer, which is expected Nov. 18.

stories.title: Winnipegger raises money for CancerCare Manitoba with giant jack-o’-lanterns
stories.summary: Chris Okell carves out heavyweight pumpkins in honour of his mom who loved Halloween — a promise he's upheld every year while trying to raise money for cancer.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Chris Okell carves out over 1,000-pound pumpkins displayed in his driveway in honour of his mom who loved Halloween.

Chris’ mom, Marietta Okell, passed away in 2010 from pancreatic cancer, and asked Chris to promise her that he will keep carving pumpkins for the kids. It’s a promise he’s upheld every year while trying to raise money in hopes to find a cure for cancer.

“I’m going to keep going for as long as I can and continue to raise money for anybody who needs this, because I lost three people this year alone,” said Okell. “Is there a cure? I hope so, and if there is, let it free. Let people stop suffering.”

People can donate online through CancerCare Manitoba or in person at 39 Baisinger Dr.

Watch the video above for the full story.

stories.title: Elections across Canada see rise in advance voting. Could it lead to a higher overall turnout?
stories.summary: More Canadians appear to be choosing to cast their ballots early, and in some elections, advance polling has seen record numbers.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Winnipeg – More Canadians appear to be choosing to cast their ballots early, and in some elections, advance polling has seen record numbers.

A record number of voters cast their ballots ahead of Winnipeg’s municipal election, with a total of 50,767 votes cast. This is a 21.2 per cent increase from 2022, when the previous advance voting record was set in the city.

“There’s definitely been an uptick in advance voting in all elections,” said Malcolm Bird, a professor of political studies at the University of Winnipeg.

“I think part of this has to do with an effort by the political parties and by elections organizations to promote it, in the hopes that it will encourage more people to vote in general.”

The trend extends beyond Winnipeg, with Toronto nearly doubling its advance voting turnout this year compared with its last election four years ago.

According to the City of Toronto, 225,550 eligible voters cast their ballot during the six days of advance voting. That is up from about 130,000 in the 2023 mayoral byelection and approximately 116,000 in the last general municipal election in 2022.

The trend isn’t limited to municipal elections.

Advance voting for Quebec’s provincial election earlier this month was also up from 2022, with 25.59 per cent, or 1.6 million electors, voting early. Four years ago, the percentage of advanced voters was 24.8 per cent.

Political experts say advance voting offers voters more flexibility.

“Generally speaking, higher turnout is because people have become used to voting early. It’s easier to vote early,” said Christopher Adams, a professor of political science at the University of Manitoba.

“I think the get-out-the-vote campaigns by candidates is much more aggressive during advance polling, because you get to lock in your supporters.”

Adams explains that voter turnout is influenced by several factors, including whether people believe their vote makes a difference, how accessible voting is and whether barriers prevent people from voting, as well as external factors such as the weather.

But while advance polling numbers appear to be rising in some elections, it doesn’t necessarily mean more people are voting overall.

“I’m always a little skeptical about when you see record numbers of advance vote, necessarily being a harbinger of major voter turnout or change or anything like that,” said Curtis Brown, vice-president of Abacus Data.

“In the last election (in Winnipeg), there was record voter turnout in advance, but we only had 37 per cent turnout.”

The question now is whether this recent surge in advance voting in Winnipeg will carry through to election day, as voters across the province, including in Winnipeg, head to the polls on Wednesday.

B.C. election turnout lowest in decades

Voter turnout in B.C.’s provincial election was the lowest seen in the last 30 years.

Preliminary voter turnout for the 2026 election sits at 48.12 per cent with 99.96 per cent of ballot boxes reporting. That’s a lower turnout than for all of the previous general elections listed on the Elections BC website, going back to 1996.

Thirty years ago, voter turnout was 71.5 per cent. In 2024, it was 58.45 per cent.

Thirty years ago, voter turnout was 71.5 per cent. In 2024, it was 58.45 per cent.

content_blocks.text: Winnipeg – More Canadians appear to be choosing to cast their ballots early, and in some elections, advance polling has seen record numbers.

A record number of voters cast their ballots ahead of Winnipeg’s municipal election, with a total of 50,767 votes cast. This is a 21.2 per cent increase from 2022, when the previous advance voting record was set in the city.
“There’s definitely been an uptick in advance voting in all elections,” said Malcolm Bird, a professor of political studies at the University of Winnipeg.
“I think part of this has to do with an effort by the political parties and by elections organizations to promote it, in the hopes that it will encourage more people to vote in general.”

content_blocks.alt: Advanced polls voting election results
content_blocks.caption: Malcom Bird is a political studies professor at the University of Manitoba. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: The trend extends beyond Winnipeg, with Toronto nearly doubling its advance voting turnout this year compared with its last election four years ago.

According to the City of Toronto, 225,550 eligible voters cast their ballot during the six days of advance voting. That is up from about 130,000 in the 2023 mayoral byelection and approximately 116,000 in the last general municipal election in 2022.
The trend isn’t limited to municipal elections.

Advance voting for Quebec’s provincial election earlier this month was also up from 2022, with 25.59 per cent, or 1.6 million electors, voting early. Four years ago, the percentage of advanced voters was 24.8 per cent.
Political experts say advance voting offers voters more flexibility.

content_blocks.alt: A election vote sign
content_blocks.caption: An election vote sign seen here in Waterloo on Oct. 8, 2019. (Dan Lauckner / CTV Kitchener)

content_blocks.text: “Generally speaking, higher turnout is because people have become used to voting early. It’s easier to vote early,” said Christopher Adams, a professor of political science at the University of Manitoba.
“I think the get-out-the-vote campaigns by candidates is much more aggressive during advance polling, because you get to lock in your supporters.”

Adams explains that voter turnout is influenced by several factors, including whether people believe their vote makes a difference, how accessible voting is and whether barriers prevent people from voting, as well as external factors such as the weather.
But while advance polling numbers appear to be rising in some elections, it doesn’t necessarily mean more people are voting overall.

content_blocks.alt: Advanced polls voting election results
content_blocks.caption: Curtis Brown is the vice-president of Abacus Data. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: “I’m always a little skeptical about when you see record numbers of advance vote, necessarily being a harbinger of major voter turnout or change or anything like that,” said Curtis Brown, vice-president of Abacus Data.
“In the last election (in Winnipeg), there was record voter turnout in advance, but we only had 37 per cent turnout.”
The question now is whether this recent surge in advance voting in Winnipeg will carry through to election day, as voters across the province, including in Winnipeg, head to the polls on Wednesday.

stories.title: Mayoral elections getting heated across midwestern Ontario
stories.summary: The race for mayor in Canada’s Prettiest Town, has been anything but pretty. Personal insults have been hurled by supporters of the two candidates against each other online for several weeks now.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The race for mayor in Canada’s Prettiest Town, has been anything but pretty. Personal insults have been hurled by supporters of the two candidates against each other online for several weeks now.

Incumbent Mayor Trevor Bazinet is seeking his first mandate from the residents of Goderich. He was appointed to the top job by his fellow councilors in August 2023, following the untimely death of then mayor, Myles Murdock.

Previous to that, Bazinet spent eight years as a Goderich councilor, and one year as deputy mayor before taking over as Mayor. Challenging Bazinet is Steve Buchanan, who used to the own the Port Albert General Store, and once ran for the Liberal party in the riding of London North.

The personal nature of this campaign has brought out voters, with more than 41 per cent of Goderich’s registered voters, already casting ballots.

Further up the coast, Ken Craig is seeking his second term as Kincardine’s mayor. Challenging him in the rapidly growing shoreline community fueled largely by the Bruce Power Nuclear plant, are former Kincardine Reeve, and former Bruce County M.P.P Barb Fisher, and two term Kincardine Councilor Bill Stewart.

In Saugeen Shores, also seeing massive growth as a result of Bruce Power, Luke Charbonneau is seeking his third term as Mayor. He’s challenged by two first-time candidates Jeff James, and Brian Putnam, both from Southampton.

There will be a new mayor in Owen Sound. Incumbent Ian Boddy is not running for re-election. 6 residents are seeking to replace him, Richard Thomas, Ray Botten, Jodi King, Carol Merton, Mike Seiler, and Andrii Zvorygin.

In Southern Huron County, George Finch is seeking his 3rd term as Mayor for the Municipality of South Huron. He’s being challenged by former South Huron Mayor Maureen Cole, and three term South Huron councilor Ted Oke.

These are just some of the races, we’ll be covering tonight, across Midwestern Ontario.

stories.title: UCP backbencher Shane Getson quits legislature on eve of fall sitting
stories.summary: Shane Getson made headlines for controversial comments, including comparing transgender surgery to livestock castration in 2025.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A plainspoken, two-term Alberta United Conservative backbencher who courted controversy is quitting the job effective immediately.

Shane Getson says he is leaving due to personal and family reasons but does not elaborate.

“I can no longer give the time and attention that I have over the last seven years,” Getson said Monday in a statement written for local newspapers and shared by caucus.

“Providing anything less would diminish both my responsibilities to the people I serve and to my family.”

Getson has represented Lac. Ste. Anne-Parkland, a mostly rural riding northwest of Edmonton, since 2019.

In his time, he was known for speeches and comments riling up the political left.

In his goodbye statement, Getson writes, “Don’t chase the wackado woke, DEI, socialist easy fix for nothing ideas because of emotions getting ahead of logic.

“At the same time, keep your ears and minds open. Listen to different perspectives.”

Getson never served in cabinet but for a time was the United Conservative caucus whip.

He made headlines for controversial comments, including comparing transgender surgery to livestock castration in 2025. He later spoke of overcoming his own childhood abuse through religion, sports and hard work.

stories.title: Londoners speak on issues while voting
stories.summary: As the final day dawns for the municipal elections, Londoners are saying what issues they want to see tackled....
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
As the final day dawns for the municipal elections, Londoners are saying what issues they want to see tackled.

Throughout the election, Ward 3 candidate’s have covered housing, traffic, and bussing issues, while residents see many different issues.

London City Hall. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

“My neighbors have eight people living in one house with no parking for their cars,” said one Ward 3 resident at the Stronach Arena and Community Centre after voting on the final day.

While at the arena a steady stream of residents voting for ward 3 during the lunch break, either coming from work or running errands.

One resident of ward 3 who’s lived in London since 1964 brought up her issues with the parking in the city stating she doesn’t feel heard.

“I paid people shoveling my driveway last winter and they had no where to park. There is a school down my street where people park, they should have a no parking sign,” said Christina Iarusso who’s husband worked for the city for over 30 years. She also stated that she called the city 4 times about a broken light outside her house that flickered till it was finally fixed.

Many residents face challenges that do not get brought up as much from parking to policing to social services, while one voter told XFM News that there isn’t enough social support.

“Living alone, it’s hard finding someone to help clean and take care of me,” said Glen Lake a 91-year-old resident of London who finds it hard trying to get the support he needs.

Some changes Lake would like to see from the new ward 3 elected, is in the road construction becoming less sporadic and more for one at a time.

“Some problems I see is the cost of living has gotten out of hand,” said Ted Williams.

Williams added he wants to see the city to become more open on opinions from the average taxpayer.

Does your vote matter?

Voting sign outside of Stronach Arena (Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM news)

Those at the polls were asked if they believe their vote matters.

“I would like to think so,” said Lake.

“No, I’m one guy and many people won’t have the same opinion as me,” said Williams.

“I don’t know. It feels like the city does what they want, I almost didn’t come to vote,” Iarusso stated.

One resident stated he thinks his vote matters and everyone else’s does, saying if you think someone is the right person you should vote for them.

In 2022 the city said voting hit a historic low where 25 per cent of eligible voters made it to the polls, which was down from 2018 that saw 38 per cent vote. With the advanced polling the city estimates that the percentage will jump 27 per cent equal to around 330,000 votes casted.

-With files from Georgia Chambers and Benjamin McFadden

stories.title: Battle for Toronto mayor could be one of the tightest as Ontario holds municipal elections
stories.summary: Incumbent Olivia Chow has the Toronto’s progressive vote cornered, while Brad Bradford became a consensus challenger from the right.
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
Torontonians went to the polls Monday to choose a mayor in the tightest race in recent memory, between left wing incumbent Olivia Chow and right wing challenger Brad Bradford, a city councillor.

It is the most closely watched of Ontario’s civic elections.

In Hamilton, incumbent mayor and former Ontario NDP leader Andrea Horwath is challenged by Keanin Loomis, a lawyer and former head of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, and Rob Cooper, a city councillor running on a tax cut platform.

In Mississauga, former mayor Bonnie Crombie, who left office to lead the Ontario Liberal Party to disappointing results in the last election, is looking to reclaim her post from incumbent Carolyn Parrish, a former Liberal MP. Both are trying to hold off the challenge from councillor Alvin Tedjo.

In Ottawa, incumbent mayor Mark Sutcliffe faces his strongest challenge from councillor Jeff Leiper.

In Toronto, it has seemed until recently like Chow’s race to lose, but lately more like a toss-up.

Bradford has been a councillor for Beaches-East York since 2018. Before that he worked in urban planning, including for Toronto. He ran in the last mayoral election in 2023, getting a little over 1 per cent of the vote.

Chow won that election by five percentage points over her closest rival Ana Bailao, a former deputy to former mayor John Tory, who had recently resigned a sex scandal. In that campaign, the political right was split, with former police chief Mark Saunders, who had previously run for the Ontario Progressive Conservatives, taking nearly 9 per cent.

Chow has the city’s progressive vote cornered. She was MP for the downtown Trinity-Spadina riding (since redrawn) for eight years until 2014, and is the widow of NDP icon and former leader Jack Layton. Both were also Toronto city councillors.

If she loses, it will be the first time since the present-day amalgamated City of Toronto was created in 1998 that an incumbent mayor has lost a bid for re-election.

Early in this race, Bradford became a consensus challenger from the right, freeing him to focus on presenting an alternative to Chow.

Bradford ran on crime, congestion and cost of living. His slogan “Toronto is not broken, but it is stuck” allowed him to channel public concern about safety on the streets; encampments and drug use in city parks; violence and disorder on public transit; worsening traffic and general urban affordability without veering too far into negativity. News stories during the campaign, such as court cases about bike lanes and a shooting at a street festival, helped keep his message top of mind.

Chow enjoyed the strategic advantage of incumbency, with little need to further boost her profile. Instead, she directed many of her debate minutes against Bradford, to the point that he complained she was fear-mongering, especially about his plan to turn Toronto Water into a corporate utility like Toronto Hydro, which Chow said raised fears about privatization.

In September, there was a brief news cycle about whether Ontario Premier Doug Ford, brother of the late former mayor Rob Ford, meant to formally endorse Chow when he told reporters they have a “phenomenal relationship,” she is doing “an incredible job,” and the media should “read between the lines” about his views on the election.

Bradford’s campaign said in a statement this was a sign of Chow’s weakness against the premier, with whom she frequently negotiates and cooperates. “She protests, the Premier pushes, she folds,” it said. Bradford, for his part, has repeatedly invoked Prime Minister Mark Carney when pitching his platform, such as his plan to separate Toronto’s operating and capital budgets.

Polls in the final week showed the two candidates within the margin of error of each other, with Chow’s numbers a little higher.

Over the campaign, it is Bradford’s numbers that have increased most. At the outset, voting intentions on the political right threatened to split again, with Bradford the consensus candidate and former federal Conservative cabinet minister Chris Alexander the longshot spoiler, polling hopelessly in single digits among a constituency likely to favour Bradford.

Alexander’s late decision to drop out appears to have contributed to Bradford’s boost in polling numbers, and created a sense of momentum in the campaign’s last days.

So on voting day, with the polls showing a practical tie, both camps can sense imminent victory, Chow’s because she was ahead all along and made no major missteps, and Bradford’s because the desire for change is a powerful vote driver.

On a warm autumn day, with the sun still high at dinner time, a motivated electorate will have no excuses for failing to vote.

Toronto’s weather on Monday remained clear, calm and ideal for get out the vote strategies and last minute texted encouragements.

Polls close at 8 pm. Ballots are digitally scanned, and results are expected to be available soon afterwards.

stories.title: They called it an administrative error. Now a P.E.I. PC Party official faces 42 charges
stories.summary: As MLAs prepare to return to historic Province House for the fall sitting of P.E.I.’s legislature next week, the governing Progressive Conservatives are facing serious questions about their political fundraising.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown – As MLAs prepare to return to historic Province House for the fall sitting of P.E.I.’s legislature next week, the governing Progressive Conservatives are facing serious questions about their political fundraising.

P.E.I. RCMP have laid 42 charges against the party’s official agent over donations made last year. The allegations include allowing donations from people who weren’t eligible to contribute, knowingly accepting amounts above legal limits, knowingly making false statements in documents filed with the chief electoral officer, and failing to meet reporting and receipt requirements.

Speaking to reporters ahead of a First Nations-First Ministers’ meeting in Ottawa on Monday, P.E.I. Premier Rob Lantz appeared to downplay the allegations.

“These are administrative issues with our submissions to Elections P.E.I., and it’s before the courts now,” Lantz said, echoing comments he made to local media earlier this month.

“It’ll work itself out.”

In August, Elections P.E.I. referred irregularities involving the party’s donations to the RCMP. Police say their investigation is now complete.

“This is not something that we take lightly,” said media relations officer Cpl. Gavin Moore. “It’s important that people report if they do see irregularities and that these things can be brought to light.”

In 2025, the annual contribution limit was $3,350 per person, per party. According to CTV News calculations, seven donations allegedly exceeded their combined legal limits by more than $11,000.

Breakdown of the 42 charges of alleged offences under Election Expenses act, in plain language:

10 charges of allowing donations from people who weren’t permitted to contribute

9 charges of failing to issue required receipts or ensure they were properly completed or handled

8 charges of knowingly making false statements in documents filed with the chief electoral officer

7 charges of knowingly allowing and accepting contributions exceeding the annual donation limit

4 charges of failing to file required contribution records

3 charges of failing to record contributors’ names and addresses for donations exceeding $250

1 charges of failing to ensure required financial statements and the auditor’s report were filed

The allegations have not been proven in court.

Matt MacFarlane, leader of P.E.I.’s Green Party, said Lantz “should be taking some ownership.”

“This is not something where you want to blame your volunteers,” he said. “This is something where a leader should step forward and say, ‘We’ve made a mistake. We’ve done wrong. We need to do better.’”

MacFarlane pointed to the allegations of knowingly making false statements and accepting donations above legal limits.

“These are very important laws in our province to ensure an equal playing field for all parties,” he said.

In a statement sent to CTV News, the PC Party said it has co-operated fully with Elections P.E.I. throughout the process.

The party said its 2025 contributions received a clean audit from an independent auditor, who found its financial statements were accurate and in line with accounting standards.

“The matters identified by Elections PEI arose through its separate compliance review process,” the statement said.

The PC Party’s official agent is scheduled to appear in Charlottetown provincial court on Thursday.

stories.title: BC Ferries board cuts ties with CEO Nicolas Jimenez
stories.summary: B.C. Conservatives called for Jimenez’s firing last year after company awarded $1-billion contract to Chinese state-owned company
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Nicolas Jimenez is out as CEO at BC Ferries in a “leadership transition” launched by the company’s board, just two days after the election of the B.C. Conservatives, who asked for his firing last year.

A news release from BC Ferries said Brian Anderson, the company’s vice-president of strategy and planning, has been appointed as the interim chief executive officer, effective immediately.

The release said the board of directors had also started a “revitalization review” to address growing demands for safe, reliable services.

The B.C. Conservatives, who secured a two-third majority in Saturday’s provincial election, called last year for Jimenez to be fired after the company awarded a $1-billion contract to a Chinese state-owned company to build four new vessels.

The party also called for the firing of board chair Joy MacPhail, saying she and Jimenez had shown “a complete failure of judgment” by pushing forward with the contract with China Merchants Industry Weihai Shipyards despite Canada’s trade dispute with China.

Eric McNeely, provincial president of the BC Ferry and Marine Workers’ Union, said on Monday that he saw indications last year that a review was taking place over the Chinese contract.

“I think there were some real questions around that time about why we wouldn’t build ferries in B.C. or in Canada, and then some questions sort of emerging about who’s accountable for decisions made by BC Ferries when there is so much government money in play,” said McNeely.

McNeely said about 4,500 union members at BC Ferries have lacked a collective agreement since November 2025, and he hoped the change in leadership could reset that labour relationship.

“I think with new leadership, there’s a potential opportunity to find labour peace as we go into the fall period, as opposed to what was happening under previous leadership where management was giving themselves increases while unionized members continue without,” said McNeely.

The BC Ferries board said in its news release that it appreciated Jimenez for his contributions to the company and a search for a permanent successor would follow the revitalization review.

Jimenez told the House of Commons transport committee last year that BC Ferries received six compliant bids to replace its four oldest ships, all from foreign countries.

While two Canadian shipyards pre-qualified for the competition, he said, neither chose to formally submit a proposal.

The organization chose the proposal that offered the best combination of value, quality, delivery, speed and protections for customers, Jimenez said.

Jimenez was previously president and CEO of provincial auto insurer Icbc.

“I think there were some real questions around that time about why we wouldn’t build ferries in B.C. or in Canada, and then some questions sort of emerging about who’s accountable for decisions made by BC Ferries when there is so much government money in play,” said McNeely.
McNeely said about 4,500 union members at BC Ferries have lacked a collective agreement since November 2025, and he hoped the change in leadership could reset that labour relationship.

“I think with new leadership, there’s a potential opportunity to find labour peace as we go into the fall period, as opposed to what was happening under previous leadership where management was giving themselves increases while unionized members continue without,” said McNeely.
The BC Ferries board said in its news release that it appreciated Jimenez for his contributions to the company and a search for a permanent successor would follow the revitalization review.
Jimenez told the House of Commons transport committee last year that BC Ferries received six compliant bids to replace its four oldest ships, all from foreign countries.
While two Canadian shipyards pre-qualified for the competition, he said, neither chose to formally submit a proposal.
The organization chose the proposal that offered the best combination of value, quality, delivery, speed and protections for customers, Jimenez said.
Jimenez was previously president and CEO of provincial auto insurer Icbc.

stories.title: Carney says Canada looking into 'reforming or even abolishing' the Indian Act
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said he shares the view that Canada should be looking into "reforming or even abolishing the Indian Act."
stories.author: Stuart Thomson
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney said he shares the view that Canada should be looking into “reforming or even abolishing the Indian Act” after meeting with First Nations leaders on Monday.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew first raised the issue publicly when he told reporters earlier in the day that Canada should abolish the Act and that such a move was “long overdue.”

Carney credited Kinew for his advocacy and said that he was open to the idea of modernizing, reforming or abolishing the Act, based on a consultation process that is still “to be determined.” The prime minister admitted that “not everybody” at the meeting with premiers and First Nations leaders was in agreement with the proposal.

“I am committed to a process that moves Canada beyond the Indian Act, and I am directing my ministers to work in partnership with First Nations to chart that path together,” said Carney on Monday.

Carney said that if the Indian Act is abolished, then “fully modernizing the governance relationship is the desirable end state.”

AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said she looked forward to discussing the idea with the Assembly of First Nations.

“There is a diversity of First Nations from coast to coast to coast. We’re in every province and territory in this beautiful country that we all share, and that question is going to be up to them to decide, right? And they’re going to have to decide for themselves,” said Woodhouse Nepinak.

The meeting in Ottawa brought Carney together with some provincial premiers, chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations and Woodhouse Nepinak. The gathering comes as Carney tries to win over First Nations leaders for a slate of planned major projects, including a pipeline from Alberta to the West Coast, that are already facing legal jeopardy .

Carney said the leaders also discussed a proposed First Nations Sovereign Wealth Fund, which he described as “an opportunity to share directly in the wealth that the country is creating.” Carney said he has instructed Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne to look into the fund and other ways that First Nations can benefit from the major projects.

'Very much an open question': Carney's West Coast pipeline project could run into legal pitfalls

Carney pitches major project powers to skeptical First Nations as advancing 'Indigenous economic growth'

The First Nations Sovereign Wealth Fund could also work in tandem with the Canada Strong Fund, the government’s proposed sovereign wealth fund, Carney said.

“There have been various models that have been suggested. I think all need to be explored. One could work alongside the Canada Strong Fund. Some in the room, not us, suggested that, or different models could be developed,” said Carney.

By Patrice Bergeron The Canadian Press

St-Pierre Plamondon was criticized for his absence from a summit on Monday in Ottawa between premiers and Indigenous representatives.

A spokesperson for the new PQ government announced the planned meeting.

Last week, St-Pierre Plamondon’s team had suggested that he would not attend the federally organized meeting due to scheduling issues.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

The Quebec government is in transition after the Oct. 5 election that gave the PQ a minority rule.

In a social media post, the leader of the official Opposition Liberals, Charles Milliard, criticized the premier for leaving Quebec’s seat empty, even though he had promised to collaborate with the rest of Canada.

But the new minister of relations with First Nations and Inuit, Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay, said St-Pierre Plamondon’s absence was a “deliberate and well-considered” choice.

“The government of Quebec meets directly with Indigenous nations, nation to nation, on our territory,” he wrote on social media. “Not at a table organized by Ottawa, according to its framework, its schedule and parameters that remain very fuzzy.”

The premiers of Alberta and British Columbia were also absent from the meeting in Ottawa.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: 'The U.S. is coming closer to our position': Carney describes small intensification of trade talks
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Monday that there has been a small intensification in trade talks with the United States.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Monday that there has been a small intensification in trade talks with the United States, but the prospect of a deal will depend on the Americans moving closer to the Canadian position.

“To the extent any progress has been made, it’s because the U.S. is coming closer to our position,” said Carney, during a press conference in Ottawa.

In answer to a reporter in French, the prime minister said there has been a small intensification of trade talks with our southern neighbour, but that there has been no change in pressure to make a deal for the Canadian government.

There has been very little movement on the trade file between the two countries after negotiations fell apart in late August. Carney paused negotiations, citing last-minute demands from U.S. negotiators that made a deal untenable for Canadian interests.

Key sticking points included U.S. tariffs on Canadian medium and heavy-duty trucks, French-language labelling and streaming discoverability rules and U.S. oversight on Canadian trade policy.

Last Wednesday, Carney spoke with Trump at length about geopolitical and trade issues.

“Canada is ready to sign an agreement that is in the interests of Canadians, all Canadians, with very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in in August,” said Carney. “To the extent to which the U.S. is moving towards accepting those aspects, then there’s a greater prospect of a deal.”

The U.S. midterms have put more political pressure on U.S. President Donald Trump in recent weeks, with polls pointing to American voters’ frustration with the president’s record on inflation and cost of living concerns.

Trump has attended rallies in reliably Republican states, including Texas, Alabama and Oklahoma.

On Friday, Trump told reporters Canada “was working very hard” to get a trade deal with the U.S.

During a rally in Michigan on Sunday, Trump said the trade conflict with Canada could end “really soon” and said the Canadians are “willing to give us anything at this moment.”

That same day, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett told Fox News’ The Sunday Briefing, that talks between Canada and the U.S. were “gathering steam” and noted United States Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had been in contact with his Canadian counterparts all week.

In a statement, spokesperson for Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, Eve Loignon-Giroux, said Canada remains in “constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities.”

“We stand ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada’s interests,” she added.

On Friday, Trump issued a presidential proclamation exempting several Canadian goods from Section 338 tariffs, after lobbying efforts from Republican Sen. Susan Collins from Maine.

Collins is fighting to keep her seat in her state that relies heavily on trade with Canada.

Andrew Hale, fellow at Washington-based Advancing American Freedom, said he sees little evidence of an imminent deal beyond Trump’s campaign messaging for the midterms.

“Aside from campaign rhetoric, I’ve seen little evidence that we are (closer to a deal),” said Hale. “With so many of these announcements, I find that they’re performative messaging, and they often lack substance.”

Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute, said he sees Trump’s upbeat rhetoric primarily as domestic political messaging and doesn’t expect the midterms to soften the administration’s negotiating stance.

“I find it difficult to believe that those positions are going to change dramatically ahead of the midterms to try to get a result,” he said.

Obregon said it doesn’t make sense for Canada to give the U.S. a trade victory or a demonstration of one ahead of the midterms on Nov. 3.

“Ultimately that’s what you were aiming for with retaliation — that this tariff war would become costly for the American side and for the administration, specifically, and it’s sort of bearing out that way,” he said.

National Post, with files from Tracy Moran

stories.title: BC Ferries CEO Nicolas Jimenez out as board launches leadership change
stories.summary: Vancouver - Nicolas Jimenez is out as CEO at BC Ferries in a "leadership transition" launched by the company's board.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Nicolas Jimenez is out as CEO at BC Ferries in a “leadership transition” launched by the company’s board, just two days after the election of the B.C. Conservatives, who asked for his firing last year.

A news release from BC Ferries said Brian Anderson, the company’s vice-president of strategy and planning, has been appointed as the interim chief executive officer, effective immediately.

stories.title: New Brunswick strikes deal to explore recovering metals from old mine waste
stories.summary: A U.S.-based firm is looking to turn decades-old mining waste at the Nigadoo mine near Bathurst, N.B. into something valuable.
stories.author: Reeti Rohilla, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Could the waste left behind by an old mine help pay for its own cleanup?

That’s the idea behind a new agreement between New Brunswick and a U.S.-based firm that’s looking to turn decades-old mining waste at the Nigadoo mine near Bathurst, N.B., into something valuable.

The mine once produced copper, lead, zinc and silver but has been shut down for nearly 50 years.

The province says some valuable metals May still be hiding in the waste left behind.

In an agreement announced Monday in Fredericton, Regeneration Enterprises says it wants to find out if those metals can still be recovered.

“The recovery of the metals, the critical minerals, whatever they might be, are then used to fund the restoration, as opposed to the public having to pay for it,” said Michael McPhie, Regeneration Enterprises’ managing director.

The company says the site represents a $35 million liability for the province.

“Part of our work is to remove that off the balance sheet for the province,” said McPhie.

“By recovering the metals, not only can we clean up the site, but we can provide a net benefit back to the people of New Brunswick by removing that liability.”

The province says no provincial money is going into exploration right now. However, future government funding hasn’t been ruled out.

“It’s two things. One: it is an opportunity for us to be able to unlock mineral wealth from a tailings facility. And two: have a proper, robust environmental remediation and reclamation of that particular site,” said Natural Resources Minister John Herron.

The Conservation Council of NB says targeting an already-damaged site could be better than disturbing untouched land.

“If the result of doing this testing and doing the mining to get the minerals out of the tailings — if the end result is that the mine will be rehabilitated, I think that’s a good thing,” said Beverly Gingras, the group’s executive director.

“There definitely seems to be some benefits. But, you know, as with everything, the devil’s in the details.”

Gingras says there are still environmental concerns and the question of who would have to pay if things go wrong.

“So there might be, in terms of if they start trying to reprocess these tailings ponds, are they going to be disturbing some settled heavy metals that might find its way into our watersheds? I don’t know. So there might be some environmental concerns for sure,” she added.

The company, which is working with Pabineau First Nation, expects to know within a year whether the project is financially viable.

If it is and approvals come through, processing could begin within two to three years.

“It’s two things. One: it is an opportunity for us to be able to unlock mineral wealth from a tailings facility. And two: have a proper, robust environmental remediation and reclamation of that particular site,” said Natural Resources Minister John Herron.
The Conservation Council of NB says targeting an already-damaged site could be better than disturbing untouched land.

“If the result of doing this testing and doing the mining to get the minerals out of the tailings — if the end result is that the mine will be rehabilitated, I think that’s a good thing,” said Beverly Gingras, the group’s executive director.
“There definitely seems to be some benefits. But, you know, as with everything, the devil’s in the details.”
Gingras says there are still environmental concerns and the question of who would have to pay if things go wrong.

“So there might be, in terms of if they start trying to reprocess these tailings ponds, are they going to be disturbing some settled heavy metals that might find its way into our watersheds? I don’t know. So there might be some environmental concerns for sure,” she added.
The company, which is working with Pabineau First Nation, expects to know within a year whether the project is financially viable.
If it is and approvals come through, processing could begin within two to three years.

stories.title: Year-round daylight time has a dark side. Here’s how Canada can prepare for it
stories.summary: Changes are coming on Nov. 1 to B.C., Alberta, Manitoba, Northwest Territories and parts of Northwestern Ontario
stories.author: Zosia Bielski
stories.content:
This Nov. 1, as a large swath of Canada does away with seasonal time change and shifts to year-round daylight time instead, experts are warning about the health consequences of this move, which will bring darker mornings through the winter.

For people in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Northwest Territories and parts of Northwestern Ontario, the shift means no more adjusting every spring and fall – plus one more hour of light in the evenings.

In government polls on time change, those in favour of permanent daylight time voiced their desire for an extra hour of light after work to see friends and family, exercise and shop.

But for all the perks, the move comes at a cost. Through winter, without setting the clocks back, more of the mornings will be shrouded in darkness, forcing workers and students to commute well before sunrise.

Scientists caution that darker mornings do a number on our sleep, hitting adolescents, early shift workers and those with sleep disorders the hardest. Shortened hours of rest have been linked to numerous health harms, from depression and cardiovascular risk, to workplace injuries.

Researchers have even discovered dips in productivity, school attendance and grades at the edges of time zones where sunrise comes latest.

With so many concerns, why is half of Canada embarking on its own experiment with permanent daylight time? That’s the question from authors of a strongly worded paper published ahead of the Nov. 1 changes in the Canadian Medical Association Journal.

“Ending biannual clock adjustments may eliminate transition harms that last a few weeks,” wrote the authors, “but the health effects of permanent [daylight] time are likely to be chronic.”

The authors are pushing for countermeasures – better pedestrian infrastructure to make travel safer through darker mornings, later start times for students, as well as public-health messaging on nighttime sleep habits.

The Globe spoke, separately, with two of the paper’s co-authors, Patrick Baylis, an associate professor at the University of British Columbia’s Vancouver School of Economics, and Ralph Mistlberger, professor of psychology at Simon Fraser University.

Tips for adjusting to time changes

💡boost light exposure in the morning with lamps that deliver bright blue and white light at home, school and work.

☀️shift to warmer light as the day progresses.

📱shut down devices well before bedtime. Light from screens can prevent the biological cues that stimulate sleep.

Mistlberger: The sun rises very early in the summer, and many of us are sleeping through a good deal of that. With daylight time, we are essentially “saving” some of that missed sunshine by tacking it on to the end of the day.

When people are polled on time change, it’s always, “We don’t like switching, but we love those summer evenings. Why not have more of those?” Those warm evenings with the sun setting at 10 p.m., they fill us with this good feeling. Why wouldn’t you vote for that, without any other information?

And that’s been the problem – it’s a knowledge translation problem.

More than the long summer evenings, what people will end up noticing is that in winter, the sun might not even rise until 9 a.m. when they’re at work already. Meaning they will have not seen any daylight in the morning.

What has struck me here is that more health experts were not consulted on this. It’s hard to penetrate the powers of populism. Governments want what the people want, but people don’t always know what’s good for them.

Everywhere this has been tried and abandoned, it’s because ultimately, people didn’t like it. They liked the idea of summer evenings but they don’t like the reality of dark winters.

Mistlberger: It all comes down to morning light and our internal biological clocks. The effect of later sunrise is that it’ll be more difficult to wake up early in the dark, and more difficult to go to bed early and fall asleep.

At the same time, our social clock will not change: we’ll still have to get up at the same time for our regular work and school schedules. The mismatch between the social clock and our biological clock is called “social jet lag.” With year-round daylight savings time, there will be an extended period where social jet lag is increased in the winters.

When there is misalignment and short sleep, you get a whole spectrum of negative health outcomes. What we know from copious epidemiological evidence is that people who sleep only five or six hours are at greater risk of developing diabetes, metabolic disorders, cancer and cardiovascular disorders.

Mistlberger: Teenagers are also the least able to avoid social media and the phone in front of their face in bed at night. It’s a source of light, sound and busyness.

All of that is stimulating the nervous system, allowing you to stay up later than you should. The artificial screen light also suppresses melatonin, the biological signal for, “It’s biological nighttime. Go to bed.”

So now you’ve got artificial light in the evening but also less natural light in the morning. The two will conspire to make people more socially jetlagged.

Baylis: Early morning shift workers. People with longer commutes, since they need to start earlier. In general, people with less flexible schedules that require them to get up early are most likely to be affected. Other vulnerable populations, besides students, would be those who are naturally inclined toward staying up later – people who already struggle to sleep an adequate amount.

From a transportation safety perspective, we should also be thinking about individuals commuting in rural or lower-income communities with more limited lighting, particularly in areas with fewer sidewalks.

Baylis: It’s all related. This affects sleep and then sleep affects health. Then, sleep and health affect schooling outcomes, which then shape economic outcomes.

Mistlberger: Studies have looked at whether there’s a difference in people’s health, academic outcomes, earnings and productivity from one edge of the time zone to the other. This really blew me away – it’s shocking. One study in Florida discovered that being on the edge of the time zone where sunrise is earlier was equivalent to changing class size from 40 students to 20 students. When you have fewer students per teacher, you get better academic outcomes, and that was the effect of this time zone position.

Baylis: The economic evidence was surprising to me. This pattern shows up where you see less productivity and lower wages on the western edge of the time zone, where sunrise comes later. You can imagine workers being less effective at work because they’re sleepier. If everybody in an area is experiencing sleep loss and getting less done during the day, it can have compounding effects. Whereas if you’re in a city where people are well rested, you can see how it would lead to higher overall levels of productivity, with more productive firms looking to locate there. They’re all tiny things that stack on each other.

Baylis: Nothing new needs to be invented here. But particular attention needs to be paid to deploy existing safety technologies on routes likely to see much more early morning foot traffic. It might be installing new lights in school zones.

Baylis: We know that adolescents really suffer under late sunrises. California’s state-level intervention shifted public middle and high school start times later. Shifting start-times to be more aligned with the sun has beneficial effects on student performance.

Mistlberger: At work, organizations will have more control over this but they won’t do it unless they’re informed about the value of it to their workers’ productivity and safety.

Baylis: It’s been in place there for a long time and people don’t seem to find it objectionable. It’s not doing annoying things to schedules in the spring and fall, and it’s not putting people through the early morning challenges we’re concerned about.

Mistlberger: Yukon has actually been on permanent daylight time since 2020. Governments say, “It doesn’t seem to have affected them.” But the sun rises so late there, it’s late no matter what time system you choose. It’s not informative.

It would not surprise me if we abandon this after a short period of time. I wish we weren’t doing it but I’m very curious. There’s a little scientist inside of me thinking, this is going to be interesting.

The interviews have been compiled, edited and condensed for clarity.

Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press

While it’s clear that few enjoy resetting their clocks twice a year, the issue of daylight versus standard time is more divisive.

But research points to the health advantages of permanent standard time with its earlier sunrises. At the same time, several global test cases illustrate the unintended consequences of doing daylight time year-round.

Internationally, three large-scale experiments with permanent daylight time proved unpopular.

During the oil crisis in 1974, the United States implemented permanent daylight time to save energy. Within a year, officials backpedaled, following outcry over pedestrian accidents, children trundling to school in pitch black conditions. (That hasn’t deterred American lawmakers from floating new legislation to give permanent DST another try.)

Chile ventured the concept in 2015 but backtracked a year later, after protests from fruit growers, who found dark mornings delayed their work day, productivity plummeting by 15 per cent.

In 2014, Russia abandoned its own three-year trial after traffic accidents spiked and people in the northern reaches complained of brutally gloomy mornings.

Along with experts studying sleep and circadian rhythms, the authors of a recent paper in the Canadian Medical Association Journal argue that permanent standard time would have been the wiser option, since it preserves more morning light and better coordinates our work and school schedules with our bodies, which naturally want to follow the sun.

A 2025 Stanford modeling study looked at circadian rhythms, noting how aligned or misaligned they become through seasonal time changes, permanent daylight time and permanent standard time. Then, they related the information to cardiovascular risks and a range of health issues. Biannual switching proved the most harmful, followed by permanent daylight time, with standard time holding the most health benefits. The researchers concluded that standard time was the recommended system .

Despite this, government polling on time changes often omits permanent standard time as an option, frustrating experts. Public surveys tend to offer just two choices: permanent daylight time, or changing the clocks twice annually – a deeply unpopular option.

The authors of the CMAJ paper are urging provincial governments making the shift this November to watch for the health consequences of later sunrises, to help inform policy choices going forward.

stories.title: Londoners head to polls as mayoral candidates make final push on election day
stories.summary: Londoners headed to polling stations Monday to cast their ballots in the 2026 municipal election, with incumbent Mayor Josh Morgan and a field of challengers vying for the city’s top job.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Londoners headed to polling stations Monday to cast their ballots in the 2026 municipal election, with incumbent Mayor Josh Morgan and a field of challengers vying for the city’s top job.

Voting is open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., with unofficial results to be posted on the City of London’s website as they become available after polls close.

Morgan arrived at his polling station with his 18-year-old daughter, while first-time mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose also brought her daughter along to vote.

Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson says she voted in the advance polls, and was out canvassing voters on election day.

For many Londoners, voting was an opportunity to take part in the democratic process and encourage others to do the same.

“I just wanted to model a civic engagement for my son, start him early,” said voter Michael Yang. “And it’s, you know, very important to be involved.”

Imaan Saeed said she believes voting matters because of the people who fought for the right to participate in elections.

“So many people have fought for our ability to be able to vote,” Saeed said. “So yeah, I think it is important that even our little vote will make a difference.”

However, not everyone who went to the polls was able to cast a ballot.

Jesse Clay said he was unable to vote after discovering his name had been crossed off the voters’ list by mistake.

“The rest of my family went into an advanced poll last week, and I’ve just come in to vote today, and it turns out they accidentally crossed my name off instead of my 19-year-old’s name,” Clay said. “So I am not able to vote today.”

The experience raises questions about how election officials handle potential errors and ensure votes are counted accurately.

Matt Farrell, a politics professor at Fanshawe College, said human error is possible but that safeguards are in place to help protect the integrity of elections.

“Now these things don’t happen very often,” Farrell said. “And generally speaking, there are some procedures in place and oversight and redundancies to ensure that that kind of thing doesn’t happen.”

Farrell said that when errors do occur, they are typically isolated and unlikely to change the outcome of an election.

He added that recounts are a normal part of election administration and May be triggered when results are particularly close, depending on the rules in place.

“For London… if it’s a really close election that looks like a tie, that’ll be a recount,” Farrell said.

There are different types of recounts, Farrell explained. Administrative recounts are conducted by election officials, while judicial recounts can be ordered through the courts in certain circumstances.

A candidate who believes there was a problem with the counting process May also seek to have a recount ordered by a judge, he said.

Despite the possibility of isolated errors, Farrell said voters can have confidence in the overall process.

“By and large, our elections are safe and they’re reliable,” he said. “And Londoners can feel confident that their vote is being tabulated and reported accurately.”

More information about the election is available on the city’s election resources webpage .

stories.title: Canada-U.S. trade talks ‘moving quickly’ at political level ahead of midterms: sources
stories.summary: Multiple sources tell Global News that talks are “moving quickly” but express skepticism at a deal being reached before Americans vote on Nov. 3.
stories.author: Mackenzie Gray, Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The once-stalled trade talks between the U.S. and Canada are now “moving quickly” at the political level, multiple sources with direct knowledge of the negotiations have told Global News.

But despite talks moving forward after almost two months of stalemate, the sources expressed skepticism that a deal can get done before the American midterm elections on Nov. 3. Others noted that U.S. President Donald Trump routinely says deals have been struck, only to blow them up again — such as during the last round of U.S. trade talks in August.

The most recent discussions have stayed at the political level,with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic Leblanc leading the Canadian side, the sources said. More formal negotiations between trade representatives have not yet taken place, according to comments from Canada’s lead negotiator Janice Charette last week.

Sources told Global News that the Canadian side views this as a window to reach a deal with Trump’s administration ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Meanwhile Reuters, citing four Canadian and two U.S. sources, said the two countries are working on a deal to ease Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel and autos ahead of those elections.

“Canada is ready to sign an agreement that is in the interest of Canadians, all Canadians. We have very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August,” said Prime Minister Mark Carney in a press conference Monday.

“To the extent to which the U.S. is moving towards accepting those aspects, then there’s a greater prospect of a deal. But if there is (a deal offered), we’ll judge it as a whole.”

Asked how he knows that Trump will sign the next agreement “in pen” — meaning standing by whatever agreement is reached by the two countries — Carney responded simply “I don’t.”

Trump’s tariff war has become a political issue for Republicans, particularly in key Senate races in Michigan and Maine, as the GOP braces for what looks like a drubbing in the midterms.

Global News granted the sources anonymity to speak openly about the politically sensitive negotiations.

If a deal were to be struck over the coming week, two sources said the Americans would need to make multiple concessions on issues that led to talks breaking down on Aug. 21. Those issues included Canada’s freedom to strike trade deals with other countries, and what U.S. tariffs on auto, steel and aluminum would apply to under a new deal.

Whether all the various players in the Trump administration would agree to those concessions is an open question.

Last week, Carney signaled the Trump administration has already shown some flexibility on their previous demands.

“They’ve already moved on several (of Canada’s red lines), by the way, since we rightly walked away from a deal that wasn’t in Canada’s interest,” Carney said on the Real Talk with Ryan Jespersen podcast.

Trump, for his part, told supporters on Sunday that he expects his trade war with Canada to end “pretty soon.”

As the sources noted, there’s no indication Canada will take the U.S. president at his word on that. During the same speech to supporters, in Port Huron, Michigan, Trump launched into his usual invective against Canada, suggesting the country has been “ripping off” the U.S. for years. But as the midterms approach, it suggests that Canada-U.S. trade is rattling around somewhere in Trump’s mind.

Trade talks between the two counties have been off since Canada walked away from negotiations in late August. After the talks collapsed, Carney said the U.S. made a last-minute push for language that would limit Canada’s ability to enter into trade deals with other countries, water down French language requirements, and hurt the country’s struggling auto industry.

The Trump administration responded with additional tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of Canadian goods, and Ottawa responded in kind with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs.

On Friday, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins — in a tough fight to hold her seat in Maine — revealed that Trump agreed to lift tariffs on Canadian corrugated paper, plastic boxes and several types of agricultural machinery important to her state.

“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Collins said in a statement.

But while Trump lifted some tariffs, he imposed new ones on Canadian goods like cocoa powder, paints and varnishes, shampoos, vinyl flooring, archery equipment and carpets. The Americans will now apply 50 per cent tariffs on sewage sludge and some types of municipal waste.

The trash issue appeared to seemed to strike a chord with Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, who appeared at the Port Huron rally with Trump.

“Those Canadians send truck after truck loaded with their trash into our state,” Rogers, in a competitive race with Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, said to boos from the crowd.

“The president, just this week, announced he’s going to tariff those trash trucks.”

With files from the Canadian Press and Reuters.

Others noted that U.S. President Donald Trump routinely says deals have been struck, only to blow them up again — such as during the last round of U.S. trade talks in August.

stories.title: ‘Go out and do brave things’: Canadian diver becomes first woman to dive from an iceberg
stories.summary: Molly Carlson made history with a 15-metre plunge from an iceberg off Newfoundland.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta and Anne Leclair
stories.content:
Canadian cliff diver Molly Carlson has taken her sport into icy new territory, becoming the first known woman in the world to dive from an iceberg.

The Montreal-based diver completed the roughly 15-metre, or 50-foot, plunge from an iceberg off the coast of Twillingate, Newfoundland, into the North Atlantic Ocean back in June.

Carlson told Global News on Monday that the feat took months of preparation and required her to first learn how to ice climb before searching for an iceberg that was safe enough for the dive.

She said icebergs can be at risk of rolling, adding that part of the one she jumped from broke off moments after her dive.

“After I jumped off, it started breaking on the backside. So the timing was insane. If we were on there for five more minutes, who knows what this story could have been like.”

Footage of the achievement was shared online by project lead Red Bull Canada last week. Carlson has since gained more than one million followers on Instagram.

Carlson said the project was about more than completing a world-first. She wanted it to represent her experience with extreme anxiety and show other women that fear does not have to prevent them from accomplishing extraordinary things.

“I struggle a lot with my mental health,” Carlson said. “For me, it was important to pick a project that not only was challenging and beautiful and intense, but also did something to represent what’s on the inside.”

Carlson compared that experience to an iceberg, most of which sits below the water’s surface.

“Everyone kind of sits 10 per cent above the surface, the highlight reels, the perfect everything, but deep down we are all human. We’re all scared. We all have emotions. We all have fear,” she said.

“Knowing that fear doesn’t get the final say was really special to me.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Knowing that fear doesn't get the final say was really special to me."

“I truly want women to know that they could go out and do brave things too, no matter how insane they might sound.”

Carlson is now turning her attention to what she jokes is her next “iceberg”: the ring on her finger.

She is planning her wedding to fellow cliff diver Aidan Heslop after the couple announced their engagement earlier this month.
