stories.title: Holt’s makes a big bet on caviar
stories.summary: Paris institution Caviar Kaspia makes its debut in Canada with outposts at Holt Renfrew’s restaurants in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal
stories.author: Andrew Sardone
stories.content:
For almost a century, Caviar Kaspia has been a Paris institution, dishing out mother-of-pearl spoonful after mother-of-pearl spoonful of inky roe. The restaurant opened on Rue des Mathurins in 1929 and, in 1953, moved a few blocks south to its blue awninged storefront on Place de la Madeleine.

When the fashion hordes descend on the city – for the ready-to-wear collections in September and February and couture shows in January and July – tightly packed tables in its second-floor dining room fill up with a swanky swirl of celebrity editors, industrious executives, front row A-listers, gilded clients and hospitable publicists. Over tins of Ossetra, twice-baked potatoes, bowls of pickles and ice-cold vodka carafes, they gossip and table-hop and try not to be too obvious when they crane their necks to take in the glittering scene.

Before the advent of social media, this decadent tableau was a bit of an insider secret. Today, it’s a viral sensation and an often-impossible reservation. That buzz has turned Caviar Kaspia into as much of a luxury brand as the French houses that host their post-show parties in its private dining room. The restaurant now operates eight permanent and seasonal locations, including outposts at the Mark Hotel on New York’s Upper East Side and along the Bosphorus in Istanbul. This holiday season, it’s also partnering with Holt Renfrew on its Canadian debut at the retailer’s restaurants in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal.

“I think the experience of going to Caviar Kaspia kind of trumps the caviar to a certain point,” says Joseph Tang, Holt Renfrew’s fashion director. “You’re really there to live and breathe Paris with every single major fashion person.” To channel that buzz, chefs and front-of-house staff from the three Holts Cafés travelled to Paris in September to master creating the perfect blini, practice gently unfolding a pancake onto a diner’s plate and be coached on the finery and formalities of caviar consumption. “It was equally as important to bring the ceremony of the table back to Canada,” Tang says.

Open from Nov. 2 until Feb. 28 to tap into the celebratory marathon through the holiday season and Lunar New Year, the Cafés’ tables will become a stage for all this pomp and circumstance. Ordering off the Caviar Kaspia menu will earn you a spot with a signature blue tablecloth and a special place setting. The menu will include caviar-topped standards like potato rösti pizzas and grilled cheddar and Monterey Jack sandwiches plus new options including chicken nuggets.

And there will be merch. In addition to caviar itself, including 30 to 250 grams of Baeri roe packed in custom tins in Holt Renfrew magenta, there are vintage-inspired T-shirts, sweatshirts, ball caps and tote bags.

Holt Renfrew’s big bet on caviar is happening during a zeitgeisty moment for the once-exclusive salted Sturgeon eggs. Single-serving caviar bumps dished out on the side of your hand now pop up on restaurant menus around the world and direct-to-consumer retailers have upended the monopolies (and pricing) of high-end distributors. But the conventions of the Caviar Kaspia experience, wherever you indulge in it, are a reminder that its consumption is meant to be more of a ritual than scooping out a tin with a ruffled potato chip.

Caviar Kaspia’s CEO Ramon Mac-Crohon, who has been with the company since 2001, says that everything at the restaurant is theatre, citing its ornate matryoshka serving vessels that hinge open to reveal a dark tin nestled in sparkling crushed ice. What’s consistent from night to night and location to location is the aesthetic built around that azure hue. “The main ingredient, for me, is, like Hermès orange, the Kaspia blue. When you’re looking at a table, you could be anywhere in the world, but it’s Kaspia.”

According to Tang, creating these moments is part of Holt Renfrew’s deeper push into immersive retail. “We’re covered in fashion. We have all the best brands around the world,” he says. “But this allows us to share a little bit of the experiences that we get to see when we travel and bring that back to the customer.”

For more, visit holtrenfrew.com.

The Globe and Mail Style Magazine travelled as a guest of Holt Renfrew, which did not review or approve this article. Stories are based on merit; The Globe does not guarantee coverage.

stories.title: Montreal Jewish chef left curious by prospective diners asking about her views on 'genocide in Palestine'
stories.summary: "Is this normal? Is this the new normal?,” Chef Raegan Steinberg asks in a social media post.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
It was Steinberg’s response to a question from a prospective diner, asking about her views on the “genocide in Palestine.”

“There’s a boycott list that’s been going around since October 7,” she explains in an interview with National Post. It points to Montreal businesses that have allegedly expressed support for Israel. And Steinberg is on it.

“I don’t think I can do anything about it. I think no matter what you do, people will assume a lot of things about you and your policies and your politics.”

However, she points out, “I’ve been very adamant about not discussing politics. I definitely don’t want that to define us. I just thought it was interesting that we were receiving that line of questioning, and I was fairly certain that other fellow restaurateurs were not receiving the same line of questioning.”

As a Jewish restaurateur and chef, she says: “I don’t hide the fact that I’m Jewish, right? I don’t think I should have to. Absolutely not. No. But I also don’t think I need to discuss foreign policy in order to conduct business in Montreal, Quebec. … We all just want to make great food, feed our families, go home. You know, sleep well, wake up the next day, do it all again.”

Broadly speaking, she says she has a lot of respect for the younger generation spending their money at businesses that align with their values: “I respect that 100 per cent.” And if all restaurants are facing this kind of challenge, she says, “then it’s fair game … but I have a feeling that that’s not the case, and that was more or less, proven to me.”

In her post she asks: “I’m just wondering if this happens to other restaurateurs or is it specific to Jewish people? I don’t even know. Is this normal? Is this the new normal?” Afterwards, she spoke with a small collection of fellow Montreal restaurateurs and chefs. The majority of them haven’t faced similar questions. Jewish restaurants were “definitely a higher percentage of the few people that I spoke to, but I think that some Jewish restaurants are more targeted than others.”

At the same time, she insists she is not complaining and does not want to attract negative attention: “I don’t think there’s like a negative stain on us or anything like that. We’re very happy, you know. I just think it’s important for people to know what goes on behind the scenes sometimes.”

Referred to as “a top chef,” by Canadian restaurant guide, Tastet, Steinberg is most notable for three popular restaurants in the Montreal area: Arthurs Nosh Bar in Saint-Henri, Dirty Greens and Arthurs Nosh Bar at Le Cathcart, as well as Romies in Old Montreal.

The prospective diner wrote to her, saying: “Hello!! I’d like to come try the food but I’m mindful where I spend my money these days. I saw your restaurant on the boycott list but I wanted to confirm with you what your views are about the genocide in Palestine (as the boycott lists might be misinformed). Look forward to hearing back. Thank you!”

Steinberg responds that she is “not really even sure how to go about (responding). Anyways, just wondering if anyone else gets these kind of questions.”

Steinberg says she was heavily influenced in her choice to become a chef by her father. She eventually pursued culinary training at the Art Institute of Vancouver, later returning to Montreal to work at the renown Joe Beef .

Then she and her partner, Alexandre Cohen, embarked on Back of House Catering before opening Arthurs Nosh Bar in 2016, a Montreal brunch staple on Notre-Dame Street West. She says the restaurant bears her father’s name as a tribute to him and offers Jewish cuisine reinvented with Moroccan influences.

Later she launched Dirty Greens at Le Cathcart, offering gourmet salads. Then in the fall of 2024, Raegan and Alexandre opened Romies, a contemporary American bistro. And in 2026, they opened Arthur’s Dinette in the NDG neighbourhood.

stories.title: ‘Immediately stop using’: Electric snow throwers sold at Home Hardware recalled
stories.summary: More than 37,000 electric snow throwers sold in Home Hardware are being recalled due to an “electric shock hazard.”
stories.author: Christl Dabu
stories.content:
More than 37,000 electric snow throwers sold at Home Hardware are being recalled due to an “electric shock hazard.”

“The power cable on the affected units May break when exposed to extreme cold weather, causing a potential electric shock injury,” according to an advisory published by Health Canada on Monday.

The recall is for the Benchmark-branded 22-inch, 15 amp electric snow thrower, with model number YF6022 on the back of the base. It has the word “Benchmark” written on the side, and red and black base and wheels and a black handle.

“Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled product and contact Home Hardware for instructions on how to destroy the product in exchange for a refund,” according to the notice.

As of Oct. 5, 2026, Ontario-based Home Hardware has received 19 reports of broken power cords in Canada but no reported injuries, according to the recall notice.

The company reported that 37,667 affected electric snow throwers were sold in Canada, between November 2020 and May 2026.

Suzhou Murray Electronics & Machinery Co., Ltd., is the manufacturer, and the supplier is Sumec Hardware & Tools. Both are based in Jiangsu, China.

Customers seeking more information are advised to call Home Hardware Stores Limited at 1-877-940-5081, email contactus@homehardware.CA , or visit the company website .

Consumers are encouraged to report health or safety incidents by filling out the Consumer Product Incident Report Form .

“Please note that the Canada Consumer Product Safety Act prohibits recalled products from being redistributed, sold or even given away in Canada,” according to the advisory.

stories.title: N.S. government announces funding to grow boatbuilding industry
stories.summary: The Nova Scotia government says it is investing over $350,000 to help boatbuilders and boat repair businesses in the province expand into new markets.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia government says it is investing over $350,000 to help boatbuilders and boat repair businesses in the province expand into new markets.

The province says the funding from its Community Economic Development Fund is going to the Nova Scotia Boatbuilders Association.

It says the association will use the money to promote local companies at industry trade shows and missions, in trade publications and through online communications and strategic partnerships.

The Nova Scotia Boatbuilders Association was established in 1998 to diversify the industry beyond the domestic fishing boat market.

The province says the investment will help local boatbuilders deliver on national defence priorities and compete internationally for naval contracts.

The executive director of the Nova Scotia Boatbuilders Association says the boatbuilding industry maintains small vessels for several of the province’s key industries, including fisheries and defence.

“This investment helps to ensure the ongoing health of our industry, and the rural communities where much of the work takes place, as we navigate an unusually complex trade environment,” said a statement from executive director Jan Fullerton.

stories.title: Meghan Roach steps down as Roots CEO as go-private transaction closes
stories.summary: Deal with Marquee Brands, announced in August at price of $4.10 per share, passed a shareholder vote earlier this month
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Roots Corp. Root-T says Meghan Roach has stepped down as president and chief executive as its go-private transaction with Marquee Brands has closed.

Roach has been in the CEO role since 2020 after first joining the company as interim chief financial officer in 2019.

The company says in a news release she will continue to serve in an advisory role to ensure a smooth leadership transition.

The go-private transaction was announced in August at a price of $4.10 per share and passed a shareholder vote earlier this month with more than 99-per-cent support.

The company says Roots shares are now expected to be delisted “shortly” from the Toronto Stock Exchange.

Marquee Brands also manages the Martha Stewart, Laura Ashley and Roberto Cavalli labels and intends to expand Roots to other markets such as Korea, India and Mexico.

stories.title: Toronto fundraiser Elizabeth Tory was a maestro at working a room
stories.summary: A devoted volunteer with Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre and other organizations, she was legendary in Canadian charity and business circles for her drive, accomplishments and wit
stories.author: Virginia Galt
stories.content:
Elizabeth Tory, an intrepid volunteer with formidable powers of persuasion, tapped a vast network in support of various causes. She recruited surgeons and captains of industry to canvass for hospital fundraisers and once enlisted her hairstylist’s help to buttonhole an elusive donor as he settled into his chair for a trim.

Liz, as she was known by most, was legendary in Canadian charity and business circles for her drive, accomplishments and rapier wit. In the course of a life dedicated to community service, Ms. Tory played a strategic role on the boards of Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, the Toronto Symphony Orchestra and the Art Gallery of Ontario, among others, while also spearheading multimillion-dollar campaigns for donations. It was unpaid, enormously valuable work. At the grassroots level, for years she went door-to-door in the same Toronto neighbourhood collecting money for cancer research. Her daughter, Jennifer, tagged along when she was a child.

Ms. Tory died at her Toronto condo, in the company of her four children, ON Oct. 3. At 94, she had succumbed to age-related ailments. The woman with six holes-in-one to her credit finally gave up golf two years ago and was active until the end as a member of the art gallery’s nominating committee vetting candidates for board service.

Her husband, John A. Tory, a trusted behind-the-scenes adviser in the Thomson and Rogers business empires, died suddenly of a hemorrhagic stroke in 2011. As a team, they were regarded as one of Canada’s most influential power couples, say those who knew them both.

Liz Bacon was a vibrant, outgoing nursing student when her sister Anna, a law school classmate of John’s, introduced them. He was as reserved as she was ebullient, their daughter Jennifer Tory says.

“My dad was very shy, notwithstanding he was a very successful businessman and had to be out there with all different types of people. Without her, he might have been a real hermit and stayed home at lot more. … I think that’s part of the reason he adored her.”

A voracious reader, Ms. Tory held her own at business events and was a maestro at working a room.

The late Peter C. Newman, author of The Canadian Establishment book series, made this observation: “Liz Tory, whose husband masterminds the exponential growth of the Thomson empire, is probably the most sought-after social animator, partly because she is so well-organized (serving on a dozen committees as well as running her own company, Tudor Travel) but mainly because she has an instinct for how group effort can be meshed into meaningful results.” She later sold the travel business to American Express, her daughter said.

While the volunteer hours she put in were equivalent to a full-time job, none of this came at the expense of family, says her eldest son, former Toronto mayor John H. Tory. In addition to being a strong, supportive wife, she was a fiercely proud mother to her children, John, Jennifer, Jeffrey and Michael. She relished her role as grandmother and great-grandmother although she was not the sort of person one would describe as “cuddly,” her son John said at the funeral, drawing laughs from many in the church who had been at the receiving end of her zingers.

The Tory family’s community impact is perhaps most deeply evident at Toronto’s Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, where in addition to Liz’s – and now Jennifer’s – board service, the Torys have been major benefactors for more than five decades. Two weeks after the Tory family matriarch died, Sunnybrook celebrated the 50 th anniversary of the Tory Trauma Program, which is the largest of its kind in Canada, chief executive officer Andy Smith said in an interview. It provides care for medical emergencies ranging from heart attacks and brain hemorrhages to accidents, burns and mass casualties.

As he spoke, the trauma team was on standby to receive patients from Alberta if needed following the devastating Wainwright military base fire that claimed four lives and injured dozens of others.

John A. Tory and Liz Tory, early in their marriage, consulted Sunnybrook doctors and executives on their most pressing needs and decided on a substantial donation to support trauma treatment. Jennifer Tory, a retired bank executive, has built on that philanthropy and followed in her mother’s footsteps as a member of the Sunnybrook Foundation board. Liz served on the hospital board for 14 years and subsequently sat on the foundation board.

“Liz transcended to the highest levels of foundation leadership, where it was about much more than money. It was about the spirit that she brought and imparted,” Dr. Smith says. She had a way of inspiring others and bringing them on board.

Elizabeth Emma Bacon was born in Toronto on Jan. 15, 1932. She was the second of four children born to Howard Bacon, who owned a trucking business, and Helen Bacon (née Solomon). She attended Jarvis Collegiate in downtown Toronto, where she was an excellent athlete and sang in musical productions.

“Liz Tory came from modest beginnings to lead an extraordinary life of family and community contribution,” her children wrote in the death notice.

She was a student at the Wellesley Hospital School of Nursing when she met John A. Tory and did not resume her nursing studies after marrying him and having their first child at the age of 21. She was of a generation where women were not widely expected to work outside the home while raising families but volunteer work was encouraged.

The bold confidence she inherited from her mother served her in good stead when her mother-in-law, Jean Tory, introduced her to the worlds of wealth and charity. “She didn’t know she was releasing a tiger,” Liz Tory later told Globe and Mail society columnist Rosemary Sexton.

Her first volunteer job with Jean was with the Toronto Symphony Orchestra, where Liz Tory stayed on as a volunteer for more than 70 years. She was always in high demand from other not-for-profit organizations and charities wanting to boost their impact.

Her children John and Jennifer say their mother was fearless and unabashedly direct in enlisting others to donate money or time. She was sharp, funny and made people laugh, although at times it was a somewhat nervous laugh.

They both recall a memorable exchange at a meeting of the Art Gallery of Ontario board, where a list of potential board nominees was being considered. The other board members seemed satisfied with the list, then Liz said, “I think my copy has a page missing.” When asked what she meant, she responded, “Well, I don’t know, the page that has the women’s names on it.” They had presented a slate entirely of men.

The zingers did not come quite as frequently toward the end of her life, although Liz firmly asserted her independence when her children took her on an exploratory tour of a retirement home. When informed of the menu and dining schedules, Liz quipped that that it was kind of like prison where you were told what time you were going to eat and who you were going to eat with, her son John recounted in an interview.

The “nice young woman” leading the tour gamely carried on the movie room where Liz asked, “Do you have porn night?” It was a joke, “and she would say it in a way that couldn’t be other than funny,” he added. “But it was a serious message for us that … she was going to live at home if she possibly could and we abided by her wishes.”

The condolences offered to the family after her death were fond and effusive. Ms. Tory had a remarkable ability to remember people’s names and the names of their children. When she volunteered at Sunnybrook, she would invite doctors home to dinner. CEOs, caregivers, hairstylists, the condo concierge and her golf caddy were among the friends who paid tribute. When the former mayor of Toronto goes to shops in his mother’s neighbourhood, he said, he is best known as Liz Tory’s son.

stories.title: Quebec Liberal candidate speaks out after losing seat to PQ in recount
stories.summary: QUÉBEC - A Quebec Liberal Party candidate who lost her seat following a judicial recount is accusing a judge of unfairly rejecting ballots.
stories.author: Patrice Bergeron The Canadian Press
stories.content:
QUÉBEC - A Quebec Liberal Party candidate who lost her seat following a judicial recount is accusing a judge of unfairly rejecting ballots.

Affine Lwalalika wrote on social media to question the court’s decision to award the Vachon riding to the Parti Québécois’s Stephan Fogaing.

Lwalalika claims in her post that several ballots deemed valid on election night were rejected during the recount because one or more pencil marks were either very faint or appeared outside the designated circle even if the circle also contained a checkmark.

The Liberal candidate had won the seat by 10 votes on election night, but that decision was overturned following the recount requested by the PQ.

Fogaing was declared the winner last week by a margin of three votes.

The PQ formed a minority government on election night, winning 59 of the 127 seats at the legislature.

The party welcomed the addition of a 60th elected representative.

The Liberal Party said last week that it was challenging the judge’s invalidation of certain ballots during the recount.

“Should an additional mark, one that contains no offensive language, is minor and often very faint, and includes no drawing or element that could identify the voter, be enough to invalidate a clearly expressed vote? That is what we will be bringing before the courts,” Lwalalika wrote.

She added that “the intent of these voters was unequivocal and that these ballots should be declared valid following a new judicial review.”

In an email sent to The Canadian Press, Élections Québec noted that the Election Act does not provide for an appeal process to overturn the result of a judicial recount.

However, it adds that the law allows for a challenge on two grounds: either that the election or the related proclamation is irregular, or that a fraudulent electoral maneuver was carried out.

In either case, “the facts alleged must be such as to have changed or significantly affected the outcome of the election,” the statement clarifies.

The challenge must be filed with the Court of Quebec and heard by three judges within at least 10 days after each party has been notified. The judgment is then rendered by a majority of the judges, according to Élections Québec.

The court could rule that the election is void, that the member whose election is contested is duly elected, or that another person has been elected.

If the election is declared void, another election must be held. However, if the court decides that one of the candidates is elected, the result is forwarded to the legislature’s secretary general so that the elected candidate May be sworn in.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Eric Bauza, the Canadian voice behind Bugs Bunny, has died at age 46
stories.summary: Toronto voice actor, the latest to take over from Mel "Man of a Thousand Voices" Blanc, said Daffy Duck was his favourite.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
actor who was the voice of such Looney Tunes characters as Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, has died at the age of age 46, according to his family.

Bauza’s page on the entertainment database imdb.com lists more than 400 credits stretching back to the early 2000s and including work on TV’s Phineas and Ferb, Dora the Explorer, Lego Star Wars: The Yoda Chronicles, and numerous movies and video games.

His most recent work included this summer’s Coyote vs. Acme, where he voiced Bugs, Daffy, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig, Road Runner, Tweety and more.

His many awards included Emmys for his works on Looney Tunes Cartoons (2022), Bugs Bunny Builders (2023) and Teen Titans Go! (2025). He is listed in the credits for an upcoming TV movie Bye Bye Bunny: A Looney Tunes Musical, still in production.

Media reports say he passed away Sunday from hypertensive cardiovascular disease, a group of conditions caused by long-term high blood pressure.

National Post spoke to Bauza in 2021 for the release of Space Jam: A New Legacy. He said he’d been a fan of Looney Tunes cartoons since he was a boy, and the he’d loved the original Space Jam movie in 1992. “And I can tell you right now I’m a kid in a candy store,” he said of starring in the sequel.

Born in Scarborough, Ont., ON the outskirts of Toronto in 1979, Bauza attended Cardinal Newman High School (now St. John Henry Newman).

Film review: Years in the making, Coyote vs. Acme sings a sad toon

The most Canadian saying might not be from Canada, eh?

“School cafeteria was my Greek theatre, the forum, that’s where I held court,” he told the Post. “They made the mistake — or maybe the right trajectory — of allowing me to do the morning announcement. Me behind the microphone in high school. You can imagine. It was a field day.”

He graduated from the radio, TV and film program of Toronto’s Centennial College in 2000 and later moved to the U.S.

He said the enjoyed the relative anonymity of being a voice actor — “I could go to the grocery store and no one will bother me” — but added that there were times when being able to sound like a cartoon could be a bonus.

“Being able to do Daffy Duck at U.S. Customs at the airport will get you through in under two minutes,” he said, using the voice as he spoke. “They just listen to this voice and they stamp that passport and you’re off to the races. They go from these tough-as-nails guardians of the nation to these six-year-old kids asking if I can do a voicemail for them.”

Bauza was just the latest voice actor to take over from the late Mel Blanc, nicknamed The Man of a Thousand Voices, who originated Bugs, Daffy, Porky and others, and who died in 1989.

“Daffy for me has always been the favourite of the bunch,” Bauza said when asked for his favourite character. “He is definitely the guy that just tries so hard and always fails. I think that’s like everyone on Earth.”

The day before his death, Bauza shared a photo of himself with The Simpsons director David Silverman at the annual LightBox Expo event in California.

In a statement reported by the Hollywood Reporter , Channing Dungey, chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks, said: “Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world. He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life.”

stories.title: 34-year-old man sentenced for vicious random stabbing attack on elderly woman
stories.summary: Betty O’Loughlin regularly walked her dog along Brydges Street in east London every morning. But in the early hours of Aug. 19, 2024, the 78-year-old was viciously attacked and stabbed six times by a complete stranger.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Betty O’Loughlin regularly walked her dog along Brydges Street in east London every morning. But in the early hours of Aug. 19, 2024, the 78-year-old was viciously attacked and stabbed six times by a complete stranger.

At the sentencing hearing at the London Courthouse on Monday, Justice Michael Carnegie told the court as she rushed home to her apartment, “She went to change her clothes and realized she was covered in blood.”

The court heard after the incident she never really left her apartment and kept to herself.

O’Loughlin survived the random attack but unfortunately died a year later from complications not related to the stab wounds.

Last December, Cristefer Young-Hough, a 34-year-old with a history of mental health issues and substance abuse plead guilty to aggravated assault as well as assault causing bodily harm after he subsequently punched a corrections office in the face while in custody at the Elgin-Middlesex Detention Centre in London.

Suffering from schizophrenia, Justice Carnegie told the court that in the moments after his arrest by London Police, he boasted about the incident.

“He commented that he had stabbed a little old lady and that it had been so easy,” Carnegie said.

The judge said he also asked, “What took you so long?”

Young-Hough told his mother in a text message, “I figured if the system was frame me for stabbing someone, I might as well go out and stab someone.”

The court heard he has lived in several shelters over the years and has a lengthy criminal record.

Justice Carnegie sentenced Young-Hough to a total of six years for both attacks. With credit for time served, he has about 32 months left to serve in prison.

He has is prohibited from carrying any weapons, including firearms, for life.

stories.title: A Montreal man on the run from authorities takes pet raccoon for rabies vaccination
stories.summary: Montreal - A Montreal man who says he is on the run from provincial authorities for housing a raccoon has taken his pet for a rabies vaccination.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The first time the Quebec environmental enforcement officers came for his raccoon, Louka Berman said he stashed the mammal in a park.

Berman said three officers from the provincial wildlife authority came to his Montreal apartment in early October with a warrant to seize the raccoon. He said he let them in but then grabbed the raccoon and ran.

When he returned, he said one of the officers told him he’d be fined for obstruction of justice.

Louka Berman, who lives in Montreal, found an injured baby raccoon in May and nursed it back to health. Now, he and the raccoon he named Pepper are on the run from provincial authorities. (Oct. 26, 2026)

Weeks later, ON Oct. 22, Berman said he once again took the raccoon and ran after seeing enforcement officers pulling up in the street next to his apartment.

“I didn’t take that chance. I’m being super paranoid. I mean, they want to kill my baby, why wouldn’t I be paranoid? So I just assumed the worst,” he said.

Berman named the raccoon Pepper. Together, the pair has now spent weeks dodging authorities, becoming local celebrities in Montreal and even collecting some money due to their online viral fame.

Now, Berman said he is living a nomadic life with the pet. He said he sleeps in his car or with friends. He leaves Pepper outside and he said the raccoon either stays in the same area or makes his way back to Berman.

“It’s been peaceful, but we’re not out of the woods yet,” he said.

Berman said he has also cashed in over $10,000 from a cryptocurrency that was launched by someone else who created the “Pepper coin” and used the raccoon as the face of the new currency.

He said the person who developed the coin reached out online and offered him a cut of the transaction fees.

Louka Berman and his pet raccoon Pepper outside Saint-Damien, Que., ON Monday, Oct. 26, 2026.

Another online fundraiser has collected over $3,000 since it was first posted on Oct. 15.

Berman said he hasn’t organized either, but hopes the money could be used to help build a new sanctuary for wild animals.

On Monday, he took his raccoon to meet the co-owner of a refuge north of Montreal and get vaccinated for rabies. Quebec is currently dealing with an outbreak of raccoon rabies, although it has not yet reached Montreal or the north shore of the St. Lawrence River.

“It’s good because it’s going to shut a lot of people up (who said), ‘What if (it) has rabies?’ No, (it’s) vaccinated, there’s nothing you can say,” he said.

The bond between raccoon and man started when Berman found the injured baby animal in May. He left his job, thinking he would nurse Pepper back to health for a few weeks before freeing him.

Pepper would have none of it. Whenever Berman brought it to a park, the raccoon would find its way back to him.

In September, a video of Berman riding a bike with Pepper on his shoulder went viral on social media. He was quickly dubbed Montreal’s “raccoon guy.”

The provincial government doesn’t see it that way.

In order to keep a wild animal like a raccoon captive, people need to apply for a permit with the provincial environment ministry, Daniel Labonté, a spokesperson for the ministry, told The Canadian Press. However, Labonté added, even with a permit, keeping a raccoon as a pet is not allowed.

A first offence to this regulation could lead to a fine from $1,000 to $5,000, he said.

Labonté said the province’s wildlife authority received a report about “an individual who was riding a bicycle with a raccoon on his shoulder” and investigated the situation, but would not comment further.

The Montreal branch of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals told The Canadian Press it does not condone domesticating wild animals like raccoons.

“These are animals that should, as much as possible, remain in their natural habitat. We advise citizens not to intervene with this species unless it is necessary,” a spokesperson wrote in an email statement.

This isn’t the first time an orphaned baby raccoon found itself on the government’s radar. In 2013, Jacques Lessard and Rachel Garenne nursed a raccoon they named Nymous back to health. When the government captured Nymous, Lessard and Garenne said they fought to get it back and eventually got a special permit to keep it.

Now they operate the refuge near Launaudière, north of Montreal, near where Garenne offered to meet Berman and administer the rabies shot to Pepper.

Nymous passed away in 2015, after complications from a sterilization operation, said Lessard. Tears started to well up in his eyes as he talked about how Pepper’s story reminded him of that experience.

“It’s so hard,” he said.

Louka Berman with his pet raccoon Pepper outside Saint-Damien, Que., ON Monday, Oct. 26, 2026.

While recent governmental restrictions mean they can’t take in Pepper, Garenne was able to meet with Berman and Pepper in a grassy area around two kilometres away from the refuge.

Pepper snacked on a blueberry muffin and trail mix on a picnic table as Garenne and Berman chatted about the raccoon’s health. Berman periodically grabbed or play-fought with Pepper in what looked like a comfortable routine.

“It’s not a dangerous animal. I know people with dogs that are 10 times more dangerous. Does this look dangerous?” said Berman, holding up Pepper.

Berman has little doubt that the government would euthanize Pepper if the raccoon was seized.

“If the animal doesn’t deserve to die, there’s no reason why it should. I think that’s a simple mindset,” he said.

Labonté said the ministry tries to find a shelter or free seized animals, but that euthanasia remains an option as a last resort.

Berman said he is working on getting the necessary permits to open a modest refuge where he could keep up to 15 animals.

“As long as Pepper is alive, I think it’s just always going to find support — or until they decide to leave us alone, we’ll see what comes first,” said Berman.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Youth-led climate trial begins in federal court in Vancouver
stories.summary: Vancouver - The first youth-led climate trial in Canadian history has begun at the federal courthouse in downtown Vancouver, where 15 plaintiffs are arguing that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.
stories.author: Brieanna Charlebois The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The first youth-led climate trial in Canadian history has begun at the federal courthouse in Vancouver, where 15 plaintiffs argue that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.

Catherine Boies Parker, who is representing the youth plaintiffs, said in her opening statement Monday that the case is not about the existence of climate change but rather whether the government is “constitutionally required to stop making it worse.”

“The plaintiffs are asking this court to hold Canada legally accountable for its role in continuing and worsening the climate crisis that is causing harm,” she said.

She said the Charter must provide youth a “degree of protection from their own government’s actions” that she says are contributing to the “greatest threat to personal security that humans have ever faced.”

Boies Parker told the court that her clients are not asking it to develop or implement policies or decide what steps the government should make to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions.

Those decisions should be left to the legislative and executive branches of government, she said.

The role of the court, she said, is to determine if the plaintiffs have a constitutional right to protections.

“When the government acts in a manner that interferes with the physical and emotional integrity of its people, especially its most vulnerable people, the rule of law requires the court to assess whether that interference is consistent with the constitution,” she said.

“That responsibility doesn’t disappear just because the issues are complex,” she said, adding that “unsupervised action May contribute to irreversible harm to children and future generations that have no access to a ballot box.”

She said Canada has been aware of the impacts of climate change as far back as 1988, and has “repeatedly recognized” the dangers of greenhouse gases and made commitments to reduce its emissions.

But despite decades of international commitments and legislative promises, Canada has “repeatedly failed to set sufficient targets (and) repeatedly failed to meet those insufficient targets,” Boies Parker said.

BJ Wray, counsel for Canada’s Department of Justice, told the court in opening arguments that the Charter was “never intended to solve existential crises.”

Wray noted the scope of the Charter that protects the right to life, liberty and security of a person will be an issue for the court to grapple with.

To that, Justice Simon Fothergill said he is “mindful that this could have implications” on other issues, such as housing or health care, that are essential to people’s well-being but “for which the government doesn’t currently recognize a free-standing obligation.”

Wray told the court that Canada is in compliance with its international obligations and it has been reducing greenhouse gas emissions since 2005.

“That is the trajectory that we are on.”

Wray told the court that the outcome the plaintiffs are seeking “can’t be achieved through legal orders” and “can only be achieved through complex international statecraft, over many years.”

Wray said the evidence Canada will present will show that eliminating the impacts of global climate change or “providing the plaintiffs with a safe climate system” is not something the country can do on its own.

“Canada’s evidence will show that global climate change requires a global solution,” and the remedy sought by the plaintiffs is “an outcome that cannot be achieved as there is no way for Canada on its own to ensure a safe climate system,” Wray said.

“The charter ought not to be used to impose on Canada an obligation it cannot fulfil on its own, and we say that this claim should be dismissed,” Wray concluded.

Boies Parker earlier said she was anticipating the government would say it can’t fix climate change on its own, but she argued it can make it better or worse.

The trial comes about seven years after the case was first filed in 2019.

Boies Parker told the court the impacts of climate change have intensified since then, citing the 2021 heat dome in B.C., Canada’s record-breaking 2023 wildfire season, flooding and other extreme weather events that she said “have caused physical and psychological harm.”

The 15 youth are from seven provinces and two territories and are expected to testify about how they have suffered what their lawyers say are “specific harms connected directly to the government’s conduct.”

Boies Parker said those harms include respiratory illness worsened by wildfire smoke, displacement due to extreme weather, mental health impacts, such as climate anxiety and loss of cultural connections to the land that has been lost due to climate disasters.

One of the 15 plaintiffs, a Yellowknife native, was the first to testify at the trial.

Kira Young, now 20 and a varsity athlete at McMaster University, recounted being forced to evacuate from her hometown in the summer of 2023 as a wildfire approached. She described feeling “existential dread and instability.”

“It felt like a destabilization of everything I had known,” she told the court, as she recounted fleeing to Edmonton with her brother and father, while leaving her mother — an essential worker — behind. It was a week before she learned her home was not threatened and they were allowed to return.

“I worry about experiencing something similar in the future,” she said.

She has since been diagnosed with Still’s Disease, an autoinflammatory disorder that she told the court is “exacerbated by heat and smoke.”

Young testified she joined the case about three years ago, when she was 17.

“I am so scared that the suffering and the pain and hardship that I spent the last hour describing is just the beginning of what’s to come for me and youth across Canada, but I don’t believe that that is destined,” she said when asked why she felt compelled to join.

The trial is expected to continue into late November, with closing arguments scheduled for February.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.
paragraphs: Vancouver - The first youth-led climate trial in Canadian history has begun at the federal courthouse in Vancouver, where 15 plaintiffs argue that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing the trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions.

Catherine Boies Parker, who is representing the youth plaintiffs, said in her opening statement Monday that the case is not about the existence of climate change but rather whether the government is “constitutionally required to stop making it worse.”
“The plaintiffs are asking this court to hold Canada legally accountable for its role in continuing and worsening the climate crisis that is causing harm,” she said.

She said the Charter must provide youth a “degree of protection from their own government’s actions” that she says are contributing to the “greatest threat to personal security that humans have ever faced.”
Boies Parker told the court that her clients are not asking it to develop or implement policies or decide what steps the government should make to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions.
Those decisions should be left to the legislative and executive branches of government, she said.
The role of the court, she said, is to determine if the plaintiffs have a constitutional right to protections.

“When the government acts in a manner that interferes with the physical and emotional integrity of its people, especially its most vulnerable people, the rule of law requires the court to assess whether that interference is consistent with the constitution,” she said.

“That responsibility doesn’t disappear just because the issues are complex,” she said, adding that “unsupervised action May contribute to irreversible harm to children and future generations that have no access to a ballot box.”
She said Canada has been aware of the impacts of climate change as far back as 1988, and has “repeatedly recognized” the dangers of greenhouse gases and made commitments to reduce its emissions.

But despite decades of international commitments and legislative promises, Canada has “repeatedly failed to set sufficient targets (and) repeatedly failed to meet those insufficient targets,” Boies Parker said.
BJ Wray, counsel for Canada’s Department of Justice, told the court in opening arguments that the Charter was “never intended to solve existential crises.”
Wray noted the scope of the Charter that protects the right to life, liberty and security of a person will be an issue for the court to grapple with.

To that, Justice Simon Fothergill said he is “mindful that this could have implications” on other issues, such as housing or health care, that are essential to people’s well-being but “for which the government doesn’t currently recognize a free-standing obligation.”
Wray told the court that Canada is in compliance with its international obligations and it has been reducing greenhouse gas emissions since 2005.
“That is the trajectory that we are on.”
Wray told the court that the outcome the plaintiffs are seeking “can’t be achieved through legal orders” and “can only be achieved through complex international statecraft, over many years.”

Wray said the evidence Canada will present will show that eliminating the impacts of global climate change or “providing the plaintiffs with a safe climate system” is not something the country can do on its own.

“Canada’s evidence will show that global climate change requires a global solution,” and the remedy sought by the plaintiffs is “an outcome that cannot be achieved as there is no way for Canada on its own to ensure a safe climate system,” Wray said.
“The charter ought not to be used to impose on Canada an obligation it cannot fulfil on its own, and we say that this claim should be dismissed,” Wray concluded.
Boies Parker earlier said she was anticipating the government would say it can’t fix climate change on its own, but she argued it can make it better or worse.
The trial comes about seven years after the case was first filed in 2019.

Boies Parker told the court the impacts of climate change have intensified since then, citing the 2021 heat dome in B.C., Canada’s record-breaking 2023 wildfire season, flooding and other extreme weather events that she said “have caused physical and psychological harm.”

The 15 youth are from seven provinces and two territories and are expected to testify about how they have suffered what their lawyers say are “specific harms connected directly to the government’s conduct.”

Boies Parker said those harms include respiratory illness worsened by wildfire smoke, displacement due to extreme weather, mental health impacts, such as climate anxiety and loss of cultural connections to the land that has been lost due to climate disasters.
One of the 15 plaintiffs, a Yellowknife native, was the first to testify at the trial.

Kira Young, now 20 and a varsity athlete at McMaster University, recounted being forced to evacuate from her hometown in the summer of 2023 as a wildfire approached. She described feeling “existential dread and instability.”

“It felt like a destabilization of everything I had known,” she told the court, as she recounted fleeing to Edmonton with her brother and father, while leaving her mother — an essential worker — behind. It was a week before she learned her home was not threatened and they were allowed to return.
“I worry about experiencing something similar in the future,” she said.
She has since been diagnosed with Still’s Disease, an autoinflammatory disorder that she told the court is “exacerbated by heat and smoke.”
Young testified she joined the case about three years ago, when she was 17.

“I am so scared that the suffering and the pain and hardship that I spent the last hour describing is just the beginning of what’s to come for me and youth across Canada, but I don’t believe that that is destined,” she said when asked why she felt compelled to join.
The trial is expected to continue into late November, with closing arguments scheduled for February.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

stories.author: Ian Bickis The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WINNIPEG - The owners of Manitoba’s Port of Churchill say they’re working with Dubai-based DP World Inc. to potentially boost traffic at the arctic port.

Oct. 26, 2026

GAC[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/manitoba/port-of-churchill-owners-and-dubai-based-dp-world-looking-to-boost-trade-route/article_d6e3334b-8ef6-51bd-977d-1451db69f1d4.html)

By Ian Bickis The Canadian Press

Indigenous-owned Artic Gateway Group says the memorandum of understanding it has signed with DP World focuses on port operations and possibly creating a transportation corridor linking Manitoba to global markets.

The supply chain memorandum also includes the CentrePort Canada inland shipping hub based beside the Winnipeg airport, as well as the Hudson Bay Railway that links it to the Port of Churchill.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

No dollar investment commitments were announced with the memorandum.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew has championed a Port of Churchill expansion, which would include a liquefied natural gas export terminal that could cost more than $70 billion to build.

The port has done little traffic in recent years, but it has seen renewed interest as Canada looks to diversify trade routes and thinning sea ice expands the potential shipping season.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

stories.summary: Biochemistry professor Stephanie Bishop is among four new and renewed Canada Research Chairs at Western University.

Stephanie Bishop among new and renewed Canada Research Chairs at Western

By Emily Leighton,

October 26, 2026

Western's four new and renewed Canada Research Chairs span the fields of antimicrobial resistance, mental health, wearable medical devices and water quality. (Western Communications)

Topic Research

[](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.westernu.ca%2F2026%2F10%2Fwestern-canada-research-chair-antibiotic-resistant-infections%2F&t=New%20Canada%20Research%20Chair%20at%20Western%20targets%20antibiotic-resistant%20infections)

[](http://twitter.com/share?text=New%20Canada%20Research%20Chair%20at%20Western%20targets%20antibiotic-resistant%20infections&url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.westernu.ca%2F2026%2F10%2Fwestern-canada-research-chair-antibiotic-resistant-infections%2F&via=westernu)

[](http://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.westernu.ca%2F2026%2F10%2Fwestern-canada-research-chair-antibiotic-resistant-infections%2F&title=New%20Canada%20Research%20Chair%20at%20Western%20targets%20antibiotic-resistant%20infections)

[](http://www.printfriendly.com/print?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.westernu.ca%2F2026%2F10%2Fwestern-canada-research-chair-antibiotic-resistant-infections%2F&title=New%20Canada%20Research%20Chair%20at%20Western%20targets%20antibiotic-resistant%20infections)

Explore All News

As bacteria evolve to outsmart antibiotics, once-reliable treatments are becoming less effective.

For biochemistry professor Stephanie Bishop, the search for solutions begins with understanding how bacteria adapt and survive.Named Western’s newest Canada Research Chair (CRC), she is investigating the metabolic changes associated with antibiotic resistance – and whether those changes could reveal new ways to fight back.

The federally funded CRC program recognizes some of the world’s “most accomplished and promising minds,” supporting research excellence in engineering, natural sciences, health sciences, humanities and social sciences.

Bishop’s appointment brings Western’s total number of CRCs to 63. Three other Western CRCs were renewed or advanced as part of the government’slatest investment in Canadian research.

As the Tier 2 CRC in Microbial Metabolomics at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry, Bishop will focus on the bacteria responsible for gonorrhea, a common sexually transmitted infection that is becoming increasingly difficult to treat.

Gonorrhea affects an estimated 82 million people worldwide) each year, according to the World Health Organization. The emergence of strains resistant to existing antibiotics is raising concerns about the future effectiveness of available treatments.

Bishop’s research uses metabolomics to map the small molecules involved in bacterial activity, offering a window into how bacteria function, grow and respond to their environments.

Stephanie Bishop

Her team is particularly interested in a biological trade-off. Genetic mutations that make gonorrhea-causing bacteria resistant to antibiotics can also interfere with their ability to grow.

Some bacteria, however, find a way around that disadvantage, adjusting their metabolism to compensate for the effects of the mutations. Understanding these adaptations could reveal new vulnerabilities for researchers to target with drugs.

“The goal of my research program is to identify new targets for drug development, helping ensure gonorrhea remains treatable in the years to come,” said Bishop.

The new CRC position draws on Western’s existing strengths and specialized infrastructure for infectious disease research, including the new Pathogen Research Centre, the Imaging Pathogens for Knowledge Translation (ImPaKT) facility and advanced technology dedicated to metabolomics research.

“Western has made strategic investments in research infrastructure and people to create a world-class environment for researchers to engage in globally impactful research,” said Bishop.

Kelly Anderson,Schulich Medicine & Dentistry, renewed Tier 2 CRC in Public Mental Health Research

Ana Luisa Trejos, Engineering, renewed Tier 2 CRC in Wearable Mechatronics

Explore All News
As bacteria evolve to outsmart antibiotics, once-reliable treatments are becoming less effective.

For biochemistry professor Stephanie Bishop, the search for solutions begins with understanding how bacteria adapt and survive.Named Western’s newest Canada Research Chair (CRC), she is investigating the metabolic changes associated with antibiotic resistance – and whether those changes could reveal new ways to fight back.

The federally funded CRC program recognizes some of the world’s “most accomplished and promising minds,” supporting research excellence in engineering, natural sciences, health sciences, humanities and social sciences.
Bishop’s appointment brings Western’s total number of CRCs to 63. Three other Western CRCs were renewed or advanced as part of the government’slatest investment in Canadian research.

As the Tier 2 CRC in Microbial Metabolomics at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry, Bishop will focus on the bacteria responsible for gonorrhea, a common sexually transmitted infection that is becoming increasingly difficult to treat.

Gonorrhea affects an estimated 82 million people worldwide) each year, according to the World Health Organization. The emergence of strains resistant to existing antibiotics is raising concerns about the future effectiveness of available treatments.
Bishop’s research uses metabolomics to map the small molecules involved in bacterial activity, offering a window into how bacteria function, grow and respond to their environments.
Stephanie Bishop
Her team is particularly interested in a biological trade-off. Genetic mutations that make gonorrhea-causing bacteria resistant to antibiotics can also interfere with their ability to grow.

Some bacteria, however, find a way around that disadvantage, adjusting their metabolism to compensate for the effects of the mutations. Understanding these adaptations could reveal new vulnerabilities for researchers to target with drugs.
“The goal of my research program is to identify new targets for drug development, helping ensure gonorrhea remains treatable in the years to come,” said Bishop.

The new CRC position draws on Western’s existing strengths and specialized infrastructure for infectious disease research, including the new Pathogen Research Centre, the Imaging Pathogens for Knowledge Translation (ImPaKT) facility and advanced technology dedicated to metabolomics research.
“Western has made strategic investments in research infrastructure and people to create a world-class environment for researchers to engage in globally impactful research,” said Bishop.

stories.title: U.S. firm signs deal to explore closed New Brunswick mine
stories.summary: Fredericton - The New Brunswick government has signed an exploration deal with a firm that plans to extract minerals from a long-closed mining site.
stories.author: Eli Ridder The Canadian Press
stories.content:
U.S.-based Regeneration Enterprises says it wants to pull metals from rock and chemical waste left at the Nigadoo mine site in northern New Brunswick.

The company says it will fund the environmental clean up of the mine using revenue generated from selling the metals.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

Regeneration Enterprises managing director Michael McPhie says he is not asking for provincial funding during any phase of the project.

Instead, McPhie says the project will save taxpayer dollars as his company will take over the degrading site from the provincial government.

Provincial Natural Resources Minister John Herron says this is the type of investment New Brunswick is trying to attract as it works to revive its mining industry.

“This project will convert something that has been a liability for decades and turn it into new investment, good jobs and a cleaner site,” Herron said in a statement Monday.

Production at the mine, located near Bathurst, N.B., first started in 1956, according to a University of New Brunswick research paper. The mine was permanently shuttered in 1977 after repeated closures.

McPhie told reporters at a mining conference in Fredericton that zinc, lead, germanium, gallium, indium, silver and copper are among the minerals his company could pull from the abandoned mine.

He added a crew is headed to the site in the coming days to conduct tests that will determine if the project is feasible.

Those results are expected within one year and production could start within two to three years, he said.

Regeneration is a social enterprise company backed by Apple, Caterpillar and others with the goal of recovering metals from old mines and restoring the land.

A spokesperson said the New Brunswick government is expected to make another mining-related announcement at the conference on Tuesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Galloway agent tells of impact of sexual assault allegations on author's career
stories.summary: Vancouver - The literary agent for Steven Galloway has described what he views as the detrimental impact that unproven allegations of rape and sexual assault had on the author at the height of his "promising" career a decade ago.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The literary agent for Steven Galloway said it would have been “impossible” to sell any new work by his client in the years after a former student made unproven allegations of rape and sexual assault against the author a decade ago.

Henry Dunow described what he viewed as the detrimental impact of the claims on Galloway’s “promising” career during a British Columbia Supreme Court hearing in the author’s defamation lawsuit against his accuser and other defendants.

Dunow said he thought of Galloway as a literary “star” with a bright future ahead.

But the allegations, which emerged in 2015, derailed that trajectory, he said.

An author’s “social capital” and platform carry great importance in the industry, in a way more than the words on the page, Dunow told the hearing on Monday.

Galloway, the former chair of creative writing at the University of B.C., denies the allegations, and he was never charged.

He is suing his accuser, known as A.B., whose assault claims were found unsubstantiated by a former judge hired by the university.

The lawsuit alleges A.B. and other defendants defamed Galloway by publishing the unproven allegations online and through other forums.

Several people originally named as defendants in the lawsuit filed in 2018 have settled with Galloway and offered public apologies.

The court learned earlier this month that A.B. was no longer asserting in her defence that Galloway assaulted her, rather that she reported he had done so.

The woman, whose name is under a publication ban, is not testifying in the case, citing mental health struggles.

Galloway, the author of “The Cellist of Sarajevo” and “The Confabulist” was fired by the university and has said his career was destroyed by the allegations.

He testified earlier this month that he could no longer write, his income from book royalties had “cratered” and he was selling boats for a living.

Dunow told the hearing the allegations resulted in the cancellation of a $100,000 contract for a three-novel series Galloway pitched about a ventriloquist detective, meant to be a playful departure from his earlier, serious works.

He later agreed during cross-examination by A.B.‘s lawyer Arden Beddoes that “The Confabulist” hadn’t met expectations following the success of “The Cellist of Sarajevo,” though he said a so-called “sophomore slump” was not uncommon.

The New York-based agent said he believed A.B.‘s allegations had also thwarted the realization of a film option for “The Cellist of Sarajevo” dating back to around 2011.

Galloway’s lawyer, Dan Burnett, also called an expert witness on Monday who had produced a report on the author’s estimated financial losses after the allegations.

Darren Benning told the court he found Galloway’s total past and future income losses starting from late 2015 to retirement age totalled more than $7 million.

If Galloway’s income had been 25 per cent lower, allowing for potential contingencies, he said the loss would be $4.9 million. If it were 25 per cent higher, the estimated loss would be more than $9 million, Benning said.

The case has drawn intense attention in the Canadian literary scene.

A group of authors, including Margaret Atwood, signed an open letter in November 2016 calling for an investigation into how the university handled Galloway’s case.

The court has previously heard that Galloway and A.B. had a two-year affair, which he has said ended in 2013.

Galloway testified she was a former student who was older than him, whom he’d met sometime in 2011 when she took a writing course from a colleague of his.

“I remain ashamed of having had an affair period, let alone an affair with a student at the university I was at,” he told an earlier hearing. “I should not have been cheating on my wife, and I should have not been doing it with a student.”

A.B.‘s former husband testified last week, called as a witness by Galloway’s lawyers.

Atwood has recently penned opinion articles supporting Galloway, writing in The Globe and Mail that testimony from A.B.‘s ex-husband saying he was exchanging text messages with A.B. about a hockey game at the time of her alleged 2011 rape in Galloway’s office, was like the “Aha!” moment in a Sherlock Holmes novel.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Shotgun fired in Zorra Township home invasion, suspects at large
stories.summary: A shotgun has been fired in a Zorra Township home invasion Monday. The suspects remain at large.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A shotgun has been fired in a Zorra Township home invasion Monday. The suspects remain at large.

Just after midnight, OPP said they were called to a home on 29th Line. They said two people went into the home and one of them had a shotgun. The home was allegedly broken into and were confronted by the homeowner.

During the incident, an altercation took place between the homeowner and suspects, leading to the shotgun being fired. One of the suspects were hit and has suffered unknown injuries.

Both suspects then drove from the scene and have not been arrested.

The homeowner sustained minor injuries in the incident.

The first suspect is described as a man, around six feet tall, with a large stomach, wearing a black bandana.

The second suspect is described as a man wearing a black balaclava.

Investigators think this was a targeted incident and there isn’t a known threat to public safety.

Shotgun discharged during home invasion. #OxfordOPP is investigating a targeted home invasion in Zorra Township in which a suspect was injured after the shotgun was discharged during a struggle with the homeowner. Two suspects remain outstanding. Police are asking anyone with… pic.twitter.com/2GW9dxdtYZ — OPP West Region (@OPP_WR) October 26, 2026

Anyone with information or sees a person with an apparent gunshot wound is asked to contact Oxford OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Residents nearby are asked to check security footage and dash cam footage for any suspicious activity.

stories.title: Father of Jewish students in London, Ont. says daughters won't give into fear after swastika drawn near home
stories.summary: Darren Slavens says his daughters, both Western University students, responded with courage after a swastika was drawn near their home.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
The father of two Jewish students attending Western University in London, Ont. says his daughters remain courageous and will continue to be proud of their faith after a swastika was drawn near their off-campus home.

“While I wanted to draw attention to the incident, I wanted to focus more on their response,” Darren Slavens told National Post on Monday. “These kids are warriors… Instead of fear and intimidation, these kids have responded with courage and pride and that’s what our community needs right now.”

He added that he was happy for the support shown by non-Jewish allies.

He posted a video to Instagram after the incident last week, believing that the swastika was drawn in the front yard of his daughters’ home. He told National Post that he later learned that it was drawn next door.

In the video, he said he was “furious” that the community had to “deal with this garbage.” He said it made his “blood boil” but he felt “unbelievable pride” in his daughters and their friends.

“To those who believe they can frighten Jewish students into hiding their identity, I’ve got news for you. You’re dealing with the wrong generation,” he said. Rather than victims, “our kids are growing up to be warriors. Warriors of courage. Warriors of conviction.”

The incident occurred in the parking lot of off-campus housing for mostly Jewish students in downtown London. Video footage shows a man spraying the pavement with liquid, drawing a Nazi swastika on the ground.

“Chabad at Western’s Rabbis arrived on the scene within minutes to support Jewish students and ensure they felt safe and cared for,” said the statement. “They immediately contacted the London Police Service and the hate crime unit to help emphasize the urgency and seriousness of the incident, contributing to a swift police response.”

Police said they were told that a man who was “completing construction work” in the city used equipment to create what appeared to be the Nazi symbol. Police were provided with photos and videos of the incident from nearby residents.

A 56-year-old London resident identified by police as Gordon Botaitis was arrested on Oct. 23 and charged with one count of offence motivated by hatred.

It was proud of the “students who responded with solidarity and defiance” and commended local police for acting quickly. However, they called for enforcement to be consistent nationwide and for extremism to be “stopped before it takes root.”

“We urge authorities at all levels to confront the radicalization spreading across our campuses and throughout the country, where antisemitic libels and conspiracies about Jews and Israelis fuel hatred, violence and even terrorism,” said Cija.

Meanwhile, Slavens — who posts frequently about Israel and Zionism — said he’s used to receiving hate mail and hate comments, but this time he said there was a number of people giving their support, which he called “heartwarming.”

“I still hold the university and universities across this country responsible. They are a key source of the dehumanization of Jews through allowing the lie of genocide, the lie of apartheid, and the Free Palestine movements to flourish on campus,” he said.

“Something must be done in this country to stop the tropes on campus and on social media, and this event has shown me our kids have the courage and the knowledge to continue this fight against Jew hate”

Western University did not immediately respond to National Post’s request for comment.

In September, there was a string of antisemitic incidents in Ontario, including a shooting at a Belleville synagogue on Yom Kippur that left a police officer in critical condition.

Later that month, a 19-year-old Whitby man was arrested for making threats online to shoot up a synagogue. Less than a week later, a 33-year-old Kitchener man was arrested for making antisemitic comments online “directed at members of the Jewish community.”

stories.title: Three Ontario elections to watch that are not Toronto
stories.summary: Toronto's mayoral race will make the most headlines, but the contests in Hamilton, Mississauga and Ottawa are worth following.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
With residents in 444 Ontario cities and towns deciding who will lead them for the next four years, today is Canada’s busiest day in municipal politics.

While many municipalities have their niche issues — like the cleanup of former General Motors land in St. Catharines or Mississauga’s Ridgeway Plaza — the topics most important to voters are consistent: taxes, transit, housing, homelessness and local infrastructure.

And like so many urban centres across Canada, public safety is also paramount to deciding whether a candidate’s proposed policies will meaningfully address the issue of rising crime rates and increased public drug use.

Most eyes are sure to be locked on Toronto’s results, but here are three other adjacent races worth watching.

Incumbent Carolyn Parrish and former mayor and Ontario Liberal Party Leader Bonnie Crombie are the central figures in this closely watched contest, but councillor Alvin Tedjo has emerged as a potential spoiler.

Councillor Dipika Damerla is also in the running alongside 10 other candidates on the second-longest ballot outside Toronto.

Parrish, a long-time city councillor and former four-term Liberal MP, is seeking her first full term, having replaced Crombie when she left municipal politics for provincial politics in 2024. Crombie, also a former Liberal MP, failed to win a seat in the 2025 Ontario general election and announced her intention to reclaim the mayoralty.

During a leaders’ debate on Oct. 1 at Food Banks Mississauga’ warehouse, Parrish and Crombie got into a heated back-and-forth, shouting at one another at times and launching personal barbs. Parrish called Crombie a “blonde bombshell,” and Crombie accused her successor of being a mayor who “just sits behind her desk,” the National Observer reported.

“She can be very Trumpian,” Crombie said of Parrish to the outlet. “I took her to task on her comments, but I never resorted to name-calling.”

Parrish reportedly said she May have lost her “cool a bit,” but doesn’t “believe anyone behaved particularly well.”

Damerla, meanwhile, told the Bramptonist that the debate “felt like it was kindergarten” at times, and Tedjo said bickering “is part of the problem,” City News reported . Both said it showed a need for change in leadership.

Criminal offences in the Mississauga and Brampton area have been on a downward trend since 2023, according to the Peel Regional Police website , but a 2025 annual report shows drug violations were up 14 per cent since the year prior.

The candidates’ approaches vary on police staffing, funding for law enforcement, the use of surveillance technology and the role of mental health and social service workers in responding to drug-related issues.

Crime and public safety (11 per cent) are tied with housing as the most important issue facing the city, according to an Abacus Data poll released last week.

That same poll indicates a three-way race between Crombie (26 per cent), Tedjo (25 per cent), and Parrish (22 per cent), with 16 per cent still undecided.

A L iaison Strategies poll last week, however, finds Crombie leading with 35 per cent among decided and leaning voters, followed by Tedjo (31 per cent) and Parrish (28 per cent). Damerla is a distant fourth in both.

The nation’s capital also has 14 people on the mayoral ballot, among them incumbent mayor Mark Sutcliffe and his main challenger, longtime progressive councillor Jeff Leiper.

Two other candidates likely to pinch votes from either include Neil Saravanamuttoo, an economist and regular critic of City Hall, and homebuilder Alex Lawson, a political outsider vowing top-down reforms.

“I think it’s important for the people of Ottawa to understand the ideology behind some of the candidates who are running for mayor,” Sutcliffe said earlier this month, per the Ottawa Citizen.

“It’s a competition of ideas. It’s a competition of agendas.”

In July, Sutcliffe stood by fundraising and endorsement emails from two former Ontario politicians — former MPP and provincial cabinet minister Madeleine Meilleur and former MPP, MP and cabinet minister John Baird — that framed his opponents as radicals, CBC reported .

Meilleur said Leiper and Lawson represent the “ideological extremes of the political spectrum,” while Baird’s labelled the former as a “hard left, ideological and out of touch candidate.”

In response, Lawson called it “petty name-calling,” and Leiper argued, “malicious American-style politics has no place in our municipal politics.”

Ottawa has not elected a leftist candidate as mayor since Marion Dewar in 1978, the Citizen reported.

Citywide crime as of Aug. 17 is up eight per cent over the same period last year, according to the Citizen . Sexual violations are up 24 per cent, assaults are up five per cent, instances of violent crime grew four per cent and property crime inched up six per cent.

“The increase in the vulnerable population is overwhelming the social agencies that manage them. People aren’t feeling as safe as they used to with some of the social disorder and the open drug use and whatnot,” Ottawa Police Service Chief Eric Stubbs told the Citizen late last year.

All the candidates’ platforms differ in how they balance police staffing and budgeting, enforcement and response to drug addiction and mental health crises.

paragraphs: With residents in 444 Ontario cities and towns deciding who will lead them for the next four years, today is Canada’s busiest day in municipal politics.

While many municipalities have their niche issues — like the cleanup of former General Motors land in St. Catharines or Mississauga’s Ridgeway Plaza — the topics most important to voters are consistent: taxes, transit, housing, homelessness and local infrastructure.

And like so many urban centres across Canada, public safety is also paramount to deciding whether a candidate’s proposed policies will meaningfully address the issue of rising crime rates and increased public drug use.
Most eyes are sure to be locked on Toronto’s results, but here are three other adjacent races worth watching.

Incumbent Carolyn Parrish and former mayor and Ontario Liberal Party Leader Bonnie Crombie are the central figures in this closely watched contest, but councillor Alvin Tedjo has emerged as a potential spoiler.
Councillor Dipika Damerla is also in the running alongside 10 other candidates on the second-longest ballot outside Toronto.

Parrish, a long-time city councillor and former four-term Liberal MP, is seeking her first full term, having replaced Crombie when she left municipal politics for provincial politics in 2024. Crombie, also a former Liberal MP, failed to win a seat in the 2025 Ontario general election and announced her intention to reclaim the mayoralty.

During a leaders’ debate on Oct. 1 at Food Banks Mississauga’ warehouse, Parrish and Crombie got into a heated back-and-forth, shouting at one another at times and launching personal barbs. Parrish called Crombie a “blonde bombshell,” and Crombie accused her successor of being a mayor who “just sits behind her desk,” the National Observer reported.
“She can be very Trumpian,” Crombie said of Parrish to the outlet. “I took her to task on her comments, but I never resorted to name-calling.”
Parrish reportedly said she May have lost her “cool a bit,” but doesn’t “believe anyone behaved particularly well.”

Damerla, meanwhile, told the Bramptonist that the debate “felt like it was kindergarten” at times, and Tedjo said bickering “is part of the problem,” City News reported . Both said it showed a need for change in leadership.

Criminal offences in the Mississauga and Brampton area have been on a downward trend since 2023, according to the Peel Regional Police website , but a 2025 annual report shows drug violations were up 14 per cent since the year prior.

The candidates’ approaches vary on police staffing, funding for law enforcement, the use of surveillance technology and the role of mental health and social service workers in responding to drug-related issues.
Crime and public safety (11 per cent) are tied with housing as the most important issue facing the city, according to an Abacus Data poll released last week.
That same poll indicates a three-way race between Crombie (26 per cent), Tedjo (25 per cent), and Parrish (22 per cent), with 16 per cent still undecided.

A L iaison Strategies poll last week, however, finds Crombie leading with 35 per cent among decided and leaning voters, followed by Tedjo (31 per cent) and Parrish (28 per cent). Damerla is a distant fourth in both.

Two other candidates likely to pinch votes from either include Neil Saravanamuttoo, an economist and regular critic of City Hall, and homebuilder Alex Lawson, a political outsider vowing top-down reforms.
“I think it’s important for the people of Ottawa to understand the ideology behind some of the candidates who are running for mayor,” Sutcliffe said earlier this month, per the Ottawa Citizen.
“It’s a competition of ideas. It’s a competition of agendas.”
