stories.title: Carney, premiers to meet with First Nations leaders in Ottawa for first time in years
stories.summary: Ottawa — First Nations leaders meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney and some of the country's premiers today in what the Assembly of First Nations is calling a historic occasion.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A historic meeting between Prime Minister Mark Carney, premiers and First Nations was meant to build bridges between communities and work out issues related to major projects development, the respecting of rights, health and public safety amid rising tensions.

But it ended with calls from Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew to abolish the controversial Indian Act, and agreement from Carney something must be done about the legislation from 1876 that governs First Nations — something protestors outside the Ottawa venue were warning about before the announcement was even made, and something likely to generate heated debate.

Carney said he will instruct his ministers to work with First Nations to move Canada beyond the Indian Act, which he said could mean reforming it or abolishing it altogether. He said changes would only be made in partnership with First Nations leadership.

The Indian Act gives Ottawa sweeping powers over First Nations communities and people, including by defining who qualifies for recognition, what reserves can and can’t do, dismantles traditional forms of governance and, at one point, outlawed ceremonial practices.

It even governs First Nations people after death, with the Indigenous Services minister required to approve of wills for people living on reserve, or to void them altogether if they see fit.

While there is a general consensus among First Nations chiefs the legislation is outdated and restrictive, there is little consensus on if it should repealed, and, if it is, what takes its place. There is broad support, however, for changing rules on how the Indian Act determines who qualifies for status, but the federal government and Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty have not committed to changing registration rules.

Earlier in the day, Kinew told reporters during a break in the meeting that Canada needs a relationship between First Nations and the government “that reflects who Indigenous people are as Canadians.”

Kinew, a member of Ojibways of Onigaming First Nation, held up his own status card and said abolishing the Indian Act should be high on the national political agenda, and that he received an “open-minded reception” from leadership in the closed-door meeting when he made the pitch.

“The suggestion of reforming, potentially abolishing and fully modernizing governance, is that a process, co-developed, needs to be put in place, and the federal government is open to that process,” Carney said.

Carney echoed Kinew’s remarks that the idea of abolishing or modernizing the Indian Act was discussed openly in the room — and an idea he was similarly “very open to.”

“Not everybody, but other participants raised the desirability. So it’s already starting from the right place in that it’s not the federal government deciding something should be done. It’s responding to a request,” Carney said.

“I think this was the spirit of this meeting — certainly the spirit I took — the ability to sit down together and develop that co-development, gives me hope that we can we can finally move forward from this.”

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said there are some protections in the Indian Act for First Nations, and First Nations should be able to decide how to move forward.

“Look, that’s a question that was just posed today in the room among First Nations. Some First Nations; others would be very reserved,” Woodhouse Nepinak.

“But there is, you know, a diversity of First Nations from coast to coast to coast, where in every province and territory in this beautiful country that we all share. And that question is going to be up to them to decide.”

Protestors outside the venue were warning that their representatives in the meeting, who were largely made up of regional chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations, would inappropriately discuss First Nations rights without a mandate from community members.

Mohawk policy analyst and protest organizer Russ Diabo has frequently accused the Assembly of First Nations of working toward Indian Act abolition with the federal government. Asked about Woodhouse Nepinak telling the room in her opening remarks she has a mandate from chiefs to discuss rights, Diabo said the AFN charter does not represent the grassroots.

“Our traditional governments are direct democracies where the people are involved in decision-making,” Diabo told The Canadian Press on the sidewalk in front of the Diefenbaker Building..

“What we should be returning to is traditional forms of government which involve people in decision making, otherwise we see manipulation happening all the time.”

After Kinew’s remarks, Diabo said governments were already working on abolishing it without consent.

The chief of Onion Lake Cree Nation, which reportedly sent a cease-and-desist letter to the Assembly of First Nations ahead of the meeting to make clear the body does not represent his community or negotiate on its behalf, expressed concern about the future of the Indian Act.

“First Nations must determine their own path toward self-determination. That cannot be a process designed in Ottawa and presented to our nations for approval. It must be developed with us, respect our treaty relationships and proceed only with our free, prior and informed consent,” Chief Pete Chief said in a media statement.

“But that future must be determined by First Nations themselves, not dictated by the federal government or negotiated on our behalf by organizations we have not authorized to represent us.”

First Nations chiefs are frequently critiqued by members of their community when they meet with premiers or Carney behind closed doors.

Asked about those critiques already forming online regarding talk of Indian Act abolition, Woodhouse Nepinak said First Nations should be able to determine for themselves how they’re governed.

“I know those conversations are hard to have, but if we don’t have them, you’ll see the disputes,” she said.

Lawyer Pam Palmater likened the talks of abolishment to the Stephen Harper era, saying the federal government would love nothing more than to drop its fiduciary and treaty obligations to First Nations.

“Saw this coming with Carney’s conservative extractive agenda,” Palmater wrote on social media.

Monday’s closed-door meeting is the first such gathering since the Kelowna Accord talks of 2005, which brought premiers and then-prime minister Paul Martin together with Indigenous leaders to discuss ways to close the socioeconomic gaps in Indigenous communities.

The Kelowna agreement was not implemented after the Conservative government under former prime minister Stephen Harper took office just a few months later.

This meeting came as Carney’s government works to speed up major project approvals and development — efforts some First Nations chiefs say threaten their rights.

Jeronimo Kataquapit, who was protesting the major projects push outside the meeting venue in Ottawa, chided the federal government and the Assembly of First Nations over the lack of youth representation at the meeting.

“These major projects cannot move forward without our free, prior and informed consent, and it’s the youth that stand to be the most impacted by the decisions made today by all leadership, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous alike,” Kataquapit said from the sidewalk in front of the Diefenbaker Building.

Protester Katisha Paul, an advocate for youth and women, questioned the Assembly of First Nations’ mandate to negotiate on First Nations’ behalf.

“I’m not in that room today but I can imagine and speculate that the voices of our ancestors are not being heard, they’re not being voiced and they’re not being amplified because many of those elected band council chiefs have lost their ways,” Paul said.

Tensions between Ottawa and First Nations spiked soon after Carney was elected in 2025 when his government passed legislation to create a new office tasked with streamlining major project developments and approving projects within one year.

First Nations leaders warned the compressed timelines would interfere with their rights and lead to court challenges. Provincial governments have enacted similar legislation.

But tensions are boiling over for a number of other reasons as well, including the lands claim process in British Columbia, the newly announced Pacific Link pipeline project in Alberta and development of the mineral-rich Ring of Fire in Ontario. In many cases, it’s youth who are pushing back on First Nations leaders, the premiers and prime minister.

Carney said Monday in his opening remarks it’s “sobering” to consider that this is the first meeting to bring together federal, provincial and First Nations leaders in two decades.

“Our task is twofold. First is to work together to create opportunities for all our peoples, while building a country that is stronger, more sovereign and more independent,” he said.

“And secondly, our task is to live our values fully of a fair and inclusive Canada.”

While some First Nations are opposed to Carney’s development agenda and those of the provinces, others are open to the idea of increasing economic activity in their territories.

Nisga’a Nation President Eva Clayton told reporters ahead of the meeting she supports Carney’s plans and that she and other modern treaty holders are at the meeting to support Canada.

Chiefs in the meeting room told reporters the talks behind closed doors were constructive and that they felt their voices were heard, but that they wanted more action on actively involving their communities in the Natural Resources Transfer Acts. That call was pushed for by former Assembly of First Nations national chief Matthew Coon Come.

The British Columbia Assembly of First Nations said in a media release after the meeting it failed to live up to its potential.

“The structure, format and agenda of this meeting were solely reflective of federal and provincial interest,” Regional Chief Terry Teegee said.

“The prime minister and premiers have an obligation to meet directly with First Nations to engage in reciprocal dialogue on issues of shared importance, not simply those items which align with this government’s priorities.”

After the meeting, Carney committed to looking into a First Nations sovereign wealth fund that would allow for communities to invest in major projects in an easier way, funding for First Nations policing and improving First Nations health.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Did Ontario's minimum wage just go up?
stories.summary: There are four categories of workers affected by the province's minimum wage hikes.
stories.author: Soma Ray-Ellis
stories.content:
Q: I’m a minimum wage earner in Ontario, and my pay has recently gone up. Can I expect it to keep increasing annually?

A: Ontario’s minimum wage rates are subject to annual increases based on the rate of inflation measured through the province’s Consumer Price Index (CPI). Minimum wage is the lowest amount an employer is allowed to pay a worker by law.

This index measures changes in the cost of goods and services purchased by Ontario consumers, including food, transportation and shelter.

Ontario’s minimum wage is adjusted annually based on the CPI. The government announces the new rate by April 1, and the new rate takes effect on Oct. 1.

This year, as you’ve mentioned, minimum wage has increased.

The Ontario government states that about 35 per cent of minimum wage workers are employed in the retail trade sector, while about 24 per cent work in accommodation and food services.

Overall, there are four categories of workers affected by minimum wage hikes in Ontario.

The first is general minimum wage workers, which includes employees in the retail trade, accommodation, and food services sectors.

As of Oct. 1, 2026, their wage has increased to $17.95 per hour from $17.60 per hour.

The second category is student minimum wage, which applies to students younger than 18 who work 28 hours a week or less while school is in session, or work during school breaks or summer holidays.

Their wage has increased to $16.90 per hour from $16.60 per hour.

The third category covers employees who work as hunting, fishing and wilderness guides.

A wilderness guide is an employee who guides, assists or teaches groups/individuals participating in activities in the wilderness.

This includes backcountry skiing, snowshoeing, canoeing, hiking and survival training.

Wages for this group are based on blocks of time rather than by the hour.

Their rate for working less than five consecutive hours in a day is now $89.75, up from $88.05.

Their rate for working five or more hours in a day is now $179.50, up from $176.15.

The last group of minimum wage earners to receive a rate hike are homeworkers.

A homeworker is defined as an employee who is paid to perform work in their own home.

This includes those who write software for a high-tech company, call centre employees, and employees who sew for a manufacturer.

Their rate is now $19.70 per hour, up from $19.35 per hour.

Keep in mind that students of all ages employed in this category must receive the homeworker’s minimum wage.

Ontario maintains the second-highest minimum wage rate among provinces in Canada, second to British Columbia, where it is $18.25 per hour.

If a minimum wage increase comes into effect partway through an employee’s pay period, it will be treated as two separate pay periods, and the employee will be entitled to at least the minimum wage that applies in each of them.

Additionally, if an employee’s pay is based wholly or partly on commission, it must amount to at least the minimum wage for each hour the employee has worked.

stories.title: Ontario promised four hours of daily care in long-term care homes, but records show nearly 300 are failing
stories.summary: Internal records show nearly 300 Ontario long-term care homes fail to meet the promised four hours of daily resident care.
stories.author: Frédérik Plante
stories.content:
At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic in November 2020, Ontario Premier Doug Ford promised more hands-on care for long-term care homes’ residents.

“By increasing the hours of daily direct care for residents, we will improve their quality of life and ensure they are more comfortable and safe,” Ford said at the time.

His government pledged to reach four hours of daily care by nurses and personal support workers for each long-term care resident by 2024-25. But records obtained by the Star through a freedom-of-information request reveal large disparities between homes and widespread failure to reach the standard.

A year past the government’s deadline, nearly 300 long-term care homes still don’t meet the promised standard of four hours of daily care, the records show.

Research has shown that more daily hours of care is associated with better outcomes for long-term care residents , including better mood, fewer falls and lower use of antipsychotic drugs .

The Canadian Institute for Health Information found that short-staffed long-term care homes had a higher risk of infection and a higher mortality rate. Ontario’s Long-Term Care COVID-19 Commission recommended in 2021 that the minimum of four hours of hands-on care by personal support workers and nurses should be implemented “ on an urgent basis .”

A Ministry of Long-Term Care spokesperson said that Ontario is “making record investments to ensure people at every stage of life can access the care they need.” This includes $44.1 million in the province’s 2026 budget “to ensure every resident continues to receive an average of four hours of direct care each day,” the Ministry said in an unsigned statement.

The Ford government said it met its goal, with the provincial average increasing slightly above four hours of daily care last year. But far from every resident benefits from that minimum.

The COVID-19 Commission found that the government’s promised timeline was “too slow” and that, by the time the standard would be reached, four hours of daily care would likely be insufficient as the “acuity of long-term care residents continues to increase.”

The facility that provided the least amount of direct care to residents in the first three quarters of 2025-26 — the most recent data obtained by the Star — was St. Lawrence Lodge in Brockville. St. Lawrence, a not-for-profit home with 224 licensed beds, recorded an average of two hours and 21 minutes of care per resident over that period, with a low of one hour and 16 minutes during the second quarter.

An unrelated Ministry of Long-Term Care inspection conducted in the fall of 2025 shows numerous other issues at St. Lawrence, including unspecified allegations of staff to resident physical and emotional abuse, neglect and retaliation. The inspection found several deficiencies, including a resident with a documented bed sore who was not assessed and another whose wounds were not treated properly.

Lisa Harper, the administrator of St. Lawrence, did not return the Star’s calls.

Ninety-one long-term care homes did not have data on care provided in 2025-26 because of various “data quality issues,” according to Ministry records. Among those without recent data, 73 had previously failed to provide four hours of care per resident, ON average, between 2023 and 2025.

This means that less than half of Ontario’s 705 long-term care homes have met the provincial government’s promised standard.

Among the 20 facilities giving the least amount of daily care per resident, four homes belong to the same for-profit licensee: Caressant Care Nursing and Retirement Homes Limited.

An August routine compliance inspection at one of these, the Caressant Care home on McLaughlin Road in Lindsay, found that staff “were verbally abusive when providing care” to a resident, did not provide sufficient personal care, failed to properly address a resident’s pain and put others “at increased risk of heat-related illness” when their rooms were left at temperatures above 26°C. The inspection resulted in several written notifications and orders to remedy deficiencies, but no penalty.

Betty Hazen, the facility’s executive director, declined to answer the Star’s questions. Natalie Dechert, Caressant Care’s Vice President of Operations, said that “while many of our homes are consistently meeting or exceeding these provincial targets, we recognize there is ongoing work to do in certain locations to ensure consistency.”

She said that the company is making progress and “remains deeply focused on delivering the safe, compassionate care our residents deserve.”

ByThames Valley District School Board - Oct 26, 2026

General News

All Notices and Updates

Thames Valley District School Board congratulates Kim Davy, a valued art teacher at H.B. Beal Secondary School, for receiving the prestigious Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award from the Canadian Society for Education through Art (CSEA/SCEA) and the journal Canadian Art Teacher (CAT).

Kim Davy is one of just five educators from across Canada named as award recipients this fall, and the only recipient representing Ontario. The Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award is a national recognition program that celebrates outstanding K-12 art educators who contribute to sharing knowledge and fostering meaningful learning through the visual arts.

Kim was nominated for the award by a BealArt alumna who wanted to honour the exceptional impact she has had on students through her work in the classroom.

"I am deeply passionate about the power of Art Education to drive personal growth and development," said Kim Davy. "As an educator, my primary mission is to support and empower students as they find their voice, build technical skills, and expand their creative awareness. I encourage them to focus on their unique artistic journeys—where "mileage on the hands" reflects a dedication to practice, and deep research fosters an authentic voice. By inviting students to take risks, I help them learn to trust the creative process."

"Within the Bealart community, staff and students uplift one another through coordinated teamwork, critical dialogue, technical growth, and conceptual exploration. Ultimately, my hope is that our students cultivate lifelong skills that extend far beyond the classroom, shaping them into future creators and engaged community members."

As part of the recognition, Kim participated in a CAT Conversation on October 15, joining fellow award recipients in an 80-minute discussion focused on creative programming and art education.

Congratulations to Kim Davy on this outstanding achievement and recognition of her work in art education!

ByThames Valley District School Board - Oct 26, 2026

Thames Valley District School Board congratulates Kim Davy, a valued art teacher at H.B. Beal Secondary School, for receiving the prestigious Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award from the Canadian Society for Education through Art (CSEA/SCEA) and the journal Canadian Art Teacher (CAT).

Kim Davy is one of just five educators from across Canada named as award recipients this fall, and the only recipient representing Ontario. The Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award is a national recognition program that celebrates outstanding K-12 art educators who contribute to sharing knowledge and fostering meaningful learning through the visual arts.
Kim was nominated for the award by a BealArt alumna who wanted to honour the exceptional impact she has had on students through her work in the classroom.

"I am deeply passionate about the power of Art Education to drive personal growth and development," said Kim Davy. "As an educator, my primary mission is to support and empower students as they find their voice, build technical skills, and expand their creative awareness. I encourage them to focus on their unique artistic journeys—where "mileage on the hands" reflects a dedication to practice, and deep research fosters an authentic voice. By inviting students to take risks, I help them learn to trust the creative process."

"Within the Bealart community, staff and students uplift one another through coordinated teamwork, critical dialogue, technical growth, and conceptual exploration. Ultimately, my hope is that our students cultivate lifelong skills that extend far beyond the classroom, shaping them into future creators and engaged community members."
As part of the recognition, Kim participated in a CAT Conversation on October 15, joining fellow award recipients in an 80-minute discussion focused on creative programming and art education.
Congratulations to Kim Davy on this outstanding achievement and recognition of her work in art education!

stories.title: Ontario is on track get everyone a family doctor or primary care provider by 2029, province says
stories.summary: The Ford government says more than half a million people have been connected to a family doctor or primary care team through Health Care Connect.
stories.author: Megan Ogilvie; Kerry Gillespie
stories.content:
Nearly two years after promising to fix Ontario’s primary care system, the Ford government says more than half a million people have been connected to a family doctor or primary care team.

Health officials on Monday said this puts the province on track to connect every Ontarian to primary care by 2029 — a pledge made by the Ministry of Health when it launched its Primary Care Action Plan in January 2025 .

Since then, the province has committed $3.4 billion to primary care, including creating and expanding primary care teams , opening new medical school spots and boosting the primary care workforce .

Health Minister Sylvia Jones said Ontario leads the country with nearly 90 per cent of people connected to a family doctor or primary care team. By that accounting, that still leaves roughly 1.8 million Ontarians without access to such care.

“We know there is more work to do,” Jones said.

She said the government has increased the number of family physicians in Ontario by 14 per cent since 2018 and is taking additional steps to increase numbers further by training more doctors and attracting them from other jurisdictions.

“We are making it easier for nurses and physicians to move and practice here in Ontario — with over 2,300 nurses and more than 570 doctors from the U.S. choosing to practice in Ontario in 2025 alone,” Jones said.

The government has added 340 undergraduate seats and 551 postgraduate family medical positions, she said, noting the province is “investing in the largest medical school education expansion in a generation.”

Jones also pointed to progress with Health Care Connect, the provincial program that connects people to primary care in their community. More than 470,000 people have been cleared from Health Care Connect since January 2025, she said, with wait times at their lowest levels in more than a decade.

The province had pledged to clear the Health Care Connect wait-list by the spring of 2026 — and stated last fall it was on track to do so . Health officials did not say Monday why they had not met their own government targets.

Last year, Ontario’s auditor general highlighted issues with Health Care Connect, stating the program was not as effective as it could be, with too few doctors using the service and patients lagging on wait-lists. The findings were released in an audit of the province’s oversight of access to primary care, which at the time concluded the Health Ministry was failing to get more Ontarians a family doctor.

The audit highlighted a lack of provincial co-ordination in physician recruitment , while a separate audit on oversight of medical education found the government had underestimated the number of medical school seats needed to train family doctors. According to the auditor, the province needs 2,000 more family physicians to ensure all Ontarians could be connected to primary care.

The Ministry of Health acknowledged that many long-standing issues with Health Care Connect have been resolved and the tool is now working well to connect patients. As of Oct. 1, ministry figures show that of the roughly 61,000 people on Health Care Connect list, 15 per cent have been waiting more than a year, while nearly 40 per cent have only been waiting three months.

Dr. Adil Shamji, Liberal primary care critic and MPP for Don Valley East, said the Ford government still has a long way to go in solving the primary care crisis, noting that people coming off the Health Care Connect list doesn’t mean they found a doctor.

“Some of them, their phone number has changed, they moved, in some cases they May have died, and they’ve just been removed off the list,” Shamji said. He added the government needs to increase their focus on physician retention, getting nurse practitioners publicly funded and speeding up credentialing of internationally trained doctors.

Research has shown an increasing number of doctors who train as family physicians are fleeing the profession to other areas of practice , including emergency medicine.

Dr. Jane Philpott, the former liberal health minister who was appointed in 2024 by the Ontario government to lead the Primary Care Action Team, said Monday that two rounds of funding have gone toward expanding and creating primary care teams.

So far, more than 300 new and expanded primary care teams will connect some 800,000 patients by the end of the current fiscal year. In 2027-28 and 2028-29, the government is projecting it will be able to attach more patients — some 1.2 million — to primary care teams than has happened so far.

Philpott said those “ambitious targets” come down to clinicians and administrators in the system learning and improving their community outreach.

“We asked them to do more,” Philpott said. “We received proposals for even higher targets and we expect that across the province as the system sorts itself out … we expect our attachment rates to go up.”

stories.title: Ice unit investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (October 26, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit have arrested and charged a London man after an investigation involving the online luring of a person believed to be a youth.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 26, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit have arrested and charged a London man after an investigation involving the online luring of a person believed to be a youth.

On October 20, 2026, a man began communicating online with an individual he believed to be a 14-year-old female. During the conversation, the suspect offered to pick up the youth and take her for a drive.

The suspect later provided his phone number, and the conversation continued by text message. The communication became sexual in nature. The suspect sent sexually explicit images over the phone and requested images in return. The suspect also agreed to meet the individual he believed to be 14 years old, in person.

Through the investigation, members of the London Police Service ICE Unit identified the suspect as an adult male, residing in London.

During the investigation, police learned the suspect was using the Snapchat username "biskylover."

On October 22, 2026, officers attended the location where the meeting had been arranged and arrested the suspect.

As a result of the investigation, Dylan Jonathan Carter, 25, of London, has been charged with:

Make available sexually explicit material to person under or believed to be under 18 years of age;

Make available sexually explicit material to person under or believed to be under 16 years of age;

Luring a person under 18 years of age by means of telecommunication; and

Luring a person under 16 years of age by means of telecommunication.

The accused remains in custody and is expected to appear in London court on October 27, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Investigators believe there May be additional victims, and as such, we are releasing the accused’s image.

London Police Service is a member of the Provincial Strategy to protect children from sexual abuse and exploitation on the internet. The Strategy has been made possible by a grant from the Ministry of the Solicitor General.

Anyone who has had similar interactions with the accused, or who has information that May assist investigators, is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Teens use machete to rob boy, 15, at Whitby cinema. Victim suffers ‘significant laceration’
stories.summary: Police say the teen was robbed after going to the movie theatre to “meet a female he knew through social media.”
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
A 15-year-old boy suffered a “significant laceration” after he was robbed and stabbed by a group of teens armed with a machete at a Whitby movie theatre on Sunday, Durham police say.

It was around 12:40 a.m. when officers from Central West Division were called to Landmark Cinemas at 75 Consumers Dr. , near Thickson Road South and Highway 401, for an “armed person call,” Durham Regional Police said in a news release.

stories.title: Ready. Set. Reset: How the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre improved ready-to-treat to treatment wait times
stories.summary: October 26, 2026
stories.content:
Photo from left: Meghan Koczwara and Christine Rossi, radiation therapists in the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre preparing the Ethos linear accelerator (used to deliver radiation therapy) for a patient.

October 26, 2026

After only twelve weeks, beginning in March 2026, the Radiation Therapy team at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre improved radiation therapy wait times by 34 per cent.

Some key figures to keep in mind:

The target for patient wait times for this project is measured from when a patient is considered ready to treat to the start of radiation treatment.

This project also included the target for patient wait times at LHSC from first consultation to the CT simulation appointment, which is three days. The CT simulation appointment is often the first step in planning for radiation therapy treatment, is three days.

The provincial benchmark is for the patient to be treated within their urgency category wait time window. The target for most patients is to begin treatment within a wait time window of 14 days from being ready-to-treat. And within that, the aim is that at least 85 per cent of patients should be starting their treatment in that period.

After the Radiation Therapy team implemented RESET into their workflow in August 2026, they saw 90.7 per cent of patients meet their wait time target from ready-to-treat to receiving their treatment.

When leaders in Radiation Therapy closely examined patient wait times for radiation treatment and CT simulation appointments, they noted that the issue was not about individual performance.

“Everyone was working hard and following the processes available to them. The team initially expected the system to self-correct as pressures changed from day to day, but a deeper investigation revealed that was not happening. Instead, delays were occurring throughout the pathway, creating barriers that prevented patients from moving efficiently from consultation to treatment,” explains Carina Feuz, Manager, Radiation Planning in the Verspeeten.

There were six areas that the team needed to focus on to improve these wait times:

Demand and backlog management

CT simulation

Treatment planning

Treatment delivery

Stabilizing the roles of staff and ensuring their well-being

Accountability and reporting as the project progressed

The three main goals of the project were:

Reduce patient demand where appropriate

Increase capacity where needed

Improve patient flow through the treatment pathway

Dr. David D'Souza, Division Chair/Head of Radiation Oncology at the Verspeeten notes that there are multiple steps and collaborators that work in the cancer centre to get patients assessed and started on radiation.

"The 14-day target was set to ensure that across Ontario, there was equitable and timely access to radiation," D'Souza explains. "Our performance at the Verspeeten is measured and compared with other centres in the province. The rationale is that an adequately resourced system should be able to do the work required to get a patient started on treatment within that target. Longer waits can lead to poorer treatment outcomes. The importance of including the CT simulation appointment in this project is that it is the first step in getting patient to treatment. If a patient waits more than three days, it becomes challenging to “catch up” and get a patient started on time."

Feuz explains, “We recognized there were opportunities for improvement. It wasn’t about any one person or one team. It was about understanding how the entire pathway was functioning and where we could make changes together.”

The Radiation Efficiency Scheduling & Execution Transformation (RESET) launched in March 2026 in response to patient wait times that were longer than the provincial target for Urgency Three patients – which are patients that should receive their first treatment within 14 days from their ready-to-treat date.

The other categories are Urgency One patients, who should receive their first treatment within one day from consultation, and Urgency Two patients, who should receive their first treatment within seven days from their ready-to-treat date.

Working in partnership with LHSC’s Project Management Office, the initiative used data and insights from staff to identify practical changes using existing resources to reduce bottlenecks, restore timely access for patients, and create a more sustainable operating model of care.

“Rather than simply scheduling appointments as space became available, teams began focusing on whether patients moving through the system were truly ready for the next step in their treatment journey,” Feuz says. “And CT simulation booking was aligned more closely with treatment readiness, helping create a smoother and more predictable flow.”

Early indicators helped leaders and frontline staff understand when trends were emerging and what actions were required. If a change appeared to be part of a larger pattern, leaders determined whether they should stay the course, activate contingency plans, or take more direct action. This disciplined approach helped create a shared understanding across the pathway and increased clarity around decision-making.

The program established clear rules to review cases as the patient moved through each stage of care. These reviews helped identify barriers, adjust bookings when necessary, and ensure patients continued progressing through the system in a timely manner.

“If ready-to-treat performance started to decline or shift, that served as a signal for us to respond,” Feuz says. “Each threshold had a specific action associated with it, which meant we could monitor access delays and intervene before a backlog was established.”

Clerks, physicians, physicists, radiation therapists, dosimetrists, electronic technologists, and leaders all had a role in helping patients move more efficiently through the pathway.

“The numbers were important,” Feuz notes, “but what mattered most was how the plan was implemented across the program and the positive impact it had on patient access to timely care.”

"The impact of RESET has been huge," shares Dr. D'Souza. "Since many of our patients travel for over an hour to get to our centre, in addition to convenience, these changes have made it easier for a patient to access the resources needed in a timely manner in order for them to receive radiation treatment. There is more flexibility in getting patients booked into a time slot that works for them. It also means that those suffering with symptoms like pain are getting relief sooner."

There were honest conversations throughout the process, and staff feedback was sought before, during, and after implementation. Many of the improvements that contributed to the program’s success came directly from frontline teams.

“A lot of the changes were staff generated,” says Feuz. “The success of RESET was because of the team here in Radiation Therapy. It was a huge team effort. We would not have achieved this success without everyone’s commitment.”

The shared goal was never simply to improve a metric. It was to ensure patients received the care they needed without unnecessary delays.

“We wanted patients to remain at the forefront,” Feuz says. “That’s why we were doing this. We wanted them to receive the best care possible and to receive it in a timely way.”

It is important to recognize that growth continues across both patient volumes and in terms of complexity of the patients the Verspeeten sees. Planning for additional capacity remains a critical component of the cancer centre's strategy.

Today, the Radiation Therapy team continues to monitor trends, review indicators regularly, and escalate concerns before they become larger issues.

RESET has demonstrated that sustainable improvement comes not from any single metric or intervention, but from a shared commitment to keeping patients moving through their care journey and ensuring timely access to treatment when it matters most.

"While the data shows improvement in access times, the true success of RESET can be measured in the experience of patients”, Feuz shares. "By identifying issues earlier, responding to trends proactively, and working together across the entire radiation therapy pathway, the team has helped ensure more patients receive the care they need, when they need it. And that remains the goal moving forward."

stories.title: Replica firearms seized
stories.summary: London, ON (October 26, 2026) – Two suspects were arrested within minutes of a 9-1-1 call early Sunday morning after a witness reported a dispute in the south end of the city.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 26, 2026) – Two suspects were arrested within minutes of a 9-1-1 call early Sunday morning after a witness reported a dispute in the south end of the city.

At approximately 4:10 a.m., ON October 25, 2026, two males attended an address near Chiddington Avenue and Chiddington Gate and began to argue with a resident, prompting a witness to call police.

Additional information was received that the suspect males were in possession of firearms.

Officers responded, located, and arrested both suspects.

There were no reported injuries.

During a search incident to arrest, officers located two replica firearms.

As a result of the investigation, Hamza Al Said, 18, of Ottawa has been charged with the following offences:

Carry concealed weapon; and

Utter threats.

Mohamad Al Saleh, 21, of Ottawa, has been charged with the following offences:

Utter threats; and

Breach of recognizance.

Both accused have since been released and are expected to appear in London court on November 26, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Veteran mayors fall across province amid winds of change
stories.summary: Hamilton's Andrea Horwarth trails in early results as peers in Milton, Niagara Falls and beyond are defeated.
stories.author: Rob Ferguson; Robert Benzie
stories.content:
The winds of change swept away prominent mayors across Ontario on Monday night, including Hamilton’s Andrea Horwath and Drew Dilkens in Windsor.

Other incumbents — some of them veterans with decades in office — were turfed in Milton, Waterloo, Niagara Falls, Fort Erie and Sarnia.

Horwath, the former Ontario NDP leader and one-term mayor, was trounced. She finished a distant third behind winner Keanin Loomis and runner-up Rob Cooper, a city councillor.

It was a comeback for Loomis, a former head of the Hamilton chamber of commerce, who narrowly lost to Horwath in 2022.

Hamilton mayoral hopeful Keanin Loomis was leading in early results Monday.

“We didn’t quit, we didn’t walk away, we stayed, we listened,” he told supporters. “It’s a true Hamilton story.”

In Windsor, Mayor Drew Dilkens lost his bid for a fourth term — which he said upon entering the race in August would be his last in the border city, where auto and other manufacturing industries have been hit by the Trump tariffs.

The new mayor is Fred Francis, a city councillor who had criticized Dilkens for failing to revive Windsor’s flagging downtown after being in power since 2014. With all 85 polls reporting, Francis had 47.6 per cent support and Dilkens 33.8 per cent.

“If you can’t get the job done in 12 years, four more years won’t make a difference,” Francis, the younger brother of former mayor Eddie Francis, said during the campaign.

In Milton, Gord Krantz, 89, who was the longest serving mayor in Canada, having been chief magistrate since 1980, fell to challenger George Minakakis, the chair of Milton Hydro.

Minakakis’s campaign message was that fast-growing Milton is “a very different town from what it was 20 or 30 years ago.”

Niagara Falls Mayor Jim Diodati, who endorsed Premier Doug Ford in last year’s Ontario election, failed in his bid for a fifth term and fell to city Councillor Lori Lococo, who campaigned on the need for accountability and change.

As polls closed — and before the defeat of so many veteran mayors who were his allies — Ford insisted his “government is ready to work with everyone who is elected tonight on the issues that matter most to Ontario families.”

Fort Erie Mayor Wayne Redekop, who had been in office since 2014, fell to Niagara Regional Councillor Tom Insinna.

Mayor Mike Bradley of Sarnia, who held the post since 1988, had his 11-term winning streak broken by Carrie McEachran, who has been the CEO of the Sarnia-Lambton Chamber of Commerce.

Waterloo’s first-term Mayor Dorothy McCabe was another incumbent who went down to defeat. Challenger Shannon Weber, who lost to McCabe by just 331 votes in 2022, had 52.1 per cent of the vote to 29.6 per cent for McCabe with 45 of 55 polls reporting.

Next door, Kitchener Mayor Berry Vrbanovic romped to victory with 56.6 per cent of the vote to Cindy Ward’s 15.1 per cent with 40 of 44 polls reporting.

In Ottawa, first-term Mayor Mark Sutcliffe, a former talk radio host and Ford favourite, fended off a spirited challenge from progressive three-term Councillor Jeff Leiper. With all polls reporting, Sutcliffe had 44.7 per cent of the vote to Leiper’s 33.9 per cent.

In London, Mayor Josh Morgan was on track to become the first chief magistrate of the Forest City to win a second term in 16 years. With 160 of 200 polls reporting, he had 45 per cent support compared to his main challenger Susan Stevenson at almost 26.5 per cent.

First-term Barrie Mayor Alex Nuttall coasted to an easy victory, winning 66.6 per cent of the vote to 25.3 per cent for challenger Tanya Saari.

stories.title: Doerkson says he’ll prioritize B.C.’s finances, work toward West Coast pipeline as next premier
stories.summary: BC Conservative Leader won a large majority government in a snap election called two years early by Ndp’s Eby
stories.author: Jesse Winter, Ian Bailey
stories.content:
British Columbia ’s next premier, a former rodeo rider and newspaper publisher who many people hadn’t heard of five weeks ago, says his first priorities will be taking an in-depth look at the province’s deeply indebted finances, and working with Alberta and Prime Minister Mark Carney to jump-start the planned oil pipeline to the West Coast.

BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson won a large majority government Saturday in a snap election called two years early by NDP Leader David Eby.

“British Columbians voted for change last night and for whatever reason, they liked the platform that we put forward,” Mr. Doerkson said at a news conference Sunday. “I intend to get to work right away.”

The loss has the BC NDP bitterly regretting the high-stakes gamble of calling the election, the timing of which appeared aimed at taking advantage of the disarray in the Conservative caucus. The Conservatives had elected a deeply unpopular leader in the spring, but she resigned two days before Mr. Eby made the election call.

Mr. Doerkson was named interim leader and was soon thrown into a campaign, uniting a fractious caucus behind him.

NDP MLA and cabinet minister Adrian Dix, who was re-elected, called Saturday’s result one of the most disappointing nights in the modern history of the BC NDP. After nine years of government under the leadership of John Horgan and Mr. Eby, the party is heading into opposition.

“Clearly, given the results, it was a mistake to call the election,” Mr. Dix told reporters after the results came in.

Mike Farnworth, who has served as B.C. transportation minister and was also narrowly re-elected, agreed calling the snap election was a bad idea.

“In hindsight, I don’t think it’s rocket science to say we probably shouldn’t have,” he said in an interview Sunday.

He said the caucus and the party will have to take time to reflect on the outcome and what comes next.

Mr. Eby resigned as party leader in a somber speech Saturday night, accepting responsibility for the outcome of the vote. He said he would continue to represent his riding.

“This is obviously something I do with a very heavy heart,” he said to supporters at his party’s gathering in Vancouver. “But it is time for new leadership within our party.”

The results with 99 per cent of the polls reporting showed 64 Conservatives elected, 27 for the NDP and two for the Greens. The NDP lost 20 seats compared to the party’s result in the last election in 2024.

At his news conference Sunday, Mr. Doerkson listed some of his first priorities.

He said briefings with the public service will begin in coming days with “some urgency” so the government will be able to swiftly advance its agenda once it’s sworn in.

He said after being sworn in, he would immediately launch an independent review of the province’s finances, citing the record-high $14-billion deficit and the need to find a way to bring it to balance eventually.

Other initiatives include an expert commission on hospital emergency rooms and wait times, as well as a tax break aimed at returning $1,000 to every British Columbian.

He said he hopes to engage with Mr. Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith to get the Pacific Link pipeline, between Alberta and B.C., moving.

Without being specific, Mr. Doerkson said he has been “thrilled” about recent announcements by the Prime Minister. “We’ll work very closely with him, and of course, our neighbours.”

Mr. Doerkson said Sunday that he hopes to use a session of the B.C. legislature next spring to repeal an Indigenous rights law passed unanimously by the legislature in 2019, the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, or Dripa. Critics worry the province is at risk of many lawsuits if Indigenous groups believe the province’s laws are not in alignment with Dripa.

“I am still committed to the repeal of Dripa. It has not worked in this province, and, frankly, it has caused more problems to date than, I think, potentially anything else,” he said.

The premier-designate said he looks forward to working with First Nations communities in the province, noting that he has received complimentary messages from some of those communities.

He said he had not ruled out holding a session of the legislature this fall.

Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney said Mr. Doerkson’s win offers lessons that other Conservatives should take to heart.

“Yet another reminder to Conservative parties: ignore the crazy fringe of the hard populist right. Don’t let the tail wag the dog. Let them stay in their little fringe parties,” Mr. Kenney posted on social media Saturday night.

“Instead, propose bold, thoughtful policy reforms rooted in conservative principles that appeal to the broad mainstream,” Mr. Kenney wrote.

Manitoba NDP Premier Wab Kinew said the B.C. results should be a warning for other politicians and consultants looking to eke out tactical advantages without considering voters themselves.

Politics is not a game, he said.

“It is a serious responsibly that isn’t to be played with. There’s no partisanship in these comments, it’s all about reminding people that we have a serious obligation to take our democracy and our duties with the utmost of care.”

Voter turnout appears to have played a significant role in Saturday night’s outcome.

Elections B.C. reported Sunday afternoon only 48 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot, a record low.

While the Conservatives took nearly half of all the votes cast, they netted fewer actual votes than in the 2024 election, as did the NDP.

paragraphs: British Columbia ’s next premier, a former rodeo rider and newspaper publisher who many people hadn’t heard of five weeks ago, says his first priorities will be taking an in-depth look at the province’s deeply indebted finances, and working with Alberta and Prime Minister Mark Carney to jump-start the planned oil pipeline to the West Coast.
BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson won a large majority government Saturday in a snap election called two years early by NDP Leader David Eby.

“British Columbians voted for change last night and for whatever reason, they liked the platform that we put forward,” Mr. Doerkson said at a news conference Sunday. “I intend to get to work right away.”

The loss has the BC NDP bitterly regretting the high-stakes gamble of calling the election, the timing of which appeared aimed at taking advantage of the disarray in the Conservative caucus. The Conservatives had elected a deeply unpopular leader in the spring, but she resigned two days before Mr. Eby made the election call.
Mr. Doerkson was named interim leader and was soon thrown into a campaign, uniting a fractious caucus behind him.

NDP MLA and cabinet minister Adrian Dix, who was re-elected, called Saturday’s result one of the most disappointing nights in the modern history of the BC NDP. After nine years of government under the leadership of John Horgan and Mr. Eby, the party is heading into opposition.
“Clearly, given the results, it was a mistake to call the election,” Mr. Dix told reporters after the results came in.
Mike Farnworth, who has served as B.C. transportation minister and was also narrowly re-elected, agreed calling the snap election was a bad idea.
“In hindsight, I don’t think it’s rocket science to say we probably shouldn’t have,” he said in an interview Sunday.
He said the caucus and the party will have to take time to reflect on the outcome and what comes next.
Mr. Eby resigned as party leader in a somber speech Saturday night, accepting responsibility for the outcome of the vote. He said he would continue to represent his riding.
“This is obviously something I do with a very heavy heart,” he said to supporters at his party’s gathering in Vancouver. “But it is time for new leadership within our party.”

The results with 99 per cent of the polls reporting showed 64 Conservatives elected, 27 for the NDP and two for the Greens. The NDP lost 20 seats compared to the party’s result in the last election in 2024.
At his news conference Sunday, Mr. Doerkson listed some of his first priorities.
He said briefings with the public service will begin in coming days with “some urgency” so the government will be able to swiftly advance its agenda once it’s sworn in.

He said after being sworn in, he would immediately launch an independent review of the province’s finances, citing the record-high $14-billion deficit and the need to find a way to bring it to balance eventually.
Other initiatives include an expert commission on hospital emergency rooms and wait times, as well as a tax break aimed at returning $1,000 to every British Columbian.
He said he hopes to engage with Mr. Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith to get the Pacific Link pipeline, between Alberta and B.C., moving.
Without being specific, Mr. Doerkson said he has been “thrilled” about recent announcements by the Prime Minister. “We’ll work very closely with him, and of course, our neighbours.”

Mr. Doerkson said Sunday that he hopes to use a session of the B.C. legislature next spring to repeal an Indigenous rights law passed unanimously by the legislature in 2019, the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, or Dripa. Critics worry the province is at risk of many lawsuits if Indigenous groups believe the province’s laws are not in alignment with Dripa.
“I am still committed to the repeal of Dripa. It has not worked in this province, and, frankly, it has caused more problems to date than, I think, potentially anything else,” he said.
The premier-designate said he looks forward to working with First Nations communities in the province, noting that he has received complimentary messages from some of those communities.
He said he had not ruled out holding a session of the legislature this fall.
Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney said Mr. Doerkson’s win offers lessons that other Conservatives should take to heart.

“Yet another reminder to Conservative parties: ignore the crazy fringe of the hard populist right. Don’t let the tail wag the dog. Let them stay in their little fringe parties,” Mr. Kenney posted on social media Saturday night.
“Instead, propose bold, thoughtful policy reforms rooted in conservative principles that appeal to the broad mainstream,” Mr. Kenney wrote.
Manitoba NDP Premier Wab Kinew said the B.C. results should be a warning for other politicians and consultants looking to eke out tactical advantages without considering voters themselves.
Politics is not a game, he said.

“It is a serious responsibly that isn’t to be played with. There’s no partisanship in these comments, it’s all about reminding people that we have a serious obligation to take our democracy and our duties with the utmost of care.”

stories.title: B.C. election turnout slumps to new low as fewer than half of voters cast ballot
stories.summary: Voters did not seem persuaded that a snap election was necessary, despite Eby’s efforts to make it about winning a new mandate
stories.author: Joe Friesen
stories.content:
Voter turnout in B.C. hit a new low in Saturday’s provincial election as fewer than half of registered voters cast a ballot, an indication, observers say, that many voters rejected the rationale for the snap vote.

According to preliminary results from Elections BC, about 48 per cent of voters cast a ballot, which would be the lowest level recorded going back as far as 1928. In 2024, voter turnout was about 58.5 per cent, and in 2020, it was about 53.9 per cent.

The stunning electoral turnaround that saw the Conservatives, led by interim party leader and now premier-designate Lorne Doerkson, sweep the incumbent NDP government from office was a remarkable rebuke for outgoing Premier David Eby.

With two years left in his mandate and with an opposition party that was without a permanent leader and in disarray, Mr. Eby called the vote on Sept. 22 with his party leading in the polls. Voters, however, did not seem persuaded that an election was necessary, despite Mr. Eby’s efforts to make it about winning a new mandate to tackle the U.S. trade war.

On Saturday, they punished the government, electing a sizable Conservative majority and ending a nine-year run in charge for the NDP that began in 2017 under premier John Horgan, who died in 2024.

Geoff Meggs, who was chief of staff to Mr. Horgan, said it appears that many of the party’s voters simply stayed home.

“Dave Eby’s campaign angered them. They were never persuaded by his arguments in favour of an election,” Mr. Meggs said.

He said in some ways it’s not surprising that the party’s support took a hit. The NDP campaign, when it eventually pivoted away from the trade argument for the election, proposed complex policies focused on affordability, such as one to regulate grocery prices, that didn’t capture the imagination of voters.

And while Mr. Eby raised fears about what the Conservatives would do if they won power, he didn’t clearly underline what his government had accomplished, according to some political observers.

“He didn’t campaign on the very real achievements of the NDP over the years since 2017 and proposed things that didn’t resonate with British Columbians,” Mr. Meggs said.

The NDP received about 274,000 fewer votes than in the previous election, while the Conservatives got about 49,000 fewer. The Green Party increased its tally by about 23,000.

The low turnout for the provincial election is in contrast with relatively strong turnout during the recent municipal elections. In Vancouver, municipal voter turnout was up seven percentage points for the Oct. 17 vote at 43.4 per cent, compared with 36.3 per cent in 2022. Across the province, municipal-election turnout was 32.8 per cent, according to the Union of B.C. Municipalities, up by about three percentage points from four years ago.

Allan Tupper, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of British Columbia, said the timing of the two elections, just one week apart, was odd and May have had an impact on how many votes were cast. With two sets of signs on local lawns and campaigns competing for often overlapping pools of volunteers, citizens May have experienced some election fatigue.

“It just seemed there was no energy for this thing,” Prof. Tupper said. “I think Eby didn’t size it up right. The opposition organized itself very quickly.”

In the Quebec provincial election of Oct. 5, turnout was a relatively high 67 per cent, while the Alberta referendum of Oct. 19, which asked whether to hold a vote on separation, had preliminary turnout of more than 62 per cent.

Duff Conacher, co-founder of Democracy Watch, a non-profit that works on democratic reform, said studies show that voter turnout is high when voters believe something important is at stake, when the leaders appear viable and competent and the race appears close.

Turnout was above 70 per cent in B.C. in all the elections held from 1983 to 2001 and hasn’t been higher than about 62 per cent since.

Mr. Conacher said it’s a worrying sign that voter participation appears to have dipped below 50 per cent this time, but it’s not surprising given recent trends.

stories.title: London man charged in hate-motivated incident involving swastika symbol
stories.summary: A 56-year-old London man is facing a charge following an investigation into a hate-motivated incident in the city’s downtown.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A 56-year-old London man is facing a charge following an investigation into a hate-motivated incident in the city’s downtown.

London police say Gordon Botaitis was charged with one count of offence motivated by hatred after a symbol resembling a swastika was created in a gravel parking lot in the 0-100 block of St. George Street.

Police were made aware of the incident on Oct. 22. They say a man completing construction work at the property used equipment believed to be a pressure washer to create the symbol.

Nearby residents captured video and photographs of the incident and provided them to police. The property owner was notified and removed the symbol.

On Oct. 23, police identified and arrested the suspect. The investigation was reassigned to the London Police Service Hate Crime Unit, which determined the incident was motivated by hatred.

Botaitis was released from custody and is expected to appear in London court on Jan. 18, 2027.

stories.title: Shuffling of U.S. tariffs will offer little relief to Canada, experts say
stories.summary: Along with lifting some tariffs and adding others, Trump administration has said trade negotiations with Canada are ‘gathering steam’
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
The shifting front line in the U.S-Canada trade war will lessen the economic pain in border states while still targeting Canadian manufacturing capacity, experts say.

The lifting of 50-per-cent tariffs on 22 categories of goods by the United States and the addition of 100 new categories will have a roughly equivalent impact in terms of dollars – about $2.5-billion in goods were exempted with about $2.6-billion newly targeted – but will also shift some of the focus away from products U.S. businesses need for their own operations.

Senator Susan Collins of Maine has taken credit for lifting the tariffs on some packaging products, which she said had impacted Maine businesses such as apple and blueberry growers.

Alongside its tariff adjustments, the Trump administration has also said that it’s nearing a trade deal with Canada. Kevin Hassett, the top economic adviser in the White House, told Fox News on Sunday that negotiations are “gathering steam” and that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been speaking with Canadian officials “all week.”

According to Wolfgang Alschner, a law professor with a specialty in business and trade at the University of Ottawa, there are lots of examples of integrated cross-border supply chains where tariffs hurt U.S. businesses and consumers as much or more than they strike at Canada.

“With tighter North American integration, it made total sense for states like Maine to trade with Quebec for supplies for local industries. Now of course with the border being a harder border you really have to re-evaluate those relationships,” Mr. Alschner said.

He said some of the new tariffs are on finished retail products such as shampoo, which won’t have a strong localized impact in any particular geographic market – such as a border state with a tense and close Senate election battle raging.

“I think that makes perfect sense from a defensive point of view. You ideally want to spread out the pain,” Mr. Alschner said.

Some other new tariffs could turn up the pain on specific industries in Canada.

One example is in the hardwood flooring market, where U.S. tariffs against China and Vietnam have caused those countries to shift exports to more open nations such as Canada.

According to William Pellerin, partner with law firm McMillan LLP and co-leader of its international trade group, even before the new tariffs on Canadian hardwood, his group of eight flooring manufacturing clients based mainly in Quebec and Ontario were struggling to compete domestically against imports.

“[China and Vietnam] totally flooded the market at prices that are ludicrously low. The Canadian producers have been able to survive by selling products to the U.S.,” Mr. Pellerin said.

Many of the companies are benefiting from federal work-share programs to keep the lights on. “A lot of the companies had layoffs, a number are on work-share, with workers on maybe three days a week,” he said.

But in the longer term, Mr. Pellerin said restricting imports of overseas hardwood May be the only path forward.

Kyle Peacock, principal at Peacock Tariff Consulting, said he has identified another pattern in the types of industries that are being targeted: U.S. companies with Canadian manufacturing sites that could see production shifted back to America.

“We had that on lip balm,” Mr. Peacock said. Since the first round of tariffs, he said five of seven Canadian sites making the wax or other parts of lip balm have either stopped shipping to the U.S. or are planning to relocate. In New Brunswick, social media darling Eclair Lips announced in October it would no longer make its lip balm in Canada, moving production to Vermont.

But even trade relief doesn’t necessarily change the case for manufacturers “re-shoring” operations back to the U.S.

A week ago, Polyethics Industries in Orillia, Ont., announced 118 layoffs, which Mr. Peacock said is part of the company shifting capacity to its factory in Antwerp, Ohio. The company makes polyethylene plastic products such as garbage bags that are now subject to tariff relief, but while Mr. Peacock has consulted with them, he still expects the company to move the remaining production to the U.S. in the coming weeks.

According to him, the company faced other rising costs, such as soaring diesel prices and transportation costs thanks in part to the U.S. war with Iran. Tariff relief won’t be enough to move the needle.

“That’s one piece of a very big pie that’s making us move,” Mr. Peacock said he was told.

stories.title: B.C.'s premier designate plans to speak with Whitecaps about future in Vancouver
stories.summary: Vancouver - British Columbia's premier designate says he doesn't know what the plan is to keep the Whitecaps in Vancouver.
stories.author: Gemma Karstens-Smith The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - British Columbia’s premier designate says he doesn’t know what the plan is to keep the Whitecaps in Vancouver.

Lorne Doerkson spoke to media Sunday, hours after his B.C. Conservatives were elected in about two-thirds of the province’s 93 ridings.

“I love the Whitecaps and there’s a great amount of support for them here,” said the party’s interim leader. “But I’ll be straight up with you — I don’t know the plan going forward.

“But I do want to have a conversation with the Whitecaps because — trust me when I say this — British Columbia loves the Whitecaps.”

The team has been for sale since December 2024 and the current ownership group has repeatedly said they want it to stay in Vancouver.

Both the Whitecaps and Major League Soccer have said the team’s ability to generate revenue is limited, in part because it does not own its home stadium and that has made it difficult to attract buyers willing to keep the ‘Caps in the city.

The 55,000-seat venue is owned and operated by PavCo, a provincial Crown corporation.

Whitecaps sporting director and CEO Axel Schuster said last month the club had reached an agreement to extend its lease at BC Place through the 2027 “sprint season.”

The condensed campaign will run from February through May, with each of the league’s 30 teams playing a 14-game regular season before the single-elimination playoffs.

MLS will then move to a summer-to-spring calendar, starting in July 2027.

What happens to the Whitecaps after the sprint season remains unclear, Schuster said.

“People should know we’re here, we’re staying in the sprint season,” he said. “So the club is not going yet, and nothing is happening yet. … And the only way you can show us your support and help is buying tickets and come to the games.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Olivia Chow, Brad Bradford battle to the wire in Toronto’s mayoral election
stories.summary: As voters head to the polls Monday, Chow is at risk of becoming first incumbent to lose since the city amalgamated in 1998
stories.author: Jeff Gray
stories.content:
A hard-fought race to lead Toronto between incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow and her leading challenger, east-end city councillor Brad Bradford, comes to an end on Monday, as Torontonians vote in a municipal election that recently published opinion surveys have suggested is too close to call.

If Mr. Bradford – a former city planner who has sat on council since 2018 and only took 1.28 per cent of the vote in his first bid for mayor three years ago – were to win, Ms. Chow would become the first incumbent in the mayor’s chair to lose since the current city was created by amalgamation in 1998.

Pollster David Valentin of Liaison Strategies, who has been tracking the race closely, says whether Mr. Bradford can put it over the top will depend on turnout, and particularly on whether downtown residents show up. Those in many areas of the city’s centre, he says, have been more likely to vote in recent years – and are more likely to support Ms. Chow.

Mr. Valentin says the result could hinge on whether the Bradford campaign’s door knockers can outpace the NDP-backed Ms. Chow’s traditionally strong get-out-the-vote operation.

“For me, the question really is, does he have the machine? Does he have the people power to get this done?” Mr. Valentin said.

The rest of Ontario’s municipalities are also going to the polls on Monday, with several races some observers believe could be tight battles for incumbents.

In Mississauga, former mayor and former provincial Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie is among the candidates gunning for her old job, facing off with current Mayor Carolyn Parrish. Local councillor Alvin Tedjo is also running in what has been a bitterly contested race.

In Hamilton, Mayor Andrea Horwath, a former Ontario NDP leader, faces a battle against a field of candidates that includes local business advocate Keanin Loomis, whom she beat only narrowly in 2022, and councillor Rob Cooper.

Ms. Chow, 69 – a former MP and councillor, long-time NDP stalwart and widow of former party leader Jack Layton – rode into Toronto’s city hall three years ago on her trademark flower-festooned bike, after narrowly winning a by-election prompted by the sudden resignation of mayor John Tory over an affair with a staffer.

Facing an inherited $1.8-billion budget hole blamed partly on the aftermath of COVID-19, she brought in two large property-tax hikes in a row (after promising “modest” increases) and signed an unprecedented multibillion-dollar financial deal with Premier Doug Ford, which included $1.2-billion in operating cash over three years and the transfer of the expensive Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway to the province. The moves were among the reasons the city won a credit-rating upgrade to AA-plus from S&P Global Ratings.

In her campaign, she has pledged to reduce fares for frequent transit riders and provide free school lunches, while keeping future property-tax hikes “in and around” the rate of inflation. But she has faced flak for muting her criticism of Mr. Ford’s controversial plans for the province’s waterfront Ontario Place site. And while the city has cleared many of the homeless encampments in its parks on her watch, many in Toronto still complain about the number of drug users or mentally ill people on the streets and in the transit system.

The 40-year-old Mr. Bradford, who worked to appeal to conservatives and suburbanites despite having been a city planner in favour of bike lanes, has repeatedly charged the city was “stuck” under Ms. Chow’s status quo. He vows to freeze property taxes, commission an external “line-by-line” review of spending and eliminate the city’s land-transfer tax on sales of homes under $1.1-million. The tax has been a key revenue source for the perennially cash-strapped municipality since it was introduced 20 years ago.

He also pledged to hire 1,000 additional police officers, capitalizing on widespread fears of disorder and crime – fears that persist despite low overall crime rates. Last September, he appeared on the cover of the tabloid Toronto Sun, posing with the softball bat he said he keeps in his bedroom to protect his family from home invaders.

Ms. Chow has charged that Mr. Bradford’s cost-cutting plans would mean shutting libraries and raising transit fares, which he denies. She also told viewers of Thursday’s final televised debate that Mr. Bradford’s tax freeze would still leave the city’s annual 1.5-per-cent building levy untouched.

In recent weeks, the two campaigns have clashed as Ms. Chow and high-profile allies, including environmentalist David Suzuki and former mayor David Miller, have charged that Mr. Bradford’s promise to hive off the Toronto Water department into a separate, publicly owned company is a step toward privatization.

Mr. Bradford says his plan would allow Toronto to finance new water pipes with debt instead of higher rates, cutting water bills by 25 per cent – and vows that the new entity would remain publicly owned under the new provincial law that allows the change. In last week’s debate, Mr. Bradford told Ms. Chow the criticism was “misinformation” and “scare tactics.”

Looming over the campaign was the shadow of Mr. Ford, who has often intervened in Toronto affairs and is a former city councillor and the brother of the late mayor Rob Ford.

The Premier, whose bid to override Ms. Chow’s objections and allow jets at the city’s waterfront island airport was blocked by Ottawa this summer , has in recent days carried out his threat to unilaterally rip out a stretch of the city’s west-end bike lanes. Mr. Bradford, who now agrees with the removal of those lanes despite previously supporting their installation, accuses Ms. Chow of failing to stand up to Mr. Ford.

Despite Mr. Bradford’s conservative thrust and the presence of former Ford aides on his campaign, the Premier all but endorsed Ms. Chow in September, in remarks his office later tried to recant, saying the Premier was not endorsing anyone. Before she was elected, he had warned she would be “unmitigated disaster” but he has since then frequently sung her praises.

Meanwhile, in several of Toronto’s 25 wards, there are races that are expected to be competitive, including in some where incumbents have stepped down, throwing the composition of the next council into question. In addition to Mr. Bradford’s former seat in Beaches-East York, there are open races in Toronto-Danforth, University-Rosedale and Parkdale-High Park.

stories.title: U.K. won’t join Canada-led defence bank, but pledges cooperation
stories.summary: The two countries will "work in close partnership" on investment opportunities and challenges, according to a joint media statement.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
The British government has turned down Ottawa’s attempts to have it join the international Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, though London says it will work in lockstep with Canada to meet Nato spending targets.

The Dsrb is meant to reduce borrowing costs for military spending by pooling credit strength among allies.

Canada has tried for months to convince the U.K. to join the project, but London has instead been pursuing its own program called the Multilateral Defence Mechanism.

Both countries agreed Sunday to craft a framework for cooperation between both banks, “having mutually concluded that it is best to develop two distinct but complementary institutions.”

The two will “work in close partnership” on investment opportunities and challenges, according to a joint media statement.

The Dsrb will be based in Canada and has the support of countries such as Belgium, Turkey and Ukraine.

content_blocks.text: Ottawa — The British government has turned down Ottawa’s attempts to have it join the international Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, though London says it will work in lockstep with Canada to meet Nato spending targets.
The Dsrb is meant to reduce borrowing costs for military spending by pooling credit strength among allies.
Canada has tried for months to convince the U.K. to join the project, but London has instead been pursuing its own program called the Multilateral Defence Mechanism.
Both countries agreed Sunday to craft a framework for cooperation between both banks, “having mutually concluded that it is best to develop two distinct but complementary institutions.”
The two will “work in close partnership” on investment opportunities and challenges, according to a joint media statement.
The Dsrb will be based in Canada and has the support of countries such as Belgium, Turkey and Ukraine.
