stories.title: Lorne Doerkson leads B.C. Conservatives to power with thumping two-thirds majority
stories.summary: Vancouver - British Columbia has turned blue, electing a B.C. Conservative government with an overwhelming two-thirds majority.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
flag wire: true flag sponsored: false article_type: pubinfo.section: cms.site.custom.site_domain : thestar.com sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/toronto_star bHasMigratedAvatar : false firstAuthor.avatar :

By Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press

Vancouver - British Columbia’s premier-designate Lorne Doerkson’s long to-do list includes lowering taxes, while reviewing the provincial finances, working with Alberta and the federal government on the proposed Pacific Link pipeline and repealing Indigenous legislation.

Doerkson laid out his priorities at a news conference Sunday, just hours after his party was elected with about two-thirds of the province’s 93 seats in the legislature.

He said he has spoken to the lieutenant-governor and named Kim Henderson, a former deputy to the premier to previous Liberal governments, to lead his transition team.

“We are going to do this properly, and we are going to do it with obviously some urgency,” he said. “When this government is sworn in, it will be ready on Day 1, and it will hit the ground running.”

Doerkson did not rule out calling a fall legislative session, and if it were to return this year, his government would move to lower taxes.

“Our first priority for the legislature is raising the basic personal exemption to $32,000,” he said. “That is about $1,000 a year back in the pocket of nearly every working British Columbian.”

His government, he said, will also follow through on the election promise to not raise taxes or introduce new ones.

“When I make a promise to British Columbians, I will keep it, and that starts for sure right now.”

The incoming premier said his government will also launch an independent review of the provincial finances.

Current forecasts peg the provincial deficit of $14 billion and B.C. has had eight credit-rating downgrades in three years.

Provincial debt has become a significant challenge, Doerkson said.

“Our interest payment is choking our economy and choking British Columbia,” he said.

The trade conflict with the United States is the biggest economic threat facing the province, he said, and he repeated promises to supercharge the provincial economy through additional resource-projects.

“Among my first calls as premier, will be to the prime minister and to (Alberta) Premier Smith to get the Pacific Link (pipeline project) moving,” he said. “Our resources are the strongest hand that British Columbia hold and we will for sure play them.”

Hamish Telford, associate professor of political science at the University of the Fraser Valley, said Doerkson’s plan to “supercharge” the economy is outside of his control.

He said private companies — not Doerkson — are making the investment decisions.

“They are going to do that based on market demand, and the price that they can offer consumers in other parts of the world,” he said.

Doerkson said that he is still committed to the repeal of the Declaration on the Rights of the Indigenous Peoples Act.

Dripa is “a thick piece of legislation,” that his government wants to repeal as quickly as possible because it has not worked, he said.

“Frankly, it has caused more problems to date than I think potentially anything else,” he said, noting it could be repealed in the spring session.

But Telford said Doerkson’s economic agenda hinges in part on securing Indigenous support for those projects.

“And if he repeals Dripa, he is going to set his government off to a very bad start with First Nations across British Columbia, who are almost universally in favour of maintaining Dripa,” he said.

Doerkson promised a government of respect for all, while speaking directly to his party’s base in rural and northern B.C.

“I know what it means when the mill closes, when the (emergency-room) shuts at night and when there’s fire on the ridge,” he said. “Under this government, you will never be an afterthought.”

He promised that he would use his first 100 days in office to set up an expert commission to keep hospital emergency rooms open and cut down wait times.

Elections BC said Sunday that the Conservatives won 64 seats but results for four of them were extremely close.

In Burnaby South-Metrotown, 66 votes divide the winning New Democrat Paul Choi from the Conservative candidate and there were 58 rejected ballots.

Three ridings that went to the Conservatives; Kelowna Centre, Cowichan Valley and Ladysmith-Oceanside, were all within fewer than 150 votes.

Elections BC says that under the Elections Act, a recount is automatic if the preliminary results show a difference of 100 votes or fewer.

The Conservative’s resounding win even drew the attention of the White House, with U.S. President Donald Trump posting on his social media account that the Conservative Party has won in British Columbia for the first time in almost 100 years.

The post is accompanied by a composite of photos of Trump, Prime Minister Mark Carney, the B.C. legislature and a map of Canada with the province coloured in red.

Doerkson rejected any implications of being aligned with Trump.

“I’m an ally to British Columbia, and we should have taken the opportunity years ago to protect ourselves against these attacks,” he said.

A statement from the B.C. Conservatives released Sunday says Henderson will be chair of the transition team on a volunteer basis and will be taking an unpaid leave from the pipeline firm Trans Mountain Corp. where she took on the post of interim vice-president a year ago.

She spent more than a decade serving the previous Liberal governments of Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell as deputy minister, cabinet secretary and head of the B.C. public service.

Outgoing Premier David Eby announced his resignation as NDP leader, although he won his seat in Vancouver-Point Grey on Saturday.

Manitoba Premier Web Kinew didn’t mention Eby by name, but told reporters in Ottawa Sunday that the election results should be a lesson learned.

“There’s no partisanship in these comments,” Kinew said. “It’s all about reminding people that we have a serious obligation to take our democracy and our duties with the utmost of care.”

Doerkson said he has always started his work the moment after being elected.

“And for me, that isn’t going to change,” he said. “I intend to get to work right away. I intend work for British Columbia hard, because four years come quick.”

Eby’s decision to call a snap election two years early will go down as one of the most disastrous miscalculations in Canadian political history.

The NDP has been reduced to about 27 ridings and the Greens won two, with Leader Emily Lowan securing a seat on Vancouver Island.

Preliminary results show the popular vote went to the Conservatives with about 48 per cent of the vote, while the NDP won about 37 per cent and the Greens 11 per cent.

Doerkson emerged from obscurity when he was named interim leader of the Conservatives just two days before Eby’s fateful election call on Sept. 22.

Voter turnout figures show about 1.8 million cast ballots, representing about 48 per cent of registered voters.

A statement from the office of the clerk of the legislative assembly said Sunday that oath ceremonies for those elected won’t take place until the certified results of the general election are available, which is expected on Nov. 18.

“Arrangements will be made with the three caucuses for oath ceremonies to proceed after that date,” the statement said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week
stories.summary: Canada
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week:

Corporate earnings

Some of corporate Canada’s biggest names will report their results this week. Celestica Inc. is set to report results on Monday, followed by Precision Drilling Corp. on Tuesday. Agnico Eagle Mines Ltd. and Canadian Pacific Kansas City Ltd. are set to report on Wednesday. Restaurant Brands International Inc., Teck Resources Ltd., Spin Master Corp., Air Canada and TMX Group Ltd. are scheduled for Thursday. The week ends with Cameco Corp., Canadian National Railway Co., Imperial Oil Ltd. and Magna International Inc. on Friday.

Interest rate announcement

The Bank of Canada will release its interest rate decision and fall monetary policy report on Wednesday. Financial markets are betting there is a good chance the central bank will raise its key interest rate target from its current level of 2.25 per cent where it has been set since October last year.

Canada-EU summit

Canada will host a Canada-EU Summit in Montreal starting on Thursday. Prime Minister Mark Carney has been working on establishing closer links with Europe, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed Canada could become the first associate member of the European Union.

Statistics Canada will offer its latest reading of the overall economy on Friday when it releases its gross domestic product by industry figures for August and its preliminary estimate for September. The figures will offer an early estimate of how the Canadian economy fared for the third quarter as a whole.

Weston speech

Galen Weston, chairman of Loblaw Cos. Ltd., and CEO of George Weston Ltd., will give a speech to the Canadian Club Toronto on Friday. Weston is expected to talk about the erosion of trust in the private sector and its role in Canadian prosperity.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Five takeaways from B.C.’s election
stories.summary: U.S.-Canada trade war didn’t help Ndp’s fortunes on Saturday, which saw Conservatives win a majority and Greens pick up some of the popular vote
stories.author: Jesse Winter, Ian Bailey
stories.content:
British Columbia voters elected a Conservative majority government on Saturday after a snap election called by the NDP backfired.

Here are five takeaways from the provincial election.

David Eby resigned as leader of the NDP after his party was badly defeated in an election that didn’t have to happen. Mr. Eby acknowledged his responsibility for the outcome of the election, which he called two years earlier than required. He lamented that many of his colleagues lost their seats, including seven cabinet ministers.

The standings, with 99.6 per cent of polls reporting, stood at 64 seats for the Conservatives, 27 for the NDP and two for the Greens. The results reduced the NDP by 20 seats.

“A number of my colleagues, some of the hardest-working MLAs I know for their communities, were not elected tonight. It breaks my heart, and I accept full responsibility for that outcome,” a crestfallen Mr. Eby said in his concession speech.

Lorne Doerkson managed to pull together a party win mere weeks after he was abruptly named interim Conservative leader, after Kerry-Lynne Findlay quit after just over three months of turmoil.

The B.C. Conservatives went into the race as an underdog. Even during the campaign, there was turbulence linked to comments from some candidates.

Much of the NDP campaign focused on attacking what Mr. Eby framed as the most controversial and “dangerous” candidates. But for some, those attacks didn’t seem to find their mark. Mr. Doerkson refused to drop Heather Maahs as a candidate, even after her anti-Lgbtq comments from a 2022 podcast resurfaced. Ms. Maahs won her seat Saturday night.

Mr. Eby’s Forests Minister Ravi Parmar called out David Williams, the incumbent MLA for Salmon Arm-Shuswap, over a Facebook post that showed much of B.C., the Yukon, Alberta and Saskatchewan as “The Republic of Western Canada” and a “protectorate” of the United States.

Mr. Williams was re-elected as well.

At the outset of the campaign, Mr. Eby tried to frame the election in existential terms, saying he needed a strong mandate from B.C. voters to protect the province from U.S. President Donald Trump and the ongoing trade war.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford used a similar justification when he called a snap election in 2025, saying he needed a mandate to respond to Trump’s economic threats.

Mr. Ford led his Progressive Conservatives to a third straight majority, but Mr. Eby arrived at election day with the B.C. Conservatives running ahead in public-opinion polling, and ultimately lost.

Fewer than half of eligible B.C. voters turned up at the polls. Saturday’s voter turnout of 48 per cent is the lowest since 1996, and six percentage points lower than the 54-per-cent turnout from 2020, an election that was held while the province – and the world – was still in the grip of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The last time B.C. voters went to the polls, when Mr. Eby secured a slim majority, turnout was 58.4 per cent. When former premier John Horgan lead the NDP to victory in 2017, turnout was 61 per cent.

Throughout the campaign, Mr. Doerkson made repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People Act a central plank of his platform, a promise roundly criticized by Indigenous leaders. The B.C. Assembly of First Nations was strongly opposed to the move, as was a powerful chief in Mr. Doerkson’s own riding .

While Mr. Doerkson didn’t mention Dripa by name in his victory speech, he did make several references to Indigenous people and their communities, saying the groups need to work together with the province to “supercharge” B.C.’s economy by cutting red tape.

“This future is one we will build together as partners with the certainty all of us need.”

He also invoked a fear in some Conservative circles that expanding reconciliation efforts might put private property rights in question.

“I also believe in the protection of private property rights,” Mr. Doerkson said, earning a loud cheer from his supporters, “and parks that are open to all British Columbians.”

The BC Greens increased their share of the popular vote, which May have hurt the NDP, particularly in close ridings.

In 2024, the Greens took 8.2 per cent of the popular vote. On Saturday night, the party led by Emily Lowan took 11 per cent.

“We did it,” Ms. Lowan said in an election-night speech that framed what she sees as a coming fight against the new government’s likely agenda.

“I am scared for what’s to come. The Conservative agenda is one of cuts to the programs that we rely on the most,” Ms. Lowan said. “It’s one of culture wars and needless attacks on human rights.”

At 26 years old, Ms. Lowan is among the youngest leaders of a political party with an elected member in Canadian history.

Despite her youth, she traded jabs with the more seasoned leaders of the NDP and Conservatives, men more than 20 years her senior. She won her seat of Saanich North and the Islands handily, with almost 50 per cent of the vote. Jeremy Valeriote also won his seat of West Vancouver-Sea to Sky for the Greens.

While the Greens only managed to keep their two existing seats, their share of the vote in some key ridings appeared to allow a Conservative candidate to take the win.

For example, the Saanich-South riding went to the Conservatives’ Cathie Ounsted with 10,549, or 39.2 per cent. Former journalist Richard Zussman, for the NDP, was close behind with 9,332, or 34.7 per cent. The Greens’ Lisa Lapointe took 6,985 for 25.9 per cent – well shy of the winner’s circle, but a large enough share to have split the vote on the left.

stories.title: Who is Lorne Doerkson, B.C.’s next premier?
stories.summary: The interim B.C. Conservative leader delivered a rollicking victory speech as he revelled in a sweeping majority win, secured in a snap provincial election.
stories.author: Darryl Greer
stories.content:
British Columbians got their best look so far at Lorne Doerkson on Saturday night, their premier-designate , and self-described “guy from Williams Lake.”

The interim B.C. Conservative leader delivered a rollicking victory speech as he revelled in a sweeping majority win, secured in a snap provincial election called by outgoing Premier David Eby in a disastrous political miscalculation.

Doerkson had emerged from obscurity to unify a fractured Opposition that was a political basket case just six weeks ago. The party had seen waves of defections under former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

The former bronco rider said he knew all about coming back from indignity.

“I have watched a lot of people get thrown at a rodeo and I’ll say I’ve been thrown a few times myself,” Doerkson said.

“But what I’ve learned, what I have learned from that (is) you pick up yourself, dust yourself off and you get back on.”

Doerkson, who has worked as a newspaper publisher and auto dealer, was once little known outside Williams Lake and his home riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin, which he has represented since 2020.

But that all changed on Sept. 20, when he was hurriedly installed as interim leader of the Conservatives — having returned from a trip to Africa — after the resignation of Findlay, whose divisive leadership had been tearing the party asunder.

Two days later, Doerkson was campaigning to become premier after Eby’s early election call.

“I didn’t expect this, I certainly didn’t seek this and I certainly did not plan two years ago to somehow put all of these stars into alignment,” Doerkson said in a campaign interview.

“I mean, the fact is, (in) politics every day is an exciting day and the next one you have no idea what is about to happen.”

His first task was returning Conservative defectors to the fold, including seven who said just days earlier that they were joining the upstart CentreBC party.

He was sometimes being a scarce presence on the campaign trail. But Doerkson and the Conservatives consistently led Eby and the NDP in opinion polls, as the premier faced intense criticism over an early election call that he seemed to struggle justifying.

Before his elevation, Doerkson had stayed mostly out of the culture-war fray, his time in the legislature spent mostly hyper-focused on his riding and region, beset by wildfires and hospital emergency room closures.

Doerkson’s time as publisher of the local newspaper had put him squarely at the heart of the community. As a former rodeo rider, he framed positions on health care from his perspective as a former visitor to emergency rooms.

Scott Tucker, who owns the local Home Hardware in Williams Lake, has been Doerkson’s financial agent since he entered politics, and said in a recent interview that he had known the man for about 15 years or more.

They’re both Rotarians and would encounter each other at community events, where Doerkson was more often than not the master of ceremonies.

Tucker said Doerkson is “not one to go it alone,” describing him as someone who seeks out guidance and input from others, drawing on his experience in business, and volunteering and dealing with different points of view.

Doerkson was certainly gracious in victory.

He thanked Eby for his public service, saying “it asks a lot of a person and a lot of their family.”

“He has given to this province for years, of both of those things. So thank you very much, David Eby,” said Doerkson, who also thanked Green Leader Emily Lowan for “all that she’s done to inspire thousands of young British Columbians.”

His acknowledgment of his political rivals drew warm applause.

But the night belonged to the guy from Williams Lake.

– With files from Brenna Owen

stories.title: First Nations, Carney, premiers to gather for ceremony ahead of historic meeting
stories.summary: The ceremony comes a day before what's seen as a historic meeting with the prime minister and premiers, the first since the Kelowna Accord talks of 2005.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume
stories.content:
First Nations leaders are gathering with Prime Minister Mark Carney and the country’s premiers in Ottawa today for a ceremony ahead of a historic meeting on Monday.

Monday’s meeting will the first such gathering since the Kelowna Accord talks of 2005, which brought premiers and then-prime minister Paul Martin together with Indigenous leaders to discuss ways to close the socioeconomic gaps in their communities.

First Nations will be represented in the closed-door meeting on Monday largely by regional chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations.

The Privy Council Office has not said which premiers will be attending the meeting, although Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith have both said they will be absent.

The ceremonies will be held in Ottawa with knowledge keepers, elders, First Nations leaders and community members.

National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak says it’s important to start the meeting with ceremony to ensure all participants are entering with the right frame of mind, grounded in First Nations spirituality.

stories.title: What Danielle Smith is still getting wrong, according to this even-tempered separatist
stories.summary: Analysis: Keith Wilson says Alberta has rejected independence, and he accepts that. But the premier has work to do with party dissenters.
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
“The people have spoken, I accept what they’ve said,” says Keith Wilson, co-founder of the Let Alberta Decide campaign and one of the more even-tempered advocates for Alberta independence. “And they really want, in my view, the premier to make an earnest effort at seeking fairness for Alberta. That’s how I interpret this.”

Albertans spoke clearly on Oct. 19. Roughly three-quarters of voters endorsed remaining in Canada; about one-quarter backed starting the constitutional process for a future binding separation referendum. Turnout was historic. A slight majority supported the Ucp’s proposals for greater provincial control over immigration, while the constitutional questions received more mixed results that fall short of a clear mandate for rewriting Confederation.

Premier Danielle Smith’s address to the province on Tuesday was crisp: Alberta remains a province of Canada, and for as long as she is premier she will not hold another referendum on separation. The government will honour the referendum results and continue asserting provincial autonomy through political and legal channels rather than the exit ramp.

Her message to UCP members was equally direct: the next election is 12 months away (fixed for Oct. 18, 2027). Division within the party hands the Opposition New Democrats the win. The UCP is a big-tent party but not an independence party. Candidates and members of constituency association boards must support a strong Alberta within a united Canada; those who cannot reconcile and seek to turn the party into a vehicle for independence are invited to find another party. Ordinary members remain free to hold personal views.

After months of badgering, shaming and demands to purge anyone with separatist sympathies from the conservative fold, I was relieved to hear the distinction. I also wondered how it landed with those who had pushed hardest for independence.

“I was glad to hear she’s not treating this as ‘mission accomplished,’” Wilson says. “She’s treating this as she has marching orders from the voters and it’s to seek serious change in how Alberta is treated within Confederation. So that to me is very positive, and I hope for her success in that, and whatever role I can provide to help with that, I’ll do.”

He cautions, however: “I think her messaging to the (UCP) membership was an error,” and if uncorrected it risks the very division she aims to prevent, in his view.

I listened to Smith’s video more than once. What I heard was precise: separatists are not welcome as UCP candidates or on constituency boards.

“You and I are political nerds,” Wilson observes, “and those nuances mean a lot to us. But the voters aren’t. And they just hear, ‘If you’re a separatist, you’re not welcome,’ whereas what she was saying was, ‘If you’re a separatist, you’re not welcome in these two very specific, discrete roles.’

“I know what she meant, but that’s not what came across,” he adds. “It’s coming across that she’s dismissing these people and one of the fundamental consistent grievances of Albertans who support independence is their frustration that they feel Ottawa dismisses them.” Framing that lands as dismissal, doesn’t help the reconciliation the party needs and “risks creating that wedge she’s seeking to avoid,” he says.

At times, Wilson says, it felt as if the premier was addressing Jeff Rath and Mitch Sylvestre, leaders of other pro-separatist campaigns who had made the issue personal against her. “I can understand her frustration,” he notes. Social media accuses them of Smith derangement syndrome; their attacks have been vicious. “They cost us a lot of support and I can understand why the premier would be unhappy with them.” Plenty of Albertans see the damage and reject the lumping together of every independence advocate.

“When I reflect on some of her wording,” he continues, “I even felt … she was kind of almost speaking to me at one point or at least people in my camp.” The reception, though, has been “you’re with us or against us” — decide now if you’re a separatist. “I don’t think that May have been her intention but that’s how it’s coming across. It’s a messaging problem; I don’t think it’s an intention problem.”

The pro-independence campaigns are not interchangeable. Some accept the referendum outcome and will engage constructively inside existing structures; others will not. Alberta’s experiment with direct democracy — historic turnout, rigorous third-party funding rules, and a hand-count process whose full administrative cost is still being tallied — did not produce catharsis for the most strident voices still calling for Smith’s head. There are, however, champions prepared to accept the result and work with the government for structural change. Wilson is among them. He needs to know, explicitly, that he remains welcome in the party of which he is still a member.

This is not our first conversation. We disagree on independence, but lawyer-to-lawyer I respect Wilson’s work ethic and motives. He has spent a career standing up for people facing powerful institutions — ranchers in a BSE crisis, families living beside industrial emissions, citizens confronting extraordinary emergency powers during COVID — and he is unrelenting. “I’m looking for work for the first time since I was 14 years old,” he chuckles. “I can’t believe I did this to myself … I normally run 30 files and I’m down to two.” Unlike others, he did not work this campaign from the corner of a desk; he was all in.

He has no political ambition. People have told him outright he should be the next premier. “Absolutely not,” he says.

What does he expect from the government? Structural change so that “the future of my children and grandchildren’s prosperity (is not) dependent on whether or not the sitting premier is getting along with the sitting prime minister.” He views the premier’s pledge against another referendum as imprudent: an export tax or other sudden federal hit would create immense pressure. And he’s not convinced the rest of Canada fully grasps Alberta’s grievances despite the coverage. Quebec’s new minority PQ government under Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon May create some leverage for greater provincial autonomy, but he is not optimistic it will push to open the equalization formula.

“I think the best, surest pathway to achieve that change is for the premier to be successful in bringing the party back together, recognizing the legitimate objectives of those of us who are separatists. Having us all put our shoulder to the wheel to support her … and for her to be ambitious about the change.”

“But it doesn’t have to be separation?” I ask. “You accept that?”

“Of course,” he says.

He has not spoken with Premier Smith about the results; their last private conversation was in 2025, when she asked if he was all in on independence. In my estimation, they are due for a follow-up.

At times, Wilson says, it felt as if the premier was addressing Jeff Rath and Mitch Sylvestre, leaders of other pro-separatist campaigns who had made the issue personal against her. “I can understand her frustration,” he notes. Social media accuses them of Smith derangement syndrome; their attacks have been vicious. “They cost us a lot of support and I can understand why the premier would be unhappy with them.” Plenty of Albertans see the damage and reject the lumping together of every independence advocate.

“When I reflect on some of her wording,” he continues, “I even felt … she was kind of almost speaking to me at one point or at least people in my camp.” The reception, though, has been “you’re with us or against us” — decide now if you’re a separatist. “I don’t think that May have been her intention but that’s how it’s coming across. He needs to know, explicitly, that he remains welcome in the party of which he is still a member.

This is not our first conversation. We disagree on independence, but lawyer-to-lawyer I respect Wilson’s work ethic and motives. He has spent a career standing up for people facing powerful institutions — ranchers in a BSE crisis, families living beside industrial emissions, citizens confronting extraordinary emergency powers during COVID — and he is unrelenting. “I’m looking for work for the first time since I was 14 years old,” he chuckles. “I can’t believe I did this to myself … I normally run 30 files and I’m down to two.” Unlike others, he did not work this campaign from the corner of a desk; he was all in.
He has no political ambition. People have told him outright he should be the next premier. “Absolutely not,” he says.

content_blocks.text: “The people have spoken, I accept what they’ve said,” says Keith Wilson, co-founder of the Let Alberta Decide campaign and one of the more even-tempered advocates for Alberta independence. “And they really want, in my view, the premier to make an earnest effort at seeking fairness for Alberta. Roughly three-quarters of voters endorsed remaining in Canada; about one-quarter backed starting the constitutional process for a future binding separation referendum. Turnout was historic. stories.title: Who is Nathan Fielder? The Canadian filmmaker behind new Elizabeth Homes documentary
stories.summary: Nathan Fielder's new documentary, You Can See Everything, landed in cinemas on Oct. 16, bringing in US$15 million in its opening weekend.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Nathan Fielder’s new documentary, You Can See Everything, landed in cinemas on Oct. 16, bringing in US$15 million in its opening weekend and marking the biggest opening weekend for a documentary in North America in more than 20 years.

The Canadian-American comedian and filmmaker had already risen to fame with his TV shows including The Rehearsal and Nathan for You, but the Oscar buzz around You Can See Everything combined with the film’s near-perfect scores on review platforms like Letterboxd and Metacritic has launched Fielder to a new level of fame.

Here’s what we know about his life and career.

Nathan Fielder is a 43-year-old comedian, actor, writer, and filmmaker, known for his awkward, deadpan delivery and TV projects that blur the lines between reality and performance.

He was born in Vancouver and attended Point Grey Secondary School, where he was part of the school’s improv group alongside fellow student and actor-comedian Seth Rogen.

As a teen, Fielder worked as a magician in Vancouver, at a store and at birthday parties and bar mitzvahs. In a recent interview with W Magazine , Fielder said: “I was doing magic, and I worked at a magic shop from when I was 13 until I was 20. I had to stop, because if you don’t stop, people will forever say to you, ‘Show me a trick.’”

In 2005, he graduated with a degree in business from the University of Victoria “with really good grades” — a tagline for one of his TV shows years later.

In 2008, Fielder made his first appearance on CBC’s news parody show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, where he had a recurring segment called “Nathan on Your Side” in which he played a consumer advocate.

The role helped him land writing roles at Comedy Central in the U.S., where he worked on the sketch-variety series Important Things with Demetri Martin.

Fielder became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2025, according to reports.

In 2013, Fielder launched his own Comedy Central series, Nathan for You, a docu-reality show in which he offered struggling businesses outlandish advice, drawing on his real business degree.

In one episode, he suggested a frozen yogurt shop add a “poo” flavour; in another, he placed an ad for a pet store at a pet cemetery; and elsewhere he had a hotel test a soundproof “sex box” by placing a child inside to shield them from a porn shoot staged in the same room.

The show further established Fielder’s socially awkward and absurd style that has become his signature.

Nathan for You ran for four seasons, earning a near-perfect 97 per cent score on review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes , with the New York Times hailing it “the television series with the most incisive take on the 21st-century economy” in a 2015 review.

The show won three awards at the 2014 Canadian Comedy Awards and in 2019 won a Writers Guild of America Award in the Comedy/Variety Sketch Series category.

In 2022, Fielder launched his show, The Rehearsal, in which he constructed scenarios allowing real people to rehearse real-life events.

One of Fielder’s most notable moments came in the second season of The Rehearsal, where he learned to pilot a Boeing 737 and hired actors to play passengers as he flew over the Mojave Desert. He also recreated the life of hero pilot Captain Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger by being “birthed” as Sully and breastfed from an oversized puppet.

The Rehearsal received four Emmy Award nominations and is in the “Universal Acclaim” category on Metacritic , with Screen Rant calling season two “daring, profound, and subversively hilarious.”

Fielder also starred in and directed Showtime series The Curse, a black comedy in which he and Emma Stone portray a couple trying to bring their vision for eco-conscious housing to life and produce a TV show called “Flipanthropy.”

Fielder’s inspiration for the show was a real-life incident that happened to him when he had just moved from Canada to L.A., according to co-creator Benny Safdie . A woman approached him and asked for money, and when he apologized for not having any cash, she said, “I curse you.” He went to an ATM, took out $20 and returned to ask if the curse was lifted, to which the woman said yes.

Fielder has also held small parts in the 2017 comedy-drama The Disaster Artist, which also starred Seth Rogen, and Hbo’s mockumentary Tour de Pharmacy, among others. He co-directed the Sacha Baron Cohen satirical series Who Is America?, which aired in 2018.

You Can See Everything is a three-hour documentary which follows Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the days before her prison sentence begins. Fielder co-directed the film with Lance Oppenheim.

Holmes was convicted of four federal charges of wire fraud in 2022 for misrepresenting to investors what the Theranos technology was capable of and how widely its machines were being adopted. Theranos falsely claimed it could perform a range of medical tests using a small amount of blood from a single finger prick. Holmes was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison in November 2022.

In You Can See Everything, Holmes grants Fielder and Oppenheim extraordinary access to her life with partner Billy Evans and their two children. For the film, Fielder lived with Holmes in her seaside rental for 34 days.

Of the small team of roughly seven on-site crew members, several also hail from Canada, including editor Adam Locke-Norton and Ottawa-born producer Tatiana Bears.

You Can See Everything is the latest in a string of pop culture projects based on Holmes, which includes HBO documentary The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley and Hulu’s The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried as Holmes.

On Thursday, Fielder and Oppenheim surprised viewers at a Toronto film screening of You Can See Everything. Oppenheim praised Canada’s filmmakers at the screening, calling them some of the “best on the planet.”

content_blocks.text: In 2022, Fielder launched his show, The Rehearsal, in which he constructed scenarios allowing real people to rehearse real-life events.

One of Fielder’s most notable moments came in the second season of The Rehearsal, where he learned to pilot a Boeing 737 and hired actors to play passengers as he flew over the Mojave Desert. He also recreated the life of hero pilot Captain Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger by being “birthed” as Sully and breastfed from an oversized puppet.
The Rehearsal received four Emmy Award nominations and is in the “Universal Acclaim” category on Metacritic , with Screen Rant calling season two “daring, profound, and subversively hilarious.”

content_blocks.text: What else has Nathan Fielder done in his career?

Fielder also starred in and directed Showtime series The Curse, a black comedy in which he and Emma Stone portray a couple trying to bring their vision for eco-conscious housing to life and produce a TV show called “Flipanthropy.”

Fielder’s inspiration for the show was a real-life incident that happened to him when he had just moved from Canada to L.A., according to co-creator Benny Safdie . A woman approached him and asked for money, and when he apologized for not having any cash, she said, “I curse you.” He went to an ATM, took out $20 and returned to ask if the curse was lifted, to which the woman said yes.

What is Nathan Fielder’s new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything?
You Can See Everything is a three-hour documentary which follows Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the days before her prison sentence begins. Fielder co-directed the film with Lance Oppenheim.

Holmes was convicted of four federal charges of wire fraud in 2022 for misrepresenting to investors what the Theranos technology was capable of and how widely its machines were being adopted. Theranos falsely claimed it could perform a range of medical tests using a small amount of blood from a single finger prick. Holmes was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison in November 2022.

stories.title: Americans in Canada urge fellow expats to vote in high-stakes midterm elections
stories.summary: American Democrats living in Canada are prepared to shout their political choices from the rooftops ahead of next month’s midterm elections — while some of those who back Republican candidates seem leery of speaking out fearing a backlash from their neighbours.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — American Democrats living in Canada are prepared to shout their political choices from the rooftops ahead of next month’s midterm elections — while some of those who back Republican candidates seem leery of speaking out fearing a backlash from their neighbours.

Tammy Wilsker Mermelstein, a Texas voter who moved to the Greater Toronto Area last year, will be voting in a U.S. election from Canada for the first time.

While she used to be a Republican and voted that way until 2016, Wilsker Mermelstein said she has never voted for U.S. President Donald Trump. She said it’s crucial for people to vote this year as “Texas is in play.”

“Texas has not elected a Democrat in high office for at least two decades, probably longer, and this is the first solid chance,” she said. “They say every vote counts. This is really going to be an election where every vote matters, even in states where people aren’t used to having their vote matter if they’re in the minority.”

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections which could see the Democrats seize control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives from the Republicans. Democratic control of one or both chambers could significantly alter the path of Trump’s presidency, including the possibility of new impeachment proceedings against him, and investigations of some of his key allies and agency heads.

Expat participation in U.S. elections is typically low, though the Federal Voting Assistance Program estimates there were more than 430,000 eligible U.S. voters in Canada as of 2024.

The organization estimates turnout among Americans in Canada was about 10 per cent in the 2024 general election, while the domestic voting rate that year was about 76 per cent. The organization estimates the overall turnout among all eligible overseas U.S. citizens at 11 per cent.

Kathryn Sikkink, a professor at the Harvard Kennedy School who has volunteered with the U.S. Vote Foundation, said participation in voting abroad May be low because some citizens find it difficult. Some, she said, don’t even realize they’re eligible to vote.

The U.S. Department of State website says U.S. citizens can get an absentee ballot by mail, email or fax, or by downloading it from the internet, though options vary by state.

Most U.S. citizens can vote absentee for federal office candidates in U.S. primary and general elections. Some states also allow U.S. citizens living abroad to vote for local and state office candidates, and on referendums.

Georganne Burke, the chapter lead for Republicans Overseas in Canada, said it has been a “contentious year” as Americans living in Canada have watched “the back and forth” between the two governments over trade.

“They want to make sure that whatever’s going on in the States stays kind of healthy in case they have to go back home. So people, they are more engaged, I think, than they have in the past,” she said.

A dual citizen, Burke moved back to the U.S. a few months ago after spending 38 years in Toronto and Ottawa.

A Republican and Trump supporter, Burke said she estimates there is a roughly three-to-one Democrat to Republican ratio among American expats living in Canada.

“I know that most Republicans are very motivated to vote,” she said. “They’re very quiet about it. They don’t talk because they’re not received in a very friendly way in Canada, which is kind of unfortunate.

“Democrats are also motivated to vote, especially if they’re in one of those toss-up states, like Michigan.”

When The Canadian Press sought to speak with various American voters via social media pages and message boards, lots of Democrats stepped forward. Not one Republican did.

Burke said it’s a civic duty to vote in elections. She also said while some of the things Trump says and does make her “cringe,” she focuses on his accomplishments.

“A lot of the thing that he has done in the United States have made a huge difference for Americans, including dealing with the border problem in Mexico,” she said. “And I know it drives people crazy, but he is reshoring, as he puts it, American industry to the United States to employ Americans. That’s his job.”

Trump’s trade war with Canada has become a leading ballot box issue in some key states ahead of the U.S. midterms.

Trump rapidly escalated his trade war and rhetoric against Canada after trade negotiations fell apart in August. The president signed an order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America and the United States hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs. A few weeks later, Ottawa responded with its own retaliatory duties.

Jessica Matwick, a dual citizen who lives in Ottawa and is involved with Democrats Abroad and Indivisible Ottawa, said every eligible voter should get out and vote “to put a stop to an unhinged administration and a legislative body that has abdicated their responsibility to keep the executive in check.”

“The attacks on Canadian sovereignty and destructive tariff war are actions I cannot remain silent about,” said Matwick, who moved back to Canada in late 2016 and votes in Virginia. “I still have family living in the U.S. and many friends who I am concerned about.

“My heart hurts knowing that the damage that has been done in a relatively short period of time will take years and years to repair.”

Cody Littlefield, who moved to Canada from the U.S. in 2019 and now lives in Calgary, said he tries to vote in every election. A California voter, he said this election presents an opportunity for voters to send a message that what’s happening in the U.S. “is not acceptable.”

“The future of the country really matters to me,” said Littlefield, adding that he and his family May eventually move back to the U.S.

“There are some people who will never go back and maybe they just really don’t care about the domestic stuff, but I would say the foreign policy still does affect them.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: First Nations, Carney and premiers set to gather for day of ceremony
stories.summary: Ottawa - First Nations leaders are gathering with Prime Minister Mark Carney and the country's premiers in Ottawa today for a ceremony ahead of a historic meeting on Monday.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - First Nations leaders gathered in Ottawa on Sunday for ceremonies ahead of a historic meeting on Monday with some premiers and Prime Minister Mark Carney, while grassroots activists planned their strategy to protest the meeting while heavily invoking the 2012 Idle No More movement.

National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak told reporters Sunday afternoon that First Nations want to be partners with the provinces in making a strong economy that works for everyone.

“We see geopolitical unrest around the world for many people including Canada. And we want to work toward prosperity for First Nations, and make sure that this meeting isn’t a one-and-done,” she said.

As part of the ceremonies, premiers were given a handful of tobacco they were encouraged to pray upon. They then followed Woodhouse Nepinak to a tree on the grounds of the Diefenbaker Building where they placed the tobacco at the trunk.

Monday’s meeting will be the first such gathering since the Kelowna Accord talks of 2005, which brought premiers and then-prime minister Paul Martin together with Indigenous leaders to discuss ways to close the socioeconomic gaps in their communities.

First Nations will be represented in the closed-door meeting on Monday largely by regional chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations.

The Privy Council Office has not said which premiers will be attending the meeting. Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who is Ojibwe, attended the day of ceremony along with New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt, Prince Edward Island Premier Rob Lantz, Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham and Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith have both said they will be absent from the Monday meeting.

St-Pierre Plamondon explained that he wants to prioritize a different approach with Indigenous peoples and that he has several meetings scheduled in the near future, including one with the chief of the Assembly of First Nations of Quebec and Labrador.

Smith said she will not be attending because the meeting overlaps with the resumption of question period in her province as well as the aftermath of a historic referendum on separation.

Woodhouse Nepinak said it’s important premiers attend as First Nations have a role in national unity.

“There is no shortage of issues, and the quicker we all get back to the table, the better this country will be,” she said.

The ceremonies were held in Ottawa with knowledge keepers, elders, First Nations leaders and community members.

Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty was at Sunday’s ceremony, alongside Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty and Northern Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand.

Prime Minister Mark Carney did not attend the ceremonies, which NDP MP Leah Gazan said is a sign of disrespect.

“You cannot preach partnership abroad while neglecting the relationships, rights and obligations that must be honoured at home,” Gazan wrote on social media.

When asked what he made of some of his colleagues not attending the ceremonial gathering, Kinew said ceremony is an integral part of the conversation.

“We have to acknowledge that there’s something greater than ourselves, no matter how you conceive of that,” Kinew said.

“That could be a spiritual thing, that could just be a reminder that none of us are as important as the province or country or territory or community that we represent. Ceremony is an effective way to do that.”

The meeting comes as Carney works to speed up major project approvals and development — efforts some First Nations chiefs say threaten their rights.

Tensions between Ottawa and First Nations spiked soon after Carney was elected in 2025 when his government passed legislation to create a new office tasked with streamlining major project developments and approving projects within one year.

First Nations leaders warned the compressed timelines would interfere with their rights and lead to court challenges. Provincial governments have enacted similar legislation.

But tensions are boiling over for a number of other reasons as well, including the lands claim process in British Columbia, the newly announced Pacific Link pipeline project in Alberta and development of the mineral-rich Ring of Fire in Ontario.

The Assembly of First Nations has been preparing for the meeting for months by holding town halls with chiefs to discuss actions they want to see governments take. Gina Wilson, who recently served as deputy minister at Indigenous Services Canada, helped to advise chiefs as they lined up their priorities for the meeting.

The AFN released a handful of position papers last week on economic development, policing and public safety, employment and health.

Mohawk policy analyst Russ Diabo said he’s worried the meeting will focus entirely on economics and avoid tougher conversations about First Nations rights. He has helped to organize a counter-meeting of grassroots leaders and advocates and a protest of the meeting itself, saying he does not trust the AFN to act in the best interest of communities.

The collective met on Sunday afternoon at an Ottawa community centre to strategize, heavily invoking the 2012 Idle No More protest movement that took over Canadian cities as former prime minister Stephen Harper attempted to pass legislation similar to Carney’s.

Indigenous leaders said the bill, intended to ramp up resource development, would trample on their rights while giving governments and businesses more authority to develop resources without thorough environmental assessments.

Leaders allied with the Idle No More movement staged protests, rallies and blockades on railway lines and highways and earned widespread support from across the country.

Kanahus Manuel, whose father Arthur Manuel worked closely with Diabo, called the strategy meeting a war room.

“I’m happy to stand tomorrow and stand on this front line,” she said. “I’m here to stand with my family to say again what Russ said: That the band council system does not represent us, the Assembly of First Nations do not represent us.”

A youth activist and founder of the Indigenous rights movement Okiniwak said he’s disappointed by First Nations leadership across the country, including his own, in how they’ve reacted to the major projects agenda.

But he also cautioned the group to keep the attention where it matters: the premiers and the prime minister.

“Don’t forget that your own people are inside there too. Things aren’t as black and white as it May seem,” Ramon Kataquapit said.

“They want to fight for the very things that we’re fighting for, but they just happen to be within the system that was imposed on them in the same way that it’s imposing on us.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 25, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. An earlier version’s extended headline said Prime Minister Mark Carney would be at Sunday’s ceremony. He will not be at the ceremony, and the government is instead being represented by Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty.

The ceremonies were held in Ottawa with knowledge keepers, elders, First Nations leaders and community members.
Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty was at Sunday’s ceremony, alongside Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty and Northern Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand.
Prime Minister Mark Carney did not attend the ceremonies, which NDP MP Leah Gazan said is a sign of disrespect.
“You cannot preach partnership abroad while neglecting the relationships, rights and obligations that must be honoured at home,” Gazan wrote on social media.
When asked what he made of some of his colleagues not attending the ceremonial gathering, Kinew said ceremony is an integral part of the conversation.
“We have to acknowledge that there’s something greater than ourselves, no matter how you conceive of that,” Kinew said.

“That could be a spiritual thing, that could just be a reminder that none of us are as important as the province or country or territory or community that we represent. Ceremony is an effective way to do that.”
The meeting comes as Carney works to speed up major project approvals and development — efforts some First Nations chiefs say threaten their rights.

Tensions between Ottawa and First Nations spiked soon after Carney was elected in 2025 when his government passed legislation to create a new office tasked with streamlining major project developments and approving projects within one year.
First Nations leaders warned the compressed timelines would interfere with their rights and lead to court challenges. Provincial governments have enacted similar legislation.

But tensions are boiling over for a number of other reasons as well, including the lands claim process in British Columbia, the newly announced Pacific Link pipeline project in Alberta and development of the mineral-rich Ring of Fire in Ontario.

The Assembly of First Nations has been preparing for the meeting for months by holding town halls with chiefs to discuss actions they want to see governments take. Gina Wilson, who recently served as deputy minister at Indigenous Services Canada, helped to advise chiefs as they lined up their priorities for the meeting.
The AFN released a handful of position papers last week on economic development, policing and public safety, employment and health.

Mohawk policy analyst Russ Diabo said he’s worried the meeting will focus entirely on economics and avoid tougher conversations about First Nations rights. He has helped to organize a counter-meeting of grassroots leaders and advocates and a protest of the meeting itself, saying he does not trust the AFN to act in the best interest of communities.

The collective met on Sunday afternoon at an Ottawa community centre to strategize, heavily invoking the 2012 Idle No More protest movement that took over Canadian cities as former prime minister Stephen Harper attempted to pass legislation similar to Carney’s.

Indigenous leaders said the bill, intended to ramp up resource development, would trample on their rights while giving governments and businesses more authority to develop resources without thorough environmental assessments.
Leaders allied with the Idle No More movement staged protests, rallies and blockades on railway lines and highways and earned widespread support from across the country.
Kanahus Manuel, whose father Arthur Manuel worked closely with Diabo, called the strategy meeting a war room.

“I’m happy to stand tomorrow and stand on this front line,” she said. “I’m here to stand with my family to say again what Russ said: That the band council system does not represent us, the Assembly of First Nations do not represent us.”

A youth activist and founder of the Indigenous rights movement Okiniwak said he’s disappointed by First Nations leadership across the country, including his own, in how they’ve reacted to the major projects agenda.
But he also cautioned the group to keep the attention where it matters: the premiers and the prime minister.
“Don’t forget that your own people are inside there too. Things aren’t as black and white as it May seem,” Ramon Kataquapit said.
“They want to fight for the very things that we’re fighting for, but they just happen to be within the system that was imposed on them in the same way that it’s imposing on us.”

stories.title: First Nations, minister and premiers gather for day of ceremony
stories.summary: First Nations leaders are gathering with PM Mark Carney and the country's premiers in Ottawa today for a ceremony ahead of a historic meeting on Monday.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — First Nations leaders gathered in Ottawa on Sunday for ceremonies ahead of a historic meeting on Monday with some premiers and Prime Minister Mark Carney, while grassroots activists planned their strategy to protest the meeting while heavily invoking the 2012 Idle No More movement.

National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak told reporters Sunday afternoon that First Nations want to be partners with the provinces in making a strong economy that works for everyone.

“We see geopolitical unrest around the world for many people including Canada. And we want to work toward prosperity for First Nations, and make sure that this meeting isn’t a one-and-done,” she said.

As part of the ceremonies, premiers were given a handful of tobacco they were encouraged to pray upon. They then followed Woodhouse Nepinak to a tree on the grounds of the Diefenbaker Building where they placed the tobacco at the trunk.

Monday’s meeting will be the first such gathering since the Kelowna Accord talks of 2005, which brought premiers and then-prime minister Paul Martin together with Indigenous leaders to discuss ways to close the socioeconomic gaps in their communities.

First Nations will be represented in the closed-door meeting on Monday largely by regional chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations.

The Privy Council Office has not said which premiers will be attending the meeting. Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who is Ojibwe, attended the day of ceremony along with New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt, Prince Edward Island Premier Rob Lantz, Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham and Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith have both said they will be absent from the Monday meeting.

St-Pierre Plamondon explained that he wants to prioritize a different approach with Indigenous peoples and that he has several meetings scheduled in the near future, including one with the chief of the Assembly of First Nations of Quebec and Labrador.

Smith said she will not be attending because the meeting overlaps with the resumption of question period in her province as well as the aftermath of a historic referendum on separation.

Woodhouse Nepinak said it’s important premiers attend as First Nations have a role in national unity.

“There is no shortage of issues, and the quicker we all get back to the table, the better this country will be,” she said.

“You cannot preach partnership abroad while neglecting the relationships, rights and obligations that must be honoured at home,” Gazan wrote on social media.

“We have to acknowledge that there’s something greater than ourselves, no matter how you conceive of that,” Kinew said.

“That could be a spiritual thing, that could just be a reminder that none of us are as important as the province or country or territory or community that we represent. Ceremony is an effective way to do that.”

Gina Wilson, who recently served as deputy minister at Indigenous Services Canada, helped to advise chiefs as they lined up their priorities for the meeting.

The AFN released a handful of position papers last week on economic development, policing and public safety, employment and health.

Mohawk policy analyst Russ Diabo said he’s worried the meeting will focus entirely on economics and avoid tougher conversations about First Nations rights. He has helped to organize a counter-meeting of grassroots leaders and advocates and a protest of the meeting itself, saying he does not trust the AFN to act in the best interest of communities.

stories.title: Tackling homelessness will be a key challenge for incoming Ontario mayors, councils
stories.summary: The rise in homelessness is one of the most pressing issues mayors and councillors elected next week across Ontario will have to face as the struggle to fund housing, mental health and addiction services persists.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The rise in homelessness is one of the most pressing issues mayors and councillors elected next week across Ontario will have to face as the struggle to fund housing, mental health and addiction services persists.

A seminal study from the Association of Municipalities of Ontario warned last year that the province was at a “tipping point” in the homelessness crisis.

It found nearly 80,000 Ontarians were homeless in 2024. That number rose to about 85,000 people in 2025 and the association expects it to rise again.

“Eighty-five thousand is breathtaking in the sense that it’s shocking how big that number is in a province as wealthy as we are,” said Riley Brockington, president of AMO, which represents the province’s 444 municipalities.

More than half of those people have been homeless for more than six months, the association said.

The vast majority of Ontario’s municipalities are struggling with the issue and it’s eating up more and more of their annual budgets, Brockington said. Without the ability to run deficits, it puts municipalities in a bind.

Brockington, an Ottawa city councillor who was acclaimed in his ward ahead of Monday’s election, said the province and the federal government need to step up with stable, long-term funding.

It’s the only way to try to get a handle on homelessness, he said. “We’re calling for a national housing strategy with some real money.”

The Amo’s ask is big: $11 billion over 10 years. That would cover supportive, transitional and community housing for 75,000 people, along with money for prevention programs.

The association is also asking for $2 billion over eight years to deal with the rise in encampments. There were nearly 2,000 encampments across Ontario last year, it said.

The encampments have been popping up all over the province, including in many smaller towns where there are no shelters.

“We believe every person in Ontario needs a safe place to call home every night, but it’s very expensive,” Brockington said. “This is why the burden cannot be on the shoulders exclusively of municipalities.”

The frustrating part for municipalities, Brockington said, is the fact that every level of government agrees on the path forward: more housing, particularly supportive housing.

While municipalities are appreciative of every dollar from the federal and provincial governments, much of that comes in the form of time-limited funding, Brockington said.

“Municipalities need to be able to budget and have some assurances going forward that the money will still be there,” he said. Otherwise, it will be the same scramble every year, he said, with little ability to plan long term.

A recent report from the Financial Accountability Office of Ontario said provincial spending on homelessness programs has fluctuated since 2020, before reaching a projected $948 million in 2026-27. But that figure is expected to decline to $708 million in 2028-29 because of time-limited funding, the report said.

Northern and rural Ontario are driving the growth of homelessness, which is increasing 37 per cent in northern Ontario and 31 per cent in mostly rural communities in one year, AMO found.

Another troubling statistic the association uncovered: about 20,000 youth are homeless across the province.

And on any given night in Toronto, more than 1,000 teens and children are in the city’s shelters or on its streets.

For Mark Aston, the CEO of Covenant House Toronto, Canada’s largest charity serving youth in crisis, prevention is key. Covenant House has a crisis shelter, offers transitional housing and wraparound support services including education and employment support.

“It is getting more difficult for young people to get out of that situation because of a whole bunch of things: affordability, the job market, and also acute crisis and disabling conditions that need co-ordinated specialized services to help young people,” he said.

Covenant House has seen great prevention results by going into Toronto’s schools, Aston said, adding that the program is very successful, with more than 90 per cent of at-risk young people avoiding homelessness.

“We have solutions, we just really need to get attention to this and do a bit of scaling,” Aston said, arguing that the program should be in every single school in the province. Covenant House also has its own on-site school that helps youth complete their secondary education.

The reason is simple, Aston said. Between 30 to 50 per cent of adults experiencing chronic homelessness can trace their journeys back to their youth.

“That’s when they first experienced homelessness,” Aston said. “So if you don’t solve the problem when somebody’s young, it can become really entrenched, really pervasive.”

For young people, the largest driver of homelessness is family pressure, conflict or breakdown, he said, while for adults the leading cause is eviction.

When a young person becomes homeless, early intervention is key. Aston said Covenant House gives them space to breathe, connects them with health-care workers, mental health professionals and tries to reconnect them with family — but not necessarily the family that May have driven them away.

“If you can do that and you can maintain those connections and you can provide them with housing, with social supports, with community, it can really be life altering for those young people,” he said. “You can change the trajectory of where they’re going.”

Aston has a message for all incoming mayors.

“I think the mayors across Ontario should make a commitment to end youth homelessness,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 25, 2026.

stories.title: How young fish harvesters are helping save a rapidly aging industry
stories.summary: Lillian Saul is not exactly a newcomer to the fishing industry, but at 30 she’s one of the younger captains on the water in Newfoundland and Labrador.
stories.author: Garrett Barry
stories.content:
Flatrock, N.L. – Lillian Saul is not exactly a newcomer to the fishing industry, but at 30 she’s one of the younger captains on the water in Newfoundland and Labrador.

“I’ve invested everything into this,” she said from her new home in Twillingate, ON Newfoundland’s northeast coast. “The last 11 years of my life have been building up to this… I’ve basically invested my entire adult life into fishing.”

Saul is part of a youth movement in an industry that has been aging rapidly. The province’s Fish, Food and Allied Workers Union estimated more than 33 per cent of certified fish harvesters in their membership are 54 or older.

Thousands of those workers are expected to leave their jobs over the coming decade.

It’s starting to weigh on industry players, who have launched a new program to try to lure young and new prospective fish harvesters into the fishery and into businesses like Saul’s.

The Fishing Industry New Entrants Initiative, a project by the Ffaw union in partnership with other fishery organizations, is backed by more than a million dollars from Newfoundland and Labrador’s provincial government. It aims to ramp up fishing industry presence at career fairs, immigration offices and schools across the province.

Saul, an American, first moved to Newfoundland and Labrador to pursue a graduate degree at Memorial University, where she planned to study fisheries regulation. But while pursuing permanent residency, she says she was unable to leave Canada, and work in the fishery ultimately set her on her current path.

“In Alaska, there’s so many young women in their 20s that run their own boats,” she said. “So that’s kind of where it got me thinking that that could be me.”

Employment in fishing

In more remote and rural areas of the province, fishing is still a big draw for young people but close to St. John’s it competes with job offers from businesses in the city.

“The fishery do have a black eye from the public, unfortunately, and that’s sad,” said Chad Waterman, a 37-year-old crab harvester in Flatrock, near St. John’s.

“I don’t think, still, people realize how big of an economic driver the fishery is.”

Employment in the fishing industry, in both vessels and in seafood processing plants, has stagnated in Newfoundland and Labrador. Statistics Canada surveys suggest direct fish harvesting jobs in the province fell from about 4,300 in 2011 to 3,100 in 2025.

Meanwhile, the value of the fishery has improved: commercial fish landings topped $1.2 billion in Newfoundland and Labrador in 2025, more than twice what they were in 2011.

Waterman said the fishery could use a bit more good press like the marketing campaign the New Entrants Initiative began running in October.

The boom-and-bust of the fishery can be a big struggle, Waterman admits, something that can dissuade people from entering that industry. The prices in Newfoundland and Labrador for many species can vary greatly from year to year.

Still, he said, the good years outweigh the bad. While family connections and a bit of coincidence set him onto a life in the fishery, he’s not looking back.

Saul said she thinks the regulatory burden on businesses in the fishing industry ought to be eased which might help bring new blood onto the waters.

“Every single time you want to progress, there’s ten barriers right there in front of you,” she said. “You have to do so much stuff on the computer, it’s all very difficult.”

stories.title: ‘It’s long overdue’: Flood mitigation efforts underway in two Manitoba First Nations
stories.summary: Much needed flood mitigation efforts are underway in two Manitoba First Nations that are prone to flooding every spring.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Peguis First Nation, Man., – Much needed flood mitigation efforts are underway in two Manitoba First Nations that are prone to flooding every spring.

The $61.1 million flood mitigation project is aimed at protecting hundreds of homes and infrastructure in both Peguis First Nation and the neighbouring Fisher River Cree Nation.

The first phase of the long-term initiative will see clay dikes built to protect central Peguis and up to 500 vulnerable houses across both communities, situated about 160 kilometres north of Winnipeg.

There will also be improvements to roadways to maintain access during the flooding.

“It’s long overdue,” said Stan Bird, who is the chief of Peguis.

“We’re talking generations of our people who have been affected by the flood, but we still have people that are out of the community as a result of the flood.”

In 2014, more than 100 people were displaced due to high water levels in the community. In 2022, over 2,000 people were forced out of their homes.

Bird says his community has been calling on the provincial and federal governments to provide this help for years.

“It’s a start,” he said.

Fisher River Cree Nation Chief David Crate echoed that sentiment.

“Enhancing protections for homes, access routes and essential community infrastructure will help reduce flood risks, support the safety of our residents and strengthen our community’s resilience for generations to come,” he said in a statement.

Earlier this week, Federal Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty and Manitoba Infrastructure Minister Lisa Naylor announced the work is underway in both communities , with Ottawa reimbursing eligible provincial costs through its Emergency Management Assistance Program (Emap).

“These measures reflect our shared commitment to addressing long-standing risks and protecting what matters most,” Minister Gull-Masty said in a statement.

“Together, we are taking practical steps to build stronger, more resilient communities and reduce the impact of flooding on families.”

Repeated seasonal flooding has forced evacuations for years, leaving residents uncertain about the safety of their homes and community infrastructure.

Lorne Cochrane, who is the director of operations for Fisher River CN, hopes these measures bring change.

“With these proactive measures protecting our community and our assets, it gives us a comfort that we can do things without having to worry and won’t have to evacuate and rush out at the last hour trying to sandbag homes,” he said.

Peguis resident Fred Sinclair said he’s happy to see these measures finally be implemented.

His home in Peguis has been subject to severe damage in recent years, including major flooding to his basement.

“The water was halfway up my basement, and I lost everything down there,” he said.

The project offers Sinclair hope that the next spring flood won’t mean more damage.

“It’s too bad that we have to live like that with dikes around us, but as long as it’s going to avoid flooding, I don’t mind,” he said.

stories.title: The blue wave that swept B.C. and seven more takeaways from the Conservative's big win
stories.summary: Just under 2 million British Columbians had their political say on Saturday night across 93 ridings. Here are some take-aways from the night.
stories.author: David Carrigg
stories.content:
Just under two million British Columbians had their political say on Saturday across 93 ridings.

The decision was a resounding rejection of B.C. NDP Leader David Eby and his party. Eby triggered the snap election on Sept. 22, just two years into his four-year term.

Here are some take-aways from the night:

Within a half-hour of results starting to arrive it was clear that the B.C. Conservative party had won a significant majority. Fifteen minutes later, it was official.

University of B.C. political scientist Stewart Prest said that it quickly became apparent that the Tories were leading in over 60 ridings.

“When the party is quickly winning half the vote across the province, they’re almost certain to win a commanding majority,” he said.

After the 2024 election there were 47 NDP MLAs, 44 Conservative MLAs and two Greens. As of midnight Saturday, the Conservatives had 64 seats, the NDP 27 and the Greens two.

The Conservatives won six of Surrey’s 10 seats in 2024 — Surrey North, Surrey South, Surrey-Cloverdale, Surrey-Panorama, Surrey-Serpentine River, and Surrey-White Rock.

This year, the party swept the city in stunning fashion.

Longtime NDP MLAs Jagrup Brar in Surrey Fleetwood, Amna Shah in Surrey City Centre, Jessie Sunner in Surrey Newton and Garry Begg in Surrey Guildford all lost their seats.

The Conservatives also swept in Delta and Richmond.

The blue wave travelled farther into Vancouver this election.

The Conservative party was able to win one Vancouver seat (Vancouver-Quilchena) in 2024, and this year also secured Vancouver-Langara, Vancouver-Yaletown, and Vancouver-Fraserview.

It was a double political hit for the defeated Vancouver-Yaletown incumbent NDP candidate, Terry Yung. His wife, Sarah Kirby-Yung, was voted off of Vancouver city council last week.

Eby was able to narrowly hang onto his seat in Vancouver-Point Grey.

Just six months ago, Caroline Elliott was narrowly defeated by Kerry-Lynne Findlay in the race to be Conservative party leader.

On Saturday, Elliott easily won the riding of West Vancouver-Capilano, vacated by Lynne Block so that Elliot could run. Block moved to North Vancouver-Seymour, which she also easily won.

Among the losers this election was former Conservative MLA Dallas Brodie, who ran again in Vancouver Quilchena as a OneBC candidate and secured less than 1,000 votes.

Also, popular former Conservative Elenore Sturko finished third in Surrey South as a CentreBC candidate.

The comeback attempt by Andrew Weaver, the former Green party MLA and leader, failed as he was defeated as candidate for CentreBC in Oak Bay-Gordon Head. The riding was won by NDP incumbent Diana Gibson.

In 2024 more than two million people turned out to vote in the provincial election, representing 58.74 per cent of all registered voters.

In this election, the vote total amounted to 1,770,371 or 47.97 per cent of registered voters. This is the first time the percentage has been below 50 per cent in at least a decade and indicates that NDP voters stayed home, Prest said.

Less than two hours after results began to roll in, Eby stood before a subdued crowd in downtown Vancouver and resigned as party leader.

Prest said Eby had no choice.

“He will be remembered as the premier who called an unnecessary election with a working majority, bet the house on orange and lost everything,” Prest said. “He was more focused on the politics of the job than actual policy and getting things done.”

On Thursday, pollster Leger gave the Conservatives a five per cent lead, with 44 per cent of decided voters compared with 39 per cent for the NDP and 13 per cent for the Greens.

This was roughly in line with other earlier-published polls. Just before the election, poll collator 338Canada predicted 45 per cent of the vote for the Conservatives, 39 per cent for the B.C. NDP and 12 per cent for the Greens.

With most polls reporting, the Conservatives won 48.06 per cent of the vote, the NDP took 37.37 per cent of the votes and the Greens had 10.97 per cent.

Green Leader Emily Lowan won the Saanich North and the Islands riding on Saturday night.

The party won its first seat in 2013 with Weaver taking the riding of Oak Bay-Gordon Head.

In 2017, there were three Green MLAs elected, and two in 2024, including Jeremy Valeriote in West Vancouver-Sea to Sky. Valeriote was able to retain his seat Saturday, giving the party two seats.

While Lowan won, the balance of power on Vancouver Island shifted. Long a stronghold for the NDP, in 2024 the Conservatives broke through by winning Courtenay-Comox and North Island.

This election the Conservative won five ridings including North Island. They did, however, lose Courtenay-Comox.
