stories.title: For Antoni Cimolino, leaving the Stratford Festival is such sweet sorrow
stories.summary: The outgoing artistic director is saying farewell after nearly 40 years. It’s been one heck of a love story, Aisling Murphy reports
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Antoni Cimolino pats his chest for emphasis. Ba-dum. Ba-dum. Ba-dum. The gesture is part and parcel of learning the text of William Shakespeare; actors usually do it to capture the rhythm of iambic pentameter, which, when executed correctly, makes the Bard’s language feel like a heartbeat.

At the top of today’s rehearsal, however, Cimolino is making a point about accents. The cast of Saturday, Sunday, Monday , an Italian family drama set in Naples and the last play Cimolino will helm as the Stratford Festival’s artistic director, will not be using them. But certain words need to be said a certain way, he says with a wry smile: ragù, mamma and papà had better be stressed in the right spot.

A gold wedding band glints on his ring finger as he gesticulates, his decades of research into Italian playwright Eduardo De Filippo spilling into the room.

In the buttery sunlight of the rehearsal hall, it’s not particularly clear if Cimolino, 65, has yet made peace with his decision to leave the Stratford Festival. Saturday, Sunday, Monday will play its final performance at the Avon Theatre on Oct. 24; his official last day will be Nov. 15.

In his preamble to the play’s first table read, his eyes ever-so-subtly glimmer as he speaks. Today marks a difficult milestone: It’s his final first day of rehearsal in the top job. He’s been in the position for 14 years, but the 39 seasons he’s spent working for the festival in different capacities have constituted more than 80 per cent of his adulthood. It’s a tough goodbye to swallow, no matter how long he’s had to get used to it.

But for a blissful afternoon, there is only the work at hand – the play, the actors and the promise of telling an audience a story that will somehow change how they see the world.

After rehearsal, Cimolino slips out a side door, his script tucked under his jacket. His steely dark curls – the same ones that in 1992 made him such a dashing Romeo – bounce as he walks toward Ontario Street. For 14 summers, the city’s shops and restaurants have relied on his programming to attract tourists to the 33,000-person town; it’s almost as if the storefronts stand a little straighter when he passes.

Eventually, he crests the hill. He’s moving quickly: As ever, there’s work to be done at the festival.

The Tom Patterson Theatre opened to the public in 2022, and is considered one of Cimolino's defining accomplishments as the Stratford Festival's artistic director. Christopher Katsarov; Jennifer Roberts/The Globe and Mail

Cimolino officially announced his departure last summer, but he was ready to leave in 2024.

The renovated Tom Patterson Theatre, perhaps Cimolino’s greatest achievement as the festival’s artistic director, was open and operational; the worst impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, for the most part, had come and gone. After 37 years at the Stratford Festival – as an actor, director, administrator and devoted figurehead – he could see a finish line. He was ready to spend more time with his wife and children; he’d missed enough dinners and birthdays.

But the Stratford Festival’s board disagreed. The company was still recovering from the pandemic, and no one but Cimolino could be trusted to steer the ship through whatever came next. He agreed to do two more years, emphatic that the contract extension would be his last. There was no pay bump or perk that made delaying his plans any less of a sacrifice. “They wanted me to stay. I stayed,” he recalls.

The intervening years weren’t easy. The company sold fewer tickets in 2024 than in 2023, but then excelled in 2025, with 482,579 tickets distributed across the longest season in festival history. That same year, the company completed a lengthy search process, and landed on Jonathan Church, a highly respected British theatre producer, as Cimolino’s successor.

Church has moved into the office Cimolino once shared with executive director Anita Gaffney. Next year’s season has been announced. For better or worse, the stage is set for Stratford’s next act.

Cimolino’s first act took place in Sudbury, Ont., where he was born in 1961, the second child of working-class Italian parents Gino and Vera Cimolino. His father was a construction foreman; his mother worked in housekeeping at a local hospital.

He didn’t speak a word of English until kindergarten. But in high school, he became a master of public speaking, a debate team captain whose assertive baritone would become his defining hallmark as an actor. For a while, he and his family thought he’d grow up to be a lawyer.

Then came the Stratford Festival.

The first few Stratford shows he saw – Candide in 1978, Richard II in 1979 – didn’t do much for teenage Cimolino. But the 1979 production of Love’s Labour’s Lost at the 1,833-seat Festival Theatre stopped him in his tracks. “The theatre itself kind of blew my mind,” he says. “The spatial relationship, the way we were all so focused on the play. There was this connection between them onstage and us in the audience. I’m still in awe of that.”

He was going to be an actor at the Stratford Festival. He’d make sure of it. His parents didn’t quite share his enthusiasm when he told them of his chosen life path – “that was a profoundly unhappy day” in the Cimolino household, he recalls with some amusement – but he was determined to find his way to the festival. He enrolled in the University of Windsor’s acting program, and a few years later graduated from the school with a diploma and the woman who would become his wife, fellow actor Brigit Wilson.

But Stratford didn’t wait for him. His first few auditions for the company were unsuccessful – he wanted it too badly, he recalls. That audition experience coloured how he later hired young actors at the festival. “The theatre doesn’t always take what you have,” he says. “It takes what it needs. That’s hard for a young actor to learn. But you have to learn it.”

In 1988, he finally made it in. Actor Seana McKenna remembers a day they shared on stationary bikes the following year, when he seemed unsure if he’d stay at the festival long term. “We really didn’t have that much to do,” she shares of those early acting years with a laugh.

Obviously, he stuck it out. According to actor Lucy Peacock, he was charming and funny, one of the few young artists who would show up for the festival’s voluntary warm-ups. “He had the commitment and that wish to grow and learn,” she recalls. “He was a fine actor, playful and skilled and willing – he always wanted to know what he could do to help.”

Cimolino’s Romeo in 1992 marked an apex in his acting career – he was recognized for playing the role even when he travelled abroad. He was handsome, hardworking and hungry to improve: If he’d wanted to, he could have played plenty more Romeos.

But according to actor Colm Feore, who played Mercutio alongside Cimolino’s Romeo, the future figurehead wasn’t interested in that. On days off from his own rehearsals, Cimolino snuck into others’, watching how productions came together across the festival. “He wanted to know how the magic happens,” Feore says. “He wanted to look behind the curtain, and when he did, he found that far more attractive than standing in front of it.”

Richard Monette, artistic director of the Stratford Festival from 1994 until 2007, was Cimolino’s professional mentor, but their relationship was deeper than that: Monette was a doting godfather to Cimolino’s children Sophia and Gabriele. At the festival, the men were close to inseparable; Cimolino served as Stratford’s executive director, Monette’s operational counterpart, from 1998 until 2006.

Over cardamom buns and crisp Diet Cokes at Stratford’s Café Bouffon, Cimolino – who admits that the attention around his departure this year has made him squirm – lights up when asked about Monette.

“Many of the directors at that time were autocratic, kind of cruel and humiliating,” Cimolino explains of Monette’s specific breed of leadership. “Richard didn’t do that. He was gentler.” Monette taught Cimolino to be careful with actors’ feelings during curtain calls – where people bow, and when, can carry unintended commentary on their performance, he says. Monette showed him how and when to deal in compassion rather than power.

Monette’s sudden passing in 2008, from a pulmonary embolism, was crushing: “I was a fan, and I really believed in him,” Cimolino says. Monette was generous to a fault – he once surprised company actor Sara Topham, who was honeymooning in Paris with her husband, with a lavish meal at the Eiffel Tower.

Sometimes Cimolino witnessed company members taking advantage of Monette’s kindness, and it made his blood boil, he confides. Those who treated Monette poorly were not invited back under Cimolino’s tenure. “There’s always been that sense of justice in my heart,” he says.

Monette served as artistic director of the Stratford Festival for 14 years – the exact same amount of time as Cimolino.

Owing to a tumultuous string of leadership debacles, the years that followed Monette’s retirement were among the festival’s most chaotic. Cimolino, however, was on an upward trajectory: After his nine-year stint as the company’s executive director, he was named general director in 2006.

The Stratford Festival, looking to shake things up, replaced Monette with a triumvirate structure in which three directors – Des McAnuff, Marti Maraden and Don Shipley – would co-lead the company. It ultimately proved disastrous. Conflicts were regularly reported by the press; programming choices betrayed a lack of unity within the festival’s leadership team. “It wasn’t an easy thing, it wasn’t a happy thing,” Cimolino says. “I failed to keep the group together. Everyone wanted the same thing – these were good people, talented people.”

Things became calmer – sort of – when Maraden and Shipley resigned in 2008. McAnuff, whose splashy approach to Shakespeare and musical theatre divided festival audiences and critics, became the company’s sole artistic director. Cimolino stayed on as general director. “We worked well together,” McAnuff says. “He had a natural talent for administration.”

In 2011, McAnuff announced he’d stay until the end of the 2013 season. From there, the job was Cimolino’s to lose. In 2010, Cimolino had been the founding chair of Culture Days, a nationwide celebration of arts and culture in Canada; for decades, he’d made clear his investment and belief in the arts, with Stratford as an epicentre for them.

A search was done; the requisite hiring protocols were followed. But most everyone knew the Cimolino era was coming. He was the obvious choice, a gifted director who knew where all the company’s bodies were buried. He remained calm in a crisis; to this day, he’s not known to yell. (“There were times he could have been a bit more forceful,” says board chair Larry Stevenson, otherwise praising Cimolino’s composure.)

On March 10, 2012, a new world order was announced. Antoni Cimolino was the Stratford Festival’s next artistic director.

Thirty-nine years is one hell of a love story. But like any great love affair, Cimolino’s has had bumps: He’s keenly aware of the time he missed with his children Gabriele and Sophia, now 33 and 30, when they were growing up. He can list by heart the vacations that became overwhelmed by media interviews, most often following deaths of long-time company members back home.

In 2020, Cimolino drew criticism for how the Stratford Festival had historically treated its Black employees. Black artists, including E.B. Smith, spoke out against “as cast” contracts which, prior to rehearsals, gave actors little insight into how they might be used – or tokenized – in a given production.

In June of that year, the festival released a statement underscoring its “complicity in unjust systems,” and committed to continuously evolving its understanding of anti-racism, but Cimolino knows that response could and should have come sooner. He wishes, too, that he had reached out more intentionally to artists struggling with mental-health issues during the pandemic lockdowns. He wonders often what more the festival could have done to support its most vulnerable employees during such an unspeakably lonely time.

Indeed, the pandemic was awful – it’s not an era Cimolino enjoys remembering. He spent those early months of COVID calling donors, taking walks around the river with friends and quietly fretting about the future of the festival. Prior to March, 2020, he’d never considered even the possibility of cancelling a season outright.

“I watched him go through hell,” says Wilson, his wife and a contracted actor during the season lost to COVID. The day Broadway went dark was a hard one, she says; the evening Cimolino told her she no longer needed to worry about learning her lines for the summer was worse. He and executive director Gaffney were worked to the bone, each toiling around the clock to ensure the festival could someday reopen in full swing.

At home, Cimolino and Wilson snatched moments of lightness where they could find them. “All of a sudden I looked over and there was a man beside me on the couch watching Netflix,” Wilson says. “I said, ‘Who are you?’ He said, ‘I’m your husband.’” Before long, their house was overtaken by recording equipment and ring lights. Cimolino’s hours were somehow even longer than they’d already been. But they could chat between Zoom calls.

“He loves so many things – his family, mainly. He’s made huge sacrifices for the amount of time he’s given to the place, but there has never been any doubt in my mind that his family has come first,” says Donna Feore, a close friend and the festival’s artistic associate for musical theatre development. “Is he hardworking? Yes. But a workaholic? No, I don’t think so.”

Against the odds, the festival muddled through the pandemic, and even launched the digital streaming service Stratfest@Home. Cimolino is widely credited with keeping the festival afloat through his fundraising and advocacy work in 2020. “Stratford is really connected to Antoni,” says Larry McCabe, a restaurateur and Stratford city councillor. “Without him, I don’t think we’d be sitting in such a robust and thriving city.”

For the next year – the first step on the long road to achieving balance – he’ll be travelling in theatre-free bliss. Long visits with his children in Taiwan and Halifax are on the books, plus a big trip to Cyprus. He’s counting down the days to his granddaughter Penelope’s first Christmas. He plans to binge the works of Cormac McCarthy, and, hey, he might even watch Heated Rivalry . He’ll finally have the time.

Just don’t let him hear you say he’s retiring. He’ll likely be back as a guest director at the Stratford Festival, and he and his wife have no plans to move elsewhere. The decimation of theatre education in this country is on his radar; so too is the lack of training available for mid-career artists looking to deepen their practice. The Stratford Festival’s Antoni Cimolino Excellence Fund – a small piece of his legacy which aims to provide cross-training funding for Canadian theatre artists, among other things – will help plug that gap.

But Cimolino knows intimately that the festival will always need more – more money, more time, more staff, more shows. He’ll forever feel a pull to the place, just as he’ll forever treasure his time in rehearsal: Memories such as sharing luxe chocolates with actors and goofing off in the cavernous Festival Theatre are among his favourites.

When we reach the end of our final interview, he brings his hand to his chest before shaking my hand goodbye. He’s not correcting an accent or scanning a passage of Shakespeare’s poetry; there’s something deeper to the gesture. More personal.

Once more, I see evidence of that iambic heartbeat – Cimolino’s, the festival’s, the city’s – its tempo decelerating for the first time in close to four decades.

McAnuff, whose splashy approach to Shakespeare and musical theatre divided festival audiences and critics, became the company’s sole artistic director. Cimolino stayed on as general director. “We worked well together,” McAnuff says. “He had a natural talent for administration.”

In 2011, McAnuff announced he’d stay until the end of the 2013 season. From there, the job was Cimolino’s to lose. In 2010, Cimolino had been the founding chair of Culture Days, a nationwide celebration of arts and culture in Canada; for decades, he’d made clear his investment and belief in the arts, with Stratford as an epicentre for them.

A search was done; the requisite hiring protocols were followed. But most everyone knew the Cimolino era was coming. He was the obvious choice, a gifted director who knew where all the company’s bodies were buried. He remained calm in a crisis; to this day, he’s not known to yell. (“There were times he could have been a bit more forceful,” says board chair Larry Stevenson, otherwise praising Cimolino’s composure.)
On March 10, 2012, a new world order was announced. Antoni Cimolino was the Stratford Festival’s next artistic director.

Thirty-nine years is one hell of a love story. But like any great love affair, Cimolino’s has had bumps: He’s keenly aware of the time he missed with his children Gabriele and Sophia, now 33 and 30, when they were growing up. He can list by heart the vacations that became overwhelmed by media interviews, most often following deaths of long-time company members back home.

In 2020, Cimolino drew criticism for how the Stratford Festival had historically treated its Black employees. Black artists, including E.B. Smith, spoke out against “as cast” contracts which, prior to rehearsals, gave actors little insight into how they might be used – or tokenized – in a given production.

In June of that year, the festival released a statement underscoring its “complicity in unjust systems,” and committed to continuously evolving its understanding of anti-racism, but Cimolino knows that response could and should have come sooner. He wishes, too, that he had reached out more intentionally to artists struggling with mental-health issues during the pandemic lockdowns. He wonders often what more the festival could have done to support its most vulnerable employees during such an unspeakably lonely time.

Indeed, the pandemic was awful – it’s not an era Cimolino enjoys remembering. He spent those early months of COVID calling donors, taking walks around the river with friends and quietly fretting about the future of the festival. Prior to March, 2020, he’d never considered even the possibility of cancelling a season outright.

“I watched him go through hell,” says Wilson, his wife and a contracted actor during the season lost to COVID. The day Broadway went dark was a hard one, she says; the evening Cimolino told her she no longer needed to worry about learning her lines for the summer was worse. He and executive director Gaffney were worked to the bone, each toiling around the clock to ensure the festival could someday reopen in full swing.

At home, Cimolino and Wilson snatched moments of lightness where they could find them. “All of a sudden I looked over and there was a man beside me on the couch watching Netflix,” Wilson says. “I said, ‘Who are you?’ He said, ‘I’m your husband.’” Before long, their house was overtaken by recording equipment and ring lights. Cimolino’s hours were somehow even longer than they’d already been. But they could chat between Zoom calls.

“He loves so many things – his family, mainly. He’s made huge sacrifices for the amount of time he’s given to the place, but there has never been any doubt in my mind that his family has come first,” says Donna Feore, a close friend and the festival’s artistic associate for musical theatre development. “Is he hardworking? Yes. But a workaholic? No, I don’t think so.”

Against the odds, the festival muddled through the pandemic, and even launched the digital streaming service Stratfest@Home. Cimolino is widely credited with keeping the festival afloat through his fundraising and advocacy work in 2020. “Stratford is really connected to Antoni,” says Larry McCabe, a restaurateur and Stratford city councillor. “Without him, I don’t think we’d be sitting in such a robust and thriving city.”

For the next year – the first step on the long road to achieving balance – he’ll be travelling in theatre-free bliss. Long visits with his children in Taiwan and Halifax are on the books, plus a big trip to Cyprus. He’s counting down the days to his granddaughter Penelope’s first Christmas. He plans to binge the works of Cormac McCarthy, and, hey, he might even watch Heated Rivalry . He’ll finally have the time.

Just don’t let him hear you say he’s retiring. He’ll likely be back as a guest director at the Stratford Festival, and he and his wife have no plans to move elsewhere. The decimation of theatre education in this country is on his radar; so too is the lack of training available for mid-career artists looking to deepen their practice. The Stratford Festival’s Antoni Cimolino Excellence Fund – a small piece of his legacy which aims to provide cross-training funding for Canadian theatre artists, among other things – will help plug that gap.

But Cimolino knows intimately that the festival will always need more – more money, more time, more staff, more shows. He’ll forever feel a pull to the place, just as he’ll forever treasure his time in rehearsal: Memories such as sharing luxe chocolates with actors and goofing off in the cavernous Festival Theatre are among his favourites.

When we reach the end of our final interview, he brings his hand to his chest before shaking my hand goodbye. He’s not correcting an accent or scanning a passage of Shakespeare’s poetry; there’s something deeper to the gesture. More personal.
Once more, I see evidence of that iambic heartbeat – Cimolino’s, the festival’s, the city’s – its tempo decelerating for the first time in close to four decades.

content_blocks.text: The first few Stratford shows he saw – Candide in 1978, Richard II in 1979 – didn’t do much for teenage Cimolino. But the 1979 production of Love’s Labour’s Lost at the 1,833-seat Festival Theatre stopped him in his tracks. “The theatre itself kind of blew my mind,” he says. “The spatial relationship, the way we were all so focused on the play. There was this connection between them onstage and us in the audience. I’m still in awe of that.”

His parents didn’t quite share his enthusiasm when he told them of his chosen life path – “that was a profoundly unhappy day” in the Cimolino household, he recalls with some amusement – but he was determined to find his way to the festival. He enrolled in the University of Windsor’s acting program, and a few years later graduated from the school with a diploma and the woman who would become his wife, fellow actor Brigit Wilson.

content_blocks.text: But Stratford didn’t wait for him. His first few auditions for the company were unsuccessful – he wanted it too badly, he recalls. content_blocks.text: In June of that year, the festival released a statement underscoring its “complicity in unjust systems,” and committed to continuously evolving its understanding of anti-racism, but Cimolino knows that response could and should have come sooner. He wishes, too, that he had reached out more intentionally to artists struggling with mental-health issues during the pandemic lockdowns. He wonders often what more the festival could have done to support its most vulnerable employees during such an unspeakably lonely time.

content_blocks.text: Indeed, the pandemic was awful – it’s not an era Cimolino enjoys remembering. He spent those early months of COVID calling donors, taking walks around the river with friends and quietly fretting about the future of the festival. Prior to March, 2020, he’d never considered even the possibility of cancelling a season outright.

content_blocks.text: “I watched him go through hell,” says Wilson, his wife and a contracted actor during the season lost to COVID. The day Broadway went dark was a hard one, she says; the evening Cimolino told her she no longer needed to worry about learning her lines for the summer was worse. He and executive director Gaffney were worked to the bone, each toiling around the clock to ensure the festival could someday reopen in full swing.

content_blocks.text: At home, Cimolino and Wilson snatched moments of lightness where they could find them. “All of a sudden I looked over and there was a man beside me on the couch watching Netflix,” Wilson says. “I said, ‘Who are you?’ He said, ‘I’m your husband.’” Before long, their house was overtaken by recording equipment and ring lights. Cimolino’s hours were somehow even longer than they’d already been. But they could chat between Zoom calls.

stories.title: Cuban ambassadors ask Canada to renew its rejection of U.S. embargo and fuel blockade
stories.summary: Havana is urging Ottawa not to drop its public opposition to the decades-long U.S. embargo as Washington ramps up pressure on countries supporting Cuba.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Havana is urging Ottawa not to drop its public opposition to the decades-long U.S. embargo as Washington ramps up pressure on countries supporting Cuba.

“We are confident that Canada will stay with us, as they have done in the past,” Cuban Ambassador to Canada Rodrigo Malmierca Diaz told The Canadian Press.

“The blockade and this intensification is, in practice, killing people.”

The United Nations is set to vote next week on a motion Cuba has put forward nearly every year since 1992. It calls for the termination of “the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba.”

Canada has voted in favour of this motion multiple times.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has been trying to overthrow Cuba’s Communist government through a de facto oil blockade. Washington cut off Venezuelan shipments in January and has threatened to impose tariffs on countries that sell oil to the island nation.

Washington claims Cuba poses a national security threat to the United States. Malmierca said the Caribbean nation is being collectively punished by an American pressure campaign that is harming the health and education of Cubans.

An economic crisis has gripped Cuba since 2020, triggering critical shortages and severe blackouts that peaked after January’s fuel blockade.

Havana insists its economic struggles stem from six decades of American sanctions, but critics point to the inefficiency of its Communist regime. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International say Cuba’s government engages in arbitrary arrests, tortures political prisoners and limits media and political parties.

Cuba produces only 40 per cent of the fuel it needs. Shortages have led to frequent blackouts that have threatened health care systems and crippled the island’s economy. Air Canada and other airlines cancelled flights to Cuba in February because of shortages of aviation fuel.

Ottawa has pledged to distribute $13 million in humanitarian aid for Cubans through international organizations — not the Cuban government. Past Canadian development funding has gone to things like solar panels aimed at making the island less reliant on foreign fuel.

“The people are resisting because we are convinced that the most valuable thing we have is the independence, the sovereignty of Cuba. And we are not going to surrender that,” Malmierca said.

“We would like to have a normal relationship with the U.S. We are ready for dialogue.”

Malmierca said countries that have supported Cuba have told Havana they’re being warned by Washington their access to American trade or aid could be curbed if they continue supporting UN motions to end the blockade.

He said Cuba is “not naive” and knows Canada is facing its own economic pressure from the Trump administration.

“This year is a particular moment because of all this aggressivity of the U.S. government against Cuba,” he said. “They are in a kind of offensive with other countries, trying to exercise influence for them to change their votes. We know they are using threats.”

The Canadian Press asked the U.S. State Department for comment but didn’t receive a response.

U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz this week urged countries to vote against the motion, dismissing it as a product of “70 years of propaganda” meant to distract from corruption in Havana. He said Washington has been lobbying European countries to vote against the motion.

“Do not let them abuse your vote for their oppression,” he said at a Monday event he hosted. “Do not give in to this lie.”

In a statement, Global Affairs Canada said it is still pondering how it will vote on the UN motion next week.

“As with all UN resolutions, Canada’s voting position is being considered in advance of the vote,” wrote spokesperson Thida Ith.

“Canada continues to call for the Cuban government to implement needed reforms to respect the political and economic rights of the Cuban people, and to release all political prisoners.”

In July, Havana called for a UN debate on the American embargo in the context of the island’s fuel crisis. Washington suggested it was a waste of resources to debate a motion that had already been debated nine months prior, and insisted that the decision to hold a debate be put to a recorded vote.

The vote passed and a debate was held. Canada was among 30 countries that abstained from the motion on holding a debate.

Civil society groups such as the Canadian Network on Cuba said they fear Ottawa May be pulling back from Cuba.

A document The Canadian Press obtained through a freedom-of-information request shows Ottawa had frank exchanges with Cuba about its liquidity crisis before Trump ramped up pressure on the Communist government.

The document — a briefing book prepared by Global Affairs for its deputy minister — shows the deputy minister met with three Canadian firms during a visit to Havana in February 2023 to discuss their Cuban clients’ unpaid bills.

The document says the aim of the meeting was to reassure the three firms that Ottawa “has their back … without unduly encouraging new investors and traders who risk not being paid for their goods/services.”

The companies mentioned in the document are the National Bank, mining firm Sherritt and hotel chain Blue Diamond, now called Royalton. None of the companies responded to The Canadian Press when asked whether they still have accounts in arrears in Cuba.

Sherritt and Royalton have both ceased operations in Cuba. Havana has blamed their withdrawal on American pressure tactics.

The briefing book for the deputy minister reveals some of the nature of Canada’s discussions with Cuba, with Ottawa pushing for details on small and medium-sized enterprises and Havana requesting more aid.

“Canadian firms are facing mounting payment arrears with Cuban buyers. Many Canadian firms in Cuba are SMEs and the situation is threatening their sustainability,” reads the February 2023 document for the deputy minister.

“We sought bilateral meetings for you, that would allow you, for example, to engage on human rights and new economic actors (private sector SMEs and entrepreneurs). The Cuban side wanted rather to talk to you about new tourism initiatives and more Canadian international development projects.”

The briefing book proposed that Canada “leverage Cuba’s desire for increased assistance in our dialogue on other priorities (e.g. human rights)” — but added that the cheapest and most effective things Canada could offer would be technical help with reforming the agriculture sector and rules for smaller businesses.

Malmierca said Cuba is implementing 176 reform measures which came out of parliamentary and public consultations. He said these measures will allow a larger role for the private sector, foreign investment incentives and municipal autonomy.

“In Cuba, we work according to the rule of law,” he said. “Cuba is a society that is continuously trying to improve.”

He said a trade fair in Havana next month is going largely virtual due to the current electricity shortages, and Cuba will hold an event in Toronto ahead of time to drum up interest from Canadian entrepreneurs.

“We can maintain not only the economic relationship, but we can increase it in better conditions in the near future.”

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: British Columbians vote in early election, with David Eby's job on the line
stories.summary: British Columbians go to the polls today in an early election called by NDP Leader David Eby in the biggest gamble of his political life.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria — British Columbians go to the polls today in an early election called by NDP Leader David Eby in the biggest gamble of his political life.

The five-week campaign saw the major parties fight over issues from health care to housing, the province’s record deficit and the increasing cost of living.

Polls open at 8.a.m. and close at 8 p.m. in the snap election that Eby called two years early, initially saying he needed a new mandate to tackle challenges posed by U.S. President Donald Trump.

Voters head to the polls in B.C.’s 2026 snap election. Live updates here.

But Eby said Friday the election was needed to end the frustrations of a “stalled out” legislature where the NDP held a one-seat majority, and he regretted not making that clearer.

Interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson secured his party’s top job two days before the election call in September, and managed to woo back legislators who quit the party under the divisive leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

It’s Green Party Leader Emily Lowan’s first provincial election and Eby spent the closing days of the campaign urging her party’s supporters to consider voting NDP to prevent splitting the vote.

The legislature at dissolution officially consisted of 47 New Democrats, 29 Conservatives, two Greens and 13 Independents, with two vacant seats.

But that does not take into account that most of the nominal Independents were Conservatives who returned to the party after Doerkson became interim leader — they May not all be reflected in the official numbers, but the Conservatives went into the election holding about 37 seats.

Elections BC has said votes cast on election day will be counted by hand, despite electronic tabulators being used for the first time in 2024. The agency cited the tight timelines in the snap election and the technical requirements to get the machines up and running.

Mail-in and absentee ballots won’t be counted until about two weeks after election day, with Elections BC saying it needed time to ensure that only eligible voters vote, and only once.

More than 891,000 advance votes were cast, representing about 24 per cent of all registered voters.

The campaign saw the NDP propose a new tax bracket for those making more than $1 million to help fund health care, while pledging price caps on some basic groceries and to create a training program for qualified international medical graduates already living in B.C.

The Conservatives promised no tax increases and to raise B.C.’s basic personal income tax exemption from $13,216 to $32,000, resulting in a $1,000 tax cut for most individual workers.

Doerkson said his top priority was repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act.

The Greens promised to tax household wealth over $50 million, to open a community health centre in every riding, and to reform the province’s oil and gas royalty framework.

Other parties contending for votes include CentreBC, led by former Conservative Elenore Sturko, and OneBC, whose interim leader Dallas Brodie is another former Conservative.

Voters head to the polls in B.C.’s 2026 snap election. Live updates here.
But Eby said Friday the election was needed to end the frustrations of a “stalled out” legislature where the NDP held a one-seat majority, and he regretted not making that clearer.

Interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson secured his party’s top job two days before the election call in September, and managed to woo back legislators who quit the party under the divisive leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay.
It’s Green Party Leader Emily Lowan’s first provincial election and Eby spent the closing days of the campaign urging her party’s supporters to consider voting NDP to prevent splitting the vote.
The legislature at dissolution officially consisted of 47 New Democrats, 29 Conservatives, two Greens and 13 Independents, with two vacant seats.

The campaign saw the NDP propose a new tax bracket for those making more than $1 million to help fund health care, while pledging price caps on some basic groceries and to create a training program for qualified international medical graduates already living in B.C.

Doerkson said his top priority was repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act.
The Greens promised to tax household wealth over $50 million, to open a community health centre in every riding, and to reform the province’s oil and gas royalty framework.
Other parties contending for votes include CentreBC, led by former Conservative Elenore Sturko, and OneBC, whose interim leader Dallas Brodie is another former Conservative.

stories.title: Cuban ambassadors ask Canada to renew rejection of U.S. embargo and fuel blockade
stories.summary: Havana is urging Ottawa not to drop its public opposition to the decades-long U.S. embargo as Washington ramps up pressure on countries supporting Cuba.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Havana is urging Ottawa not to drop its public opposition to the decades-long U.S. embargo as Washington ramps up pressure on countries supporting Cuba.

“We are confident that Canada will stay with us, as they have done in the past,” Cuban Ambassador to Canada Rodrigo Malmierca Diaz told The Canadian Press.

“The blockade and this intensification is, in practice, killing people.”

The United Nations is set to vote next week on a motion Cuba has put forward nearly every year since 1992. It calls for the termination of “the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba.”

Canada has voted in favour of this motion multiple times.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has been trying to overthrow Cuba’s Communist government through a de facto oil blockade. Washington cut off Venezuelan shipments in January and has threatened to impose tariffs on countries that sell oil to the island nation.

Washington claims Cuba poses a national security threat to the United States. Malmierca said the Caribbean nation is being collectively punished by an American pressure campaign that is harming the health and education of Cubans.

An economic crisis has gripped Cuba since 2020, triggering critical shortages and severe blackouts that peaked after January’s fuel blockade.

Havana insists its economic struggles stem from six decades of American sanctions, but critics point to the inefficiency of its Communist regime. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International say Cuba’s government engages in arbitrary arrests, tortures political prisoners and limits media and political parties.

Cuba produces only 40 per cent of the fuel it needs. Shortages have led to frequent blackouts that have threatened health care systems and crippled the island’s economy. Air Canada and other airlines cancelled flights to Cuba in February because of shortages of aviation fuel.

Ottawa has pledged to distribute $13 million in humanitarian aid for Cubans through international organizations — not the Cuban government. Past Canadian development funding has gone to things like solar panels aimed at making the island less reliant on foreign fuel.

“The people are resisting because we are convinced that the most valuable thing we have is the independence, the sovereignty of Cuba. And we are not going to surrender that,” Malmierca said.

“We would like to have a normal relationship with the U.S. We are ready for dialogue.” Malmierca said countries that have supported Cuba have told Havana they’re being warned by Washington their access to American trade or aid could be curbed if they continue supporting UN motions to end the blockade.

He said Cuba is “not naive” and knows Canada is facing its own economic pressure from the Trump administration.

“This year is a particular moment because of all this aggressivity of the U.S. government against Cuba,” he said. “They are in a kind of offensive with other countries, trying to exercise influence for them to change their votes. We know they are using threats.”

The Canadian Press asked the U.S. State Department for comment but didn’t receive a response.

U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz this week urged countries to vote against the motion, dismissing it as a product of “70 years of propaganda” meant to distract from corruption in Havana. He said Washington has been lobbying European countries to vote against the motion.

“Do not let them abuse your vote for their oppression,” he said at a Monday event he hosted. “Do not give in to this lie.”

In a statement, Global Affairs Canada said it is still pondering how it will vote on the UN motion next week.

“As with all UN resolutions, Canada’s voting position is being considered in advance of the vote,” wrote spokesperson Thida Ith.

“Canada continues to call for the Cuban government to implement needed reforms to respect the political and economic rights of the Cuban people, and to release all political prisoners.”

In July, Havana called for a UN debate on the American embargo in the context of the island’s fuel crisis. Washington suggested it was a waste of resources to debate a motion that had already been debated nine months prior, and insisted that the decision to hold a debate be put to a recorded vote.

The vote passed and a debate was held. Canada was among 30 countries that abstained from the motion on holding a debate.

Civil society groups such as the Canadian Network on Cuba said they fear Ottawa May be pulling back from Cuba.

A document The Canadian Press obtained through a freedom-of-information request shows Ottawa had frank exchanges with Cuba about its liquidity crisis before Trump ramped up pressure on the Communist government.

The document — a briefing book prepared by Global Affairs for its deputy minister — shows the deputy minister met with three Canadian firms during a visit to Havana in February 2023 to discuss their Cuban clients’ unpaid bills.

The document says the aim of the meeting was to reassure the three firms that Ottawa “has their back … without unduly encouraging new investors and traders who risk not being paid for their goods/services.”

The companies mentioned in the document are the National Bank, mining firm Sherritt and hotel chain Blue Diamond, now called Royalton. None of the companies responded to The Canadian Press when asked whether they still have accounts in arrears in Cuba.

Sherritt and Royalton have both ceased operations in Cuba. Havana has blamed their withdrawal on American pressure tactics.

The briefing book for the deputy minister reveals some of the nature of Canada’s discussions with Cuba, with Ottawa pushing for details on small and medium-sized enterprises and Havana requesting more aid.

“Canadian firms are facing mounting payment arrears with Cuban buyers. Many Canadian firms in Cuba are SMEs and the situation is threatening their sustainability,” reads the February 2023 document for the deputy minister.

“We sought bilateral meetings for you, that would allow you, for example, to engage on human rights and new economic actors (private sector SMEs and entrepreneurs). The Cuban side wanted rather to talk to you about new tourism initiatives and more Canadian international development projects.”

The briefing book proposed that Canada “leverage Cuba’s desire for increased assistance in our dialogue on other priorities (e.g. human rights)” — but added that the cheapest and most effective things Canada could offer would be technical help with reforming the agriculture sector and rules for smaller businesses.

Malmierca said Cuba is implementing 176 reform measures which came out of parliamentary and public consultations. He said these measures will allow a larger role for the private sector, foreign investment incentives and municipal autonomy.

“In Cuba, we work according to the rule of law,” he said. “Cuba is a society that is continuously trying to improve.”

He said a trade fair in Havana next month is going largely virtual due to the current electricity shortages, and Cuba will hold an event in Toronto ahead of time to drum up interest from Canadian entrepreneurs.

“We can maintain not only the economic relationship, but we can increase it in better conditions in the near future.”

stories.title: Canada's anti-immigrant sentiment softening, according to new poll
stories.summary: 45% of Canadians polled said we have too many immigrants, 31% indicated we have about the right number, and 13% said we don't have enough.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
Canadians in the Atlantic region and on the Prairies are most likely to think there are too many immigrants coming to this country while British Columbians and Quebecers are least likely to see it that way, according to a new poll.

When you look at all 10 provinces, 45 per cent of Canadians polled said we have too many immigrants, 31 per cent indicated we have about the right number, and 13 per cent said we don’t have enough, according to the poll conducted earlier this month by Ekos for the Association for Canadian Studies.

“We’re still seeing the large plurality of Canadians saying there are too many immigrants,” said Jack Jedwab, the association’s president.

“But clearly relative to the previous three years, we are seeing some change in feeling around that and some loosening of concern on the part of Canadians.”

Manitoba and Saskatchewan respondents were most likely to say Canada has too many immigrants (52 per cent), followed by Atlantic Canada (50 per cent), then Alberta and Ontario (both at 46 per cent).

British Columbians were least likely to say Canada has too many immigrants (39 per cent), followed closely by Quebecers (40 per cent).

The poll comes ahead of Mark Carney’s Liberal government announcing immigration levels for the next three years in the coming weeks before presenting a budget on Nov. 5.

British Columbians topped the list of those who said Canada has about the right number of immigrants (34 per cent), followed by Alberta and Quebec (both at 32 per cent). Those polled in Manitoba and Saskatchewan were least likely to say Canada has the right number of immigrants (26 per cent).

British Columbians were also the most likely to say Canada doesn’t have enough immigrants (18 per cent), followed by Quebec (16 per cent), Atlantic Canada (13 per cent), and Ontario (12 per cent).

Immigration concerns have declined across the board, but they’re still high in Atlantic Canada and lowest in B.C. and Quebec, according to the poll.

Quebecers were most likely to strongly agree with the need for a common set of values (42 per cent strongly agreed with that, and another 42 per cent somewhat agree).

Only 31 per cent of respondents in Manitoba and Saskatchewan strongly agreed with the need for a common set of values, while 42 per cent somewhat agreed.

But a near equal share believes cohesion requires people accepting others with different values, according to the poll.

In all 10 provinces, 40 per cent of respondents strongly agreed with that statement, while another 39 per cent somewhat agreed.

Those who indicated Canada has too many immigrants was down 13 percentage points from a separate Leger poll conducted in March 2025. Those who say we don’t have enough was up 10 percentage points over that same period.

In Atlantic Canada, the number of respondents indicating there are too many immigrants has dropped eight percentage points since March 2025, from 58 per cent to 50 per cent.

In B.C., that number dropped 17 percentage points from 56 per cent in March 2025 to 39 per cent. In Quebec it tumbled 18 percentage points to 40 per cent.

For all 10 provinces, immigration concerns have fallen 13 percentage points from March 2025 until this month, from 58 per cent to 45 per cent.

The new poll indicates a majority of Canadians believe that a cohesive society requires a common set of values. For all 10 provinces, 39 per cent of those polled strongly agreed with that sentiment, while 44 per cent somewhat agreed with it.

Among those who feel Canada has too many immigrants, 89 per cent say social cohesion requires shared common values. Sixty-four per cent of them say it requires accepting different values.

“The people who believe that we need shared common values for cohesion are far more inclined to say there are too many immigrants,” Jedwab said.

“On the other hand, those saying we need to accept different values are far more inclined to say that we’ve got about the right number or, in fact, not enough.”

We're still seeing the large plurality of Canadians saying there are too many immigrants

Among those who say Canada has too many immigrants, 51 per cent indicated they’re very attached to Canada.

“These people are saying, ‘I don’t feel as good about Canada because there are too many immigrants,'” Jedwab said.

That attachment jumps to 70 per cent for the folks who think we have the right number of newcomers.

Immigrants are less likely than non-immigrants to feel that there are too many immigrants, according to the poll.

Among those born here, 47 per cent said we have too many immigrants, 31 per cent indicated the number’s about right, and 12 per cent indicated there’s not enough.

For those born outside Canada, 35 per cent said we have too many immigrants, 29 per cent said the number’s about right and 20 per cent said there’s not enough.

“Some of the softening we’re seeing in attitudes towards immigration seem to be coming from that immigrant cohort whose anxiety I think is also diminishing,” Jedwab said.

The survey of 1,222 Canadian adults was conducted online Oct. 9-15 using Ekos’ Probit research panel.

The national margin of error is ±2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

When you look at all 10 provinces, 45 per cent of Canadians polled said we have too many immigrants, 31 per cent indicated we have about the right number, and 13 per cent said we don’t have enough, according to the poll conducted earlier this month by Ekos for the Association for Canadian Studies.
“We’re still seeing the large plurality of Canadians saying there are too many immigrants,” said Jack Jedwab, the association’s president.
“But clearly relative to the previous three years, we are seeing some change in feeling around that and some loosening of concern on the part of Canadians.”
Manitoba and Saskatchewan respondents were most likely to say Canada has too many immigrants (52 per cent), followed by Atlantic Canada (50 per cent), then Alberta and Ontario (both at 46 per cent).
British Columbians were least likely to say Canada has too many immigrants (39 per cent), followed closely by Quebecers (40 per cent).
The poll comes ahead of Mark Carney’s Liberal government announcing immigration levels for the next three years in the coming weeks before presenting a budget on Nov. 5.

British Columbians topped the list of those who said Canada has about the right number of immigrants (34 per cent), followed by Alberta and Quebec (both at 32 per cent). Those polled in Manitoba and Saskatchewan were least likely to say Canada has the right number of immigrants (26 per cent).
British Columbians were also the most likely to say Canada doesn’t have enough immigrants (18 per cent), followed by Quebec (16 per cent), Atlantic Canada (13 per cent), and Ontario (12 per cent).
Immigration concerns have declined across the board, but they’re still high in Atlantic Canada and lowest in B.C. and Quebec, according to the poll.
Quebecers were most likely to strongly agree with the need for a common set of values (42 per cent strongly agreed with that, and another 42 per cent somewhat agree).
Only 31 per cent of respondents in Manitoba and Saskatchewan strongly agreed with the need for a common set of values, while 42 per cent somewhat agreed.
But a near equal share believes cohesion requires people accepting others with different values, according to the poll.
In all 10 provinces, 40 per cent of respondents strongly agreed with that statement, while another 39 per cent somewhat agreed.

Those who indicated Canada has too many immigrants was down 13 percentage points from a separate Leger poll conducted in March 2025. Those who say we don’t have enough was up 10 percentage points over that same period.
In Atlantic Canada, the number of respondents indicating there are too many immigrants has dropped eight percentage points since March 2025, from 58 per cent to 50 per cent.
In B.C., that number dropped 17 percentage points from 56 per cent in March 2025 to 39 per cent. In Quebec it tumbled 18 percentage points to 40 per cent.
For all 10 provinces, immigration concerns have fallen 13 percentage points from March 2025 until this month, from 58 per cent to 45 per cent.

The new poll indicates a majority of Canadians believe that a cohesive society requires a common set of values. For all 10 provinces, 39 per cent of those polled strongly agreed with that sentiment, while 44 per cent somewhat agreed with it.
Among those who feel Canada has too many immigrants, 89 per cent say social cohesion requires shared common values. Sixty-four per cent of them say it requires accepting different values.
“The people who believe that we need shared common values for cohesion are far more inclined to say there are too many immigrants,” Jedwab said.
“On the other hand, those saying we need to accept different values are far more inclined to say that we’ve got about the right number or, in fact, not enough.”
We're still seeing the large plurality of Canadians saying there are too many immigrants
Among those who say Canada has too many immigrants, 51 per cent indicated they’re very attached to Canada.
“These people are saying, ‘I don’t feel as good about Canada because there are too many immigrants,'” Jedwab said.
That attachment jumps to 70 per cent for the folks who think we have the right number of newcomers.
Immigrants are less likely than non-immigrants to feel that there are too many immigrants, according to the poll.
Among those born here, 47 per cent said we have too many immigrants, 31 per cent indicated the number’s about right, and 12 per cent indicated there’s not enough.
For those born outside Canada, 35 per cent said we have too many immigrants, 29 per cent said the number’s about right and 20 per cent said there’s not enough.
“Some of the softening we’re seeing in attitudes towards immigration seem to be coming from that immigrant cohort whose anxiety I think is also diminishing,” Jedwab said.
The survey of 1,222 Canadian adults was conducted online Oct. 9-15 using Ekos’ Probit research panel.
The national margin of error is ±2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: The housing crisis is no longer shaping big-city politics. Why not?
stories.summary: In both Vancouver and Toronto, debates about planning and housing have been blunted by a lull in the market and rising housing supply. But experts say that is a temporary reprieve
stories.author: Alex Bozikovic
stories.content:
In 2019, the City of Toronto announced that it was going to create Housing Now. Then-mayor John Tory launched a program by that name to urgently build mixed-income housing on city land. Seven years later, not one of those homes has been completed.

Yet, despite housing costs and availability dominating local politics for years, it has not been a defining issue in Toronto’s municipal election campaign ahead of the vote on Monday. Nor has it been in Vancouver, where the Green Party’s Pete Fry defeated incumbent mayor Ken Sim on Oct. 17 to end ABC Vancouver’s hold on the mayor’s office. This year, candidates have devoted more attention to other issues, principally taxes and municipal spending, perceptions of public safety, homelessness and transit.

Part of the explanation is that, as the housing market has softened, elected officials no longer see planning reform and housing construction as an urgent priority. The current drop in rents and prices May be weakening the political resolve for change – even as a recent slowdown in construction points to another shortage in the near future.

“New people are likely coming to our cities whether we want them to or not,” says Mark Richardson, a housing advocate with the Toronto group HousingNowTO. (The group’s name refers to the city program.) “We will be ill-prepared for it. Rents will start climbing again, bidding wars will return to some neighbourhoods, and people will act surprised that this has happened again – even though it’s predictable.”

In the Vancouver region, “People feel the crisis is easing,” says Alexandra Flynn, a housing policy expert and associate professor at the University of British Columbia’s Peter A. Allard School of Law. “Asking rents in Vancouver are down from their 2023 peak and condo prices are still falling, so for some voters, the sense of emergency isn’t what it was.”

In Depth: The population is shrinking in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we put more housing there?

The market in both cities has been influenced by two trends: A high number of newly completed homes has coincided with a sharp decline in demand owing to decreased immigration.

At Vancouver City Hall, these changing conditions have altered the conversation. Mr. Sim and his ABC party came to power in 2022 promising to address housing affordability, including through zoning reform. The province has also weighed in: David Eby’s NDP government in 2023 passed a bill mandating higher-density housing near mass transit, and another bill widely permitting “small-scale multiunit housing.”

However, in Vancouver, specific city planning changes that would make it easier to build housing have sputtered. This summer, responding to vocal opposition from some residents’ groups, council voted to reject the proposed Villages Plan, which would have allowed new low-rise housing in 17 neighbourhoods. That set back the city’s effort to accommodate more homes across established residential areas, a centrepiece of the recently revised Official Development Plan .

Although housing May not be a primary election issue, it nevertheless remains a major source of concern among voters. A recent Ipsos poll of British Columbians found that housing affordability and availability is the third most pressing issue .

“It is strange how little politicians are speaking to housing affordability,” says Daniel Oleksiuk, director of the advocacy group Abundant Housing Vancouver. “Politicians don’t seem to want to address this in 2026, but they will have to face the facts eventually.”

He added that Mr. Fry has not set a clear direction on housing policy, and the new councillors – a majority, including several from the left-wing Cope party – do not have clear records on housing. “There is an opportunity for those people to see whether they want to open up more of the city’s neighbourhoods or not.”

In Toronto, “This has not been a housing election,” says Matti Siemiatycki, director of the Infrastructure Institute at the University of Toronto. “In the last few years, housing was the top issue – it’s really a good reminder of how quickly the winds can shift.”

This marks a change from the period between 2020 and 2024, when all three levels of government were actively trying to accelerate housing construction. The federal Housing Accelerator Fund tied funding to municipal commitments to reform planning and increase housing supply.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow has focused her re-election campaign on a property-tax freeze, capping transit fares and school food programs. Her principal opponent, Brad Bradford, has emphasized public safety, traffic congestion and “cost of living.”

On housing, Ms. Chow has emphasized protections for existing tenants, overseen the creation of Toronto’s public builder, and has emphasized the role of government in building social housing and partnering with private builders, as in the Housing Now program. She has set a broader target of 65,000 new rent-controlled homes approved – not built – by 2030.

Mr. Bradford, a professional urban planner who worked at City Hall before running for office, has taken a different tack. While promising tenant protections and financial supports for non-profit builders, he has also proposed eliminating the city’s land transfer tax on a first home purchase up to $1.1-million, a savings for homebuyers that his campaign estimates at $18,000 that will cost the city around $300-million annually.

Mr. Richardson, the housing advocate, argues that the current downturn is a missed opportunity for governments to invest in affordable rental housing.

“Construction materials, construction labour and land are never going to be cheaper than they are now in Toronto,” he says. “This is a Boxing Day sale on housing, and the fact that our governments at all three levels are mostly twiddling their thumbs, not exploiting this opportunity to greatly invest in affordable rental housing, is just sad.”

Housing starts in both Toronto and Vancouver have fallen sharply in recent years. In the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, condominium housing starts are down 90 per cent from their 2021 peak, according to the research group Urbanation. The number of apartment units under construction, including condominiums and purpose-built rentals, has fallen 45 per cent in three years.

In the Vancouver region, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. notes that overall housing starts and condominium housing starts remain low, which presents a longer-term risk to affordability, as buyers face increased competition for fewer homes.

The lack of building today will mean fewer new homes in two to five years. Shaun Hildebrand, president of the Toronto real estate research group Urbanation, expects completions to fall more than 60 per cent to 2029 from their current levels.

“The housing crisis is not easing – it is changing shape,” Mr. Hildebrand says. “While renters and buyers have seen some relief, it is short-term. The underlying problem of a structural shortage of supply remains, and it is getting worse because we have largely stopped building. We are already seeing rents find their floor and rental vacancy start to come back down.”

Rising rents could prompt a new sense of political urgency about housing, Mr. Richardson suggests, once middle- and upper-income people are feeling the pinch again. “A couple of years ago, this was an emergency and a wartime effort,” he says. “Now that the pressure on wealthier people has softened, it is no longer a wartime effort. Now it’s just inconvenience.”

stories.title: Wainwright fire a wake-up call for country unprepared for mass casualties, experts say
stories.summary: Experts warn health care system has limited capacity to handle multiple mass-casualty events, particularly those involving burn injuries
stories.author: Pippa Norman
stories.content:
Dr. Damian Paton-Gay raced through the halls of the Wainwright Health Centre on Saturday night as chaos swirled around him. Nearly every corner of the 100-bed Alberta hospital was crammed with gurneys holding patients suffering from severely scorched skin and in need of intensive care.

His job was to take stock of the condition of the 39 injured soldiers arriving from the nearby military base where they had been engulfed by flames during a training exercise. Calmly but swiftly, he determined which needed to go elsewhere for specialized treatment, and how soon first responders could get them there.

For Dr. Paton-Gay, this was a first – a scene of mayhem that he said would prompt someone watching a medical drama to say, “Well, this TV show is taking a bit of artistic license.”

But this scenario is precisely the type of mass casualty event that senior leadership in both the civilian and military health care systems in Canada have been simulating – and warning that the country is woefully unprepared for.

A domestic producer is an organization that processes and sometimes recovers skin from sources within Canada. Donor recovery operations only recover, but do not process skin.

For two years now, this group of experts have run war games involving the repatriation of hundreds of war zone casualties arriving from overseas for a sustained period to determine how Canadian health care systems would fare. Burns have featured heavily in the exercises.

What played out on Saturday night in Wainwright, a town about 200 kilometres east of Edmonton, is just a glimpse of how the capacity of Canada’s health care system can be challenged in an instant, said Adalsteinn Brown, dean at the University of Toronto’s Dalla Lana School of Public Health, and one of the experts involved in these planning simulations.

If the Wainwright fire and another tragedy elsewhere in Canada occurred around the same time, the system would falter, Dr. Brown said.

“If we continually run the systems as close as we can to the bone, we don’t focus on resilience, we don’t build in that capacity, and we don’t practice being ready to deal with not just one but many. Then we’ll find ourselves in real fundamental existential difficulties with the health system,” Dr. Brown said.

The Canadian Armed Forces relies on the country’s civilian, public health care system, which is often operating at maximum capacity, for specialized care. Canada also depends heavily upon imports for critical supplies such as skin and blood bags, leaving its supply chains vulnerable in the event of war or another large-scale mass casualty event. Those involved in the simulations are campaigning for better co-ordination of health care preparedness at a national level, especially between the civilian and military systems, to ensure Canada emerges resilient in the face of a crisis much larger than Wainwright.

In December, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned in a speech in Berlin that, “Conflict is at our door.” He added, “Russia has brought war back to Europe, and we must be prepared for the scale of war our grandparents or great-grandparents endured.”

For Canada, this call to action doesn’t mean only investing into arms and soldiers, but also, health care: “You really can’t talk about the defence of Canada without investing in a resilient civilian health care system,” Major-General Scott Malcolm, surgeon-general of the Canadian Armed Forces and a participant in the Canadian war games, said.

Similar disasters in the past have done little to spark change, said Gen. Malcolm. He referenced Quebec’s Lac-Mégantic disaster in 2013, during which a fiery explosion killed 47 people. That prompted calls to be better equipped for burn care in Canada, he said. But little changed.

Being prepared for an influx of burn patients is top of mind for Gen. Malcolm because of the types of injuries being documented in Ukraine, which are different than wars past.

“We’re seeing burns and a greater volume of patients in general,” he said. This has raised flags at home for the surgeon-general, where the Armed Forces often rely on the civilian health care system and lack burn surgeons among their ranks.

Modelling shows that capacity, supplies and specialized personnel in the civilian system are limited in terms of surge capacity.

When Dr. Paton-Gay was making calls from the Wainwright Health Centre on Saturday night, one of the things he asked was how much space hospitals could open up for the incoming burn victims. Were there existing patients who could be moved around to open up room in intensive and emergency care? How many?

Seven of the injured soldiers landed in his own intensive care unit at the Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton where he works full-time as a physician.

Dr. Paton-Gay walked into his Edmonton home on Sunday morning roughly 12 hours after receiving the call for aid in Wainwright. By Monday morning at 7 a.m., he was back at work in the ICU to begin his first shift of a seven-day stretch.

“There is some fatigue,” he said. “But no one’s going to shy away from caring for people who volunteered their service to protect our country.”

Many of his waking hours this week, as well as those of his colleagues, have been spent caring for the burn patients.

“It’s minute by minute for the nurses at the bedside,” he said.

The care includes painful dressing changes that often require painkillers or sedation, ensuring the patients’ airways remain open, frequent surgical procedures, and keeping their bodies free of infection and at the right temperature. It’s precise work and critical, until they are ready for the intensive surgeries necessary to replace their damaged skin.

This aspect of their recovery underscores another feature of the Canadian health care system that mass casualty experts say is deficient – a steady supply of tissues, such as skin, cornea and tendon. In the U.S., there are more than 100 establishments accredited by the Association for Advancing Tissue and Biologics whose members’ work includes tissue recovery, distribution and storage. In Canada, there are 15 organizations dedicated to supplying tissue to those in need.

Canada imports the majority of its tissues from the U.S., said Dr. Graham Sher, chief executive of Canadian Blood Services. The country has long been self-sufficient in blood, but tissues have been left behind owing to a lack of federal investment, he said.

That vulnerability is why, more than a year ago, Gen. Malcolm approached the national organization to increase the country’s sovereign supply of skin. This request was backed in June by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, who announced a $75-million investment into Canadian Blood Services to support its work with the Armed Forces.

“If we ran into a circumstance, where needs arose at the same time in our neighbours to the south or in Europe, we would be challenged,” Gen. Malcolm said.

“We simply don’t produce enough tissue in Canada, right now, in peacetime, to meet our demands.”

The Globe and Mail asked the provincial health agency Acute Care Alberta about how much skin will be required to treat victims of the Wainwright fire, and where it will be sourced from.

Acute Care Alberta declined to provide specifics about individual patients’ treatment requirements. Spokesperson Jennifer Vanderlaan wrote in an e-mail: “When donor skin is required, Give Life Alberta tissue banks in Edmonton and Calgary maintain supplies from deceased donors. If local demand exceeds supply, hospitals can also request donor skin from tissue banks in other provinces.”

It’s difficult to say how much skin Canada needs to be better prepared. With the caveat that there’s “not a lot of science to it,” Gen. Malcolm said he’s calling for an expansion of tissue banks across the country, with each location housing about 1.5-million square centimetres, roughly the area of 11 standard parking spaces.

“You never know truly how many casualties you’re going to have,” he said.

For now, planning to bolster Canada’s national skin supply chain is still in early stages, said Jody Faught, vice-president of supply chain at Canadian Blood Services.

In Quebec, where the province operates its own blood and tissue supply separate from the rest of the country, Héma-Québec spokesperson Josée Larivée confirmed the organization has been co-ordinating with the armed forces and Ottawa.

Quebec has previously been reliant on the U.S. for tissues. Today, it’s closing in on an agreement with the federal government, Ms. Larivée wrote in an e-mail, to have 1.5-million square centimetres of skin, or enough to “simultaneously treat approximately 75 to 150 severely burned patients.”

Wainwright is proof for Dr. Paton-Gay that the system and supplies supporting a country’s health care workers matter. “We can trust that people will do remarkable things, if they’re provided a system that supports them,” he said.

stories.title: Canada spent second most out of 32 countries on health care with little to show for it': Fraser report
stories.summary: Fraser report puts Canada second in spending among comparable nations, but near last in most measures of medical availability of resources.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
A new report from the Fraser Institute notes that, of the 32 high-income countries offering universal health care, Canada ranks among the highest for spending but falls consistently at the bottom when it comes to results.

The report , “Comparing Performance of Universal Health Care Countries,” by Mackenzie Moir and Nadeem Esmail, is the latest annual look at the topic by the Fraser Institute.

It examined countries that were members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (Oecd), offered universal or near-universal and had a gross national income per capita of more than US$13,935. Of the 38 Oecd countries, four — Mexico, Costa Rica, Estonia and the United States — do not have universal health care and two others — Türkiye and Colombia — did not meet the income cutoff.

Of the remaining 32 countries, Canada ranked second highest for spending as a percentage of GDP in 2024, the most recent year of comparable data. Only Chile spent more.

However, across 13 indictors of the availability of medical resources and timely access to medical services, Canada was generally below average among Oecd countries.

Notably, it ranked 30th out of 32 countries for the availability of doctors, 26th out of 31 for hospital beds dedicated to physical care, 28th out of 31 for the availability of MRI machines, and 28th out of 31 for CT scanners.

More specifically, Canada was found to have 2.8 doctors per thousand people. The average was 4.1, and the top countries in the category — Greece, Austria, Iceland and Norway — had more than five per thousand people.

Canada fared better on availability of nurses, with 10.5 per thousand people where the average was 10.1. However, this put our country in 14th place for this measurement, with top countries Switzerland, Iceland, Luxembourg and Ireland all recording more than 16 nurses per thousand people.

Canada’s MRI machine tally was 10.7 per million residents, barely more than half the Oecd average of 20.6 per million. CT and PET scanners were similarly near or below half the average in other countries. Canada had a better ranking for a type of scanner known as a gamma camera, placing third with 14.3 per million people. It also had 17.2 mammographs per million people, putting it in 13th place, though still below the average of 23.4.

Meanwhile, among the nine countries for which comparable wait times measures are available, Canada ranked dead last for the percentage of patients reporting they were able to make a same- or next-day appointment when sick, at 22 per cent.

When it came to timely access, our country also placed eighth out of nine for patients who waited more than one month to see a specialist (65 per cent) and had the highest percentage of patients (58 per cent) who waited two months or more for non-emergency surgery.

“There’s a clear imbalance between the high cost of Canada’s health-care system and the actual care Canadians receive,” said Nadeem Esmail, director of health policy studies at the Fraser Institute and co-author of the report.

The report did not make specific recommendations, but noted: “To improve health care for Canadians, our policymakers should learn from other countries around the world that also provide universal health care, often at lower costs to taxpayers and with significantly better access and shorter wait times.”

The methodology used in the report is based on that used in previous reports published between 2016 and 2025, the Institute said. It looked at 13 indicators, representing two broad categories: availability of resources, and access to resources.

It also noted that the population age profiles in the 32 countries vary significantly, and that older populations require higher levels of health-care spending. “For this reason, this study presents indicators measuring health-care expenditures and the availability of resources adjusted according to the age-profile of the country,” it added.
