stories.title: His cancer gave him just months to live. A new early-stage Toronto treatment has been a 'lifesaver' — and could offer hope to other patients
stories.summary: Although most investigational drugs fail to pass clinical trials, experts view invikafusp alfa with cautious optimism.
stories.author: Kevin Jiang; Megan Ogilvie
stories.content:
Joe Szostak was in the middle of a family vacation in Florida in February of 2023 when, while getting changed one morning, he noticed a peculiar lump in his right armpit, the size of a ping-pong ball.

Over the next two weeks, Szostak said the lump swelled to the size of an orange. By April, it had grown to the size of a grapefruit: “I couldn’t even hold my arm up properly.”

Szostak’s doctors eventually determined he had squamous cell carcinoma, a common form of skin cancer. But by the time the then-67-year-old noticed the growth, it had metastasized, spreading through his body. Physicians gave him two to three months.

“Then I had to come home and share that with my son,” Szostak told the Star. “I don’t wish that conversation on anyone.”

Today, Szostak’s condition has stabilized. He credits his recovery in large part to a new, investigational immunotherapy he received as part of a Phase 1/2 clinical trial at Uhn’s Princess Margaret Cancer Centre.

“I’ve been on this trial for probably well over two years now, with surprisingly no complications, no adverse effects,” Szostak said. “It’s a lifesaver.”

One out of every $10 spent on cancer treatments in Canada goes towards Keytruda. Experts warn that something has to give.

Although it’s still early in the process, and most investigational drugs fail to pass clinical trials, experts are approaching the drug — called invikafusp alfa — with cautious optimism. Only a few dozen patients have received it. But, if successful, it could open the door to new treatment pathways for patients who have run out of options.

Cancer drugs that target the immune system are revolutionizing how some kinds of tumours are treated, but existing immunotherapies still leave too many patients behind. Only about 20 per cent of patients with solid tumours respond to current immune-targeting drugs, which is why experts say research into investigational therapies like the one Szostak took are so important.

“What’s exciting about immunotherapy is that it works even in some patients who have very advanced disease; they still can have a complete response” and be rescued, said Dr. John Bell, senior scientist at the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute and scientific director of BioCanRx, Canada’s Immunotherapy Network.

“Cancer is a very complex disease and we’re never going to have one pill or one immunotherapy that’s going to work,” said Bell, who was not involved in the clinical trials. “But combinations of them have a real chance to cure people — and keep them cured.”

Developed by U.S. biopharmaceutical company Marengo Therapeutics, invikafusp alfa is administered via intravenous infusion and is currently in Phase 2 clinical trials. If successful, it could take up to 10 years for this therapy to reach clinics, the Toronto investigators say. Results of the phase 1/2 clinical trial were published Friday in Nature Medicine.

Dr. Lillian SIU, medical oncologist and senior scientist at Uhn’s Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, said trials of the investigational immunotherapy show promise.

Although Szostak was advised to get his affairs in order following his terminal diagnosis, he refused to give up. In April, over eight hours, a surgeon removed the grapefruit-sized tumour. Over the next year, he underwent immunotherapy, then chemotherapy and radiation treatments.

Szostak lost his hair, feeling in his toes and hands, and suffered a blood clot that made his arm swell up “like the Michelin man.” By the end of 2023, he’d lost 50 pounds and his cancer spread. He developed a lesion under his right arm and a nodule in each lung.

Desperate, Szostak approached a company in the U.S. that offered to sequence the genome of his cancer to identify potential drugs. After shelling out “several thousand dollars,” it produced a 38-page report.

He shared the findings with oncologists at hospitals including Princess Margaret, with low expectations — and was surprised when the Toronto cancer centre called him back about a new trial.

Szostak became one of a few dozen patients around the world with access to invikafusp alfa.

Compared to previous treatments, it was like “night and day,” Szostak said. “When I walk out of my infusion treatments every three weeks, I feel ... I could run around the block.”

Other participants reported side effects: “Some patients had feverish chills the night of the first infusion, and then it gets better over time,” said Dr. Lillian SIU, a co-senior author on the study and a medical oncologist and senior scientist at Princess Margaret. “But it was overall a safe and tolerable drug.”

SIU is also a scientific adviser to Marengo Therapeutics, which developed the drug, and holds equity.

“I feel better than I did in 2022,” before he got diagnosed, said Joe Szostak.

Szostak was one of just 58 patients across 10 cancer centres in Canada, France, Spain and the U.S. to receive the new drug. Only 27 received a dose that could affect their health.

In this select group, roughly 15 per cent saw their tumours shrink enough to meet clinical criteria for a response, while around 44 per cent had less shrinkage.

Importantly, 18 of these patients’ cancers had stopped responding to previous immunotherapies. But after taking invikafusp alfa, two-thirds of this group stabilized or saw their tumours shrink.

“I want to emphasize that this is an investigational drug,” noted SIU. “The identification of anti-cancer activity is not a primary goal — safety is the primary goal” of the trials so far.

The drug, known as a selective dual T cell agonist, is a first-in-class therapy — meaning it functions in a way like no other treatments before it.

It works by activating two specific types of white blood cells that, while relatively rare in the body, are common within tumours. Unlike other immunotherapies that elicit a broader immune response, invikafusp alfa is more selective in its approach, potentially reducing side effects.

Experts warn that too many young people face difficulties in accessing tests and follow-up care

Invikafusp alfa has passed the Phase 1 portion of the trials, meaning it’s been shown to be safe at an optimized dose among a small group of participants. Phase 2, which involves more patients and investigates efficacy and short-term side effects, is underway. A Phase 3 trial will test the drug on a larger pool of patients to evaluate efficacy and test for signs of toxicity.

Only 31 per cent of industry-sponsored pharmaceuticals make it past Phase 2, while about 58 per cent pass Phase 3, explained Christine Williams, an immunologist and executive vice-president of the Ontario Institutes for Cancer Research, who wasn’t involved in this research trial.

Dr. Zhen Su, president and CEO of Marengo Therapeutics, said it will be critical to understand how invikafusp alfa works in different patients, which patients are most likely to respond and whether it’s effective when combined with standard cancer treatments. The company expects to publish further Phase 1/2 results next year.

Clinical trials act as “a bridge between research and changes in clinical care,” Williams said, noting they are an important way for patients to get early access to innovative treatments.

Dr. Erica Tsang, a medical oncologist and clinical investigator at Princess Margaret, is running another clinical trial with invikafusp alfa, testing if it can be used to treat cancers at the earliest possible stage.

It will involve patients whose cancer might come back and who have regular blood tests to look for molecular markers of cancer, with the goal of changing the disease’s trajectory. Tsang called the research “uncharted territory.”

More than two years later, Szostak’s cancer has stabilized; the lesion under his arm is no longer visible on scans, one nodule in his lungs has shrunk by more than half and the other has remained stable.

Szostak has been able to return to much of his regular life. He walks five kilometres a day, cycles on a regular basis and spends time with his wife and adult son.

Szostak feels grateful for the chance to join the trial. “I feel better than I did in 2022 — before my diagnosis — when I was probably feeling some of the early effects of cancer.”

stories.title: Ontario lacks aging strategy as senior population surges, advocates say
stories.summary: Report says province should focus on community programs and supports that help people stay healthier and avoid hospitals or nursing homes.
stories.author: Moira Welsh
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford’s promise to add 58,000 new or renovated nursing home beds has led to just 11,000 completed spaces, while advocates say the province still has no overarching aging plan for cheaper and healthier options in the community.

Instead of focusing primarily on the $6.4-billion construction project, Dr. Samir Sinha says the province needs a strategy for proactive, community-based health and social supports for an aging population that, according to Statistics Canada, will include 1.1 million Ontarians aged 85 and older within 20 years.

While the Progressive Conservative government says it has injected billions of dollars into home care and community services, a recent report by the National Institute on Ageing (NIA) said Ontario is a policy laggard compared with Alberta, British Columbia and Nova Scotia, all of which have “strong and distinct” aging strategies backed by dedicated funding.

“Ontario’s approach remains largely fragmented — relying on a network of locally delivered programs without a formally recognized or resourced system-level co-ordinating or capacity-building structure,” said the report co-authored by Sinha, who is the Nia’s director of health policy research and a Sinai Health geriatrician. He presented the findings at a recent meeting of Canadian health ministers in Winnipeg.

Canada’s “rapidly aging population,” the NIA said, is “placing new demands on the communities in which people live and the services they rely on. In particular, increasing numbers of Canadians are aging alone, living on fixed incomes, and managing multiple chronic conditions.”

An international examination of community programs that help people stay healthier and avoid hospitals or nursing homes shows that comprehensive policies bring “greater clarity and predictability for older persons and their families, caregivers and care providers around what exists to enable both healthy aging and aging in the right place,” the report said.

Advocates such as Sinha have long called for an aging strategy but say time is running out for government action.

In 2026, Ontario became a “super-aged” province , with one in five residents now 65 or older, according to Statistics Canada. And with the massive millennial generation beginning to turn 50 in 2031, the demands of an older society will not fade with the baby boomers, the oldest of whom are now turning 80.

Ontario therefore needs not just an aging strategy, but a plan that supports people at different stages of life, said Laura Tamblyn Watts, CEO of CanAge, a national advocacy group.

“There are actually three distinct generations within that designation, and they have very different needs,” said Tamblyn Watts.

Many in their mid-60s, she noted, are no longer considered “old” and with longevity offering extra decades of life, policymakers “must prepare” for a variety of options to keep people healthy and engaged, avoiding the social isolation that is linked to depression and dementia.

Concerns about housing and health are increasingly part of political discussions at Queen’s Park.

The Green Party’s Aislinn Clancy has questioned the government on plans to help older Ontarians remain at home and Liberal MPP Stephanie Smyth (Toronto—St. Paul’s) is working on a private member’s bill that focuses on aging.

“By expanding community-based programs and making social connections more accessible,” Smyth said, “we can improve quality of life, ease pressure on the health-care system and potentially delay the need for long-term care.”

Cost comparisons show significant savings from government investments in the community with programs that provide transportation, proactive health care and wellness hubs for social connections.

Daily hospital fees range from $700 to $1,200. Nursing homes cost roughly $200 a day. Community programs range from $63 for “supportive care” to $127 in home care, according to Advantage Ontario, which represents long-term care, seniors’ housing, supportive housing, and community service agencies.

Donna Duncan, CEO of the Ontario Long-Term Care Association, which represents nursing homes, said she welcomes the Nia’s focus on community supports.

“Most people want to age at home and in their own communities, and services like meals, transportation, respite and friendly visiting help them do that safely and for longer,” Duncan said.

“We know Ontario needs both. More than 50,000 people are waiting for a long-term-care home, and the residents we care for today have more complex medical needs than ever. For them, 24/7 nursing and personal care is the right care, and the work underway with government to build and redevelop homes needs to continue.”

Financial planners break down what each level of care actually costs — and how to plan for the

Duncan also noted a pilot program operated by the Ministry of Long-Term Care that enables some homes to serve as community hubs where people can access nursing, dementia care, wound care and personal support while still living independently.

In an interview, Sinha said the province’s programs for older adults are siloed under the budgets of the Ministry of Health, Ministry of Long-Term Care and the Ministry for Seniors and Accessibility.

“Who is stepping back and actually saying, ‘What is the overall game plan to create a sustainable health care system?’ ”

The Health Ministry said it is doing just that.

“Our government is taking action to provide more people with the right care, in the right place, at every stage of life,” said Lily Barnes, spokesperson for Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

The ministry has “tripled” funding for home and community care, spending $5.6 billion this year, Barnes said in an email. That money will “strengthen and expand home and community care services, helping thousands more patients access home and community care.”

She also cited “record investments into our home care workforce” that includes better wages for personal support workers and $300 million to “help thousands of people launch their careers as PSWs.”

The $5.6 billion “sounds like a lot,” said Sinha, but is a “tiny” slice of the ministry’s current $91.8-billion health budget.

“We can start to understand why long-term care wait-lists are climbing, and hospitals have a lot of patients occupying beds who don’t want or need to be there — often because we don’t have enough home care or community supports.”

stories.title: Privacy commissioner looking into Crime Stoppers tip line hack. Here’s what you need to know
stories.summary: The breach could render tipsters vulnerable to identity theft, fraud and in some cases risk their public safety, according to experts.
stories.author: Abby O’Brien
stories.content:
The federal privacy commissioner is examining a large-scale Crime Stoppers data breach that exposed nearly 1.5 million Canadian tips, prompting some local branches to pause the program amid security and safety concerns for tipsters.

Despite the breach falling outside their mandate, Vito Pilieci, spokesperson for the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, said the agency has offered “expertise and guidance” in the aftermath of the breach, and is seeking more information from Navigate360 “before determining next steps.”

Pilieci said he was not in a position to comment further.

As first reported by CBC, the information was stolen last March by a hacking group seeking to disprove the company’s claim that its platform was “anonymous” and “secure.”

All told, more 8.3 million tips were exposed, according to the investigation, 1.5 million of which were submitted by Canadians. In some cases, names of the tipsters or other personal information, like phone numbers or addresses, were included in the data.

The breach, unprecedented in both scope and severity, according to experts who spoke to the Star, could render tipsters vulnerable to offences like identity theft and fraud, and in some cases, risk their public safety. Some local programs, including in Toronto, have opted to pause accepting tips after learning the extent of the leak.

“It could be really dangerous if (this information) got into the wrong hands,” said Lisa Danay Wallace, a lawyer specializing in information technology and privacy. “It takes it a big step further, into physical risk.”

A coalition of hackers, dubbed Internet Yiff Machine, stole data from P3, the tip software used by the charity since 2018, in March. A week later, the organization said Navigate360 informed them that the system was “safe and fully operational.”

Crime Stoppers says it was told by Navigate360 in May that the data — a total of 91GB — had been recovered.

In a statement shared Thursday, Crime Stoppers Toronto said it took months to gain clarity on the extent of the breach. The Guelph Wellington branch shared a similar statement on Thursday.

In that time, a copy of the hacked data was made available to researchers and journalists by Distributed Denial of Secrets, an American non-profit that publishes hacked documents, if deemed to be in the public interest.

CBC’s reporting, published on Wednesday, was the first time the Toronto branch was made aware that the leaked information had been accessed by an outside party.

Some of the leaked tips contained personal information, such as full names, addresses and phone numbers, along with allegations they reported to the non-profit. Some of the tips resulted in arrests or charges, with tipsters receiving cash rewards.

“This creates a unique situation where very sensitive, highly sensitive information has been breached,” Danay Wallace said.

But the risk is not only to the tipsters; the leaked tips could harm the reputations of those being reported, particularly if the allegations contained within were unfounded.

“People that are being accused in these tips; they’re still innocent until proven guilty, too,” said Danay Wallace.

Toronto Crime Stoppers saw the most tips of any Canadian city exposed in the breach, a total of 179,891, including more than 14,000 names.

Spokesperson Sean Sportun says the organization has not had the opportunity to review the leaked tips.

“(Navigate360) has not given us the text of the tips, despite repeated requests through our lawyers, so we can’t see what each one says,” Sportun said in a written statement to the Star. The organization says it continues to seek the stolen tips from Navigate360, along with a “full account of what happened.”

Toronto Crime Stoppers announced Thursday it was pausing its tips program and is currently asking the public to direct reports to Toronto police. Sportun says it will not readopt the program until it “can stand behind the system that protects (its tips.)”

“This week’s reporting shows the data has travelled beyond Navigate360, and we don’t know who else May have a copy,” he said. “So we are acting as if it could be misused.”

Along with Toronto police, Hamilton, and Peel, York, Halton and Durham police services have also suspended the intake of tips.

The Crime Stoppers of Canada Association says that the tip program and software has since been secured.

“Navigate360 has advised us that third-party cybersecurity experts have investigated the breach, identified vulnerabilities and completed remediation,” association vice president Craig MacPhail told the Star.

The national tip program remains in operation.

MacPhail says the national association respects the decision of independent branches and continues to work with local programs to implement additional measures and oversights.

“These measures strengthen protections for current and future submissions, said MacPhail. “They cannot undo the exposure of information already taken, which remains a serious concern.”

stories.title: Hate-motivated incident
stories.summary: London, ON (October 24, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service have charged a London man following an investigation into a hate-motivated incident that occurred in the downtown core.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 24, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service have charged a London man following an investigation into a hate-motivated incident that occurred in the downtown core.

On October 22, 2026, police were made aware of an incident that took place in the rear parking lot of a property located in the 0-100 block of St. George Street. It was reported that a male who was completing construction work at the address used equipment, believed to be a pressure washer, to create a symbol resembling a swastika in the gravel surface of the parking lot.

Nearby residents captured video and photographs of the incident and provided the information to police. The property owner was notified and attended the location, removing the symbol.

On October 23, 2026, members of the London Police Service identified and arrested the suspect male.

The investigation was reassigned to members of the London Police Service Hate Crime Unit, and the incident was determined to have been motivated by hatred.

As a result of the investigation, Gordon Botaitis, 56, of London, has been charged with one count of offence motivated by hatred.

The accused was released from custody and is expected to appear in London court on January 18, 2027, in relation to the charge.

Hate has no place in our city. The London Police Service is committed to protecting the safety and well-being of all members of our community and recognizes the significant harm that hate-motivated incidents can cause. Everyone deserves to feel safe and respected in our city. Any incident believed to be motivated by hate will be taken seriously and thoroughly investigated. The London Police Service remains committed to working with our community to address hate and ensure London remains a safe and inclusive place for all.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Teachers, support staff rally across province amid stalled contract talks
stories.summary: The rallies come as negotiations between the province and teachers’ unions remain at a standstill.
stories.author: Jake Ross
stories.content:
Thousands of teachers and support staff across the province rallied on Saturday in a show of support for public education, and as their contract talks remain in limbo.

Protests were held in Toronto, Ottawa, London, Sudbury and Thunder Bay to push for better funding, improvements to teacher retention and recruitment, smaller class sizes and plans to address violence in schools, among other issues they want to highlight at the bargaining table.

stories.title: With Osap cut off, can Ontario's private colleges be saved?
stories.summary: The loss of access to Osap grants, and now loans, amid fraud allegations at 8 schools, is sparking fears for the future.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
A clampdown on international students. No new partnerships with public colleges. Then, no access to Ontario Student Assistance Program aid grants. And, for now, no access to Osap loans.

Private colleges have been dealt a number of blows by both the federal and Ontario governments — but it’s the most recent move by the province that could lead to the demise of a number of these mainly for-profit businesses.

Such schools offer quick credentials, typically serving non-traditional students and often in niche programs, but with a much higher tuition price tag, so they rely on student aid funds to keep up enrolment.

Without it, “we are expecting more program pauses and potentially school closures if the Osap freeze continues,” said Taylor Buck, the administration and communications assistant at Career Colleges Ontario.

The government implemented the ban on Osap for all private colleges amid concerns about fraud at a handful, but says it plans to reinstate it under a stringent new process come January. Online programs, however, will remain ineligible.

With at least one private college already suspending programs amid financial uncertainty, the organization that oversees almost 300 such schools worries that’s just the start.

Minister Nolan Quinn asks Ontario Provincial Police to investigate “criminal allegations.”

“We can’t comment on individual institutions or situations not yet made public, but colleges cannot operate indefinitely without the tuition funding their students rely on, and students cannot wait until the new year for certainty,” Buck also said in a statement to the Star.

“There needs to be a path forward now for students at compliant institutions.”

More than eight colleges are now being inspected and targeted by the province amid concerns of misuse — with some allegations already referred to the OPP.

Career colleges sometimes offer programs not easily available elsewhere — trucking or flight schools, for example — and their shorter duration appeals to mature students, lower-income students, those already in the workforce as well as newcomers looking to boost credentials. (International students don’t qualify for Osap.)

About one-third of Ontario’s roughly 600 private colleges qualify to receive Osap funds.

The Canadian Press has reported that in 2024-5, seven private colleges received $385 million in Osap — the same amount that students in all of the province’s public colleges received that same year.

Laurel Schollen, a higher education expert at the University of Toronto’s Ontario Institute for Studies in Education, said that without Osap, students would need to afford such programs; “it will put some into desperate straits.”

While the quality of some has come under fire, critics have blamed the government for poor oversight despite repeated warnings — from provincial auditors, and even Career Colleges Ontario itself.

“It’s a very dramatic move, and it’s one of those situations where I think most of the evidence suggests there’s a small number of players that May be problematic,” said Glen Jones, a higher education expert at Oise, who believes the government doesn’t “have the data to make a distinction” so shut down student aid to all.

Career colleges are regulated by legislation, he noted, but “one of the challenges is the ability of the government to monitor whether all of those regulations are being fulfilled. There are supposed to be regular inspections, and the last study we did, one of the issues that arose was how frequently the government (inspected) institutions.”

Just last week, Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn said a sector-wide, third-party audit that recently flagged concerns around misuse continues, and that ministry “investigators began in-person inspections at eight private career colleges,” an investigation that “extends to the sector as a whole.”

He has promised that private college students stuck in limbo will have access to third-party loans, but provided no details.

“To protect against irregularities or fraud, Osap will not resume for private post-secondary institutions until the strengthened validation process is in place” in the new year, he said, and “will include caps on Osap-funded enrolment, the exclusion of predominantly online-only programs, and strengthened student identification and verification controls.”

In 2025-26, some 242 private colleges were eligible for Osap, representing 121,000 students.

Jones also noted that private college graduates have the highest default rates when it comes to Osap repayment, which the government should be paying attention to. In 2023, public universities had a default rate of 1.9 per cent, public colleges 5.5 per cent, and private colleges 7.4 per cent.

Mothercraft, established almost 100 years ago, trains early childhood educators while running daycares and parent support programs. Despite its charitable and non-profit status, it falls under private career college legislation.

The Osap freeze has created “a lot of anxiety and stress for those students that had been counting on loans,” said executive director Michele Lupa, adding the school has deferred tuition payments for about a dozen students for now until the province works out a plan for third-party loans.

“We’re trying to minimize their stress while they’re in the first semester of a very intense program,” she said. She said she worries about the future of the school’s online programming and if it will be permanently excluded.

About half of Mothercraft’s graduating class of 120 will have learned online, but with the requirement for an in-person placement.

While colleges worry about their future, students do, too. Alisson Almeida, who has a bachelor of science in biology from York University, now attends Aaps College for a diploma in pharmaceutical quality control to help “close the gaps on my resume.”

“I wouldn’t have been able to even start the program if I was not approved for Osap,” said the 42-year-old who was approved for $18,000 in Osap this year. The college, he added, “is being very generous to me; they will allow me to complete the program, even though we have no certainty of how this is going to work.”

Alisson Almeida, who has a bachelor of science in biology from York University, now attends Aaps College in Toronto for a diploma in pharmaceutical quality control to help “close the gaps on my resume.”

Some believe this is an opportunity for public colleges, which were also hit hard by the limits to international students — using programs run with private colleges to help boost their budgets — now that some for-profit schools face peril.

What’s needed now is a comprehensive look at the role of the private college sector, says Paul Axelrod, professor emeritus at York University.

“Are students getting their money’s worth? Did they find jobs?” he said, adding while demand is there for shorter courses, the government “will only learn about (effectiveness) if they do a systematic survey of people who have attended them and are attending them, and how have things changed.”

He said the province in the long term should be leaning into public colleges, which have seen programs axed, staff laid off, campuses closed and even school mergers because of budget issues.

Axelrod noted the government’s recent changes to Osap overall, moving to a loan-heavy system instead of nonrepayable grants, was prompted by ballooning costs in the private college sector.

Most experts agree, however, that this latest move by the government has tainted all private career colleges when so far a small number remain under suspicion.

“There’s a difference between treating the entire sector as corrupt rather than taking ownership for the fact that there wasn’t a lot of oversight,” said Elizabeth Buckner of Oise, who has studied the private sector in higher education.

“It allowed certain institutions to take advantage, and that those institutions need to be investigated and punished and closed down. But a niche mom-and-pop school that’s providing (education in a) field for 40 years is not the same.”

stories.title: Kelowna-area candidates make final push before election day
stories.summary: BC NDP Leader David Eby said Tuesday that Conservatives have taken the region for granted, arguing they cannot assume voters will automatically support them.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
With election day approaching, candidates in Kelowna-Mission and Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream are making their final pitches to voters, with public safety, healthcare, affordability and jobs among the key issues.

In Kelowna-Mission, Conservative candidate Gavin Dew is hoping to keep the riding in Conservative hands, pointing to healthcare and public safety as priorities.

“Conservatives are very committed to getting the 33,000 unused square feet of space at Kelowna General Hospital opened,” Dew said. “We’re very committed to mandatory care at Okanagan Correctional Centre.”

Dew is running against NDP candidate Miriam Rycroft, Green candidate Saoirse MacKinnon, and Abraham Nordine of OneBC.

BC NDP Leader David Eby said Tuesday that Conservatives have taken the region for granted, arguing they cannot assume voters will automatically support them.

“We have to work harder in this region; we need to earn every vote,” Eby said, while on a campaign stop in Kelowna.

Dew disputed that characterization, criticizing the local NDP campaign.

“It’s difficult for me to see the NDP as working extra hard in this region when my local candidate has yet to show her face in Kelowna,” he said.

Rycroft’s photo is absent from the NDP campaign website’s candidate biographies, and a drive through the riding did not turn up NDP election signs promoting her candidacy.

On the eve of the election, a regional campaign manager said Rycroft was unavailable for an interview.

In neighbouring Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream, NDP candidate Binny Boparai is hoping to make gains in a riding that has traditionally favoured Conservatives.

Boparai, a farmer and business owner, said she believes voters May be ready to consider a different party.

“I think people are ready to give a different party a shot because I’m the type of candidate that shows up and answers the tough questions,” she said.

Boparai identified the cost of living and job creation as key priorities, arguing that stronger regional economic growth could help address a range of concerns.

“If we have growth, economic growth in our region, that’s going to bring on good jobs and that solves a lot of the other underlying issues,” she said.

Conservative candidate Pavneet Singh, also a business owner, identified homelessness and the economy among the issues facing the riding.

Singh argued that expanding natural resource development could help create jobs and strengthen the provincial economy.

“LNG will be double and triple by 2035, and we have resources. People want to go to work, and we have to create jobs, and economy will be better once we do that,” Singh said.

Singh also urged voters to reject another NDP term, saying: “British Columbia cannot afford one more term of NDP.”

Green candidate Carter Mochinski and OneBC candidate Alexandra Wright are also running in Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream.

stories.title: Toronto’s municipal election faces voter turnout test after 2022 record-low
stories.summary: Factors such as rising political toxicity, election fatigue and loss of local media have contributed to apathy among voters
stories.author: Patrick White
stories.content:
Ala’a Adib raises her fist and raps the door in well-practised rhythm.

Knock-knock-knock-knock-knock.

“It does start to hurt after a while,” she says, studying her knuckles while listening for movement beyond the door at 44 Willowridge Rd., a public housing complex where just 17 per cent of eligible voters cast ballots in the last city election. In the surrounding ward of Etobicoke North, home to 115,000 people, just 6,800 votes was good enough to elect the incumbent councillor, Vincent Crisanti.

She tries again. Knock-knock-knock-knock-knock. The door swings open to reveal a man in a Megadeth T-shirt and a waft of marijuana smoke. She doesn’t miss a beat.

“Hi, I’m Ala’a and I’m running for city council,” she says. “The vote is coming up this Monday. I want to make sure we have affordable housing, safer communities and faster, reliable transit.”

“Right on, I’ll check it out,” says the man. The door closes, ending a 10-second pitch to boost her candidacy and bolster the deteriorating foundations of local democracy.

Toronto notched a record-low turnout of 29.2 per cent in the 2022 election. The ebb affected the entire province. Just one out of three eligible voters went to the polls, down considerably from Ontario’s historical average of 40 per cent. Recent municipal results from B.C. and a surge in advance voting suggest the tide could be turning, but it’s difficult to project whether the sentiment will stretch eastward.

Academics have pointed to a jumble of factors, including the COVID-19 pandemic, rising political toxicity, election fatigue, loss of local media and a political system that snubs new and young Canadians. But the effect is clear: weaker mandates, weaker candidate fields and weaker democracies.

“People here just don’t feel like their lives are going to change based on decisions the city is making,” Ms. Adib says about the Toronto Community Housing building, where daily life is organized around fickle elevator service and long trips for groceries.

After the abysmal 2022 turnout, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) set out to study the problem. It determined that voters show up when they have a sense of civic duty, trust the political system and want political change.

“When these things are not there, that’s when we see apathy taking over,” AMO executive director Lindsay Jones says.

But AMO found many local electorates didn’t get that change option in 2022. A record number of candidates had been acclaimed with no competition.

Since then, the organization has run a series of free workshops for anyone interested in running for councils, some targeting youth, Indigenous peoples and people with racialized backgrounds. More than 6,000 people signed up. AMO also ran social media ads encouraging people to come forward.

When the nomination period ended this year, the acclamation picture had improved dramatically. Candidate acclamations are down from 548 in 2022 to 400 this year. And the number of municipalities where the entire council was acclaimed has dropped from 32 to 19.

B.C. managed a marginal increase in voter turnout during its Oct. 17 municipal elections, from 29.2 per cent in 2022 to 32.8 per cent. The bump was more pronounced in several major municipalities, with Vancouver turnout increasing by about seven percentage points and Richmond turnout up by 16 percentage points. A number of prominent incumbents, including Vancouver mayor Ken Sim, were given the boot.

“People turn out when they want to make a change,” says political strategist and former Vancouver city councillor Geoff Meggs. “That always draws extra people.”

It’s difficult to tell whether the change sentiment will translate nationally. B.C. has long held its own political microclimate.

Polling in Toronto has shown the race between incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow and her main challenger, Brad Bradford, to be neck-and-neck.

Toronto turnout is generally highest when there’s a member of the Ford family on the ballot. Rob Ford’s insurgent campaign to “end the gravy train” at City Hall drew 51 per cent of eligible voters in 2010. The subsequent 2014 election victory for John Tory over Doug Ford drew 55 per cent.

Those polarizing elections – and large turnout they attracted – have few analogues today.

“I don’t foresee a big surge in Ontario turnout,” University of Ottawa political studies professor Daniel Stockemer says.

In his recent research on the factors that contribute to high turnout, Dr. Stockemer hypothesized that a candidate’s youth could be key to attracting new voters.

The theory didn’t hold up to his statistical analysis of 47 elections in 28 countries.

“I was kind of disappointed by the finding,” he said.

“There’s a problem, a democratic deficit right now,” he added. “I thought younger candidates could boost youth turnout, but it actually does very little.”

Ms. Adib hopes he’s wrong. At age 35, she’s hoping her age can spur younger generations in the ward to vote.

In 2020, her brother, 21-year-old Adan (Sache) Dubet, was shot and killed. He had attended Toronto Metropolitan University and planned to become a lawyer. She started a charity, Smiles For Sache, that provides a Ramadan meal program, youth mentorship and other initiatives.

“That gives me the confidence to put myself out here,” she says, moving on to another door, another pitch, another potential voter.

stories.title: David Eby’s surprise B.C. election culminates in narrow race between NDP, Conservatives
stories.summary: Timing of NDP Leader’s decision has become a frequent issue for him throughout the campaign
stories.author: Mike Hager, Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Five Sundays ago, NDP Leader David Eby was gearing up to call a surprise election.

But that day, he received a surprise of his own: Embattled B.C. Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned after just four months on the job.

And, he acknowledged during a recent editorial meeting with The Globe and Mail, he was just as shocked to see her replaced that same day by Lorne Doerkson, a 58-year-old former small-town newspaper publisher from the Interior and two-term MLA whom most people had never heard of.

Despite his unknown opponent, Mr. Eby called the election two days later on Sept. 22.

The timing of this decision became a frequent issue for him throughout the campaign.

Greg Lyle, a Sunshine Coast-based pollster who is president of Innovative Research Group, said the call meant the NDP was fighting an election with far more uncertainty. With Ms. Findlay gone, Mr. Lyle said, it proved much more difficult to tie Mr. Doerkson to the same grievances and goals animating the greatest existential threat to B.C.’s economy: U.S. President Donald Trump.

Mr. Eby “thought he was going to be running against Kerry-Lynne and he ended up with someone else, but they had two full days to figure this thing out or to not call the election,” said Mr. Lyle, who began polling for Kim Campbell’s Progressive Conservative Party in the 1993 federal election.

“At that point, you just don’t call it and you would have a perfectly good excuse: ‘It’s not a responsible thing to call an election when there’s so much disarray in the main opposition, we’re going to give them a chance to catch their breath.’”

The Conservatives appear to have caught their breath anyway. Most opinion polls show them either statistically tied with the NDP, or slightly ahead.

The New Democrats have governed the province for nine years, since the late John Horgan formed government with the support of three Green Party MLAs in 2017. Mr. Eby succeeded Mr. Horgan as leader and premier in 2022. Two years ago, he won a slim majority government with 47 seats, compared with 44 for a resurgent BC Conservative Party and two for the Greens.

During a campaign appearance this week, Mr. Eby acknowledged that him snapping his term in half is still front of mind for many voters.

“The No. 1 question that people ask me is why are we having an election. … Look. I get it. I know that people have a lot going on. I know they didn’t want an election right now. I hear the frustration and I understand it,” he said.

But, Mr. Eby said in the lone leaders’ debate, he requires the stability of a majority mandate to make the “big swings” that British Columbians need government to deliver.

Over the course of the race, the Conservatives dropped two candidates after the NDP highlighted their past anti-Islamic and antisemitic statements.

However, the party kept Katy Merrifield as campaign director despite controversy over an anti-Islamic social-media post she had made in June. She took it down within hours of posting, and after the backlash erupted earlier this month, she explained that, as a rape survivor, she posted in anger upon hearing about an independent “Rape Gang Inquiry” in Britain. She said she misdirected her fury at the entire religion instead of the “extremism used to justify these horrific crimes.”

The New Democrats, meanwhile, had to explain why Mr. Eby and his doctor wife, who earn multiple times the province’s median household income, were benefiting from their child using one of B.C.’s scarce $10-a-day subsidized daycare spots .

Regardless of who forms government, neither of the main parties presented clear paths back to fiscal stability in the near or even medium term amid rising deficits, a mounting debt load and tumbling credit ratings.

Economists say tax hikes proposed by the NDP and Greens could raise less revenue than projected and discourage economic activity, while the Conservatives’ tax cut could put B.C. further in the red.

The Ndp’s plan shows the deficit falling from roughly $13.8-billion this fiscal year (after adjusting for the government’s pause to its planned expansion of provincial sales taxes on professional services) to $11.97-billion in fiscal 2028-29.

To achieve even that modest reduction, the party’s plan relies on a tax increase on the top 4 per cent of earners and up to $730-million a year of new revenue from “targeted economic growth” tied to major projects. However, planned new spending would absorb most of the new revenue.

Meanwhile, the Conservatives said their plan will bring B.C.’s annual deficit down to $10.8-billion by 2029-30, which would still be more than twice the province’s 2023-24 shortfall. The plan was harshly criticized for relying on rosy growth predictions.

To reach its target, the party said it would reduce the province’s contingency reserve fund, enact a hiring freeze, review spending at most ministries and cut outside consultants.

The plan bakes in $2.6-billion of extra revenue from faster growth over three years. But a tax cut achieved by raising the province’s personal income tax exemption level to save most workers $1,000 a year would offset that extra revenue by about $3.4-billion annually.

Both the NDP and the Conservatives pledged to fully fund the health care system.

To help people with the crushing cost of necessities, the NDP pledged to suspend 10 cents a litre of the provincial motor fuel tax, and promised up to another 20 cents off by asking the BC Utilities Commission to cap the price of gasoline.

The Conservatives promised to cut the 10-per-cent provincial sales tax on Canadian alcohol.

Political scientist Stewart Prest of the University of British Columbia said the two parties focused the final stretch of the campaign on Surrey , Vancouver’s southeastern suburb and the second most populous city in the province. Many of its 10 ridings could swing to elect a new party.

“Surrey is pretty clearly the chief battleground of this election, and that’s not new,” he said. “We have seen Surrey specifically, but then the Fraser Valley more broadly as the battleground of elections.”

Both the NDP and Conservatives have promised to expand SkyTrain service in Surrey. The Conservatives have released what they call a Surrey Success Plan with commitments on SkyTrain, scrapping the Massey Tunnel replacement in favour of a new bridge as well as building a new hospital.

Among other commitments, the NDP has promised a new Surrey Charter to provide the city’s leaders with more authority in managing the city.

“There’s a sense of unmet need there, a frustration that is palpable, that the people need things in Surrey, that they are not necessarily getting them at the pace they need them,” Dr. Prest said.

Saturday’s election outcome will show whether Mr. Eby can continue the streak of Canadian politicians benefiting from having Mr. Trump as a foil.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford called a snap election last year on the basis he also needed a mandate to respond to economic threats posed by the Trump administration. Mr. Ford led his Progressive Conservatives to a third straight majority.

stories.title: ‘He ran into the fire’: Military medic critically injured saving fellow soldiers in CFB Wainwright fire
stories.summary: His mother says Cpl. Liam Keane kept running into the deadly fire to save fellow soldiers until his own injuries overtook him.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Sarah Ryan
stories.content:
A 23-year-old Canadian Armed Forces medic remains in critical condition after his mother says he repeatedly ran into the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright to save his fellow soldiers, continuing until his own injuries overtook him.

Cpl. Liam Keane is stationed out of Edmonton with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

His mother, Tami Flexhaug, said the day her son learned he would become a military medic was one of the happiest days of his life. She said Keane is passionate about his career and approached his job with his whole heart.

“It has been shared with us during the incident he ran into the fire multiple times to save his fellow soldiers,” Flexhaug said in a written statement to Global News.

“Liam was doing exactly what he was well trained to do, his job, for this we and his military family and those who knew him are very proud of him. He continued till his own injuries overtook him.”

Flexhaug said her family was also told Keane spoke before he was airlifted from the scene. “This gives us much hope,” she said.

Flexhaug said she has received an outpouring of messages describing the kind of soldier and person her son is.

Keane previously received a commendation for showing kindness and compassion to a patient while training.

“He is kind, caring and compassionate, a very special young man, always going above and beyond,” Flexhaug said. “He had a real love for his trade and did it exceptionally well.”

Keane underwent his first surgery Thursday, which Flexhaug said went well. She said the family is taking each day as a blessing.

“His injuries are complex and extensive, but we have hope and know he is in the very best hands,” she said.

Flexhaug said her son would want to thank everyone for their kindness, including first responders and Stars. Stars (Shock Trauma Air Rescue Service) is an air ambulance service that provides critical care and rapid emergency medical transport across Western Canada.

“If it wasn’t for them, we would not have him today,” she said.

She is asking people to continue keeping Keane in their thoughts and prayers.

stories.title: Morgan pitches $10M hotel-tax fund for downtown revitalization plan, Stevenson questions priorities
stories.summary: Incumbent London mayoral candidate Josh Morgan says if re-elected, he’ll direct $1 million a year from the city’s Municipal Accommodation Tax (MAT) toward the Downtown Master Plan for the next decade.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Incumbent London mayoral candidate Josh Morgan says if re-elected, he’ll direct $1-million a year from the city’s Municipal Accommodation Tax (MAT) toward the Downtown Master Plan for the next decade.

On Friday, Morgan held a campaign announcement to announce his proposal to tap into some of the municipal tax on hotel room stays to cover $10 million of the $48 million, 10-year plan approved by a majority of city council in June.

Morgan said he would seek other ways to fund the remaining $38 million, “We have an economic development reserve fund (at city hall), we have the capacity to fund this in ways that are innovative and creative, and we continue to find new ways that are not property tax related.”

However, mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson questioned the proposed use of hotel-tax revenue.

“I would be interested to hear what the hotels have to say about that,” Stevenson told CTV News. “We’ve only got two-ish million a year, of which $1.6 million is already going towards the Canada Life Place (expansion) repayments for the next few years.”

Stevenson, who did not support the plan when council approved it, still questions its priorities.

“There are 58 initiatives, $48 million over ten years. We need to do the basics. Londoners want a safe downtown, and they want parking, and that’s what private investment needs,” she asserted.

Morgan is also proposing an expansion of the Office to Residential Conversion program that provides financial incentives to offset some of the costs of transforming office buildings into apartments.

The redbrick building owned by Farhi Holdings has been vacant and boarded up for years.

Morgan said, “We will create a new stream (that’s) dedicated towards small scale office to residential conversions and a specific allocation for heritage assets.”

Incumbent councillors Shawn Lewis, Skyler Franke, and Peter Cuddy flanked Morgan at Friday’s announcement.

He added that incumbents Paul Van Meerbergen and Hadley McAlister had to cancel, but supported his downtown funding proposal.

Morgan was also joined by Coun. Steve Hillier and Coun. Jerry Pribil who are not seeking re-election.

He characterized the presence of so many municipal politicians at this announcement, and other campaign events as a sign of his collaborative approach, “The mayor has one vote on council. A mayor cannot get things done without the support of their colleagues. A mayor should not be thinking about overriding colleagues. They should bring them together with plans that work and plans we can all get behind.”

Stevenson suggested Morgan’s support from incumbent candidates would mean more of the same at city hall.

“These are the same councillors that have supported illegal drug use in our shelters and our highly supportive housing and our social housing. The same ones who voted for the $500,000 to $800,000 BRT bus shelters,” she said.

Both candidates say they offer voters different approaches to leading the city.

Stevenson replied, “Whether it’s ending illegal drug use, taxes at less than 1 per cent, coordinated road construction plans, or transparency, its (vote for) me or the status quo with Josh.”

A complete list of candidates running in the municipal election can be found on the City of London website.

Election Day is Monday, Oct. 26.

stories.title: The dangers of Brad Bradford’s Toronto
stories.summary: Capitalizing on misplaced fear is no way to build a better city
stories.author: Alex Bozikovic
stories.content:
Brad Bradford is scared of Toronto, and he thinks you should be too.

That is the unmistakable theme of the campaign from the outgoing city councillor as he challenges Mayor Olivia Chow. His campaign rhetoric has painted a consistent picture of a dirty and dangerous Toronto filled with disorder. And the implied lesson is clear. In these dark times, only one man – accompanied by the 1,000 police officers he’s pledged to hire – can save us. That is a standard challenger’s narrative.

But in Toronto of 2026 , it has a problem: it is not true. During the three years of Ms. Chow’s mayoralty, the City of Toronto has become a significantly safer place, and is one Canada’s safest cities. Murders, shootings and violent crime are all down substantially. Last year’s homicide total was the lowest in 50 years. Car thefts, which spiked after the height of the pandemic, are down dramatically in the past three years.

An objective observer can only come to one conclusion: The bike-riding NDPer has been a law-and-order mayor. She has also given the police department everything on its wish list. In a strange turn of events, she even earned the enthusiastic endorsement of the Toronto Police Association, the labour organization which represents more than 8,700 police and civilian members of the police service.

How then has public safety become such a central focus of the municipal conversation?

When we talk about public safety today, what we are mostly talking about is “public disorder.” That euphemism refers to the presence of unhoused people. When an executive driving downtown sees a tent from their car, that is disorder. When she sees someone nodding off on the subway, that too, is public disorder. When a provocateur on Instagram yells with disgust about the people he is stepping over on the sidewalk – disorder.

Those visible problems are driven, in large part, by the opioid crisis and by a generation of cutbacks to mental health services. These larger issues predate Ms. Chow’s mayoralty and are mainly out of the city’s control. That said, dealing with homelessness is the city’s task and the situation has improved significantly on her watch.

Unfortunately, our culture is inclined to view a big city as an inherently dangerous and disorderly place. This assumption has been baked into our politics by generations of rhetoric and too much of American TV.

The presence of unhoused people does not mean danger. But many of us feel that it does. That fear is a problem of its own. It points to apparent solutions that are forceful and costly. Take Mr. Bradford‘s key promise to hire 1,000 police officers. How exactly would that make Torontonians feel safer? Will there be a police officer on every streetcar, in every park, all the time? How will those officers deal with people they encounter who need treatment?

None of this works as policy. It only works as a narrative, and only if you imagine a shadowy Gotham full of leering villains. But stories have power, and Ms. Chow has not risen to this rhetorical challenge. She has declined to define a clear alternative vision, one of attractive public places and streets filled with happy people. She has not told the story – the true story – of a city that remains livable, lively and safe.

That positive vision is badly needed, and it is achievable. A Toronto of better parks with richer amenities (including cafés where citizens gather and chat) is another way to attack this problem. People feel safe around other people.

For now, Mr. Bradford‘s campaign of darkness reflects poorly on the city and on him. The fact is that Toronto is a vibrant place. The streets are filled with a rich mix of humanity, of people who want to be here and who are ready to look out for their neighbours. Mr. Bradford’s bad vibes might just land him a win in Monday’s municipal election. In that case, we will find out if he is fit to run the city or just to run against it.

stories.title: Beth Lew-Williams wins Cundill History Prize for book on anti-Chinese discrimination
stories.summary: Princeton professor Beth Lew-Williams has won this year’s Cundill History Prize for “John Doe Chinaman: A Forgotten History of Chinese Life under American Racial Law.”
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — Princeton professor Beth Lew-Williams has won this year’s Cundill History Prize for “John Doe Chinaman: A Forgotten History of Chinese Life under American Racial Law.”

Lew-Williams received the US$75,000 award during a ceremony in Montreal on Friday for the book that explores the laws that constrained the lives of Chinese immigrants in the 19th century American West.

In a press release Cundill jurors praise her work for being “dazzlingly innovative and hard-hitting.”

Award organizers say the book examines court records, immigration files and personal accounts to show the extent of anti-Chinese discrimination and “restores individuality and humanity to lives once obscured by prejudice.”

The runners-up for the prize, who each receive US$10,000, are Jonathan Cheng for “Korean Messiah: Kim II Sung and the Christian Roots of North Korea’s Personality Cult” and Alexander Lee for “The First Ghetto: Venice and the Jews.”

The prestigious prize is run by McGill University and recognizes history writing in English.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct 23, 2026.

Kaitlyn McGrath, The Canadian Press

stories.title: BC Spca urges election candidates to commit to pet-friendly housing laws
stories.summary: Vancouver - As British Columbia chooses a new provincial government on Saturday, the Spca has launched its own campaign urging voters to call on election candidates to commit to changing laws so that families with pets will have equal access to housing.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - As British Columbia chooses a new provincial government on Saturday, the Spca has launched its own campaign urging voters to call on election candidates to commit to changing laws so that families with pets will have equal access to housing.

The plea comes after Erin Hayman’s family spent months hunting for a place to live with their pets when they lost their home in the Bald Range wildfire, which destroyed about 150 structures in the district of Summerland, B.C. in August.

stories.title: ‘Waiting too long’: Calls to strengthen Safe Social Media Act ahead of second reading debate
stories.summary: Young people in Canada are among those calling on the federal government to strengthen a bill aimed at making social media safer for kids online.
stories.author: Katie Griffin
stories.content:
Ottawa - Young people in Canada are among those calling on the federal government to strengthen a bill aimed at making social media safer for kids online.

“I think we have been waiting too long for action,” said Aany Vital Ramos.

The 17-year-old high-school student has grown up with social media and wants to help make the digital world safer for herself and others after seeing how harmful it can be.

“I’ve seen a lot of young people use it for opportunities, whether for education, communication, or self-expression. But I also see some of the issues… like cyberbullying, seeing harmful content, or the effects social media can have on their well-being,” she said.

“Limiting these types of regulations to only social media doesn’t necessarily also go through the underlying risk because I know a ton of youth who are on these gaming platforms, platforms like Roblox, platforms like Discord, who also want to be protected.”

Bill C-34, the government’s Safe Social Media Act , will be called for debate at second reading in the House of Commons next week.

“It’s been 14 years since Amanda Todd died as a result of sextortion and cyberbullying. That’s 14 years that our Parliament has waited, and dithered, and taken, you know, quite frankly, far too long,” said Sara Austin, founder and CEO of Children First Canada.

The organization is the national voice on children’s rights to digital safety.

“We know that kids don’t just have a right to be protected from harmful content, they have the right to have their data protected. And we’ve seen countless ways that children’s privacy has been violated, not just by social media companies and AI chatbots, but by educational technology companies that have access to very sensitive data.”

Children’s Privacy Code

This comes as Canada’s privacy commissioner this week launched this country’s first Children’s Privacy Code.

It outlines expectations for organizations that handle children’s personal information, including that they must communicate with them in an age-appropriate way and without profiling or manipulating them.

“Kids have to know what’s going to be done with their information. They have to have the ability to say ‘yes’ or to say ‘no’. They have to be able to say I don’t want this anymore. They have to understand what’s happening with their information,” said Privacy Commissioner Philippe Dufresne.

Dufresne admits there needs to be more enforcement powers.

“I have some powers under the legislation to do some investigations, to make some recommendations, to work with companies to make things better. That’s what we did with TikTok, specifically with respect to kids’ information. That’s what we did with Grok in terms of the deep fakes situation. We’re going to continue to use all of the tools. We need more tools. We need more enforcement powers. And there’s some current bills in Parliament that are going to be debated on that,” he said.

Advocates hope the code and Safe Social Media Act will make technology safer for children and hold companies accountable.

“We have seen kids’ data exposed at scale and putting them really at danger. And so, this new digital code will really play a meaningful role in protecting children and giving parents and other caregivers the assurance that our kids can operate more safely in the digital world,” Austin said.

Vital Ramos said protection in the digital realm hasn’t happened fast enough and wants to ensure young people are part of the conversation.

“If Bill C-34 is about building a safer digital future, then it should be built with us, with our experiences, strengthened by our voices,” she said.

stories.title: Complaint to Competition Bureau alleges Israeli companies misled Canadians about West Bank real estate
stories.summary: Bureau says it will review allegations that properties in occupied Palestinian territories in the West Bank were marketed as being in Israel
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie
stories.content:
A group of lawyers and civil society members have filed a complaint with the Competition Bureau over Israeli real estate events in Toronto and Montreal, alleging that illegal properties were marketed to Canadians under false pretenses.

The complaint alleges at least four Israeli real estate companies and one Canadian marketing firm promoted properties in occupied Palestinian territories in the West Bank while misleading consumers to believe they were in Israel.

The Competition Bureau says it will review the complaint filed by Global Echo Litigation Center and the Canadian Lawyers for International Human Rights and determine if an investigation into the companies is warranted.

James Yap, president of the lawyers’ association and a Windsor university law professor, said Canadians who May have purchased West Bank properties could be opening themselves up to serious legal consequences under international law, such as complicity in war crimes.

Canada and much of the international community have long held that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal and an obstacle to peace in the Middle East.

The territory has been occupied by Israel since 1967, but settlement activity has significantly increased since the onset of the latest war in the Gaza Strip, triggered by the 2023 Hamas attack on Israel that killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. Israel’s retaliatory offensive has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and displaced most of Gaza’s two million residents.

Ottawa advised Canadian businesses in August to avoid engaging with Israeli settlements, warning that failing to do so could open them up to legal and financial risk.

“The Canadian government talks a lot about upholding international law,” Yap said. “We have our prime minister bemoaning the deterioration of the international rules-based order. They condemn the settlements as illegal. They talk about taking steps, taking action. This is a chance for the Canadian government to actually take action.”

The complaint, filed on behalf of six Canadians, compiles photos, social media posts and promotional materials of condo projects in the occupied West Bank being marketed at various real estate events from 2024 to 2026.

One photo of an Israeli real estate company’s booth at the 2024 Great Israeli Real Estate Event in Montreal suggests the company promoted condo projects in Ma’ale Adumim and Adam, two Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, alongside Israeli real estate.

The company’s booth advertised the developments with the message of finding one’s “dream home in Israel.”

Another company’s booth at the same 2024 event advertised it as “your real estate agency in Jerusalem” while listing the locations of four Israeli settlements in the West Bank and two Israeli cities. The company is more explicit on its website, stating that its homes in West Bank settlements in Efrat, Mitzpe Yericho and Ma’ale Adumim are in Israel.

A Canadian marketing firm that helps North Americans buy Israeli real estate similarly lists a West Bank condo development as being in Israel on its website but it used more ambiguous language at a real estate event in Toronto.

The firm promoted a condo project in the Givat HaMatos settlement, located in East Jerusalem in the occupied West Bank, at the 2026 Israel Real Estate Briefing in Toronto with the tag line “own a piece of Jerusalem.”

The lawyers behind the complaint to the Competition Bureau argue the ambiguity isn’t enough to absolve the companies.

Under Canadian law, courts use a “general impression” test to determine if an advertisement is false or misleading. If an ad is literally true but omits essential information that would influence a consumer’s behaviour, it could violate the Competition Act.

The lawyers argue that by promoting these properties at events titled the Great Israeli Real Estate Event and the Israeli Real Estate Briefing, and omitting mention of their true location in internationally-contested territories, the real estate companies misled Canadians.

Ariel Katz, a competition law expert who reviewed the complaint but was not involved in its filing, said he finds the evidence compelling, but couldn’t say if the Competition Bureau would be likely to launch an inquiry.

“This is a highly politically charged topic, right? So whatever decision they make, they might be under enormous pressure,” Katz said.

Israel contends that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are not illegal because of Jewish people’s historic connection to the land.

While the complaint deals with allegations of false advertising, Katz said the West Bank properties that were allegedly promoted at the events are considered illegal under international law, and Ottawa could ban the marketing of such properties altogether.

The lawyers behind the complaint say they’re leaving the door open for future legal action that could target the illegality of the properties themselves.

The Canadian Press asked Global Affairs Canada if the sale of West Bank property is illegal in Canada and whether Canadians could be legally liable if they purchased such property but did not receive an answer before publication.

Emily Schaeffer Omer-Man, founder of Global Echo Litigation Center, said her law firm has been monitoring a “circuit” of Israeli real estate events in the United States, United Kingdom, France and other countries.

She said the complaint before the Competition Bureau gives Canada a chance to “pave the way” for other countries to follow suit in cracking down on these kinds of sales.

Marlee Wasser, one of the complainants, said she’s a granddaughter of Holocaust survivors and sees the sale of Israeli settlement property in Canada as normalizing genocide in the West Bank, where Israeli settlers have attacked and displaced Palestinians.

She added that protests outside Israeli real estate events have been used to justify restricting peoples’ right to protest in Canada.

The mayor of Vaughan, Ont., proposed a bubble zone bylaw – which ultimately passed – restricting protests near places of worship, schools and hospitals shortly after protesters demonstrated outside a local synagogue where an Israeli real estate event was being held in 2024.

For Basel Adra, an Oscar award-winning documentarian and community engagement manager at Global Echo Litigation Center, the complaint before the Competition Bureau is a chance for Canada to do “what’s right.”

The Palestinian filmmaker of “No Other Land,” a documentary about the destruction of a West Bank community, says there’s daily construction in the West Bank, building homes and roads for Israeli settlers.

While he’s never personally seen a Canadian settler in the West Bank, Adra said there are settlers from all over the world, especially America, in Israeli communities in the region.

Adra said he’s been attacked by settlers several times, and last week a group of settlers invaded his family’s land and cut down olive trees.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said in June there was an average of six settler attacks on Palestinian communities in the West Bank each day of 2026 thus far that caused casualties or property damage, higher than any other year on record.

stories.title: Canadian woman dies in U.S. over fear of crossing through B.C. for medical care
stories.summary: A U.S. immigration lawyer says his Canadian client died after failing to seek medical care over fears she would be detained and deported by U.S. authorities.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
A U.S. immigration lawyer says his Canadian client died after failing to seek medical care over fears she would be detained and deported by U.S. authorities.

Paige Adamson, 61, died on Sunday in the U.S. enclave of Point Roberts , which is only accessible from Canada.

Lawyer Len Saunders said Adamson was injured and needed medical attention, but was afraid to cross through B.C. to Bellingham to seek medical care because the last time she returned to the U.S., she was interrogated and threatened with deportation.

“She was advised not to leave the U.S., because if she did leave and come back, she could be taken into custody and taken down to Tacoma,” Saunders said.

“So she was fearful of reentering Canada, then trying to return to the United States.”

Point Roberts does have a medical clinic, but it is not clear if Adamson sought medical attention there or if she could be treated there.

Saunders said Adamson had lived in the U.S. for 14 years and had a green card, but was expected to attend a deportation hearing next month.

He added that about six other Canadians living in Washington State are facing deportation.

There is no word on what caused Adamson’s death, but friends said she had fallen recently and died at home on Sunday.

stories.title: German Canadian Club rolling out the barrel for Oktoberfest in London
stories.summary: They will be tapping the kegs and dancing to polka music at the German Canadian Club on Cove Road in London.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
They will be tapping the kegs and dancing to polka music at the German Canadian Club on Cove Road in London.

2,000 people are expected over the weekend in the big tent for the annual Oktoberfest.

“We’ve been doing this here for 94 years”, said Mike Marienwald, one of the organizers for the event. “But for the past 4 years its been under the big tent and it’s fantastic.”

Besides the traditional German music and dancers, there’s the food and it’s more than just homemade pretzels.

“We have German sausage and schnitzel, sauerkraut, red cabbage, potato salad and goulash,” said Friedhelm Hoffmann, organizer.

With six bands on hand there will be plenty of dancing and of course Oktoberfest wouldn’t be complete without the suds.

“The beer is Paulaner and it comes directly from Germany and it takes two weeks to get here by boat,” said Hoffman.

Due to the success of Oktoberfest, Saturday night is sold out however, tickets are still available for Friday night, Saturday afternoon which is family day and Sunday afternoon.

“I say Oktoberfest is now universal, but this celebration we have here is one of a kind,” said Marienwald.
