stories.title: Who will be Toronto’s next mayor? What to know before the Oct. 26 election
stories.summary: A look at Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford’s platforms, voting information and when results are expected
stories.author: Arisa Valyear
stories.content:
Toronto, like the rest of Ontario, is holding municipal elections on Monday, which includes a vote for the mayor of Canada’s most populous city. Incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow and former urban planner and Beaches-East York councillor Brad Bradford are leading the race in the days approaching the election. An additional 51 candidates are on the ballot, with Chris Alexander still listed, despite having dropped out of the race earlier this month. (His announcement was made too late for his name to be removed.) A full list of candidates can be viewed on the City of Toronto website .

Before Torontonians head to the polls on Monday, here’s what to know about the 2026 mayoral election, including platform highlights, how to vote and when the results will be announced.

Of the 53 names on the ballot this year, Ms. Chow and Mr. Bradford are the two primary candidates. Opinion polls through the campaign gave Ms. Chow a solid lead but survey results have been tightening in recent weeks, suggesting a potential dead heat.

On Oct. 21, a Liaison Strategies survey – a national public opinion research firm – found the race almost deadlocked. A random sampling of 1,000 Toronto residents for the poll between Oct. 18 and 19 showed Mr. Bradford at 49 per cent of the vote, and Ms. Chow at 47 per cent. The poll has a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Ms. Chow has been openly endorsed by environmentalist David Suzuki, Blue Rodeo front man Jim Cuddy, former Ontario premier Kathleen Wynne and Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles. She has also received support from singer Leslie Feist and writer and filmmaker Sarah Polley.

Mr. Bradford’s supporters include Rush’s Geddy Lee , former Postmedia CEO Paul Godfrey, Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke and former federal cabinet minister Lisa Raitt.

In September, Premier Doug Ford openly praised and supported Ms. Chow and their working relationship. “We’re going to continue supporting the mayor. She’s doing an incredible job. So, read between the lines,” he said at a news conference on Sept. 16. A day later, Mr. Ford’s office issued a statement saying the comments were not a formal endorsement .

On public safety: Public safety has been a hallmark of both mayoral campaigns, with Mr. Bradford and Ms. Chow vowing to add more officers to Toronto’s police force. Mr. Bradford pledged to take his seat on the Toronto Police Service Board (a civilian oversight body that oversees the Toronto Police Service) and to place officers at every TTC station.

Ms. Chow’s campaign promises that she will invest in youth violence prevention programs and add 15,000 new youth jobs through the Toronto Youth Employment Strategy. Mr. Bradford has pledged to add the same number of jobs for youth in the private sector.

On affordability and taxes: Mr. Bradford says he will initiate a one-year property tax freeze, eliminate the land transfer tax on principal residences below $1.1-million and cut residents’ water bills by up to 25 per cent. Ms. Chow’s office said she would keep property taxes “at or around” the rate of inflation. She’s also pledged to ban surveillance pricing on groceries (algorithm-driven pricing that varies based on customer-collected data), reduce taxes for independent grocery stores and more. In addition to free snacks and breakfasts offered to students through the city’s school food program, Ms. Chow has vowed to extend the program to lunches if re-elected.

On tenant-related issues: A Bad Landlords Task Force will be part of Ms. Chow’s mandate if voters choose to re-elect her. Buildings will be canvassed and inspected by enforcement officers and court-ordered repair requests will be issued, according to her campaign website . Ms. Chow promises that if the landlord refuses the repairs, the city will complete them and bill the landlord.

Mr. Bradford is pledging a number of initiatives, including a promise to enforce Toronto’s pre-existing renoviction bylaw via a public dashboard that tracks the city’s building applications, licences issued, investigations, charges and more. He’s also pledging a “costed staffing plan” for Toronto Building to ensure tenant complaints are met with in-person dispatchers. Additionally, Mr. Bradford is promising a “cool room” in every rental home and an expansion of the Air Conditioner Benefit for low-income seniors and those with medical needs.

On traffic and transit: Mr. Bradford is putting forward a plan to reduce congestion in the city that includes getting shovels in the ground on the Eglinton East LRT by 2030. He is also promising to remove bike lanes on Bloor Street West in Etobicoke (from South Kingsway to Resurrection Road) and remove Scarborough’s red bus lanes on Kingston Road, Morningside Avenue, Kennedy Road and Midland Road. He’s proposed transitioning the Kingston Road and Morningside Avenue from red lanes to HOV.

Mr. Bradford has also said he would push forward a public safety plan on e-bikes, including banning mini-motorcycles in bike lanes, painted lanes and elsewhere.

Ms. Chow has also promised to maintain the TTC fare freeze for a fourth year, as well as initiate free TTC rides for those who pay for 10 trips in a week. Additionally, she’s proposed AI traffic lights, hiring traffic agents, establishing a new command centre for city traffic operations and better co-ordination on construction and road closures, as well as the aforementioned fare freeze and maximum cost on rides per week.

Voters must be Canadian citizens, at least 18 years old and Toronto residents. Non-residents are eligible, but only if the voter or their spouse own or rent property in the city. Eligible voters can vote only once, regardless of how many properties they own or rent in Toronto. Those with multiple Toronto addresses can use the City’s MyVote tool to determine their voting location.

Election day is Oct. 26, with polls opening at 10 a.m. and closing at 8 p.m. Advance voting took place from Oct. 6 to 11, and the cut-off date for mail-in ballots was Oct. 14.

Voters must bring identification that shows their name and address. The City of Toronto accepts driver’s licences, digital phone bills, mortgage statements, void cheques and more. Passports are not considered an acceptable piece of identification since they don’t include addresses. A full list of eligible forms of identification can be found on the City of Toronto website .

Voting closes at 8 p.m. on Oct. 26, with results expected to be released throughout Monday night.

With reports from Jeff Gray, Patrick White and Laura Stone.

content_blocks.text: How close is the race between Brad Bradford and Olivia Chow?

content_blocks.text: Of the 53 names on the ballot this year, Ms. Chow and Mr. Bradford are the two primary candidates. Opinion polls through the campaign gave Ms. Chow a solid lead but survey results have been tightening in recent weeks, suggesting a potential dead heat.

content_blocks.text: On Oct. 21, a Liaison Strategies survey – a national public opinion research firm – found the race almost deadlocked. A random sampling of 1,000 Toronto residents for the poll between Oct. 18 and 19 showed Mr. Bradford at 49 per cent of the vote, and Ms. Chow at 47 per cent. The poll has a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

content_blocks.text: How do their platforms compare?

content_blocks.text: On public safety: Public safety has been a hallmark of both mayoral campaigns, with Mr. Bradford and Ms. Chow vowing to add more officers to Toronto’s police force. Mr. Bradford pledged to take his seat on the Toronto Police Service Board (a civilian oversight body that oversees the Toronto Police Service) and to place officers at every TTC station.

content_blocks.text: Ms. Chow’s campaign promises that she will invest in youth violence prevention programs and add 15,000 new youth jobs through the Toronto Youth Employment Strategy. Mr. Bradford has pledged to add the same number of jobs for youth in the private sector.

content_blocks.text: On affordability and taxes: Mr. Bradford says he will initiate a one-year property tax freeze, eliminate the land transfer tax on principal residences below $1.1-million and cut residents’ water bills by up to 25 per cent. content_blocks.text: Who is eligible to vote in the Toronto election?
content_blocks.html: Who is eligible to vote in the Toronto election?

content_blocks.text: Voters must be Canadian citizens, at least 18 years old and Toronto residents. Non-residents are eligible, but only if the voter or their spouse own or rent property in the city. Eligible voters can vote only once, regardless of how many properties they own or rent in Toronto. Those with multiple Toronto addresses can use the City’s MyVote tool to determine their voting location.

stories.title: Jeffrey Rath, Mitch Sylvestre said to be fired from Alberta Prosperity Project weeks ago
stories.summary: News of the pair’s ‘for cause’ removal was kept quiet to avoid derailing the referendum campaign, movement leader says
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Separatist leaders affiliated with the Alberta Prosperity Project say the group’s two most prominent members – Jeffrey Rath and Mitch Sylvestre – were fired by the organization six weeks ago, but the news was kept quiet to avoid derailing the referendum campaign .

In a Thursday night social-media post, Tanya Clemens said the App’s board, of which she says she’s a member, had decided in mid-September to remove Mr. Sylvestre and Mr. Rath from their roles with the group “for cause.”

“I didn’t want an internal dispute to become the story when we were trying to have such an important conversation with Albertans about their future,” Ms. Clemens said, explaining why they didn’t publicize the news earlier.

Ms. Clemens said that there were concerns about who was given access to the App’s membership database, how the group approached the referendum campaign, and how the two men conducted themselves leading the movement.

“I believe there are legitimate questions about whether some of those actions complied with their legal obligations, and I think those questions deserve a legal examination,” she said.

The revelation of their apparent firings sparked a wave of finger-pointing and accusations in the wake of Monday’s referendum result, in which 75 per cent of the Alberta electorate rejected the separatist cause and chose to remain a part of Canada.

Mr. Sylvestre says he is still in charge of the Prosperity Project; Mr. Rath described meetings that unseated him and Mr. Sylvestre as “imaginary.”

Chris Scott, an independence advocate who says he sits on the board, said the APP terminated Mr. Sylvestre as chief executive and Mr. Rath as legal counsel on Sept. 14. They were removed as directors 10 days later, he said.

There is documentation, Mr. Scott says, to prove that the two men had been removed from the group. In a video, he enumerated a list of allegations that he says led the board to dismiss Mr. Sylvestre and Mr. Rath.

Alberta’s separatist movement has spent more than a year in the international spotlight. But after Monday’s sharp rebuke from the electorate, it has started to look inward.

On Tuesday, Premier Danielle Smith said it was time to turn a new page and reiterated her commitment to not holding another referendum on the issue as long as she’s Premier.

The next day, she issued an ultimatum to separatists within her United Conservative Party intent on transforming the UCP into a vehicle for the movement: accept the results or leave the party.

Some independence leaders responded by pledging support for Ms. Smith while others have turned against her.

Mr. Sylvestre and Mr. Rath have said that they won’t leave the UCP and will push to elect allies to the provincial board of the party at its annual meeting next month.

Other separatists, including Mr. Scott and Keith Wilson, a lawyer who co-founded the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, have lined up behind the Premier.

Mr. Scott, in a video posted Thursday night, said he plans to run for a UCP board position at the late-November AGM. But he contends that a separatist takeover of the party would be “a disaster.”

“I do not believe that this plan to try and take over the UCP and create a separatist party after we had only 25 per cent of Albertans even vote to have a conversation about Alberta independence – I do not believe that will bear fruit at all,” he said.

Mr. Scott alleged that the App’s membership list was given to two conservative strategists during the referendum campaign. Mr. Sylvestre previously told The Globe and Mail that it is a list of roughly 250,000 supporters.

Communications from the APP have continued under Mr. Sylvestre’s name. A Wednesday e-mail from the group thanking supporters for their efforts was signed in his name.

On Thursday night, Mr. Rath suggested that the board meetings never happened.

“Neither Tanya Clemens or Chris Scott were lawfully registered as board members at the time these imaginary board meetings were held,” Mr. Rath wrote on social media, signing off as general counsel for the group.

Mr. Scott replied, writing that Mr. Rath approved meeting minutes in November, 2025, that showed Mr. Scott and Ms. Clemens were board members.

Mr. Rath replied: “Chris you aren’t a director. Get over it.”

stories.title: 'Transformed the landscape': What Terry Fox taught cancer doctors
stories.summary: In the years since Fox's death, researchers have focused on precision-targeted genetic treatment that has led to “curative outcomes.”
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
Toronto — “The poster child is lung cancer,” said Lillian SIU, a clinical trial specialist at Toronto’s Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, over a bistro lunch on Thursday with Terry Fox’s family members and a few of the cancer researchers who will benefit from a record-breaking new donation in Fox’s name, publicly announced an hour earlier.

In cancer medicine, SIU said, many of the diagnostic concepts are blunt and outdated, such as describing lung cancer as either “small cell” or “non small cell” based on how tumours appear under a microscope. It makes every patient’s tumour seem the same as all the others, and so their prospects seem similar.

But lung cancers are not all the same. Now, the genetics of tumours can be sequenced, and often this reveals they come in genetic subtypes that respond to certain treatments and not others.

Tumours might look the same, but to genomic sequencing they reveal their specific “vulnerabilities,” SIU said. So, in this emerging science, lung cancer is recognized as having many subgroups, and people who recently might have been expected to die quickly can now expect to live 10 years or more if they have a certain type that is vulnerable to a targeted genetic intervention.

Cancer is a genetic disease, SIU said. As with lung cancer, so with all the others. The cancer that killed Terry Fox, for example, osteosarcoma, had a 20 per cent survival rate after five years in 1980, when he ran his Marathon of Hope. Today it is 80 per cent.

This is the promise of “precision medicine,” the underlying principle of the Marathon of Hope Cancer Centres Network, the manifestation of Fox’s dream that was the focus of Thursday’s announcement.

Marco Marra, a medical geneticist at the University of British Columbia and Terry Fox Leader in Cancer Genome Science, called it “the ultimate tribute” to Fox, a network connecting the research of more than 1,300 scientists among 57 cancer centres across the country.

These include melanoma researcher Ian Watson of McGill University. He said melanoma has gone from a cancer that was incurable to one that responds to precision-targeted genetic treatment leading to “curative outcomes.” His goal is that these outcomes should be within reach for all late-stage melanoma patients. Precision medicine, based on biomarkers in each patient’s genome, has “transformed the landscape,” he said.

“We know the model works, but now we need to take it further,” said Marra.

The first phase of Marathon of Hope network, launched in 2019, involved research on tissue samples from biobanks. Some were from patients who gave samples prospectively when they were diagnosed. Some were from people who were dead.

Phase two will use genomic information directly from actual current patients, and use to this to devise targeted treatments focused on the promise of genetic biomarkers for personalized medicine.

“It’s more challenging,” SIU said, and the goal remains lofty, to sequence the genome of each patient newly diagnosed with cancer. There can be inefficiencies, seeking out more genetic information than is needed to treat the cancer. But the promise is massive.

Now, it is also well-funded by both government and philanthropy.

At the ceremony Thursday in Toronto to unveil a new short video that illustrates the network’s activities, with music by Leslie Feist, the Terry Fox Foundation announced its largest single gift ever.

Larry Tanenbaum, a part owner of the Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment, and his wife Judy, gave $25 million from their family foundation, which is matched by the federal government for a $50-million influx of actual funding for this phase two of the network.

“Progress is real, but it is not yet enough,” Tanenbaum said.

As a thank you, former Toronto Maple Leafs captain Darryl Sittler presented the Tanenbaums with a framed photograph of Sittler presenting Fox with Sittler’s 1980 NHL All Star Game jersey before a welcoming crowd at Toronto’s City Hall during his run in 1980.

“I was Terry’s hero. He was mine,” Sittler said.

“He asked all of us to keep going,” said Fred Fox, Terry’s older brother.

He said Terry did not run to become a famous Canadian hero, though he did, perhaps the greatest in that pantheon. He simply ran to raise money to help people with cancer, with a provisional goal of a dollar from every Canadian, which in 1980 would have been just shy of $25 million, a total that has been long since surpassed. The Terry Fox Foundation has raised more than $1 billion since he died on June 28, 1981.

Fox ran every day for 143 days in the summer of 1980, from the Atlantic Ocean to the north shore of Lake Superior, where he learned his cancer had spread to his lungs, forcing him to stop. A statue marks this place today, outside Thunder Bay. He died the next year, age 22, the youngest ever Companion of the Order of Canada, its highest rank.

A newly released documentary film, Run Terry Run, is compiled of behind the scenes footage from his run, from reels that had been unwatched for years.

His niece, Kirsten Fox, who works in community development for the Terry Fox Foundation in B.C. and Yukon, said they were rediscovered in storage at a sweetspot in time, early enough that they had not physically deteriorated, and late enough that the cost of digitization had become affordable. She described some of its poignant scenes, including Terry leaving the highway for a swim and the boyish joy he displayed.

After the ceremony Thursday, a long-time Terry Fox Run participant strode away across the cobblestones of Toronto’s historic Distillery District.

“He and I would have made a great pair,” said Bill McGuire, meaning he still has his right leg, and Terry had his left.

McGuire lost his leg to a similar type of cancer, sarcoma. He has done the Terry Fox Run for 37 years, first on two legs, then in a wheelchair and for the past two decades on just one leg and crutches, as he does not like his prosthetic. Lately, he has raised about $20,000 each time.

In 1980, McGuire was an avid runner, even doing marathons, and he recalls being amazed to hear of this young guy running across the country. “He wasn’t looking to sell ads on his T-shirt. He’s just doing it,” McGuire said. He was a “quintessential Canadian.”

McGuire reflects that his own experience with cancer has made him a better person, no longer “borderline jaded” as before, but grateful, hopeful, and appreciative of the chance to carry on Fox’s fundraising legacy.

stories.title: Albertans’ vote reignites push from provinces for more control over immigration
stories.summary: Roughly 1 million Albertans voted yes to immigration reform questions on the referendum ballot Monday. While the results are preliminary and non-binding, they have sparked a renewed conversation about immigration policy across Canada.
stories.author: Heather Wright
stories.content:
Toronto - Roughly 1 million Albertans voted ‘Yes’ to immigration reform questions on the referendum ballot Monday. While the results are preliminary and non-binding, they have sparked a renewed conversation about immigration policy across Canada.

“I think the provinces have always wanted a greater say in immigration policy, it’s a concurrent power under the constitution,” said Geoffrey Cameron, a political science professor at the University of Guelph.

“So I think what we’re hearing from other provinces right now is they want the federal government to give them more of a say over the numbers they get in existing programs,” he said.

While Ottawa sets the overall annual immigration levels and makes the final decisions on admissibility, each year provinces and territories nominate a set number of economic immigrants through Provincial Nominee Programs. Quebec is the exception as it sets its own immigration targets, selects its own economic immigrants and runs its own settlement services.

When asked in Ottawa on Wednesday whether Alberta could get a deal similar to Quebec’s, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s response was brief. “We’ll see,” he said in French.

Alberta’s premier says her province is looking at Quebec’s deal with Ottawa in terms of shaping a revamp in its own deal with the federal government.

“We have been looking for some inspiration from Quebec’s 1991 Canada Quebec accord. They have had this kind of authority over economic migrants for some time,” Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said Thursday. Smith noted that it is early in this process but that conversations with the prime minister have begun.

“We talked yesterday morning, and he is accepting that Albertans want to have a more collaborative approach between his government and ours on issues of immigration,” she said. “And so I told him that we would be working on putting a proposal together.”

After several years of cutting immigration numbers, Ottawa has recently hinted levels could soon see a modest increase, citing slow population growth and the government’s infrastructure plans, which require a surge in skilled workers.

Speaking in Ottawa on Wednesday, Carney stressed that any change would be “sustainable.”

“It’s a question of making those judgments in a way that works for Canadians, works for Canada and is sustainable,” he said. “I just want to underscore we will not budge from overall levels that are sustainable. We’re getting them to that level now.”

Provinces call for more immigrants, not fewer

Alberta is not alone in wanting more autonomy. While experts say most provinces are asking Ottawa for more immigrants, not fewer, they want a greater say in who comes.

“They want a larger share of total immigration to Canada to be allocated to them, where they can select on the basis of occupations they see as in demand in their provinces,” Cameron said.

Both Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Labrador have come out recently calling for more say in who comes to their provinces.

“Prince Edward Island supports a greater provincial and territorial role in immigration planning and decision-making,” the province said in a statement. “We understand our labour market needs and the pressures on public services, so we should have a meaningful role in shaping immigration levels and programs.”

In a statement Newfoundland and Labrador said “as immigration is a shared constitutional responsibility, Newfoundland and Labrador has continued to advocate for a stronger provincial role in economic immigration.”

Meanwhile Saskatchewan says it “has and will continue to push for greater control over immigration.” The province says with respect to immigration, our focus is on meeting the specific skilled labour needs of our industries.” It adds that “this complements and does not replace the need to train more people here at home to address skilled labour needs…”

Premiers will meet in Ottawa on Monday, with immigration expected to be among the many issues discussed.

“We talked yesterday morning, and he is accepting that Albertans want to have a more collaborative approach between his government and ours on issues of immigration,” she said. “And so I told him that we would be working on putting a proposal together.”

After several years of cutting immigration numbers, Ottawa has recently hinted levels could soon see a modest increase, citing slow population growth and the government’s infrastructure plans, which require a surge in skilled workers.
Speaking in Ottawa on Wednesday, Carney stressed that any change would be “sustainable.”

“It’s a question of making those judgments in a way that works for Canadians, works for Canada and is sustainable,” he said. “I just want to underscore we will not budge from overall levels that are sustainable. We’re getting them to that level now.”
Provinces call for more immigrants, not fewer
Alberta is not alone in wanting more autonomy. While experts say most provinces are asking Ottawa for more immigrants, not fewer, they want a greater say in who comes.
“They want a larger share of total immigration to Canada to be allocated to them, where they can select on the basis of occupations they see as in demand in their provinces,” Cameron said.
Both Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Labrador have come out recently calling for more say in who comes to their provinces.

“Prince Edward Island supports a greater provincial and territorial role in immigration planning and decision-making,” the province said in a statement. “We understand our labour market needs and the pressures on public services, so we should have a meaningful role in shaping immigration levels and programs.”

In a statement Newfoundland and Labrador said “as immigration is a shared constitutional responsibility, Newfoundland and Labrador has continued to advocate for a stronger provincial role in economic immigration.”

Meanwhile Saskatchewan says it “has and will continue to push for greater control over immigration.” The province says with respect to immigration, our focus is on meeting the specific skilled labour needs of our industries.” It adds that “this complements and does not replace the need to train more people here at home to address skilled labour needs…”
Premiers will meet in Ottawa on Monday, with immigration expected to be among the many issues discussed.

stories.title: U.S. ambassador offers Canada help almost a week after Wainwright tragedy
stories.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says the United States has offered to help following the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says the United States has offered to help following the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta.

Four soldiers were killed and 39 injured on Oct. 17 when a fire that began during a training exercise on an anti-grenade launching range was picked up by fierce winds.

The military says the fire swept in less than a minute about a kilometre away to where a different training exercise was taking place on the base about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

Twenty-seven soldiers remain in hospital, including 13 in critical condition, many of them with severe burns.

In a social media post today almost a week after the tragedy, Hoekstra said the U.S. government has made a formal offer of assistance and resources to Canada’s federal government to help support the recovery of soldiers affected by traumatic burns “should it be deemed necessary.”

Our prayers remain with all affected by the tragedy at @CanadianForces Base Wainwright. To support the recovery of soldiers affected by traumatic burns, the U.S. government has made a formal offer of assistance and resources to the Government of Canada, should it be deemed… — Ambassador Pete Hoekstra (@USAmbCanada) October 23, 2026

The military says there are three different investigations into the tragedy and could not say when more answers will be available about how the tragedy occurred.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026

With files from Kyle Duggan and Nick Murray in Ottawa

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadian woman died after declining hospital care in U.S. due to deportation fear, son says
stories.summary: Paige Adamson, a U.S. permanent resident, refused to seek treatment after she fall at her home in Point Roberts, Wash.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The son of a Canadian woman who died after a fall at her home in Point Roberts, Wash., earlier this month said she refused to seek treatment, fearing she would be detained by U.S. authorities or prevented from returning to the country.

Dylan Adamson said his 61-year-old mother, Paige Adamson, was afraid to leave the United States because immigration authorities had recently commenced deportation proceedings, alleging she illicitly voted in a state election in 2018.

Health care is limited in Point Roberts, which is cut off from the rest of the United States and accessible by land only by travelling through British Columbia.

Adamson said his mother refused to be taken to a hospital because she was afraid of what might happen if she crossed the border.

He said he only learned of his mother’s fall after speaking with a firefighter who attended the scene of her death last Sunday, within a week of the accident.

“I’m just at a loss. Just because of a vote, my mom is dead. Just because of a stupid technicality, my mom is dead,” he said in an interview on Friday.

The fall came about a month after Paige Adamson, a permanent resident of the United States who had been living in Point Roberts since 2012, was heading home from a dinner to celebrate her birthday in nearby Tsawwassen, B.C., when U.S. border officials held her for hours and questioned her about voting in the country.

Dylan Adamson said his mother did not recall registering to vote or casting a ballot, and the ensuing deportation proceedings sent her into a “panic.”

On top of that stress, he said dental troubles had been affecting her ability to eat.

“She was very skinny when I saw her. I saw her a couple months ago. So, she was very frail and she tripped.”

Adamson said he understood from speaking with her friends in Point Roberts that she tripped and fell on a vacuum, striking her side, “around her stomach, hip side.”

He said he had also learned that paramedics who saw his mother before her death told her she needed to go to a hospital, but she signed a form declining further care.

“She would have went to the hospital. The only reason she didn’t is out of fear,” said Adamson, who lives in Maple Ridge, B.C.

Had he known about his mother’s fall, he said he would have driven to see her right away.

He said he expects to learn more details about her death from a medical examiner on Saturday.

Immigration lawyer Len Saunders said he first heard from Paige Adamson just after she was put into deportation proceedings over allegations she had illicitly registered to vote and cast a ballot in Washington state.

Saunders provided The Canadian Press with photos he said Adamson shared with him showing a transcript of her questioning by a border officer, along with a notice requiring her to appear before an immigration judge in Seattle on Nov. 4.

The notice alleged Adamson “falsely represented” herself as a U.S. citizen in order to register to vote in Whatcom county, then voted in the Nov. 6, 2018 election.

She was subject to removal from the United States on that basis, it said.

Saunders, who is based in Blaine, Wash., said he told Adamson he hadn’t been taking on deportation cases since the closure of a courtroom in the city some years ago, but he referred her to lawyers in Seattle and they kept in touch.

He said Adamson told him she was “losing sanity” over the ordeal.

Saunders said Adamson told him she hadn’t been feeling well, but she was afraid of travelling to see her doctor in Bellingham, Wash., because of the deportation action.

The lawyer said he was “shocked” to learn of her death.

“Quite frankly, when I first heard that, I thought it was suicide. I thought, you know, she’s just so stressed out,” he said.

Saunders said Adamson’s case is part of a recent U.S. government crackdown on people who aren’t American citizens but who have registered to vote, sometimes unknowingly, or cast a ballot without realizing they were ineligible to do so.

“You go into (the Department of Motor Vehicles) and you get your driver’s licence, and quite often they register you to vote,” he explained.

“People think, ‘Okay, if I can register, I can vote.’ So, a lot of these people did register and did vote, but it wasn’t done maliciously. They were naive.”

In the past, Saunders said U.S. authorities wouldn’t typically seek to deport such people as long as they removed themselves from voter lists and attested to registering or voting without knowing they shouldn’t have.

“I’ve never seen someone put in deportation proceedings at a port of entry as a permanent resident for voting. I’ve never seen it in 25 years.”

But that’s changed, Saunders said, noting the shift follows a U.S. government directive earlier this year to look into voter lists and enforce non-compliance.

Saunders said he’s heard of several cases of Canadians who are permanent residents of the United States travelling to Canada last month, then facing questions about possibly registering to vote and voting as they returned home.

He said border officials advised each of them against leaving the country “because they could be at risk when they come back of being put into custody and taken on a one-way trip” to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centre.

“Like, these officers put the fear of God into all of these Canadians,” he said.

“When you go down to one of these detention centres, it’s not (for) days, it’s weeks, or months,” he added.

The transcript of Adamson’s Sept. 15 questioning shows the U.S. border officer asked her whether she had ever filled out a voter registration form in the country, to which she replied “No,” although she did recall a state-level ballot.

“Did they send you a ballot to vote?” the officer asked.

“Yes. It comes with everybody’s mail. I don’t remember when it was. Ten years ago, maybe,” Adamson replied.

Asked whether she received a ballot at her most recent address in Point Roberts, Adamson said, “No. I don’t know. It’s junk mail. I just threw it away. Right?

“Sorry, I am tired,” the transcript reads.

Saunders said he has helped many Canadians become U.S. citizens by naturalization over the years, including those who’d registered to vote or voted, telling them “as long as we can show that you deregistered,” the process should be successful.

“We’d deregister them, we’d do an affidavit, I would take them to their interview in Seattle when they became an American, and it was a non-issue.”

Now, Saunders said he won’t submit someone’s naturalization application if there’s any indication they May have registered to vote or voted in the United States.

“I don’t want to be liable for someone getting deported.”

stories.title: Son says Canadian died in U.S. after declining hospital care due to deportation fear
stories.summary: The son of a Canadian woman who died after a fall at her home in Point Roberts, Wash., earlier this month says she refused to seek treatment as she feared she would be detained by U.S. authorities or prevented from returning to the country.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The son of a Canadian woman who died after a fall at her home in Point Roberts, Wash., earlier this month says she refused to seek treatment as she feared she would be detained by U.S. authorities or prevented from returning to the country.

Dylan Adamson says his 61-year-old mother was afraid to leave the United States because immigration authorities had recently commenced deportation proceedings, alleging she illicitly voted in a state election in 2018.

Health care is limited in Point Roberts, which is cut off from the rest of the United States and accessible by land only by travelling through British Columbia, and Adamson says his mother, Paige Adamson, refused to be taken to a hospital because she feared being unable to return home due to the deportation action.

Adamson says he only learned of his mother’s fall after speaking with a firefighter who attended the scene of her death last Sunday, within a week of the accident.

The fall came about a month after Paige Adamson, a U.S. permanent resident, was heading home from a birthday dinner in nearby Tsawwassen, B.C., when American border officials held her for hours and questioned her about voting in the country.

Dylan Adamson says his mother did not recall registering to vote or casting a ballot, and the ensuing deportation proceedings sent her into a “panic.”

Adamson, who lives in B.C., says he’s been told paramedics who saw his mother before her death said to her that she needed to go to a hospital, but she signed a form declining further care because she was afraid of crossing the border.

“I’m just at a loss. Just because of a vote, my mom is dead. Just because of a stupid technicality, my mom is dead.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Sarnia Mayor Bradley raises concerns as U.S. deploys drones on Great Lakes waterways
stories.summary: The mayor of Sarnia is raising concerns after the U.S. deployed surveillance drones in the Great Lakes. It comes after at least one of the unmanned vessels was spotted in the St. Clair River recently between Sarnia and Port Huron.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
The mayor of Sarnia is raising concerns after the U.S. deployed surveillance drones in the Great Lakes. It comes after at least one of the unmanned vessels was spotted in the St. Clair River recently between Sarnia and Port Huron.

“This is a huge slap again to Canada on our sovereignty, and the lack of communication,” said Mike Bradley, who saw the unusual watercraft, and wondered what it was.

It turns out, what he saw was a so-called Saildrone. Bradley says he has since learned that U.S. Coast Guard, under the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, is deploying the unmanned watercraft.

Six of the 33 foot drone sailboats are patrolling the Great Lakes gathering data.

“We have no understanding of what they’re going to do with the information. And we have thousands of boaters, thousands of boaters who use this area for boating. And now they’ve got this drone following them, sailing around, collecting their information. They’re saying they’re looking for drug smuggling, and immigration issues, and all that. But there’s really no evidence that’s a big problem on the great lakes,” exclaimed Bradley.

The drone patrols come as relations between the two countries have reached their lowest point in decades.

The presence of the strange watercraft is unnerving to some Sarnia area residents.

“It’s their right to guard their border, but I wish they’d keep an eye on other things instead of Canada. I don’t think we’re anything to worry about. As if we’re going to attack them,” said Ed Daly

“I really don’t get what’s going on with the States, and I wish things were a lot different. We’ve always had a good relationship,” remarked Craig Cormier.

“You’re invading my privacy, kind of, right? I don’t think that’s right,” said Patricia Myers.

Paul Samson, head of the Canada U.S. Relations program at the Centre for International Governance and Innovation, says Canadians shouldn’t necessarily be alarmed.

“My assessment of this is just that’s kind of like posturing, and it’s trying to be annoying. Sure, they might be taking photographs and doing some kind of intelligence gathering, but it’s actually just for the purpose of kind of asserting power and kind of being bullying,” he explained.

In the meantime, unrelated to the Saildrone surveillance, U.S. President Trump is scheduled to appear at a rally in Port Huron, just across the river from Sarnia on Sunday.

stories.title: In this rural Alberta district, a slim majority back separation despite provincial result
stories.summary: The referendum question in the west-central riding saw 48.8 per cent of votes to remain in Canada, 51.2 per cent agreeing to a second ballot
stories.author: Temur Durrani
stories.content:
Standing on his acreage near the eastern foothills of the Canadian Rockies, Jim Fowler is breathing a long sigh of relief. The 68-year-old, whose homestead is adorned with pro-unity flags, simply refused to believe that a majority of his province would ever feel the need to separate from his country.

His love for Canada is unabashed, he said, and his patriotism goes way back: His mother was one of more than 800,000 women dubbed bomb girls, who worked out of secret plants on the Allied front during the Second World War to manufacture munitions.

Mr. Fowler, however, lives in the west-central town of Rocky Mountain House. He knows how his neighbours and friends think; conversations with some of them have been incredibly difficult in the past few months. “We try not to talk about it too much,” he said, “but it’s been hard to escape our political differences.”

And so, despite his own convictions, he’s not surprised that his neck of the woods is one of the only two ridings in the province where a slim majority of voters supported the beginning of a legal process toward a binding secession referendum.

Provincially, 75 per cent of Albertans voted to stick with Canada. But people in the electoral district of Rimbey–Rocky Mountain House–Sundre were so split that, by final count, the difference was just 615 votes. The separation question saw 48.8 per cent of votes for Alberta to remain in Canada and 51.2 per cent agreeing to a second secession ballot.

The battle over the province’s future has led to divisiveness at dinner tables, coffee shops, schools, grocery stores, playgrounds and community centres, residents in the small municipalities that comprise the riding told The Globe and Mail. They worry, they said, that these ruptures will be lasting.

“Let me give you an example,” Mr. Fowler said on a sunny afternoon, just days after the referendum. “One of my friends here drove by a little while ago, pulled in, and saw my place. And he says to me, ‘I see you got those stupid Canadian flags there, eh?’ ”

He understands the impulse. “Ottawa has not been the easiest to work with or kindest to Alberta. It’s true that they don’t seem to understand our way of life,” Mr. Fowler said. “But come on, we can’t be serious about separatism being the solution to that frustration.”

Across this rural district of around 34,000 registered electors, the idea of Alberta sovereignty is certainly not new.

With its rich farming and fur trade history, growth over the past century here has been largely propelled by oil, gas, coal and lumber. For many who supported separatism, their vote wasn’t necessarily a desire to dissolve Canadian unity altogether, they said. Instead, it served as a vehicle to voice long-standing angst over federal energy policies, equalization payments and a perceived lack of autonomy for Alberta.

“I think it’s high time we changed the status quo,” said Nichole Stewart, who runs the Lighthouse, a holistic healing centre on Rocky Mountain House’s downtown strip.

She describes her town of about 8,000 as being proud of its quietude, “especially compared to those big, louder-than-necessary cities like Edmonton.” Cozy cafés, gift shops and Western-wear clothing stores line its main street. Cats roam freely in neighbourhoods. And just under 20 churches of various denominations are part of the predominantly blue-collar area.

The referendum, though, has caused deep fissures. “There’s just so much judginess now that you can’t even have an Alberta flag flying without someone needing to say something about it to you,” the 40-year-old Ms. Stewart said.

Case in point: Shane Boniface, the mayor of Rocky Mountain House, declined an interview because he said any more commentary on the matter would create further hurdles for his community to move on from the referendum.

But for Ms. Stewart, separatism is a serious affair. Her fury toward Ottawa reached its peak amid COVID-19 lockdowns, during which she felt vaccine mandates stripped away her privacy and freedom of choice.

“I’m just so sick of just complacency all the time,” she said. “We keep sending all this money elsewhere to Ukraine and wherever, and we’re adding so much more to this country than getting back from it. I just feel like Alberta – we’re so strong on our own, we don’t really need the rest of Canada to have our own strong economy and people.”

A short drive away, past multiple anti-abortion billboards on the highway, the strife is especially palpable in the town of Rimbey – population 2,500.

Ghosts, goblins and ghouls of the inflatable and kitschy variety have quickly replaced much of the outdoor decor of many homes for Halloween after the largest electoral event in Alberta’s history. But pro-separation signs are still aplenty. They can be spotted in cul-de-sacs of single-family units, outside large ranches and even scattered haphazardly on several streets.

One sign in Nugent, just outside Rimbey, declares Alberta as the 51st State: “We’re Done,” it boldly asserts with American insignia. In town, another hollers: “Quebec GOT TO Vote, WHY Can’t WE?”

“You have to understand, we’ve been just done by this woke agenda of the radical left and Carney’s Liberals, with all this money for left-wing causes like Lgbtq initiatives or the BLM movement,” said Ron Lapka, 56, as his wife, Sue Ceasar, also 56, nodded along.

“There’s a saying that’s attributed to Al Capone that goes: You can get more done with a kind word and a gun than you can get with a kind word alone. And when it comes to Alberta’s independence, kind words just aren’t cutting it for us any more,” he said.

Ms. Ceasar, who works as a community nurse while her husband has retired, believes most of Rimbey voted for separation. “There’s maybe just one guy there that has those unity signs,” she chuckled, pointing at a house nearby. “The rest of us are on the same page. We’re mostly home-schoolers, churchgoers and, you know, just very grassroots-oriented.”

In fact, there are many pro-unity signs exhibited across Rimbey. But while people in those homes were willing to explain their thinking, they said they were afraid to provide their names to The Globe out of fear of backlash from their neighbours.

John Willow was the only exception. “Everyone should have a right to express their opinion. That’s the point of democracy,” said the 59-year-old, whose Forever Canadian sign stands out in a corner filled with Independent Alberta flags.

“I just want people now to accept this result and move on with their lives. We all need to learn how to respect each other again and learn to move forward, as hard as that May be for some more than others.”

stories.title: Winnipeg police suspend Crime Stoppers tips following data breach
stories.summary: Winnipeg police have suspended their use of Crime Stoppers. Instead, it said it will try to accommodate anonymous information submitted via its tip line when possible.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The Winnipeg Police Service is suspending its use of Crime Stoppers, following a data breach at the organization.

Police said they were made aware that some data related to Winnipeg was included in the breach. A data breach at Crime Stoppers, an agency that accepts anonymous information about crime, was the subject of an investigation by CBC published Wednesday , which reported that more than 1.5 million tips were affected.

“The Winnipeg Police Service has suspended its use of Crime Stoppers while we review the information that has become available and assess the additional safeguards and security measures being implemented by Crime Stoppers and its service providers,” police said.

Police said that Crime Stoppers operates as a separate, independent organization and manages its own platforms, including the ones that manage information submissions.

“We recognize the important role Crime Stoppers has played in supporting community safety and investigations over many years and appreciate the seriousness with which it is approaching this matter,” Winnipeg police said.

To submit information to police during the suspension of Crime Stoppers services, people can make online reports or call the Winnipeg police tip line at 204-986-6178. When possible, police said they will try to accommodate requests for anonymity.

stories.title: Halifax man faces new charges in U.S. Consulate bomb threat case
stories.summary: Ali Assakereh was arrested in August for allegedly placing a propane tank and flammable liquids in his car and parking it near the consulate
stories.author: Devin Stevens
stories.content:
Halifax Regional Police have laid two additional charges against the man accused of threatening to bomb the city’s U.S. Consulate in August.

Ali Assakereh, 54, was arrested Aug. 10 for allegedly placing a propane tank and flammable liquids in his car and parking it near the consulate, prompting evacuations across a large section of downtown Halifax.

He was already facing charges of mischief and uttering threats, as well as a charge under a section of the Criminal Code that prohibits threats against internationally protected people, including diplomats.

The Crown has said it considers the latter offence to be terrorist activity, which allows it to seek an increased penalty of up to life in prison.

Police said in a news release on Friday that they’ve laid two additional charges related to hoax terrorist activity.

Assakereh is scheduled for a court appearance next month.

stories.title: St-Pierre Plamondon pledges $28-million for Quebec homelessness response
stories.summary: Government plans to add 1,000 new spots in warming centres and emergency shelters across the province
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
Quebec’s premier promised Friday to bring a new-found political will to the battle against homelessness, as he announced $28-million in emergency funding.

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon announced the new funding on Friday in Montreal, in his first major announcement since he was sworn in as premier on Wednesday. St-Pierre Plamondon, who has also named himself homelessness minister, said the money is in addition to $18-million that was previously allocated, bringing the total amount to $46-million.

“I think in order to succeed, we need to be facing directly the nature of the problem, not pretend it’s not there,” he told journalists. “It’s the first step. Then you need to take political will, to show political will. And that’s what we’re doing today.”

St-Pierre Plamondon said the money will go toward adding 1,000 new spots in warming centres and emergency shelters across Quebec. The Montreal area, which is home to nearly half of the province’s unhoused population, is slated to get $18-million out of the total.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada joined the premier for the announcement at the shelter Accueil Bonneau.

She said she is thrilled the new provincial government has made homelessness its first order of business. She said the city had come up with a homelessness strategy for the winter, but needed $20-million from the provincial government to implement its plan.

“All our Montrealers, our citizens, our Quebeckers that are in the streets deserve to have a roof over their heads and that’s what we have to aim for,” said the mayor. “Having this announcement today makes that a reality and it’s the first step in the shared objective.”

The announcement comes days after media reported that a woman experiencing homelessness died in Sorel-Tracy, Que. The premier said the woman tried to access a shelter she frequently visited, but there was not enough room for her.

“That’s not a narrative we can accept as a society. It doesn’t work,” said St-Pierre Plamondon. “Quebec . . . is among the wealthiest places in the world, and we will do whatever it takes to restore dignity for everyone.”

Quebec’s chief coroner has ordered a public inquiry into the deaths of five individuals experiencing homelessness in Montreal between Sept. 23, 2025 and March 25, 2026.

The Quebec coroner’s office has investigated the deaths of 500 people experiencing homelessness since 2020, according to St-Pierre Plamondon.

The premier added that the government will hold a summit on homelessness, as proposed by former premier Pauline Marois, in early 2027. The summit will gather key actors from the community sector and all levels of government to identify the causes of homelessness and their remedies.

“There’s addiction, mental health problems, the housing crisis,” said the premier, adding he has been inspired by the “housing-first” model seen in Finland and Texas where those experiencing homelessness are provided with homes and psychosocial support.

While Friday’s announcement is solely for emergency services, he said his government will work to implement long-term solutions, such as providing community organizations with recurring funding and building 20,000 subsidized housing units.

He said the previous administration had prioritized “affordable” housing run by the private sector and non-profit organizations.

“Social housing is making a comeback,” said St-Pierre Plamondon. “I remember that, right from the start of the 2018 term, they claimed that the private sector would take care of it. And look where that got us.”

He also pledged to implement policies to “balance” the housing market. He said that once housing supply outpaces demand, landlords and developers will no longer have an incentive to have high tenant turnover or to hike rents beyond what is recommended by the province’s housing tribunal.

“Until we restore the market to equilibrium, it’s going to be difficult because we can’t monitor the honesty of each of the nine million people on our territory,” he said.

Alia Hassan-Cournol, executive director of women’s shelter La rue des Femmes, said she feels optimistic about the new sums, despite not yet knowing how much will be allocated to her organization.

“We really hear the change in tone,” she said.

stories.title: Trump, seeking to help Maine Sen. Susan Collins, exempts some Canadian imports from his 50% tariffs
stories.summary: Washington (AP) — President Donald Trump, seeking to help Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a tough reelection battle in Maine, is exempting some imports — including plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery — from the 50% tariffs he slapped on $20 billion worth of Canadian products over the summer. The changes will take effect Oct. 30.
stories.author: Paul Wiseman The Associated Press
stories.content:
Washington (AP) — President Donald Trump, seeking to help Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a tough reelection battle in Maine, is exempting some imports — including plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery — from the 50% tariffs he slapped on $20 billion worth of Canadian products over the summer. The changes will take effect Oct. 30.

The White House said the president was seeking to offset “the burden to U.S. commerce while better serving the public interest.’’

stories.title: We're hearing more about rabies in the news. Here's what to know about the virus
stories.summary: Toronto - Public health officials in B.C. and Quebec are dealing with rabies in wild animals that have come into contact with people or domestic pets. In Vancouver, it was a single skunk but in parts of Quebec, there is an outbreak of rabies in raccoons that has transmitted the virus to three cats.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Public health officials in B.C. and Quebec are dealing with rabies in wild animals that have come into contact with people or domestic pets. In Vancouver, it was a single skunk but in parts of Quebec, there is an outbreak of rabies in raccoons that has transmitted the virus to three cats.

On Friday, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia), which is responsible for national rabies surveillance, said that the number of animal cases fluctuates from year to year, but preliminary data suggests “increased rabies activity in raccoons, particularly in Quebec, is a major factor contributing to the higher number of confirmed rabies cases reported this year.”

stories.title: Elks, Riders turn to backups for season finale
stories.summary: It's a battle of the backups Saturday when the Edmonton Elks face the Saskatchewan Roughriders in their CFL regular-season finale.
stories.author: Jeff DeDekker
stories.content:
Regina – It’s a battle of the backups Saturday when the Edmonton Elks face the Saskatchewan Roughriders in their CFL regular-season finale.

With both teams already assured of playoff berths, they’re resting several starters, including their starting quarterbacks.

Jack Coan, in his third season with the Riders, will make his first CFL start in place of Trevor Harris. A former starter at Wisconsin and Notre Dame, the 27-year-old quarterback has patiently waited for his opportunity to lead the Riders.

“I think it was difficult for me at first, but as I’ve gone on, I really had a change of perspective,” said Coan, who last started a professional game with the Xfl’s San Antonio Brahmas in 2023. “This is such a great experience, and I have a chance to get better each and every day, no matter what.”

The Elks (13-4) have clinched first place in the West and will host the division final on Nov. 7, while the Riders (9-8) have yet to determine their playoff path. A Saskatchewan win Saturday would secure third place and a division semifinal matchup against the B.C. Lions, but the Riders could also finish fourth and cross over to the East Division playoffs.

Coan has appeared in just four games with the Riders, completing 14 of 31 passes for 153 yards and one touchdown. He’s also rushed 16 times for 54 yards and three touchdowns.

Riders head coach Corey Mace has watched Coan develop under offensive coordinator Marc Mueller and has high expectations for the quarterback.

“I’m looking for him to command and go out and execute. He’s been in the system for three years, he’s bided his time, and he’s just been waiting for an opportunity,” said Mace. “This is an important game for us, and it’s an important game for him, so I’d like to see him operate at his best.”

Mace has decided not only to rest Harris but to keep the veteran quarterback out of uniform Saturday. Saskatchewan’s depth chart lists Tommy Stevens and rookie Brayden Schager as backups. Schager, who has spent the season on the practice roster, could see his first regular-season action.

The Riders are also resting receiver KeeSean Johnson, running back A.J. Ouellette, defensive lineman James Vaughters, offensive lineman Jermarcus Hardrick and defensive back DaMarcus Fields.

The Elks are also making a quarterback change, with Taylor Powell starting in place of Cody Fajardo, who will dress but isn’t expected to play.

Unlike Coan, Powell has CFL starting experience. The 28-year-old went 4-6 in 10 starts over three seasons with the Hamilton Tiger-Cats.

Powell, who signed with the Elks as a free agent in the off-season, will make his first CFL start since Aug. 17, 2024, when he suffered a concussion while playing for Hamilton in a 47-22 loss to Edmonton.

Powell says he’s learned from watching Fajardo lead the Elks to first place in the West.

“It doesn’t have to be flashy to play championship football. It just comes down to protecting the ball, and we talk a lot about just playing through the smoke,” said Powell, who has 2,874 career passing yards with 14 touchdowns and nine interceptions.

The Elks are resting 12 players Saturday, including defensive lineman Malik Carney, defensive back Tyrell Ford, receiver Austin Mack and tailback Justin Rankin.

Remarkable Season: A win Saturday would give the Elks 14 victories, their most since winning 16 games in 1989. Edmonton would also double its win total from 2025, when it finished 7-11.

Passing Fancy: Harris is the only remaining CFL quarterback to have attempted every pass for his team this season, a streak that will end when Coan starts Saturday. The 40-year-old ranks 10th in CFL career passing yards with 43,067 in 212 games. Harris has thrown for a career-high 5,370 yards this season, surpassing 5,000 for the second time.

Deee-Fence: The Elks boast the CFL’s top-ranked defence, allowing 24.8 points per game through 17 contests. Edmonton last led the league in fewest points allowed in 2015.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Canada plunges into early flu season as vaccines begin to roll out
stories.summary: Experts agree that vaccination is the best way to prevent serious illness and complications from influenza.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Infectious disease experts say Canada’s flu season started about seven weeks earlier than usual this year, but with proper interventions, there is no need to sound the alarm bells just yet.

According to data from Health Canada, 6.1 per cent of tests detected influenza in the week ending Oct. 17.

For the same week in 2025, 0.8 per cent of tests came back positive.

Health Canada defines the epidemic threshold at five per cent, a mark Canada didn’t surpass until mid-November last year.

“It’s still within the range of not being unusual, but it absolutely started earlier,” Dr. Isaac Bogoch, an infectious disease specialist at the University Health Network in Toronto, told Global News.

Bogoch said it is difficult to know exactly why flu season started earlier this year but noted that Australia’s flu season ended later than usual.

B.C. has been hit particularly hard early in the season with positivity rates between 10 and 15 per cent seen as early as late-September, according to one expert.

“It started also on the west coast of the United States where it’s warmer all the way down in California,” Dr. Brian Conway, medical director of the Vancouver Infectious Disease Centre, told Global News. “So evidently, the virus has entered from the Pacific Rim, perhaps the southern hemisphere that’s ending its flu season and it has made its entry into the West Coast, particularly into British Columbia.”

Doctors say the dominant flu strain this year is of the H1N1 strain, which is what caused the 2009 swine flu epidemic.

H1N1 is a subtype of Influenza A and spreads the same as any other respiratory virus.

Bogoch said typically a year dominated by H1N1 sees less hospitalizations than an H3N2 dominant year.

“But I can’t stress this enough, at an individual level, it doesn’t matter. Influenza is influenza is influenza and you might feel really ill,” he said.

South of the border, American health officials have identified a genetic mutation of the H1N1 virus that is spreading amongst the population. The G155E mutation allows the virus to better evade human immunity.

Dr. Jesse Papenburg, an infectious disease specialist at the Montreal Children’s Hospital, told Global News he has not heard of the mutation being in Canada yet, but ultimately it would not change the way that health officials respond.

“We saw that last year where there was an H3N2 strain subclade K that had very important genetic changes, changes in places that we know are important for the immune system to be able to recognize it,” he said. “At the same time, what we saw in the field was that the vaccines still offered protection that was somewhere in a similar ballpark to what we see usually with estimates ranging from 40 to 60 per cent.”

The vaccine this year does cover the H1N1 strain, but Papenburg said it is impossible to know just how effective it’ll be until people start getting it.

“The truth is that we will only know how well the vaccine works once we’ve proved enough cases to be able to do interim analyses on vaccine effectiveness in the field,” he said. “People should never be basing their decision on whether or not they should get vaccinated based on the fact of this.”

Regardless of the strains the vaccine targets, Papenburg said what it does reduce is the severity of the illness, decreasing the likelihood of hospitalization or death but almost 50 per cent.

“We’d love to see it higher than that. But at the same time, reducing your risk, especially if you happen to be in one of the vulnerable populations where the risk is already really high, it’s really substantial,” he said.

Most provinces begin launching vaccine appointments around mid-October, but several provinces began offering the shot earlier this year.

P.E.I. and Nova Scotia began offering vaccine appointments in early October. B.C. began offering the vaccine to vulnerable populations on Oct. 5 and expanded that to all people on Oct. 13. Alberta told pharmacies to start giving out doses as soon as they arrived, ahead of the Oct. 19 launch date.

Saskatchewan and Manitoba have been offering flu shots since Oct. 13 with Quebec following suit one week later. Ontario is currently offering vaccines to vulnerable populations with eligibility opening to everyone on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Ottawa ‘disappointed’ after union announces strike votes for 120,000 workers
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal government says it's "disappointed" after Canada's largest federal public service union announced 120,000 workers will take part in nationwide strike votes starting next month.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government says it’s “disappointed” after Canada’s largest federal public service union announced 120,000 workers will take part in nationwide strike votes starting next month.

The Public Service Alliance of Canada says voting will take place from Nov. 16 to Jan. 22.

The union and Treasury Board have been in contract negotiations for a year and a half and Psac in May called a government wage offer of less than one per cent per year “insulting.”

The Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat says it’s “disappointed” the union has chosen to proceed with a strike vote while the groups are still working through the mediation process.

The government says that for the past year and a half, it has engaged with the union on all of its proposals and several days of mediation recently led to progress on certain points.

The Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat says it respects the right to strike but the best deals are reached at the bargaining table.

stories.title: Hyland Cinema and Forest City Film Festival Team Up for the First Time in Festival History
stories.summary: This year, Hyland Cinema and the Forest City Film Festival come together for the first time. This is an import...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
This year, Hyland Cinema and the Forest City Film Festival come together for the first time.

This is an important development for Forest City’s independent cinema scene, bringing together the Forest City Film Festival’s celebration of filmmakers and the Hyland Cinema’s unique film experiences.

The film festival features films from Southwestern Ontario, Canada, and internationally. Meanwhile, the Hyland Cinema has made a name for itself as a home for art house, independent, and international films.

“We talked about what shows our audience and the festival’s audience would be interested in to maximize how many people we can get to come to a show.” Dalton Pike, a manager at the Hyland, stated.

The Hyland Cinema has long offered London audiences an alternative to the traditional multiplex experience, with programming that includes independent productions, international titles and special screenings.

The Forest City Film Festival shares a similar focus on bringing distinctive stories to the big screen, with programming that celebrates regional talent while introducing audiences to films from further afield.

By working together, the two organizations can help expand the reach of festival programming and reinforce the importance of accessible, community-focused cinema.

On Saturday, October 16th, the Hyland had its first screening of the festival. They premiered Club Kid , the directorial debut by comedian and actor Jordan Firstman.

“We thought Club Kid would work well with our crowd, because we do a lot of films that are in talks to be Academy Award-nominated,” Pike said.

The Hyland Cinema also screened Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney on Wednesday. Following a Q&A with the Canadian director Matthew Rankin.

Club Kid and Ladies and Gentlemen, Brain Mulroney is shown on a poster at the Hyland Cinema on Wednesday, October 21st. Callum Contursi/XFM News

The collaboration comes as the Forest City Film Festival continues to grow as a showcase for regional filmmaking. The festival runs from October 15 to 25, featuring screenings, filmmaker conversations and industry events across London.

Source: Forest City Film Festival

stories.title: Israeli companies misled Canadians about West Bank real estate, complaint alleges
stories.summary: A group of lawyers and civil society members have filed a complaint with the Competition Bureau over Israeli real estate events in Toronto and Montreal, alleging that illegal properties were marketed to Canadians under false pretences.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A group of lawyers and civil society members have filed a complaint with the Competition Bureau over Israeli real estate events in Toronto and Montreal, alleging that illegal properties were marketed to Canadians under false pretences.

The complaint alleges at least four Israeli real estate companies and one Canadian marketing firm promoted properties in occupied Palestinian territories in the West Bank while misleading consumers to believe they were in Israel.

The Competition Bureau says it will review the complaint filed by Global Echo Litigation Center and the Canadian Lawyers for International Human Rights and determine if an investigation into the companies is warranted.

James Yap, president of the lawyers’ association and a Windsor university law professor, said Canadians who May have purchased West Bank properties could be opening themselves up to serious legal consequences under international law, such as complicity in war crimes.

Canada and much of the international community have long held that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal and an obstacle to peace in the Middle East.

The territory has been occupied by Israel since 1967, but settlement activity has significantly increased since the onset of the latest war in the Gaza Strip, triggered by the 2023 Hamas attack on Israel that killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. Israel’s retaliatory offensive has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and displaced most of Gaza’s two million residents.

Ottawa advised Canadian businesses in August to avoid engaging with Israeli settlements, warning that failing to do so could open them up to legal and financial risk.

“The Canadian government talks a lot about upholding international law,” Yap said. “We have our prime minister bemoaning the deterioration of the international rules-based order. They condemn the settlements as illegal. They talk about taking steps, taking action. This is a chance for the Canadian government to actually take action.”

The complaint, filed on behalf of six Canadians, compiles photos, social media posts and promotional materials of condo projects in the occupied West Bank being marketed at various real estate events from 2024 to 2026.

One photo of an Israeli real estate company’s booth at the 2024 Great Israeli Real Estate Event in Montreal suggests the company promoted condo projects in Ma’ale Adumim and Adam, two Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, alongside Israeli real estate.

The company’s booth advertised the developments with the message of finding one’s “dream home in Israel.”

Another company’s booth at the same 2024 event advertised it as “your real estate agency in Jerusalem” while listing the locations of four Israeli settlements in the West Bank and two Israeli cities. The company is more explicit on its website, stating that its homes in West Bank settlements in Efrat, Mitzpe Yericho and Ma’ale Adumim are in Israel.

A Canadian marketing firm that helps North Americans buy Israeli real estate similarly lists a West Bank condo development as being in Israel on its website but it used more ambiguous language at a real estate event in Toronto.

The firm promoted a condo project in the Givat HaMatos settlement, located in East Jerusalem in the occupied West Bank, at the 2026 Israel Real Estate Briefing in Toronto with the tagline “own a piece of Jerusalem.”

The lawyers behind the complaint to the Competition Bureau argue the ambiguity isn’t enough to absolve the companies.

Under Canadian law, courts use a “general impression” test to determine if an advertisement is false or misleading. If an ad is literally true but omits essential information that would influence a consumer’s behaviour, it could violate the Competition Act.

The lawyers argue that by promoting these properties at events titled the Great Israeli Real Estate Event and the Israeli Real Estate Briefing, and omitting mention of their true location in internationally-contested territories, the real estate companies misled Canadians.

Ariel Katz, a competition law expert who reviewed the complaint but was not involved in its filing, said he finds the evidence compelling, but couldn’t say if the Competition Bureau would be likely to launch an inquiry.

“This is a highly politically charged topic, right? So whatever decision they make, they might be under enormous pressure,” Katz said.

Israel contends that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are not illegal because of Jewish people’s historic connection to the land.

While the complaint deals with allegations of false advertising, Katz said the West Bank properties that were allegedly promoted at the events are considered illegal under international law, and Ottawa could ban the marketing of such properties altogether.

The lawyers behind the complaint say they’re leaving the door open for future legal action that could target the illegality of the properties themselves.

The Canadian Press asked Global Affairs Canada if the sale of West Bank property is illegal in Canada and whether Canadians could be legally liable if they purchased such property but did not receive an answer before publication.

Emily Schaeffer Omer-Man, founder of Global Echo Litigation Center, said her law firm has been monitoring a “circuit” of Israeli real estate events in the United States, United Kingdom, France and other countries.

She said the complaint before the Competition Bureau gives Canada a chance to “pave the way” for other countries to follow suit in cracking down on these kinds of sales.

Marlee Wasser, one of the complainants, said she’s a granddaughter of Holocaust survivors and sees the sale of Israeli settlement property in Canada as normalizing genocide in the West Bank, where Israeli settlers have attacked and displaced Palestinians.

She added that protests outside Israeli real estate events have been used to justify restricting peoples’ right to protest in Canada.

The mayor of Vaughan, Ont., proposed a bubble zone bylaw – which ultimately passed – restricting protests near places of worship, schools and hospitals shortly after protesters demonstrated outside a local synagogue where an Israeli real estate event was being held in 2024.

For Basel Adra, an Oscar award-winning documentarian and community engagement manager at Global Echo Litigation Center, the complaint before the Competition Bureau is a chance for Canada to do “what’s right.”

The Palestinian filmmaker of “No Other Land,” a documentary about the destruction of a West Bank community, says there’s daily construction in the West Bank, building homes and roads for Israeli settlers.

While he’s never personally seen a Canadian settler in the West Bank, Adra said there are settlers from all over the world, especially America, in Israeli communities in the region.

Adra said he’s been attacked by settlers several times, and last week a group of settlers invaded his family’s land and cut down olive trees.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said in June there was an average of six settler attacks on Palestinian communities in the West Bank each day of 2026 thus far that caused casualties or property damage, higher than any other year on record.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.
