One photo of an Israeli real estate company’s booth at the 2024 Great Israeli Real Estate Event in Montreal suggests the company promoted condo projects in Ma’ale Adumim and Adam, two Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, alongside Israeli real estate.
The company’s booth advertised the developments with the message of finding one’s “dream home in Israel.”

Another company’s booth at the same 2024 event advertised it as “your real estate agency in Jerusalem” while listing the locations of four Israeli settlements in the West Bank and two Israeli cities. The company is more explicit on its website, stating that its homes in West Bank settlements in Efrat, Mitzpe Yericho and Ma’ale Adumim are in Israel.

A Canadian marketing firm that helps North Americans buy Israeli real estate similarly lists a West Bank condo development as being in Israel on its website but it used more ambiguous language at a real estate event in Toronto.

The firm promoted a condo project in the Givat HaMatos settlement, located in East Jerusalem in the occupied West Bank, at the 2026 Israel Real Estate Briefing in Toronto with the tagline “own a piece of Jerusalem.”
The lawyers behind the complaint to the Competition Bureau argue the ambiguity isn’t enough to absolve the companies.

Under Canadian law, courts use a “general impression” test to determine if an advertisement is false or misleading. If an ad is literally true but omits essential information that would influence a consumer’s behaviour, it could violate the Competition Act.

The lawyers argue that by promoting these properties at events titled the Great Israeli Real Estate Event and the Israeli Real Estate Briefing, and omitting mention of their true location in internationally-contested territories, the real estate companies misled Canadians.

Ariel Katz, a competition law expert who reviewed the complaint but was not involved in its filing, said he finds the evidence compelling, but couldn’t say if the Competition Bureau would be likely to launch an inquiry.
“This is a highly politically charged topic, right? So whatever decision they make, they might be under enormous pressure,” Katz said.
Israel contends that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are not illegal because of Jewish people’s historic connection to the land.

While the complaint deals with allegations of false advertising, Katz said the West Bank properties that were allegedly promoted at the events are considered illegal under international law, and Ottawa could ban the marketing of such properties altogether.
The lawyers behind the complaint say they’re leaving the door open for future legal action that could target the illegality of the properties themselves.

The Canadian Press asked Global Affairs Canada if the sale of West Bank property is illegal in Canada and whether Canadians could be legally liable if they purchased such property but did not receive an answer before publication.

Emily Schaeffer Omer-Man, founder of Global Echo Litigation Center, said her law firm has been monitoring a “circuit” of Israeli real estate events in the United States, United Kingdom, France and other countries.
She said the complaint before the Competition Bureau gives Canada a chance to “pave the way” for other countries to follow suit in cracking down on these kinds of sales.

Marlee Wasser, one of the complainants, said she’s a granddaughter of Holocaust survivors and sees the sale of Israeli settlement property in Canada as normalizing genocide in the West Bank, where Israeli settlers have attacked and displaced Palestinians.
She added that protests outside Israeli real estate events have been used to justify restricting peoples’ right to protest in Canada.

The mayor of Vaughan, Ont., proposed a bubble zone bylaw – which ultimately passed – restricting protests near places of worship, schools and hospitals shortly after protesters demonstrated outside a local synagogue where an Israeli real estate event was being held in 2024.

For Basel Adra, an Oscar award-winning documentarian and community engagement manager at Global Echo Litigation Center, the complaint before the Competition Bureau is a chance for Canada to do “what’s right.”

The Palestinian filmmaker of “No Other Land,” a documentary about the destruction of a West Bank community, says there’s daily construction in the West Bank, building homes and roads for Israeli settlers.
While he’s never personally seen a Canadian settler in the West Bank, Adra said there are settlers from all over the world, especially America, in Israeli communities in the region.
Adra said he’s been attacked by settlers several times, and last week a group of settlers invaded his family’s land and cut down olive trees.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said in June there was an average of six settler attacks on Palestinian communities in the West Bank each day of 2026 thus far that caused casualties or property damage, higher than any other year on record.

stories.title: Toyota Canada recalls more than 24,000 vehicles over seating issue
stories.summary: Toyota is recalling more than 24,000 vehicles due to a seating issue that May increase the risk of injury in a crash.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Toyota is recalling more than 24,000 vehicles in Canada due to an issue with seats that May increase the risk of injury in a crash.

The recall affects Sienna Hybrid minivans from model years 2022 to 2026, according to a notice published by Transport Canada on Oct. 20 and updated Oct. 23.

The notice said the mechanisms that lock the second-row seat recliners in position May disengage under certain conditions when a seatbelt pretensioner activates.

As a result, the seatbacks could move during a crash, potentially increasing the risk of injury to occupants.

Toyota advised owners not to use the second-row seats to transport passengers until the recall repairs have been completed.

The automaker will notify affected owners by mail and instruct them to take their vehicles to a dealership. Dealers will update the software in the supplemental restraint system (SRS) electronic control unit, which controls the seatbelt pretensioners.

Owners can check whether their vehicle is affected by entering their vehicle identification number (VIN) on Toyota Canada’s recall lookup page ⁠ or contact Toyota at 1-888-869-6828 for more information.

stories.title: B.C. election at a glance: Hand count for most votes due to snap call's 'logistics'
stories.summary: It's the last full day of campaigning in British Columbia's election ahead of final voting day Saturday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Friday is the last full day of campaigning in British Columbia’s election ahead of final voting day Saturday.

Here’s a look at some of the latest developments on the campaign trail.

Hand count for most ballots

Elections BC has confirmed that votes cast on election day will be tallied manually, in a departure from 2024, when electronic tabulators were used to count paper ballots for the first time in a general election.

Elections BC spokesperson Colleen Hildebrandt says the decision to go with a hybrid model, where advance votes are counted with a tabulator and votes on election day are counted by hand, was made as soon as the snap election was called two years early because of the tight timeline.

About 600 tabulators were used for advance voting across just over 300 locations she said, but scaling up for election day would have required between 2,500 and 3,000 machines deployed across 1,200 voting locations.

Each machine has technical requirements, including testing, verifying for accuracy as well as training staff to use them, she said.

“So, the time it takes to actually get … that to happen, it requires a lot of training and materials and shipping of supplies and testing that and making sure everything is ready to go. And to do that across 1,200 locations is quite complex.”

Elections BC’s annual report lists technology procurement as something that is typically done 12 months ahead of a scheduled election.

When a snap election was called in 2020, Elections BC used the same type of model, Hildebrandt said.

Votes counted with electronic tabulators are expected to be the first results reported after voting closes at 8 p.m.

Elections BC also says the election-night count will not include absentee or mail-in ballots, which will be tallied at the final count scheduled for Nov. 6 to Nov. 10.

Elections BC’s report on the 2024 election says electronic tabulation allowed the first preliminary results to be reported within five minutes of polls closing, and 59 per cent of preliminary results to reported within half an hour.

It said that in past elections first results typically started to be reported around 45 minutes after polls closed.

Doerkson rallies with clark and mccallum

The B.C. Conservatives held a rally in Surrey on Thursday night, with mayor-elect Doug McCallum endorsing Lorne Doerkson as the province’s next premier.

Also present at the rally were former B.C. premier Christy Clark, and former Surrey mayors Linda Hepner and Dianne Watts.

McCallum told the rally that he was standing with people who had changed Surrey and it was time to change B.C.

The 82-year-old McCallum is about to embark on his third separate stint as Surrey’s mayor, after defeating incumbent Brenda Locke in the Oct. 17 municipal elections.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Rogers plans to charge extra for bill payments with a credit card
stories.summary: Rogers says it will begin charging most customers across Canada a 1.6 per cent processing fee next year for bill payments made using a credit card.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Rogers says it will begin charging most customers across Canada a 1.6 per cent processing fee next year for bill payments made using a credit card.

Those changes will take effect starting Jan. 17, 2027, and do not apply in Quebec, according to the company’s website.

Separately, the company said Friday that it was looking for “alternatives” to cover a loss tied to a Crtc ban from earlier this year.

Telecom companies, in March, were banned from charging customers fees to cancel or change internet and cellphone plans.

Rogers says charging a fee to process bill payments using a credit card is “increasingly common,” and it “reflects the fees we are charged by credit card companies.”

“When customers choose to pay their bill by credit card, we are charged a payment processing fee. These costs have gone up nearly 40 per cent since 2020, and we now pay about $150 million a year in fees,” said a Rogers spokesperson in a statement to Global News.

“It’s increasingly common across many sectors for a charge to apply when consumers choose to pay by credit card – and this change helps us recover our costs.”

The spokesperson also confirmed to Global News that if a bill payment is made using the Rogers Bank Mastercard, the same processing fee will still be charged.

To avoid being charged an additional fee, Rogers says customers can make bill payments using other methods, including a debit card or direct debit from bank accounts.

On Friday, Rogers reported earnings to shareholders from its most recent quarter , which included overall revenue of $5.44 billion, up from $5.35 billion in the same quarter last year.

But revenue from its mobile division declined slightly.

The average monthly revenue per mobile user was $55.22, down from $56.70 a year ago, and the company’s chief financial officer Glenn Brandt pointed the finger at the Crtc, saying the regulator’s ban on fees to cancel or change plans had the “largest impact.”

“The purpose of those setup fees was exactly that — to offset costs of account changes or new accounts coming on,” Brandt told analysts on a conference call Friday.

“The charge disappeared (due to) the Crtc decision. The costs don’t.”

Brandt said Rogers put in place some “early initiatives” during the quarter to recover some of those costs, but “there’s still more work to do.”

He added: “We’re now moving back to finding alternatives for covering those costs.”

Telecommunications companies in Canada, for the most part, are allowed to charge these sorts of fees depending on the type of service that is being billed.

Rogers’ rival Telus, in 2022, faced pushback from the Crtc for requesting to charge similar fees to its customers, specifically for home phone services.

“We received a request from a company that wanted to charge a fee to customers paying by credit card for services we regulate. We refused that request,” the Crtc says on its website from 2024.

“For services we don’t regulate (such as mobile and Internet services and phone services in urban centres), companies don’t need our approval to charge a fee.”

It adds: “We’re very concerned about companies who charge their customers credit card processing fees on services we do not regulate. If companies start or continue this practice, we’ll explore means to take action since it affects vulnerable customers.”

Global News reached out to the Crtc Friday regarding the new credit card fees Rogers plans on charging its customers.

“Affordability is an important consideration for the Crtc. The Crtc has taken action to increase choice and competition and help lower the cost of telecommunications services for Canadians. We will continue to advance this work so that Canadians benefit from more affordable, reliable, and high-quality services.”

– with a file from The Canadian Press

stories.title: What we know and don't know about the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: Edmonton - Military officials provided an update Thursday on the investigation into the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright earlier this month.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Military officials provided an update Thursday on the investigation into the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright earlier this month.

Officials say four soldiers were killed and dozens more were injured when a fire swept over the base on Oct. 17. On Thursday, officials said 27 injured soldiers remained in various hospitals, with 13 in critical condition. Twelve others have since been released.

The dead have been identified as: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

Here’s what we know and don’t know so far about the events of Oct. 17.

When and how did the fire start?

The fire started “as a result of a training event that was taking place on the anti-grenade launcher range,” Brig.-Gen. Vanessa Hanrahan, head of the military police, told Thursday’s press briefing. She said the training was “routine.”

It’s not clear exactly how the fire started. Officials said no gas infrastructure was damaged. Hanrahan told reporters there was “no indication that there was an explosion of any kind that resulted in the fire” or that an explosion was triggered by the fire.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland of the 1st Canadian Division told reporters that, just before 4 p.m. local time, the fire spread to the pairs range, where soldiers train in pairs to provide covering fire.

Why did they continue training despite the fire?

Military officials wouldn’t touch on that question when pressed by reporters Thursday. Hanrahan said it’s part of the military police investigation.

“The investigative team is still out there determining all of the decision-making that happened once the fire started, up to and including when they responded to the incident involving the tragedies of today,” she said.

“So it would be inappropriate for me to speculate now about all of those decisions and any of the other aspects of the investigation. Once the investigative team has time to review all the evidence and do what it is they need to do, I’ll be in a better position to provide accurate information.”

How did the fire spread so quickly?

On Thursday, Rutland said high winds contributed to the fire’s spread.

“Uncommonly high winds took a pre-existing range fire towards the pairs range and it overtook (the soldiers’) position,” he said.

“The fire crossed the base fire guard and burned beyond the training base.”

Hanrahan said in her opening remarks that firefighters were unable to suppress the fire because it was in a “permanent danger area” of the base. Instead, the fire was being monitored, she said.

Permanent danger areas can be contaminated with unexploded munitions.

What were the soldiers doing at the time of the fire?

Rutland began his part of the briefing by correcting information he had given previously.

“I said the injured soldiers were conducting a section attack range. This was incorrect,” Rutland said.

“They were setting up for a pairs range. This is where two soldiers attack a target, taking turns covering and firing for one another. In our training sequence, soldiers re-qualify on their weapon individually, then conduct a pairs range, and then move on to the next progression, which is a section attack range.”

Who is leading the investigation and how long will it take?

There are several investigations in the works and it’s not clear how long they’ll take.

A military-led board of inquiry will look into the broader circumstances and make recommendations.

“Normally, those investigations are done to illustrate systemic issues for us to take actions on,” Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan said Thursday.

The military says a board of inquiry is “a fact-finding investigation” to determine how an incident happened and how similar incidents can be prevented in the future.

Rutland said previously the overall investigation would take at least a month, but on Thursday he broadened that timeline to account for the inquiry.

“This underestimated the scope of the upcoming board of inquiry, which will take as long as it takes to examine all facets of the situation,” he said.

Hanrahan said that inquiry has not been launched but it will be in the “near future.”

Hanrahan said the military police investigation is being conducted “independently from the Canadian Armed Forces chain of command.”

“Their role is to establish the facts and determine whether any criminal or service offence May have occurred,” she told reporters, adding 30 people are working on the investigation.

“The involvement of the military police should not be interpreted as an indication that an offence has taken place.”

She said the investigation’s findings will “be provided to Canadians” but did not say how long it will take.

The Alberta Chief Medical Examiner’s office, which probes fatalities in the province, is also conducting an investigation. No timeline was provided for that investigation either.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

— With files from Kyle Duggan and Nick Murray in Ottawa

stories.title: Victims urged to come forward in human trafficking investigation
stories.summary: The London Police Service has charged a Mississauga man in connection with a human trafficking investigation.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The London Police Service has charged a Mississauga man in connection with a human trafficking investigation.

In June, police say they were contact by a woman, who reported being a victim of human trafficking, assaults, and exploitation, spanning back to 2019.

An investigation was launched and officers said the suspect was involved in similar relationships with women throughout the years. They said one victim was exploited in the sex trade, which the suspect benefitted financially from, and had tried to recruit more women for sexual exploitation.

The LPS added that multiple incidents of violence were reported throughout the investigation.

On Wednesday, search warrants were executed in Etobicoke and Woodbridge with the help of the Toronto Police Service. Items seized included cash, four cell phones, and multiple Percocet pills.

The suspect was then found and arrested in Woodbridge.

32-year-old Jesse Nigel Anthony Jones has been charged with:

Three counts of assault

Material benefit resulting from trafficking persons

Material benefit from sexual services

Failure to comply with release order

Trafficking in person comprehensive

Possession of a schedule one substance

Investigators are urging any victims to come forward. Anyone who May have had contact with him or who has any relevant information is asked to contact the LPS at 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Eby calls Doerkson a ‘Trojan horse’ as B.C. election campaign winds down
stories.summary: NDP Leader says voters should look beyond the Conservative Leader while acknowledging concerns over his decision to call an early election
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
NDP Leader David Eby is describing interim BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson as a “Trojan horse” because of the more extreme elements of his party, as campaigning wraps up ahead of Saturday’s provincial election.

Eby also expressed some regret about the way he handled the early stages of the campaign, acknowledging British Columbians were “surprised and frustrated” by his decision to go to the polls two years early.

He had said at the time that the election was necessary to respond to the threat posed by U.S. President Donald Trump , but he now says he wishes he’d been clearer about the “stalled” nature of the legislature, where the NDP held a one-seat majority.

Eby was speaking at a campaign stop in Surrey where both he and Doerkson have been focused in the last week of the election.

He says British Columbians May think they know what they are getting with Doerkson, but he May not even be the Conservatives’ leader after the election.

Doerkson rallied in Surrey on Thursday night alongside former premier Christie Clark and Surrey mayor-elect Doug McCallum, but is campaigning in Eby’s home riding of Vancouver-Point Grey today.

Doerkson has no availability with reporters today, for at least the third day this week.

Friday is the last full day of campaigning in the election ahead of final voting day Saturday when most ballots will be counted by hand.

Elections BC confirmed that votes cast on election day will be tallied manually on Saturday, in a departure from 2024, when electronic tabulators were used to count paper ballots for the first time in a general election.

That was hailed as a success in Elections BC’s report on the polls, but the agency said in a statement that it was going back to a manual count due to “short time frames and complex operational logistics of a snap election.”

stories.title: 'Huge mistake' to assume decisive Alberta referendum means West is happy: Preston Manning
stories.summary: Much of the angst being felt in the West, and even in other parts of Canada, are rooted in federal intrusion, says Reform Party founder.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Despite Alberta’s decision to remain a province of Canada rather than hold another referendum, anger is still simmering at the surface, says Preston Manning.

The former Calgary MP and leader of Canada’s Reform party, which later morphed into the Conservative Party of Canada, doesn’t believe that the issues that prompted Alberta’s referendum have been solved.

Much of the angst being felt in the West, and even in other parts of Canada, are rooted in federal intrusion, said Manning. “The big question now is … remain and do what?”

On Oct. 19, Albertans went to the polls to respond to a list of 10 questions , ranging from immigration, inter-provincial relations and the desire to secede. Preliminary, unofficial results for the last question about separating show a 75-25 split against it.

Premier Danielle Smith, who recently vowed there would be no more secession referendums, should define what it means to build a strong and sovereign province within the federation, said Manning.

“It means beefing up the provincial activity in every area the constitution assigns to the provinces, and pushing the envelope in the joint jurisdiction areas, which are agriculture, environment and, of course, immigration, and presumably she’s going to be doing that,” he told National Post.

The major areas of federal intrusion are natural resources, health, municipal governance, along with property and civil rights.

One solution that would quash some discontent is for the federal government to show that it can compromise. “Civil rights is a provincial responsibility, and so one thing the federal government could do is to pass a statute, an act respecting provincial sovereignty, whereby it repealed or amended those statutes that authorized the intrusion.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney has not addressed what can be done in any of his speeches, said Manning. Carney urged Albertans to vote for a united Canada while speaking in Edmonton on Oct. 16. But he has not shown a “flicker of recognition of what was the cause of this. Not just the referendum, but all the forces behind it,” Manning said.

It’s a “huge mistake” to assume that all is well after a 75-25 split, said Manning. It’s a problem not only in Alberta, he added. It extends to Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia — “a whole bunch of other provinces that are not happy with federal-provincial relations.”

It would make sense to put forward a “grand bargain” between the federal and provincial governments that could satisfy both parties. The federal government could offer to withdraw from certain areas, while the provinces could withdraw from trade and commerce, a major area of federal jurisdiction that the provinces have “invaded.”

There are also smaller solutions that would prove the federal government is listening, like not challenging the notwithstanding clause or negotiating a new immigration accord with Alberta (or any province that wants one), similar to the one struck with Quebec in 1991.

“These would not be difficult. But it would send a signal: ‘We hear that you’ve got angst about this and that. We’re responding,'” he said.

These issues are all coinciding with the turmoil caused by tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump and his rhetoric against Canada.

“Trump is sitting on top of a populist movement,” said Manning. “But what part of the country has had more experience with populist movements that became government than any other part of North America? Western Canada — all the third-party tradition of populist groups, and there’s lessons to be learned from that.”

One lesson is to understand how you get to the leader of such a movement. “You don’t get to him necessarily by talking to his five top advisors on Wall Street or in Washington. You get to a populist leader through his followers, and Carney has no sense of how you do that.”

He added: “There’s another way to handle Trump on tariffs, but not the way Canada’s done it.”

What Canada has done is use anti-Americanism as a tool. It’s “easy to use” in an election, he said, but difficult to turn it off after. Even Trump’s rhetoric about Canada becoming the 51st state started as a joke but “Canadian politicians took it deathly serious. Now it becomes a chip in a game.”

The entire situation could have been handled differently. And Manning is hoping that the angst felt in the West, and other parts of the country, can eventually be settled with policies that will make Canada prosperous and secure “down the road, not just tomorrow.”

After a more than 50 years in politics, at 84 years old, Manning said that it’s his love of the country that keeps him involved.

“I think we have a magnificent country, and I think it can be governed better,” he said.

stories.title: Maine senator says ‘tariff exemptions’ coming for some Canadian goods
stories.summary: Republican Sen. Susan Collins says some 'tariff exemptions' will be granted on certain Canadian agricultural goods by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins says some “tariff exemptions” will be granted on certain Canadian agricultural goods by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration, with less than two weeks to go before the midterm elections.

In a post on social media, the senator said she was “pleased to have secured additional tariff exemptions for products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.”

“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” she said.

“In my repeated conversations with Ambassador Greer, Secretary Lutnick, and other senior Administration officials, I have asked for tariff relief for these important products and I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner.”

Neither Trump nor the White House have confirmed her statement as of publication and it is not clear whether any lifting of tariffs will include additional tariffs on other sectors, or how long any potential relief might last.

Global News has reached out to the White House for additional information.

The U.S. midterms are scheduled for Nov. 3.

More to come.

stories.title: U.S. to drop some tariffs on Canadian exports, says Maine senator
stories.summary: A United States senator says nine categories of Canadian exports will be exempted from U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs on Canada.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump is lifting some tariffs on Canadian exports at the end of this month, but adding tariffs to dozens of new products, including Canadian garbage and sewage.

As the trade war with Canada becomes a ballot box issue in key races ahead of November’s midterm election, Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, said Friday nine categories of Canadian exports will be exempted from tariffs. Those include corrugated paper, plastic boxes and several types of machinery important to her state’s agricultural industries.

Collins is in a tough re-election battle and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, has made the trade war with Canada a key issue in the tight race.

“Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense,” Collins said in a media statement Friday.

Collins said the tariff exemptions are for products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.

The executive order signed Friday by Trump says the tariffs will disappear from those products on Oct. 30, and that the changes are being made after Trump received new advice from senior executive branch officials.

“In my judgment, the modification in this proclamation will offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce, is consistent with the public interests and the interests of the United States, is required by the public interests, and will better serve the public interest,” the order reads.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded to Collins’ announcement of limited tariff relief by posting on social media, “Now get rid of the rest.”

However, the same executive order will also impose new tariffs on dozens of new categories as cocoa powder, paints and varnishes, shampoos, vinyl flooring, archery equipment and carpets. It also will apply 50 per cent tariffs on sewage sludge, and some municipal waste.

Trump’s trade war with Canada has become a political flashpoint in states such as Maine and Michigan ahead of November’s midterms.

Trump slammed an array of Canadian products with 50 per cent tariffs in August after trade talks with Ottawa broke down. The president also signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.

Ottawa responded with retaliatory tariffs on specific American imports.

Trump again escalated trade tensions the following month by banning imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some liquor and whey products.

Earlier this week, a U.S. food importer filed a legal challenge against the Depression-era trade statute — Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 — that Trump used to hit Canada with the heavy duties and trade embargoes.

Collins has repeatedly broken with Trump over his tariffs on Canada. Maine shares a border with Quebec and New Brunswick and relies heavily on trade with Canada.

Collins has argued on the campaign trail that her behind-the-scenes advocacy has secured tariff relief, pointing to the Trump administration’s decision to lift duties on road salt and concrete.

Jackson has countered that Mainers “can’t eat road salt” and small carve-outs won’t reverse the wider economic damage caused by Trump’s tariffs and trade war.

Jackson responded to his challenger’s tariff announcement Friday by saying Collins “enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire.”

“Mainers needed help long before Susan Collins needed saving. But apparently, families struggling to pay their bills wasn’t enough of an emergency. Her losing her job is,” Jackson posted on social media.

“We deserve a senator who stands up to Trump — not one who rubber-stamps his agenda and begs for relief from the chaos she helped create.”

Collins said she has had multiple conversations with United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and other Trump administration officials to ask for tariff relief.

“I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner,” she said.

While Collins has taken credit for the latest tariff relief, it could become a road map for other Republicans in border states trying to navigate Trump’s unpopular policies in their tight races.

The Michigan and Maine races in particular could prove critical to control of Congress. Democrats need to achieve a net gain of four seats to get the Senate majority.

Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers also recently broke with Trump over the trade war with Canada, despite previously supporting the president’s policies. He faces a tight race with Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

In a campaign ad posted on social media earlier this month, Rogers said people in Michigan “know that Canada is not our enemy.”

“We need to end this tariff war now,” Rogers said in the ad, which shows the Republican sitting at a bar and holding a Labatt’s beer.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

By Emily Leighton,

Most pregnancies after living kidney donation are uncomplicated, according to a new Canadian study that provides a clearer picture of pregnancy outcomes among kidney donors.

The study, published in _JAMA_and led by researchers at Western University and London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (LHSCRI), compared pregnancies among living kidney donors in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia with those of women in similarly good health who had not donated.

“For many potential donors, the decision isn’t just about their health today, but what life might look like years down the road,” said Dr. Amit Garg, senior author of the study and professor at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry in the departments of medicine and epidemiology and biostatistics.

### “We want people to have the clearest possible information about what donation could mean for them, including if they hope to have children.” – Dr. Amit Garg, Schulich Medicine & Dentistry professor

Using provincial health-care data, including data from ICES, researchers compared 385 pregnancies among kidney donors with 1,540 pregnancies among women who had not donated.

Most pregnancy outcomes examined were similar between the two groups. Rates of gestational diabetes, caesarean delivery, premature birth and neonatal intensive care admissions were comparable, as were rates of serious maternal complications and postpartum hemorrhage.

The researchers did identify a small increased risk of hypertensive disorders, which involve high blood pressure during pregnancy. Among kidney donors, 11.9 per cent of pregnancies involved hospitalization with gestational hypertension, preeclampsia or eclampsia, compared with 8.3 per cent among non-donors.

The study also found that babies born to kidney donors were more likely to be smaller than expected for their stage of pregnancy. Researchers say further investigation is needed to confirm this secondary finding.

The research builds on an earlier Ontario study involving 131 pregnancies after kidney donation. By expanding the scope to 385 donor pregnancies across three provinces, the team was able to provide more precise estimates of pregnancy-related risks.

Garg, a nephrologist at London Health Sciences Centre, scientist at LHSCRI and senior scientist at ICES, has counselled more than 1,000 prospective kidney donors over the past two decades.

“Understanding the magnitude of risk, and when complications are most likely to occur, gives us a much better foundation for conversations with prospective donors,” he said. “These findings can help people make informed decisions and guide their care during pregnancy.”

stories.title: Liberals tabling bill to prohibit Maid for mental illness alone on Tuesday
stories.summary: The Liberal government will table its bill permanently barring people with mental illness alone from accessing an assisted death on Tuesday.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Liberal government will table its bill permanently barring people with mental illness alone from accessing an assisted death on Tuesday, National Post has learned.

A senior government source confirmed that the long-awaited bill would be put on the House of Commons notice paper on Friday evening and that the bill is expected to be tabled during Tuesday’s sitting. The source was granted anonymity as they were not authorized to discuss the bill publicly.

Two weeks ago, Justice Minister Sean Fraser took the unusual step of telegraphing what he expected to put into the bill, including making permanent the prohibition to medical assistance in dying (Maid) for people seeking it on the sole basis of a psychiatric illness.

Whether to open up Maid to people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness has been one of the most heated issues in the history of legalized assisted death in Canada. Once tabled, the bill will certainly be hotly debated by MPs as well as advocates and critics of Maid.

He also announced the bill would allow people to make advance requests for Maid if diagnosed with an illness that would threaten their ability to provide final consent, up to the last moments before the lethal injection.

On Friday, the source reaffirmed that that would be done by decriminalizing the act for doctors who administer Maid to patients who made an advance request. It will then be up to provinces to determine if they want to allow advance requests for Maid.

Outside Quebec, euthanizing someone in the absence of capacity is a serious offence in the absence of a valid waiver of final consent. While Quebec has permitted the practice since 2024, Alberta has already banned advance requests.

Foreshadowing the bill, Fraser said on Oct. 7 that the legislation will grant access to Maid “to people who have provided consent at a time when they still have capacity but know that they have been diagnosed with an illness that will take that capacity from them subsequently.

“These are not easy decisions. But we believe they are the correct ones,” the minister said.

Following the announcement, some groups expressed concern that individuals might be coerced into signing advance requests for Maid and called for further safeguards.

In a statement Wednesday, Dementia Justice Canada called on the government to require an independent legal assessment by a lawyer before death.

“Requiring independent legal advice before an advance request is signed could help ensure that the person understands the request and makes it freely,” reads a release by group chair and lawyer Heather Campbell Pope.

In June, a special parliamentary committee recommended the Liberal government draw a line in the sand and indefinitely exclude people with mental illness alone from eligibility for Maid. Expanding Maid for mental illness, set to take effect March 17, 2027, had already been deferred, twice.

The joint committee of MPs and senators said key issues haven’t been addressed, including whether it’s possible to predict with any certainty whether a person’s mental illness is incurable. Dr. Sonu Gaind, past chief of psychiatry at Toronto’s Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, told the committee that doctors are right less than half the time, comparing the ability to predict long-term prognosis to a coin toss.

Current and former chairs of psychiatry departments at universities across Canada warned the committee that making Maid available to people with depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, substance abuse and other mental illnesses would facilitate avoidable deaths and erode suicide prevention efforts.

The committee said “grave concerns and deep divisions” continue to exist. A recurring theme was the pressing need for better access to mental health services and concerns long waits for care could exacerbate suffering, driving Maid requests. The committee also heard stories of “questionable conduct” by some Maid providers, as well as doctors “with a seemingly cavalier attitude toward ending a life,” committee co-chair Liberal MP Marcus Powlowski wrote in a supplemental opinion.

However, the committee’s decision wasn’t unanimous. Three senators as well as a Bloc Québécois MP, Luc Thériault, wrote dissenting opinions and called on the government to bring the question of expansion to the Supreme Court of Canada. Fraser has declined to do so.

First legalized in 2016 for people whose deaths are “reasonably foreseeable,” Canada’s Maid law was amended in 2021 to remove the “reasonably foreseeable” provision. The amendments under Bill C-7 also included a restriction on mental illness alone as a qualifying condition for Maid, an exclusion that was originally set to expire on March 17, 2023, but was later pushed back to 2024 and then again, to March 2027.

Currently, dementia is an eligible diagnosis for Maid in Canada, provided people have the capacity to make a reasoned request and don’t lose that capacity before they want their lives ended. Dementia is considered a neurological disorder, not a mental illness.

National Post, with files from Sharon Kirkey

Cnardi@postmedia.com

stories.title: U.S. to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian products: report
stories.summary: Back in late August, the U.S. levied 50 per cent tariffs on nearly US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
The U.S. is removing the 50 per cent tariffs on certain Canadian products as the trade war with Canada becomes a ballot box issue in key races ahead of November’s midterm election.

Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, said nine categories of Canadian exports will be exempted from tariffs, including corrugated paper, plastic boxes and several types of machinery important to her state’s agricultural industries.

In a post on X on Friday, Collins said she helped to secure the exemptions.

“I am pleased to have secured additional tariff exemptions products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers,” she wrote.

“In my repeated conversations with Ambassador Greer, Secretary Lutnick, and other senior Administration officials, I have asked for tariff relief for these important products and I will continue working directly with Administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner.”

Collins said the tariff exemptions are for products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.

In a fact sheet published Friday , the White House confirmed it is removing certain products — such as plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes — from the scope of the Section 338 tariffs, while replacing those with tariffs on “certain valves, carpets, waste products, and others.”

The fact sheet went on to state that the tariffs apply to all goods regardless if they are covered by the current Canada-U.S.-Mexico (Cusma) trade agreement.

The White House said the president was seeking to offset “the burden to U.S. commerce while better serving the public interest.”

Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement, “Trump’s desperate, 11th hour attempt to save Susan Collins’ political career is an admission that American voters are rejecting his toxic tariff policies.”

The changes take effect Oct. 30, 2026.

Canada’s Trade Minister, Dominic LeBlanc, says they are assessing the latest measures, reiterating that it continues to work towards a mutually beneficial trade deal with the United States.

“The Government of Canada takes note of the latest tariff measures from the United States,” read a statement sent to CityNews. “As always, our focus remains clear: building a stronger, more competitive, and more resilient economy for workers, businesses, farmers and all Canadians. While we assess these latest steps, Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada’s interests.”

The association that represents Canada’s forestry sector says while they are reviewing the full impact of the latest measures, what they really need is “stable, rules-based trade, not constantly changing tariffs.”

“Moving a limited number of forest products off one tariff list while adding even more does not amount to relief. Canadian lumber, furniture, kitchen cabinetry and other wood products remain caught up in a growing web of U.S. duties and tariffs that increase costs for American consumers and create uncertainty for businesses and workers on both sides of the border,” said Derek Nighbor, the President and CEO of the Forest Products Association of Canada.

Back in late August, the U.S. levied 50 per cent tariffs on nearly US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods.

Trump’s trade war with Canada has become a political flashpoint in Collins’ state just ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Trump slammed an array of Canadian products with 50 per cent tariffs in August after trade talks with Ottawa broke down. The president also signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America.

Ottawa responded with retaliatory tariffs on specific American imports.

Trump again escalated trade tensions the following month by banning imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some dairy products.

Collins has repeatedly pushed back on Trump’s tariffs on Canada. Maine shares a border with Quebec and New Brunswick and relies heavily on trade with Canada.

Files from The Canadian Press and The Associated Press were used in this report

stories.title: Driver charged in fatal Stratford pedestrian collision
stories.summary: A 38-year-old St. Catharines resident has been charged with dangerous driving causing death following a fatal pedestrian collision in Stratford earlier this year.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 38-year-old St. Catharines resident has been charged with dangerous driving causing death following a fatal pedestrian collision in Stratford earlier this year.

Stratford police said the charge stems from an incident on Aug. 16, 2026, when officers responded shortly after 11 a.m. to a report of a pedestrian being struck by a vehicle.

The pedestrian, identified as an 86-year-old Stratford resident, died from injuries sustained in the collision.

Police said their investigation has now concluded, resulting in the driver involved being charged with the Criminal Code offence of dangerous driving causing death.

The accused turned himself in to police and was arrested on Oct. 11. He was later released from custody on an undertaking and is scheduled to appear in court on Nov. 9.

Police have not released any additional details about the circumstances surrounding the collision.

stories.title: “I can’t continue school”: Private college students May have to wait until new year for Osap freeze to end
stories.summary: Lani Miko was getting excited because she only had 37 days left before becoming an H.V.A.C Technician, but that optimism has turned to dread, after Ontario’s student loan program, ceased payments to students of private career colleges, earlier this month.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Lani Miko was getting excited because she only had 37 days left before becoming an H.V.A.C Technician, but that optimism has turned to dread, after Ontario’s student loan program, ceased payments to students of private career colleges, earlier this month.

“I’m worried the school is going to close, and worried if I’m going to be able to finish my hours,” says the Hensall native. Miko isn’t alone. Melissa Hilton actually quit her private college program, when Ontario Student Assistance Program (O.S.A.P.)funding was frozen, ON October 6th.

because there’s no guarantee that the next payment is going to come through in January,” says Hilton, who lives in Exeter. Ontario froze O.S.A.P funding for students at all 242 private colleges operating in the province, after irregularities in student assistance funding was found at six career colleges.

Eight more are now under investigation. “Why are you penalizing all students at other schools that have followed the rules, follow the regulations? They get audited regularly, so you can see who are legitimate students, and who are not,” says Miko.

The province says they’re working with banks to offer private career college students, suddenly without O.S.A.P, loans. “So, your solution is, you took a loan out to go to school, we’re withholding that. But, you need to apply for another loan, which then puts you in even more debt when you’re done,” she says.

The Ministry of Colleges and Universities says they’re working on a new validation process for O.S.A.P approvals for Ontario’s private career colleges, but that won’t likely be ready until the new year, leaving students like Miko and Hilton, with their dreams and lives, ON hold.

“That’s the thing. Do you work with an employer and tell them that you might be gone in six months? It’s just a bunch of questions, that you can’t answer,” says Hilton. “I’m a single mom. I have bills to pay. I have to run the household.

And now I’m like, I already have a second job, but I’m on leave from that, so I could go to trade school. So, what do I do?” questions a frustrated Miko. The Ministry of Colleges and Universities says, “While the Ministry’s initial investigation focused on a few schools, with the Ministry since taking action not to renew O.S.A.P at six campuses, in recent weeks we’ve seen signs of systemic issues.

stories.title: Ford promotes MPP who resigned from cabinet over hotel expenses
stories.summary: Stan Cho’s appointment as parliamentary assistant prompts outcry from opposition parties who accuse the government of a lack of accountability
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has promoted a former Toronto cabinet minister who resigned this summer after billing thousands in local hotel stays, prompting outcry from opposition parties who accused the government of a lack of accountability.

Mr. Ford on Thursday named Toronto MPP Stan Cho as the new parliamentary assistant to Education Minister Paul Calandra. The roles are assigned by the premier to help cabinet ministers, and come with a $22,500 pay bump on top of an MPP’s $157,350 salary. Parliamentary assistants also often address questions in the legislature about their ministries when cabinet ministers are absent.

The offices of Mr. Cho and Mr. Ford did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday about the MPP’s new role. Nor did Mr. Calandra’s office.

Mr. Cho resigned as Minister of Tourism, Culture and Gaming on July 17 after it was revealed he spent more than $16,000 on hotels in the past three years, despite representing a Toronto riding not far from the Ontario legislature.

At the time, Mr. Ford called the expenses “totally unacceptable,” and said Mr. Cho has taken responsibility for his mistake. Mr. Cho, who remained a member of the Progressive Conservative caucus, said at the time he had repaid the money. He said he billed for the stays when the legislature sat late, but did “not stop to ask how it would look to a person in my riding working a double shift.”

Mr. Cho and more than a dozen others in the caucus – including others in cabinet – charged a total of more than $120,000 since 2023 on hotels, according to public disclosure documents. The opposition has accused the government members of entitlement and frivolous spending, alleging that they abused the rules.

The hotel stays were filed under “special circumstances” expenses that allow members of the legislature who live within 50 kilometres of Queen’s Park to charge for hotels under exceptional circumstances, such as snowstorms or night sittings.

Mr. Ford has previously said the hotel expenses of other top spenders in his caucus would also be repaid in full.

The Premier’s decision to give Mr. Cho more responsibility and a raise did not sit well with Ontario’s opposition parties. The legislature is set to return Tuesday after an extended 21-week break, which the government said was necessary to not interfere in Monday’s municipal elections but was decried as undemocratic by the opposition.

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles on Friday called on Mr. Ford to fire Mr. Cho – not to give him a raise.

“Stan Cho spent tens of thousands of taxpayer dollars on luxury Toronto hotels despite living fifteen minutes from Queen’s Park. Instead of holding him accountable, Doug Ford gave him a $22,500 pay bump with the people’s hard-earned tax dollars,” Ms. Stiles said in a statement.

“While the people of Ontario are putting groceries back on the shelves, spending hours in hospital waiting rooms, and sending their kids to overcrowded classrooms, Doug Ford is giving his MPPs a blank cheque to party on the taxpayer dime.”

Interim Ontario Liberal Leader John Fraser also criticized the promotion.

“Stan Cho billed taxpayers more than $16,000 for hotel stays just a few subway stops from home. When he got caught, he paid it back, and three months later Doug Ford paid him back with a raise,” he said in a statement.

“There is no accountability in this government, because no matter how badly a minister screws up, the Premier always takes care of his friends.”

Mr. Fraser also noted that the number of parliamentary assistants has grown. According to publicly available lists, all but two of the 79 PC MPPs have either a cabinet or parliamentary assistant role.

stories.title: Warm, sunny weekend ahead for southwestern Ontario
stories.summary: Residents across southwestern Ontario can look forward to another stretch of sunny and seasonably mild weather heading into the weekend, according to meteorologist Gary Archibald.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
Residents across southwestern Ontario can look forward to another stretch of sunny and seasonably mild weather heading into the weekend, according to meteorologist Gary Archibald.

Archibald said a ridge of high pressure has kept conditions quiet and clear across much of eastern North America in recent days, helping to set the stage for favourable weather through at least Sunday.

“Just like last weekend, I’m anticipating a beautiful fair-weather weekend,” Archibald said. “Saturday and Sunday look good.”

Friday’s high is expected to reach 16 C, about four degrees above the seasonal average, while overnight temperatures are forecast to dip to around 4 C under mainly clear skies.

Archibald said any cloud cover seen over the past several days has largely been limited to fair-weather clouds, a trend that is expected to continue across the lower Great Lakes region.

“It bodes well for a great-looking weekend,” he said.

Skies are expected to remain clear Friday evening, with temperatures falling to about 8 C by 8 p.m., 6 C by 10 p.m. and 4 C around midnight. Light easterly winds of 10 km/h or less are also forecast.

Looking ahead, Archibald said sunshine and temperatures in the upper teens are expected to continue through the weekend and into Monday in London and much of southwestern Ontario.

A cooler pattern is forecast to arrive by the middle of next week, with daytime highs settling into the lower teens. There is also the possibility of showers toward the end of the work week.

“A similar-looking forecast for the Midwest as well,” Archibald said. “Sunny for Saturday and then clouds moving in Monday, with a possible passing shower.”

Despite the cooler temperatures expected next week, conditions will remain typical for late October, with readings near seasonal norms.

stories.title: Quebec premier announces $28 million for warming centres and emergency shelters
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec's new premier says the provincial government will spend $28 million in emergency funding to address homelessness.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec’s premier promised Friday to bring a new-found political will to the battle against homelessness, as he announced $28 million in emergency funding.

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon announced the new funding on Friday in Montreal, in his first major announcement since he was sworn in as premier on Wednesday. St-Pierre Plamondon, who has also named himself homelessness minister, said the money is in addition to $18 million that was previously allocated, bringing the total amount to $46 million.

“I think in order to succeed, we need to be facing directly the nature of the problem, not pretend it’s not there,” he told journalists. “It’s the first step. Then you need to take political will, to show political will. And that’s what we’re doing today.”

St-Pierre Plamondon said the money will go toward adding 1,000 new spots in warming centres and emergency shelters across Quebec. The Montreal area, which is home to nearly half of the province’s unhoused population, is slated to get $18 million out of the total.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada joined the premier for the announcement at the shelter Accueil Bonneau.

She said she is thrilled the new provincial government has made homelessness its first order of business. She said the city had come up with a homelessness strategy for the winter, but needed $20 million from the provincial government to implement its plan.

“All our Montrealers, our citizens, our Quebecers that are in the streets deserve to have a roof over their heads and that’s what we have to aim for,” said the mayor. “Having this announcement today makes that a reality and it’s the first step in the shared objective.”

The announcement comes days after media reported that a woman experiencing homelessness died in Sorel-Tracy, Que. The premier said the woman tried to access a shelter she frequently visited, but there was not enough room for her.

“That’s not a narrative we can accept as a society. It doesn’t work,” said St-Pierre Plamondon. “Quebec … is among the wealthiest places in the world, and we will do whatever it takes to restore dignity for everyone.”

Quebec’s chief coroner has ordered a public inquiry into the deaths of five individuals experiencing homelessness in Montreal between Sept. 23, 2025 and March 25, 2026.

The Quebec coroner’s office has investigated the deaths of 500 people experiencing homelessness since 2020, according to St-Pierre Plamondon.

The premier added that the government will hold a summit on homelessness, as proposed by former premier Pauline Marois, in early 2027. The summit will gather key actors from the community sector and all levels of government to identify the causes of homelessness and their remedies.

“There’s addiction, mental health problems, the housing crisis,” said the premier, adding he has been inspired by the “housing-first” model seen in Finland and Texas where those experiencing homelessness are provided with homes and psychosocial support.

While Friday’s announcement is solely for emergency services, he said his government will work to implement long-term solutions, such as providing community organizations with recurring funding and building 20,000 subsidized housing units.

He said the previous administration had prioritized “affordable” housing run by the private sector and non-profit organizations.

“Social housing is making a comeback,” said St-Pierre Plamondon. “I remember that, right from the start of the 2018 term, they claimed that the private sector would take care of it. And look where that got us.”

He also pledged to implement policies to “balance” the housing market. He said that once housing supply outpaces demand, landlords and developers will no longer have an incentive to have high tenant turnover or to hike rents beyond what is recommended by the province’s housing tribunal.

“Until we restore the market to equilibrium, it’s going to be difficult because we can’t monitor the honesty of each of the nine million people on our territory,” he said.

Alia Hassan-Cournol, executive director of women’s shelter La rue des Femmes, said she feels optimistic about the new sums, despite not yet knowing how much will be allocated to her organization.

“We really hear the change in tone,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version incorrectly identified Alia Hassan as director of a women’s shelter called La rue des Femmes. In fact, Alia Hassan-Cournol is the executive director of La rue des Femmes.

stories.title: Trump says Canada 'working very hard' to make a trade deal with U.S.
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said Canada is "working very hard" to make a trade deal with the U.S.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – U.S. President Donald Trump said Canada is “working very hard” to make a trade deal with the U.S., despite talks remaining at a standstill since August.

“Canada is working very hard to make a deal with us, and I hate to say this, but we have all the cards,” Trump told reporters in Washington on Friday.

Carney, who is currently visiting Istanbul where he signed a strategic partnership with Turkey, said the timing of a trade deal remains up to the U.S.

“We could sign it this afternoon if the U.S. were there,” said Carney, during a press conference on Friday. “If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that.”

When asked specifically if Canada could sign a deal with the Americans before the U.S. midterms on Nov. 3, Carney did not close the door on that possibility and reiterated that it’s up to the U.S., who are “hard to predict.”

There has been very little movement on the trade file between the two countries after negotiations fell apart in late August. Carney paused negotiations, citing last-minute demands from U.S. negotiators that made a deal untenable for Canadian interests. Key sticking points included U.S. tariffs on Canadian medium and heavy duty trucks, French-language labelling and streaming discoverability rules and U.S. oversight on Canadian trade policy.

On Wednesday, Carney told reporters he spoke with Trump “for quite some time” about geopolitical and trade issues.

On Thursday, the Advisory Committee on Canada–U.S. Economic Relations met for the first time since Sept. 4. Present at that meeting was Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette and Canadian Ambassador to the U.S. Mark Wiseman.

Charette told a business audience in Toronto on Thursday that communication channels remain open with American counterparts.

“I have said publicly that pens are down and the doors are open,” she said, at the Toronto Global Forum. “Canada stands ready to continue discussions towards actually trying to achieve our objectives around stabilizing the relationship, you have seen reference, I think, publicly in the last couple of days, conversations are going on at multiple levels.”

Despite those open channels, there has also been a notable escalation in rhetoric from U.S. officials in recent weeks, in the lead-up to the U.S. midterms.

During a podcast appearance earlier this month, U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra warned Canadian politicians to “to keep your nose out of American politics.” In late September, White House trade adviser Peter Navarro also told Canadian lobbyists to “get the hell out of our country.”

On Wednesday, the U.S. embassy in Ottawa published a “fact sheet” listing quotes from Canadian politicians accusing them of openly describing “plans to influence American politics.”

The named politicians include Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Liberal MP Anthony Housefather.

Carney expressed disappointment with Hoekstra’s allegations that Canadian officials are interfering in American elections.

“I’m disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role to make these suggestions,” said Carney, during a press conference in Istanbul on Friday. “We have a very deep diplomatic presence in the United States.”

Earlier this week, Global Affairs Canada issued a directive to Canadian diplomats working in the U.S. to stay away from candidates running in the midterm elections, according to a report by Bloomberg News.

Carney said the guidance was issued before the fact sheet was published by the U.S. envoy, reminding diplomats to be careful who they are seen with.

“We have lots of interaction with American companies, citizens, individuals, stakeholders more broadly,” he said. “We’re very, very careful to not be seen to, not be seen to interfere.”

The prime minister said the allegations have “no merit” and Canadian officials have no intention of interfering with U.S. democratic processes.

In the upcoming midterms the Republican Party is expected to lose control of Congress. Trump’s personal approval ratings have taken a hit, thanks to voter frustrations over inflation, the economy and U.S. military action in Iran.

When asked if he was concerned about Republican officials potentially laying the groundwork to blame Canadians for their midterm losses and justify further tariffs, Carney said he doesn’t see that as a likely outcome.

“I have said publicly that pens are down and the doors are open,” she said, at the Toronto Global Forum. “Canada stands ready to continue discussions towards actually trying to achieve our objectives around stabilizing the relationship, you have seen reference, I think, publicly in the last couple of days, conversations are going on at multiple levels.”
Despite those open channels, there has also been a notable escalation in rhetoric from U.S. officials in recent weeks, in the lead-up to the U.S. midterms.

During a podcast appearance earlier this month, U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra warned Canadian politicians to “to keep your nose out of American politics.” In late September, White House trade adviser Peter Navarro also told Canadian lobbyists to “get the hell out of our country.”
On Wednesday, the U.S. embassy in Ottawa published a “fact sheet” listing quotes from Canadian politicians accusing them of openly describing “plans to influence American politics.”
The named politicians include Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Liberal MP Anthony Housefather.
Carney expressed disappointment with Hoekstra’s allegations that Canadian officials are interfering in American elections.

“I’m disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role to make these suggestions,” said Carney, during a press conference in Istanbul on Friday. “We have a very deep diplomatic presence in the United States.”

Earlier this week, Global Affairs Canada issued a directive to Canadian diplomats working in the U.S. to stay away from candidates running in the midterm elections, according to a report by Bloomberg News.
Carney said the guidance was issued before the fact sheet was published by the U.S. envoy, reminding diplomats to be careful who they are seen with.
“We have lots of interaction with American companies, citizens, individuals, stakeholders more broadly,” he said. “We’re very, very careful to not be seen to, not be seen to interfere.”
The prime minister said the allegations have “no merit” and Canadian officials have no intention of interfering with U.S. democratic processes.

In the upcoming midterms the Republican Party is expected to lose control of Congress. Trump’s personal approval ratings have taken a hit, thanks to voter frustrations over inflation, the economy and U.S. military action in Iran.

When asked if he was concerned about Republican officials potentially laying the groundwork to blame Canadians for their midterm losses and justify further tariffs, Carney said he doesn’t see that as a likely outcome.

stories.title: Canada will be 'a living hell' if it becomes associate member of EU, claims MEP
stories.summary: German MEP Christine Anderson said becoming an associate member of the EU would turn Canada "into a living hell" during a recent debate.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
A Member of European Parliament (MEP) said that becoming an associate member of the EU would turn Canada “into a living hell” and asked “is Mark Carney stupid enough to fall for it?” during a debate on Thursday.

Speaking at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, ahead of the EU-Canada summit in Montreal next week, German MEP Christine Anderson accused the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, of looking to wipe out industry, censor speech and “flood” Canada with “even more illegal migrants.”

“Ursula von der Leyen wants to lure Canada into an associate membership of the EU,” she said. “Apparently (she) is no longer content with merely terrorizing the people in the EU with her insane regulations, bureaucracy, and cronyism.”

Arguing that von der Leyen’s motivations aren’t related to trade because Ceta (an existing free-trade agreement between Canada and the EU) is already in place, Anderson said: “She is looking for yet another people whose industry she can wipe out, whose prosperity she can destroy, whose speech she can censor, and whose countries she can flood with even more illegal migrants, thus turning Canada into a living hell.

“The question is: Is Mark Carney stupid enough to fall for it, or will he do right by the Canadian people and tell Ursula von der Leyen to bugger off?”

Anderson suggested that if Canada were to become an associate member of the EU, “maybe a new freedom convoy would then be in order,” referring to the 2022 protests that were organized to oppose COVID restrictions.

Later on in the debate, European Parliament Vice President Younous Omarjee reminded speakers to show respect to Carney during their comments. “You can of course criticize the gentleman, but some comments are not acceptable,” he said.

But not all the MEPs speaking at Thursday’s debate shared Anderson’s views. Members reacted to the scope of Canada’s proposed associate membership, which was outlined by European Commissioner Jozef Síkela at the start of the meeting and would involve supply-chain integration, the creation of a technology space for joint research, and coordinated economic-security policies.

Belgian MEP Kathleen Van Brempt said, “In a world filled with Trumps, Europe needs stable and reliable partners,” adding, “Canada is such a partner,” while Poland’s Dariusz Joński echoed this sentiment, saying: “We need reliable and strong allies, and Canada is one of them.

But French MEP Angéline Furet expressed concerns about the impact on European factories and industries, and Latvia’s Rihards Kols added that the EU does not need “quasi member states,” but instead needs “to deliver on the agreements that we have already signed.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the European Union’s invitation to become its first-ever “associate member” in September with a speech in the Parliament’s hemicycle in Strasbourg, which was well-received by the MEPs in the room — including Anderson’s colleague, Terry Reintke, who attended in a Sidney Crosby Team Canada jersey .

The summit in Montreal on Oct. 29 and 30 is expected to deepen the alliance between the EU and Canada, focusing on cooperation on trade, defence and security, technology, energy and critical minerals.

However, as Síkela noted in his address, negotiations remain ongoing and the scope of what associate membership would actually mean for Canada will be defined over the coming year. “Nothing is done until it’s done,” he said.

Meanwhile, Anderson stirred controversy in Canada in 2023 when she was denounced by Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre after meeting three Tory MPs.

Dean Allison, Colin Carrie and Leslyn Lewis were photographed having dinner with Anderson in February that year, drawing concern from Canadian groups including the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija).

Anderson represents the Alternative for Germany party (AfD), which was classified as “extremist” by Germany’s spy agency in 2025 .

In a written statement responding to the concerns, Poilievre called Anderson’s views “racist, hateful” and “vile.”

“The MPs were not aware of this visiting member of the European Parliament’s opinions, and they regret meeting with her,” the statement said. “Frankly, it would be better if Anderson never visited Canada in the first place.”

Poilievre’s office also issued a separate statement attributed to the three MPs. “It is, of course, not uncommon for members of Parliament to meet with visiting elected officials from other countries,” it read, adding, “We were not aware of the views or associations of her and her political party. We do not share or endorse her views and strongly condemn any views that are racist or hateful.”

stories.title: ‘It’s cold, but it’s real nice’: American travellers give P.E.I.’s tourism season added momentum
stories.summary: Passengers stepping off the Carnival Sunshine were happy to finally be on land after a nor’easter forced their ship to skip a stop in Halifax.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown – Passengers stepping off the Carnival Sunshine were happy to finally be on land after a nor’easter forced their ship to skip a stop in Halifax.

Their arrival comes as Port Charlottetown works to extend Prince Edward Island’s tourism season, with cruise visits continuing into early November. The extension gives local businesses that would typically close after Labour Day more opportunities to stay open.

“We’re really excited to be here. We’ve been on this ship for five days now,” said Peter Walter, from Melville, Tenn.

“We’re here to see everything Prince Edward Island has to offer,” said his wife, Sandi.

The port’s efforts include international marketing, building awareness of the destination and investing in infrastructure, said CEO Mike Cochrane. It works with major cruise lines and itinerary planners around the world to promote what Prince Edward Island and Atlantic Canada have to offer in September and October.

Those efforts appear to be paying off. The Island reached a record 1.87 million visitors in 2025, while visitation outside the peak season has increased at least 18 per cent since 2019.

Cochrane said the benefits extend beyond restaurants, taxis and tour guides to fishing and farming communities, as local products gain exposure to audiences from around the world.

“When you can plan on thousands of people at your doorstep on a particular day, ON a particular time… it’s a planned business opportunity,” Cochrane said.

Tourists spent $520.7 million across the province in 2024, according to provincial figures.

It’s all good news for commercial helicopter pilot Charles Racine, who offers sightseeing tours.

“We get to take on more people and more passengers,” he said. “It’s a great time to see the Island in all its fall colours.”

For some visitors, it was their first time this far north.

“We had the opportunity to visit Charlottetown and we took it,” said DJ Blackwell, from North Carolina.

“Canada is different,” said Billy Trevillian, from Cartersville, Virgnia. “So far, it’s cold, but it’s real nice.”

But the chill wasn’t getting in the way of enjoying the Island’s main attractions.

“As Anne said, she’s glad that we have a world where there’s an October,” said Adrian Gilbert with a laugh. “We wanted to come here and enjoy October in the spirit of Anne of Green Gables.”

“As long as I stay warm, I’ll be alright,” said her husband, David.

P.E.I. was named North America’s Best Cruise Destination for 2026 at the World Cruise Awards.

It’s the first Atlantic Canadian destination to receive the title, joining previous recipients including Hawaii, Alaska and Florida.

The port says the recognition gives it another selling point with cruise lines, which plan itineraries two to three years in advance.

The industry generated $49 million in economic output for the province in 2024 and supported about 280 jobs.

Port Charlottetown is already expecting 42 cruise ships and 80,000 visitors next October.

“That means what we’re doing is 100 per cent bang on,” Cochrane said.

stories.title: Canada, EU ‘closing in’ on digital trade deal ahead of summit: minister
stories.summary: International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu was in Ireland on Thursday to push forward negotiations ahead of next week's Canada-EU Summit in Montreal.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Canada and the European Union are continuing negotiations on a digital trade agreement that would make it easier for businesses to buy and sell across borders.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu was in Ireland on Thursday to push forward negotiations ahead of next week’s Canada-EU Summit in Montreal.

In a statement, Sidhu says Canada and the EU are “closing in on an agreement” to help “create less friction” around e-signatures and e-contracts, paperless trade, secure cross-border data flows, duties on electronic transmissions and e-commerce.

Sidhu says Canada exported nearly $15 billion in digital services to the EU in 2024 and there is an opportunity now to grow that further with an agreement in place.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has been working on establishing closer links with Europe, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has suggested Canada could become the first associate member of the European Union.

The two sides are expected to announce the next steps in the deepening partnership at the Canada-EU Summit.
