stories.title: National security strategy to address array of threats coming soon: Carney adviser
stories.summary: David Morrison told MPs on the House of Commons public safety and national security committee this week he hopes the strategy will be public within a few weeks.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
A senior federal adviser says the Liberals are poised to release a new national security strategy — the first such policy in more than two decades.

David Morrison, senior diplomatic and international affairs adviser to Prime Minister Mark Carney, says the strategy will look to bolster Canada’s defences against an array of security threats.

Morrison told MPs on the House of Commons public safety and national security committee this week he hopes the strategy will be public within a few weeks.

Privy Council Office spokesperson Mélany Gauvin says the coming strategy will increase Canada’s focus on economic security.

In 2004, the Liberal government of Prime Minister Paul Martin released Securing an Open Society, the most recent complete national security policy.

Two years ago, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau directed officials to deliver a renewed national security strategy in 2025.

stories.title: Thunder Bay's next mayor will have to grapple with homelessness, housing crisis
stories.summary: Candidates vying to lead one of northern Ontario's largest municipalities agree that public safety, homelessness and aging infrastructure will have to be among the top priorities for Thunder Bay's next council.
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press
stories.content:
flag wire: true flag sponsored: false article_type: pubinfo.section: cms.site.custom.site_domain : thestar.com sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/toronto_star bHasMigratedAvatar : false firstAuthor.avatar :

By Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press

Candidates vying to lead one of northern Ontario’s largest municipalities agree that public safety, homelessness and aging infrastructure will have to be among the top priorities for Thunder Bay’s next council.

Nine candidates are competing to replace long-serving mayor and former member of Parliament Ken Boshcoff, who is retiring from municipal politics. He was first elected councillor in 1979 and served two stints as mayor, first from 1997 to 2003 then again in 2022.

Trevor Giertuga, who’s running for mayor after serving as city councillor since 2000, said the rise in crime and homelessness is the main challenge facing the city. If elected, he said he would increase police resources and build more housing.

“I would like to see us return back to neighbourhood policing with more boots on the ground in the areas, so we could target high-risk areas or high-crime areas,” he said, noting that Thunder Bay used to have a crime prevention council whose members included Indigenous leaders, business owners and others in the community.

Statistics Canada’s crime severity index, based on police-reported data, for Thunder Bay increased 18 per cent from 2024 to 2025. The Thunder Bay police website shows the city’s crime severity index has been higher than both provincial and national averages from 2020 to 2024.

The District of Thunder Bay’s Social Services Administration Board estimated in an August report that there were 1,129 homeless people in the city by the end of last year and that at least 58 per cent of them identified as Indigenous.

Earlier this month, the city’s long-awaited temporary shelter village with 80 private cabins and shared washroom and kitchen facilities welcomed its first residents. But Giertuga said the city needs more permanent housing instead of temporary solutions to homelessness.

“The village has opened and although I was opposed to it, we’re in it now, so it’s a matter of making sure it’s run properly,” he said, adding that the $12.5 million spent on the project should have gone toward permanent housing.

Moe Comuzzi, a real estate broker with extensive business experience who is also running for mayor, said the temporary village is a well thought out project and she would be committed to moving it forward if elected.

“It gives people dignity and the opportunity to have a nice, warm, safe place to help them,” she said. “Whether or not they need services for mental health and addictions, the services will be there for them ... or whether they’re just waiting for an affordable home that takes a little bit of time to build.”

Comuzzi said building more housing and infrastructure is part of the goal to attract more investment and growth, as the city is an economic hub in northern Ontario.

“Industry, small business, and mining, critical minerals — I mean the opportunities are endless,” she said.

Giertuga said he would also focus on increasing the city’s tax base to avoid steep rate hikes for residents. He said Thunder Bay has a $30-million infrastructure funding gap and city council has been raising the capital budget by five per cent a year to make that gap smaller.

But he said promising to freeze property taxes is not realistic.

“Other candidates have put forward a tax freeze for 2027 and I ask, ‘then how, where, are we going to get the money or what services are we prepared to cut?’”

Comuzzi also said a tax freeze is not feasible.

“Everybody’s feeling the pinch at the grocery store and at the gas station. Businesses are feeling that stress too. So, growing Thunder Bay for all of us is the right step in the right direction,” she said.

Since Thunder Bay is a regional service hub in northern Ontario, Giertuga said he would also advocate for more federal and provincial funding to help the city serve people from nearby communities.

“We have 30,000 people in the city that are not on our census that have come from outlying communities, and not just unhoused people, people coming for cancer treatment, people coming for other medical treatment, people coming for all sorts of different reasons,” he said.

For mayoral candidate Volker Kromm, a project manager and business leader, the rise in poverty is a key issue.

“These last couple of years, we’ve seen a steady decline and such an increase in the effects of poverty on the streets and the drug culture and the cost of living and the whole of the affordability issue,” he said.

“The poverty is growing, there aren’t enough jobs. In some cases, there isn’t the training available, and these people can’t afford to live here because there aren’t enough affordable houses, so they end up on the streets.”

Thunder Bay’s 10-year housing and homelessness plan says getting enough affordable housing will continue to be a problem since the average cost of building a single new unit is $450,000 and “the available funding does not stretch far.”

Kromm said the city needs to better co-ordinate with federal and provincial government agencies and other groups that help homeless people and those struggling with addiction.

“We have a lot of great social service organizations ... They’re doing the best that they can, but they work separate,” he said.

Lindsay Martin, executive director of the Elizabeth Fry Society of Northwestern Ontario, said her organization supports homeless women and gender-diverse people, including those who struggle with substance use and mental health issues, but has never had much contact with or support from the city.

“A lot of NGOs, or non-for-profits or charitable organizations, they rely on community, they rely on government funding, and the municipality doesn’t necessarily step in to support organizations like Elizabeth Fry Society,” she said.

“It would be good if they started to co-ordinate with work that’s already being done and support it in that way.”

Martin said the next city council should advocate for more support from the province to address issues that lead to homelessness, such as lack of affordable housing and mental health care.

“Without housing, folks are out there struggling ... temperatures drop to -35 here at times, and that’s a death sentence for people who are unhoused in our community,” she said.

Peter Diedrich, a mayoral candidate who worked for decades in telecom, technology and venture capital consulting, agreed that more co-ordination with higher levels of government is key to addressing long-standing issues in Thunder Bay.

“The role of a new mayor and a new council is to actually make that co-ordination process work and work flawlessly,” he said.

“It’s not just a municipal problem. Much of the funding and resources need to be coming from provincial and federal sources, and I don’t think that I should go as mayor without a good plan. I don’t want to go and beg for money.”

Diedrich said collaboration with the province is part of his goal to build more housing, have 90 per cent fewer homeless people and zero tent encampments in Thunder Bay in four years. He criticized the previous administration for allowing designated encampment sites in parks, “where children are playing with their families.”

Kromm said a lot of people he met during the election campaign expressed disappointment and frustration about the work of previous city councils.

“I was shocked a little bit at the lack of enthusiasm that people have for the municipal election,” he said.

“When I’m knocking on doors, they say, ‘Oh, I guess we’ll have to sit down and kind of take a look at the issues,’” Kromm said. “If they’re a business or a homeowner that’s been affected by some of the homelessness or the crime issues, then they’re keenly engaged, but still, it’s a fairly small percentage of people that are responding.”

The city said a total of 9.52 per cent of eligible voters, or more than 8,700, cast their ballots in advance as of Thursday morning. The overall turnout in Thunder Bay’s 2022 election was 43 per cent.

Kromm said people need to pay closer attention to what the candidates are saying.

“Take a look at the councillors, take a look at their skill sets, what do they bring to the table?” he said. “If you vote on name recognition, you’re going to get what you’ve always had.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Affordability measures, consumer protection legislation coming: Alberta government
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta's government says it has a suite of legislation coming this fall to protect Albertans, their pocketbooks and their personal information.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Alberta’s government says it has a suite of legislation coming this fall to protect Albertans, their pocketbooks and their personal information.

Speaking to reporters Friday, government house leader Joseph Schow said the province will soon table new bills to lower the cost of auto insurance and give Albertans new protection when it comes to their utility bills.

New consumer protection rules around ticket resales and used vehicles are also in the works, Schow said, as are stronger rules around the development of artificial intelligence data centres.

Alberta’s politicians are set to return to the legislature Tuesday just as Premier Danielle Smith’s government enters the final calendar year of its mandate.

The next general election is set for Oct. 18, 2027.

Schow said helping Albertans, not the looming election, is driving the legislative agenda. “Each of these initiatives I’ve laid out are addressing some of the very real concerns that we have heard from Albertans,” he said.

The legislature is also set to resume just over a week after Alberta’s historic referendum in which voters overwhelmingly supported keeping the province in Canada.

Voters also approved of the government taking action on a number of immigration reforms, though by slim margins. Smith has said the government would be proceeding with caution. Schow confirmed Friday that no legislation was coming on that topic until at least the spring.

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said Smith’s government seems more concerned with “culture war” politics. He was referring to Schow saying the government had legislation coming that would ensure public sector hiring is “merit based.”

Schow said it was about boosting public confidence and trust in hiring decisions. Nenshi said it was a coded message against diversity hiring. “When they use ‘merit,’ that means don’t hire the ethnic people for these jobs (and) don’t hire women for these jobs,” Nenshi said.

The president of the Alberta Union of Provincial Employees, which represents about 22,000 government employees, also called out the proposal, saying it sounded like a “thinly veiled act of institutionalized racism” meant to divide Albertans against each other.

“The government already ensures that only the best candidates are hired,” Sandra Azocar said in a statement.

“The government is looking for a scapegoat for a problem that does not exist.”

Nenshi also questioned why the government planned to bring in new rules for data centres after spending the last two years positioning Alberta as an ideal place for companies to build.

In July, Smith and tech giant Meta announced a $13-billion AI data centre project in Sturgeon County, just north of Edmonton. The project was quickly met by protests in the community. In a subsequent series of town hall meetings on data centres, hundreds of angry residents confronted Smith’s technology minister.

Nenshi said he thought the government was unprepared for the backlash and reiterated that the NDP has been calling for a pause on data centre development until a thorough policy framework is in place.

Schow said he couldn’t provide specifics but said the government had heard Albertans’ concerns about grid stability, power bills and water usage.

“We are not afraid of moving forward with new technologies, but we will do it in a reasonable, responsible manner,” he said.

Schow also confirmed the government will be taking action in other areas, such as: legislation around bike lanes; stiffer penalties for illegal dumping; new safeguards around voter information; standards for school report cards; and new rules on reporting incidents at daycare centres.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

stories.title: American visitors flock to Charlottetown as P.E.I. pushes to extend tourism season
stories.summary: Passengers stepping off the Carnival Sunshine were happy to finally be on land after a nor’easter forced their ship to skip a stop in Halifax.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown – Passengers stepping off the Carnival Sunshine were happy to finally be on land after a nor’easter forced their ship to skip a stop in Halifax.

Their arrival comes as Port Charlottetown works to extend Prince Edward Island’s tourism season, with cruise visits continuing into early November. The extension gives local businesses that would typically close after Labour Day more opportunities to stay open.

“We’re really excited to be here. We’ve been on this ship for five days now,” said Peter Walter, from Melville, Tenn.

“We’re here to see everything Prince Edward Island has to offer,” said his wife, Sandi.

The port’s efforts include international marketing, building awareness of the destination and investing in infrastructure, said CEO Mike Cochrane. It works with major cruise lines and itinerary planners around the world to promote what Prince Edward Island and Atlantic Canada have to offer in September and October.

Those efforts appear to be paying off. The Island reached a record 1.87 million visitors in 2025, while visitation outside the peak season has increased at least 18 per cent since 2019.

Cochrane said the benefits extend beyond restaurants, taxis and tour guides to fishing and farming communities, as local products gain exposure to audiences from around the world.

“When you can plan on thousands of people at your doorstep on a particular day, ON a particular time… it’s a planned business opportunity,” Cochrane said.

Tourists spent $520.7 million across the province in 2024, according to provincial figures.

It’s all good news for commercial helicopter pilot Charles Racine, who offers sightseeing tours.

“We get to take on more people and more passengers,” he said. “It’s a great time to see the Island in all its fall colours.”

For some visitors, it was their first time this far north.

“We had the opportunity to visit Charlottetown and we took it,” said DJ Blackwell, from North Carolina.

“Canada is different,” said Billy Trevillian, from Cartersville, Virgnia. “So far, it’s cold, but it’s real nice.”

But the chill wasn’t getting in the way of enjoying the Island’s main attractions.

“As Anne said, she’s glad that we have a world where there’s an October,” said Adrian Gilbert with a laugh. “We wanted to come here and enjoy October in the spirit of Anne of Green Gables.”

“As long as I stay warm, I’ll be alright,” said her husband, David.

P.E.I. was named North America’s Best Cruise Destination for 2026 at the World Cruise Awards.

It’s the first Atlantic Canadian destination to receive the title, joining previous recipients including Hawaii, Alaska and Florida.

The port says the recognition gives it another selling point with cruise lines, which plan itineraries two to three years in advance.

The industry generated $49 million in economic output for the province in 2024 and supported about 280 jobs.

Port Charlottetown is already expecting 42 cruise ships and 80,000 visitors next October.

“That means what we’re doing is 100 per cent bang on,” Cochrane said.

stories.title: Wolf attack in northern Saskatchewan injures contractor
stories.summary: A person suffered non-life-threatening injuries after being attacked by a wolf in northern Saskatchewan earlier this week, the province's community safety ministry has confirmed.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A person is recovering after they were attacked by a wolf in northern Saskatchewan earlier this week, according to the province’s community safety ministry.

The attack occurred on Saturday, along Highway 914 in a remote northern area, according to a statement from the Saskatchewan Ministry of Community Safety. It said the person received treatment for non-life-threatening injuries.

They were treated at Cameco’s Key Lake mill, the company said in an email to Global News. The company confirmed that the person attacked worked with the corporation as a contractor and was off-site during the incident.

As a result of the attack, the wolf was captured on Tuesday and euthanized. The animal will be subject to a necropsy at Prairie Diagnostic Services in Saskatoon.

The Saskatchewan Conservation Officer Service’s Wildlife Human Attack Response Team is investigating.

Despite wolves being common, attacks are generally rare in the province as the animals tend to avoid human contact, according to the ministry.

“People travelling, working or recreating in areas where wolves May be present should avoid attracting wildlife with food or garbage, remain aware of their surroundings, and never approach or feed wolves,” it added.

“If you encounter a wolf, do not run or turn your back on it. Face the animal, make yourself appear large, and slowly back away while giving the wolf space to leave the area.”

To report an aggressive or strangely behaving wolf, people can contact the Turn in Poachers and Polluters (Tipp) line at 1-800-667-7561. If it is an emergency, call 911.

stories.title: Jets trade star goaltender Connor Hellebuyck to New Jersey Devils, team confirms
stories.summary: Goaltender Connor Hellebuyck has been traded from the Winnipeg Jets to the New Jersey Devils, the team confirmed Friday.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The Winnipeg Jets have traded star goaltender Connor Hellebuyck to the New Jersey Devils.

In exchange for the goaltender, the team received the Devils’ second-round pick in the 2029 draft and their seventh-round pick for the 2027 draft. The Jets also acquired three forwards, Alexander Command, Dawson Mercer and Nick Bjugstad, in addition to goaltender Nico Daws.

Hellebuyck went public with a trade request in August and was suspended by the team after he chose not to attend training camp. The netminder played on the Jets for his entire NHL career until the team dealt him to the Devils Friday.

Kevin Cheveldayoff, the general manager of the Winnipeg Jets spoke with the media on Friday afternoon, hours after the team announced Hellebuyck was traded.

“At the end of the day, Connor made his choice to do (this) how he chose to do it. And as an organization, we just had to act accordingly, and we did,” Cheveldayoff told reporters.

“Each manager is going to choose to deal with their own set of challenges in their own way. I know how I operate and, again, I know my beliefs. I believe in organization. I believe in our ownership. I think we have an ultra-competitive group in that room of players.”

Cheveldayoff began Friday’s news conference by thanking Hellebuyck for his contributions to the team.

“He was a big part of our family. We accomplished some pretty good things. We obviously didn’t accomplish the end-all goal that we all wanted,” he said.

Command, 18, was the Devils’ first-round pick in the 2026 draft. He was chosen 12th overall and represented Sweden at the 2026 World U-18 Championships, winning gold.

Mercer had four assists for New Jersey in 10 games. He’s been a Devil for six seasons, playing 420 career games, scoring 213 points and 120 penalty minutes.

The third forward acquired by the Jets, Bjugstad, is recovering from surgery. Last season he played 61 games with nine points scored. He will be on the Jets’ injury reserve, the team said.

The Jets’ newly-obtained goaltender, Daws, played four games as a Devil this season and posted a 2-2-0 record with a .874 save percentage. In the 59 career NHL games.

“We addressed some needs that we had in our forward group here right now. We added depth to the organization, we added assets that I can use now – either for drafting or at the trade deadline. And at the end of the day, that’s the goal that I set out to try to accomplish here,” the Jets GM said.

Command was high on the Jets’ list heading into this year’s NHL draft, he said, adding that the forward is already texting with his new teammates.

“I think there’s some great synergy with a lot our young prospects coming up,” he continued.

The Jets and Devils will meet at the Canada Life Centre on Nov. 10. They will also face off in Newark, New Jersey weeks later on Nov. 28.

Kelly Moore, sports director at 680 Cjob and the Manitoba Hockey Hall of Fame media inductee for 2024, told Global News that the Jets trading the goaltender was a long time coming. He said the move will help the jets in seasons to come.

“This will help the Winnipeg Jets in the present and for sure in the future, getting a young prospect like Alexander Command,” Moore said, describing the 18-year-old as “a complete player.”

Mercer will be ready to step into the lineup and make his presence known, the analyst added. He said the Jets have been looking for a player to fill the role Mercer is expected to take on since talks of trading Hellebuyck began.

“For Winnipeg Jets fans, the saga is over,” Moore said. “(And) the Jets get a player that they have been long interested in, Dawson Mercer. And they also get a great young prospect in Alexander Commander.”

Looking to the rest of the Jets’ season, Moore praised current goalie, Stuart Skinner’s, recent performances. He said the acquisition of Daws will further bolster the team’s goaltending.

In his time as a Jet, Hellebuyck won the Hart Memorial Trophy as the league’s most valuable player, three Vezina Trophies as the top goaltender and the Olympic Gold for Team USA in the 2026 games.

— With files from The Canadian Press.

stories.title: U.S. price-fixing case advances against Canadian frozen potato giants
stories.summary: New Brunswick’s McCain Foods Limited and J.D. Irving-owned Cavendish Farms were among five defendants seeking the case’s dismissal.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An Illinois judge says a class-action lawsuit alleging two Canadian companies participated in a frozen potato price-fixing scheme in the U.S. can continue.

New Brunswick’s McCain Foods Limited and J.D. Irving-owned Cavendish Farms were among five defendants seeking the case’s dismissal.

The case began in 2024 with commercial and consumer plaintiffs alleging the companies conspired to increase the price of frozen french fries, tater tots and other products.

They alleged the industry’s “good ol’ boys network” used a data analytics platform called PotatoTrack to share sales and pricing information.

The defendant companies, which together control about 98 per cent of the U.S. market, argued the case should be dismissed.

Last month a U.S. judge allowed most claims under a federal antitrust law to continue, but rejected some claims made under the laws of various states.

McCain and Cavendish did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.

stories.title: Nova Scotia police watchdog clears officers in murder plot, extortion investigation
stories.summary: Two officers were cleared of wrongdoing following an investigation into allegations the pair had conspired to commit murder and that one had tried to blackmail the other.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Nova Scotia’s police watchdog has cleared two officers of wrongdoing following an investigation into allegations the pair had conspired to commit murder and that one had tried to blackmail the other.

The Serious Incident Response Team released a report saying it received a referral from another police force in May regarding two members of the Annapolis Royal Police Service.

The independent agency says its investigation focused on a conversation between two officers in May of last year, which dealt with harming a person known to police.

The team also investigated an allegation that one of the officers threatened to release a recording of the conversation unless the other complied with a request concerning a workplace matter, though no details were provided.

stories.title: Canadian banking fees hard for consumers to see or anticipate, report says
stories.summary: The fees most Canadian banks charge their customers are hard to see or anticipate, and the associated costs can add up quickly over time, a new report says.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The fees most Canadian banks charge their customers are hard to see or anticipate, and the associated costs can add up quickly over time, a new report says.

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, a federal watchdog, released a report Friday which reviewed how Canadian banking fees are structured, disclosed and experienced by consumers. It was conducted on request by the federal government in Budget 2025 .

The report examined some of the most common fees consumers see, including for deposit accounts and related banking services.

It found there is a general lack of transparency in some of the ways banks charge their customers, which are often complex and leave little wiggle room for consumers that May grapple with the costs.

“Canadians should be able to clearly understand what they are paying for banking services,” said Shereen Benzvy Miller, commissioner of the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada in a release.

“When fees make the full cost harder to see, it affects both affordability and competition.”

To help avoid confusion, the agency suggests banks offer personalized, usage-based information to customers.

Some examples of fees examined in the report include those for account maintenance, excess transactions, the use of an ATM, non-sufficient funds and overdraft protection, currency conversion and cross-border debit, prepaid product payments and fees charged for customers to transfer-out funds to another bank.

The report says many of the fees can be combined, depending on the transaction or service, and consumers May not fully understand how those costs will add up before completing those transactions — even with current point-in-time disclosures.

Some of these fees and overall costs to consumers are avoidable or can be reduced in certain circumstances, but consumers May not be aware.

These include fees that add up when a customer exceeds their account limits, multiple fees on a single ATM withdrawal, when a fee on prepaid payments is withdrawn from that same prepaid payment and reduces its available balance over time, and when the cost of overdraft protection May cost less than a combination of fees for non-sufficient funds or dishonoured payments.

“Consumers May find it difficult to monitor their transaction usage throughout the billing cycle and to anticipate when excess transaction fees will be charged,” the report says.

“Banks are not required to notify consumers when they are approaching or have exceeded their transaction limits. As a result, consumers May only become aware that excess transaction fees have been charged after the end of the billing period.”

The report suggests changes be made to require that banks provide notifications when customers are nearing their transaction limits or May incur excess fees.

It adds: “Repeated reminders would increase the salience of these costs and May prompt consumers to reassess their account usage or consider alternative options that better align with their needs.”

Earlier this year, the federal government capped the fee banks can charge its customers for having non-sufficient funds , or NSFs, at $10.

Deciding which bank to go with can also be a challenge for consumers, the report says, noting that when consumers are deciding which bank’s fee structure aligns with their specific needs, many banks make comparing their products and services too complex.

For example, account holders May not be aware when the features they are entitled to no longer align with their needs, and when alternatives are available that are more helpful and cost effective.

Some banks have fees or processes that May also discourage consumers from switching accounts or banks. This includes transfer-out fees some banks charge customers to move money from one account to another.

The report says there are also barriers that make it difficult for consumers to compare products and services across institutions, including limited visibility into total banking costs over time.

“More transparency makes it easier for consumers to compare options and save money, and financial institutions have stronger incentives to compete for their business,” said Benzvy Miller, the watchdog’s commissioner.

The report from the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada comes amid an ongoing lawsuit and pending settlement that alleges Cibc unfairly charged non-sufficient funds fees to customers multiple times for the same transaction. A similar settlement involved TD Bank in 2024.

stories.title: Teachers, are you assigning more pencil and paper assignments in the age of AI? Let us know
stories.summary: As reading skills decline in Canadian schools, we want to hear from teachers taking steps to improve scores and help students think more critically
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
The reading skills of Canadian high-school students are in decline, according to the most recent test scores from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development.

Other countries saw a similar trend.

The results were concerning to Andreas Schleicher, the Oecd’s director for education and skills, who told The Globe that in the age of artificial intelligence , students will need strong reading skills more than ever.

For a future story, we would like to hear from teachers across the country about the reading skills of their students and the steps they’ve taken to mitigate the effects of AI and help their classroom think more critically.

How have you changed your classroom practices when it comes to reading and writing? Are you assigning more paper and pencil assignments? Are you requiring oral presentations or other analog-type work?

Share your story in the box below, or send us an e-mail at audience@globeandmail.com .

stories.title: U.S. case alleging price-fixing advances against Canadian frozen potato giants
stories.summary: Florenceville-Bristol - An Illinois judge says a class-action lawsuit alleging two Canadian companies participated in a frozen potato price-fixing scheme in the U.S. can continue.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Florenceville-Bristol - An Illinois judge says a class-action lawsuit alleging two Canadian companies participated in a frozen potato price-fixing scheme in the U.S. can continue.

New Brunswick’s McCain Foods Limited and J.D. Irving-owned Cavendish Farms were among five defendants seeking the case’s dismissal.

Defendants also include U.S. potato product companies Lamb Weston and J.R. Simplot, along with Circana, a third-party data provider whose PotatoTrack analytics platform the firms allegedly used to conspire with each other.

The case began in 2024 when grocer Redner’s Markets filed the initial complaint. It was consolidated with similar actions from commercial and consumer plaintiffs in 2025 alleging the potato companies conspired to increase the price of frozen french fries, hash browns, tater tots and other products.

The plaintiffs cited several examples of the companies increasing their prices by similar amounts at similar times, sometimes the same day, or within days of each other.

They alleged the industry’s “good ol’ boys network” used the PotatoTrack platform to share sales and pricing information for the American frozen potato sector, with the claimed price-fixing beginning in 2021.

The allegations have not been tested in court.

Court documents say frozen products make up about half of the entire U.S. potato market and the frozen sector was worth US$68 billion in 2023.

The plaintiffs claimed frozen potato prices increased 62 per cent between January 2022 and December 2024. Meanwhile, they claimed the companies’ input costs declined 33 per cent between October 2023 and the middle of 2025.

The defendants, including McCain and Cavendish, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.

The potato companies argued in court that their costs spiked and compressed profit margins for years during the COVID-19 pandemic, giving an “obvious alternative explanation” for the price increases.

The judge ruled the argument did not undermine the conspiracy allegations, instead noting pandemic-era constraints could give the companies “an even greater incentive to conspire to fix prices.”

Court papers say Lamb Weston has 40 per cent of the U.S. frozen potato market, McCain has 30 per cent, Simplot stands at 20 per cent and Cavendish has about seven to eight per cent. Together they control about 98 per cent of the market.

The defendant companies made a joint submission arguing the case should be dismissed because the plaintiffs had “failed to adequately plead the existence of a conspiracy in order to state a claim.”

McCain made additional arguments saying the U.S. district court for the northern district of Illinois lacked jurisdiction over the company and that the court was not the proper venue.

Circana argued the plaintiffs did not plausibly allege it participated in a conspiracy and didn’t provide any motive for it to have done so.

Circana describes itself as a leading technology, AI and data company for a range of businesses, including consumer packaged goods companies.

The plaintiffs claimed PotatoTrack provides “individual item level data” for all frozen potato shipments from the four processors to food service customers in the U.S. and foreign countries. They claimed each company receives reports showing their data on one side, and data from the other three companies on the other.

They claim PotatoTrack reports compile proprietary pricing data on all products sent to food service outlets, such as restaurants, schools and hospitals.

Judge Jeffrey I. Cummings largely rejected the arguments from the defendants and allowed most aspects of the case under a federal antitrust law to proceed to the next stage in his Sept. 17 ruling. He disallowed a number claims made under laws of various U.S. states.

While the use of PotatoTrack was the main argument of the plaintiffs, they also argued potato company executives are “unusually close for competitors” and could share pricing information by hiring each other’s former employees.

They cited the producers all belonging to the same collection of trade organizations and sharing co-packing arrangements where pricing can be discussed.

They claimed the producers sometimes use the same third-parties to store their product and that personnel could check out the inventory and product destinations of other companies in real time.

The plaintiffs alleged the companies exchanged letters with effective dates of price increases included.

They also claim the companies tried to conceal their communications, alleging that Lamb Weston employees in particular were told to send text messages “to avoid creating emails that could be discovered in the event of an antitrust investigation.”

The defendants argued that in order for the case to proceed the plaintiffs needed to allege the companies had direct agreements with each other, rather than through a third-party service like PotatoTrack. The judge said that argument was incorrect.

“All told, these allegations support a plausible inference that the information exchange occurring at the same time as historic price increases resulted in those anticompetitive effects,” the judge wrote.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

— By Devin Stevens in Halifax.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version of the story had a headline that incorrectly stated a U.S. price-fixing case was advancing against Canadian companies. In fact, a case is advancing against the companies that alleges price-fixing is taking place, but those allegations have not been tested in court.

content_blocks.text: Court documents say frozen products make up about half of the entire U.S. potato market and the frozen sector was worth US$68 billion in 2023.
content_blocks.html: Court documents say frozen products make up about half of the entire U.S. potato market and the frozen sector was worth US$68 billion in 2023.

content_blocks.text: The plaintiffs claimed frozen potato prices increased 62 per cent between January 2022 and December 2024. Meanwhile, they claimed the companies’ input costs declined 33 per cent between October 2023 and the middle of 2025.
content_blocks.html: The plaintiffs claimed frozen potato prices increased 62 per cent between January 2022 and December 2024. Meanwhile, they claimed the companies’ input costs declined 33 per cent between October 2023 and the middle of 2025.

content_blocks.text: The defendants, including McCain and Cavendish, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.
content_blocks.html: The defendants, including McCain and Cavendish, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.

content_blocks.text: The potato companies argued in court that their costs spiked and compressed profit margins for years during the COVID-19 pandemic, giving an “obvious alternative explanation” for the price increases.
content_blocks.html: The potato companies argued in court that their costs spiked and compressed profit margins for years during the COVID-19 pandemic, giving an “obvious alternative explanation” for the price increases.

content_blocks.text: The judge ruled the argument did not undermine the conspiracy allegations, instead noting pandemic-era constraints could give the companies “an even greater incentive to conspire to fix prices.”
content_blocks.html: The judge ruled the argument did not undermine the conspiracy allegations, instead noting pandemic-era constraints could give the companies “an even greater incentive to conspire to fix prices.”

content_blocks.text: Court papers say Lamb Weston has 40 per cent of the U.S. frozen potato market, McCain has 30 per cent, Simplot stands at 20 per cent and Cavendish has about seven to eight per cent. Together they control about 98 per cent of the market.
content_blocks.html: Court papers say Lamb Weston has 40 per cent of the U.S. frozen potato market, McCain has 30 per cent, Simplot stands at 20 per cent and Cavendish has about seven to eight per cent. Together they control about 98 per cent of the market.

content_blocks.text: The defendant companies made a joint submission arguing the case should be dismissed because the plaintiffs had “failed to adequately plead the existence of a conspiracy in order to state a claim.”
content_blocks.html: The defendant companies made a joint submission arguing the case should be dismissed because the plaintiffs had “failed to adequately plead the existence of a conspiracy in order to state a claim.”

content_blocks.text: McCain made additional arguments saying the U.S. district court for the northern district of Illinois lacked jurisdiction over the company and that the court was not the proper venue.
content_blocks.html: McCain made additional arguments saying the U.S. district court for the northern district of Illinois lacked jurisdiction over the company and that the court was not the proper venue.

content_blocks.text: Circana argued the plaintiffs did not plausibly allege it participated in a conspiracy and didn’t provide any motive for it to have done so.
content_blocks.html: Circana argued the plaintiffs did not plausibly allege it participated in a conspiracy and didn’t provide any motive for it to have done so.

content_blocks.text: Circana describes itself as a leading technology, AI and data company for a range of businesses, including consumer packaged goods companies.
content_blocks.html: Circana describes itself as a leading technology, AI and data company for a range of businesses, including consumer packaged goods companies.

content_blocks.text: The plaintiffs claimed PotatoTrack provides “individual item level data” for all frozen potato shipments from the four processors to food service customers in the U.S. and foreign countries. They claimed each company receives reports showing their data on one side, and data from the other three companies on the other.
content_blocks.html: The plaintiffs claimed PotatoTrack provides “individual item level data” for all frozen potato shipments from the four processors to food service customers in the U.S. and foreign countries. They claimed each company receives reports showing their data on one side, and data from the other three companies on the other.

content_blocks.text: They claim PotatoTrack reports compile proprietary pricing data on all products sent to food service outlets, such as restaurants, schools and hospitals.
content_blocks.html: They claim PotatoTrack reports compile proprietary pricing data on all products sent to food service outlets, such as restaurants, schools and hospitals.

content_blocks.text: Judge Jeffrey I. Cummings largely rejected the arguments from the defendants and allowed most aspects of the case under a federal antitrust law to proceed to the next stage in his Sept. 17 ruling. He disallowed a number claims made under laws of various U.S. states.
content_blocks.html: Judge Jeffrey I. Cummings largely rejected the arguments from the defendants and allowed most aspects of the case under a federal antitrust law to proceed to the next stage in his Sept. 17 ruling. He disallowed a number claims made under laws of various U.S. states.

content_blocks.text: While the use of PotatoTrack was the main argument of the plaintiffs, they also argued potato company executives are “unusually close for competitors” and could share pricing information by hiring each other’s former employees.
content_blocks.html: While the use of PotatoTrack was the main argument of the plaintiffs, they also argued potato company executives are “unusually close for competitors” and could share pricing information by hiring each other’s former employees.

content_blocks.text: They cited the producers all belonging to the same collection of trade organizations and sharing co-packing arrangements where pricing can be discussed.
content_blocks.html: They cited the producers all belonging to the same collection of trade organizations and sharing co-packing arrangements where pricing can be discussed.

content_blocks.text: They claimed the producers sometimes use the same third-parties to store their product and that personnel could check out the inventory and product destinations of other companies in real time.
content_blocks.html: They claimed the producers sometimes use the same third-parties to store their product and that personnel could check out the inventory and product destinations of other companies in real time.

content_blocks.text: The plaintiffs alleged the companies exchanged letters with effective dates of price increases included.
content_blocks.html: The plaintiffs alleged the companies exchanged letters with effective dates of price increases included.

content_blocks.text: They also claim the companies tried to conceal their communications, alleging that Lamb Weston employees in particular were told to send text messages “to avoid creating emails that could be discovered in the event of an antitrust investigation.”
content_blocks.html: They also claim the companies tried to conceal their communications, alleging that Lamb Weston employees in particular were told to send text messages “to avoid creating emails that could be discovered in the event of an antitrust investigation.”

content_blocks.text: The defendants argued that in order for the case to proceed the plaintiffs needed to allege the companies had direct agreements with each other, rather than through a third-party service like PotatoTrack. The judge said that argument was incorrect.
content_blocks.html: The defendants argued that in order for the case to proceed the plaintiffs needed to allege the companies had direct agreements with each other, rather than through a third-party service like PotatoTrack. The judge said that argument was incorrect.

content_blocks.text: “All told, these allegations support a plausible inference that the information exchange occurring at the same time as historic price increases resulted in those anticompetitive effects,” the judge wrote.
content_blocks.html: “All told, these allegations support a plausible inference that the information exchange occurring at the same time as historic price increases resulted in those anticompetitive effects,” the judge wrote.

stories.title: Small plane experienced engine failure before fatal Ottawa crash, investigation finds
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Transportation Safety Board of Canada says a small airplane experienced engine failure before it crashed near the Ottawa International Airport last year, killing the pilot and injuring two passengers.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The Transportation Safety Board of Canada says a small airplane experienced engine failure before it crashed near the Ottawa International Airport last year, killing the pilot and injuring two passengers.

The board’s report says various pieces detached from the engine and oil sprayed across the windshield of the privately registered Grumman AA-5A at 5:45 p.m. on July 31, 2025, causing the pilot to divert to the international airport and start descending.

stories.title: Toronto election: Chow holding decisive lead over Bradford, new poll indicates
stories.summary: A new poll released Friday suggests Olivia Chow is holding a decisive lead over Brad Bradford in Toronto’s mayoral contest.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A new poll released Friday suggests Olivia Chow is holding a decisive lead over Brad Bradford in Toronto’s mayoral contest.

The Pollara Strategic Insights’ survey indicates the incumbent leads her main challenger 55 per cent to 44 per cent among decided voters, including those who have already voted.

The online poll suggests 48 per cent of respondents have positive feelings about Chow, while only 36 per cent feel the same about Bradford.

Chow leads Bradford on working with other levels of government, affordability, safety and taxes, and there is no consensus on which candidate will bring change or who will be best for the economy and jobs.

Several polls recently have put Bradford slightly ahead of Chow. Others still place her ahead of Bradford – including a Pollara survey released Tuesday – indicating there is no clear favourite, according to the research firms that publish the polls.

A Liaison Strategies survey released Wednesday puts Bradford at 49 per cent support and Chow at 47 per cent among decided and leaning voters, with three per cent choosing someone else.

In this most recent poll, Chow has lost a five-point lead she had in a Liaison Strategies poll published Oct. 13 .

Another poll published Tuesday by Mainstreet Research also revealed a very narrow race with a slight advantage for Bradford. The firm put Bradford’s support at 48.9 per cent support and Chow at a “nearly equal” 47.5 per cent, Mainstreet said in a statement.

Both candidates have been hitting the pavement daily in the final week before the Oct. 26 election to reach those precious undecided voters who May push the vote slightly more on either side.

Chow is looking to secure her first full term after winning the 2023 mayoral byelection, while Bradford is seeking to become Toronto’s sixth mayor since amalgamation on Jan. 1, 1998.

Between Oct. 16 and 21, Pollara conducted a hybrid online and telephone survey of 1,094 Toronto residents aged 18 and older who are eligible to vote: 697 online panel completes and 397 live telephone interviews. Data was weighted to reflect the age, gender and regional composition of Toronto’s adult population, based on the most recent census figures. While online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error, a probability sample of this size would be accurate to ± 3.0%, 19 times out of 20. Vote results include those who have already voted at the advance polls (26%), who were asked how they voted. This research was commissioned by Cupe Local 416 (Toronto Civic Employees’ Union).

Liaison Strategies surveyed a random sample of 1,000 Toronto residents from Oct. 18 to Oct. 19, 2026, using conventional phone and Interactive Voice Recording (IVR) technology. The margin of error is +/- 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. The margin is higher for subsamples, including decided and leaning voters.

Mainstreet Research conducted its survey between Oct. 16 and Oct. 18, 2026 with a sample size of 1,000 adults, 18 years of age or older, living in Toronto. The survey was conducted using conventional phone Interactive Voice Response (IVR) technology. The margin of error for the poll is +/- 3.1% at the 95% confidence level. Margins of error are higher in each subsample.

The Pollara Strategic Insights survey was fielded Oct. 13 to 19, 2026. It surveyed Toronto residents aged 18+ eligible to vote (695 online panel, 404 live telephone). The poll was commissioned by Cupe Local 416 (Toronto Civic Employees’ Union). It was weighted to census data by gender, age and region. It states that “because the sample includes an online panel, no margin of error applies”. A probability sample of 1,099 would carry a margin of error of +/- 3.0 percentage points, 19 times out of 20, and more for subgroups. Subgroups with an unweighted base under 100 should be read with caution, it says.

stories.title: AI concerns continue to hit Big Tech stocks Friday as oil prices rise again
stories.summary: Stocks are opening lower Friday on Wall Street as Big Tech companies tied to artificial intelligence swing lower again and oil prices rise.
stories.author: Elaine Kurtenbach And Michelle Chapman
stories.content:
Stocks are opening lower Friday on Wall Street as Big Tech companies tied to artificial intelligence swing lower again and oil prices rise.

The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent in the early going Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 547 points, or one per cent. The Nasdaq composite was down 0.4 per cent.

Concerns about the cost of building out AI have weighed heavily on on stocks this week , though a sell-off eased early Friday.

AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that the booming sector May be under threat from the rising costs of borrowing money to build data centers and buy more AI chips.

Among tech stocks, Meta fell 2.1 per cent.

Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent , fell slightly before the market opened Friday after reporting stronger than expected revenue for the latest quarter, though profits fell short. The Facebook and Instagram parent company, which closed down seven per cent on Thursday, also said it’s creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.

Tesla was a bit higher in premarket trading after closing down 3.1 per cent on Thursday as the electric vehicle maker reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.

The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4 per cent at Thursday’s close, but it made slight gains before Friday’s market open. The chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value and movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other.

The Toronto Stock Exchange was down close to one per cent.

European markets were lower. France’s main index fell one per cent, though yields on French government bonds eased a bit. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.97 per cent.

Oil prices reached levels not seen since May amid halting efforts to bring the U.S. and Iran back to the negotiation table.

The price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 1.8 per cent to just above US$115 a barrel, its highest level since March. U.S. benchmark crude oil jumped 1.8 per cent to $101.22 per barrel.

Gasoline prices in the U.S. are rising again. The national average for a gallon of regular gas rose two cents to $4.29 Friday, according to the AAA, compared with $3.07 a gallon a year ago.

Higher oil prices have weighed on stocks. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped four per cent on Thursday and has shot up from less than $97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.

Turkey hosted meetings Friday with the foreign ministers of Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and European nations — the UK, France, Germany and Italy — to discuss conflicts in the Middle East and efforts to resolve the Russia-Ukraine war.

In Europe, Germany’s DAX dropped 0.8 per cent to 25,171.50, while the CAC 40 in Paris fell 0.7 per cent to 7,756.34. Britain’s Ftse 100 declined 0.5 per cent to 10,670.55. Asian markets were mostly higher.

The U.S. dollar rose to 156.92 Japanese yen from 156.77 yen. The euro fell to $1.1195 from $1.1218.

The Canadian dollar rose about a tenth of a cent to 71.52 U.S. cents.

stories.title: St. Thomas police suspend Crime Stoppers participation after cybersecurity breach
stories.summary: The St. Thomas Police Service has temporarily suspended its participation in the St. Thomas-Elgin Crime Stoppers program following a cybersecurity breach involving a third-party platform used to manage anonymous tips.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The St. Thomas Police Service has temporarily suspended its participation in the St. Thomas-Elgin Crime Stoppers program following a cybersecurity breach involving a third-party platform used to manage anonymous tips.

In a news release issued Friday, police said the breach involves Navigate360’s P3 platform, the system used by Crime Stoppers organizations to receive and manage anonymous information from the public.

Police said the decision to pause participation was made immediately as officials assess the scope of the breach and determine what safeguards May be required before continuing involvement in the program.

The St. Thomas Police Service said the incident involves a third-party Crime Stoppers platform that operates independently from police internal information systems. Investigators are working to verify the impact on the St. Thomas-Elgin Crime Stoppers program, including any potential risks to individuals who submitted information, confidential data and ongoing police investigations.

“Crime Stoppers and its volunteers have made valuable contributions to the St. Thomas community for decades, strengthening public safety through a longstanding partnership and valuable support for police investigations,” Chief Marc Roskamp said in the release.

“The safety of people who provide information, the protection of confidential information and public trust must guide our response. We will reassess our participation once we have the verified findings and security assurances needed to make an informed decision.”

Police are asking residents to report crimes and public safety concerns directly to the St. Thomas Police Service while the suspension remains in effect.

Anyone with information about a crime or public safety concern can contact police at 519-631-1224. Non-emergency incidents can also be reported through the service’s online reporting system.

Police said anyone requiring immediate assistance should call 911.

stories.title: New $24M federal investment fuels Western-led bid to cure HIV
stories.summary: Western-led international research initiative to develop an accessible HIV cure received $24 million in federal funding.
stories.author: Jeff Renaud
stories.content:
A Western-led international research initiative to develop an accessible HIV cure has received $24 million in federal funding to promote its equitable approach to advancing treatment. The six-year project aims to deliver promising treatments for first-in-human clinical trials while building capacity for cost effective production and delivery in Canada and Uganda.

The new investment supports Immunequity, a large-scale collaboration led by Western and involving researchers from the University of British Columbia, the University of Ottawa, Université de Montréal and the University of Manitoba, alongside partners in Uganda and industry. The federal New Frontiers in Research Fund’s Transformation stream supports Canadian-led interdisciplinary projects tackling major global challenges with the potential for lasting change.

Immunequity, led by Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry’s Eric Arts, aims to develop an HIV cure that can be made affordable and accessible in countries where the need is greatest. The international team will combine new treatment approaches with frugal biomedical technologies that lower the cost of making, delivering and monitoring the treatment. It will also help build the policies, partnerships and manufacturing capacity needed to bring these innovations to people in Uganda and across sub-Saharan Africa.

Nearly 40 million people worldwide live with HIV. Most require daily medication for life.

The ultimate goal is to reimagine how HIV cures are developed with scientific innovation, affordability, manufacturability and equitable access as inseparable goals. Immunequity brings together Canadian and Ugandan researchers from the outset, rather than developing a cure in Canada and addressing access in lower-income countries later.

“This substantial investment will help Western researchers and our partners tackle a long-standing health challenge that continues to affect millions around the world,” said Western President Alan Shepard. “We’re grateful for the initiative and leadership of all those involved in the Immunequity partnership.”

For Arts, Western’s Canada Research Chair in HIV Pathogenesis and Viral Control, the funding represents a major step forward for an idea that has been years in development.

“The pattern for too long has been to develop a treatment in a high-income country and, years later, it makes its way to lower-income countries. And these countries May not even have the capacity to produce it,” said Arts, a microbiology and immunology professor at Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry. “We have an opportunity to change that with Immunequity.”

While maintaining the quality and safety needed for widespread use in sub-Saharan Africa, Immunequity will also advance frugal innovations to make HIV diagnosis and monitoring and biotherapeutic production more affordable and practical. The biomedical engineering team will develop smaller, more efficient manufacturing approaches to ensure safe, temperature-controlled transportation and storage of therapeutics.

To support this work, the Western team also includes medical biophysics professors Maria Drangova and David Holdsworth, engineering professors James Lacefield and Arghya Paul and Margaret Mutumba, director of Western’s Africa Institute and Frugal Biomedical Innovations.

Eric Arts (Megan Morris/Schulich Medicine & Dentistry)

“This support from the Canadian government provides the opportunity to really make a difference,” said Arts, Immunequity’s principal investigator. “Studying a disease and being able to treat a disease are two very different things.”

The first priority is to produce a biotherapeutic, a treatment made from living organisms, at Western’s new Pathogen Research Centre, creating a potential HIV cure suitable for first-in-human studies.

Currently under construction at Western Research Parks, the Pathogen Research Centre will bring advanced containment, real-world testing environments and clinical-scale therapeutic manufacturing together under one roof. The $44-million facility is expected to be ready for occupancy in 2027.

Immunequity is pursuing two promising approaches to an HIV cure in parallel. At UBC, Peter Zandstra and his collaborators are advancing a distinct biotherapeutic approach alongside Western’s, giving Immunequity two opportunities to advance its goal of an effective, scalable and accessible HIV cure.

The six-year program is expected to include the first-in-human studies in Canada and Uganda, building on years of research to prepare the new treatments for clinical testing.

“An investment of this scale would not have been possible with an idea alone,” said Arts. “We first had to generate substantial preclinical evidence showing these therapeutic approaches have the potential to work in humans.”

Ugandan partners include Dr. Cissy Kityo Mutuluuza, DSc’25,and colleagues at the Joint Clinical Research Centre and Makerere University in Kampala, building on decades of HIV research and clinical experience in Uganda. The project also involves industry partners, including Toronto-based SHC Therapeutics, and expertise in biomanufacturing and commercialization.

“For Uganda, this is the chance to prove an HIV cure works at home, working alongside Canada rather than years behind it. What makes this support for Immunequity so transformative is that it embeds health equity directly into the scientific process from day one,” said Kityo Mutuluuza. “Together, we are setting a new blueprint for how therapies should be co-developed and delivered globally.”

Core faculty members of the Immunequity team. Dr. Cissy Kityo Mutuluuza (front centre), Ugandan HIV/Aids researcher and executive director of the Joint Clinical Research Centre, visisted Western in June 2025 for early planning meetings and to receive an honorary degree. (Maria Drangova/Schulich Medicine & Dentistry)

The goal is to develop a scientifically effective therapy that can be manufactured at scale and made affordable across different health-care settings.

“One of the real strengths of this collaboration is that Canada has the depth of expertise and infrastructure to assemble a world-class team of its own,” said Arts. “We have the scientific, engineering and manufacturing capabilities to advance this work here in Canada. Working with partners in Uganda every step of the way gives us an opportunity to help develop a potential HIV cure that can also be produced and made accessible where it is needed most.”

Learn more about how Western is optimizing health for all.

stories.title: More Ontario police forces pause Crime Stoppers use after cyber breach
stories.summary: Police in Halton, Peel and York regions, Hamilton and Kingston have announced suspensions after Toronto Crime Stoppers paused its phone, online and app-based tip intake.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Several Ontario police forces are suspending their use of Crime Stoppers as concerns grow over a cybersecurity breach that potentially exposed identifying information included in some anonymous tips.

Police in Halton, Peel and York regions, Hamilton and Kingston have announced suspensions after Toronto Crime Stoppers paused its phone, online and app-based tip intake .

“Crime Stoppers’ brand as we know it is essentially dead,” tech analyst Carmi Levy told Global News.

“This is catastrophic. If you called in information on any crime at all, and you assumed that information would be held confidential, that has now been blown up.”

In March, hackers stole data from P3, the tip-management software Toronto Crime Stoppers has used since 2018, Chair Sean Sportun said in a statement Wednesday.

Navigate360, which provides the P3 platform, “repeatedly” assured Toronto Crime Stoppers the system was secure, Sportun said. A month after the attack, the provider said some Canadian data had been stolen but that Toronto submissions were not affected, he added.

Sportun said the organization was told in June tips submitted to the platform between January 2022 and November 2025 were affected. A month later, it pegged the figure at 176,859 tips affected, adding 12,392 of them May contain personal information.

“We never ask for your name, and we don’t want it. But people sometimes include details to explain what they saw,” Sportun said.

“Before a tip goes to investigators, our practice is to remove those details. It has come to light that some of those original tips containing potentially identifying information were stolen from P3.”

In September and October, Navigate360 gave Toronto Crime Stoppers a list of 14,973 names found in the breach. However, Sportun said the list “lacks detail necessary to measure the risk involved” because it did not identify who the names belonged to.

Toronto Crime Stoppers continues to press Navigate360 for details.

Navigate360 did not immediately return Global News’ request for comment.

Sportun added that “anonymously sourced information” reported this week had not been shared with Toronto Crime Stoppers. An investigation by CBC published Wednesday reported that more than 1.5 million Canadian Crime Stoppers tips were affected.

Sean Sparling, a former deputy chief of the Sault Ste. Marie Police Service, told Global News officers across Canada use Crime Stoppers “on a daily basis.”

He said he relied on Crime Stoppers for many of his own investigations.

“Knowing Crime Stoppers and how well it’s organized, how well it works and its importance to the law enforcement community and the safety of our communities, I fully expect they’re going to recover from this,” Sparling said.

Crime Stoppers programs in Peel and Hamilton said in separate statements Thursday they continue to press Navigate360 for more information.

Police forces in Kingston, York and Halton regions said Thursday they’re assessing the impact of the breach on their operations.

Toronto police said Wednesday the service is temporarily suspending its use of Crime Stoppers while it assesses new safeguards and other measures.

Each police force said members of the public can submit information through existing police reporting channels, though those methods are not anonymous.

Anyone facing an immediate emergency should call 911.

“Until we have a safer way to protect you, please do not send us tips by phone, online or through the app,” Sportun said.

“Pausing our program means that option isn’t available now, and we did not make this decision lightly. We are pausing because those people deserve a system we can fully stand behind.”

stories.title: At the annual Witches Walk in this Ontario village, women are free to be whoever they want
stories.summary: Coldwater has just over 1,100 residents, but the sleepy, historic place attracts thousands of visitors every year through its cosplay events
stories.author: Writing and photography Laura Proctor
stories.content:
On the first bitterly cold night of October, a group of women are warming their hands by a bubbling cauldron in Coldwater, Ont. They’re talking about witches. More specifically, they’re talking about why thousands flock to the Coldwater Witches Walk every year.

“There are a lot of women here who are being who they want to be for one night,” says Jodi Derrick, a local resident and Witches Walk devotee. Derrick came to the event on the evening of Oct. 16 with her friend, Christine Nicholls, and Christine’s sister, April Brown. The three women shared drinks and laughs at her house before donning their witches hats and heading downtown.

Christine Nicholls, Jodi Derrick and April Brown leave for the Coldwater Witches Walk on Oct. 16, an annual tradition that includes costume contests and a haunted house.

The event brings out thousands of people every year, most of them women.

Coldwater has just over 1,100 residents, but this sleepy village attracts thousands of visitors every year through its cosplay events – including a steampunk festival, a fairy festival and the Witches Walk, which started in 2008 and has since exploded in popularity. Witches Walk attendees take part in costume contests, browse witchy wares from artisans and brave the haunted house that’s set up in Coldwater’s historic mill.

The crowds that take over the town are mostly women, who say they feel free to look and act how they want at the event: ugly, scary, striking, powerful, boisterous and loud. They can stalk through the shadows at night, while also feeling safe to be out in the dark.

But the cackles and pointed hats aren’t just for cisgender women. As one attendee pointed out, the event is for anyone who feels like they belong outside of traditional societal expectations, those who might have been called a witch or something similar, in a different time.

“They used to burn women at the stake because they labelled them as witches – but they were just different. They just didn’t conform to the norm,” says Brown, a former nurse who cracks jokes about her prosthetic leg.

“As times have moved on, we’ve progressed. We can be who we want to be. We don’t have to conform to someone else’s idea of who a woman is.”

stories.title: Precedent-setting human trafficking sentence handed down in Saskatchewan
stories.summary: A case Saskatchewan Crown prosecutors are calling precedent-setting for human trafficking convictions in the province has concluded with a judge’s sentencing decision.
stories.author: Grace Miller
stories.content:
A case Saskatchewan Crown prosecutors are calling precedent-setting for human trafficking convictions in the province has concluded with a judge’s sentencing decision. Judge Miguel Martinez handed down prison sentences of four years for Sohel Hadiar for human trafficking offences and 14 years for Muhammad Musam on charges of human trafficking and sexual assault.

Senior Crown prosecutor Leslie Dunning said this case will be used to inform future human trafficking cases in Saskatchewan.

“We didn’t cite any Saskatchewan human trafficking cases, all of what we cited mainly came out of Ontario. So this is one of the precedent-setting cases for human trafficking in the province,” said Dunning.

The judge found the Bengali men, Hadiar and Musam, took advantage of a Bengali woman’s vulnerability. She is referred to as S.K. to protect her identity.

Court heard the men withheld S.K.’s citizenship documentation and threatened to break her work permit in an effort to exploit her. The judge determined the men forced the victim to work up to 12 hours a day, six days a week with very little pay.

The two moved S.K. between the Saskatchewan communities of Gull Lake, Elrose and Tisdale for jobs at their restaurants.

Both men will have to pay restitution to S.K. of more than $17,000.

The courtroom also heard the victim impact statement from the woman, in which she said the abuse ruined her life.

S.K. wrote about feeling stuck in her life and feeling scared of being trafficked again if she tried to improve her situation.

“I don’t think much about my future anymore and focus on keeping my head down,” said S.K.

“How could they do this to a Bengali sister for just a little money?”

S.K. also said her family in Bangladesh know about the abuse and are facing intense public scrutiny.

She said her mother sometimes asks her why she had to try to come to Canada. S.K. said she asks herself the same question.

stories.title: U.S. claims of Canadian political interference have ‘no merit,’ Carney says
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says there is "no merit" to American claims that Canadians might be interfering in U.S. politics ahead of November's midterm elections.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says there is “no merit” to American claims that Canadians might be interfering in U.S. politics ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Officials in the Trump administration, including U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra , have claimed Canadian politicians are interfering in the democratic process south of the border.

Hoekstra has said the administration is watching Canadian politicians closely ahead of the midterms and warned them to butt out of American politics.

Carney has consistently rebutted accusations of electoral interference and told reporters in Turkey today that he’s “disappointed” the U.S. envoy is spreading those claims.

Canadian diplomats were told this week not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections amid a period of “heightened sensitivity.”

The prime minister says Canada has deep diplomatic ties to the United States but is careful to avoid even the perception of interference in electoral processes.

stories.title: Quebec coroner’s report questions suicide conclusion in death of 18-year-old
stories.summary: A Quebec coroner says evidence does not establish suicide in the death of 18-year-old Emmanuel Diafouka. His family is calling for police to reopen the investigation.
stories.author: Felicia Parrillo
stories.content:
Warning: This story includes the topic of suicide. Please read at your own discretion.

For Emmanuel Diafouka’s parents, the fight for answers has never stopped.

On Jan. 30, 2025, their 18-year-old son was found dead from a gunshot wound to the head in a park in Dollard-des-Ormeaux.

Police concluded his death was a suicide and the family says investigators closed the case in less than a week.

But his family never accepted that explanation.

Now, a coroner’s report says that while Diafouka died of a close-range gunshot injury to the head and that DNA and other evidence pointed him handling the weapon, there was insufficient evidence to conclude that he intended to kill himself.

“I will not say that we are happy – it’s not the word I can use – but it’s like they gave us some hope regarding the next step,” said Jean-François Diafouka, the boy’s father.

The coroner’s report also identifies the weapon as a shortened .22 calibre semi-automatic rifle, which is a prohibited firearm.

His parents want to know where the gun came from and whether someone else was involved in their son’s death.

“For me it’s clear that there’s other people involved in the death of my son,” said Jean-François. “Since the beginning, that’s my point.”

The family, which has involved the Center for Research-Action on Race Relations (Crarr) in their quest to get answers, say they also believe race is part of the story. They question whether enough was done to get to the bottom of their son’s death.

“It shows the need for the police department, any police department, to be more rigorous and sensitive when dealing with the death of a youth under very mysterious circumstances,” said Fo Niemi, Crarr’s executive director.

Global News reached out to the Montreal police for comment but have yet to hear back.

A complaint filed last year with the Police Ethics Commissioner over Montreal police’s handling of the case is still awaiting a decision.

The family continues to demand that police reopen the investigation into Emmanuel’s death.

If you or someone you know is in crisis and needs help, resources are available. In case of an emergency, please call 911 for immediate help.

For immediate mental health support, call 988. For a directory of support services in your area, visit the Canadian Association for Suicide Prevention at suicideprevention.CA.

On Jan. 30, 2025, their 18-year-old son was found dead from a gunshot wound to the head in a park in Dollard-des-Ormeaux.
Police concluded his death was a suicide and the family says investigators closed the case in less than a week.
But his family never accepted that explanation.

Now, a coroner’s report says that while Diafouka died of a close-range gunshot injury to the head and that DNA and other evidence pointed him handling the weapon, there was insufficient evidence to conclude that he intended to kill himself.
“I will not say that we are happy – it’s not the word I can use – but it’s like they gave us some hope regarding the next step,” said Jean-François Diafouka, the boy’s father.
The coroner’s report also identifies the weapon as a shortened .22 calibre semi-automatic rifle, which is a prohibited firearm.
His parents want to know where the gun came from and whether someone else was involved in their son’s death.
“For me it’s clear that there’s other people involved in the death of my son,” said Jean-François. “Since the beginning, that’s my point.”

The family, which has involved the Center for Research-Action on Race Relations (Crarr) in their quest to get answers, say they also believe race is part of the story. They question whether enough was done to get to the bottom of their son’s death.

content_blocks.text: “It shows the need for the police department, any police department, to be more rigorous and sensitive when dealing with the death of a youth under very mysterious circumstances,” said Fo Niemi, Crarr’s executive director.
Global News reached out to the Montreal police for comment but have yet to hear back.
A complaint filed last year with the Police Ethics Commissioner over Montreal police’s handling of the case is still awaiting a decision.
The family continues to demand that police reopen the investigation into Emmanuel’s death.
