stories.title: Ward 3 candidates’ proposals on safer roads
stories.summary: Better bus service and safer roads around Fanshawe College are priorities for at least two candidates running ...
stories.author: Georgia Chambers
stories.content:
Better bus service and safer roads around Fanshawe College are priorities for at least two candidates running in Ward 3.

Both issues matter to the Fanshawe community, especially after a year of major construction near the college to prepare for the city’s new Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system.

With thousands of students and staff travelling to campus each day by car, bike and bus, XFM wanted to know what candidates are proposing when it comes to transit and roads. Earlier this week, XFM sent a list of questions to all six candidates seeking to represent the east London ward.

Zak Rahim and Leroy Osbourne responded.

What transit improvements does Ward 3 need most?

“So what Ward 3 really needs is frequency of transit and connectivity where people are and where they need to get where they need to go,” Rahim said.

“So if you’re deep in a residential area, you’re not walking 10 minutes, 15 minutes to get to a main corridor,” Osbourne said.

Should planning north and west BRT routes continue or pause?

Both support a pause.

“Right now, we haven’t proven to taxpayers to Londoners that we got a good plan. We just have promises,” Osbourne said.

“So before we commit to new, you know, new legs of the BRT, the north or west leg, I want to see what that spending will actually deliver,” Rahim said.

What would you do to improve road safety?

Osbourne wants to enforce calmer traffic, and upgrade down Huron Street.

“Give a safe area that’s off the road. And we start rethinking how we use sidewalks and turning into multi use paths,” Osbourne said.

Rahim purposes traffic calming by schools, filling sidewalk gaps along Highbury Avenue and better snow plowing on bike lanes.

“When we make it safer for our kids to walk or bike to school, we can get away from that car dependency,” Rahim said.

London’s municipal election is open October 26, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m..

stories.title: Artist Delcy Morelos’s Ombligo (navel) engages all the senses
stories.summary: The sculpture is on display at the Museum of Contemporary Art Toronto until Feb. 14
stories.author: Tatum Dooley
stories.content:
There are some artworks that simply feel destined for Dia Beacon, the upstate New York museum home to postwar heavyweights working in minimalism, conceptualism and land art, as if they were custom-made to live next to Louise Bourgeois, Richard Serra and Michael Heizer. Bogotá-based artist Delcy Morelos’s large-scale installation Ombligo (navel) is one such piece. Lucky for us in Toronto , it’s up at the Museum of Contemporary Art Toronto until Feb. 14, and not in upstate New York.

In the past week, I’ve heard Ombligo (navel) compared to a basket, a hammock, a web, a cocoon, an egg, the bump of a pregnant stomach or a very shapely breast. I think it looks like the safety netting found at indoor playgrounds or under trapezes. It’s funny the way our brain makes connections when we’re confronted with something we’ve never seen before.

Morelos is known for her installations built from organic materials. In this case, a mixture of corn, tapioca, tobacco and various unnamed materials that recall medicinal and nourishing properties, while also filling the air on the third floor with an overpowering aroma. As soon as the elevator doors open, the sculpture engulfs you in scent. Put simply, the smell is earthy . It smells good, but is so overpowering it veers into abjection. It feels like being steeped in a very strong tea of cinnamon, cloves, dirt, maybe even diesel. At a certain point, you simply have to let go and give in to the experience.

One might assume that, after spending more than an hour in that space, your nose would adjust to the scent – it does not. The scent remains cloying, as if the sculpture were taking over every molecule in the room. Scents in museums are often a gimmick; that’s not the case here. With the presence of smell, taste and touch are also introduced. It’s as if you can feel the humidity emanating from the piece and imagine it would be cool to the touch. The artwork engages all the senses.

Ombligo (navel) is made from locally sourced materials, including corn roots harvested from Crooked Farmz, an urban micro-farm in Downsview Park. The sisal, a traditional fibre used for rope, is from Yucatan, Mexico, and supplied specifically for this exhibition. Morelos marries the geometry found in minimalism with the cosmologies of ancestral cultures across the Andes and Amazon. Mud, a constant in her work, is embedded in the knowledge her grandmother, a descendant of the Indigenous Emberá people, passed down to her. Land art is an easy way to categorize Morelos’s practice, except that it pushes back against colonialism rather than asserting it, as so many land artists have.

For Morelos, the sculpture is a play on the grid, a container found throughout art history rooted in restraint, constraints and minimalism. Morelos considers the grid a patriarchal structure that she subverts through the sculpture’s bulbous shape. Ombligo (navel) combines structure – the traditional process of weaving and basketmaking, itself a grid – with the organic shape of a sphere. The earthly materials introduce unpredictability. In Morelos’s hands, the grid becomes nurturing, vast and uncontained.

There’s something deeply maternal about the piece, a feeling the title prompts. Ombligo, translated as navel, is the place that connects each of us with our mother. The roots that make up the piece are a metaphor for umbilical cords, searching through the dirt to find nutrients. Following this line of thinking, the sculpture’s shape becomes a cradle. Morelos compares the sculpture’s attributes – its darkness and humidity – to the mother’s womb: comfortable and cozy.

The sculpture took two weeks to build, with 20 staff members working on it. This alone speaks to the work’s remarkable scale. It’s equally tactile and tangible; there’s no escaping its mass. The ground, usually firmly beneath us, is now suspended above. From afar, it reads as a dark opaque mass, a swelling nest. Only on closer inspection does the transparency show, with light fighting to be seen through the mesh-like material. The sculpture is not only physically larger than the viewer, but it also looms metaphorically, creating a sense of scale in the psyche.

Without the added context of an art gallery, didactic text and friendly docents, it feels straight out of science fiction. Is Ombligo (navel) a planet hurtling toward the ground? An alien ship levitating above? A home for the stranded? A nest for a dragon? How can something so natural be unnatural?

It’s hard to write about this work without connecting it back to the self. It’s a sculpture that demands the viewer become aware of their body in space, and, if they’re willing, of their own fragility. This achievement is why it belongs next to Bourgeois, Serra or Heizer, artists who engulf the viewer and nudge them closer to the abyss. Ombligo (navel) elicits either serenity or panic. Regardless of your reaction, Ombligo (navel) asks for surrender.

stories.title: Developers up their perk game, Elora's fraught debate and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Oct. 23
stories.summary: Plus, this week’s lowest fixed and variable mortgage rates in Canada
stories.author: Moira Wyton
stories.content:
This week: A luxury hotel firm stirs up debate in a quaint Ontario town and B.C. developers get more creative with their perks to lure buyers. Plus, why you should pay off your mortgage before you retire, and one property worth a look.

It’s easy to see why Elora was one of the first places I was told to visit when I spent a summer in Toronto. The historic former mill town has reinvented itself as a high-end tourist destination perfect for weddings and weekend getaways. But behind the town’s picturesque exteriors, the growing presence of a luxury hotel company has sparked a debate about who gets to decide how a community grows and changes.

As Greg Mercer reports, Kat Florence seems to divide the village as deeply as the gorge that runs through it. The company first made a purchase in Elora in 2020, and eventually bought at least 19 properties worth $32-million, according to publicly available records. Their projects, including a former hotel restored into posh accommodations, have contributed to the town’s recent economic boom. But the company has also helped fuel concerns over increasing real estate values and the significant rise in tourism some locals say is overwhelming the community.

Some critics say Kat Florence has come to wield too much power, alleging its promise of donations to the township has given it a rubber stamp to fast-track zoning and permitting – something both the company and township flatly deny. And Kat Florence has also been pushing back against its loudest critics, suing three people for defamation and serving at least a dozen residents with cease-and-desist letters. Read Greg’s deep dive on Elora and how, like many Canadian tourist destinations, an influx of new money and people has some wondering whose town it is.

Would you like a luxury car, a kitted out garage or cold hard cash with that? Potential home buyers are being offered increasingly creative and generous incentives by developers trying to move their unsold units in B.C. Polygon Homes, for example, seemingly has something for everyone: a $100,000 electric BMW (or cash equivalent) for buyers of some $1.1-million-plus high-rise units in North Vancouver, $25,000 toward new homes in Abbotsford for firefighters, police, nurses and other front-line workers, and decked-out garages with storage systems and e-bikes worth $30,000 for outdoor enthusiasts in Squamish.

It May seem outlandish, but as Kerry Gold reports, this is part of the new normal. Just a few years ago, prospective investors would line up to purchase preconstruction homes, a far cry from developers’ struggles to get potential buyers through the door now. Wesgroup Properties in Vancouver is even offering “try before you buy” weekends in their show units with fully stocked fridges and gift cards for local retailers to sell people on the full lifestyle.

And as developers and marketers told Kerry, the strategies are likely here to stay. “This market is forcing developers to rethink how we sell homes, and I think some of those changes will stay with us even when the market improves,” Joey Coupland, senior vice-president of sales at Wesgroup, told Kerry. Read her piece to see how buyers are responding .

Rates shown are the lowest available for each term/type and category (insured vs. uninsured) as of market close on Thursday, Oct. 22 .

Your home can be part of your retirement plan, but just make sure you pay it off before then. Retirement preparation focuses mostly on saving and investing, and for good reason. But as Rob Carrick argues , we need to pay more attention to future-proofing our retirement plans, and mortgages are one of the biggest risks of all.

“Homeowners of all ages are vulnerable to the utterly unexpected rise in mortgage rates this year, but none more than retirees,” Rob writes. In your working years, you have more options to offset a few hundred more dollars a month, whether via a raise, a promotion, or another job. Retirees can cut their spending, and that’s about it. “Beyond working, what are you going to do? Invest more aggressively? Buy lottery tickets?” Rob asks.

It’s cause for concern, because the amount of mortgage debt held by retirees is growing. With risks that rates will rise for years to come, it’s a club you want to do your best to stay out of. “Pay your mortgage off before retirement and you can watch the rate drama ahead as a disinterested bystander,” Rob suggests.

Quilts are becoming must-have statement pieces , not just worn family heirlooms to curl up with on the couch. Homespun interiors in general are having a moment as people push back on the rise of technology and seek out warm, tactile and uniquely human spaces.

But these aren’t your grandparents’ quilts. As Alexandra Petros reports, Canadian designers are reinventing the quilt with fresh techniques, styles and customizations. From bedspreads with bespoke tags displaying the name of the family cottage to minimalist designs and fresh colour combinations, here’s how quilts can help you inject texture and personality into your spaces.

838496 4th Line E, Mulmur, Ont. – Full gallery here

What do you do when you want an old home but your spouse doesn’t want the hassle and quirks? For the owners of this Regency-inspired cottage , the answer was to build a new home in an old style – and with some actually old bones. Interior designer Marylou Morgan spent years sourcing antique features and furniture before her and her husband’s house was completed in 1995, more than 150 years after the Regency era ended.

The four-bedroom, four-bathroom home is now a beautiful step back in time underpinned with modern comforts, electricity and geothermal heating. Perched on a parcel of the Niagara Escarpment with panoramic views, the T-shaped building greets visitors with a large veranda and bellcast roof. The massive wooden front door is one Morgan salvaged from a nearby 1840s farmhouse that had gone into receivership, and it informed the scale of the design by architect Jamie Wright of Young + Wright in Toronto.

The house is filled with other antique treasures Morgan sourced from abandoned historic homes and buildings across the province, from distressed wood floors to the mud room door with a fanlight above it. But while the age of hosting balls is over, a screened-in porch that opens with double doors to both the living room and the English Country-style kitchen makes an ideal space to entertain, rain or shine.

What do you think is the asking price for the property?

a. $3,500,000 b. $3,750,000 c. $4,000,000 d. $4,250,000 d. The asking price is $4,250,000.

stories.title: Rogers posts $482-million quarterly profit, revenue edges up
stories.summary: Profit down from $5.71-billion a year ago, when the telco saw $5-billion non-cash gain related to Mlse
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Rogers Communications Inc. RCI-B-T reported a jump in free cash flow in its third quarter but posted about flat revenue and lower new subscription numbers, as it works toward a minority sale of its sports holdings.

The company reported $1.3-billion in free cash flow, up 65 per cent from last year and beating analyst expectations.

The free cash flow followed 46 per cent lower capital expenditures in the quarter. Earlier this year, the company said it planned to cut capital spending for the year by 30 per overall, in part by selling or deferring some infrastructure projects.

The higher free cash flow in the quarter was also the result of cable, wireless and real estate sales totaling $274-million in the quarter.

Overall revenue was up 2 per cent and service revenue was up 1 per cent in the quarter. The company reported a a 9-per-cent bump in its sports and media division revenue, boosted by strong Toronto Blue Jays performance and the earlier start of the NHL regular season.

The company reiterated its plans to sell a minority stake in its recently consolidated sports holdings in the first half of 2027, but did not provide any further updates.

Over all, the Toronto-based telecom, sports and media company “reported an update which we characterize as slightly positive,” said analyst Jerome Dubreuil in a note to investors Friday, pointing to the strong free cash flow but noting “weak” subscriber additions.

The company added 17,000 net new postpaid mobile phone subscribers, down from 111,000 last year and below analyst expectations of 56,000.

Analysts said the subscriber figures reflect the company’s strategy to focus on selling higher value products instead of chasing a greater number of lower-paying customers. Meanwhile, Canadian population growth was flat in the quarter, meaning fewer new customers to compete over.

“In wireless, we stayed focused on financials versus chasing subscriber volume in what is typically a busy back-to-school quarter,” chief executive officer Tony Staffieri told analysts on a call Friday morning.

Improving overall average revenue per user (Arpu) – an industry metric that reflects how much the company ears from a customer – and free cash flow “is more important than tiny changes in volume growth,” said Toronto-Dominion Cowan analyst Vince Valentini in a note to investors.

For the company’s overall base of mobile phone subscribers, Arpu declined by about 2.6 per cent in the period.

Speaking to analysts Friday morning, Rogers chief financial officer Glenn Brandt said the drop was in part the result of a new policy which bans telecoms from charging certain setup fees.

“We continue to look to find ways to either eliminate or reduce those costs,” Mr. Brandt said. Where the company can’t eliminate them, he said, it will “try and offset them.”

When asked about finding efficiencies in the business, Mr. Brandt said the company has also had a “substantial reduction in costs” as a result of “more resourcing of our call center work offshore.”

Rogers reported a 91-per-cent loss in net income in the quarter, the result of an accounting change last quarter. Rogers recorded a $5-billion non-cash gain in the same quarter last year related to its holdings in Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment, and that was not repeated this year.

The company reported adjusted net income of $701-million, down 3 per cent from last year.

Cable revenue was flat compared to last year, though its margins improved.

stories.title: Trailer park users seek answers as their summer home set to close next October
stories.summary: The 42 trailers that make up the Bluewater Trailer Park in Kincardine are all tucked away for winter. Amongst them, Lyle Cowan’s summer trailer.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The 42 trailers that make up the Bluewater Trailer Park in Kincardine are all tucked away for winter. Amongst them, Lyle Cowan’s summer trailer.

“We have people there that we’ve known for 50 years. It’s like home for us,” said the Milton resident, who spends part of his summer’s in Kincardine.

Next year at this time, the Bluewater Trailer Park will likely be empty. The Municipality is closing the trailer park, because a 2023 legal analysis says the park is out of compliance.

The Municipality says part of the park lands were donated to the municipality in the 1880’s, strictly to be used as a public park, walkway, or garden.

“As a result of that, municipal council decided to move forward with a plan to bring the park back in compliance, more clearly stated as that of public use. The seasonal long term rentals of those sites did not comply with the intent of the bequeathed,” said Municipality of Kincardine Mayor Ken Craig.

The prime piece of real estate the trailer park lies on, mere metres away from Lake Huron, has been a tourist camp or trailer park for more than 100 years. In 2024, Cowan and his fellow trailer park summer tenants were given three years to vacate, which comes to a close next October.

“They have no plan. They have no estimates, and they have no schedule. So, basically they’ve got the cart before the horse. They’ve closed the park, and they’re not telling the towns people how much they’re going to spend to do this. If you can reimagine this space into something else, then go ahead and do it. But, get that plan in place, and tell people in the city how much it’s going to cost. We have enough parks already that need work,” said Cowan.

Kincardine was receiving approximately $33,000 in rent from Bluewater Trailer Park summer tenants each year considered well below market value by a 2023 staff report.

Craig says the municipality plans to turn the Bluewater Trailer Park, into a public park, walkway, or garden in 2028 following some community consultation in 2027.

“Might be a phased project, might be all at once, but it will be more in compliance with the original intent of that land. The intent of the bequeath was to have it widely available to all the residents of Kincardine,” said Craig.

Cowan and his fellow Bluewater Trailer Park users are holding out that a possibly new collection of councillors, coming out of Monday’s municipal election, will determine a different future for the Bluewater Trailer Park, and it’s 42 summer tenants.

“It was a surprise, but, there’s still hope. Hope to come yet,” he said.

stories.title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet set to continue
stories.summary: A coroner's inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony in the presence of police is set to resume Friday morning after adjourning early on Thursday.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A coroner’s inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony in the presence of police is set to resume Friday morning after adjourning early on Thursday.

The inquest into the death of 29-year-old Regis Korchinski-Paquet was paused roughly an hour into Thursday’s proceedings after her mother made a new allegation against police.

Claudette Beals testified that she saw officers push her daughter toward the balcony.

The presiding coroner, Dr. David Cameron, told jurors Thursday counsel were strategizing on how to best have them hear evidence related to the circumstances of Korchinski-Paquet’s death “in a clear and fair manner.”

Beals is expected to continue her testimony today.

Earlier Thursday, she said that the family struggled at times to deal with Korchinski-Paquet’s seizures and would have benefited from support and education regarding epilepsy.

The inquest has heard Korchinski-Paquet experienced seizures from epilepsy and had two on May 27, 2020, the day she died.

Her seizures were often followed by periods of erratic and aggressive behaviour, the inquest has heard.

stories.title: Boon or boondoggle? N.S. weighs $10B data centre’s promised economic benefits
stories.summary: Living more than 200 kilometres from the site of a major artificial intelligence data centre proposal isn't stopping Michael McCluskey from voicing his opposition to the project.
stories.author: Devin Stevens
stories.content:
Living more than 200 kilometres from the site of a major artificial intelligence data centre proposal isn’t stopping Michael McCluskey from voicing his opposition to the project.

The retired military veteran and training professional from Dartmouth, N.S., has added his name to a Change.org petition that has already collected more than 18,000 signatures since the project was announced last Friday.

Anthropic, an American AI company, plans to lease the Point Tupper, N.S., site for its first Canadian data centre, the first major AI facility to be publicly proposed in Nova Scotia.

However, McCluskey said he just views it as the latest in a long history of Nova Scotia chasing grand economic development projects that never seem to deliver.

He said the site won’t be able to serve any other purpose if Anthropic walks away, and he’s worried the province will be left holding the bag when economic benefits don’t appear.

“They don’t put (data centres) anywhere that’s prospering,” McCluskey said in an interview.

“They don’t put them in San Francisco. They don’t put them in Los Angeles …. What they’re looking for are disadvantaged, economically desperate areas?”

EverWind plans to build the 18,600-square-metre data centre by late 2027 and lease it for 20 years to Anthropic under undisclosed financial terms. San Francisco-based Anthropic says Canada is the sixth-largest worldwide user of its Claude AI model, which is driving the project.

EverWind calls the data centre the biggest private investment in provincial history. It originally planned to build a wind-powered hydrogen plant exporting energy from its Cape Breton marine terminal. The company said it’s still pursuing this hydrogen project.

The proposal has thrust Nova Scotia into a debate that has exploded across Canada in recent months as massive AI corporations race to build computing capacity in areas with enough electricity and water to feed the resource-gobbling sector.

The facilities can range in size from a micro data centre about the size of a refrigerator to a hyperscale campus that consumes a level of power comparable to a small city.

A recent York University report found that Canada’s existing 194 data centres have a combined capacity to draw 1.6 gigawatts of electricity. More than 14-times that amount — about 22.7 gigawatts — are either under construction or in the announcement stage across 213 sites.

The proposals are supersized. Existing data centres have an average capacity of about 11 megawatts and cover an average of 0.05 square-kilometres, about the size of six Canadian football fields. New proposals average about 122 megawatts spread over more than eight square kilometres, almost 1,000 football fields.

York researchers say a 122-megawatt operation will use the same amount of power annually as 49,000 to 78,000 Canadian homes.

EverWind’s data centre will be 95 megawatts in the first phase, and the company has plans for a 325-megawatt expansion by mid-2028.

Paris Marx, a Newfoundland and Labrador-based tech critic and author of “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” said data centre opposition is forming quickly in Canada because communities have seen U.S. headlines about skyrocketing power rates and water consumption over the last 18 to 24 months.

He said if the EverWind project moves ahead, he expects it will follow a global trend where the costs to communities are higher than first projected.

“The benefits just aren’t there to the degree that we expect,” he said in an interview.

“There are not a lot of jobs that are associated with data centres beyond the construction phase. Obviously, we need to employ people to build them. They don’t employ a ton of people to actually run them.”

EverWind expects to create 2,000 jobs during construction and 215 permanent jobs between the data centre and the four wind farms that will eventually power it.

The salaries for the permanent jobs would range between $135,000 and $185,000 per year, the company said, with about half of those jobs in the data centre and half in the wind farms.

Sean Mullin, with the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, said data centres May not create the same amount of jobs as something like an auto factory, but even a couple hundred positions can make a big difference in a small community.

“We’d rather have that economic activity here than somewhere else. And then that also benefits the country in the sense that we have more compute capacity to serve the rest of the country,” he said in an interview.

Kody Blois, a Nova Scotia MP and parliamentary secretary to the prime minister, said at EverWind’s announcement last week that AI is transforming the global economy and Ottawa wants to seize the opportunity.

“These are really important jobs right here in the region. They matter to families, they matter to communities,” he said.

EverWind CEO Trent Vichie said there were already more than 20 Nova Scotian contractors working on the site and economic spinoffs will multiply the direct benefits.

“More people in restaurants, more people buying from local businesses,” he said last Friday. “It’s really providing an anchor to strengthening the community that’s already here today.”

Marx said he doubts the project will actually proceed, saying data centres are seen as a backup at the moment when other projects, such as hydrogen, fail to gain traction. He noted EverWind has already hit roadblocks a planned hydrogen project in Newfoundland.

EverWind said in an email that it’s participating in an auction to sell hydrogen to Europe and that the data centre adds a major industrial use for its renewable energy portfolio and infrastructure while the international hydrogen market develops.

“The data centre helps maintain investment momentum in wind, transmission and shared infrastructure that can also support hydrogen and ammonia over time,” the company said.

“While these investments complement each other, they are not dependent on one another.”

Anthropic lost more than US$80 billion during the first half of 2026, according to Reuters. That’s up from a US$13-billion loss in the first half of 2025. The company is planning an initial public offering of shares as early as November that could value the company at US$1.5 trillion.

The firm declined an interview request this week but has told investors that its plan to spend $518 billion on AI infrastructure over the next decade is needed because computing power is the key constraint on AI development. It has said future demand for AI systems is expected to exceed available supply, according to Reuters.

CEO Dario Amodei and the company’s five other co-founders established Anthropic as a public benefit corporation, a designation that for-profit companies select to balance financial goals and social impact.

The company has also committed to setting aside five per cent of its shares to a public benefit fund which will grow along with Anthropic’s valuation.

The fund will explore large donations to non-profits or direct distributions to specific populations. The company says it has already committed US$200 million to studying and addressing potential impacts of AI technology on the labour market.

But Marx remains skeptical about whether AI companies have a good business model.

“I think that there are also a lot of market questions as to whether something like this will even be necessary, or if a client like Anthropic will actually show up,” he said.

Marx said he doubts the project will actually proceed, saying data centres are seen as a backup at the moment when other projects, such as hydrogen, fail to gain traction. He noted EverWind has already hit roadblocks a planned hydrogen project in Newfoundland.

EverWind said in an email that it’s participating in an auction to sell hydrogen to Europe and that the data centre adds a major industrial use for its renewable energy portfolio and infrastructure while the international hydrogen market develops.
“The data centre helps maintain investment momentum in wind, transmission and shared infrastructure that can also support hydrogen and ammonia over time,” the company said.
“While these investments complement each other, they are not dependent on one another.”

Anthropic lost more than US$80 billion during the first half of 2026, according to Reuters. That’s up from a US$13-billion loss in the first half of 2025. The company is planning an initial public offering of shares as early as November that could value the company at US$1.5 trillion.

The firm declined an interview request this week but has told investors that its plan to spend $518 billion on AI infrastructure over the next decade is needed because computing power is the key constraint on AI development. It has said future demand for AI systems is expected to exceed available supply, according to Reuters.

CEO Dario Amodei and the company’s five other co-founders established Anthropic as a public benefit corporation, a designation that for-profit companies select to balance financial goals and social impact.
The company has also committed to setting aside five per cent of its shares to a public benefit fund which will grow along with Anthropic’s valuation.

The fund will explore large donations to non-profits or direct distributions to specific populations. The company says it has already committed US$200 million to studying and addressing potential impacts of AI technology on the labour market.
But Marx remains skeptical about whether AI companies have a good business model.
“I think that there are also a lot of market questions as to whether something like this will even be necessary, or if a client like Anthropic will actually show up,” he said.

content_blocks.text: The retired military veteran and training professional from Dartmouth, N.S., has added his name to a Change.org petition that has already collected more than 18,000 signatures since the project was announced last Friday.
Anthropic, an American AI company, plans to lease the Point Tupper, N.S., site for its first Canadian data centre, the first major AI facility to be publicly proposed in Nova Scotia.

He said the site won’t be able to serve any other purpose if Anthropic walks away, and he’s worried the province will be left holding the bag when economic benefits don’t appear.
“They don’t put (data centres) anywhere that’s prospering,” McCluskey said in an interview.
“They don’t put them in San Francisco. They don’t put them in Los Angeles …. What they’re looking for are disadvantaged, economically desperate areas?”

“We’d rather have that economic activity here than somewhere else. And then that also benefits the country in the sense that we have more compute capacity to serve the rest of the country,” he said in an interview.

stories.title: A new home, with the addition of a few old bones
stories.summary: Years of collecting architectural treasures from abandoned historic homes culminated in this Regency-inspired cottage in Mulmur, Ont.
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
838496 4 th Line E, Mulmur, Ont .

Asking Price: $4,250,000

Taxes: $9,254 (2026)

Land Size: 50 acres

Agent: Suzanne Lawrence, Royal LePage RCR Realty

In 1991, Marylou Morgan and her husband impulsively purchased 50 acres of idle pasture in the rolling hills of Mulmur, Ont.

The couple had no plans to buy a country property at the time, recalls Ms. Morgan, but the renovation of their Toronto house forced them out of the city for a few days. To pass the time, they looked at real estate.

The parcel carved out of a traditional 100-acre farm along the Niagara Escarpment had already been sold, but the purchaser was trying to back out of the deal, the agent informed them.

The time wasn’t right, Ms. Morgan says, but the couple figured they might never have another opportunity to acquire land with a panoramic view that stretches as far as Toronto when the light is right.

The couple faced another dilemma: Ms. Morgan was an interior designer with a particular affinity for the Regency era, which influenced architecture roughly from the early 1800s until Queen Victoria took the British throne in 1837. They had always lived in older houses, but her husband was not keen on updating gnarly plumbing, wiring and heating again.

“My husband wanted a new home, and I wanted an old home.”

The couple put off building while they concentrated on funding the schooling of their five children.

The delay gave Ms. Morgan a few years to assemble furniture and architectural elements from abandoned historic homes scattered around the province.

“I had items stored all over,” she says of the collection piled up in storage spaces in Lindsay, Kitchener-Waterloo and her mother’s garage in Toronto.

During a visit to Bowmanville, Ont., Ms. Morgan learned from an antiques dealer that a nearby property with a Regency-style house dating to about 1840 was in receivership.

Ms. Morgan negotiated with the accountants to gain access to the old stone building, then returned with a builder friend to carefully extricate the elegant wooden staircase, fireplace surrounds, decorative trim and front door.

The substantial door became the starting point for determining the proportions in the new house.

“It told me how high the ceiling had to be to accommodate the front door.”

When the couple was ready to build, Ms. Morgan turned to architect Jamie Wright to choose a site in the undulating landscape and design a house in the Ontario Regency Cottage style.

The Toronto-based firm of Young + Wright was part of a partnership that designed the city’s SkyDome stadium and other notable buildings, but occasionally Mr. Wright took on residential projects for friends.

Ms. Morgan asked the architect to design a T-shaped building with living and dining areas at the front of the home. Visitors would arrive at a gracious veranda with a bellcast roof.

After more than one year of construction, the couple moved in in 1995.

Today the two-storey house has four bedrooms and four bathrooms, plus two additional bedrooms on the lower level.

Ms. Morgan’s antique finds were incorporated throughout the house: the mud room door with a fanlight above came from the village of St. Jacobs, and the distressed wood floors were pried from a factory in Bolton.

She found artisans from surrounding areas to copy period woodwork and trims.

“It’s a dying art, but there are young people with the mindset of saving some of the older things,” she says.

Double doors open from the living room and the kitchen to a screened porch that stands between the two rooms.

“You can easily put 50 people in your house and have a cocktail party – and never worry about the weather,” she says.

In 2019, the couple added a primary suite on the main floor and built a detached two-car garage.

The modern systems include geothermal heating and cooling.

“I think we were one of the first people in the area to have geothermal,” says Ms. Morgan.

Outside, Ms. Morgan planted extensive perennial gardens. She improved the soil with compost collected from the municipality’s site on an old airstrip in the area.

The couple and visiting children and grandchildren often spend time in the area skiing, golfing and hiking the Bruce Trail.

Nearby Creemore, Ont. offers restaurants, shops, parks and Pilates classes.

“There’s always something going on in the village,” says Ms. Morgan.

Ms. Morgan brought in a European carpenter to build the kitchen in English country style.

There’s a commercial-grade stove, a centre island and a casual dining area.

A visit to a fishing camp inspired the maple countertops.

“They’re great for upkeep,” says Ms. Morgan.

A vintage icebox becomes the self-serve bar during parties.

“It really is a hub,” she says of the room where everyone tends to gather.

stories.title: These chefs left the city to open rural and small-town restaurants. Was it a good move?
stories.summary: Some of the country’s most interesting chefs are taking their skills – and their customers – on a different kind of journey
stories.author: Gayle MacDonald
stories.content:
Some of Canada’s most interesting chefs are turning up in the most unlikely places.

In small towns, fishing villages and on working farms across Canada, accomplished chefs are opening ambitious restaurants far from the big cities where they made their names. And diners are following them, unfazed by the hours of driving often required to get there.

Helped by the growth of agri-tourism and interest in food provenance, the popularity of rural restaurants is reflected in this year’s Canada’s 100 Best restaurant list, which includes a half dozen such spots, from the Michelin-star eatery The Pine in Creemore, Ont., to Pluvio in Ucluelet, B.C.

Jacob Richler, editor-in-chief and publisher of Canada’s 100 Best , says the appeal of rural restaurants has “everything to do with the feeling that what you are experiencing belongs to that particular setting.” Diners want to know who grew the vegetables, raised the meat or caught the fish. Plus, many are looking for more than just a nice meal: One-quarter want an experiential dining experience, according to OpenTable Canada’s 2026 Dining Trends Report .

“It’s not conventional fine dining, and no urban restaurant can deliver it quite like a country one can,” he says.

The Globe spoke with three chefs, for whom leaving the city was as much a personal decision as a culinary one. They were drawn to small towns for different reasons: family, a slower pace, relief from high city rents, and, perhaps most importantly, the chance to cook closer to where their food is grown, raised and caught.

By the time Guillaume Asselin decided to leave Montreal, the chef had become so busy running a restaurant, a catering company and a sugar shack that he barely had time for the thing that had drawn him into the business in the first place.

“I missed cooking,” he says.

After seven years owning and operating the popular east-end Montreal bistro Les Affamés, Asselin was exhausted. He had also grown frustrated by the distance between his kitchen and the food arriving in it.

“I wanted to have the best produce and know where everything comes from,” he says. “I wanted to do things from seed to the vegetables on the plate. I wanted the animals I raised to have a nice life.”

In 2019, he told his partner, Marie Daudelin, that he wanted land and a true farm-to-table restaurant. Daudelin was game: She had always dreamed of running a country inn, she told him, like something out of Gilmore Girls .

The couple ventured southwest into the fertile Montérégie countryside and found Saint-Anicet, home to a 126-acre farm that had sat empty for four years.

“A week later we made an offer,” says Asselin, who was no farm hand but was determined to learn.

Le Mangeoir visits begin with a farm tour, followed by a five-course meal. Dominick Gravel; C'est Finnie/Supplied

The romantic vision required unromantic work. The couple scraped paint, rebuilt fences, planted gardens and renovated neglected outbuildings.

What emerged was Le Mangeoir, a 32-seat table champêtre, or farm-to-table , and four-room farm stay.

A visit begins with a tour of the farm. Then the guests gather around a large harvest table for a five-course meal.

The farm raises all of the restaurant’s meat – pigs, cows, goats, rabbits, chickens and ducks – and produces almost everything that appears on the plate. There are laying hens, vegetable gardens, berries and an expanding orchard of apple, cherry and pear trees. A small boutique sells cuts of meat with Asselin’s preserves, pickles and hot sauce.

“Le Mangeoir’s financial viability depends on how the farm, restaurant and accommodation work together,” says Asselin, who notes that producing their own ingredients costs less than buying equivalent products elsewhere. “This model requires significant, ongoing investment, a great deal of personal involvement and a very long-term vision, particularly when you don’t have millions of dollars to start with.”

Cooking only what the farm can provide forces creativity, says Asselin. Dominick Gravel/Supplied

He loves the challenge of cooking only what he grows or nurtures. It has made him more inventive, and he says the work is more rewarding.

Goat has become a house specialty. Jerusalem artichokes might appear three ways; a purée, crisp chips or pickled. Asselin ferments pine cones, and makes kimchi as well as his own spices.

Guests, he says, love the authenticity of his farm-to-table meals. He loves the slower pace of country life. “I work just as much, maybe more, but it never feels like work,” he says. “I just live.”

In Montreal, his days came with the sound of traffic. “Here, I listen to the goats, the birds, the ducks,” he says. “It’s beautiful.”

Benjamin Cormier spent years believing that success meant leaving home. Now, at 42, the chef has built the life he never even knew he wanted, just 30 minutes from the small fishing community he grew up in.

“I thought I had to be a big-city boy,” says Cormier, chef-owner of Origines Cuisine Maritime in Caraquet, a charming Acadian coastal town in northeast New Brunswick. “But this place did not hold me back. In fact, it has helped me.”

His route back home was anything but planned. Cormier grew up in nearby Lamèque, an island community where commercial fishing and peat moss are the mainstays. He recalls the first traffic light arrived when he was 17.

After studying hotel and restaurant management in Ottawa, Cormier landed a job in his early 20s managing a restaurant attached to the New Brunswick Aquarium in Shippagan, a town next to Lamèque. A few months later, he stepped in to help cook when the chef quit. “I’ve never left the kitchen, and that was 19 years ago,” he says.

Cooking competitions followed, then an apprenticeship at Moncton’s acclaimed Little Louis’ Oyster Bar and Fine Cuisine. Within 18 months, he was sous chef, and eventually executive chef, a position he held for eight years and loved.

Then serendipity intervened again. Organizers of an annual wine dinner in Caraquet suddenly found themselves without a restaurant (the owner went bankrupt) and called Cormier, the local boy cooking in Moncton. Cormier agreed to be guest chef. Soon, people were whispering in his ear about coming home.

He was intrigued but wary. He had a good thing going in Moncton, the most populated city in New Brunswick. So, he hedged his bets, cooking at Little Louis’ during the week and driving three hours to run weekend pop-ups in Caraquet.

“I did that for six months and we were sold out every night,” he says. Eight years ago, he made the move to Caraquet permanent.

Origines is a relaxed, 60-seat restaurant where the cooking is ambitious and firmly rooted in the peninsula. Menus change weekly with the seasons and tides: cooked oysters with pickled ramps, chorizo and hollandaise; Arctic char tartare; scallops with pork belly. His customers think nothing of driving three, four and five hours to eat there, often staying in local hotels.

Becoming truly local took time. Cormier says he had to earn farmers’ trust and collect fishermen’s cellphone numbers so they would call him before selling their catch elsewhere. Now he’s on their speed dial.

What he appreciates most is how he’s close to family. His father, once a resolute plain-food-with-ketchup man, eats at Origines every week or two. Cormier’s partner, Monique Snow, runs the front of house.

When it comes to profitability of a rural restaurant, Cormier says there are some downsides. It costs more to get some higher-end products delivered, and you can’t reach the same ceiling of profitability as city restaurants.

“One could argue that the choice is not only financial,” says Cormier, who was able to pay off the restaurant quickly. “We work less days and we don’t have any issues paying all our bills and having a profit at the end of the year.”

He added, “The overall quality of life is improved once a business owner no longer has debt or financial stress, which is what I personally chose and I’m happy I made that choice.”

Cormier knows hard work got him here, but luck was a factor, too. “Never in my wildest dreams did I think this would happen when I came back home,” says Cormier, who travels internationally at the invitation of chefs he knows around the world. “This move has been the best thing that ever happened to me.”

Jeremy Austin travelled halfway around the world to discover that the restaurants he wanted to create belonged close to home.

Raised in Thornbury, Ont., Austin spent years cooking in Europe and Asia, working alongside Michelin-starred chefs and absorbing the food cultures around him.

By the time he and his wife, Cassie, were living in Shanghai, the pace of big-city life was wearing thin. They wanted to be closer to family and had long talked about opening a restaurant together.

“When we started travelling the world, we knew we wanted to bring those stories back home,” Austin says. “The best way to do that was through a tasting menu.”

The idea began modestly, with small groups eating at a table in Cassie’s parents’ Creemore farmhouse. In 2020, the couple opened The Pine in a tiny, 700-square-foot Collingwood space; four years later, they moved it to a former Shell gas station in Creemore.

Across 20-plus courses at The Pine, Austin draws heavily on Chinese dishes, then reshapes them into something that reflects what grows nearby. The countryside gives them access to some of the best ingredients, but also imposes limits, he says.

“It’s a double-edged sword but it makes us resourceful.”

The Pine has had a Michelin star for the past three years.

In May, he opened Lore in Collingwood, which was Michelin-recommended in September. Reinterpreting traditional Canadian dishes, Lore’s poutine becomes potato dumplings with braised short rib and aged-cheddar fondue, while the Caesar cocktail inspires B.C. albacore tuna with tomato broth and pickled surf clams.

Being a big fish in a smaller pond has given Austin the freedom – and confidence – to experiment and create food that is deeply personal to him. There are some unexpected costs to running two rural restaurants: Snow removal has cost him around $13,000 each season. But the cheaper lease “allows us to have intimate spaces and not need to do as many covers each night as we would in the city.”

But what he loves most is the community he gets to live and work in.

He and Cassie can hike on a Sunday afternoon, take a drive in the country or bring their daughter to the beach. “Why would I ever want to trade that for anything else?”

In small towns, fishing villages and on working farms across Canada, accomplished chefs are opening ambitious restaurants far from the big cities where they made their names. And diners are following them, unfazed by the hours of driving often required to get there.

Helped by the growth of agri-tourism and interest in food provenance, the popularity of rural restaurants is reflected in this year’s Canada’s 100 Best restaurant list, which includes a half dozen such spots, from the Michelin-star eatery The Pine in Creemore, Ont., to Pluvio in Ucluelet, B.C.

Jacob Richler, editor-in-chief and publisher of Canada’s 100 Best , says the appeal of rural restaurants has “everything to do with the feeling that what you are experiencing belongs to that particular setting.” Diners want to know who grew the vegetables, raised the meat or caught the fish. Plus, many are looking for more than just a nice meal: One-quarter want an experiential dining experience, according to OpenTable Canada’s 2026 Dining Trends Report .

stories.title: In a softer market, Vancouver developers sweeten their deals
stories.summary: Creative promotions, such as luxury cars and electric bikes, are becoming a more common tactic to boost sales
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
With unsold housing sitting on the market, developers are stepping up their game to sell units to an increasingly choosy buyer, and the promotions are getting more creative.

Polygon Homes just announced a $25,000 incentive toward the purchase of a home in their Abbotsford Cooper Meadows master-planned community for firefighters, police officers, nurses, search and rescue responders, corrections officers and teachers. The company is also offering a $100,000 luxury electric BMW for buyers of select units in their 22-storey Elle tower in central Lonsdale, North Vancouver, B.C. Buyers can opt for the car or choose cash.

Down the street, Polygon is offering a subsidy on the first three years of financing at their completed Lennox project. They’re offering a similar mortgage helper at their Squamish project, Three Summits. Also in Squamish, they are offering a fully decked-out garage in their Terrain townhome development aimed at outdoor enthusiasts, with storage systems and electric bikes worth about $30,000.

In the spring, Wesgroup Properties drew attention for its “Try it before you buy it” promotion, which let selected families spend a weekend in its fully furnished presentation suite at the Ace on Commercial Drive, complete with a stocked fridge and gift cards for nearby retailers.

It’s part of the new normal for developers navigating a challenging market downturn, selling units that are either complete or close to completion. It’s a far cry from past years when buyers would line up to buy preconstruction homes. For Polygon, most of their homes are still under construction, but they are doing everything they can to stimulate demand. Polygon president and chief executive officer Neil Chrystal estimates that new home prices have fallen by 15 to 30 per cent, depending on location.

Mr. Chrystal said he’s never seen such generous promotions, such as the one for first responders.

“Many builders are selling their homes below cost, and when we introduced this incentive for a distinct group of potential home buyers, we were trying to help stimulate demand required in today’s market,” Mr. Chrystal said.

“We are doing everything within our power to create good value.

“We’re in our 47th year, and it’s never been like this before. It’s kind of shocking,” he added. “But that said, I think the values in today’s market are becoming very, very good. And I think a lot of people that we do see buying today are getting exceptional value. And they’re moving forward with their lives in a home that makes sense for them and a growing family.”

Marketing firms have had to pivot to sell units that are newly built instead of those presold years ahead of construction. Joey Coupland, senior vice-president of sales at Wesgroup, said the new strategies are likely here to stay. Buyers now want to be sold on the full experience if they’re going to buy in.

“This market is forcing developers to rethink how we sell homes, and I think some of those changes will stay with us even when the market improves.

“The way the market is right now, as developers, we’re having to rethink everything and get more creative and more innovative and more customer-focused. Walking through a show suite and getting a sales presentation isn’t enough any more. The brochure doesn’t capture all of the exciting things about a neighbourhood. And so, we just have to do more.”

At the Ace project on Commercial Drive, dozens of people applied to spend a weekend at the show suite. Wesgroup screened applicants carefully, ensuring they were fully approved for financing and intending to buy, not just looking for a free weekend getaway. Two families were ultimately chosen, and one of them purchased in the building. That might not sound like it was worth all the effort, but the promotion attracted a lot more buyers who wanted to check out the property and who also ended up buying. For that reason, it was deemed a success that they will likely replicate with another Vancouver project they have coming up, said Ms. Coupland. A developer in Bulgaria even copied it, she said.

“With ‘Try it before you buy it,’ I think some people might have thought it was just a creative marketing idea or potentially gimmicky. It was definitely a creative way to get people’s attention, but attention alone doesn’t sell homes. And buyers still have to love the home, love the location, and the value has to work for them,” she said.

Offering discounts and enticements aren’t always enough, she added.

“The big discount is a creative way to get people’s attention, but you definitely need more.”

Mr. Chrystal said it’s not true that developers are refusing to lower prices and opting to hold onto inventory, as suggested by NDP Leader David Eby.

“I don’t think he understands our industry because there’s no home builder in Ontario or British Columbia who is hoarding homes. We are actively trying to sell all the homes that we build. And his take on it is just, it’s just wrong. We already have so many taxes on new homes it’s almost comical to add one more layer of tax.”

Generally, developers prefer to sell housing units so they can free up cash and acquire other properties. Monthly carrying costs for financing, insurance, utilities and other costs are considerable.

“We’re also one of the few home builders that’s fairly well diversified, and we don’t need to make a profit on all these homes. We’re happy to move them and get somebody in [the unit] who can start their families and get out of a basement suite, and move forward.

“There are a lot of things going on behind the scenes that shake the confidence of young people and buyers. Again, this is one of those windows of opportunity.”

stories.title: Buyer gets Surrey condo way below seller’s purchase price
stories.summary: Two-bedroom corner suite sells for $510,000 after lowering asking price
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
13350 Central Ave., No. 3511, Surrey, B.C.

Asking price: $519,000 (July, 2026)

Previous asking prices: $549,000 (June, 2026); $599,000 (April, 2026)

Selling price: $510,000 (August, 2026)

Previous selling price: $601,000 plus GST (2023)

Taxes: $2,806.10 (2025)

Monthly maintenance fee: $596.25

Days on the market: 14

Property days on market: 127

Listing agent: Ian Watt, Hellen Murch Realty

This two-bedroom, two-bathroom corner suite has 718 square feet of living space, with an open galley kitchen and laminate floors.

The three-year-old unit has sweeping views from floor-to-ceiling windows and a balcony. The building has a rooftop lounge on the 44th floor, a gym, a shared office space, a parking stall, and it’s within walking distance of the SkyTrain, the library, and a recreation centre.

“Because it’s the 35th floor, it’s got stunning views, and it’s up on the hill,” said listing agent Ian Watt.

The sellers had purchased the unit as a presale and paid taxes on the purchase price. They hoped to recoup the amount they’d paid for it, but the market wouldn’t respond, said Mr. Watt. He held open houses every weekend, but oftentimes no one showed. He said the only offers were “obscenely low,” and that many who passed through the unit were merely casual observers.

“You have to do whatever it takes,” he said. “Sometimes open houses are great. We can sometimes meet sellers, or meet another buyer. But the truth is, nobody is really serious about buying real estate right now.”

Once the sellers lowered the price, they got a decent offer.

“This young person who bought it got a fabulous deal on an almost brand-new unit at a discount,” said Mr. Watt.

Mr. Watt said the value of a home in this market isn’t based on the original purchase price or its assessed value. It comes down to what a buyer is willing to pay.

“Unless you have something absolutely unique or it’s a good deal, it’s not going to sell.”

The sale closed Sept. 28.

stories.title: Ottawa working closely with EU on foreign aid amid U.S. pullback, secretary of state Randeep Sarai says
stories.summary: Sarai is overseeing a shift in foreign aid as Carney’s government cuts back on global health spending and encourages more private funding
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Canada’s deepening ties with Europe could help fill some of the massive gaps left behind as the United States pulls back from foreign aid and embraces a “transactional” approach, says the secretary of state for international development.

“When we put all our heads together, I think the opportunities are endless,” Randeep Sarai told The Canadian Press.

He said this effort includes recent talks with the European Union on leveraging private dollars and philanthropy for aid, while maintaining some government funding for the world’s most vulnerable.

Sarai is overseeing a shift in foreign aid as the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney cuts back on global health spending and encourages more private funding in development projects.

Ottawa is cutting spending across government, seeking new trade partners and boosting the defence budget to make Canada less vulnerable to U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and threats of annexation.

The Trump administration shut down the United States Agency for International Development, Usaid, leading to what Harvard University researchers estimate to be hundreds of thousands of preventable deaths.

In April, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development reported that the U.S. in 2025 accounted for 17 per cent of spending by rich countries on foreign aid, down from 30 per cent a year prior.

U.S. spending on foreign aid dropped by 57 per cent in 2025.

Most major donor states, including Canada, have cut back on aid funding. Ottawa spends about 1.6 per cent of its budget on foreign aid.

“Taxpayer dollars are very valuable. So if we can bring in the private sector along with them, the goal is (that) eventually the private sector will invest on their own. But initially, we’ll use the taxpayer dollars to entice them,” Sarai said.

Sarai added that Europe has looked to Carney for guidance on so-called blended finance because of his experience as a United Nations official.

Carney’s UN role was to advise governments on climate finance, including ways for governments to work with the private sector and philanthropists to transition to net-zero carbon emissions.

Ireland hosted a meeting of EU development ministers earlier this month and invited Canada to attend.

Sarai said much of the discussion in Dublin was about how to leverage private capital without abandoning support for the world’s most vulnerable people.

Sarai said Canada and European countries are also working with other nations with a reputation for robust foreign aid, including Japan, Korea and Gulf nations.

He said American officials have “come back, to some degree” on aid spending by funding vaccines for children in poor countries.

“Their aid has to benefit the American economy and American people,” Sarai said.

“They have very clear guidelines on that and transactional nature of it, but that’s their direction. So I would say it’s very different from the other G7 partners, but at least we know where we’re at.”

The push for more private dollars in aid has many critics.

Co-operation Canada, a coalition of most Canadian aid groups operating abroad, said the sector supports innovative funding, with some caveats.

“If we are to use public funds to incentivize private capital, then there need to be some guardrails around … that we’re we’re using our public funds in the most efficient way possible,” said Paul Farran, the group’s advocacy director.

He said aid dollars shouldn’t be used to subsidize endeavours that the private sector wouldn’t have otherwise funded.

“Our international assistance should first and foremost be used to alleviate poverty and inequalities,” Farran said.

Sarai said Canada is not going to surrender its support for the world’s poorest to market forces.

He said that applies to Canada’s programming in the 32 nations the UN describes as the world’s least developed countries, as well as projects that focus on sexual health and reproductive rights.

He said the government has a different approach in high-growth countries, where it pursues “mutual economic prosperity” through projects that benefit Canadian companies and investors while creating jobs abroad.

“The Vietnams, Indonesias, Philippines in the world, we believe that they can now take care of those areas themselves. We don’t need to invest in those particular areas for them,” he said.

Sarai cited a new aid project in Thailand which will see Canada’s development finance institution FinDev lend cash for microloans to women in rural areas looking to launch or expand businesses.

Canada is lending roughly $85-million, which is being matched by $280 million from the Japanese bank Smbc and the Asian Development Bank.

Last month, The House finance committee, which has a majority of Liberal MPs, called on Carney last month to provide predictable and clear aid funding in the Nov. 5 budget.

Aid groups told the committee that the federal government says its supports for refugees inside Canada amount to more than 17 per cent of its total development assistance. While that’s a standard reporting practice for Western countries, the aid groups said it makes it hard to tell how much Canadian cash is actually going abroad.

The MPs on the committee argued aid spending should be “guided by poverty and fragility” and should have “increasing transparency in the international assistance envelope.”

The MPs also urged Canada to “reaffirm gender equality and women’s economic empowerment as drivers of poverty reduction and, therefore, as central priorities.” Carney caused confusion a year ago by suggesting Canada no longer has a feminist foreign policy.

Co-operation Canada supports those calls and is urging Carney to reverse cuts to global health programs.

Farran said Canada should earmark $5.5 billion annually for “core” development aid abroad, which would boost funding for things like building schools or helping women advocate for political rights.

He also said Ottawa owes the public more clarity on how it is spending foreign aid and where it’s cutting back.

stories.title: The death of the dinner party
stories.summary: When was the last time you host a dinner party? Not for special occasion, just for the sake of it. How about the last time you went to one? Odds are, it’s been awhile. With generations living in smaller homes, drinking less, and with less expendable income, they’re becoming a rarer occurrence. But with the […]
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
When was the last time you host a dinner party? Not for special occasion, just for the sake of it. How about the last time you went to one? Odds are, it’s been awhile. With generations living in smaller homes, drinking less, and with less expendable income, they’re becoming a rarer occurrence. But with the demise of the dinner party, what else are we losing?

Host Catherine Jette is speaking with Cathrin Bradbury, a columnist for the Toronto Star , about what the dinner party was and what we’re losing as a society as we push its existence to the fringes.

stories.title: Here’s why fish are returning to this former toxic waste site
stories.summary: The $400-million tar ponds cleanup was completed in 2014 and featured concrete encapsulation, followed by massive areas being filled in with soil and then topped with lawns.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Sydney, N.S. - At first glance it May seem hard to believe, but scenic Open Hearth Park in Sydney, N.S., with its vast green spaces, is located on the same site as the former Sydney tar ponds.

The massive toxic hazardous waste site was once filled with slag from steel plants, and local rivers were polluted with run off from the nearby coke ovens.

“At one point there were more than 4 million litres of sanitary sewage going into that space each day,” said Donnie Burke, senior director of Build Nova Scotia, who is tasked with monitoring the water quality in the area.

The pollution in the industrial Cape Breton started building up in the late 1800s. The long-term environmental impact was devastating, placing a major strain on the wildlife and fish.

“The fish were very stressed and they had deformities,” Burke said.

But Katherine Jones, a biologist at Cape Breton University, has good news to report. She examined samples of the tiny mummichog fish living in Coke Ovens Brook, Muggah Creek and Wash Brook and discovered their health has dramatically rebounded because water pollution levels have improved in recent years.

“The fish don’t show any bone abnormalities, or fin rot or fin erosion and their asymmetry has also improved,” Jones said. “Asymmetry is a sign of developmental stress, so fish that are more symmetrical have experienced less stress while they are developing.”

Other species of healthy fish have also returned.

“I have witnessed with staff here, trout fry in the Coke Ovens Brook and we saw gaspereau come up,” Burke said. “Recently we were informed that people saw seabass in the channel.”

The $400-million tar ponds cleanup was completed in 2014 and featured concrete encapsulation, followed by massive areas being filled in with soil and then topped with lawns. Open Hearth Park now features sports fields, flowing rivers, walking trails and a dog run.

“It took a long time and years of remediation and they have done a very good job,” said Melissa Breakwell, who comes to the park often to walk her dog. “This is wonderful.”

Burke said a beautiful public park, with cleaner water and a healthier ecosystem, represents a remarkable transformation of the entire area.

“I recall people would ask me if they had to wear respirators, coming into Sydney Harbour on a cruise ship because it was coming next to the Tar Ponds,” Burke said. “In the summertime, you now see a lot of kites flying and it is a true paradigm shift, when you think about the environmental side of it.”

Burke added that there are more than 2,000 trees planted at the park. The fields are closely monitored for subsidence and the surface and groundwater water are tested on a routine basis

“If it is stable or improving, we are then able to convey that to the public, and our trends to date have shown consistent signs of improved water quality,” said Burke, adding that is a big reason why fish are healthier and thriving at the former site of the Sydney tar ponds.

stories.title: Métis woman gets discounted sentence for selling deadly drugs
stories.summary: Despite her “moral culpability well above that of the ordinary commercial fentanyl trafficker,” the judge noted her “intergenerational trauma”
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
An Alberta judge has discounted the sentence for a Métis woman caught selling drugs she believed had already killed two people, linking her crimes to “the intergenerational legacy” of residential schools.

Justice Derek Jugnauth sentenced Kendall Delaney to six years in prison after she pleaded guilty in the Court of King’s Bench to trafficking methamphetamine and fentanyl.

“Absent the mitigating factors and the circumstances described in the Indigenous Background Report, I would regard this as an exemplary case for a sentence very significantly above the 5-7 year range,” Jugnauth wrote in a recent decision out of Edmonton.

Delaney, now 28, was arrested in the spring of 2024 by an undercover police operation set up by the Camrose Police Service and Vegreville RCMP.

The court heard that she was selling fentanyl laced with a benzodiazepine, which increases the risk of a fatal overdose.

Delaney told an undercover police officer on April 17, 2024, that “two men had recently died in her residence from fentanyl overdoses caused by the red fentanyl (she was selling), indicating that one of the deceased had been a good friend of hers.”

These circumstances place Delaney’s “moral culpability well above that of the ordinary commercial fentanyl trafficker,” said the judge in his Oct. 15 decision.

The Crown recommended she get three years in prison, calling the position “lenient” and “the minimum capable of adequately denouncing the conduct and deterring (Ms. Delaney) and others.”

Delaney tried arguing for house arrest and probation. But after the judge said he was considering giving her more time than even the Crown was seeking, she abandoned the ask for a conditional sentence and sought a prison term in the range of four to five years.

Delaney sold about two ounces of methamphetamine to an undercover officer for $380 at her home on March 10, 2024. Her six-year-old son witnessed the transaction, the judge said.

Three days later, she sold the same undercover cop an ounce of methamphetamine and 3.5 grams of cocaine for $430.

“A short time later, the undercover officer again contacted Ms. Delaney and arranged to purchase 3.5 grams of fentanyl for $220. During the discussions leading up to the sale, Ms. Delaney asked whether the officer wanted ‘blue, red or brown’ fentanyl, or a combination of the three. Ms. Delaney advised the officer that the red fentanyl was ‘literally killing ppl it’s so strong’ and suggested that anyone receiving it should be warned about its potency. The officer replied that a mixture was acceptable.”

The undercover officer went to Delaney’s home and her boyfriend handed over drugs outside.

“The fentanyl was packaged in three separate bags containing red, blue and brown fentanyl,” said the decision.

“Analysis later determined that the red fentanyl contained bromazolam, a benzodiazepine.”

The undercover officer contacted Delaney again on April 16, 2024.

“During the conversation, Ms. Delaney stated that she was not doing well because two people had overdosed during the previous week. When the officer asked to purchase additional red fentanyl and one ounce of methamphetamine, Ms. Delaney advised that the red fentanyl had caused the overdoses and noted her supply was diminished but that she would see what she could do.”

The next day, the undercover cop arranged to buy three ounces of methamphetamine from Delaney.

They travelled together to Edmonton from Vegreville, with another undercover officer in the same car, to obtain more drugs.

Once they got there, one of the undercover officers gave Delaney money to buy three ounces of methamphetamine.

She handed over the drugs and one of the undercover cops noticed Delaney had more drugs in her purse.

“During the time spent in Edmonton, Ms. Delaney advised the undercover officers on two occasions that other customers had placed orders for methamphetamine that she was obtaining on that trip.”

When Mounties stopped their car at 1:10 a.m. on April 18, 2024, Delaney “removed from her purse a bag of methamphetamine weighing approximately one ounce and a bag containing approximately 1.3 grams of cocaine and concealed both items in her vagina, which she had previously told the undercover officers she would do if stopped by police.”

Police arrested all of them and found more cocaine and methamphetamine in Delaney’s purse.

“After initially denying that she was concealing controlled substances in her body, and refusing medical treatment to extract those substances, Ms. Delaney eventually removed the concealed drugs on her own, which were then seized by police.”

Those experiences do not excuse her conduct, but they provide important context for understanding how she came before the court

The judge said he must “consider the unique systemic and background factors” that contributed to Delaney’s circumstances and determine whether they bear upon her level of moral blameworthiness.

She experienced “a significant degree of intergenerational trauma notwithstanding the limited role that her Indigenous father played in her life,” Jugnauth said.

“The fact that her father was largely absent throughout her childhood left her disconnected from her Indigenous heritage and culture.”

While that “abandonment cannot be said to have directly caused the present offences, it is nevertheless part of the intergenerational legacy experienced by Ms. Delaney. The residential school experience of her paternal grandmother was followed by family fragmentation and the loss of meaningful cultural continuity. In Ms. Delaney’s case, that legacy manifested itself in the absence of her father, a lack of connection to her Métis identity, and a childhood marked by instability and dislocation.”

The judge noted Delaney’s mother “first exposed her to crack cocaine” at the age of 19. “What followed was years-long addiction to crack cocaine and methamphetamine.”

Jugnauth gave “significant weight” to Delaney’s “acceptance of responsibility and expression of remorse; her difficult personal history; and the factors identified in the Indigenous Background Report,” said the decision.

“Her life has been marked by significant childhood adversity and the effects of intergenerational trauma. Those experiences do not excuse her conduct, but they provide important context for understanding how she came before the court.”

The judge noted Delaney’s mother “first exposed her to crack cocaine” at the age of 19. “What followed was years-long addiction to crack cocaine and methamphetamine.”

Jugnauth gave “significant weight” to Delaney’s “acceptance of responsibility and expression of remorse; her difficult personal history; and the factors identified in the Indigenous Background Report,” said the decision.

“Her life has been marked by significant childhood adversity and the effects of intergenerational trauma. Those experiences do not excuse her conduct, but they provide important context for understanding how she came before the court.”
