stories.title: What slim margins from B.C.’s last election can tell us about the coming vote
stories.summary: Many of those close calls in 2024 are still ridings to watch this weekend
stories.author: Ming Wong
stories.content:
In the 2024 B.C. provincial election, almost a quarter of 93 ridings had a slim margin of victory where the difference between the elected candidate and the runner-up was less than five percentage points.

Some of those were down to a double-digit vote difference, such as in Surrey-Guildford, where the NDP eked out a win by 22 votes. Another way to think of that number: That’s about how many people would fit in an elevator at Guildford Town Centre.

When margins are slim, every vote counts, but not every eligible vote gets cast. In the past decade, B.C. voter turnout in provincial elections has consistently hovered in the mid-50s to low 60s, which means votes are left on the table. Elections BC’s preliminary numbers show advance voting has gone down this year compared with 2024: 891,348 from 951,812.

Even the turnout from last week’s municipal elections – higher than recent years in cities such as Vancouver, Surrey and Burnaby – showed that the majority of eligible voters didn’t go to the polls.

“It’s striking that there is this enormous potential reserve of voters who if they were mobilized could conceivably make a difference at the margin,” says Richard Johnston, a professor emeritus in political science at University of British Columbia, Vancouver. But he says that part of the electorate is hard to crack.

Many of those close calls two years ago are still races to watch for 2026, where the winner and runner-up candidates are running again. Here’s an illustrated look at how tight the race was last time using everyday examples within, or close to, their respective ridings.

Past election:

Conservative Kristina Loewen won over NDP Loyal Wooldridge by a margin of 0.16 percentage points.

That was 40 votes – roughly the same number of riders of a half-full Kelowna Regional Transit bus.

What to expect:

Kelowna Centre is one of these tight races that are in ridings newly created in 2024 in response to population growth in those areas, as part of the latest electoral district boundary redrawing that happens after every other election.

This downtown riding is focused on the urban core, and will see a rematch of Ms. Loewen, who worked in real estate, and Mr. Wooldridge, a former city councillor. Also in the mix is OneBC candidate Bill Desrosiers, who works at a heavy-equipment rental company.

Conservative Bryan Tepper beat NDP incumbent Jinny Sims by a margin of 1.49 percentage points.

That was 263 votes, roughly the same number of riders of two full cars on the Expo Line SkyTrain.

Surrey is one of the fastest growing municipalities in the province, and its 10 ridings are liable to swing. Surrey-Panorama used to be a BC Liberal seat before Ms. Sims won in 2017. Previously an MP and head of the BC Teachers’ Federation, Ms. Sims is again running against Mr. Tepper, a former RCMP officer. Rounding out the candidates are CentreBC’s Manav Manro, a businessman, and Green’s Nolen Scott, who works in film.

NDP incumbent Amna Shah edged Conservative Zeeshan Wahla by a margin of 1.61 percentage points.

That was 232 votes, roughly the same number of riders of two full cars on the Expo Line SkyTrain.

For this downtown constituency newly redrawn in 2024, it’ll be a rematch between Ms. Shah and Mr. Wahla, along with Raman Sharma and Oliver Wildfong, candidates from the newly formed parties CentreBC and OneBC, respectively.

Conservative Scott McInnis won over the NDP’s Andrea Dunlop by a margin of 3.66 percentage points.

That was 670 votes, a little under the full capacity of the hot pool at Radium Hot Springs.

It would’ve been a rematch of the same three candidates from the past election except the Green’s Calvin Beauchesne opted to run for Golden City Council (and was elected.) Instead, facing off Mr. McInnis and Ms. Dunlop for the Greens will be Rana Nelson. All three are former teachers.

Conservative Jody Toor triumphed over the NDP’s Andrew Mercier by a margin of 3.81 percentage points.

That was 867 votes, about the number of patrons in the Sections P-N at a Vancouver Giants hockey game at the Langley Events Centre.

Langley-Willowbrook used to be part of a larger electoral district called Langley, which was held by BC Liberal Mary Polak for more than a decade. Mr. Mercier defeated her in 2020. When the district boundaries were redrawn, and Langley-Willowbrook was contested for the first time, Mr. Mercier lost to Ms. Toor. Both are running again, along with Shubham Joshi, a OneBC candidate, and Anisha Sandhu of the Greens.

stories.title: You called me a bad feminist. I was actually Sherlock Holmes
stories.summary: Why was I interested in the case of Steven Galloway? Because there were so many questions that needed to be answered
stories.author: Margaret Atwood
stories.content:
Margaret Atwood is the author of Book of Lives: A Memoir of Sorts. Her newsletter is In the Writing Burrow.

I’m a snoopy person. I like reading detective stories. Sherlock Holmes was my preadolescent crush. I like to know what is said to have happened, and also what really happened. What is hard-evidence knowledge, and what is only belief? There are many such questions that needed to be answered about what has become known as the Galloway affair .

For latecomers: Steven Galloway is the bestselling novelist and former golden boy of the University of British Columbia’s creative writing program. In 2015 he was accused of sexual assault by a former student with whom he’d been having an affair, and condemned for it without anyone knowing what specifically he was supposed to have done and whether or not he was actually guilty. He was suspended after the allegations were made and was fired the following June, following an investigation that found he had committed sexual harassment but did not find that he committed sexual or physical assault.

I get particularly snoopy when I’m being viciously attacked, as I was over my signing of the “ UBC Accountable ” letter, which advocated for due process for Mr. Galloway. This open letter did not support Mr. Galloway, as its detractors claimed, but called for an impartial and open investigation of Ubc’s botched handling of the Steven Galloway affair. Why were my attackers so radically opposed to one of the key rights of a democracy – the right to a fair trial before the verdict? That right, if abolished for men, would abolish it for women, too.

I got various answers at the time. Well-meaning younger friends told me I should remove my name from the letter because an investigation would “hurt women,” or it was “a bad look” for me. One male student told a pal of mine that he knew Mr. Galloway hadn’t done it, but felt Mr. Galloway should say he had and “take one for the team,” because so many women are sexually assaulted. Yes, this is true, which makes a ripoff of their stories all the more deplorable. I was called a “ bad feminist .” Some people told me that I was going against “the zeitgeist” – in other words, bucking public opinion. Hardly a moral litmus test.

My self-proclaimed enemies accused me of many other things, my favourite being that my books took up too much room on bookstore shelves. (I could identify, having spent years looking small beside The Mammoth Hunters , since Auel comes after Atwood.) A bunch of female academics put together a ramshackle anthology of essays called Refuse: Canlit on Fire that assumed Mr. Galloway was a rapist and I was a rape apologist. (It doesn’t wear well.) Some trolled or stalked me for years: If only I would recant and join “the right side of history,” I could be their friend and they would stop drilling holes in my teeth. It was all very Stalinist show-trial brain-washy.

I met other players in out-of-the way places, to protect them from being seen with radioactive me. Some had been at UBC at the time, and said “everyone” knew about the affair. Some had been at the off-campus meeting where Mr. Galloway was tried and condemned without knowing anything about it, and said it was a railroading. Several had written the UBC Accountable letter. Some were sessionals in the creative writing department who’d been among the many purged for not being True Believers. Some were journalists who were afraid to touch the thing, it was so “toxic.” Some were publishers who shook their heads – poor Steven – but felt powerless to do anything. Some had spoken out and been trashed in their turn. If you’ve ever tut-tutted about Mao’s Red Guards and said “It can’t happen here,” take a look.

Meanwhile, the barrage of online hate I was facing only made me snoopier. I wanted to be thorough, as Sherlock Holmes would have been. I got my grubby little paws on some interesting documents, including the 200 pages of text messages between the lovers during their affair: requests for dates and favours from her, I-have-a-headaches from him, and a hilarious reference to myself as “the Evil A.” I even obtained a floor plan of Mr. Galloway’s office, scene of the alleged rape. Was there any place where a drugged and unconscious body could have been hidden while Mr. Galloway was holding office hours, as he did until 5 p.m. on that day? There was not. Was there a drug that could have been administered shortly after five, knocking the victim out long enough to be undressed and raped, then wear off completely by 7:15 p.m., when she was seen laughing and chatting normally at an author reading? Medical opinion said no.

In any Sherlock Holmes story, there’s a finale when the Aha! moment arrives. How misled we readers have been! How clever the murderer! Except for these few sloppy details, which Holmes will now explain to us.

So it is with the Steven Galloway saga. The Supreme Court of British Columbia, where Mr. Galloway is suing for defamation, is the setting. Daniel Burnett, Mr. Galloway’s lawyer, is Sherlock, revealing clue after clue. I’ll cast the indefatigable Brad Cran as his Watson, doing the pick-and-shovel work on his Substack, Truth and Consequences , which covered the delays and appeals that have dragged this case out for eight years. Sherlock did not have a female sidekick, but let me mention my friend and fellow author Susan Swan, who hung in there despite the stink bombs tossed our way because she understood Article 10 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: “Everyone is entitled in full equality to a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal, in the determination of his rights and obligations and of any criminal charge against him.”

This week we got a piece of definitive testimony. The accuser’s former husband, who didn’t know about the two-year affair between Mr. Galloway and his wife, told the court that she said she wanted to “destroy” Mr. Galloway because he’d allegedly put his hands around her throat. The former husband also read into the record a series of texts they’d been exchanging at the time of the supposed rape in his office, containing sweet nothings but also comments about a hockey game they were following together, although in different locations.

You can fake screenshots of text messages, but not texts on someone’s actual phone, or so the experts tell me. They are time- and location-stamped. Before the trial began, Mr. Galloway’s accuser withdrew her defences of truth and fair comment (though did not admit she spread lies about Mr. Galloway) but these texts should, once and for all, put to bed the rape claim. I’m guessing the rest of the trial will be about the details of how Mr. Galloway was framed, and also how much money in damages he is owed.

Why bother, at my age and stage, to take such an interest? I myself was not materially psychologically damaged by the barrage hurled in my direction – not my first rodeo, I’m a hardened case. But many others were harmed. The trail of wreckage is very long, and includes not only those attacked, but also those duped into believing in the accuser, some of them very vulnerable because they really were rape survivors. Their lives have been torn apart, too.

Many of those who called Steven Galloway a rapist now understand that they were conned, and have settled and apologized . But some will remain true believers forever, because the credo “Galloway did it” is their cult identity. As Sherlock Holmes says at the end of A Case of Identity , “If I tell her she will not believe me.”

Why were my attackers so radically opposed to one of the key rights of a democracy – the right to a fair trial before the verdict? That right, if abolished for men, would abolish it for women, too.

I got various answers at the time. Well-meaning younger friends told me I should remove my name from the letter because an investigation would “hurt women,” or it was “a bad look” for me. One male student told a pal of mine that he knew Mr. Galloway hadn’t done it, but felt Mr. Galloway should say he had and “take one for the team,” because so many women are sexually assaulted. Yes, this is true, which makes a ripoff of their stories all the more deplorable. I was called a “ bad feminist .” Some people told me that I was going against “the zeitgeist” – in other words, bucking public opinion. Hardly a moral litmus test.

My self-proclaimed enemies accused me of many other things, my favourite being that my books took up too much room on bookstore shelves. (I could identify, having spent years looking small beside The Mammoth Hunters , since Auel comes after Atwood.) A bunch of female academics put together a ramshackle anthology of essays called Refuse: Canlit on Fire that assumed Mr. Galloway was a rapist and I was a rape apologist. (It doesn’t wear well.) Some trolled or stalked me for years: If only I would recant and join “the right side of history,” I could be their friend and they would stop drilling holes in my teeth. It was all very Stalinist show-trial brain-washy.

I met other players in out-of-the way places, to protect them from being seen with radioactive me. Some had been at UBC at the time, and said “everyone” knew about the affair. Some had been at the off-campus meeting where Mr. Galloway was tried and condemned without knowing anything about it, and said it was a railroading. Several had written the UBC Accountable letter. Some were sessionals in the creative writing department who’d been among the many purged for not being True Believers. Some were journalists who were afraid to touch the thing, it was so “toxic.” Some were publishers who shook their heads – poor Steven – but felt powerless to do anything. Some had spoken out and been trashed in their turn. If you’ve ever tut-tutted about Mao’s Red Guards and said “It can’t happen here,” take a look.

Meanwhile, the barrage of online hate I was facing only made me snoopier. I wanted to be thorough, as Sherlock Holmes would have been. I got my grubby little paws on some interesting documents, including the 200 pages of text messages between the lovers during their affair: requests for dates and favours from her, I-have-a-headaches from him, and a hilarious reference to myself as “the Evil A.” I even obtained a floor plan of Mr. Galloway’s office, scene of the alleged rape. Was there any place where a drugged and unconscious body could have been hidden while Mr. Galloway was holding office hours, as he did until 5 p.m. on that day? There was not. Was there a drug that could have been administered shortly after five, knocking the victim out long enough to be undressed and raped, then wear off completely by 7:15 p.m., when she was seen laughing and chatting normally at an author reading? Medical opinion said no.

In any Sherlock Holmes story, there’s a finale when the Aha! moment arrives. How misled we readers have been! How clever the murderer! Except for these few sloppy details, which Holmes will now explain to us.

So it is with the Steven Galloway saga. The Supreme Court of British Columbia, where Mr. Galloway is suing for defamation, is the setting. Daniel Burnett, Mr. Galloway’s lawyer, is Sherlock, revealing clue after clue. I’ll cast the indefatigable Brad Cran as his Watson, doing the pick-and-shovel work on his Substack, Truth and Consequences , which covered the delays and appeals that have dragged this case out for eight years. Sherlock did not have a female sidekick, but let me mention my friend and fellow author Susan Swan, who hung in there despite the stink bombs tossed our way because she understood Article 10 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: “Everyone is entitled in full equality to a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal, in the determination of his rights and obligations and of any criminal charge against him.”

This week we got a piece of definitive testimony. The accuser’s former husband, who didn’t know about the two-year affair between Mr. Galloway and his wife, told the court that she said she wanted to “destroy” Mr. Galloway because he’d allegedly put his hands around her throat. The former husband also read into the record a series of texts they’d been exchanging at the time of the supposed rape in his office, containing sweet nothings but also comments about a hockey game they were following together, although in different locations.

You can fake screenshots of text messages, but not texts on someone’s actual phone, or so the experts tell me. They are time- and location-stamped. Before the trial began, Mr. Galloway’s accuser withdrew her defences of truth and fair comment (though did not admit she spread lies about Mr. Galloway) but these texts should, once and for all, put to bed the rape claim. I’m guessing the rest of the trial will be about the details of how Mr. Galloway was framed, and also how much money in damages he is owed.

Why bother, at my age and stage, to take such an interest? I myself was not materially psychologically damaged by the barrage hurled in my direction – not my first rodeo, I’m a hardened case. But many others were harmed. The trail of wreckage is very long, and includes not only those attacked, but also those duped into believing in the accuser, some of them very vulnerable because they really were rape survivors. Their lives have been torn apart, too.

Many of those who called Steven Galloway a rapist now understand that they were conned, and have settled and apologized . But some will remain true believers forever, because the credo “Galloway did it” is their cult identity. As Sherlock Holmes says at the end of A Case of Identity , “If I tell her she will not believe me.”

content_blocks.text: For latecomers: Steven Galloway is the bestselling novelist and former golden boy of the University of British Columbia’s creative writing program. In 2015 he was accused of sexual assault by a former student with whom he’d been having an affair, and condemned for it without anyone knowing what specifically he was supposed to have done and whether or not he was actually guilty. He was suspended after the allegations were made and was fired the following June, following an investigation that found he had committed sexual harassment but did not find that he committed sexual or physical assault.

stories.title: Krose pitches plan for first 100 days if elected mayor
stories.summary: If elected, Krose commits to bring forward a motion at the first available Council meeting, requesting a coordinated implementation schedule for her priorities.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Just days before Londoners go to the polls to choose their next city council, mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose is offering a plan that would begin implementing her platform within the first 100 days.

If elected, Krose commits to bring forward a motion at the first available Council meeting, requesting a coordinated implementation schedule for her priorities.

“I have a plan that within the first hundred days, we will have certain tasks that are going to happen,” she told CTV News at an announcement near Victoria Park. “I have five key priorities, traffic, housing, safety, municipal services, as well as taxes.”

She will also seek council support for several initiatives including:

Implementation of a London Performance Dashboard displaying service standards, expenses, and results

Within 30 days, directing staff to identify three priority areas for value-for-money reviews

Request a ranked assessment of ten traffic bottlenecks

A coordinated homelessness workplan developed with housing providers and community partners within 30 days, and a milestone driven implementation plan within 100 days

“My first 100 days will establish the discipline and direction for four years of better services, safer neighbourhoods, and greater respect for taxpayers,” she adds.

Krose was joined at her event by Ward 4 candidate Elivis Birindwa.

Birindwa expressed support for Krose’s plan, “I spoke to her, her ideas resonate well with me, and honestly I’m rooting for her.”

A list of candidates running in the municipal election can be found on the City of London Website.

Election Day is Oct. 26.

stories.title: Candu attitude: Carney pegs ‘good chances’ on Canadian bid for Turkey nuclear plant
stories.summary: Istanbul — Prime Minister Mark Carney says a Canadian company's bid to supply nuclear energy to Turkey has a real shot of winning the lucrative tender.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Istanbul — Prime Minister Mark Carney said Friday a Canadian company has a real shot at winning a lucrative tender to supply nuclear energy to Turkey — a prospect he said was remote a year ago.

Carney was meeting with Turkish business leaders in Istanbul Friday, a day after he announced a new strategic partnership between Canada and Turkey to deepen co-operation on a range of files.

Energy is one of the pillars of that agreement and Carney said the AtkinsRéalis bid to supply two planned Turkish power plants with the Candu nuclear reactor now has “good chances” of succeeding, the prime minister said. He added it would have been a long-shot a year ago.

“We’re in negotiations, and those negotiations are getting more intense. Probably from here to the end of the year, or around COP 31, it will be a decision for the Turkish government,” Carney told reporters in French.

COP31 is the United Nations Climate Change Conference, set for Antalya, Turkey from Nov. 9 to 20.

“Candu has a chance,” Carney added. “Yes, there’s competition. But we have the quality of the technology, of the financing, and a true partnership with business in this country with Canada.”

Ian Edwards, president and CEO of AtkinsRéalis, confirmed in a LinkedIn post on Friday that he is also in Turkey this week.

He thanked Carney and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson, who is also on the trip, for “their partnership and continued support in advancing this important opportunity for Canadian nuclear energy.”

Edwards said AtkinsRéalis is conducting a feasibility study for the potential build-out of Candu reactors at Sinop, a city in Turkey on the Black Sea proposed for the site of a new power plant.

In June, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand welcomed her Turkish counterpart to Canada. During the trip, Turkish officials toured the Darlington nuclear facility in Ontario.

Canada’s nuclear strategy was released a week before the June trip.

The plan looks to sell more Candu reactors around the world and sets a goal of entering at least four new international markets by 2040. It also seeks to “engage six to 10 new nuclear entrant markets over a 15-year horizon, cementing Canada as their partner of choice.”

The push to sell Candu to new markets is an attempt to establish Canada as a reliable uranium export partner and to use nuclear energy as a geopolitical lever.

The prime minister said while contract decisions are ultimately made business-to-business, his role in Istanbul is to share how the Canadian market has become more welcoming to foreign firms and investors.

“We’ve made some fairly big changes in terms of the tax regime in Canada, the speed with which investment decisions are (being made), the way we’re partnering with a broader group of countries … those are a lot of changes at the same time,” Carney said.

“You have to go out and explain to people what’s changed.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray in Ottawa

stories.title: Air Canada to phase out routes to these U.S. destinations in 2027
stories.summary: Starting next summer, Air Canada will discontinue four routes to U.S. destinations.
stories.author: Joe Van Wonderen
stories.content:
Air Canada confirmed its plans to cancel four routes to U.S. destinations.

In an email shared with CTVNews.CA Thursday, the airline said that starting next summer, it will no longer fly between:

Vancouver-Nashville, Tenn.

Vancouver-Raleigh-Durham, N.C.

Toronto-Charleston, S.C.

Montreal-Seattle, Wash.

“Air Canada regularly reviews its schedule to ensure capacity is aligned with customer demand and travel patterns,” Air Canada spokesperson Sean Davidson said in an email.

The news comes as travel between Canada and the United States has plunged in recent years. Despite a steady increase in cross-border travel over the summer , Canadian-resident return trips from the U.S. in July were 25.6 per cent below their July 2024 level .

U.S. residents flew to Canada 701,800 times in August, according to StatCan .

Davidson added that Air Canada will continue to fly to Nashville, Raleigh-Durham and Seattle from other Canadian airports, but did not say anything about ongoing service to Charleston.

Expanding service to the U.S.

The company announced last week that it would open new routes between Toronto and Louisville, Ky., Montreal and Indianapolis, Ind., as well as Edmonton and Newark, N.J., to serve summer travellers in 2027.

“We’ll also increase capacity between Edmonton and San Francisco by deploying a larger Airbus A220 on the route,” Davidson told CTVNews.CA.

In a joint effort between Air Canada and United Airlines, seasonal routes from the U.S. to Canada will open next summer.

Those routes include Denver to Ottawa and Quebec City, seasonal service to St. John’s from Newark and expanded service between Washington, D.C. and Quebec City, along with further expansion to service between Denver and Winnipeg.

stories.title: Business Brief: Ottawa’s risky mining bet
stories.summary: Plus, Canada’s $1.75-billion venture capital boost and a new trade partnership with Turkey
stories.author: Jeffrey Jones
stories.content:
Good morning. Ottawa is betting big on critical minerals to strengthen Canada’s economy, but many of the mining projects it’s backing come with considerable financial risks. With taxpayers helping foot the bill, the question is whether the potential payoff will be worth it. More on that below.

Steel: Mélanie Joly has given Stelco’s U.S. owner 15 days to honour its job commitments or potentially face legal action over planned layoffs.

Venture capital: Ottawa is rolling out $1.75-billion in funding to boost Canada’s venture capital sector, though the plan falls short of demands from early-stage startup investors.

Trade: Canada and Turkey have announced a strategic partnership to deepen co-operation on energy, defence and trade, as Ottawa seeks to reduce its reliance on the U.S.

It’s Jeff Jones here, energy and resources editor at Report on Business. A top focus for our coverage is the objective championed by Prime Minister Mark Carney and his government to build everything everywhere. Energy, infrastructure, mining – Mr. Carney touts major projects as the way to shore up a national economy that’s under attack by U.S. President Donald Trump.

So far, large chunks of this promised construction boom are set for funding by various arms of the federal government. That is, you and me. Exhibit A: the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline to the West Coast from Alberta. Federally owned Trans Mountain Corp. is responsible for 45 per cent of that multibillion-dollar project, which is now deemed to be in the national interest.

Critical minerals are also a core focus of the hoped-for construction boom. But working mines often start with small prospectors, which do not have the financial wherewithal to build projects themselves. In addition, lenders fear the risks inherent in early-stage development, and stay away. Enter, once again, the feds.

For this weekend’s big read, mining correspondent Niall McGee has taken a hard look at some of the projects the government has decided to back to expand Canada’s position in the global race for critical minerals. Those include such minerals as graphite, palladium, dysprosium and terbium (check out the story to find out what those are used for). Many are led not by transnational players, but by junior companies that have not developed mines of their own.

Niall has spent months digging into this issue. His reporting shows the government is aware that there are numerous risks, but sees its role as necessary to bridge a funding gulf in mine development.

“Junior mining is one of the riskiest parts of the market to invest in. Blow-ups and cost overruns are endemic. So it seems almost inevitable that the taxpayer is going to suffer some losses,” Niall tells me.

“The government is also more or less admitting that the ride is going to be rough. The people I spoke to made it clear the priority isn’t to actually make money but to encourage the private sector to get on board.”

History shows that some flops are highly likely, but that a few of the proposed projects will attract private capital as properties are de-risked and construction gets underway.

Should the Canadian taxpayer play the role of mining financier of first resort? Read the feature to draw your conclusions.

Despite years of warnings about household debt, Canadians are sitting on nearly $20-trillion in net worth, thanks largely to rising investments. That financial cushion has helped keep the economy resilient, but a stock market downturn could put it to the test, investment reporter Tim Shufelt writes .

“We’re having conversations to see whether or not we can come back to the table for a set of detailed negotiations. We don’t know exactly when that’s going to happen. ... We’re trying to stabilize the relationship because we are not in a position where it is stable right now. It’s certainly not predictable.” — Janice Charette, Canada’s chief trade negotiator with the United States

Canada’s chief trade negotiator says there’s no timeline for resuming formal trade talks with Washington , despite ongoing communication between the two countries.

By the numbers: Statistics Canada reports August retail sales and September manufacturing sales.

Before the bell: Earnings include American Express and Rogers Communications.

Global markets drifted lower as a rout in global tech shares eased, after concerns over the ​enormous funding needs of AI had hammered Wall Street.

Wall Street futures were in negative territory, while TSX futures were in the red.

Overseas, the pan-European Stoxx 600 was down 0.54 per cent in morning trading. Britain’s Ftse 100 fell 0.59 per cent, Germany’s DAX declined 0.78 per cent and France’s CAC 40 gave back 0.66 per cent.

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei closed 0.34 per cent lower, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 0.69 per cent.

The Canadian dollar traded at 71.39 U.S. cents.

stories.title: U.S. is taking in a lot of Canadians, immigration numbers up 142%
stories.summary: Build Canada group says brain drain is a real issue, but it has some 'bold policy choices' that it says could help.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Drawing from recent data released by the White House that show immigration to the U.S. has fallen from almost every country except Canada, the non-profit civic group Build Canada is sounding the alarm on a potential brain drain from this country into the United States.

A social media post from a White House account on X shows legal immigration down this year from almost every corner of the Earth. Drop-off ranges from 16 per cent in Western Europe and 17 per cent in Southeast Asia to 89 per cent in central Africa and 99 per cent in central Asia.

The two countries bucking the trend are Mexico, where immigration numbers are up 17 per cent, and Canada, which has more than doubled its numbers, increasing 142 per cent. Or as Build Canada says in its post: “The U.S. is taking in Canadians. A lot of them.”

Pulling data from Statistics Canada and elsewhere, the group notes that 120,640 people left Canada last year , the highest number since records began in 1952. It adds that 34 per cent of immigrants with PhDs leave Canada within 25 years, compared to just 16 per cent of high school grads — the so-called “leaky bucket” problem. It also found that tech workers typically make 46 per cent more in the U.S. than in Canada.

The group warned that fewer rivals for U.S. green cards from the rest of the world will continue to make it easier for Canadians to head south, and that “those who go are mostly highly skilled and well paid.”

Lucy Hargreaves, co-founder and CEO of Build Canada, said in an interview that such numbers represent a serious problem. “It is this cohort of highly talented, highly educated Canadians who have the potential to be top earners who are going to the U.S. to work in high-growth industries, especially software grads, but also other professional services,” she said.

“We know that the wages that are on offer in the U.S. are significantly higher than Canada. The economy is growing much faster, and there is an incredible amount of opportunity, particularly if you are a young person in a field like technology, where there’s significant job opportunity and growth.”

Build Canada has been beating a drum for some time now about the brain drain, and it often comes down to a single factor: cash.

First Reading: The provincial revolt against immigration

Canada’s tech industry warns 'entrepreneurs are leaving in droves' for U.S.

Hargreaves noted that salaries are generally higher in the U.S., while capital gains taxes are more lax. “Our income tax structure is also, generally speaking, quite uncompetitive with many states,” she said. “The tax brackets for top income earners kick in at a much lower income in Canada than they do in the U.S. And cost of living in major Canadian cities is incredibly expensive.”

She added: “It’s not necessarily one of those things individually, but it’s cumulatively, when they start doing the math. They think about the power of the U.S. dollar. They think about cost of living, and then they think about the taxes. When they add it all up, it just doesn’t make a lot of financial sense to stay in Canada for many of these people who have multiple opportunities.”

But the problem also offers a solution. A recent paper by Build Canada notes: “There are ample levers to be used to tackle this issue that remain un-deployed.”

The paper lists “bold policy choices” that include forgiveness of student loans, income-tax reform (or a deduction for specific high-demand jobs) and a five-year “founder’s tax break” for founders of newly incorporated Canadian-controlled private corporations.

“These are all ideas that we’ve talked about, and I think some combination of those would make a meaningful difference to this cohort, and would send a signal to those graduates and young Canadians that the government is listening and is being responsive to their needs and trying to put their best foot forward to encourage them to stay.”

The news isn’t all bad, however. Build Canada noted that skilled people from other countries who are shut out of the U.S. by its restrictive immigration policies could choose Canada instead. It also pointed out that the federal government has promised a visa fast track for U.S. workers, and $1.7 billion in funding to bring researchers north.

“I wouldn’t criticize that,” Hargreaves said. “I think you’ve got to give credit where credit is due, but I don’t think it solves the problem that we’re talking about here.”

Her focus is on keeping people in Canada rather than the expensive process of luring them back.

“Ultimately the thing that I think would be great for Canadians to really start wrapping their heads around is that when you lose a high volume of Canadians like that, particularly early in their careers … you almost don’t know what you’re losing, right?”

She added: “You’re losing people before they even really get started. And so I think the more we can have that conversation about brain drain and the potential future growth that we might be losing with those people, the more we can quantify that and start to measure it and really understand what’s on the table, I think Canadians would start to rally around tackling the problem more seriously.”

stories.title: I’ll take the $98 pasta, please
stories.summary: Chefs across Canada are rejecting run-of-the-mill pasta dishes in favour of handmade delights, and charging $100 or more for tasting menus
stories.author: Sara Harowitz
stories.content:
Tucked away in East Vancouver, ON a nondescript strip of Powell Street known for its small handful of cozy restaurants, Angela Pastificio literally stands out. Its bright orange awning, reminiscent of egg yolk, cheerfully marks the spot: This is a house of pasta worship.

Angela’s only menu option is an eight-course, $98 pasta tasting experience. If that sounds like a lot of money for noodles, that’s because it is. Pasta is a food with humble origins; in Italy, affordable access to high-quality, handmade noodles is less of a luxury and more of a national right.

But in Canada, our seemingly insatiable appetite for Italian food has been growing steadily since the aughts, and prices have risen to meet the demand. Scan the menus at higher-end Italian restaurants and you’ll find plates of noodles for up to $29; even chain restaurants are boldly selling pasta dishes for upward of $30. And now, a new crop of Italian restaurants are taking things to the next level with expensive pasta tasting menus.

Spending nearly $100 at Angela might be hard to swallow at first, but the tasting menu is a lot of food; diners certainly won’t leave hungry. And according to chef Calvin Vogstad, what really makes Angela’s price worth it is the heightened level of skill, labour and care put into every bite.

“‘Craft’ is the best word for it,” he says. “I’ve been doing this for 10 years, and I’m still learning literally every day.”

Angela’s menu, which changes every month, features an antipasti, a salad, a progression of five pastas and a dessert. Each pasta is handmade, meaning the noodles are cut, shaped and filled without the use of an extruder (a machine with different attachments that pops out perfectly sized noodles, be it spaghetti or rigatoni).

“Every piece on your plate is different from the others because it’s all done by hand,” Vogstad says. The dough itself is not a perfect science, either: Humidity and airflow, for instance, can affect its consistency, which is why Vogstad has a small army of fans that he places in different areas of the restaurant depending on the weather. “I know that sounds ridiculous,” he says. “But it makes a serious difference.”

The result is noticeably better. Handmade noodles have snap, texture and depth of flavour that store-bought or even extruded pasta simply does not.

On top of that, Vogstad works hard to ensure that his menu is always offering something different. Don’t visit Angela expecting familiar options like fettuccine or fusilli; Vogstad’s pastas are intentionally obscure and regional. This past September, highlights included spoja lorda from the Emilia-Romagna region (delicate ridged squares filled with ricotta and Parmesan, and then finished with decadent black truffle butter) and tajarin al ragù from Piedmont (ultrathin egg-yolk noodles served with pork, veal and beef Bolognese-style sauce).

Hyperlocality and artisanship are also the key pillars of Toronto’s Pasta Privato , which opened earlier this year and is run by executive chef and owner Michael Angeloni. There, an eight-course, $150 tasting menu includes three handmade pastas from different regions in Italy. “The noodles that we’re doing are very unique,” Angeloni says. “Each one is hand-braided or hand-pulled.”

Angeloni estimates that it takes about 10 to 12 hours a day to make all of the pasta for his 28-seat restaurant. A more labour-intensive noodle like lorighittas – an elegant braided-ring shape – might take two or three hours for just 20 portions.

Back on the West Coast, most of the chefs cooking pasta tasting menus (including Vogstad) credit their skills to La Quercia , which has been serving handmade noodles in Vancouver’s Kitsilano area since 2008.

While La Quercia doesn’t have an official pasta-specific tasting menu, chef Adam Pegg will create one if guests ask for it. “I’m interested in everything, but the one thing that matters the most to me is the pasta,” he says. The tasting concept started around 2010, when a friend of Pegg’s requested La Quercia’s $100 family-style menu – but only wanted pasta dishes. It became something of a secret menu item (truly: If you know, you know) and inspired many young cooks who spent time in La Quercia’s kitchen. “I’m proud of all of them,” Pegg says. “I want everybody to succeed.”

One of those chefs was Greg Dilabio, who partnered with Pegg to open Oca Pastificio on Vancouver’s Commercial Drive in 2019. The restaurant specialized in a handmade pasta tasting menu that was wildly popular until Dilabio died suddenly in mid-2023, causing its abrupt closing. The restaurant reopened as Magari by Oca later that year (Pegg is no longer involved), and carries on the legacy left by Dilabio. A recent indulgence in Magari’s $80, seven-course tasting menu included such delights as pappardelle with housemade rabbit-sausage ragù, and the restaurant’s signature crown-like rotolo filled with smoked provolone and squash and then topped with sage butter.

Another one of La Quercia’s graduates is James Frost, who opened Victoria’s 16-seat Lumache with his wife Heather Dosman at the end of 2025. Lumache serves à la carte dishes, but its flagship offering is its $98 tasting menu, which includes a selection of antipasti and vegetable dishes, four handmade pastas and dessert. The menu changes monthly, but what always stays the same is Frost’s emphasis on the craft of pasta-making; dishes are simple and restrained, keeping the attention on the noodles.

“If you’re going to make pasta at a high level, you have to have the ability to stand behind it without putting anything on top,” he says. “In my house, we don’t mess around with loading up on garnishes.”

Frost thinks that pasta is an enduring favourite among Canadians because it’s deeply comforting. “My entire interest in Italian food can be traced back to eating pasta as a kid,” he says. For many of us, that childhood love of digging into a big, warming bowl of noodles never really goes away.

Does that mean we need to spend $100 to eat it? No, of course not. After all, we’re talking about very basic ingredients such as flour and eggs. But for a special night out, pasta tasting menus offer a more relaxed, yet equally enjoyable, alternative to the foams, emulsions and elaborate garnishes of haute cuisine.

“Pasta is a beloved food,” Frost asserts. When you serve it in a restaurant, he continues, “everyone’s already on your side.”

While La Quercia doesn’t have an official pasta-specific tasting menu, chef Adam Pegg will create one if guests ask for it. “I’m interested in everything, but the one thing that matters the most to me is the pasta,” he says. The tasting concept started around 2010, when a friend of Pegg’s requested La Quercia’s $100 family-style menu – but only wanted pasta dishes. It became something of a secret menu item (truly: If you know, you know) and inspired many young cooks who spent time in La Quercia’s kitchen. “I’m proud of all of them,” Pegg says. “I want everybody to succeed.”

One of those chefs was Greg Dilabio, who partnered with Pegg to open Oca Pastificio on Vancouver’s Commercial Drive in 2019. The restaurant specialized in a handmade pasta tasting menu that was wildly popular until Dilabio died suddenly in mid-2023, causing its abrupt closing. The restaurant reopened as Magari by Oca later that year (Pegg is no longer involved), and carries on the legacy left by Dilabio. A recent indulgence in Magari’s $80, seven-course tasting menu included such delights as pappardelle with housemade rabbit-sausage ragù, and the restaurant’s signature crown-like rotolo filled with smoked provolone and squash and then topped with sage butter.

Another one of La Quercia’s graduates is James Frost, who opened Victoria’s 16-seat Lumache with his wife Heather Dosman at the end of 2025. Lumache serves à la carte dishes, but its flagship offering is its $98 tasting menu, which includes a selection of antipasti and vegetable dishes, four handmade pastas and dessert. The menu changes monthly, but what always stays the same is Frost’s emphasis on the craft of pasta-making; dishes are simple and restrained, keeping the attention on the noodles.

“If you’re going to make pasta at a high level, you have to have the ability to stand behind it without putting anything on top,” he says. “In my house, we don’t mess around with loading up on garnishes.”

Frost thinks that pasta is an enduring favourite among Canadians because it’s deeply comforting. “My entire interest in Italian food can be traced back to eating pasta as a kid,” he says. For many of us, that childhood love of digging into a big, warming bowl of noodles never really goes away.

Does that mean we need to spend $100 to eat it? No, of course not. After all, we’re talking about very basic ingredients such as flour and eggs. But for a special night out, pasta tasting menus offer a more relaxed, yet equally enjoyable, alternative to the foams, emulsions and elaborate garnishes of haute cuisine.
“Pasta is a beloved food,” Frost asserts. When you serve it in a restaurant, he continues, “everyone’s already on your side.”

stories.title: Governments are rushing to build new critical minerals mines, but early-stage projects are rife with risk
stories.summary: Private investors have been skittish about financing new mines in Canada, but billions of dollars in public spending are shifting the dynamic
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Last spring, Prime Minister Mark Carney attended a groundbreaking for a graphite mine in Quebec. As Mr. Carney and Nouveau Monde Graphite Inc. chief executive Eric Desaulniers crunched along the gravelly construction site about 120 kilometres north of Montreal, the skies grew dark. Then as Mr. Desaulniers started his prepared remarks at a makeshift lectern, heavy rain started falling, eventually soaking everyone in attendance .

“Literally the only 15 minutes when it rained during the day,” said Mr. Desaulniers. Like many mining CEOs, he’s wired as an optimist. He didn’t view the gloomy weather as a bad omen for the project, the opposite in fact.

“When it’s raining on your wedding day, it should be a very happy marriage,” Mr. Desaulniers said.

This particular wedding could not have happened without the help of the federal and provincial governments. The Matawinie mine was referred to Mr. Carney’s Major Projects Office last year, which identified select natural resource developments for regulatory fast-tracking. More importantly though, the public sector provided a huge chunk of the money to build it.

Of the company’s total US$633-million mine funding package , the company raised about 75 per cent from government sources. That included debt investments worth roughly $459-million from Export Development Canada (EDC) and the Canada Infrastructure Bank (CIB) , and a US$143-million equity raise from Canada Growth Fund Inc. (CGF) and Investissement Québec.

If all goes to plan, when it is up and running, Matawinie will be the biggest operation of its kind in the G7, producing 106,000 tonnes of graphite concentrate a year. The critical mineral is an essential element in lithium ion batteries, fuel cells and industrial lubricants.

Building a mine of this scale would be nerve-wracking even for an experienced operator. But Nouveau Monde has never built a mine before. What’s more, graphite mines are relatively untested in the West with the economic case for large scale operations mostly unproven.

The massive government bet on Nouveau Monde is by no means a one-off. Over the past year and a half, the Carney government has ramped up its support for niche critical minerals operations, with dozens of financings, stockpiling arrangements and price floors involving some of the biggest names in mining, such as Rio Tinto PLC , and Teck Resources Ltd. , as well as “juniors” – much smaller development-stage companies – such as Mangrove Lithium , and Cyclic Materials .

The private sector has been skittish about funding new critical minerals mines in Canada in large part because of the risk. Traditionally, if a junior couldn’t raise money privately, it generally meant the investment case wasn’t there, and the project didn’t move forward. But that dynamic is being upended by the billions of dollars the government is offering to newbies allowing them to get over the hump, in the name of national interest. Ottawa hopes the support will be temporary, with an expectation that institutional investors, specialized mining funds, private equity and senior mining companies will take over once these new markets are established. But there is no guarantee that will happen, and there is also the possibility that some of the big swings could be financially disastrous.

Public support of critical minerals companies of this breadth and scale would have been unthinkable five years ago. But the world has changed irrevocably during that time with security of minerals supply front and centre. Canada is trying to wean itself from reliance on China and emerge as a viable alternative supplier of critical minerals to its G7 partners. But perhaps even more pressing is Ottawa’s contention that building new mines offers it leverage over the United States during the trade war.

“Access to critical minerals is one of the most important geopolitical cards for Canada,” said natural resources minister Tim Hodgson.

“We all watched President Zelensky get lectured about how he had no cards and how he should sign away his critical mineral supplies,” he added, referring to a tense interaction between U.S. President Donald Trump and the Ukrainian President last year at the White House. “We’re never going to let ourselves be in that position.”

But there is tension inherent in this strategy, no matter how well intentioned. Early stage mining projects are by definition risky. Many of the companies are trying to break into niches such as battery minerals and rare earths that are dominated by China. Moreover, Canadian taxpayers are being exposed to one of the diciest stages of the life cycle of a mining company: the gap between building a mine and first production – a multiyear transition when a lot can go wrong.

“If you compare a future graphite producer that’s never built a mine to a seasoned operator that has a lot of construction experience, you absolutely understand that you’re stepping in a name that has a lot more risk,” Mohamed Sidibé, an analyst with National Bank Financial, said of the government’s investment in Nouveau Monde Graphite.

On top of that, Canada is a “show me” story. It must prove it can compete in niche critical minerals.

“When you look at Canada and the history of investment with critical minerals, with lithium and graphite specifically, we haven’t had any key major success stories yet,” he said.

Christopher Ecclestone, principal and mining strategist at London, U.K.,-based Hallgarten & Company, believes much of the government spending on critical minerals mines is reckless. He has serious doubts about whether many of the projects receiving hundreds of millions of dollars apiece in funding will ultimately make it.

“Ottawa is picking champions but May in fact be paying for lipstick for pigs,” he said. “Will even the most generously funded actually get to production?”

Impossible to ignore is the 800-pound gorilla. Many Canadian companies receiving public support will be duking it out with China, a task that few in the West have been able to overcome. China’s domination in graphite is daunting; it accounted for approximately 82 per cent of natural graphite production globally in 2025, according to the United States Geological Survey . The Asian superpower is even stronger in processing. Last year, China refined 94 per cent of the world’s battery-grade graphite, according to the International Energy Agency.

“The question we have to ask is, are you funding an industry that ultimately is going to be profitable, and all it just needs is capital?” Mr. Ecclestone said. “Or are you funding an industry that is not going to be profitable, no matter what you do?”

Over the past seven years, another rookie operation, Toronto-based Generation Mining Ltd., has toiled to get its Marathon copper-palladium project in Northwestern Ontario into production. It’s not there yet and it hasn’t been for lack of trying.

Marathon is strategically important because Canada could emerge as a significant alternative Western supplier to South Africa and Russia in palladium, which is essential for catalytic converters in cars.

Despite the company delivering a feasibility study, successfully navigating the cumbersome Environmental Impact Assessment process and endlessly talking up the strategic importance of the project, its market value was too low to tap the private sector for the $300-million in equity needed to complete its $1.3-billion financing package.

“To go to the market and raise $300-million, when our market cap is $300-million, was quite difficult, or near impossible,” said Generation Mining CEO Jamie Levy.

Unable to raise the equity privately, Generation Mining turned to the government. Ottawa ended up coming to the table as a white knight investor. In September, CGF and CIB put up $190-million, or more than half the final funding round.

“If it wasn’t for those two parties,” said Mr. Levy, “we wouldn’t have been able to attract the other private capital to get this project financed.”

In the end, of the $1.3-billion total construction package for Marathon that was put together over the course of a few years, more than 40 per cent came from government sources.

It is these kinds of deep financial vacuums in critical minerals that Ottawa is increasingly filling in the name of geopolitical and national economic benefits.

“If you look at the ecosystem of funding in Canada, there are some gaps for valid projects that are in the interest of the country to move forward,” said Yannick Beaudoin, CEO of Canada Growth Fund Investment Management, a subsidiary of Crown corporation PSP Investments.

“For the private investors to be comfortable, they need to see an anchor investor in there, and that’s the role we’re playing for now.”

The success of the strategy will be largely based on Ottawa’s track record in picking winners but some of its early bets have already experienced setbacks.

Government funding agencies don’t dispute that what they are doing is risky. In fact, Ottawa is leaning into risk. Earlier this year, stressing the need for Canada to be a reliable supplier of critical minerals, EDC in a statement said it was taking on more risk, including financing earlier stage mining projects such as Torngat Metals Ltd.

Privately held Torngat plans to do something that nobody has ever done before in Canada: mine and process the heavy rare earths dysprosium and terbium on a commercial scale. The Montreal-based company plans to sell rare earth oxides to magnet makers in Germany and Japan. G7 countries are keen to diversify their supply chain away from China, which dominates the market globally for dysprosium and terbium. Over the past few years, China has restricted its exports of both rare earths as leverage during its trade war with the U.S.

In June, 2025, EDC and CIB provided $165-million in loans to Torngat for early development work on its project. At the time, the cost estimate, which included a mine and concentration plant in Nunavik, an access road and port in Labrador, and a separation plant in Sept-Iles, Que., was $1.6-billion .

Christine Burow, chief marketing officer with Torngat, said the cost of the project has since ballooned to $3-billion. She attributed the huge jump to inflation, and the fine tuning of costs that more detailed engineering work in a feasibility study allows. Despite the blowout, Ms. Burow said the project remains “technically and economically viable.”

The plan is to build most of the infrastructure in 2028 and 2029 and be in production in “the 2030 timeframe,” she said, about a year later than the company had earlier planned.

Like many early stage critical minerals ventures, Torngat’s Strange Lake project is a high wire act where the potential for something to go wrong is high.

“There is a big logistics challenge to what we’re doing,” she said.

When asked whether Torngat’s production setback had impacted the performance of Edc’s loan, Sven List, senior VP, Canadian Corporate Business with EDC, said he couldn’t get into specifics. But he stood by the government’s decision to invest in the first place.

“We think that there’s a lot of value in Torngat Metals that is keeping us very comfortable,” he said.

Torngat hopes to raise significantly more money from the Crown corporation. Ms. Burow said the company is working on a debt financing package with international export credit agencies, and is angling for EDC to be an anchor investor. Meanwhile, following in the footsteps of Nouveau Monde Graphite and Generation Mining, Torngat plans to tap the array of government funding avenues.

“We think we fit those programs really well,” she said.

In some ways what the federal government is doing writ large is following the example of Quebec, which has been taking big swings in the critical minerals industry for the best part of a decade. It hasn’t always gone well.

The province in 2018 sunk $130-million into Nemaska Lithium , which planned to build a lithium mine and processing plant in the province. The project encountered catastrophic cost overruns and ultimately filed for creditor protection, with Quebec losing most of its initial investment. Over the years, as Nemaska restructured under new ownership, and the project flipped between multiple owners, Quebec has invested an additional $1.1-billion into the project . While its current majority owner, Rio Tinto, has started building the processing plant in Bécancour, it hasn’t decided whether it will move forward on the Whabouchi mine.

In June, Quebec Auditor-General Christine Roy excoriated the province’s investment track record in the electric battery sector, including its bet on Nemaska, painting a picture of it blindly throwing money at early stage ventures without doing enough due diligence.

The investment strategy “didn’t have essential elements, such as objectives, timelines, targets,” and risks weren’t sufficiently considered and documented , she said.

While it’s still relatively early days in Ottawa’s investment journey into critical minerals, CGF is adamant it is doing its homework.

Cgf’s Mr. Beaudoin said it does “a ton of due diligence” on its investments before making them and there’s evidence to back that up. Nouveau Monde’s Mr. Desaulniers said CGF did nine months of work before investing, calling the government funding agency “super sophisticated.”

Over the past 18 months, CGF has announced more than $1-billion of critical minerals investments. One of its biggest success stories was its roughly $156-million equity investment into Foran Mining Corp. in 2025 . After the copper miner was acquired by Eldorado Gold Corp. earlier this year , CGF cashed out with a 1.7 times return on its investment, according to Mr. Beaudoin.

When asked about the overall performance of its critical minerals portfolio, Mr. Beaudoin conceded that there have been ups and downs. In the second quarter of this year, CGF booked a $38.9-million loss on its portfolio investments, owing in part to a decline in value of Nouveau Monde . But he stressed that Cgf’s ability to hold onto its investments in natural resources for 15 years or more allows it to potentially cash out when the timing is right.

But he also underlined that returns are not even necessarily the primary objective.

“All the Crown corporations have the same objective of additionality. When we put a dollar in, it needs to generate and catalyze more private dollars, either immediately, or over time,” he said. “For CGF, it’s probably more important than our return.”

But some feel that the government shouldn’t be in the business of trying to pick winners at all. Instead of investing in individual companies, Ottawa should focus on putting money into mining infrastructure, such as electricity grids, ports and transportation corridors, all of which could benefit lots of companies over decades, said Onno Rutten, VP, portfolio manager with Mackenzie Resources and Energy Evolution Team.

“There’s an obvious concentration geographically of world class lithium deposits in northern Quebec,” he said. “Let the government work with the First Nations and build out, ideally, a rail extension to the north. Otherwise everything has to be trucked, which really weighs on the economics.”

Expanding the power grid in British Columbia, he said, would not only benefit new copper projects, it could also facilitate the creation of a smelting industry. Currently much of the copper mined in the province is sent to Asia for processing.

It just needs love and attention and the government to pull everyone together and say, ‘one common smelter for 10 mines.’”

Toronto-based Canada Nickel Co. Inc., is one of the next in line. It has already lined up more than $1.5-billion in tentative funding and tax credits from Ottawa. Its Crawford project in Northeastern Ontario is expected to be the biggest nickel mine in the Western world if it gets built.

Canada Nickel CEO Mark Selby says that while the necessity of significant public funding for early stage miners isn’t ideal, it’s an absolutely crucial step for Canada to fight back against Chinese domination.

Indeed, there are some signs that is already happening.

Cgf’s Mr. Beaudoin said that earlier this year it was looking at funding several unnamed companies, but private sector financiers showed up.

“We stepped back,” he said. “This is the objective. For us to not be needed.”

Historically in Canada, if a gold or copper exploration stage company found a promising deposit, and proved it could be mined at a profit, often it would be acquired by a “senior” miner. But that age-old dynamic isn’t an option for many of the current crop of Canadian juniors because they’re forging into specialized markets that investors aren’t convinced will succeed.

Something that would reduce the risk considerably for fledgling Canadian graphite and lithium companies would be allowing partnerships with China, said Mr. Desaulniers. That’s because the Asian superpower has the engineering and technical prowess and a track record of success that stretches back decades.

Such collaborations would have been out of the question a few years ago. But with the thawing of relations between China and Canada under Mr. Carney across many business sectors, working with a former foe isn’t something we should rule out, said Mr. Desaulniers.

paragraphs: Last spring, Prime Minister Mark Carney attended a groundbreaking for a graphite mine in Quebec. As Mr. Carney and Nouveau Monde Graphite Inc. chief executive Eric Desaulniers crunched along the gravelly construction site about 120 kilometres north of Montreal, the skies grew dark. Then as Mr. Desaulniers started his prepared remarks at a makeshift lectern, heavy rain started falling, eventually soaking everyone in attendance .

“Literally the only 15 minutes when it rained during the day,” said Mr. Desaulniers. Like many mining CEOs, he’s wired as an optimist. He didn’t view the gloomy weather as a bad omen for the project, the opposite in fact.
“When it’s raining on your wedding day, it should be a very happy marriage,” Mr. Desaulniers said.

This particular wedding could not have happened without the help of the federal and provincial governments. The Matawinie mine was referred to Mr. Carney’s Major Projects Office last year, which identified select natural resource developments for regulatory fast-tracking. More importantly though, the public sector provided a huge chunk of the money to build it.

Of the company’s total US$633-million mine funding package , the company raised about 75 per cent from government sources. That included debt investments worth roughly $459-million from Export Development Canada (EDC) and the Canada Infrastructure Bank (CIB) , and a US$143-million equity raise from Canada Growth Fund Inc. (CGF) and Investissement Québec.

If all goes to plan, when it is up and running, Matawinie will be the biggest operation of its kind in the G7, producing 106,000 tonnes of graphite concentrate a year. The critical mineral is an essential element in lithium ion batteries, fuel cells and industrial lubricants.

Building a mine of this scale would be nerve-wracking even for an experienced operator. But Nouveau Monde has never built a mine before. What’s more, graphite mines are relatively untested in the West with the economic case for large scale operations mostly unproven.

The massive government bet on Nouveau Monde is by no means a one-off. Over the past year and a half, the Carney government has ramped up its support for niche critical minerals operations, with dozens of financings, stockpiling arrangements and price floors involving some of the biggest names in mining, such as Rio Tinto PLC , and Teck Resources Ltd. , as well as “juniors” – much smaller development-stage companies – such as Mangrove Lithium , and Cyclic Materials .

The private sector has been skittish about funding new critical minerals mines in Canada in large part because of the risk. Traditionally, if a junior couldn’t raise money privately, it generally meant the investment case wasn’t there, and the project didn’t move forward. But that dynamic is being upended by the billions of dollars the government is offering to newbies allowing them to get over the hump, in the name of national interest. Ottawa hopes the support will be temporary, with an expectation that institutional investors, specialized mining funds, private equity and senior mining companies will take over once these new markets are established. But there is no guarantee that will happen, and there is also the possibility that some of the big swings could be financially disastrous.

Public support of critical minerals companies of this breadth and scale would have been unthinkable five years ago. But the world has changed irrevocably during that time with security of minerals supply front and centre. Canada is trying to wean itself from reliance on China and emerge as a viable alternative supplier of critical minerals to its G7 partners. But perhaps even more pressing is Ottawa’s contention that building new mines offers it leverage over the United States during the trade war.
“Access to critical minerals is one of the most important geopolitical cards for Canada,” said natural resources minister Tim Hodgson.

“We all watched President Zelensky get lectured about how he had no cards and how he should sign away his critical mineral supplies,” he added, referring to a tense interaction between U.S. President Donald Trump and the Ukrainian President last year at the White House. “We’re never going to let ourselves be in that position.”

But there is tension inherent in this strategy, no matter how well intentioned. Early stage mining projects are by definition risky. Many of the companies are trying to break into niches such as battery minerals and rare earths that are dominated by China. Moreover, Canadian taxpayers are being exposed to one of the diciest stages of the life cycle of a mining company: the gap between building a mine and first production – a multiyear transition when a lot can go wrong.

“If you compare a future graphite producer that’s never built a mine to a seasoned operator that has a lot of construction experience, you absolutely understand that you’re stepping in a name that has a lot more risk,” Mohamed Sidibé, an analyst with National Bank Financial, said of the government’s investment in Nouveau Monde Graphite.
On top of that, Canada is a “show me” story. It must prove it can compete in niche critical minerals.
“When you look at Canada and the history of investment with critical minerals, with lithium and graphite specifically, we haven’t had any key major success stories yet,” he said.

Christopher Ecclestone, principal and mining strategist at London, U.K.,-based Hallgarten & Company, believes much of the government spending on critical minerals mines is reckless. He has serious doubts about whether many of the projects receiving hundreds of millions of dollars apiece in funding will ultimately make it.
“Ottawa is picking champions but May in fact be paying for lipstick for pigs,” he said. “Will even the most generously funded actually get to production?”

Impossible to ignore is the 800-pound gorilla. Many Canadian companies receiving public support will be duking it out with China, a task that few in the West have been able to overcome. China’s domination in graphite is daunting; it accounted for approximately 82 per cent of natural graphite production globally in 2025, according to the United States Geological Survey . The Asian superpower is even stronger in processing. Last year, China refined 94 per cent of the world’s battery-grade graphite, according to the International Energy Agency.

“The question we have to ask is, are you funding an industry that ultimately is going to be profitable, and all it just needs is capital?” Mr. Ecclestone said. “Or are you funding an industry that is not going to be profitable, no matter what you do?”

Over the past seven years, another rookie operation, Toronto-based Generation Mining Ltd., has toiled to get its Marathon copper-palladium project in Northwestern Ontario into production. It’s not there yet and it hasn’t been for lack of trying.

Marathon is strategically important because Canada could emerge as a significant alternative Western supplier to South Africa and Russia in palladium, which is essential for catalytic converters in cars.

Despite the company delivering a feasibility study, successfully navigating the cumbersome Environmental Impact Assessment process and endlessly talking up the strategic importance of the project, its market value was too low to tap the private sector for the $300-million in equity needed to complete its $1.3-billion financing package.
“To go to the market and raise $300-million, when our market cap is $300-million, was quite difficult, or near impossible,” said Generation Mining CEO Jamie Levy.

Unable to raise the equity privately, Generation Mining turned to the government. Ottawa ended up coming to the table as a white knight investor. In September, CGF and CIB put up $190-million, or more than half the final funding round.
“If it wasn’t for those two parties,” said Mr. Levy, “we wouldn’t have been able to attract the other private capital to get this project financed.”
In the end, of the $1.3-billion total construction package for Marathon that was put together over the course of a few years, more than 40 per cent came from government sources.
It is these kinds of deep financial vacuums in critical minerals that Ottawa is increasingly filling in the name of geopolitical and national economic benefits.

“If you look at the ecosystem of funding in Canada, there are some gaps for valid projects that are in the interest of the country to move forward,” said Yannick Beaudoin, CEO of Canada Growth Fund Investment Management, a subsidiary of Crown corporation PSP Investments.
“For the private investors to be comfortable, they need to see an anchor investor in there, and that’s the role we’re playing for now.”
The success of the strategy will be largely based on Ottawa’s track record in picking winners but some of its early bets have already experienced setbacks.

Government funding agencies don’t dispute that what they are doing is risky. In fact, Ottawa is leaning into risk. Earlier this year, stressing the need for Canada to be a reliable supplier of critical minerals, EDC in a statement said it was taking on more risk, including financing earlier stage mining projects such as Torngat Metals Ltd.

Privately held Torngat plans to do something that nobody has ever done before in Canada: mine and process the heavy rare earths dysprosium and terbium on a commercial scale. The Montreal-based company plans to sell rare earth oxides to magnet makers in Germany and Japan. G7 countries are keen to diversify their supply chain away from China, which dominates the market globally for dysprosium and terbium. Over the past few years, China has restricted its exports of both rare earths as leverage during its trade war with the U.S.

In June, 2025, EDC and CIB provided $165-million in loans to Torngat for early development work on its project. At the time, the cost estimate, which included a mine and concentration plant in Nunavik, an access road and port in Labrador, and a separation plant in Sept-Iles, Que., was $1.6-billion .

Christine Burow, chief marketing officer with Torngat, said the cost of the project has since ballooned to $3-billion. She attributed the huge jump to inflation, and the fine tuning of costs that more detailed engineering work in a feasibility study allows. Despite the blowout, Ms. Burow said the project remains “technically and economically viable.”
The plan is to build most of the infrastructure in 2028 and 2029 and be in production in “the 2030 timeframe,” she said, about a year later than the company had earlier planned.
Like many early stage critical minerals ventures, Torngat’s Strange Lake project is a high wire act where the potential for something to go wrong is high.
“There is a big logistics challenge to what we’re doing,” she said.

“We think that there’s a lot of value in Torngat Metals that is keeping us very comfortable,” he said.

Torngat hopes to raise significantly more money from the Crown corporation. Ms. Burow said the company is working on a debt financing package with international export credit agencies, and is angling for EDC to be an anchor investor. Meanwhile, following in the footsteps of Nouveau Monde Graphite and Generation Mining, Torngat plans to tap the array of government funding avenues.
“We think we fit those programs really well,” she said.

In some ways what the federal government is doing writ large is following the example of Quebec, which has been taking big swings in the critical minerals industry for the best part of a decade. It hasn’t always gone well.

The province in 2018 sunk $130-million into Nemaska Lithium , which planned to build a lithium mine and processing plant in the province. The project encountered catastrophic cost overruns and ultimately filed for creditor protection, with Quebec losing most of its initial investment. Over the years, as Nemaska restructured under new ownership, and the project flipped between multiple owners, Quebec has invested an additional $1.1-billion into the project . While its current majority owner, Rio Tinto, has started building the processing plant in Bécancour, it hasn’t decided whether it will move forward on the Whabouchi mine.

In June, Quebec Auditor-General Christine Roy excoriated the province’s investment track record in the electric battery sector, including its bet on Nemaska, painting a picture of it blindly throwing money at early stage ventures without doing enough due diligence.
The investment strategy “didn’t have essential elements, such as objectives, timelines, targets,” and risks weren’t sufficiently considered and documented , she said.
While it’s still relatively early days in Ottawa’s investment journey into critical minerals, CGF is adamant it is doing its homework.

Cgf’s Mr. Beaudoin said it does “a ton of due diligence” on its investments before making them and there’s evidence to back that up. Nouveau Monde’s Mr. Desaulniers said CGF did nine months of work before investing, calling the government funding agency “super sophisticated.”

But he stressed that Cgf’s ability to hold onto its investments in natural resources for 15 years or more allows it to potentially cash out when the timing is right.
But he also underlined that returns are not even necessarily the primary objective.

“All the Crown corporations have the same objective of additionality. When we put a dollar in, it needs to generate and catalyze more private dollars, either immediately, or over time,” he said. “For CGF, it’s probably more important than our return.”
