stories.title: Seventy years later, the Hungarian Revolution still has lessons to teach us
stories.summary: The year 1956 reminds us that courage can overcome fear, that solidarity can give strength to those who stand against oppression, that freedom cannot be taken for granted
stories.author: Miklós Lengyel
stories.content:
Miklós Lengyel is the Hungarian Ambassador to Canada.

In his newly adopted and beloved Canada, the exiled poet György Faludy would write of 1956 as a luminous guiding star – a fierce, internal light he prayed would shine long after he was gone.

Seventy years ago this month, Hungarians rose against Soviet occupation and communist repression, demanding political freedom, national sovereignty and the right to determine their own future. Thousands lost their lives, tens of thousands were subsequently arrested, and roughly 200,000 people – more than 2 per cent of Hungary’s population at the time – fled the country.

For Hungarians, the anniversary is profoundly a moment of remembrance. But it should not be remembered only through grief. The year 1956 was also an extraordinary moment of moral clarity: a time when the lies of an oppressive system were suddenly laid bare and ordinary people concluded that silence was no longer possible. Questions of right and wrong, oppression and freedom, could no longer be avoided.

This is why Oct. 23 still matters today. It is not simply a date on which we look backward. It is a moment of reckoning – a powerful call to ask whether the freedom inherited from those who made sacrifices for it is properly safeguarded, and whether we remain worthy of the heroes’ legacy. We must remember Hungarians who stood alone before the guns of Soviet tanks – left to face an empire, because the danger of a wider global confrontation was too immense.

Yet 1956 is not merely Hungarian history. Our Revolution marked one of the first ruptures in the Iron Curtain, and the crucible of the Revolution connected us more closely to the wider world.

The wave of enthusiasm, compassion, and acts of generosity proved that so many stood with the Hungarian cause. In remembering 1956, we celebrate not only Hungarian courage but also the generosity of those who chose to stand with our people.

The fierce purity of 1956 echoed in the Olympic pools of Melbourne, just weeks after Soviet troops launched their final, brutal assault to crush the “freedom fight.”

The Revolution became “an inextinguishable star,” demonstrating that an uprising can be crushed and still change history, and that the desire for freedom can outlast prisons, executions, exile and enforced silence. The foundations of freedom in Central and Eastern Europe, finally achieved around 1989, had been laid decades earlier in the streets of Budapest, and by the struggles of other Central and Eastern European nations who refused to accept that authoritarian rule was permanent.

The story of the Hungarian Revolution lived on – carried by those who were forced to flee the country to escape the brutal reprisals. It also became part of Canada’s history. In 1956 and 1957, Canada welcomed more than 37,500 Hungarian refugees. Their influx was later recognized by the federal government for its national historic significance, because Canada’s response fundamentally reshaped its approach to immigration and refugee policy.

Canada’s response extended far beyond providing refuge and remarkably exemplified the emerging solidarity. Governments, universities, employers, churches and various other communities helped newcomers turn the blessing of safety into a meaningful new beginning. As one of the brightest examples, the University of British Columbia received more than 200 students and professors from the forestry faculty in Sopron, who brought centuries-old European knowledge, establishing and revolutionizing sustainable forestry across Canada.

Seventy years later, this example continues to shine. Long-term commitment from both the newcomers and the hosts ensured that the journey from admission to integration have borne fruit for all.

The deeper legacy of 1956 is very much alive. Freedom, tolerance and democracy are not gifts automatically bestowed on society. There are times when people risk their lives for them, and there are freedoms that we must fight for every day. The pure manifestation of the love of freedom in 1956 continues to inspire and connect us Hungarians and Canadians. That connection remains strikingly visible in Canada today.

On Oct. 6, the Senate adopted a motion introduced by senator Charles Adler – himself a Hungarian-born refugee who came to Canada in 1957 – officially recognizing Oct. 23 as Hungarian Heritage Day in Canada and encouraging the Government of Canada and public institutions to recognize the day as such every year.

This initiative truly reflects something greater than commemoration: It testifies that the experience of the Hungarian Revolution has become part of Canada’s own national story.

Ultimately, 1956 reminds us that courage can overcome fear, that solidarity can give strength to those who stand against oppression, that freedom cannot be taken for granted, and that it is not negotiable.

That is why the anniversary belongs not only to the past. It asks something of the present.

stories.title: 'No merit' to U.S. claims Canada is interfering ahead of midterms: Carney
stories.summary: Istanbul - Prime Minister Mark Carney says there is "no merit" to American claims that Canadians might be interfering in U.S. politics ahead of November's midterm elections.
stories.author: Craig Lord The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Istanbul - Prime Minister Mark Carney says there is “no merit” to American claims that Canadians might be interfering in U.S. politics ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Officials in the Trump administration, including U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, have claimed Canadian politicians are interfering in the democratic process south of the border.

Hoekstra said earlier this month that the administration is watching Canadian politicians closely ahead of the midterms and warned them to keep their “nose out” of American politics.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says there is "no merit" to U.S. claims Canada might be interfering in American politics ahead of the midterms. He says during a trip to Turkey that Canadian diplomats are always warned to be careful of even the perception of interference. (Oct. 23, 2026)

The U.S. embassy in Canada on Wednesday released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claimed indicate “plans to influence American politics.”

The quotes, cited by the embassy as “fact” without any context, include Industry Minister Mélanie Joly’s comments about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states, which addressed Canada’s response to American-imposed tariffs.

Some of the claims on the list date back to March 2025, when President Donald Trump’s first wave of tariffs on steel and aluminum came into effect.

Another claim relates to the anti-tariff ad which the government of Ontario aired a year ago.

Carney and other Canadian officials have repeatedly dismissed claims of political interference.

“There is no merit to these claims,” Carney told reporters Friday in Istanbul. “I’m disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions.”

Canadian diplomats were told in a memo issued by Global Affairs Canada on Tuesday not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections during a period of “heightened sensitivity.”

Carney suggested in his comments to media that Canada had already given such a directive in order to avoid “unsubstantiated allegations.”

“Our Global Affairs group, well in advance of these fact sheets and allegations, has been reminding everybody, be careful who you are even seen with physically in the same place,” he said.

“We have a very deep diplomatic presence in the United States. We have lots of interaction with American companies, citizens, individuals, stakeholders more broadly. We’re very, very careful to not be seen to interfere.”

Political tensions between Ottawa and Washington ramped up after efforts to secure a deal on tariffs and other trade irritants fell apart at the eleventh hour in August. Canada and the United States have since levied new waves of tariffs on billions of dollars worth of goods crossing the border.

The prime minister said Friday that Canada is continuing to engage with the Trump administration on trade.

He said that while Canada is ready to return to the bargaining table when the United States is willing to negotiate in good faith, he isn’t in a rush to strike a deal.

“If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that,” Carney said.

Asked whether he thought an agreement was possible before the U.S. midterms, Carney said, “It’s up to the United States.”

“They’re a little difficult to predict.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

stories.title: ‘No merit’ to U.S. claims that Canada is interfering ahead of midterms: Carney
stories.summary: Istanbul — Prime Minister Mark Carney says there is "no merit" to American claims that Canadians might be interfering in U.S. politics ahead of November's midterm elections.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Istanbul — Prime Minister Mark Carney says there is “no merit” to American claims that Canadians might be interfering in U.S. politics ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Officials in the Trump administration, including U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, have claimed Canadian politicians are interfering in the democratic process south of the border.

Hoekstra said earlier this month that the administration is watching Canadian politicians closely ahead of the midterms and warned them to keep their “nose out” of American politics.

The U.S. embassy in Canada on Wednesday released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claimed indicate “plans to influence American politics.”

The quotes, cited by the embassy as “fact” without any context, include Industry Minister Mélanie Joly’s comments about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states, which addressed Canada’s response to American-imposed tariffs.

Some of the claims on the list date back to March 2025, when President Donald Trump’s first wave of tariffs on steel and aluminum came into effect.

Another claim relates to the anti-tariff ad which the government of Ontario aired a year ago.

Carney and other Canadian officials have repeatedly dismissed claims of political interference.

“There is no merit to these claims,” Carney told reporters Friday in Istanbul. “I’m disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions.”

Canadian diplomats were told in a memo issued by Global Affairs Canada on Tuesday not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections during a period of “heightened sensitivity.”

Carney suggested in his comments to media that Canada had already given such a directive in order to avoid “unsubstantiated allegations.”

“Our Global Affairs group, well in advance of these fact sheets and allegations, has been reminding everybody, be careful who you are even seen with physically in the same place,” he said.

“We have a very deep diplomatic presence in the United States. We have lots of interaction with American companies, citizens, individuals, stakeholders more broadly. We’re very, very careful to not be seen to interfere.”

Political tensions between Ottawa and Washington ramped up after efforts to secure a deal on tariffs and other trade irritants fell apart at the eleventh hour in August. Canada and the United States have since levied new waves of tariffs on billions of dollars worth of goods crossing the border.

The prime minister said Friday that Canada is continuing to engage with the Trump administration on trade.

He said that while Canada is ready to return to the bargaining table when the United States is willing to negotiate in good faith, he isn’t in a rush to strike a deal.

“If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that,” Carney said.

Asked whether he thought an agreement was possible before the U.S. midterms, Carney said, “It’s up to the United States.”

“They’re a little difficult to predict.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Stolen tips from Crime Stoppers raise fears for witnesses, informants
stories.summary: A cybersecurity breach involving a platform used by Crime Stoppers exposed nearly 180,000 tips and 15,000 associated names, leading to several police departments suspending or restricting use of the platform.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Anonymous tips have helped police investigate crimes for decades. But a cybersecurity breach involving a platform used by Crime Stoppers has raised a troubling question for people who came forward expecting their identities to remain protected: what happens when that trust is compromised?

Toronto Crime Stoppers suspended its tip-taking services after learning that nearly 180,000 tips submitted between January 2022 and November 2025 were included in data stolen from P3, a third-party platform operated by Navigate360.

The breach, which was discovered in March, also involved nearly 15,000 names associated with the affected Toronto tips. It remains unclear whether those names belong to people who submitted information, individuals identified in the tips or both.

The consequences could extend beyond Toronto. Halton Regional Police Service has confirmed that some data related to Halton was included in the breach, while Durham Regional Police Service is reviewing the incident and has removed references directing the public to Crime Stoppers from its public-facing channels.

For former Toronto police officer and security specialist Ross McLean, the exposure threatens more than the security of a database. It could undermine a vital way for people to help investigators without putting themselves at risk.

Why anonymity matters

Crime Stoppers provides a way for people to share information about suspected criminal activity without identifying themselves. That distinction can be crucial for witnesses who fear retaliation, people who know someone involved in a crime or individuals who are uncomfortable approaching police directly.

The breach is particularly concerning because information submitted through the program can involve serious criminal investigations, McLean said in an interview with CTV New Channel on Thursday.

“It’s really quite serious ... this is another thing that we’re seeing, much like Project South when information went the wrong way from the police to the bad guys,” he said.

The full contents of the stolen Toronto tips have not been provided to the charity, leaving it unable to determine exactly what information was exposed or assess the risks to individual tipsters.

Although Crime Stoppers does not ask people submitting tips to provide their names, some May include identifying details when explaining what they witnessed. Toronto Crime Stoppers said its practice is to remove such details before information is forwarded to investigators. The breach, however, involved some original submissions that could contain identifying information.

McLean said the anonymity offered by Crime Stoppers serves a purpose that conventional police reporting channels cannot always replicate.

“They (police) have to record where they got it (info) from…they can’t necessarily protect your anonymity,” he said.

What police services are doing

Toronto Crime Stoppers announced Oct. 21 that it had stopped accepting tips through its website, telephone service and app while it works on a safer alternative.

The charity said it had been seeking answers from Navigate360 for months, including information about which tips were affected and what personal details May have been exposed. It said it was told in April that Toronto’s data had not been taken, before being informed in June that the breach had affected its records.

Toronto police have also suspended their use of the Crime Stoppers tip line while reviewing the additional safeguards and security measures that will be implemented.

In Halton, police confirmed that some data related to the region was affected and said they had suspended their use of Crime Stoppers while awaiting further information about the breach’s scope and impact.

The Halton Regional Police Service emphasized that Crime Stoppers operates independently and that its tip-management platform is not connected to the service’s internal systems. It said it is investigating and assessing potential effects on police operations.

Durham police have taken a separate precautionary step, removing public-facing references directing people to Crime Stoppers while assessing the newly available information.

The Durham Regional Police Service (Drps) is aware of new information regarding the cybersecurity incident involving P3, a third-party platform used by Crime Stoppers programs to receive and manage anonymous tips. Drps works with Durham Regional Crime Stoppers in support of… pic.twitter.com/DTtyfiR1cH — Durham Regional Police (@Drps) October 22, 2026

The Durham Regional Police Service said the incident did not involve a confirmed intrusion into its internal information systems.

Both Halton and Durham police have encouraged people with information about crime or public safety concerns to contact them directly through existing reporting channels.

However, those routes do not offer the same anonymity associated with Crime Stoppers.

What should affected tipsters do?

Toronto Crime Stoppers said it will never initiate contact to ask someone for a tip number, password or other information. Anyone who receives such a request should be suspicious.

The charity has urged people not to submit new tips through its website, telephone service or app until further notice. Anyone facing immediate danger should call 911, while non-emergency reports can be made directly to Toronto police.

For people worried that their information May have been exposed, the biggest challenge is the uncertainty. Without access to the text of the stolen tips, Toronto Crime Stoppers said it cannot establish what individual submissions contained or determine the precise risks.

McLean said people affected May need to consider protective steps, depending on the nature of the information involved.

“It’s going to be the normal things you have to look at if someone hacked your banking information,” he said, referring to measures such as changing an email address and reviewing other long-standing personal information.

Those steps May not address every risk, particularly where a tip involved a serious criminal case or someone who could face retaliation if identified.

A setback for crime prevention

The immediate concern is the safety of people whose information May have been exposed. The longer-term challenge is whether the public will continue to trust anonymous reporting systems.

McLean said the loss of a reliable tip line could make it harder for police to receive information from people who do not have personal connections within law enforcement.

He also pointed to the value of anonymous tips for journalists investigating major stories, noting that reporters use secure communications methods to help protect their sources.

“Something that we really need today, probably more than ever, is a good solid tip line where people can be safe,” he said.

Toronto Crime Stoppers said it has been working with law enforcement and technology partners on a safer way to receive tips and will not resume collecting them until it has a system it considers secure.

stories.title: Air Canada will cancel these four U.S. routes starting next summer
stories.summary: Starting next summer, Air Canada will discontinue four routes to U.S. destinations.
stories.author: Joe Van Wonderen
stories.content:
Air Canada confirmed its plans to cancel four routes to U.S. destinations.

In an email shared with CTVNews.CA Thursday, the airline said that starting next summer, it will no longer fly between:

Vancouver-Nashville, Tenn.

Vancouver-Raleigh-Durham, N.C.

Toronto-Charleston, S.C.

Montreal-Seattle, Wash.

“Air Canada regularly reviews its schedule to ensure capacity is aligned with customer demand and travel patterns,” Air Canada spokesperson Sean Davidson said in an email.

The news comes as travel between Canada and the United States has plunged in recent years. Despite a steady increase in cross-border travel over the summer , Canadian-resident return trips from the U.S. in July were 25.6 per cent below their July 2024 level .

U.S. residents flew to Canada 701,800 times in August, according to StatCan .

Davidson added that Air Canada will continue to fly to Nashville, Raleigh-Durham and Seattle from other Canadian airports, but did not say anything about ongoing service to Charleston.

Expanding service to the U.S.

Those routes include Denver to Ottawa and Quebec City, seasonal service to St. John’s from Newark and expanded service between Washington, D.C. and Quebec City, along with further expansion to service between Denver and Winnipeg.

stories.title: David Eby’s B.C. election gamble
stories.summary: The BC NDP leader called a snap election in order to get a stronger mandate but now he’s neck and neck with the BC Conservatives
stories.author: The Decibel Staff, Menaka Raman-Wilms, Mike Hager
stories.content:
On Saturday, B.C. voters head to the polls in a snap provincial election . BC NDP Leader David Eby ’s rationale for the election, held two years ahead of schedule, was to get a stronger mandate amidst a trade war. His critics called it a gamble that could threaten Eby’s government. Now, the BC Conservative party is neck in neck with the NDP and a new, young challenger could come out of the election holding the balance of power.

Mike Hager , Globe reporter in Vancouver, has been covering the election campaign. He’ll take us through the controversial election call, why the Conservatives have made a comeback in the polls and what the biggest voting issues are on the ballot.

stories.title: Carney not worried about closer Turkish ties amid nation's treatment of Lgbtq+ groups
stories.summary: Istanbul - Prime Minister Mark Carney says he's not overly concerned about Canada seeking closer ties with Turkey amid criticism that the country has infringed on Lgbtq+ rights.
stories.author: Craig Lord The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Istanbul - Prime Minister Mark Carney is defending Canada’s decision to seek closer ties with Turkey as the country is accused of infringing on Lgbtq+ rights.

Carney is in Turkey for a three-day trip to strike a new strategic partnership for deeper economic and social ties with the Nato ally.

A joint statement released Thursday with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan stated Canada and Turkey have shared values, including “human rights, individual liberties, democracy and the rule of law.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney says seeking deeper bilateral ties with Turkey does not mean Canada endorses a perceived crackdown on Lgbtq+ rights in the nation. He says Canada does calibrate the "degree of engagement" based on whether a country shares its values. (Oct. 23, 2026)

In recent months, Turkish authorities have targeted multiple Lgbtq+ groups and individuals — detaining dozens of activists, breaking into association offices and raiding popular hangouts.

Last month, Canada opted against joining Germany, France and others in condemning Turkey’s campaign against Lgbtq+ organizations.

Canada signed an Oct. 7 statement from the Equal Rights Coalition denouncing the persecution of Lgbtq+ groups and the global rise in discriminatory rhetoric. That statement did not mention Turkey by name.

Carney told reporters in Istanbul on Friday that Canada’s first priority is to protect and promote human rights at home.

“Part of the way we discharge that is to be a truly sovereign nation. Part of the way we become a truly sovereign nation and reinforce our sovereignty is to have a broad range of partnerships around the world,” he said.

Global Affairs Canada’s page on travel risks in Turkey notes the arrests of Lgbtq+ protesters. It states that while the country does not criminalize homosexuality, Canadians May face “discrimination, harassment and violence based on their sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics.”

When asked what message Canadians should take from his government’s new partnership with Turkey, Carney said “engagement is not approval.” He also said the degree of engagement can depend on the other country’s values.

Carney has pursued deeper ties with other nations accused of human rights abuses over the past year, including Saudi Arabia and China. He argued Friday that being in the room with countries that don’t share Canada’s values is better than being outside.

“Because we’re engaged, we are able to raise directly with the senior authorities in these countries how we view the world and what our expectations are,” Carney said.

The prime minister said Canada raised human rights concerns during bilateral meetings with Turkish officials but would not say whether he spoke to Erdogan directly about the issue. His office says Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand raised human rights in meetings with her counterpart on Thursday.

Carney said his conversations with world leaders work best when they are “direct and open” but not reported broadly in the media.

When asked whether he thought he was legitimizing Erdogan’s actions by engaging with him, Carney said he did not.

Before Carney travelled to Turkey, experts noted his approach to international diplomacy and social values differs sharply from that of his predecessor Justin Trudeau.

“I just don’t think the Carney government wants to make that a priority in the way that, perhaps, the Trudeau government was a little more willing to see foreign policy as a tool for moralizing their preferred social values,” said Bessma Momani, political science professor at the University of Waterloo.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Carney not worried about Turkish ties despite nation’s treatment of Lgbtq+ groups
stories.summary: Istanbul — Prime Minister Mark Carney is defending Canada's decision to seek closer ties with Turkey as the country is accused of infringing on Lgbtq+ rights.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
ISTANBUL — Prime Minister Mark Carney is defending Canada’s decision to seek closer ties with Turkey as the country is accused of infringing on LGBTQ+ rights.

Carney is in Turkey for a three-day trip to strike a new strategic partnership for deeper economic and social ties with the NATO ally.

A joint statement released Thursday with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan stated Canada and Turkey have shared values, including “human rights, individual liberties, democracy and the rule of law.”

In recent months, Turkish authorities have targeted multiple LGBTQ+ groups and individuals — detaining dozens of activists, breaking into association offices and raiding popular hangouts.

Last month, Canada opted against joining Germany, France and others in condemning Turkey’s campaign against LGBTQ+ organizations.

Canada signed an Oct. 7 statement from the Equal Rights Coalition denouncing the persecution of LGBTQ+ groups and the global rise in discriminatory rhetoric. That statement did not mention Turkey by name.

Carney told reporters in Istanbul on Friday that Canada’s first priority is to protect and promote human rights at home.

“Part of the way we discharge that is to be a truly sovereign nation. Part of the way we become a truly sovereign nation and reinforce our sovereignty is to have a broad range of partnerships around the world,” he said.

Global Affairs Canada’s page on travel risks in Turkey notes the arrests of LGBTQ+ protesters. It states that while the country does not criminalize homosexuality, Canadians may face “discrimination, harassment and violence based on their sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics.”

When asked what message Canadians should take from his government’s new partnership with Turkey, Carney said “engagement is not approval.” He also said the degree of engagement can depend on the other country’s values.

Carney has pursued deeper ties with other nations accused of human rights abuses over the past year, including Saudi Arabia and China. He argued Friday that being in the room with countries that don’t share Canada’s values is better than being outside.

“Because we’re engaged, we are able to raise directly with the senior authorities in these countries how we view the world and what our expectations are,” Carney said.

The prime minister said Canada raised human rights concerns during bilateral meetings with Turkish officials but would not say whether he spoke to Erdogan directly about the issue. His office says Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand raised human rights in meetings with her counterpart on Thursday.

Carney said his conversations with world leaders work best when they are “direct and open” but not reported broadly in the media.

When asked whether he thought he was legitimizing Erdogan’s actions by engaging with him, Carney said he did not.

Before Carney travelled to Turkey, experts noted his approach to international diplomacy and social values differs sharply from that of his predecessor Justin Trudeau.

“I just don’t think the Carney government wants to make that a priority in the way that, perhaps, the Trudeau government was a little more willing to see foreign policy as a tool for moralizing their preferred social values,” said Bessma Momani, political science professor at the University of Waterloo.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ballots cast on election day in B.C. will be counted by hand, Elections BC says
stories.summary: Vancouver - It's the last full day of campaigning in British Columbia's election ahead of final voting day Saturday, when most ballots will be counted by hand.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Saturday’s election in British Columbia will be determined by the large group of people who are still undecided and sitting at home, NDP Leader David Eby said as he wrapped up the final day of campaigning.

“I’m glad you are helping the NDP,” Eby said to a group of people in Surrey where the New Democrats need to win.

Eby said there’s a history in B.C. of elections being decided on election day itself.

“For those undecided voters, for people who are considering voting Green, I’m asking for their support,” he said.

Opinion polls have shown Eby’s NDP trailing after he set off the snap election as the BC Conservatives were embroiled in leadership troubles.

He expressed some regret on Friday about the way he handled the early stages of the campaign, acknowledging British Columbians’ were “surprised and frustrated” by his decision to go to the polls two years early.

He said at the time that the election was necessary to respond to the threat posed by U.S. President Donald Trump, but he said he now wishes he had been clearer about his rationale.

“I would say my biggest regret of the last 32 days is I was ahead of British Columbians, where their understanding was about the legislature, when I called the election,” he said.

He said he “should have done a better job of letting them know how stalled out the legislature was,” referring to his party’s one-seat majority that he described as one of the most frustrating experiences of his life.

Eby paired his last-minute appeal for votes with appearances at a campaign office in Surrey, where he delivered doughnuts, and stops in Coquitlam and Langley, where he met with candidates and volunteers.

He told a group at the Surrey stop that B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson is a cover for extremists in his party who could oust him if he is elected premier.

British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby says Doerkson's party is filled with the most extreme views that the province has ever seen and it is not clear whether Doerkson will be the leader post-election. Eby says he understands people's frustration with the election call, but hopes and expects to be premier with the support of voters. (Oct. 23, 2026)

“You May think you know what you are getting, but Mr. Doerkson is a Trojan horse filled with the most extreme views that British Columbians have ever seen running for office,” Eby said Friday.

“And we don’t even know that he will be the leader postelection,” he said referring to Doerkson’s status as interim party leader.

The B.C. Conservative Party has said it will do what it takes to retain Doerkson as leader if he becomes premier, although it has not explained how it will overcome the party’s constitution that says an interim leader cannot run for the permanent leadership.

Doerkson campaigned in his rival’s home riding of Vancouver-Point Grey on Friday.

His appearance in Eby’s riding was intended to be a photo opportunity only, but he took questions from The Canadian Press, rejecting Eby’s “Trojan horse” characterization as “absurd.”

Interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson says he is committed to being premier if elected. Doerkson called NDP leader David Eby's characterization of him as a Conservative Trojan horse "absurd" during a campaign stop in Eby's riding of Vancouver-Point Grey. (Oct. 23, 2026)

“David Eby should go knock on doors, because the people I’m talking to here (indicate) he should have some concerns in his own riding,” he said.

Doerkson said he was committed to leading his party and to being premier if elected on Saturday.

New Democrats have seized on the leadership uncertainty, saying that both Caroline Elliott, who finished second in the Conservative leadership race, and federal Conservative MP Aaron Gunn, are building up support for the leadership race to replace Doerkson.

Elliott and Gunn have since issued statements of support for Doerkson, but Eby didn’t accept the claims.

“I do think it’s telling that there are Conservatives that need to deny that they are seeking leadership at the upcoming leadership race, because there will be a leadership race, and the outcome is not certain about who will be premier if the Conservatives are elected.”

The closing stages of the election campaign have been dominated by the focus on Surrey, where Doerkson rallied on Thursday night alongside former premier Christy Clark and Surrey mayor-elect Doug McCallum.

McCallum told the crowd that they had changed Surrey — which has 10 provincial ridings — and it was time to change B.C.

Eby has repeatedly said the composition of the legislature prevented him from taking big legislative swings, which he felt were needed.

“It’s a very unusual moment, I will say, in B.C. politics, but I’m asking British Columbians for their support for that positive vision about where our province can go delivering for them and their families,” he said.

The legislature at dissolution consisted of 47 New Democrats, 29 Conservatives, two Greens, and 13 Independents, with two vacant seats.

But that information from the clerk’s office does not reflect the fact that in the days before dissolution, most of the nominal Independents said they were returning to the Conservative fold, after former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay stepped down and Doerkson took over.

Taking that into account, the Conservatives went into the election holding about 37 seats.

The Independents also included former Conservatives Jordan Kealy and Hon Chan, who exited the party after it was revealed they were facing criminal charges, as well as OneBC’s Dallas Brodie and CentreBC’s Elenore Sturko.

Doerkson became interim leader on Sept. 20, just two days before Eby called the election.

Elections BC said it will be hand counting most of the ballots cast in the election.

While the votes were counted electronically in 2024, Elections BC spokesperson Colleen Hildebrandt said on Friday that they will be using a hybrid model this time because there wasn’t time to train people to use the tabulators and each machine has technical requirements.

In past elections that have been hand counted, results started being reported about 45 minutes after the polls closed, while in the 2024 election, 59 per cent of preliminary results were reported within half an hour.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

stories.title: To make sense of the shifting narrative in 'Yaga,' the actors made a murder wall
stories.summary: Toronto - Before they started filming, the stars of Crave's new supernatural crime show "Yaga" brought an onscreen trope behind the scenes to help them keep track of the story's many moving pieces: a so-called "murder wall."
stories.author: Nicole Thompson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Before they started filming, the stars of Crave’s new supernatural crime show “Yaga” brought an onscreen trope behind the scenes to help them keep track of the story’s many moving pieces: a so-called “murder wall.”

Clark Backo, who plays a straitlaced cop on the show, said she and Noah Reid went over to showrunner Kat Sandler’s apartment, where they broke down each of the show’s eight episodes and taped dozens of recipe cards to the wall to note which characters knew what, when, and what their motivations were.

“What’s a romantic moment? What’s a comedy moment? What’s important?” Backo recalled laying out on the cards. “Because (Sandler) is also melding every single genre under the sun, so there’s also making sure that we’re finding flow in that.”

Crave's buzzy new series "Yaga" is a fast-paced supernatural mystery, and its stars say it was filmed in a super condensed timeline, which led to numerous challenges. Still, Carrie-Anne Moss, Noah Reid and Clark Backo said they had a lot of fun filming the show, which also stars Hudson Williams. (Oct. 23, 2026)

The series is a mystery based on Sandler’s stage play of the same name, which is itself loosely based on the Slavic folklore character of Baba Yaga. In myth, Baba Yaga is a crone who lives in a hut that walks around on chicken feet; she flies around in a mortar and pestle and eats children.

The show centres on the disappearance of the heir to a commercial fishery, played by “Heated Rivalry” star Hudson Williams. Backo plays the police officer assigned to his case, while Reid plays a private investigator hired by the missing man’s family.

Their investigation leads them to an enigmatic university professor portrayed by Carrie-Anne Moss — an older woman rumoured to regularly seduce younger men.

The relationships between the characters aren’t always clear, and Backo said she’d occasionally refer back to a photo of the “murder wall” to make sure she kept everything straight in her head.

“There were a few moments where that really did help, but I think just the process of doing it was the most helpful: just us getting together and going through the script and marking it out.”

It was necessary in part because of the packed schedule, which Backo said gave the cast roughly an hour to film each scene — far less than what’s standard.

“Eight episodes in 32 days,” Backo said. “Which is, for people who don’t know, it’s basically two indie films in a month. And we had a lot of fun despite that.”

Reid said he and Backo would practise their lines for the next scene they were scheduled to shoot in between takes.

stories.title: Advocates flag contributions, not costs, of newcomers in Alberta referendum aftermath
stories.summary: Calgary - A union representative for a beef processing plant south of Calgary is warning of worsening labour shortages if immigration policy proposals that narrowly passed in Alberta's referendum are enacted.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - A union representative for a beef processing plant south of Calgary is warning of worsening labour shortages if immigration policy proposals that narrowly passed in Alberta’s referendum are enacted.

“These are tough and high turnover jobs with few candidates lining up to fill them,” said Faduma Ahmed, with the United Food and Commercial Workers Local 401 at Cargill’s abattoir in High River, Alta.

With 98 per cent of polls reporting in Monday’s referendum, a slim majority of votes were cast in favour of limiting access to or charging a fee for provincially funded services based on immigration status. Premier Danielle Smith’s government had argued that the cost to provide health care and education to temporary Alberta residents amounts to $1 billion a year and that a surge in newcomers has strained affordability and services.

But critics have warned that the referendum’s outcome could make Alberta less attractive to newcomers at a time when jobs desperately need to be filled.

At the Cargill plant, temporary foreign workers, refugees, permanent residents and citizens from all over the globe work side by side and all pay taxes, said Ahmed. It’s back-breaking work, with staffers often having to hoist whole carcasses.

“When we sit down to eat, we rarely think about the intense and the gruelling labour it takes to get the food onto our tables, right on our plate,” she said, adding that workers have come to her concerned about their ability to pay for health care and school for their children.

“They are foundational to keeping our economy moving, and they are navigating the exact same punishing affordability crisis as every other Albertan.”

Ahmed said the union will draw a “hard line” if the proposals become law.

“We will fight to ensure immigrant workers receive the same services they do today, up to and including making the employers pay at the bargaining table to fund the differences.”

Another sector that relies heavily on immigration is health care for seniors.

“Often we’ll find they’ll work in roles that maybe some Canadians May not be interested in,” said Leah Lechelt, executive director of the Christian Health Association of Alberta, which represents non-profits that employ 22,000 staff across the province.

She said some college programs for health-care aides have closed or reduced their enrolment simply because there haven’t been enough applications domestically.

The workforce hails from around the world, and are mostly health-care aides, but also cleaning and food-service staff, Lechelt said. They deal with vulnerable patients, so regulations largely limit those jobs to permanent residents and citizens.

“It’s really a very attractive role for somebody who is fairly new to Canada and sometimes is working on some English language proficiency skills.”

The association has established an apprenticeship program that enables those in entry-level jobs, like housekeeping, to train on-site to become health-care aides and pursue a better-paying career path.

“And then we can backfill those positions with other newcomers, maybe starting out in their journey in Canada.”

One of the referendum proposals asked whether Albertans would support the province taking more control of immigration from the federal government.

It was an idea the Business Council of Alberta has long advocated, said president Adam Legge.

“There’s a bit of a better on-the-ground intel perspective compared to a centralized decision in Ottawa,” he said.

“Oftentimes there are some skills and geographic mismatches between what Ottawa approves on an immigration basis and what is needed.”

For instance, he said there’s a huge demand for workers in the skilled trades, like heavy-duty mechanics, welders and electricians.

He said he heard from members generally that they don’t want to see anything deter people from choosing to live in Alberta.

Research by University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe commissioned by the Calgary Chamber of Commerce found immigrants paid an estimated $4.1 billion in Alberta personal income taxes in 2026.

It also found immigrants younger than 40 had a net fiscal contribution of almost $1 billion, after the cost of provincial family programs, workers’ compensation and social assistance are accounted for.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Carney's second budget will aim to help small businesses cut costs and invest more, sources say
stories.summary: The government is considering lowering the small-business tax rate and reducing the EI premium rate on smaller operations.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney’s second budget is expected to include measures for Canada’s small businesses that will aim to both trim costs and encourage investment, government sources say.

After announcing its productivity mega-deduction earlier this year to lower taxes on capital investments, especially large ones, National Post has learned that the Liberal government will try to help Canada’s smaller businesses cut costs in the upcoming budget.

The government is considering measures such as lowering the small-business tax rate (9 per cent), cutting red tape on such things as tax filing, and reducing the employment insurance (EI) premium rate on smaller operations, a government source said.

And on the business investment side, considered a key metric in boosting the sector’s productivity and growth, the government is also weighing the pros and cons of various policy options. On the table are measures such as expanding and accelerating a company’s ability to use capital cost allowance (CCA) provisions to write off expenses and depreciable assets, such as equipment and buildings.

And while there is still time to insert or remove items from the budget, one source said it’s very likely that the Nov. 5 document will include items to help small businesses with both costs and investment.

“You can walk and chew gum at the same time,” the source said.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said on Wednesday that the government’s first priority in making this budget is Canadians’ cost of living. But the second, he said, is economic growth, with the accent on helping small and medium-sized businesses seize opportunities.

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business (Cfib), which represents small and medium-sized businesses across the country, warned Thursday that much of Canada’s small business sector is at risk. Nearly two-thirds (63 per cent) of small business owners plan to leave their businesses over the next decade, the organization said in a new report, but only 6 per cent of those owners have a formal succession plan in place.

Cfib has been lobbying the government to make bold changes in this budget, including a cut in the small business income tax rate to 6 per cent, from 9 per cent.

Many economists argue that the current gap between 9 per cent and the general business rate of 15 is already too much of what they consider a distortion, which encourages companies to split themselves into smaller entities and discourages growth.

The business group has also asked Ottawa to increase the small business deduction, which is the threshold for business income that qualifies for the lower tax rate, to $700,000 from $500,000.

One of the main problems in the sector, Cfib said, is that there simply aren’t enough Canadians who want to own their own business. There’s an “entrepreneurial drought” at the beginning of the cycle, the group said, and not enough buyers when a business owner wants to retire or do something else.

According to Cfib, business exits in Canada have outpaced new entries since early 2024, which is a big problem.

“A successful handover keeps a business open and brings a new generation of entrepreneurs into the economy,” Corinne Pohlmann, Cfib’s executive vice-president of advocacy, was quoted as saying in a release. “Which is why governments need to pay attention and help make it easier to buy and sell a business.”

Carney has raised the challenges of the Canadian economy’s mediocre productivity, a metric that reflects a country’s standard of living, and the lack of corporate investment. While last month’s productivity mega-deduction initiative and budget moves for small business would create extra incentives on both fronts, the government is also facing another large deficit and escalating debt.

Champagne has indicated in recent months that the government will continue to err on the side of what he calls “investments” in the economy, instead of reducing the deficit. Champagne argues that Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7 and that leaves room to spend or cut taxes or other revenue sources, although some analysts say that position isn’t necessarily something to brag about .

“I think Canadians can understand that we have a strong fiscal position and we’re investing in the things that will generate growth to the country,” he said in July.

The proposed new mega-deduction, which the government estimates will cost the treasury $36.5-billion over the next five years, could also be included in the upcoming budget. Whether it’s included or presented as separate legislation, the measure will be one of the government’s biggest swings at boosting long-term growth.

The government hopes that the deduction changes, announced last month at an international investors’ summit in Toronto, will spur investment, particularly in capital-intensive industries such as energy, mining, transportation, and technology. The changes are expected to cut Canada’s projected tax rate on new investment, a key metric for large investors, by slightly more than half, to about 6.4 per cent from 13 per cent.

A government source emphasized that the mega-deduction will also help small and medium-sized businesses, ON top of other moves the Carney government has already made: its buy-Canadian policy, removing the federal tax on gas and diesel, eliminating the federal portion of inter-provincial trade barriers, and others. But all of those policies, combined with an array of spending moves, has left Ottawa facing another massive deficit and a greater pile of red ink.

In the government’s spring update, Champagne said the 2025–26 deficit was projected to be about $66.9 billion, down from the $78.3 billion that had been projected in last fall’s budget. That drop was due largely to a fiscal windfall from higher oil prices.

While Ottawa has been amassing large piles of debt for more than half a century, the problem has grown substantially over the last few years. The federal government has now accumulated more than $1.3 trillion in total debt, almost half of which has been added over the last five years.

stories.title: Canada working closely with EU on foreign aid as U.S. pulls back, Sarai says
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canada's deepening ties with Europe could help fill some of the massive gaps left behind as the United States pulls back from foreign aid and embraces a "transactional" approach, says the secretary of state for international development.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada’s deepening ties with Europe could help fill some of the massive gaps left behind as the United States pulls back from foreign aid and embraces a “transactional” approach, says the secretary of state for international development.

“When we put all our heads together, I think the opportunities are endless,” Randeep Sarai told The Canadian Press.

He said this effort includes recent talks with the European Union on leveraging private dollars and philanthropy for aid, while maintaining some government funding for the world’s most vulnerable.

Sarai is overseeing a shift in foreign aid as the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney cuts back on global health spending and encourages more private funding in development projects.

Ottawa is cutting spending across government, seeking new trade partners and boosting the defence budget to make Canada less vulnerable to U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and threats of annexation.

The Trump administration shut down the United States Agency for International Development, Usaid, leading to what Harvard University researchers estimate to be hundreds of thousands of preventable deaths.

In April, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development reported that the U.S. in 2025 accounted for 17 per cent of spending by rich countries on foreign aid, down from 30 per cent a year prior.

U.S. spending on foreign aid dropped by 57 per cent in 2025.

Most major donor states, including Canada, have cut back on aid funding. Ottawa spends about 1.6 per cent of its budget on foreign aid.

“Taxpayer dollars are very valuable. So if we can bring in the private sector along with them, the goal is (that) eventually the private sector will invest on their own. But initially, we’ll use the taxpayer dollars to entice them,” Sarai said.

Sarai added that Europe has looked to Carney for guidance on so-called blended finance because of his experience as a United Nations official.

Carney’s UN role was to advise governments on climate finance, including ways for governments to work with the private sector and philanthropists to transition to net-zero carbon emissions.

Ireland hosted a meeting of EU development ministers earlier this month and invited Canada to attend.

Sarai said much of the discussion in Dublin was about how to leverage private capital without abandoning support for the world’s most vulnerable people.

Sarai said Canada and European countries are also working with other nations with a reputation for robust foreign aid, including Japan, Korea and Gulf nations.

He said American officials have “come back, to some degree” on aid spending by funding vaccines for children in poor countries.

“Their aid has to benefit the American economy and American people,” Sarai said.

“They have very clear guidelines on that and transactional nature of it, but that’s their direction. So I would say it’s very different from the other G7 partners, but at least we know where we’re at.”

The push for more private dollars in aid has many critics.

Co-operation Canada, a coalition of most Canadian aid groups operating abroad, said the sector supports innovative funding, with some caveats.

“If we are to use public funds to incentivize private capital, then there need to be some guardrails around … that we’re we’re using our public funds in the most efficient way possible,” said Paul Farran, the group’s advocacy director.

He said aid dollars shouldn’t be used to subsidize endeavours that the private sector wouldn’t have otherwise funded.

“Our international assistance should first and foremost be used to alleviate poverty and inequalities,” Farran said.

Sarai said Canada is not going to surrender its support for the world’s poorest to market forces.

He said that applies to Canada’s programming in the 32 nations the UN describes as the world’s least developed countries, as well as projects that focus on sexual health and reproductive rights.

He said the government has a different approach in high-growth countries, where it pursues “mutual economic prosperity” through projects that benefit Canadian companies and investors while creating jobs abroad.

“The Vietnams, Indonesias, Philippines in the world, we believe that they can now take care of those areas themselves. We don’t need to invest in those particular areas for them,” he said.

Sarai cited a new aid project in Thailand which will see Canada’s development finance institution FinDev lend cash for microloans to women in rural areas looking to launch or expand businesses.

Canada is lending roughly $85 million, which is being matched by $280 million from the Japanese bank Smbc and the Asian Development Bank.

Last month, The House finance committee, which has a majority of Liberal MPs, called on Carney last month to provide predictable and clear aid funding in the Nov. 5 budget.

Aid groups told the committee that the federal government says its supports for refugees inside Canada amount to more than 17 per cent of its total development assistance. While that’s a standard reporting practice for Western countries, the aid groups said it makes it hard to tell how much Canadian cash is actually going abroad.

The MPs on the committee argued aid spending should be “guided by poverty and fragility” and should have “increasing transparency in the international assistance envelope.”

The MPs also urged Canada to “reaffirm gender equality and women’s economic empowerment as drivers of poverty reduction and, therefore, as central priorities.” Carney caused confusion a year ago by suggesting Canada no longer has a feminist foreign policy.

Co-operation Canada supports those calls and is urging Carney to reverse cuts to global health programs.

Farran said Canada should earmark $5.5 billion annually for “core” development aid abroad, which would boost funding for things like building schools or helping women advocate for political rights.

He also said Ottawa owes the public more clarity on how it is spending foreign aid and where it’s cutting back.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Military could begin Arctic sensor installations next summer
stories.summary: Ottawa — National Defence plans to install 47 sensor stations across the North starting as early as next summer to bolster Norad’s surveillance and early warning abilities, according to recently published regulatory filings.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — National Defence plans to install 47 sensor stations across the North starting as early as next summer to bolster Norad’s surveillance and early warning abilities, according to recently published regulatory filings.

The planned installations would start in Yukon near the Alaskan border and follow along the Arctic coast across the Northwest Territories, reaching as far out as Alert, Nunavut, the most northern inhabited point in the world.

Called Project Crossbow, the plan involves using Hercules aircraft and Chinook helicopters to airlift passive sensor installations, which resemble large shipping containers that stand on metal legs.

The initial deployments could begin as soon as next summer with initial operating capability coming online in 2029, said Royal Canadian Air Force spokesperson Lt.-Cmdr. Melanie Aqiqi.

She said in an emailed statement that Crossbow is “part of a broader network of capabilities supporting northern air domain awareness.”

The container stations will run on solar and wind power, according to a series of National Defence documents filed with a Nunavut regulatory board.

Aside from some temporary deployments required to set them up and an annual maintenance cycle, the installations will remain unstaffed throughout the year.

“This defence capability (surveillance sensors) will operate within self-powered, autonomous, ruggedized power-generating container systems designed for continuous operations in austere environments and extreme Arctic conditions,” one of the documents said.

The federal government is investing billions of dollars in a broader effort to modernize Norad’s equipment.

The project was announced in 2022 by then-defence minister Anita Anand under the Northern Approaches Surveillance system, which includes the over-the-horizon radar project.

Anand said at the time the capabilities of the joint Canada-U.S. project are classified but the new network would add “another layer of detection” to Norad.

An information package submitted to the Nunavut Planning Commission said the project is of “national significance” and the “proposed sites are required for overall system network operation.”

The sites mapped out in some of the filed plans include two in Quttinirpaaq National Park on Ellesmere Island and four within a migratory bird sanctuary on Banks Island. The documents state the project is expected to have little to no impact on wildlife.

Two sensor systems are already stationed in Alert, Nunavut and Sachs Harbour, Northwest Territories, one of the documents said.

The sites were chosen so that National Defence can easily airlift the containers in just a few days — although the exact rationale for site selection remains classified.

The sensor project is expected to be complete by 2032. Once fully deployed, the project is expected to run another 20 years.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Most pregnancies after living kidney donation uncomplicated, Canadian study finds
stories.summary: New research examines pregnancy outcomes among kidney donors, providing clearer evidence to inform donation decisions. Most pregnancies after living kidney donation are uncomplicated…
stories.content:
Stories October 23, 2026

New research examines pregnancy outcomes among kidney donors, providing clearer evidence to inform donation decisions.

Most pregnancies after living kidney donation are uncomplicated, according to a new Canadian study that provides a clearer picture of pregnancy outcomes among kidney donors.

The study, published in JAMA and led by researchers at Western University and London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (LHSCRI), compared pregnancies among living kidney donors in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia with those of women in similarly good health who had not donated.

“For many potential donors, the decision isn’t just about their health today, but what life might look like years down the road,” said Dr. Amit Garg, senior author of the study and professor at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry. “We want people to have the clearest possible information about what donation could mean for them, including if they hope to have children.”

Using provincial health-care data, including data from ICES Western, researchers compared 385 pregnancies among kidney donors with 1,540 pregnancies among women who had not donated.

Most pregnancy outcomes examined were similar between the two groups. Rates of gestational diabetes, caesarean delivery, premature birth and neonatal intensive care admissions were comparable, as were rates of serious maternal complications and postpartum hemorrhage.

The researchers did identify a small increased risk of hypertensive disorders, which involve high blood pressure during pregnancy. Among kidney donors, 11.9 per cent of pregnancies involved hospitalization with gestational hypertension, preeclampsia or eclampsia, compared with 8.3 per cent among non-donors.

The study also found that babies born to kidney donors were more likely to be smaller than expected for their stage of pregnancy. Researchers say further investigation is needed to confirm this secondary finding.

The research builds on an earlier Ontario study involving 131 pregnancies after kidney donation. By expanding the scope to 385 donor pregnancies across three provinces, the team was able to provide more precise estimates of pregnancy-related risks.

Garg, a nephrologist at London Health Sciences Centre, scientist at LHSCRI and senior scientist at ICES, has counselled more than 1,000 prospective kidney donors over the past two decades.

“Understanding the magnitude of risk, and when complications are most likely to occur, gives us a much better foundation for conversations with prospective donors,” he said. “These findings can help people make informed decisions and guide their care during pregnancy.”

stories.title: Overnight Highway 401 closure for MTO interchange improvements
stories.summary: The Ministry of Transportation (MTO) continues work on the Colonel Talbot Road interchange improvements project.
stories.content:
The Ministry of Transportation (MTO) continues work on the Colonel Talbot Road interchange improvements project. Crews are working on road and underground infrastructure, paving Tempo Road, and completing landscaping as weather permits.

Colonel Talbot Road is currently closed to traffic between Tempo Road and Glanworth Drive until Friday, November 27.

Highway 401 will be fully closed in both directions overnight from Saturday, October 24, to Sunday, October 25, to accommodate bridge work. Drivers should follow posted detour signs and allow extra time for their trips.

Westbound: Exit Highway 401 at Highway 402 and follow Highway 402 to Colonel Talbot Road.

Eastbound: Exit Highway 401 at Colonel Talbot Road and follow Highway 3 to Wellington Road to return to Highway 401.

Visit Hwy 401 Colonel Talbot project website for project information, construction updates, and current traffic restrictions.

stories.title: Human trafficking investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (October 23, 2026) – A man is facing multiple charges following an investigation by members of the London Police Service (LPS) Human Trafficking Unit.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 23, 2026) – A man is facing multiple charges following an investigation by members of the London Police Service (LPS) Human Trafficking Unit.

In June 2026, police were contacted by a woman who reported being the victim of human trafficking, assaults, and exploitation dating back to 2019.

Through the investigation, police learned that the suspect had been involved in similar relationships with multiple women over several years. Investigators received information that one victim had been exploited in the sex trade, that the suspect had financially benefited from her activities, and that he had attempted to recruit additional women for the purpose of sexual exploitation. Multiple incidents of violence were also reported during the investigation.

As a result of the investigation, ON October 21, 2026, members of the LPS Human Trafficking Unit, with the assistance of the Toronto Police Service Emergency Response Team, executed search warrants in Etobicoke and Woodbridge.

The following items were seized as a result of the searches:

A quantity of Canadian currency;

Four cellular devices; and,

Multiple Percocet pills.

The suspect was located and arrested in Woodbridge.

As a result, Jesse Nigel Jones, 32, of Mississauga, has been charged with the following offences:

Three counts of assault;

Material benefit resulting from trafficking in persons;

Procuring;

Material benefit from sexual services

Fail to comply with release order

Trafficking in person comprehensive; and,

Possession of a Schedule 1 substance.

Investigators believe there May be additional victims and are releasing a photograph of the accused as part of the ongoing investigation. Anyone who May have had contact with him, or who has information relevant to this investigation, is encouraged to contact police.

The accused remains in custody and is expected to reappear in London court on October 26, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: If Brad Bradford becomes mayor, it won’t be with the help of his ward
stories.summary: In today’s First Up: the debate over a tower in Bloor West Village and Canada and Turkey forge deals.
stories.author: Edward Keenan
stories.content:
In today’s First Up:the debate over a tower in Bloor West Village and Canada and Turkey forge deals.

Oct. 23, 2026

Updated at 8:28 p.m.

Copied to clipboard

Andrew Francis Wallace Toronto Star[](http://www.thestar.com/news/morning-digest/if-brad-bradford-becomes-mayor-it-won-t-be-with-the-help-of-his-ward/article_af27aa98-e287-4923-b00b-0052ea0f49d0.html)

ByEdward Keenan Columnist

Good morning. This is the Friday, Oct. 23 edition of First Up, the Star’s daily morning digest. Sign up to get it earlier each day, in your inbox.

We’re a weekend away from election day in Toronto and municipalities across Ontario. And eight days away from Halloween. If you’re still debating who to vote for, check out our Vote Compass tool for guidance. If you’re still not sure about your Halloween costume, I’m afraid I don’t have much help for you; I’m a last-minute scrambler. More on the final stretch of the Toronto election in just a moment. (And more on Halloween next week).

But first up, here are six things to know as you go into the weekend:

Mark Carney announced a “strategic partnership” on trade and defence with Turkey as he continues looking beyond the U.S. for partners.

Toronto Police arrested three people after a string of violent robberies, and recovered $80,000 in rare Pokémon cards.

“Maple washed”: Canada’s largest employer of veterans lost a massive contract to a subsidiary of an American firm by a difference of $100,000.

The art of protest: A pile of red bikes adorned with skulls and flowers in an Etobicoke park serves as both a sculpture and a shrine.

The margin in this riding was 10 votes. After the recount, it’s three. And the Quebec Liberals refuse to concede.

Scottie Barnes surprised fans with a CN Tower hairstyle for the Raptors’ home opener — it was a surprise to him too.

Now, let’s get this show on the road.

Brad Bradford has represented Beaches—East York for two terms as a councillor, but the 40-year-old former city planner is unlikely to win most votes there, polls say. This lack of a power base in his home ward will make him exceptional in the city’s history if he wins the mayoral election Monday, as polls suggest he could. Senior politics reporter David Rider spoke with voters from all corners of Toronto to look at how Bradford has built a mayoral campaign base on the opposite side of the city from where he built his political career.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Battleground: Meanwhile, in Beaches—East York, the race to replace Bradford on city council is one of the most hotly contested in the city with big names vying for the seat.

The final debate of the mayoral campaign took place Thursday night. City hall bureau chief Ben Spurr rounds up how the closing arguments went.

A rundown mansion on the Scarborough Bluffs became famous while vacant. But something is brewing there now, and neighbours are hopeful a “horrible waste of a beautiful property” will soon end. May Warren reports.

The deadly fire at CFB Wainwright started due to military training on a grenade launcher range. It was deemed not to be a threat, military officials said.

For a while this week, it looked like the constitution was coming to get Carney, but Susan Delacourt says updated referendum numbers mean he may get to escape the bane of previous PMs.

“I know what I saw”: New allegations from Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s mother cause chaos at the inquest into her death after she fell from a balcony during a police call.

Our trading relationship with the U.S. is never going back to what it used to be, Carney’s lead negotiator says.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly issues a formal ultimatum to Stelco: Undo layoffs within 15 days or we’ll see you in court.

Here’s the best thing about my neighbourhood: we can walk to Bloor Street West and find more than one butcher shop, more than one fruit market, more than one bakery, a bunch of restaurants, florists, clothing stores, even a community theatre and a library. It’s called Bloor West Village, and it feels like a village.

As the Star reported this week, a lot of my neighbours are panicking because of a plan to level some low-rise independent storefronts and build a 15-storey tower. They worry about parking, density and height — the usual NIMBY laundry list. I’m not worried about any of those things.

But I am worried, because I suspect that when the tower goes up, the ground-level retail is not going to look like the charming, tiny, independent businesses it replaces. It’s going to look like a forbidding glass-wall dead zone on the street. Maybe there will be a big-box retailer or a bank in there. Because that’s how we do things in Toronto. Look at condoland around the SkyDome. Look at the new offices and condos along Queens Quay East.

Heck, look at King Street West at John: on the south side, the most charming theatre district restaurant strip of brick storefronts, which could be the photo in the dictionary illustrating “urban vibrancy.” Now turn 180 degrees and look at the north side, at the high-rise Lightbox office and cinema tower — a valuable cultural institution in a street-killing wrapper. The streetscape is a block-long black hole of forbidding, indistinct reflective glass.

We know what great urban high streets look like. They look like Yorkville or Queen West or Queen East or Bloor West in the Annex or Bloor West Village. Look at photos of great streets in cities around the world and you see similar qualities. But whenever we build something new, it looks like the outside of a suburban mall. It doesn’t have to be that way. Look at Manhattan, where some of the most famous streetscapes in the world are at the base of skyscrapers. Look at Paris, where the world-famous café and pâtisserie tradition is housed almost entirely at the base of six-storey mid-rise apartment blocks.

At the new Mirvish Village where Honest Ed’s used to be, they’ve tried to adapt, reserving small spaces packed tightly together in Honest Ed’s Alley for indie businesses (and preserving much of the old Markham Street). We’ll see how that works out. But our street-level track record in Toronto with new-build high-rises isn’t great. Probably because we put all our fighting energy into density and traffic concerns and don’t really pay attention to what the main street is going to look like.

What do you think? Do you think the city should find a way to demand better street-level design in new buildings? Would you be more willing to accept a high-rise apartment tower near you if it came with spaces for cool new businesses that made your neighbourhood a better place to wander and shop? Let us know in the comments section here.

JUSTIN LING:Why is Canada still following international norms the U.S. flouts?

ADAM RADWANSKI:Chrystia Freeland’s most interesting insights have more to do with Mark Carney than Justin Trudeau.

ALTHIA RAJ:Danielle Smith’s belief in Canadian unity shouldn’t be conditional on pipelines and politics.

The Terry Fox Foundation just received its largest single gift ever: $25 million to support a national network of cancer centres. The announcement came with the launch of a touching new “Powered by Terry” video you can watch here.

Fashion Do: Coach has partnered with Penguin Random House. Chanel and Miu Miu have launched book clubs. Move over, e-readers:paper books, in all their analog glory, are back.

Fashion Don’t: Nightclubs like Wiggle Room are banning smart glasses, which are able to film you completely unnoticed. “People should know if they’re being recorded.”

Unlikely candidates were the stars of Toronto’s show in the Leafs’ wild last-minute 5-4 win over the Rangers.

The Raptors’ young bench players need to stay in their lane. As Doug Smith writes, they’re fine with that.

No surprise that many of you took part in the discourse under David Rider’s story about how bike lanes are dividing Toronto, according to Vote Compass data. Some readers argue cars are the real issue:

“Cars and Ubers are the bigger problem. But also, people’s expectations are unrealistic for getting across such a big city.” — Dave

Reader Tanya said more people use public transit than bike lanes:

“It makes me crazy that we are so focused on bike lanes when so many more people rely on the TTC! Everyone I know takes TTC at least sometimes and only a couple ever bike for transportation (as opposed to fun on a weekend).” — Tanya

Today’s word of the day is “pentu,” which means “puppy” in Finnish. We learn this as we become aware of the 24/7 “Pentulive” stream that is documenting the lives of six newborn puppies in Finland. With all the high-stakes drama in the world and the city right now, it’s nice to take a moment and find something that makes you smile.

Thanks for starting your day with us. If you enjoy First Up, please share it with a friend. And let us know what you think of the changes we’ve made, and what you’d like to see. Email firstup@thestar.ca. I’ll see you back here Monday morning.

Host: Edward Keenan

Editor: Maryam Shah

Producers: Sima Shakeri, Paige Oldfield

Senior editor: Christine Loureiro

The final debate of the mayoral campaign took place Thursday night. City hall bureau chief Ben Spurr rounds up how the closing arguments went.

items: A rundown mansion on the Scarborough Bluffs became famous while vacant. But something is brewing there now, and neighbours are hopeful a “horrible waste of a beautiful property” will soon end. May Warren reports.

items: The deadly fire at CFB Wainwright started due to military training on a grenade launcher range. It was deemed not to be a threat, military officials said.
For a while this week, it looked like the constitution was coming to get Carney, but Susan Delacourt says updated referendum numbers mean he may get to escape the bane of previous PMs.

items: “I know what I saw”: New allegations from Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s mother cause chaos at the inquest into her death after she fell from a balcony during a police call.
