items: Our trading relationship with the U.S. is never going back to what it used to be, Carney’s lead negotiator says.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly issues a formal ultimatum to Stelco: Undo layoffs within 15 days or we’ll see you in court.

content_blocks.text: THE CONVERSATION
It’s the streetscape, stupid

Here’s the best thing about my neighbourhood: we can walk to Bloor Street West and find more than one butcher shop, more than one fruit market, more than one bakery, a bunch of restaurants, florists, clothing stores, even a community theatre and a library. It’s called Bloor West Village, and it feels like a village.

As the Star reported this week, a lot of my neighbours are panicking because of a plan to level some low-rise independent storefronts and build a 15-storey tower. They worry about parking, density and height — the usual NIMBY laundry list. I’m not worried about any of those things.

But I am worried, because I suspect that when the tower goes up, the ground-level retail is not going to look like the charming, tiny, independent businesses it replaces. It’s going to look like a forbidding glass-wall dead zone on the street. Maybe there will be a big-box retailer or a bank in there. Because that’s how we do things in Toronto. Look at condoland around the SkyDome. Look at the new offices and condos along Queens Quay East.

Heck, look at King Street West at John: on the south side, the most charming theatre district restaurant strip of brick storefronts, which could be the photo in the dictionary illustrating “urban vibrancy.” Now turn 180 degrees and look at the north side, at the high-rise Lightbox office and cinema tower — a valuable cultural institution in a street-killing wrapper. The streetscape is a block-long black hole of forbidding, indistinct reflective glass.

We know what great urban high streets look like. They look like Yorkville or Queen West or Queen East or Bloor West in the Annex or Bloor West Village. Look at photos of great streets in cities around the world and you see similar qualities. But whenever we build something new, it looks like the outside of a suburban mall. It doesn’t have to be that way. Look at Manhattan, where some of the most famous streetscapes in the world are at the base of skyscrapers. Look at Paris, where the world-famous café and pâtisserie tradition is housed almost entirely at the base of six-storey mid-rise apartment blocks.

At the new Mirvish Village where Honest Ed’s used to be, they’ve tried to adapt, reserving small spaces packed tightly together in Honest Ed’s Alley for indie businesses (and preserving much of the old Markham Street). We’ll see how that works out. But our street-level track record in Toronto with new-build high-rises isn’t great. Probably because we put all our fighting energy into density and traffic concerns and don’t really pay attention to what the main street is going to look like.

What do you think? Do you think the city should find a way to demand better street-level design in new buildings? Would you be more willing to accept a high-rise apartment tower near you if it came with spaces for cool new businesses that made your neighbourhood a better place to wander and shop? Let us know in the comments section here.

items: The Terry Fox Foundation just received its largest single gift ever: $25 million to support a national network of cancer centres. The announcement came with the launch of a touching new “Powered by Terry” video you can watch here.

items: Fashion Do: Coach has partnered with Penguin Random House. Chanel and Miu Miu have launched book clubs. Move over, e-readers:paper books, in all their analog glory, are back.
Fashion Don’t: Nightclubs like Wiggle Room are banning smart glasses, which are able to film you completely unnoticed. “People should know if they’re being recorded.”

content_blocks.text: Sports

items: Unlikely candidates were the stars of Toronto’s show in the Leafs’ wild last-minute 5-4 win over the Rangers.
The Raptors’ young bench players need to stay in their lane. As Doug Smith writes, they’re fine with that.

content_blocks.text: YOUR SAY

No surprise that many of you took part in the discourse under David Rider’s story about how bike lanes are dividing Toronto, according to Vote Compass data. Some readers argue cars are the real issue:
“Cars and Ubers are the bigger problem. But also, people’s expectations are unrealistic for getting across such a big city.” — Dave
Reader Tanya said more people use public transit than bike lanes:

“It makes me crazy that we are so focused on bike lanes when so many more people rely on the TTC! Everyone I know takes TTC at least sometimes and only a couple ever bike for transportation (as opposed to fun on a weekend).” — Tanya

Today’s word of the day is “pentu,” which means “puppy” in Finnish. We learn this as we become aware of the 24/7 “Pentulive” stream that is documenting the lives of six newborn puppies in Finland. With all the high-stakes drama in the world and the city right now, it’s nice to take a moment and find something that makes you smile.

Thanks for starting your day with us. If you enjoy First Up, please share it with a friend. And let us know what you think of the changes we’ve made, and what you’d like to see. Email firstup@thestar.ca. I’ll see you back here Monday morning.

stories.title: $6M Anonymous Gift Creates Canada's First National Myeloma Biobank
stories.summary: London, ON — An anonymous $6-million gift to London Health Sciences Foundation (Lhsf) will help establish Canada’s first-ever national biobank dedicated exclusively to myeloma rese
stories.content:
London, ON — An anonymous $6-million gift to London Health Sciences Foundation (Lhsf) will help establish Canada’s first-ever national biobank dedicated exclusively to myeloma research. The ‘Canadian Myeloma Research Biobank’ will be housed at London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri) and is made possible through a collaboration between Lhsf, Lhscri and the Canadian Myeloma Research Group (Cmrg).

The gift ranks among the largest donations to multiple myeloma research nationally and is the largest known gift from a Canadian philanthropist dedicated to this area.

This partnership between Lhsf and Cmrg marks a significant advancement in cancer research and will help accelerate discoveries, improve diagnostics and expand treatment options for patients not only in London but across the country.

Together, Lhsf, Cmrg and Lhscri are bringing philanthropic support, a national network of myeloma researchers and leading research infrastructure together to advance discovery and improve care. The biobank will be an ongoing collaboration between Cmrg and Lhscri, leveraging their respective expertise, research networks and infrastructure to support sample collection and enable collaborative studies that advance multiple myeloma research across Canada.

“As someone living with multiple myeloma who has successfully received treatment through an immunotherapy clinical trial in Boston, I have seen the advances being made in treating this disease,” says the donor. “I also know the cost and frequent travel required to access these treatments can put them out of reach for many Canadians. I am proud to support this foundational effort to establish Canada’s first national multiple myeloma biobank and strengthen research here at home as we work toward a cure.”

The biobank will bring myeloma samples together in one place, using consistent methods to collect, store and analyze them. This will give researchers across Canada access to the high-quality samples they need to help advance treatment and care. With patient consent, blood, bone marrow and other biological samples will be collected and securely stored for approved research, with safeguards in place to protect patient privacy. By creating a unified national resource, the biobank will address a longstanding gap in Canada's research infrastructure and strengthen LHSC's role in myeloma research.

Multiple myeloma is an aggressive and complex blood cancer that originates in plasma cells, which are a type of white blood cell responsible for producing antibodies. Cancerous plasma cells can accumulate in the bone marrow, leading to bone damage, anemia, kidney dysfunction and a compromised immune system. An estimated 4,400 people in Canada will be diagnosed with multiple myeloma in 2026.1

While treatments including targeted therapy, chemotherapy, stem cell transplantation and immunotherapy can help control the disease, there is currently no cure, and some patients face limited options when frontline treatments stop working. Until now, myeloma samples in Canada have typically been collected for individual studies or at specific hospitals, limiting access for broader research. The biobank will make samples from across the country available through a shared national resource, supporting greater collaboration and future discoveries.

“This $6 million investment to create the Canadian Myeloma Research Biobank represents a defining moment for myeloma research in Canada,” says Engin Gul, chief executive officer of Cmrg. “It will expand access to high-quality biological samples and associated clinical data, enable deeper collaboration among researchers nationwide and accelerate the discovery of more precise and effective treatments. Most importantly, it brings renewed hope to patients and families affected by multiple myeloma and moves us closer to our ultimate goal: a cure.”

The biobank will complement Cmrg's national database, which contains disease-specific information on more than 12,000 Canadian myeloma patients. By linking biological samples with clinical data, researchers will be able to study the disease in greater depth and explore new questions about its treatment.

“Establishing this biobank at Lhscri will give researchers new opportunities to better understand multiple myeloma and how it changes over time,” says Dr. Chris McIntyre, interim vice-president of research and scientific director of Lhscri. “Studying patient samples will help researchers gain valuable insights into why some treatments work better for certain patients than others. This knowledge could lead to new discoveries and ultimately, help improve treatment and care for patients.”

The biobank, while based at Lhscri in London, Ontario, will allow researchers from across the country to study patient samples collected at different points in the course of the disease, including diagnosis, following treatment and relapse. These samples can help researchers investigate the genes and mutations associated with myeloma, how the immune system responds to the disease and how myeloma develops resistance to treatment. Samples collected today could also help answer new research questions as technology advances.

“This extraordinary gift is a powerful example of what philanthropy can make possible,” says John H. MacFarlane, president and CEO, Lhsf. “As one of the largest donations to multiple myeloma research in Canada, it demonstrates an incredible commitment to advancing research and creating new possibilities for patients facing this complex disease. We are deeply grateful for this donor's vision and generosity, and for their dedication to making an impact for patients across the country.”

Planning and implementation of the biobank are underway, with the biobank expected to become operational in 2027. Cmrg and Lhscri are establishing the infrastructure and processes needed to collect, store and share patient samples with approved researchers across Canada.

By bringing together a larger, more diverse collection of patient samples and clinical information, the biobank will support national and international research collaboration, helping researchers investigate early detection, personalized treatments and other approaches to improving patient outcomes. Access to these samples could also reduce the time needed to conduct studies and advance promising discoveries.

paragraphs: London, ON — An anonymous $6-million gift to London Health Sciences Foundation (Lhsf) will help establish Canada’s first-ever national biobank dedicated exclusively to myeloma research. The ‘Canadian Myeloma Research Biobank’ will be housed at London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri) and is made possible through a collaboration between Lhsf, Lhscri and the Canadian Myeloma Research Group (Cmrg).
The gift ranks among the largest donations to multiple myeloma research nationally and is the largest known gift from a Canadian philanthropist dedicated to this area.

This partnership between Lhsf and Cmrg marks a significant advancement in cancer research and will help accelerate discoveries, improve diagnostics and expand treatment options for patients not only in London but across the country.

Together, Lhsf, Cmrg and Lhscri are bringing philanthropic support, a national network of myeloma researchers and leading research infrastructure together to advance discovery and improve care. The biobank will be an ongoing collaboration between Cmrg and Lhscri, leveraging their respective expertise, research networks and infrastructure to support sample collection and enable collaborative studies that advance multiple myeloma research across Canada.

“As someone living with multiple myeloma who has successfully received treatment through an immunotherapy clinical trial in Boston, I have seen the advances being made in treating this disease,” says the donor. “I also know the cost and frequent travel required to access these treatments can put them out of reach for many Canadians. I am proud to support this foundational effort to establish Canada’s first national multiple myeloma biobank and strengthen research here at home as we work toward a cure.”

The biobank will bring myeloma samples together in one place, using consistent methods to collect, store and analyze them. This will give researchers across Canada access to the high-quality samples they need to help advance treatment and care. With patient consent, blood, bone marrow and other biological samples will be collected and securely stored for approved research, with safeguards in place to protect patient privacy. By creating a unified national resource, the biobank will address a longstanding gap in Canada's research infrastructure and strengthen LHSC's role in myeloma research.

Multiple myeloma is an aggressive and complex blood cancer that originates in plasma cells, which are a type of white blood cell responsible for producing antibodies. Cancerous plasma cells can accumulate in the bone marrow, leading to bone damage, anemia, kidney dysfunction and a compromised immune system. An estimated 4,400 people in Canada will be diagnosed with multiple myeloma in 2026.1

While treatments including targeted therapy, chemotherapy, stem cell transplantation and immunotherapy can help control the disease, there is currently no cure, and some patients face limited options when frontline treatments stop working. Until now, myeloma samples in Canada have typically been collected for individual studies or at specific hospitals, limiting access for broader research. The biobank will make samples from across the country available through a shared national resource, supporting greater collaboration and future discoveries.

“This $6 million investment to create the Canadian Myeloma Research Biobank represents a defining moment for myeloma research in Canada,” says Engin Gul, chief executive officer of Cmrg. “It will expand access to high-quality biological samples and associated clinical data, enable deeper collaboration among researchers nationwide and accelerate the discovery of more precise and effective treatments. Most importantly, it brings renewed hope to patients and families affected by multiple myeloma and moves us closer to our ultimate goal: a cure.”

The biobank will complement Cmrg's national database, which contains disease-specific information on more than 12,000 Canadian myeloma patients. By linking biological samples with clinical data, researchers will be able to study the disease in greater depth and explore new questions about its treatment.

“Establishing this biobank at Lhscri will give researchers new opportunities to better understand multiple myeloma and how it changes over time,” says Dr. Chris McIntyre, interim vice-president of research and scientific director of Lhscri. “Studying patient samples will help researchers gain valuable insights into why some treatments work better for certain patients than others. This knowledge could lead to new discoveries and ultimately, help improve treatment and care for patients.”

The biobank, while based at Lhscri in London, Ontario, will allow researchers from across the country to study patient samples collected at different points in the course of the disease, including diagnosis, following treatment and relapse. These samples can help researchers investigate the genes and mutations associated with myeloma, how the immune system responds to the disease and how myeloma develops resistance to treatment. Samples collected today could also help answer new research questions as technology advances.

“This extraordinary gift is a powerful example of what philanthropy can make possible,” says John H. MacFarlane, president and CEO, Lhsf. “As one of the largest donations to multiple myeloma research in Canada, it demonstrates an incredible commitment to advancing research and creating new possibilities for patients facing this complex disease. We are deeply grateful for this donor's vision and generosity, and for their dedication to making an impact for patients across the country.”

Planning and implementation of the biobank are underway, with the biobank expected to become operational in 2027. Cmrg and Lhscri are establishing the infrastructure and processes needed to collect, store and share patient samples with approved researchers across Canada.

By bringing together a larger, more diverse collection of patient samples and clinical information, the biobank will support national and international research collaboration, helping researchers investigate early detection, personalized treatments and other approaches to improving patient outcomes. Access to these samples could also reduce the time needed to conduct studies and advance promising discoveries.

Through collaboration with hospitals and research centres across Canada, the biobank will help advance myeloma research and bring new possibilities for better treatments and care to patients nationwide.

stories.title: 'Comfort kills dreams': Family says soldier killed in base fire was living his dream
stories.summary: Prince Albert - The mother of one of the four Canadian soldiers killed in a fire at a military base in Alberta says his lifelong goal was to join the Forces and wear his uniform with pride.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prince Albert - Patricia Farrell is not even a week removed from the death of her son in a military training exercise gone wrong.

She looks over an array of seven photos of Pte. Shaun Farrell. One is of him as a newborn with a mohawk. Another shows him dressed in a suit when he finished high school, smiling in front of a sports car.

“He never smiled that much, but on each photo, he’s always smiling,” his mother said Thursday.

Then she stops on one particular portrait: of her son standing before a Canadian flag wearing military fatigues.

“I see him looking at me and saying, ‘I was happy. This is what I wanted to do,’” she said.

The 23-year-old from Prince Albert, Sask., was one of four soldiers killed Saturday when a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright overtook a live-fire training exercise on a nearby grenade range.

The other soldiers killed were: Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

Military officials say the fire began in a permanent danger area, preventing base firefighters from putting it out early. The fire was being monitored when a strong and sudden wind sent flames racing toward a group of 84 soldiers from the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

The fire wounded 39. As of Thursday, 27 injured soldiers remain in various hospitals, with 13 in critical condition, officials said.

Patricia Farrell, speaking to reporters in Prince Albert, Sask., said her son enlisted last year — a lifelong goal.

“He started saying when he was probably about five years old, ‘When I grow up, I’m going to be an army man,’” she said.

The family moved to Canada from South Africa in 2017.

Living with dyslexia and Asperger’s syndrome, the family said Farrell was once told he’d never graduate high school and that he’d have a lot to overcome.

But his mother says her son — armed with a quiet but fiery tenacity — refused to let labels or low expectations define him. His personal motto, she said, was “comfort kills dreams.” He had the phrase tattooed to his side.

“He knew it wasn’t always comfortable for him as a person to achieve his dreams,” Farrell said.

“He knew that … if he was comfortable, he wasn’t going to achieve that dream, so he had to, himself, get out of his comfort zone.”

From the get-go, she said her son wanted to be in the infantry. His end goal was to join special forces, she said.

“I once was on a call with him and said to him, ‘Oh, you must only be dreaming about all the bombs and everything you’re blowing up and shooting your weapon,’” she said.

“And he said, ‘Mom, I am not dreaming about these things. I’m living my dream.’”

His mother said that over the past week, she has received beautiful messages from his fellow soldiers. And the support coming in from people in Prince Albert and across the country has been “overwhelming,” she said.

Now, the family is simply trying to process the loss.

“What goes through any parent’s mind when they lose their child, their baby?” she said.

“I’m just wondering what my future is going to be like without him in our lives and without him being around.”

A family spokesperson says funeral arrangements are being finalized and his body will be brought back to Saskatchewan by week’s end.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

— By Aaron Sousa and Daniela Germano in Edmonton

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said Shaun Farrell graduated from high school in South Africa.

stories.title: Public safety takes centre stage in closely watched Kelowna election race
stories.summary: The riding is drawing attention after the 2024 election, when Loewen narrowly defeated Wooldridge by just 40 votes.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Crime and public safety are emerging as key issues in Kelowna Centre , where candidates from the BC NDP, BC Conservatives and OneBC say addressing safety concerns is a priority ahead of the provincial election.

“Undoubtedly it comes down to making streets safer,” said NDP candidate Loyal Wooldridge.

“The number one issue is crime and safety,” said Conservative candidate Kristina Loewen.

OneBC candidate Bill Desrosiers also identified crime as a major concern. “The biggest thing for me right now is crime,” Desrosiers said.

The riding is drawing attention after the 2024 election, when Loewen narrowly defeated Wooldridge by just 40 votes.

The result made Kelowna Centre one of the closely watched battlegrounds in a region traditionally considered a Conservative stronghold.

Now, the two candidates are facing off again, with the NDP hoping to win the riding.

BC NDP Leader David Eby has made several campaign commitments in Kelowna, including expanding capacity at Kelowna General Hospital.

“Our government is committed to put $30 million into Kelowna General Hospital to build out the sixth-floor inpatient unit,” Eby said.

The NDP has also pledged to create 75 involuntary treatment beds at the Oliver correctional centre.

Wooldridge says the party has a detailed plan to fund and deliver on its commitments.

“We’re the only party that has a costed plan with these commitments that are built into how we’re going to pay for it and how we’re actually going to execute those commitments,” Wooldridge said.

Loewen, however, questions whether voters should trust the NDP to follow through on its promises.

“Why would we believe the NDP? They’ve come to Kelowna many times in the last two elections, promising many things, and they’ve failed to deliver on all of them,” Loewen said.

She pointed to the Ndp’s 2024 promise to replace the aging Cottonwoods care home, a project that was later put on hold.

While Loewen did not outline specific commitments for Kelowna Centre on addiction and mental health, she said the BC Conservatives have strategies planned to address the issues.

“We have committed to a bunch of strategies and steps around that as Conservatives, and I look forward to that being implemented,” Loewen said.

Desrosiers says improving access to detox services is an important first step in helping people struggling with addiction.

“We have to be able to get these people when they come for help because right now that window is so narrow and there is nowhere for them to go,” he said.

With crime, health care and addiction among the issues being raised on the campaign trail, voters will soon decide which candidate they believe is best positioned to address the riding’s concerns.

The outcome could once again come down to a narrow margin in a race that was decided by just 40 votes in 2024.

stories.title: B.C. online furniture retailer Cymax, once a COVID winner, is shutting down
stories.summary: Burnaby-based furniture seller lays off 135 employees, set to file for receivership
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
Cymax Group Technologies Ltd. was looking like a COVID-19 pandemic winner in 2020. The furniture e-commerce company’s monthly sales spiked to US$38-million at one point that year and it hired investment bankers to explore going public . The British Columbia company was shaping up to be a second big catch for majority shareholder Markus Frind, who’d sold his online-dating business Plenty of Fish Media Inc. to Match Group for US$575-million five years earlier.

Now Cymax is no more, a victim of changing market dynamics. The initial public offering never happened, and last week Mr. Frind, who took over as chief executive officer in 2024, decided to shut the company instead of personally funding further losses, resulting in a loss of 135 jobs. Cymax is preparing to file for receivership.

“This was one investment that went sideways,” said Mr. Frind, whose investments include an Okanagan winery and a stake in online recreational-vehicle rental marketplace RVEzy. “We tried to correct it but couldn’t.”

Burnaby-based Cymax was primarily a middleman for furniture and home-furnishing vendors to sell goods on sites of giants including Amazon.com and Walmart.com, but also operated its own websites for vendors to sell and ship their wares. The company, founded in 2004 by Iranian immigrant Arash Fasahi, operated an online freight logistics platform that matched sellers to shippers as well.

Mr. Frind initially invested $18-million in Cymax in 2015 alongside the Business Development Bank of Canada and Salman Partners, and gained majority ownership later that decade.

But sales sagged as online buying patterns normalized after the peak of the pandemic, and competitors from Asia – some of whom supplied its North American-based customers – began undercutting them by selling directly into the U.S. and Canadian markets.

Cymax had staffed up under previous CEO Rizwan Somji to meet the heightened pandemic demand, and the company lost money as sales fell. Mr. Somji left in December, 2023, and Mr. Frind stepped in three months later , figuring he could apply his knowledge of product, marketing, programming and artificial intelligence to slash costs and make the company more efficient. “There’s just so much opportunity everywhere and it’s just a matter of capitalizing on that,” Mr. Frind said at the time.

But two things were out of Cymax’s control. Mr. Frind said rising advertising costs and changes to payment terms enacted by Amazon ate into the company’s already thin margins. And domestic furniture companies were hurt by the impacts of U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs , which favoured Asian importers that some accused of unfairly dumping products into the market at low prices.

Several furniture makers that sold through Cymax faltered, including Canadian companies eSolutions Furniture Group (owner of the Bush and Bestar brands), South Shore Furniture and Prepac Manufacturing, which all shuttered last spring. Cymax revenues fell steeply, to US$10-million a month. Despite earlier cost-cutting efforts, Cymax was still losing hundreds of thousands of dollars a month by fall.

A source familiar with Cymax said the company also could have benefited from tighter operational discipline. The Globe and Mail is not naming the source as they are not authorized to discuss the matter.

Cymax also had to repay or refinance a US$6.5-million BDC loan this December. Mr. Frind figured it would cost at least C$20-million to retire the loan and fund the operating losses necessary to get the freight logistics business into stronger shape.

“We looked at that math, at the decline in advertising effectiveness, the fact that all these companies were going out of business, and you draw a trend line,” he said. “It made zero financial sense to carry on. There was no path to recovery.”

After investing tens of millions of dollars into the business already, he thought he could just as easily buy another company for the same amount it would cost to save Cymax, Mr. Frind said.

Asked what he’d learned from his experience at Cymax, Mr. Frind said, “When I stepped into this business I looked at it more as a lottery ticket. I thought, ‘Can I course correct this quickly and then get out?’”

In hindsight, he said: “Don’t try and catch a falling knife. You just end up getting cut.”

stories.title: Canada updates travel advisory for Saudi Arabia amid ongoing attacks
stories.summary: Canadians are being warned against travelling to Saudi Arabia amid ongoing attacks on the country’s capital airport.
stories.author: Joe Van Wonderen
stories.content:
Canadians are being warned against travelling to Saudi Arabia amid ongoing attacks on the country’s capital airport.

“Avoid all travel to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and to King Fahd International Airport in Dammam due to ongoing military activity,” Global Affairs Canada said in its travel advisory updated Thursday .

“Missile and drone attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia have affected operations and caused flight disruptions at several airports.”

King Khalid International Airport is currently closed and further attacks could close the Saudi airspace, Global Affairs added.

“Prepare contingency plans that don’t rely on the government of Canada’s assistance for departure,” the advisory said.

Global Affairs also warned Canadians to “avoid all travel” to the Saudi Arabian provinces of Asir, Jazan and Najran, as well as all areas within 30 kilometres of the border with Yemen.

Houthi militants attacked the airport while raging a larger war against Saudi Arabia using missiles, drones, and conventional weapons.

Office staff in Riyadh have been told to work from home as a safety precaution while the Houthis fight against the kingdom.

The Houthis, also known as Ansarallah, were labelled a terrorist entity by Ottawa in 2024.

Canada is advising travellers to follow local authorities’ instructions, be ready to shelter in place and monitor the local and international situation.

“Filming, taking photos and online sharing of images of military installations, activity or damage could lead to severe penalties pursuant to the enforcement of local laws and regulations across the region,” the notice warned.

The U.S. mission to Saudi Arabia issued a similar travel warning as Ottawa.

“Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” according to a Wednesday security alert.

“The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”

stories.title: Mixed results on Alberta referendum questions highlight urban-rural divide
stories.summary: Outcome could pose political risks for Premier Danielle Smith as she campaigns toward next year’s provincial election
stories.author: Matthew Scace, Chen Wang
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith won’t be armed with a strong mandate to challenge the federal government for more powers after her proposals on immigration and constitutional issues were either defeated or received slim majorities in Monday’s referendum.

The results also underline a stark divide between rural and urban voters on her proposals, which could pose political risks for the Premier as she campaigns toward next year’s provincial election.

“Certain areas of Calgary and Edmonton supported some [proposals], and certain areas did not,” Ms. Smith told reporters on Wednesday.

“So, I take that as, ‘Let’s proceed with caution.’ ”

Elections Alberta continued to hand-count ballots on Thursday, surpassing its 48-hour deadline to tally the votes.

The count nevertheless continued as the agency worked toward the finish line of the largest electoral event in Alberta history, with 20 million ballots counted and 99 per cent of voting areas accounted for by Thursday afternoon. There are no consequences written into Alberta law for failing to meet the deadline.

Unofficial results showed that the four referendum questions centred around Alberta taking greater control over immigration were set to earn narrow majorities by Thursday night, ranging between 52 and 55-per-cent support. Meanwhile, four proposals focused on pushing for constitutional amendments, such as judicial appointments and abolishing the federal Senate, sat below 50 per cent.

Finally, one proposal, to make proof-of-citizenship mandatory at provincial election polls, was receiving 58-per-cent support – the top performer among the nine.

The results leave Ms. Smith without the mandate she explicitly sought from Albertans in the run-up to the referendum, spending $4-million in public money encouraging them to vote Yes on the nine questions.

Over the past month, Ms. Smith has pointed to the proposals as the best way to extract concessions from Ottawa, contrasting separatists who argued that a future secession vote would provide ultimate leverage.

Andrew Coyne: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is targeting immigration. But what do the numbers say?

On Monday night, Albertans rejected the prospect of separation, with roughly 75 per cent of voters preferring to remain in Canada rather than hold a second, binding secession vote.

Ms. Smith, claiming victory on the immigration proposals, said in the referendum’s immediate aftermath that she would continue her push to give Alberta more autonomy and defend the province’s jurisdiction.

But she hedged the next day when asked how she would proceed on immigration.

Two of those questions propose charging health and education premiums to some non-permanent residents and limiting their access to social services.

“I take that as a general indication that [voters] want us to work with the federal government on getting this balance right,” Ms. Smith said. Prime Minister Mark Carney showed openness this week to working with provinces on the issue.

Geography was a significant factor in voters’ choice in the referendum. On the separation question, 41 per cent of rural voters endorsed holding a second, binding vote on leaving Canada, whereas Edmonton and Calgary polled 15 and 18 per cent, respectively.

A similar dynamic played out on the other nine questions.

In Edmonton, a majority of voters rejected all nine proposals. In Calgary, a majority of electors voted against the nine questions except for the citizenship proposal.

In midsize cities such as Red Deer, Lethbridge and Medicine Hat, a majority of voters endorsed seven of the nine questions as of Thursday evening. Two proposals – one on judicial appointments and the other on federal funding – were hovering around 49-per-cent support in midsize cities.

In rural Alberta, meanwhile, support for all nine questions surpassed 60-per-cent support.

Varying appetites for the government’s proposals will be a consideration for Ms. Smith’s United Conservative Party heading into next October’s general election, which she described on Wednesday as “the only fight that matters.”

Much of that fight will be waged in Calgary. In the 2023 provincial election, the NDP swept Edmonton while Calgary almost evenly split support for the New Democrats and UCP. The UCP won the rest of the province, with the exception of two seats.

Matt Solberg, a political adviser who sat on Ms. Smith’s transition team when she became Premier in 2022, said many of the Calgary ridings up for grabs in the next provincial election rejected the immigration proposals.

“There is a deep level of electoral math that you can do on these to say, ‘well, this message May resonate in rural Alberta, but it’s not going to resonate in these other ridings,’ ” said Mr. Solberg, partner at New West Public Affairs.

Mr. Solberg suggested that the most logical avenue for Ms. Smith will be to strike a deal on immigration with Mr. Carney.

Saskatchewan and Newfoundland joined Alberta’s push for more immigration powers this week. Quebec and Ottawa have shared a unique agreement since 1991, allowing the province to exclusively control the selection of incoming economic migrants, which Ms. Smith has frequently pointed to as her desired immigration model.

Melissa Caouette, principal at MC Consulting and former special assistant to Alberta premier Jim Prentice, suggested working with Ottawa toward a similar agreement and potentially punting the other immigration questions.

She added that an agreement with Ottawa May address some of the concerns sitting with voters who endorsed the slate of immigration proposals.

stories.title: Canada advises no travel to major Saudi Arabia airports amid ongoing attacks
stories.summary: Canadians are being warned against travelling to Saudi Arabia amid ongoing attacks on the country’s capital airport.
stories.author: Joe Van Wonderen
stories.content:
Canadians are being warned against travelling to Saudi Arabia amid ongoing attacks on the country’s capital airport.

“Avoid all travel to King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and to King Fahd International Airport in Dammam due to ongoing military activity,” Global Affairs Canada said in its travel advisory updated Thursday .

“Missile and drone attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia have affected operations and caused flight disruptions at several airports.”

King Khalid International Airport is currently closed and further attacks could close the Saudi airspace, Global Affairs added.

“Prepare contingency plans that don’t rely on the government of Canada’s assistance for departure,” the advisory said.

Houthi militants attacked the airport while raging a larger war against Saudi Arabia using missiles, drones, and conventional weapons.

Office staff in Riyadh have been told to work from home as a safety precaution while the Houthis fight against the kingdom.

The Houthis, also known as Ansarallah, were labelled a terrorist entity by Ottawa in 2024.

Canada is advising travellers to follow local authorities’ instructions, be ready to shelter in place and monitor the local and international situation.

“Filming, taking photos and online sharing of images of military installations, activity or damage could lead to severe penalties pursuant to the enforcement of local laws and regulations across the region,” the notice warned.

The U.S. mission to Saudi Arabia issued a similar travel warning as Ottawa.

“Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” according to a Wednesday security alert.

“The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”

stories.title: The 4 soldiers killed in fast-moving fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta
stories.summary: Wainwright - Four Armed Forces members were killed when a fast-moving fire overwhelmed soldiers during a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton, ON Saturday. Dozens of others were injured, with 27 remaining in hospital as of Thursday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WAINWRIGHT - Four Armed Forces members were killed when a fast-moving fire overwhelmed soldiers during a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton, on Saturday. Dozens of others were injured, with 27 remaining in hospital as of Thursday.

Here’s a look at the four who died:

Pte. Shaun Farrell

Farrell, a 23-year-old member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, was from Prince Albert, Sask.

He was born in South Africa and immigrated with his family as a teen.

He was diagnosed with dyslexia and Asperger’s syndrome but met life’s obstacles with resilience and determination, his family said in a statement.

“He consistently refused to let labels or low expectations define his potential.”

It was his lifelong goal to join the military and he wore his uniform with pride, they said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a tribute in the House of Commons, said Farrell was generous and loyal and known in his battalion as the grandmaster of chess.

“His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him,” Premier Scott Moe added in a statement.

Pte. Aidan Goulding

The 23-year-old of North Vancouver was also a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

His family said he was an exceptional athlete and, after high school, became a mechanic.

He later quit to join the Army.

“Although he was making excellent money and had a good life, he decided he wanted to defend his country. His goal was to work for Special OPs and then onto CSIS,” his mother, Sonia Monk, and older brother, Wylder Goulding, said in a statement.

“He was the guy that kept people’s spirits up, a contagious laugh and a cheeky smile, he took his role in the army seriously, and our family and his dear friends have suffered a great loss.”

They said he loved his adopted army family and was looking forward to peacekeeping in Latvia.

“Before he went to basic training, he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”

He went above and beyond in his service, added the prime minister.

“Pte. Goulding met every hardship with a joke, and when others struggled, he shouldered more than his share without ever being asked,” said Carney.

Pte. Hayden Lykkemark

The 19-year-old was from Langley, B.C., and served with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“Pte. Lykkemark was known for his gift for lightening a hard day, his quick wit. He dreamed of a career in law enforcement,” said Carney.

Trevor Plater, who coached Lykkemark in rugby his senior year at Langley Secondary School, said he was “always looking out for everybody.”

Plater added that all of the team and Lykkemark’s schoolmates thought of him as a best friend.

B.C. Premier David Eby recognized Lykkemark and Goulding in a social media post.

“In this moment of profound heartbreak, as British Columbians and Canadians, let’s wrap our arms around their families, supporting them and joining in the mourning of this horrible tragedy,” he said.

Sgt. Morgan Wong

The 26-year-old from Edmonton was a reservist with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“He was an incredible person who was always there whenever anyone needed him,” his family said in a statement.

“He loved being active and spending time with his friends and family. He was extremely proud to serve with the Canadian Armed Forces.”

They said he earned a bachelor of commerce degree from the University of Alberta, as well as certificates in real estate and civil-military leadership.

He joined the Forces in 2017, and for the last four years worked as a financial analyst and manager with the Alberta government. He also served as a first responder with St. John Ambulance.

He served in Latvia from October 2024 to June 2025, and was preparing for a second tour in Europe.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of Sergeant Morgan Wong of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, and all those who lost their lives yesterday at Wainwright,” the 49th Battalion Loyal Edmonton Regiment Association said in a social media post.

“Our thoughts and prayers are also with the injured, their loved ones and everyone affected by this tragedy.

“We will remember them.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

— By Dayne Patterson and Bill Graveland in Calgary, Nick Murray in Ottawa and Ian Bickis in Winnipeg
paragraphs: WAINWRIGHT - Four Armed Forces members were killed when a fast-moving fire overwhelmed soldiers during a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton, on Saturday. Dozens of others were injured, with 27 remaining in hospital as of Thursday.
Here’s a look at the four who died:
Pte. Shaun Farrell
Farrell, a 23-year-old member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, was from Prince Albert, Sask.
He was born in South Africa and immigrated with his family as a teen.
He was diagnosed with dyslexia and Asperger’s syndrome but met life’s obstacles with resilience and determination, his family said in a statement.
“He consistently refused to let labels or low expectations define his potential.”
It was his lifelong goal to join the military and he wore his uniform with pride, they said.
Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a tribute in the House of Commons, said Farrell was generous and loyal and known in his battalion as the grandmaster of chess.
“His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him,” Premier Scott Moe added in a statement.
Pte. Aidan Goulding
The 23-year-old of North Vancouver was also a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
His family said he was an exceptional athlete and, after high school, became a mechanic.
He later quit to join the Army.

“Although he was making excellent money and had a good life, he decided he wanted to defend his country. His goal was to work for Special OPs and then onto CSIS,” his mother, Sonia Monk, and older brother, Wylder Goulding, said in a statement.
“He was the guy that kept people’s spirits up, a contagious laugh and a cheeky smile, he took his role in the army seriously, and our family and his dear friends have suffered a great loss.”
They said he loved his adopted army family and was looking forward to peacekeeping in Latvia.
“Before he went to basic training, he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”
He went above and beyond in his service, added the prime minister.
“Pte. Goulding met every hardship with a joke, and when others struggled, he shouldered more than his share without ever being asked,” said Carney.
Pte. Hayden Lykkemark
The 19-year-old was from Langley, B.C., and served with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
“Pte. Lykkemark was known for his gift for lightening a hard day, his quick wit. He dreamed of a career in law enforcement,” said Carney.
Trevor Plater, who coached Lykkemark in rugby his senior year at Langley Secondary School, said he was “always looking out for everybody.”
Plater added that all of the team and Lykkemark’s schoolmates thought of him as a best friend.
B.C. Premier David Eby recognized Lykkemark and Goulding in a social media post.
“In this moment of profound heartbreak, as British Columbians and Canadians, let’s wrap our arms around their families, supporting them and joining in the mourning of this horrible tragedy,” he said.
Sgt. Morgan Wong
The 26-year-old from Edmonton was a reservist with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
“He was an incredible person who was always there whenever anyone needed him,” his family said in a statement.
“He loved being active and spending time with his friends and family. He was extremely proud to serve with the Canadian Armed Forces.”
They said he earned a bachelor of commerce degree from the University of Alberta, as well as certificates in real estate and civil-military leadership.
He joined the Forces in 2017, and for the last four years worked as a financial analyst and manager with the Alberta government. He also served as a first responder with St. John Ambulance.
He served in Latvia from October 2024 to June 2025, and was preparing for a second tour in Europe.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of Sergeant Morgan Wong of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, and all those who lost their lives yesterday at Wainwright,” the 49th Battalion Loyal Edmonton Regiment Association said in a social media post.
“Our thoughts and prayers are also with the injured, their loved ones and everyone affected by this tragedy.
“We will remember them.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.
— By Dayne Patterson and Bill Graveland in Calgary, Nick Murray in Ottawa and Ian Bickis in Winnipeg

stories.title: Ottawa boosts funding for 60 sports groups with $60-million
stories.summary: Secretary of State for Sport says money will help elite athletes compete on world stage and advance safe sport measures
stories.author: Catherine Morrison and Nick Murray
stories.content:
More than 60 national sports organizations will share $60-million in additional federal funding as the government moves to shore up a national sport system that has been described as chronically underfunded.

At a news conference in Ottawa on Thursday, Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said the money will help elite athletes compete on the world stage and advance safe sport measures.

“We’ve landed on a fantastic new era in Canadian sport. One of the reasons that I think we’re all here is because we believe that sport can connect people and communities in ways that very few other things can,” van Koeverden said, flanked by Liberal and opposition MPs and high-performance athletes.

The organizations set to receive the largest boosts in funding include Canoe Kayak Canada ($2.4-million), Canada Basketball ($2.3-million) and the Canadian Rugby Union ($2.8-million). Some of the money, like the $2.77-million for Alpine Canada, has already been announced.

The Future of Sport in Canada Commission’s final report, released in March, made 98 recommendations.

Former chief justice of the Ontario court of justice Lise Maisonneuve, who headed the commission, spoke at the time of widespread and ongoing abuse at all levels of sport, fragmented and confusing complaint mechanisms, power imbalances and chronic underfunding.

“An underfunded sports system is an unsafe sports system,” she said.

Van Koeverden said the government’s sport strategy is built on many pillars, including improving safety.

“It is not an option. There is not a boutique program for safe sport,” he said.

“Safe sport is a pillar and a necessity and a priority for every national sport organization, and I would say we’ve seen a lot of great progress so far.”

stories.title: Restaurateur Franco Prevedello gave Toronto fine dining a new flavour
stories.summary: Known for his exacting standards and work ethic, he opened more than a dozen restaurants and had an enduring influence on the city’s chefs
stories.author: Caroline Aksich
stories.content:
Before service at the Toronto restaurant Centro, two servers would stretch a piece of string to line up the tables and chairs to Franco Prevedello’s exacting standards. The tablecloths had to fall evenly on every side, the glassware and salt-and-pepper shakers positioned just so. Once guests arrived, he worked that meticulously ordered room with an irrepressible charm, teasing one regular, squeezing another’s shoulder, pulling up a chair to talk. He remembered their favourite wine and asked after the children. Making his rounds could take an hour, each table briefly the centre of his attention. “I don’t think people would always say, ‘Let’s go to Centro tonight,’” recalled Michael Bonacini, his former executive chef. “It was more, ‘Let’s go see Franco at Centro tonight.’”

Mr. Prevedello helped change what Toronto expected of a restaurant. When he entered the scene, fine dining largely spoke French; he helped make Italian dining glamorous, championing wood-burning ovens, Super Tuscans and dishes such as caviar-topped fettuccine Natasha. Over a 50-year career, he opened and operated more than a dozen restaurants, including Pronto, Splendido, Terra, Acqua, Nota Bene and Carbon Bar. His influence extended well beyond that portfolio, rippling through the city’s dining rooms as chefs and restaurateurs who had worked for him carried his standards into places of their own.

Mr. Prevedello died on Oct. 4 in Toronto at Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre. He was 80. He had been living with Parkinson’s disease, but died after a fall caused a brain bleed.

Over his prolific career, Mr. Prevedello collected plenty of titles: Godfather, Culinary Visionary, Grand Poobah of Pasta, Metro Maestro. The careers he shaped were more numerous still. Among them were those of Mr. Bonacini, Marc Thuet, David Lee, Frank Parhizgar, Chris McDonald, Yannick Bigourdan and David Castellan. Mr. Lee sees Toronto’s chefs as branches of a family tree, including those who never worked for Mr. Prevedello but learned from people who did.

“It all stems from Franco,” he said. Even Mark McEwan, who did business with Mr. Prevedello but never worked for him, learned by watching. “He was a mentor for me, unbeknownst to him,” he said. “He built some of the hippest, busiest, coolest restaurants in Toronto, and I learned by observation.”

Francesco (Franco) Giovanni Prevedello was born on Jan. 24, 1946, in Asolo, in Italy’s Veneto region, to farmers Atillio and Maria Prevedello. He viewed hospitality as a way to make a living and see something of the world. He enrolled at hotel school in Stresa in the early 1960s, then worked in European hotels and aboard a German cruise line. In 1965, he arrived in Toronto, where his older sister lived.

In August, 1967, while working as a waiter at the Ontario Pavilion at Expo 67 in Montreal, he met fellow waiter Barbara Jackson. A whirlwind courtship followed; they married that November. Stints at La Scala and Winston’s laid the groundwork for restaurants of his own. By the early 1980s, his ventures included Biffi Bistro, Bindi and Pronto, the latter of which he sold to Mr. McEwan in 1985. In 1986, he ran the Ontario Pavilion restaurant at Expo ’86 in Vancouver, showcasing Ontario food products. Jimmy Molloy, a friend and former Centro manager, saw those six months of serving large numbers without compromising quality as a rehearsal for Centro.

Before opening, Mr. Prevedello sent chefs to California for two months to study the cooking that would inform Centro’s Cal-Ital menu. When the restaurant opened in 1987, ON Yonge Street just north of Eglinton Avenue, its 240 seats were a declaration of ambition: a two-storey dining room with white pillars, a cobalt-blue ceiling and photographs of Venetian scenes. Mr. Prevedello was betting downtown money would travel north for dinner. It did. “Everybody who’s anybody wanted to get in there,” Mr. Bonacini recalled.

For all its grandeur, Centro had little interest in making guests feel intimidated. It had white tablecloths and linen napkins, but even the maître d’ worked without a jacket. Guests could pick up the wrong fork without fear of correction. “Dinner at Centro was fun,” Mr. Molloy recalled. Executives ordering expensive wine and veal chops and a young couple splitting a pizza received the same unstinting attention.

The ease guests enjoyed took relentless work. He was at Centro in the morning, darting out for meetings and returning to inspect, adjust and improve. He might be under a table making sure it didn’t wobble, have his hand down a blocked drain or be lecturing a produce supplier on the proper ripeness of tomatoes (“We can’t be serving cucumbers for tomatoes!”). In the late afternoon, he went home for dinner with his wife and their daughters and, his colleagues suspected, a nap. By evening, he was back, adjusting thermostats and inspecting the room before greeting guests with the warmth of a man who had all the time in the world.

Barbara Prevedello helped make that pace possible. She managed the books, keeping track of the business while her husband juggled its many moving parts. “She was his rock,” Mr. Bonacini said. Together, they also helped establish the food-rescue charity Second Harvest.

Her husband, meanwhile, “could never say no,” Mr. Bonacini recalled. His instinct to welcome everyone could leave Centro overbooked; Mr. Thuet remembered reservations scribbled on slips of paper that disappeared into Mr. Prevedello’s pockets, often never reaching the host. His hospitality could exceed his seating capacity, but he turned the wait into part of the fun, working the crowd outside with glasses of prosecco and slices of pizza. Inside, order chits stretched out from the pass to the back of the kitchen, arriving faster than Mr. Thuet could call them out.

Mr. Prevedello’s enthusiasm outlasted the working day. After service, he still wanted to debate the menu. No adjective was safe: should the shrimp be “bronzed” rather than “grilled”? Mr. Molloy recalled these discussions stretching into the early hours, until it was 9 a.m. in Italy and Mr. Prevedello had wine producers to call. “I always felt Franco was the guy that was never finished,” Mr. Molloy said. “There was always something to do, something that could make it better.”

For people trying to meet his standards, there was little respite. Even a good dish offered something to correct. Risotto was too wet or too dry, overcooked or undercooked. “It was still a delicious risotto, but it was never, ever perfect,” Mr. Bonacini recalled.

For Mr. Lee, the mere sight of Mr. Prevedello approaching the kitchen pass could sharpen his work. “If you were working and your performance was a seven or an eight, and Franco would walk by, all of a sudden your performance became a 10.”

His pursuit of perfection could erupt into yelling. Colleagues remembered a volcanic temper, but also a generosity that outlasted his anger. “Franco would fire you in the afternoon, rehire you the day after, and pay for your dental work in the same week,” Mr. Bigourdan said. “ In the same week .”

In 1997, Mr. Prevedello agreed to sell his half of Centro to general manager Tony Longo and executive chef Mr. Thuet for $1-million. The Toronto Star described a bitter ownership dispute. Mr. Thuet, however, recalled no animosity between them and spoke with enduring affection for a man he regarded as a father figure and credited with making own career possible.

Those who worked for Mr. Prevedello also remembered the concern beneath the bluster. Mr. Molloy recalled colleagues wondering why someone they thought deserved to be fired was back at work the next day. The explanation was simple: The person still had bills to pay. Mr. Prevedello could lose patience with an employee without losing concern for them as a person. “He was all bark; a big teddy bear who liked to make noise,” Mr. Molloy said.

When he saw people with ambition and the willingness to work for it, he helped them get ahead. “He liked to bring people along with him,” Mr. Molloy said. “It’s a remarkable talent.”

After Mr. Lee and Mr. Bigourdan bought a then 10-year-old Splendido from him in 2001, Mr. Prevedello remained their landlord, offering advice and patience when the rent was late. Later, he invited them to partner with him on Nota Bene. “When he believed in you, you felt you’d won the lottery,” Mr. Lee said. “To have him as our partner felt like a gift.”

At Nota Bene, which opened in 2008, that support came with firm opinions about design. Mr. Lee and Mr. Bigourdan balked at his choice of ipe wood floors and Italian leather chairs, but he insisted. “Yannick, trust me, the chairs are everything,” Mr. Bigourdan recalled him saying. They spent about $200,000 on 135 chairs. “They made the room.” Mr. Prevedello and Mr. Bigourdan went on to open Carbon Bar together in 2013, his final restaurant venture.

To Mr. Bigourdan, he was less a godfather than a “consigliere.” They met every Thursday for coffee. Business occupied “32 seconds,” Mr. Bigourdan recalled; the rest went to their joys, struggles, victories and defeats. Mr. Prevedello made time for others, too, whether they needed advice, an introduction or help getting an idea off the ground. paragraphs: Before service at the Toronto restaurant Centro, two servers would stretch a piece of string to line up the tables and chairs to Franco Prevedello’s exacting standards. The tablecloths had to fall evenly on every side, the glassware and salt-and-pepper shakers positioned just so. Once guests arrived, he worked that meticulously ordered room with an irrepressible charm, teasing one regular, squeezing another’s shoulder, pulling up a chair to talk. He remembered their favourite wine and asked after the children. Making his rounds could take an hour, each table briefly the centre of his attention. “I don’t think people would always say, ‘Let’s go to Centro tonight,’” recalled Michael Bonacini, his former executive chef. “It was more, ‘Let’s go see Franco at Centro tonight.’”

Mr. Prevedello helped change what Toronto expected of a restaurant. When he entered the scene, fine dining largely spoke French; he helped make Italian dining glamorous, championing wood-burning ovens, Super Tuscans and dishes such as caviar-topped fettuccine Natasha. Over a 50-year career, he opened and operated more than a dozen restaurants, including Pronto, Splendido, Terra, Acqua, Nota Bene and Carbon Bar. His influence extended well beyond that portfolio, rippling through the city’s dining rooms as chefs and restaurateurs who had worked for him carried his standards into places of their own.
Mr. Prevedello died on Oct. 4 in Toronto at Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre. He was 80. He had been living with Parkinson’s disease, but died after a fall caused a brain bleed.

Over his prolific career, Mr. Prevedello collected plenty of titles: Godfather, Culinary Visionary, Grand Poobah of Pasta, Metro Maestro. The careers he shaped were more numerous still. Among them were those of Mr. Bonacini, Marc Thuet, David Lee, Frank Parhizgar, Chris McDonald, Yannick Bigourdan and David Castellan. Mr. Lee sees Toronto’s chefs as branches of a family tree, including those who never worked for Mr. Prevedello but learned from people who did.

“It all stems from Franco,” he said. Even Mark McEwan, who did business with Mr. Prevedello but never worked for him, learned by watching. “He was a mentor for me, unbeknownst to him,” he said. “He built some of the hippest, busiest, coolest restaurants in Toronto, and I learned by observation.”

Francesco (Franco) Giovanni Prevedello was born on Jan. 24, 1946, in Asolo, in Italy’s Veneto region, to farmers Atillio and Maria Prevedello. He viewed hospitality as a way to make a living and see something of the world. He enrolled at hotel school in Stresa in the early 1960s, then worked in European hotels and aboard a German cruise line. In 1965, he arrived in Toronto, where his older sister lived.

In August, 1967, while working as a waiter at the Ontario Pavilion at Expo 67 in Montreal, he met fellow waiter Barbara Jackson. A whirlwind courtship followed; they married that November. Stints at La Scala and Winston’s laid the groundwork for restaurants of his own. By the early 1980s, his ventures included Biffi Bistro, Bindi and Pronto, the latter of which he sold to Mr. McEwan in 1985. In 1986, he ran the Ontario Pavilion restaurant at Expo ’86 in Vancouver, showcasing Ontario food products. Jimmy Molloy, a friend and former Centro manager, saw those six months of serving large numbers without compromising quality as a rehearsal for Centro.

Before opening, Mr. Prevedello sent chefs to California for two months to study the cooking that would inform Centro’s Cal-Ital menu. When the restaurant opened in 1987, ON Yonge Street just north of Eglinton Avenue, its 240 seats were a declaration of ambition: a two-storey dining room with white pillars, a cobalt-blue ceiling and photographs of Venetian scenes. Mr. Prevedello was betting downtown money would travel north for dinner. It did. “Everybody who’s anybody wanted to get in there,” Mr. Bonacini recalled.

For all its grandeur, Centro had little interest in making guests feel intimidated. It had white tablecloths and linen napkins, but even the maître d’ worked without a jacket. Guests could pick up the wrong fork without fear of correction. “Dinner at Centro was fun,” Mr. Molloy recalled. Executives ordering expensive wine and veal chops and a young couple splitting a pizza received the same unstinting attention.

The ease guests enjoyed took relentless work. He was at Centro in the morning, darting out for meetings and returning to inspect, adjust and improve. He might be under a table making sure it didn’t wobble, have his hand down a blocked drain or be lecturing a produce supplier on the proper ripeness of tomatoes (“We can’t be serving cucumbers for tomatoes!”). In the late afternoon, he went home for dinner with his wife and their daughters and, his colleagues suspected, a nap. By evening, he was back, adjusting thermostats and inspecting the room before greeting guests with the warmth of a man who had all the time in the world.

Barbara Prevedello helped make that pace possible. She managed the books, keeping track of the business while her husband juggled its many moving parts. “She was his rock,” Mr. Bonacini said. Together, they also helped establish the food-rescue charity Second Harvest.

Her husband, meanwhile, “could never say no,” Mr. Bonacini recalled. His instinct to welcome everyone could leave Centro overbooked; Mr. Thuet remembered reservations scribbled on slips of paper that disappeared into Mr. Prevedello’s pockets, often never reaching the host. His hospitality could exceed his seating capacity, but he turned the wait into part of the fun, working the crowd outside with glasses of prosecco and slices of pizza. Inside, order chits stretched out from the pass to the back of the kitchen, arriving faster than Mr. Thuet could call them out.

Mr. Prevedello’s enthusiasm outlasted the working day. After service, he still wanted to debate the menu. No adjective was safe: should the shrimp be “bronzed” rather than “grilled”? Mr. Molloy recalled these discussions stretching into the early hours, until it was 9 a.m. in Italy and Mr. Prevedello had wine producers to call. “I always felt Franco was the guy that was never finished,” Mr. Molloy said. “There was always something to do, something that could make it better.”

For people trying to meet his standards, there was little respite. Even a good dish offered something to correct. Risotto was too wet or too dry, overcooked or undercooked. “It was still a delicious risotto, but it was never, ever perfect,” Mr. Bonacini recalled.

For Mr. Lee, the mere sight of Mr. Prevedello approaching the kitchen pass could sharpen his work. “If you were working and your performance was a seven or an eight, and Franco would walk by, all of a sudden your performance became a 10.”

His pursuit of perfection could erupt into yelling. Colleagues remembered a volcanic temper, but also a generosity that outlasted his anger. “Franco would fire you in the afternoon, rehire you the day after, and pay for your dental work in the same week,” Mr. Bigourdan said. “ In the same week .”

In 1997, Mr. Prevedello agreed to sell his half of Centro to general manager Tony Longo and executive chef Mr. Thuet for $1-million. The Toronto Star described a bitter ownership dispute. Mr. Thuet, however, recalled no animosity between them and spoke with enduring affection for a man he regarded as a father figure and credited with making own career possible.

Those who worked for Mr. Prevedello also remembered the concern beneath the bluster. Mr. Molloy recalled colleagues wondering why someone they thought deserved to be fired was back at work the next day. The explanation was simple: The person still had bills to pay. Mr. Prevedello could lose patience with an employee without losing concern for them as a person. “He was all bark; a big teddy bear who liked to make noise,” Mr. Molloy said.
When he saw people with ambition and the willingness to work for it, he helped them get ahead. “He liked to bring people along with him,” Mr. Molloy said. “It’s a remarkable talent.”

After Mr. Lee and Mr. Bigourdan bought a then 10-year-old Splendido from him in 2001, Mr. Prevedello remained their landlord, offering advice and patience when the rent was late. Later, he invited them to partner with him on Nota Bene. “When he believed in you, you felt you’d won the lottery,” Mr. Lee said. “To have him as our partner felt like a gift.”

At Nota Bene, which opened in 2008, that support came with firm opinions about design. Mr. Lee and Mr. Bigourdan balked at his choice of ipe wood floors and Italian leather chairs, but he insisted. “Yannick, trust me, the chairs are everything,” Mr. Bigourdan recalled him saying. They spent about $200,000 on 135 chairs. “They made the room.” Mr. Prevedello and Mr. Bigourdan went on to open Carbon Bar together in 2013, his final restaurant venture.

To Mr. Bigourdan, he was less a godfather than a “consigliere.” They met every Thursday for coffee. Business occupied “32 seconds,” Mr. Bigourdan recalled; the rest went to their joys, struggles, victories and defeats. Mr. Prevedello made time for others, too, whether they needed advice, an introduction or help getting an idea off the ground. When Mr. Bigourdan asked why he kept giving away his time, Mr. Prevedello’s answer was simple: “I enjoy it. I enjoy giving my time away.”

He was a builder by instinct, whether helping people realize their ambition or bringing his own ideas to life. He loved materials, design and construction. In an essay reflecting on his career, Mr. Prevedello described the pleasure of creating a restaurant, from construction through service. “I enjoyed all of the phases of it — not just running the restaurant, but building,” he wrote. “I loved creating and establishing restaurants. Then I would move on to something else.” Mr. Bonacini believed that building a restaurant gave Mr. Prevedello more satisfaction than actually running one.

His ventures took him well beyond restaurants. He brought Italian fashion label Replay to Canada, imported wine and spirits and launched a prosecco made from grapes grown in his hometown of Asolo. His love of building also drew him into property development. As a principal at Diamante Development Corporation, he oversaw the construction of condominiums, including The Florian and Phoebe. In recent years, semi-retirement still meant spending a few days a week at condo developer Mirabella.

In later years, Mr. Thuet and his wife, Biana Zorich, hosted an annual dinner with Mr. Prevedello as guest of honour. When Parkinson’s disease made conversation difficult for him, he sat smiling amid the chefs’ banter. The group plans to continue gathering, keeping his place at the head of the table.
He leaves his wife and daughters, Bobbie and Kate Prevedello.

Then I would move on to something else.” Mr. Bonacini believed that building a restaurant gave Mr. Prevedello more satisfaction than actually running one.

stories.title: An ‘avalanche’ of foreign steel dumping in Canada? Stelco owner’s gripes don’t hold up to scrutiny
stories.summary: The volume of imports of coated steel from outside the U.S. have plunged in recent years
stories.author: Jason Kirby
stories.content:
The federal government and the U.S.-based owner of Stelco Holdings Inc. have been locked in a war of words since the steelmaker announced it will lay off 500 workers in Southern Ontario.

Ottawa accuses Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. of breaking an employment agreement it signed when buying Stelco in 2024, while Cliffs chief executive officer Lourenco Goncalves pins part of the blame instead on Canada.

The Canadian market isn’t large enough to absorb galvanized steel produced domestically, as well as an “avalanche of imports” Ottawa has failed to adequately reduce, he said during a call with investors earlier this week.

The problem is, trade data don’t back up the assertion that Canada is in the midst of an onslaught of foreign galvanized steel.

On a year-to-date basis, the volume of imports of coated steel from outside the U.S. have plunged more than 30 per cent since 2025 to the lowest level since at least 2019, and are down about 60 per cent over two years, an analysis of Statistics Canada import data shows.

Cleveland-Cliffs did not respond to a request for comment.

Since the Trump administration slapped steep tariffs on steel imports – including from Canada – with the strong encouragement of Cliffs and other steelmakers, the federal government has imposed steep tariff-rate quotas to deter steel dumping in Canada. Ottawa has also mandated federally funded projects prioritize the use of Canadian steel.

Several countries whose steel exporters have faced Canadian dumping investigations have seen shipments plunge since before the start of the trade wars, with year-to-date imports from Turkey down 84 per cent from 2024 and down 87 per cent from the United Arab Emirates.

It’s not just trade data that raises questions about Mr. Goncalves’s reasons for idling Stelco’s galvanized steel operations. The move has baffled its customers, with some pointing out that amid supply restrictions, galvanized steel prices have surged this year.

stories.title: Province-city relationship key point during Winnipeg mayoral debate
stories.summary: The relationship between those at the helm at City Hall and the Manitoba Legislative Building was a key theme during Wednesday's mayoral debate on 680 Cjob.
stories.author: Marney Blunt
stories.content:
The relationship between those at the helm at City Hall and the Manitoba Legislative Building was a key, and at times, heated talking point during Wednesday’s mayoral debate on 680 Cjob.

Incumbent candidate Scott Gillingham touted his current working relationship with Manitoba’s NDP premier Wab Kinew, and questioned candidate Kevin Klein’s – who was previously a cabinet minister with the Manitoba Progressive Conservatives – ability to work with the premier, citing his past newspaper columns criticizing the premier and prime minister.

Klein argued he has already gained Kinew’s trust while candidate Mike Vogiatzakis said the city needs a new mayor without political ties.

University of Manitoba political science adjunct professor Christopher Adams says the relationship between the city and province is critical.

“You can’t operate the city without a proper relationship with the premier,” Adams told Global News.

“When the mayor wants to do something like address homelessness, expand transit service, get a water treatment plant built – those things are heavily dependent on the provincial government and the federal government.”

Adams noted there have been communication breakdowns in the past, including between former mayor Brian Bowman and former premier Brian Pallister, which hinders the city’s ability to move forward on certain projects.

“Brian Bowman had a very difficult relationship with Brian Pallister, and Brian Pallister was not willing to be friendly to the mayor and didn’t have meetings with Bowman,” Adams said.

“When Heather Stefanson came in she did reach out to Bowman. One of the first things she did as premier was to meet with Brian Bowman in a cordial way.”

Former Winnipeg mayor Susan Thompson knows the importance of this relationship well. Thompson was the the helm at City Hall during Gary Filmon’s tenure as premier.

“In the end we developed, even today, the best relationship that could be had between the province, the city, and the capital region. It was really productive and it was well-intentioned,” Thompson told Global News.

But Thompson adds in today’s current political climate, the importance of fostering those relationships are more important now than ever before.

“We’re in extraordinary change in our society with our whole economic threat from the United States of America, it’s not being talked about enough at the civic level,” Thompson said.

“And we have a very unique opportunity to build extraordinary strong relationships between Winnipeg, First Nations, the capital region, and the province.

“And it won’t work if those relationships – and dare I saw partnerships – aren’t top of mind today.”
