stories.title: New $100-million auto parts manufacturer opens in Ingersoll
stories.summary: A major addition to Ingersoll’s industrial landscape. The Oxford County community on Thursday welcomed a new auto parts manufacturer.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
A major addition to Ingersoll’s industrial landscape. The Oxford County community on Thursday welcomed a new auto parts manufacturer.

ArcelorMittal Tailored Blanks will turn out 20 million parts per year from its new 154,000 sq. ft. plant on Newman Street. The facility transforms steel coils into tailored blanks, which are used in body panels of vehicles manufactured throughout North America.

“We’re one of the very few suppliers and manufacturers of this product. Really, again focused on making vehicles safer, and lighter, and more fuel efficient,” explained company President and CEO Todd Baker.

Based in Luxembourg, the company brings in steel from its plants in Calgary and Hamilton. The facility is equipped with state of the art automation, and has more than 60 employees. It represents a $100-million investment.

According to Ingersoll mayor Brian Petrie, the company considered 41 different locations between Vaughan and Windsor, before landing in Ingersoll, where development charges were waived.

“This was our town industrial land that we developed. And when we were looking for partners, we weren’t looking for a short-term gain, the most money we could get. We were truly looking for a long-term benefit for the community, and a partner for the long-term,” Petrie told a crowd of about 100 VIPs at Thursday’s official opening.

The opening follow’s Wednesday’s announcement from the provincial and federal governments of support for steel and auto industries hit by tariffs.

“It’s all about the jobs going across the border. This is a facility that is bringing the jobs here,” said Oxford MPP Ernie Hardeman, a member of Doug Ford’s PC government.

Todd Baker says construction of the plant had actually been delayed by two months because of the trade war. Ultimately, he says they decided they had to forge ahead.

“Effectively the industry has kind of gone on hold. People don’t know what’s going to be happening six months from now, nine months from now. And in that environment everyone just kind of holds off in making decisions. So it is a difficult time in the industry, but our view is we need to push forward” Baker explained.

By The Canadian Press

Vancouver police say the pair from Calgary were attacked near the Gastown neighbourhood at about 11 p.m. Wednesday as they walked from the concert.

Police say the male victim was repeatedly hit with a sharp object that may have been glass, cutting his left forearm, while the female victim was pushed into a light pole.

Officers arrested a 34-year-old man who had two outstanding warrants, and he has been charged with assault, assault causing bodily harm and assault with a weapon.

The male victim was treated at the scene by paramedics while police say the suspect is in custody awaiting a bail hearing.

The attack comes after an AC/DC fan was attacked and seriously injured after the band’s concert at BC Place on Aug. 13, when he was punched in the face from behind, causing him to fall and strike his head on the pavement.

stories.title: Devastating fire at CFB Wainwright started on automatic grenade launcher range, official says
stories.summary: Fire later spread to a different range in another part of the base and overran soldiers’ positions, Brigadier-General Vanessa Hanrahan says
stories.author: Jesse Winter
stories.content:
A wildfire that killed four Canadian Forces soldiers and injured dozens more at a military base in Wainwright, Alta., ON Saturday started on the base’s automatic grenade launcher range, Brigadier-General Vanessa Hanrahan told reporters on Thursday.

Brig.-Gen. Hanrahan is the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal, the top soldier in charge of Canada’s military police, which are conducting one of several concurrent investigations into the fire. The military is conducting its own board of inquiry, and Alberta’s Chief Medical Examiner is also investigating.

At a news conference Thursday afternoon, Brig.-Gen. Hanrahan said her investigation shows the fire started at what’s called the AGL range, as part of routine training in that area. She did not say whether live firing of explosive rounds ignited the fire.

Initially, the fire stayed within what is known as a “permanent danger area” of the range, which prevented firefighters from attacking it directly. According to Canadian Forces Base Wainwright’s range standing orders , permanent danger areas can be contaminated with unexploded munitions.

“It was therefore monitored throughout the day by both range control and the base firehall,” Brig.-Gen. Hanrahan said.

High winds from a forecast cold front later caused the fire to suddenly change direction and accelerate rapidly, Brig.-Gen. Hanrahan said. It spread to a different range in another part of the base and overran soldiers’ positions. Understanding exactly when, how and why that happened will be a key focus of the three investigations, she said.

The four soldiers killed were identified as Private Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sergeant Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

Initially, 39 injured soldiers were sent to various hospitals. As of Thursday, 27 remained in hospital, according to Major-General Wade Rutland, Commander of the Army’s 1st Canadian Division.

“We are heartened that 12 soldiers are no longer hospitalized, although they will still continue to receive follow-up care,” he said. “The soldiers remaining in hospital are in serious condition.”

Maj.-Gen. Rutland said the military’s board of inquiry will work “as long as it takes” in order to be thorough and uncover what happened.

“We will not shy away from answers, and whatever hard truths they May reveal,” he said.

General Jennie Carignan, Chief of the Defence Staff, reiterated her commitment Thursday that the board of inquiry results will be made public once it has finished.

The Department of National Defence has so far remained tight-lipped about the fire itself, citing the investigation. Maj.-Gen. Rutland told reporters earlier this week that troops had been aware of the fire burning roughly one kilometre away for several hours.

On Thursday, he said the fire was “not originally assessed as a threat.”

“Canadians and families are rightly asking how that assessment was reached, what information it was based on, and whether different decisions should have been made. Those are amongst the central questions the investigation must answer,” Maj.-Gen. Rutland said.

He said eight firefighters from the base’s fire platoon responded to the blaze, but did not say when. They were later joined by a second platoon, and by firefighters from the town and municipal district.

The wildfire risk in Wainwright on Oct. 17 was high. Data from the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System showed a measure called the Fire Weather Index, which gauges the expected intensity of a potential fire, was rated as “extreme.” Environment Canada issued warnings of high winds for Wainwright that day and data showed forest and grassland vegetation as very dry.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland, citing the investigation, would not comment on whether the scale of those risks was adequately communicated to troops on the ground.

However, internal communications obtained by The Globe and Mail told the military the “fire index,” a measure of risk, “was low” for CFB Wainwright on Saturday. The DND has not responded to The Globe’s questions about this apparent disparity, or whether the “fire index” referenced in the memo is the same as the Cwfis Fire Weather Index.

According to the base’s range standing orders, during periods when the fire hazard is rated as extreme, pyrotechnics, tracer rounds and incendiary rounds called white phosphorus are not to be used at any time unless authorized by the base commander. The document also says that between the “high-risk months” of August to October, live firing should be conducted during “early morning shoots” when “the fire hazard is normally low enough to permit the firing of most ammunition natures,” before approximately 10 a.m.

On Thursday, Maj.-Gen. Rutland characterized that as a guideline, not an order, and said officers conducting training must weigh a series of factors including weather, the type of munitions and the number of trainees before deciding whether it is safe to shoot live ammunition.

Wildfire experts told The Globe that conditions on the base, including the extreme fire weather index and forecast high winds, were unambiguously dangerous .

A similar situation in 2023 forced the chaotic evacuation of a BC Wildfire Service fire camp in the province’s Shuswap valley.

In that case, a cold front generated high winds that drove the Adams Lake wildfire more than 24 kilometres in a matter of hours. It swept down from heavily forested mountains and tore across a grassy airfield where firefighters had set up a base of operations. Some were forced to flee while their tents caught fire .

With reports from Reuters and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Charismatic NHL star Ron Duguay found fame well beyond the hockey rink
stories.summary: In addition to playing for the New York Rangers and other teams in the league for 12 seasons, he was known for partying with celebrities at Studio 54, romancing famous women and making television appearances
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Ron Duguay, who scored 274 goals in a dozen National Hockey League seasons, suited up for his home country in the 1981 Canada Cup tournament and claimed to have dated Cher and supermodel Cheryl Tiegs simultaneously as the nightlife-loving New York Ranger with the permed pre-Raphaelite hair, died of cancer on Thursday at 69.

The hockey heartthrob was a fan favourite at Madison Square Garden and other arenas as much for those cascading brown curls as his skating and shooting skills. He married models and was one too, signing with Elite Model Management and singing “Ooh la la” in a television commercial for Sasson Jeans in 1979. Not immune to the disco fever of the era, the native of Sudbury, Ont., was a regular at Manhattan’s most exclusive nightclub.

“I was in great shape in those years,” Mr. Duguay later told The New York Times. “I was doing extra cardio at Studio 54.”

He was a determined forechecker with an aptitude for offence whose charisma helped expand the popularity of the NHL beyond the game itself in the 1980s.

If he was one of a kind, he was also the last of his kind: Skating for the minor-league Brooklyn Aces and the Jersey Rockhoppers in 2009 at 51 for two games to raise funds for the Garden of Dreams Foundation, he became the final professional hockey player to compete without a helmet in North America. Mr. Duguay told The Hockey News in 2012 that vanity wasn’t the reason he shunned headgear, but that helmets were hot, confining and, at the time, unnecessary. (Though the NHL made helmets mandatory for players entering the league after the 1978-79 season, veteran players still had the option of wearing one or not.)

He had been receiving treatment at a City of Hope cancer treatment centre in Southern California. Colon cancer diagnosed in late 2024 had spread to his liver.

The New York Rangers organization issued a statement after Mr. Duguay’s death was announced: “Ron’s signature skating style − with his hair flowing as he moved down the ice − captivated The Garden Faithful, and his skill, tenacity, and charisma earned him the admiration of all New Yorkers.”

On Oct. 2, the Sudbury Wolves alumnus was feted at the same Sudbury Community Arena where he skated as a teenager for four seasons before the New York Rangers drafted him 13th overall on June 14, 1977. Mr. Duguay signed autographs and dropped the ceremonial puck before an Ontario Hockey League game against the Niagara IceDogs.

“He was there like a trooper,” said Joe Bowen, a Sudbury native who began his hockey broadcasting career calling Wolves games for the city’s Ckso radio station at same time Mr. Duguay played for the team. “But halfway through the game he said he had to leave. You kind of knew things weren’t going in the right direction, healthwise.”

Mr. Duguay had been involved in a long-distance relationship with former U.S vice-presidential candidate and one-time Alaska governor Sarah Palin. Earlier this year he told The New York Post that the Republican politician was “the sweetest, kindest person” and a “great companion.”

He married twice, first to California model Robin Bobo (with whom he had two daughters), then to Sports Illustrated swimsuit issue bombshell Kim Alexis, with whom he had a son.

In 2009, he teamed with Canadian pair skater Barbara Underhill in the first season of the CBC figure-skating reality show Battle of the Blades . Ms. Underhill hadn’t competed in 11 years and Mr. Duguay was also long retired.

“We had a three-week rehearsal period and it was an enormous challenge,” Ms. Underhill said. “But he was born for that show, and when the television lights flashed on he came alive. It was wild, it was a gift, and Ron was in his glory.”

Until the late 1960s, professional athletes weren’t normally considered sex symbols or adored the way musicians and movie stars were. Their nightlife was their own life; wholesomeness and aw-shucks humility was what got their mugs on the boxes of Wheaties cereal.

The cocky New York Jets quarterback and shag-rug superstar Joe Namath changed all that. And when in 1978 former Jets owner Sonny Werblin took charge of Madison Square Garden and its properties, including the Rangers, he brought with him a love of glam.

“Sonny encouraged his players to go to Studio 54,” said Larry Sloman, who wrote about the Rangers in Playboy and documented the team’s 1979-80 season in the book Thin Ice . “He loved the publicity when they made it into the gossip columns.”

Mr. Duguay partnered with teammates Phil Esposito and Ron Greschner in the short-lived Sticks restaurant in Manhattan’s Upper East Side and later co-owned another eatery, Cronies, in the same area.

In a 1981 cover story, Forum magazine dubbed Mr. Duguay the “Son of Namath” for his flashy charisma. The puck-shooter had no issue at all with athletes being hyped as sex symbols and using the allure to sell sports and other things.

“Damn right, I think it’s great,” he told Forum. “And I’m lucky I’m in New York and have a man like Sonny Werblin behind me.”

Mr. Duguay was a rock star − the Jon Bon Jovi of Broadway. In fact, his singing voice was heard on the 1979 song Hockey Sock Rock , written by Canada’s Alan Thicke. One of the other participating Rangers, Dave Maloney, later told New York Magazine that the single sold 100,000 copies but only because singer-songwriter Gordon Lightfoot, a friend of Mr. Thicke’s, bought 90,000 himself.

The free-spirited athlete who answered to Doog, Doogs or Doogie graced the front of Stan Fischler’s 1982 book The New Breed: Hockey’s Hot Young Superstars . The picture was taken by the renowned sports photographer Bruce Bennett, making Mr. Duguay a rare personality photographed by both Hockey Hall of Famer Mr. Bennett and the New York-based pop-culture artist Andy Warhol.

In a story in Mr. Warhol’s Interview magazine, the skater said his first purchases when he signed with the Rangers were a white Cadillac Eldorado and shortly afterward a metallic gold speedboat he shipped back to Canada. Mr. Warhol noted that Mr. Duguay did not wear a “hat” while on the ice and said it would be a shame if his “beautiful nose” was wrecked.

“Andy had a crush on Ron,” Mr. Sloman said.

The strapping centre/right winger maintained his good looks while wearing the NHL uniforms of the Detroit Red Wings, Pittsburgh Penguins, Los Angeles Kings and, for two stints, the Rangers. In his only Stanley Cup finals he scored two goals in five games as a 21-year-old in 1979 for the Rangers, who lost to the Montreal Canadiens.

Playing with 11 future Hall of Famers on Team Canada’s Canada Cup side in 1981, Mr. Duguay took on a checking role for the team that lost to the Soviet Union squad in the final game by an 8-1 score.

After notching 40 goals for the Rangers during the 1981-82 season, he slumped to 19 goals the following year and was shipped to Detroit in a blockbuster six-player swap. He said Ms. Tiegs and actress Farrah Fawcett called him on the day the news was announced.

Analyzing the trade for Sports Illustrated, Jack Falla wrote that Mr. Duguay was a “problem child” for the Rangers’ old-school coach Herb Brooks because of his tardiness. “There is no reason to believe that Duguay will get along any better with Red Wings coach Nick Polano, a disciplinarian, than he did with Brooks,” Mr. Falla wrote in 1983.

Mr. Duguay proved his detractor wrong by scoring 80 and 89 points, respectively, in his two full seasons in Motor City. But by the time he finished his NHL career in Los Angeles in 1989, he was relegated to journeyman status. The one-time all-star lingered in the minor leagues, playing one season with Mannheim ERC of the German Bundesliga before returning to the U.S. to skate for the San Diego Gulls and the Jacksonville Barracudas. He also coached the Florida team for parts of three seasons.

Mr. Duguay traded his hockey stick for a microphone as an in-studio analyst for MSG Network’s television coverage of Rangers games from 2007 to 2018.

The glitzy Battle of the Blades competition was a far cry from his days playing in the rowdy hockey culture memorialized in Stompin’ Tom Connors’s 1969 folk song Sudbury Saturday Night , in which “Inco” rhymes with “gettin’ stinko.”

As a member of the Sudbury Wolves in 1976, the 18-year-old phenom fought Tony Horvath, a hard-rock enforcer with the visiting Sault Ste. Marie Greyhounds. Mr. Duguay’s dad emerged from the stands and socked Mr. Horvath, who was in the penalty box. As the two tussled, Mr. Duguay left his own penalty box to come to his father’s aid.

“It was mayhem,” Mr. Bowen said. “But it had nothing to do with hockey. It was family.”

Ronald Duguay was born in Sudbury on July 6, 1957. His father, J. Fernand (Fern) Duguay, worked for Falconbridge Nickel Mines Limited as an electrician and was an avid bodybuilder. His mother was Anita Duguay (née Young), who died on Aug. 10, at 97.

Ron learned to skate at the age of four and wore the purple and gold of the suburban Valley East community team as a bantam player. When drafted by the Sudbury Wolves at 16, he quit school. As a member of the Canadian side in the 1977 World Junior Championships in the former Czechoslovakia, he recorded five points for the second-place team.

The Ontarian never played for a Canadian team as a professional. In 1990, as a 33-year-old veteran, he tried out for the Toronto Maple Leafs. At that point he was living in Southern California and had adopted a health-conscious lifestyle five years earlier in hopes of prolonging his playing career.

“When I was in New York, I was enjoying myself, but I was drinking more than I needed to,” he told The Globe and Mail at the time. “Once I made the commitment to settle down, one of the things I concentrated on was making sure my body didn’t deteriorate any further.”

Mr. Duguay was cut from the team in training camp and would never again play in the NHL.

In 2022, he was back in the New York tabloids when he confronted a photographer at the Manhattan restaurant Elio’s, where he shared a meal with Ms. Palin. At the time, the former politician and self-described hockey mom told The New York Post, “He’s my buddy. We have hockey in common.”

On Sunday, Ms. Palin shared a bedside photo on Instagram of her holding the former hockey star’s hand.

Mr. Duguay leaves his siblings, Diane Menard, Richard Duguay and Norm Duguay; and children, Shay Thomas, Amber Stavros and Noah Duguay.

paragraphs: Ron Duguay, who scored 274 goals in a dozen National Hockey League seasons, suited up for his home country in the 1981 Canada Cup tournament and claimed to have dated Cher and supermodel Cheryl Tiegs simultaneously as the nightlife-loving New York Ranger with the permed pre-Raphaelite hair, died of cancer on Thursday at 69.

The hockey heartthrob was a fan favourite at Madison Square Garden and other arenas as much for those cascading brown curls as his skating and shooting skills. He married models and was one too, signing with Elite Model Management and singing “Ooh la la” in a television commercial for Sasson Jeans in 1979. Not immune to the disco fever of the era, the native of Sudbury, Ont., was a regular at Manhattan’s most exclusive nightclub.
“I was in great shape in those years,” Mr. Duguay later told The New York Times. “I was doing extra cardio at Studio 54.”
He was a determined forechecker with an aptitude for offence whose charisma helped expand the popularity of the NHL beyond the game itself in the 1980s.

If he was one of a kind, he was also the last of his kind: Skating for the minor-league Brooklyn Aces and the Jersey Rockhoppers in 2009 at 51 for two games to raise funds for the Garden of Dreams Foundation, he became the final professional hockey player to compete without a helmet in North America. Mr. Duguay told The Hockey News in 2012 that vanity wasn’t the reason he shunned headgear, but that helmets were hot, confining and, at the time, unnecessary. (Though the NHL made helmets mandatory for players entering the league after the 1978-79 season, veteran players still had the option of wearing one or not.)
He had been receiving treatment at a City of Hope cancer treatment centre in Southern California. Colon cancer diagnosed in late 2024 had spread to his liver.

The New York Rangers organization issued a statement after Mr. Duguay’s death was announced: “Ron’s signature skating style − with his hair flowing as he moved down the ice − captivated The Garden Faithful, and his skill, tenacity, and charisma earned him the admiration of all New Yorkers.”

On Oct. 2, the Sudbury Wolves alumnus was feted at the same Sudbury Community Arena where he skated as a teenager for four seasons before the New York Rangers drafted him 13th overall on June 14, 1977. Mr. Duguay signed autographs and dropped the ceremonial puck before an Ontario Hockey League game against the Niagara IceDogs.

“He was there like a trooper,” said Joe Bowen, a Sudbury native who began his hockey broadcasting career calling Wolves games for the city’s Ckso radio station at same time Mr. Duguay played for the team. “But halfway through the game he said he had to leave. You kind of knew things weren’t going in the right direction, healthwise.”

Mr. Duguay had been involved in a long-distance relationship with former U.S vice-presidential candidate and one-time Alaska governor Sarah Palin. Earlier this year he told The New York Post that the Republican politician was “the sweetest, kindest person” and a “great companion.”
He married twice, first to California model Robin Bobo (with whom he had two daughters), then to Sports Illustrated swimsuit issue bombshell Kim Alexis, with whom he had a son.

In 2009, he teamed with Canadian pair skater Barbara Underhill in the first season of the CBC figure-skating reality show Battle of the Blades . Ms. Underhill hadn’t competed in 11 years and Mr. Duguay was also long retired.

“We had a three-week rehearsal period and it was an enormous challenge,” Ms. Underhill said. “But he was born for that show, and when the television lights flashed on he came alive. It was wild, it was a gift, and Ron was in his glory.”

Until the late 1960s, professional athletes weren’t normally considered sex symbols or adored the way musicians and movie stars were. Their nightlife was their own life; wholesomeness and aw-shucks humility was what got their mugs on the boxes of Wheaties cereal.

The cocky New York Jets quarterback and shag-rug superstar Joe Namath changed all that. And when in 1978 former Jets owner Sonny Werblin took charge of Madison Square Garden and its properties, including the Rangers, he brought with him a love of glam.

“Sonny encouraged his players to go to Studio 54,” said Larry Sloman, who wrote about the Rangers in Playboy and documented the team’s 1979-80 season in the book Thin Ice . “He loved the publicity when they made it into the gossip columns.”
Mr. Duguay partnered with teammates Phil Esposito and Ron Greschner in the short-lived Sticks restaurant in Manhattan’s Upper East Side and later co-owned another eatery, Cronies, in the same area.

In a 1981 cover story, Forum magazine dubbed Mr. Duguay the “Son of Namath” for his flashy charisma. The puck-shooter had no issue at all with athletes being hyped as sex symbols and using the allure to sell sports and other things.
“Damn right, I think it’s great,” he told Forum. “And I’m lucky I’m in New York and have a man like Sonny Werblin behind me.”

Mr. Duguay was a rock star − the Jon Bon Jovi of Broadway. In fact, his singing voice was heard on the 1979 song Hockey Sock Rock , written by Canada’s Alan Thicke. One of the other participating Rangers, Dave Maloney, later told New York Magazine that the single sold 100,000 copies but only because singer-songwriter Gordon Lightfoot, a friend of Mr. Thicke’s, bought 90,000 himself.

The free-spirited athlete who answered to Doog, Doogs or Doogie graced the front of Stan Fischler’s 1982 book The New Breed: Hockey’s Hot Young Superstars . The picture was taken by the renowned sports photographer Bruce Bennett, making Mr. Duguay a rare personality photographed by both Hockey Hall of Famer Mr. Bennett and the New York-based pop-culture artist Andy Warhol.

In a story in Mr. Warhol’s Interview magazine, the skater said his first purchases when he signed with the Rangers were a white Cadillac Eldorado and shortly afterward a metallic gold speedboat he shipped back to Canada. Mr. Warhol noted that Mr. Duguay did not wear a “hat” while on the ice and said it would be a shame if his “beautiful nose” was wrecked.
“Andy had a crush on Ron,” Mr. Sloman said.

The strapping centre/right winger maintained his good looks while wearing the NHL uniforms of the Detroit Red Wings, Pittsburgh Penguins, Los Angeles Kings and, for two stints, the Rangers. In his only Stanley Cup finals he scored two goals in five games as a 21-year-old in 1979 for the Rangers, who lost to the Montreal Canadiens.
Playing with 11 future Hall of Famers on Team Canada’s Canada Cup side in 1981, Mr. Duguay took on a checking role for the team that lost to the Soviet Union squad in the final game by an 8-1 score.

After notching 40 goals for the Rangers during the 1981-82 season, he slumped to 19 goals the following year and was shipped to Detroit in a blockbuster six-player swap. He said Ms. Tiegs and actress Farrah Fawcett called him on the day the news was announced.

Analyzing the trade for Sports Illustrated, Jack Falla wrote that Mr. Duguay was a “problem child” for the Rangers’ old-school coach Herb Brooks because of his tardiness. “There is no reason to believe that Duguay will get along any better with Red Wings coach Nick Polano, a disciplinarian, than he did with Brooks,” Mr. Falla wrote in 1983.

Mr. Duguay proved his detractor wrong by scoring 80 and 89 points, respectively, in his two full seasons in Motor City. But by the time he finished his NHL career in Los Angeles in 1989, he was relegated to journeyman status. The one-time all-star lingered in the minor leagues, playing one season with Mannheim ERC of the German Bundesliga before returning to the U.S. to skate for the San Diego Gulls and the Jacksonville Barracudas. He also coached the Florida team for parts of three seasons.
Mr. Duguay traded his hockey stick for a microphone as an in-studio analyst for MSG Network’s television coverage of Rangers games from 2007 to 2018.

The glitzy Battle of the Blades competition was a far cry from his days playing in the rowdy hockey culture memorialized in Stompin’ Tom Connors’s 1969 folk song Sudbury Saturday Night , in which “Inco” rhymes with “gettin’ stinko.”

As a member of the Sudbury Wolves in 1976, the 18-year-old phenom fought Tony Horvath, a hard-rock enforcer with the visiting Sault Ste. Marie Greyhounds. Mr. Duguay’s dad emerged from the stands and socked Mr. Horvath, who was in the penalty box. As the two tussled, Mr. Duguay left his own penalty box to come to his father’s aid.
“It was mayhem,” Mr. Bowen said. “But it had nothing to do with hockey. It was family.”

Ronald Duguay was born in Sudbury on July 6, 1957. His father, J. Fernand (Fern) Duguay, worked for Falconbridge Nickel Mines Limited as an electrician and was an avid bodybuilder. His mother was Anita Duguay (née Young), who died on Aug. 10, at 97.

Ron learned to skate at the age of four and wore the purple and gold of the suburban Valley East community team as a bantam player. When drafted by the Sudbury Wolves at 16, he quit school. As a member of the Canadian side in the 1977 World Junior Championships in the former Czechoslovakia, he recorded five points for the second-place team.

The Ontarian never played for a Canadian team as a professional. In 1990, as a 33-year-old veteran, he tried out for the Toronto Maple Leafs. At that point he was living in Southern California and had adopted a health-conscious lifestyle five years earlier in hopes of prolonging his playing career.

“When I was in New York, I was enjoying myself, but I was drinking more than I needed to,” he told The Globe and Mail at the time. “Once I made the commitment to settle down, one of the things I concentrated on was making sure my body didn’t deteriorate any further.”
Mr. Duguay was cut from the team in training camp and would never again play in the NHL.

In 2022, he was back in the New York tabloids when he confronted a photographer at the Manhattan restaurant Elio’s, where he shared a meal with Ms. Palin. At the time, the former politician and self-described hockey mom told The New York Post, “He’s my buddy. We have hockey in common.”
On Sunday, Ms. Palin shared a bedside photo on Instagram of her holding the former hockey star’s hand.
Mr. Duguay leaves his siblings, Diane Menard, Richard Duguay and Norm Duguay; and children, Shay Thomas, Amber Stavros and Noah Duguay.

stories.title: Crime Stoppers breach raises fears for tipsters as police suspend use of hacked platform
stories.summary: A cybersecurity breach involving a platform used by Crime Stoppers exposed nearly 180,000 tips and 15,000 associated names, leading to several police departments suspending or restricting use of the platform.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Anonymous tips have helped police investigate crimes for decades. But a cybersecurity breach involving a platform used by Crime Stoppers has raised a troubling question for people who came forward expecting their identities to remain protected: what happens when that trust is compromised?

Toronto Crime Stoppers suspended its tip-taking services after learning that nearly 180,000 tips submitted between January 2022 and November 2025 were included in data stolen from P3, a third-party platform operated by Navigate360.

The breach, which was discovered in March, also involved nearly 15,000 names associated with the affected Toronto tips. It remains unclear whether those names belong to people who submitted information, individuals identified in the tips or both.

The consequences could extend beyond Toronto. Halton Regional Police Service has confirmed that some data related to Halton was included in the breach, while Durham Regional Police Service is reviewing the incident and has removed references directing the public to Crime Stoppers from its public-facing channels.

For former Toronto police officer and security specialist Ross McLean, the exposure threatens more than the security of a database. It could undermine a vital way for people to help investigators without putting themselves at risk.

Why anonymity matters

Crime Stoppers provides a way for people to share information about suspected criminal activity without identifying themselves. That distinction can be crucial for witnesses who fear retaliation, people who know someone involved in a crime or individuals who are uncomfortable approaching police directly.

The breach is particularly concerning because information submitted through the program can involve serious criminal investigations, McLean said in an interview with CTV New Channel on Thursday.

“It’s really quite serious ... this is another thing that we’re seeing, much like Project South when information went the wrong way from the police to the bad guys,” he said.

The full contents of the stolen Toronto tips have not been provided to the charity, leaving it unable to determine exactly what information was exposed or assess the risks to individual tipsters.

Although Crime Stoppers does not ask people submitting tips to provide their names, some May include identifying details when explaining what they witnessed. Toronto Crime Stoppers said its practice is to remove such details before information is forwarded to investigators. The breach, however, involved some original submissions that could contain identifying information.

McLean said the anonymity offered by Crime Stoppers serves a purpose that conventional police reporting channels cannot always replicate.

“They (police) have to record where they got it (info) from…they can’t necessarily protect your anonymity,” he said.

What police services are doing

Toronto Crime Stoppers announced Oct. 21 that it had stopped accepting tips through its website, telephone service and app while it works on a safer alternative.

The charity said it had been seeking answers from Navigate360 for months, including information about which tips were affected and what personal details May have been exposed. It said it was told in April that Toronto’s data had not been taken, before being informed in June that the breach had affected its records.

Toronto police have also suspended their use of the Crime Stoppers tip line while reviewing the additional safeguards and security measures that will be implemented.

In Halton, police confirmed that some data related to the region was affected and said they had suspended their use of Crime Stoppers while awaiting further information about the breach’s scope and impact.

The Halton Regional Police Service emphasized that Crime Stoppers operates independently and that its tip-management platform is not connected to the service’s internal systems. It said it is investigating and assessing potential effects on police operations.

Durham police have taken a separate precautionary step, removing public-facing references directing people to Crime Stoppers while assessing the newly available information.

The Durham Regional Police Service (Drps) is aware of new information regarding the cybersecurity incident involving P3, a third-party platform used by Crime Stoppers programs to receive and manage anonymous tips. Drps works with Durham Regional Crime Stoppers in support of… pic.twitter.com/DTtyfiR1cH — Durham Regional Police (@Drps) October 22, 2026

The Durham Regional Police Service said the incident did not involve a confirmed intrusion into its internal information systems.

Both Halton and Durham police have encouraged people with information about crime or public safety concerns to contact them directly through existing reporting channels.

However, those routes do not offer the same anonymity associated with Crime Stoppers.

What should affected tipsters do?

Toronto Crime Stoppers said it will never initiate contact to ask someone for a tip number, password or other information. Anyone who receives such a request should be suspicious.

The charity has urged people not to submit new tips through its website, telephone service or app until further notice. Anyone facing immediate danger should call 911, while non-emergency reports can be made directly to Toronto police.

For people worried that their information May have been exposed, the biggest challenge is the uncertainty. Without access to the text of the stolen tips, Toronto Crime Stoppers said it cannot establish what individual submissions contained or determine the precise risks.

McLean said people affected May need to consider protective steps, depending on the nature of the information involved.

“It’s going to be the normal things you have to look at if someone hacked your banking information,” he said, referring to measures such as changing an email address and reviewing other long-standing personal information.

Those steps May not address every risk, particularly where a tip involved a serious criminal case or someone who could face retaliation if identified.

A setback for crime prevention

The immediate concern is the safety of people whose information May have been exposed. The longer-term challenge is whether the public will continue to trust anonymous reporting systems.

McLean said the loss of a reliable tip line could make it harder for police to receive information from people who do not have personal connections within law enforcement.

He also pointed to the value of anonymous tips for journalists investigating major stories, noting that reporters use secure communications methods to help protect their sources.

“Something that we really need today, probably more than ever, is a good solid tip line where people can be safe,” he said.

Toronto Crime Stoppers said it has been working with law enforcement and technology partners on a safer way to receive tips and will not resume collecting them until it has a system it considers secure.

stories.title: Fish are returning to the waters of Sydney, N.S. after a cleanup by the Sydney Tar Ponds Agency
stories.summary: At first glance it May seem hard to believe, but scenic Open Hearth Park in Sydney, Nova Scotia, with its vast green spaces, is located on the same site as the former Sydney Tar Ponds The massive toxic hazardous waste site was once filled with slag from steel plants, and local rivers were polluted with run off from the nearby coke ovens.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Sydney, N.S. - At first glance it May seem hard to believe, but scenic Open Hearth Park in Sydney, Nova Scotia, with its vast green spaces, is located on the same site as the former Sydney tar ponds. The massive toxic hazardous waste site was once filled with slag from steel plants, and local rivers were polluted with run off from the nearby coke ovens.

“At one point there were more than 4 million litres of sanitary sewage going into that space each day,” said Donnie Burke, senior director of Build Nova Scotia, who is tasked with monitoring the water quality in the area.

The pollution in the industrial Cape Breton started building up in the late 1800s. The long-term environmental impact was devastating, placing a major strain on the wildlife and fish.

“The fish were very stressed and they had deformities,” Burke said.

But Katherine Jones, a biologist at Cape Breton University, has good news to report. She examined samples of the tiny mummichog fish living in Coke Ovens Brook, Muggah Creek and Wash Brook and discovered their health has dramatically rebounded because water pollution levels have improved in recent years.

“The fish don’t show any bone abnormalities, or fin rot or fin erosion and their asymmetry has also improved,” Jones said. “Asymmetry is a sign of developmental stress, so fish that are more symmetrical have experienced less stress while they are developing.”

Other species of healthy fish have also returned.

“I have witnessed with staff here, trout fry in the Coke Ovens Brook and we saw gaspereau come up,” Burke said. “Recently we were informed that people saw seabass in the channel.”

The $400-million tar ponds cleanup was completed in 2014 and featured concrete encapsulation, followed by massive areas being filled in with soil and then topped with lawns. Open Hearth Park now features sports fields, flowing rivers, walking trails and a dog run.

“It took a long time and years of remediation and they have done a very good job,” said Melissa Breakwell, who comes to the park often to walk her dog. “This is wonderful.”

Burke said a beautiful public park, with cleaner water and a healthier ecosystem, represents a remarkable transformation of the entire area.

“I recall people would ask me if they had to wear respirators, coming into Sydney Harbour on a cruise ship because it was coming next to the Tar Ponds,” Burke said. “In the summertime, you now see a lot of kites flying and it is a true paradigm shift, when you think about the environmental side of it.”

Burke added that there are more than 2,000 trees planted at the park. The fields are closely monitored for subsidence and the surface and groundwater water are tested on a routine basis

“If it is stable or improving, we are then able to convey that to the public, and our trends to date have shown consistent signs of improved water quality,” said Burke, adding that is a big reason why fish are healthier and thriving at the former site of the Sydney tar ponds.

stories.title: CentreBC and OneBC vie for attention against major provincial parties ahead of election
stories.summary: Experts say a shortage of candidates will be a challenge for both smaller parties
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Toward the end of last week’s leaders’ debate during the B.C. election campaign, there was a moment for a pair of political cameos.

After the leaders of the BC Conservatives, Green Party and NDP had clashed over the course of the debate, 30 seconds each was allotted for former BC Conservative MLAs Elenore Sturko and Dallas Brodie to talk about their new parties, CentreBC and OneBC, respectively.

“We wanted to use that time to tell British Columbians what the point of us is,” Ms. Sturko said about her party in an interview on Wednesday.

That has been an existential issue for both parties. They exist in the shadows of the election coming to a conclusion this Saturday, struggling for attention and relevance in what’s mainly a showdown between the Conservatives and NDP, with the Greens in the ring.

It is the first time since 1996 that B.C. voters have been able to take their pick from more than three parties with elected members in the Legislature.

Ms. Sturko, a former Mountie who was first elected in 2022, has been telling voters that she isn’t pretending CentreBC will form government. CentreBC has only 35 candidates, and there are 93 seats in the provincial legislature.

Instead, Ms. Sturko said she hopes her party will win at least two seats in the election – but acknowledged even that will be a challenge.

“Some folks are like, `I love everything about your party. I love what your party stands for. I am a centrist. I am very worried though. If I vote for you the NDP will get in, and we hate them,’” she said.

“So that is a factor for us.”

As is NDP Leader David Eby calling a snap election two years before a vote was expected, leaving her party scrambling, Ms. Sturko said.

“We definitely would have benefited from more runway,” she said.

CentreBC was created in 2025 to offer an option for moderate voters. For a time in September, it was led by former Kamloops mayor Peter Milobar, who had quit the BC Conservatives in August over the leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

However, Mr. Milobar and some other defectors who had joined CentreBC returned to the BC Conservatives after a snap election was called. By then, Ms. Findlay was no longer the Conservative leader .

Ms. Sturko, once a star candidate for the BC Conservatives, was removed from the caucus in 2025 by former leader John Rustad, who had said at the time that she was not a team player. After sitting as an independent, she joined CentreBC in September. The member of the legislature from Surrey, who is gay, has said she was prevented from expressing her “more socially Liberal beliefs” while she was a Conservative.

Dallas Brodie of OneBC, which is running 34 candidates with an additional five unaffiliated candidates, said she would be happy to get four or five people in the legislature.

And then she clarified: “I’d be happy with two. I’d be happy with one.”

Ms. Brodie said the election came about so quickly that it was hard for her party to get organized. Still, she said she has been getting media attention. “I feel like, for a small party, we have been very good at getting our message out there.”

OneBC had two seats in the legislature before the snap election, but the other MLA is not running for re-election. Ms. Brodie had co-founded the party in 2025, after then-Conservative leader John Rustad kicked her out of his caucus, alleging she had publicly mocked and belittled testimony from former residential school students .

She was accused of mimicking individuals who recounted stories of abuses – including child sexual abuse. “I spoke the truth because it matters. I will never back down from it. It is an indisputable fact that the number of bodies discovered at Kamloops is zero,” she wrote on social media after she was ejected from caucus.

In the legislature, OneBC has proposed a bill against gender-affirming care for transgender people. Also, it has proposed banning land acknowledgements by public institutions and employees.

Asked about the two parties, pollster Shachi Kurl says there was a moment when CentreBC had a chance to captivate voters looking for a new option, but the moment has passed.

“The way things happened in this campaign really left CentreBC standing there with their hands in their pockets, so to speak,” said Ms. Kurl, the president of the Angus Reid Institute.

Ms. Kurl said a shortage of candidates is a challenge for both CentreBC and OneBC.

Political scientist Hamish Telford said he would be surprised if either party elected any candidates. However, he said they could cause what’s known as the spoiler effect, affecting election outcomes by taking votes in close ridings.

The University of the Fraser Valley professor said he expects OneBC could take votes from BC Conservatives, while CentreBC could do the same for some Conservatives and New Democrats.

stories.title: What you need to know ahead of B.C.’s provincial election, according to our experts
stories.summary: Readers asked about David Eby’s chances at winning, Conservative leadership and in which ridings the Greens are expected to do well
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
On Oct. 22, reporters Mike Hager and Ian Bailey and columnist Gary Mason answered reader questions about British Columbia’s coming provincial election .

On Sept. 22, Premier David Eby called a snap provincial election, citing the “existential” threat of U.S. President Donald Trump . The NDP Leader’s decision followed months of disarray within the B.C. Conservatives, whose leader resigned just days before the election was called. Voters return to the polls barely two years since the last provincial election.

Readers asked about Mr. Eby’s chances at winning, Conservative leadership and in which ridings the Greens are expected to do well. Here are some highlights from the Q&A.

Is calling an election when the opposition party doesn’t have a permanent leader unprecedented? Could the Lt. Governor have said no to dissolving the legislature?

Mike Hager: Scholars have told us that, though it could be seen as craven, calling the snap election two days after Kerry-Lynne Findlay was turfed as the Opposition leader and replaced on an interim basis by Lorne Doerkson is constitutional. Lt.-Gov. Wendy Lisogar-Cocchia would be loathe to weigh in on the ethics of this snap election call, as doing so would open up a whole whack of other scenarios where she would have to jump in to override future calls for an election.

Gary Mason: From everything I’ve read there is only one other situation that is similar. In 1969 in Manitoba, the Progressive Conservative government called an election while the NDP was in the midst of a leadership race which was eventually won by Ed Schreyer, who was only 33 at the time. The NDP ended up winning the election in part because voters were angry by the government’s cheap tactic.

What has Eby accomplished during his time in office?

Ian Bailey: Andrea Woo and I took a look at Mr. Eby’s record here . The outcome of the election will be crucial to determining whether Mr. Eby’s political story is over or if he gets another chapter.

How could this election impact politics at the national level, major projects, etc.?

Hager: There appears to be very little daylight between the two main parties and their support for projects of “national interest.” However, Lorne Doerkson has said the Conservatives’ No. 1 priority if they form government is to repeal the province’s 2019 Indigenous reconciliation law, which could introduce a large amount of uncertainty in B.C. and lead to more opposition to such projects.

B.C. has needs for more money for health and education, but has a growing deficit and debt. How have the parties said they’ll deal with it?

Mason: You’re zeroing in on what I consider the biggest question of the election: How does the next government balance needs in health and education with the province’s deteriorating fiscal situation? Simply put, the province can’t continue to run the kind of gargantuan and irresponsible deficits that they have been under the NDP. If the Conservatives get in, we will see if they have the courage to put the brakes on spending or continue down the same path as the NDP. But that path is completely unsustainable.

What are the chances this backfires for the NDP? Could the NDP suffer bleeding popular support to the B.C. Greens or CentreBC?

Hager: Yes, the New Democrats could certainly lose ground to the Greens in some crucial ridings. But the opposite scenario May be true as well, whereby Green supporters hold their noses and vote orange in an attempt to thwart the Conservatives from forming government. CentreBC is not thought to be a big factor in many ridings, but their star candidate, former Green Party leader Andrew Weaver, might present a challenge to the NDP in his hometown of Oak Bay.

Is a wealth tax under federal or provincial control? How can Green Party Leader Emily Lowan publicly promise this, without federal support?

Hager: Ms. Lowan announced that her party would introduce a one-time tax of 5 per cent on net wealth above $50-million, 10 per cent above $100-million and 20 per cent above $1-billion. This would raise an estimated $22.2-billion after accounting for administrative costs and behavioural responses, the party said. There are real questions about how this would work.

I called up economist Jared Walker, and he said the Greens admit they would probably face a Constitutional challenge on this tax. But, they could try it by getting Statistics Canada and CRA filings on the province’s wealthiest families, monitoring them to see if they’re moving any assets out of the province, and then hit them with this prohibitive levy. It would require a sizable investment in B.C.’s enforcement ability, but Mr. Walker said that would bear fruit in other areas like cracking down on people and businesses “bending the rules” with other taxes.

Which ridings do the Greens have a shot at and who would come in second place in those ridings?

Hager: They have a real shot to keep the two they won in the last election: West Vancouver-Sea to Sky, which they won by just 676 votes over the Conservative candidate, and Green Party Leader Emily Lowan’s riding of Saanich North and the Islands, where they beat runner-up New Democrat candidate in last time.

Is Eby’s goose cooked? Even if the best case scenario plays out for him, how does the NDP continue on with him?

Mason: Well, I’d certainly say he’s in a pot of boiling water and it’s getting hotter by the day. Look, people are not in a great mood out there. And they really feel Mr. Eby used a disingenuous excuse – Donald Trump’s tariff’s – to justify the election. No one is buying it. And the fact that it was called and overlapped with municipal elections across the province made people even more upset. And that’s before we even begin examining the Ndp’s record under Mr. Eby, which, if we’re being honest, isn’t much to brag about.

What are the implications of Doerkson being an “interim leader”? Does that mean if the BC Conservatives win the election someone else in the party May become premier?

Bailey: No. That would be something to see if after the challenges of leading the party in a campaign, Mr. Doerkson handed the prize over to someone else. My understanding is that if the Conservatives win power on Saturday, the Doerkson era of B.C. politics begins and he goes on as the premier of the province.

The B.C. Conservative party portrays themselves as party that includes candidates with widely varying beliefs. If they come to hold a majority government, what are your predictions on the longevity of the party?

Hager: Elenore Sturko was a prominent MLA for the Conservatives before defecting and now leading the upstart CentreBC. She maintains the fringe elements have unmoored the pegs of this big tent and a handful of outspoken incumbent Conservatives hold bigoted and xenophobic views.

The past year has seen a lot of recrimination and backstabbing in the party over ideological purity tests as to who is a “true” conservative. Insiders say Mr. Doerkson was chosen as leader because everyone agreed he was the least likely to sewer them. He has already turfed a couple of young candidates in no-chance ridings once their hateful viewpoints surfaced, but has stood by at least one candidate repeatedly accused of homophobia in a swing riding they desperately need.

He told us during our recent editorial board meeting that he acknowledges a “robust” debate on “culture war” issues within his caucus but will ensure a Conservative government respects everyone. With so many incumbents set to once again hold sway within the party, we can expect the unexpected!

Mason: Power does remarkable things to political parties. It can bring them together because nothing beats being in government, especially after a long spell on the Opposition benches. There are far more opportunities to reward people in your caucus when you’re in government, too. At the same time, it can sometimes lead to disgruntlement among those who feel they are continually being looked over for important positions like cabinet. But this is a predicament the Conservatives will gladly take on, I suspect. We honestly don’t know what that caucus will be like, and the driving forces within it, until they get into government if the party does.

Bailey: 1981 saw the release of the book “ Discipline of power: The Conservative interlude and the Liberal restoration ” by former Globe columnist Jeffrey Simpson about the challenges the Progressive Conservatives had after winning the 1979 election. Great book. Worth reading. And relevant to this B.C. moment.

Holding power May impose discipline on a B.C. Conservative government and maintaining that discipline will be a challenge for a Premier Doerkson and his inner circle. One of the most interesting things to watch, if the Conservatives win, will be whether they are able to go forward without visible conflicts due to divisions in the party.

What happened to the BC Liberals? What about Kevin Falcon? Will he be running at all?

Mason: I honestly don’t see any future for the BC Liberals, at least not at the moment. I haven’t heard much about Kevin Falcon since he walked away from BC United before the last election. Been keeping a low profile. His sister-in-law, Caroline Elliott, is the one in his family making all the news as a Conservative leadership runner-up and now a candidate for the party. If the Conservatives win, look for her to get a high-profile cabinet position.

But, they could try it by getting Statistics Canada and CRA filings on the province’s wealthiest families, monitoring them to see if they’re moving any assets out of the province, and then hit them with this prohibitive levy. It would require a sizable investment in B.C.’s enforcement ability, but Mr. Walker said that would bear fruit in other areas like cracking down on people and businesses “bending the rules” with other taxes.
Which ridings do the Greens have a shot at and who would come in second place in those ridings?

Hager: They have a real shot to keep the two they won in the last election: West Vancouver-Sea to Sky, which they won by just 676 votes over the Conservative candidate, and Green Party Leader Emily Lowan’s riding of Saanich North and the Islands, where they beat runner-up New Democrat candidate in last time.
Is Eby’s goose cooked? Even if the best case scenario plays out for him, how does the NDP continue on with him?

Mason: Well, I’d certainly say he’s in a pot of boiling water and it’s getting hotter by the day. Look, people are not in a great mood out there. And they really feel Mr. Eby used a disingenuous excuse – Donald Trump’s tariff’s – to justify the election. No one is buying it. And the fact that it was called and overlapped with municipal elections across the province made people even more upset. And that’s before we even begin examining the Ndp’s record under Mr. Eby, which, if we’re being honest, isn’t much to brag about.
What are the implications of Doerkson being an “interim leader”? Does that mean if the BC Conservatives win the election someone else in the party May become premier?

Bailey: No. That would be something to see if after the challenges of leading the party in a campaign, Mr. Doerkson handed the prize over to someone else. My understanding is that if the Conservatives win power on Saturday, the Doerkson era of B.C. politics begins and he goes on as the premier of the province.

The B.C. Conservative party portrays themselves as party that includes candidates with widely varying beliefs. If they come to hold a majority government, what are your predictions on the longevity of the party?

Hager: Elenore Sturko was a prominent MLA for the Conservatives before defecting and now leading the upstart CentreBC. She maintains the fringe elements have unmoored the pegs of this big tent and a handful of outspoken incumbent Conservatives hold bigoted and xenophobic views.

The past year has seen a lot of recrimination and backstabbing in the party over ideological purity tests as to who is a “true” conservative. Insiders say Mr. Doerkson was chosen as leader because everyone agreed he was the least likely to sewer them. He has already turfed a couple of young candidates in no-chance ridings once their hateful viewpoints surfaced, but has stood by at least one candidate repeatedly accused of homophobia in a swing riding they desperately need.

He told us during our recent editorial board meeting that he acknowledges a “robust” debate on “culture war” issues within his caucus but will ensure a Conservative government respects everyone. With so many incumbents set to once again hold sway within the party, we can expect the unexpected!

Mason: Power does remarkable things to political parties. It can bring them together because nothing beats being in government, especially after a long spell on the Opposition benches. There are far more opportunities to reward people in your caucus when you’re in government, too. At the same time, it can sometimes lead to disgruntlement among those who feel they are continually being looked over for important positions like cabinet. But this is a predicament the Conservatives will gladly take on, I suspect. We honestly don’t know what that caucus will be like, and the driving forces within it, until they get into government if the party does.

Bailey: 1981 saw the release of the book “ Discipline of power: The Conservative interlude and the Liberal restoration ” by former Globe columnist Jeffrey Simpson about the challenges the Progressive Conservatives had after winning the 1979 election. Great book. Worth reading. And relevant to this B.C. moment.

Holding power May impose discipline on a B.C. Conservative government and maintaining that discipline will be a challenge for a Premier Doerkson and his inner circle. One of the most interesting things to watch, if the Conservatives win, will be whether they are able to go forward without visible conflicts due to divisions in the party.
What happened to the BC Liberals? What about Kevin Falcon? Will he be running at all?

Mason: I honestly don’t see any future for the BC Liberals, at least not at the moment. I haven’t heard much about Kevin Falcon since he walked away from BC United before the last election. Been keeping a low profile. His sister-in-law, Caroline Elliott, is the one in his family making all the news as a Conservative leadership runner-up and now a candidate for the party. If the Conservatives win, look for her to get a high-profile cabinet position.

content_blocks.text: Is calling an election when the opposition party doesn’t have a permanent leader unprecedented? Could the Lt. Governor have said no to dissolving the legislature?

content_blocks.text: Mike Hager: Scholars have told us that, though it could be seen as craven, calling the snap election two days after Kerry-Lynne Findlay was turfed as the Opposition leader and replaced on an interim basis by Lorne Doerkson is constitutional. Lt.-Gov. Wendy Lisogar-Cocchia would be loathe to weigh in on the ethics of this snap election call, as doing so would open up a whole whack of other scenarios where she would have to jump in to override future calls for an election.

stories.title: Miller says government moving quickly but no timeline for new digital regulator
stories.summary: In an interview with The Canadian Press, Miller said the government is moving as quickly as possible on digital safety bill C-34, which includes a ban on social media for kids.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Culture Minister Marc Miller says while he shares concerns about how long the government’s new digital regulator will take to set up, he’s unable to say exactly when that will happen.

In an interview with The Canadian Press, Miller said the government is moving as quickly as possible on digital safety bill C-34 , which includes a ban on social media for kids.

Miller spoke at McGill University’s Democracy, Rebuilt conference in Montreal on Thursday. The conference also heard from Alex Munter, head of the Canadian Medical Association, who said he was concerned about the timeline.

When the bill was introduced, government officials said it would take 18 months to set up the regulator. The bill would be administered by the new Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada.

“Eighteen months in Ottawa is like three years,” Munter said. “We don’t have that kind of time … Parents want these toxic products out of their children’s hands now.”

Miller said in the interview he is “equally, if not more concerned, than Alex.”

He said he wants to “get things in place as quickly as possible” but isn’t able to offer a specific timeline.

In his speech, Miller talked about the dangers social media poses to kids, pointing to algorithms designed to keep kids scrolling and companies that have made kids addicted to their products.

He said sexually explicit deepfakes are shared without consent and children are targeted by predators and violent networks that encourage them to “hurt themselves or even take their own lives.”

“If this were occurring in a playground, the playground would be swarmed by police and shut down,” he said.

Miller added that instances of AI chatbots telling users how to carry out a shooting, hurt someone or take their own life “aren’t hypothetical risks or scenarios. They’re real examples that have occurred.”

Bill C-34 was introduced in June and is up for second reading in the House of Commons. If it passes second reading, it must make its way through a House of Commons committee study and through the Senate before it can become law.

The new regulator the bill would create would have five members appointed by cabinet with the authority to issue binding orders to organizations and levy fines.

It would be in charge of making decisions about whether age-verification methods used by companies are effective and respect people’s privacy, and whether social media platforms qualify for exemptions to the age ban.

Australia’s eSafety commissioner Julie Inman Grant told the conference a regulator will take time to establish.

Australia became the first country to introduce a social media ban for kids in December 2025. Grant said Australia’s regulator is now looking into non-compliance or “malicious compliance” by tech platforms.

She said before the law came into force, one platform told underage users the ban was imminent and asked if they were sure they weren’t 16 — before letting about 130,000 users through. Another gave users more than two dozen chances daily to pass third-party age estimation software tests.

Miller said he’s not “naive” about the possibility of industry pushback but he expects the Canadian regulator to have a healthy back and forth with industry.

“It has to be dynamic, fluid, and can have relationships that are built,” he said.

Miller added the government has seen “what’s happened in other countries. Malicious compliance, I believe, is real.”

Miller said Thursday he is open to making changes to the bill.

“I’ve heard throughout the summer, talking to organizations, doctors, parents, groups, kids, and where they feel this could be stronger, and I am sensitive to that,” he said in the interview.

“There is an increased concern with certain aspects of gaming that has some features that are social media-like, so the compliance of those platforms is of concern to me.”

content_blocks.text: In an interview with The Canadian Press, Miller said the government is moving as quickly as possible on digital safety bill C-34 , which includes a ban on social media for kids.
content_blocks.html: In an interview with The Canadian Press, Miller said the government is moving as quickly as possible on digital safety bill C-34, which includes a ban on social media for kids.

content_blocks.text: Miller spoke at McGill University’s Democracy, Rebuilt conference in Montreal on Thursday. The conference also heard from Alex Munter, head of the Canadian Medical Association, who said he was concerned about the timeline.

When the bill was introduced, government officials said it would take 18 months to set up the regulator. The bill would be administered by the new Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada.
“Eighteen months in Ottawa is like three years,” Munter said. “We don’t have that kind of time … Parents want these toxic products out of their children’s hands now.”
Miller said in the interview he is “equally, if not more concerned, than Alex.”
He said he wants to “get things in place as quickly as possible” but isn’t able to offer a specific timeline.
In his speech, Miller talked about the dangers social media poses to kids, pointing to algorithms designed to keep kids scrolling and companies that have made kids addicted to their products.
He said sexually explicit deepfakes are shared without consent and children are targeted by predators and violent networks that encourage them to “hurt themselves or even take their own lives.”
“If this were occurring in a playground, the playground would be swarmed by police and shut down,” he said.

Miller added that instances of AI chatbots telling users how to carry out a shooting, hurt someone or take their own life “aren’t hypothetical risks or scenarios. They’re real examples that have occurred.”

Bill C-34 was introduced in June and is up for second reading in the House of Commons. If it passes second reading, it must make its way through a House of Commons committee study and through the Senate before it can become law.
The new regulator the bill would create would have five members appointed by cabinet with the authority to issue binding orders to organizations and levy fines.

It would be in charge of making decisions about whether age-verification methods used by companies are effective and respect people’s privacy, and whether social media platforms qualify for exemptions to the age ban.
Australia’s eSafety commissioner Julie Inman Grant told the conference a regulator will take time to establish.

Australia became the first country to introduce a social media ban for kids in December 2025. Grant said Australia’s regulator is now looking into non-compliance or “malicious compliance” by tech platforms.

She said before the law came into force, one platform told underage users the ban was imminent and asked if they were sure they weren’t 16 — before letting about 130,000 users through. Another gave users more than two dozen chances daily to pass third-party age estimation software tests.
Miller said he’s not “naive” about the possibility of industry pushback but he expects the Canadian regulator to have a healthy back and forth with industry.
“It has to be dynamic, fluid, and can have relationships that are built,” he said.
Miller added the government has seen “what’s happened in other countries. Malicious compliance, I believe, is real.”
Miller said Thursday he is open to making changes to the bill.
“I’ve heard throughout the summer, talking to organizations, doctors, parents, groups, kids, and where they feel this could be stronger, and I am sensitive to that,” he said in the interview.
“There is an increased concern with certain aspects of gaming that has some features that are social media-like, so the compliance of those platforms is of concern to me.”

stories.title: Video of contact with possibly rabid skunk in B.C. prompts health authority warning
stories.summary: Vancouver - Vancouver Coastal Health is warning anyone in the city's downtown who has had contact with a possibly rabid skunk to get a medical assessment immediately after a video emerged on social media.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - Vancouver Coastal Health is warning anyone in the city’s downtown who has had contact with a possibly rabid skunk to get a medical assessment immediately after a video emerged on social media.

The video posted on Facebook on Oct. 10 shows a skunk struggling to cross a Vancouver street, attracting a number of bystanders before a man picked up the animal using a sweater and moved it onto the sidewalk.

stories.title: Canada Post CEO touts ‘early signs’ of recovery even as financial woes persist
stories.summary: At its annual public meeting, Doug Ettinger said Canada Post is winning back some of the parcel delivery market that has slipped away since 2019.
stories.author: Christopher Reynolds
stories.content:
Canada Post has begun to show “early signs” of financial recovery, its CEO says, as the beleaguered Crown corporation starts to step back from the fiscal cliff.

At its annual public meeting, Doug Ettinger said Canada Post is winning back some of the parcel delivery market that has slipped away since 2019. To make those gains, the Crown corporation is giving shipping discounts to small businesses and pushing a new direct-to-consumer online marketplace.

“I am extremely confident that the organization is not only trending in the right direction, it is poised to re-establish itself as a crucial infrastructure built to serve Canada,” Ettinger said, invoking national sovereignty to make the case for a healthy postal service.

However, its network of post offices remains “overbuilt” in cities and must be scaled down, he said Thursday.

Ettinger qualified that Canada Post will continue to serve rural and remote communities. “We will not abandon the small communities that rely on us.”

Switching the remaining four million addresses that still enjoy doorstep delivery to community mailboxes within about five years marks a key pillar of Canada Post’s plan to overhaul its business model in the face of declining letter mail and financial losses.

The Crown corporation launched an online tool Thursday that lets customers with door-to-door delivery enter their postal code to see when their area is slated for conversion to a community mailbox. The first such switch in more than 10 years was completed a few days ago in Winnipeg and Sept-Îles, Que., executives said.

By the end of 2027, about 700,000 more households from Halifax to Victoria will be collecting their mail from the compact aluminum boxes, according to Canada Post.

In August, the organization reported losses of $277 million before taxes for the second quarter of the year, marking an improvement from $407 million pre-tax loss a year earlier.

The three-month period revealed “signs of an early turning point,” said chief financial officer Rindala El-Hage, as revenue rose — from parcels in particular — and operating costs plummeted.

“These results do not resolve our structural challenges, but they show that … the trajectory can improve,” she said.

Ettinger twice referred to the “fiscal cliff” the service still faces and pointed the finger at successive governments for a sluggish response. “This is not where any of us wanted to be,” said the chief executive.

But Ettinger, who is slated to step down at the end of his second term in March, said the current government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has opened the door to overdue shifts, such as lifting the moratorium on new community mailboxes imposed by his predecessor in 2015.

Other reforms include weekend parcel delivery — under a staggered rollout across the country that kicked off this month — and expected post office closures.

To win over small businesses, they will continue to receive Canada Post’s biggest shipping discounts no matter how small the volume through the end of the year. A 15 per cent discount on fuel surcharges for domestic parcels eases the pain of price hikes tied to the soaring price of gas and diesel.

A new online marketplace dubbed Canada Shops is also in the testing phase. Launched over the summer, it aims to connect Canadian retailers with domestic shoppers.

Between 2019 and 2023, the postal service’s share of the parcel market plummeted to 29 per cent from 62 per cent, as Amazon and other competitors seized on skyrocketing demand for next-day deliveries.

“This isn’t about competing with other marketplace giants,” said chief marketing officer Rod Hart of the direct-to-consumer platform.

The update from Canada Post comes less than five months after postal workers approved a tentative agreement that will boost their wages nearly 10 per cent in the first 24 months of the five-year deal.

The green light given by most of the union’s 55,000 employees followed more than two years of labour strife. Greater use of community mailboxes, which reduce the need for letter carriers, was among the sticking points.

In December 2024, the federal government asked the Canada Industrial Relations Board to step in to quash a month-long strike, and struck an Industrial Inquiry Commission to find a path forward. That probe, led by William Kaplan, made a series of recommendations that were later adopted and rolled out in a suite of sweeping changes to Canada Post’s mandate.

Announced in September 2025, the overhaul lifted the community mailbox moratorium and ended the freeze on rural post office closures — some locations are now surrounded by suburban subdivisions — that had been in place since 1994, covering close to 4,000 outlets.

stories.title: Atikamekw baby to be reburied in home community more than 70 years after death
stories.summary: Montreal - More than 70 years after his death, an Atikamekw baby buried far from his family in Quebec City will be laid to rest in his home community.
stories.author: Frédéric Lacroix-Couture The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - More than 70 years after his death, an Atikamekw baby buried far from his family in Quebec City will be laid to rest in his home community.

After 12 years of searching, the family of Maxime Ottawa has located his burial site, exhumed his remains and confirmed his identity, bringing what relatives describe as “immense relief.”

“On Oct. 26, 2026, Baby Maxime will finally come home to Manawan, to his mother and father, to his brothers and sisters,” his niece, Manon Ottawa, said Thursday at a news conference in Montreal.

Maxime was the brother of her father, Henri Ottawa, whose wish to find out what happened to the child prompted her to begin searching in 2014.

Manawan is an Atikamekw community located about 250 kilometres north of Montreal.

In 1954, when Maxime was just six months old, he was taken from Manawan to La Tuque, Que., for medical treatment without his parents.

He was later transferred to Quebec City without his family being informed. He died on Oct. 5, 1954, after 43 days in the hospital, without his loved ones having the chance to see him one last time.

His parents only learned of his death two years later, and were unable to hold a funeral or bury him according to their traditions and beliefs.

“In 2014, four years after the death of my father Henri, I began searching, according to his wishes, to find my uncle,” Ottawa told reporters.

“I wanted to understand what had happened to him … I wanted to know the truth.”

The family’s search eventually led them to Saint-Charles Cemetery in Quebec City, where Maxime had been buried.

In October 2025, Quebec Superior Court authorized the exhumation of his remains so that forensic testing could confirm his identity and, if successful, allow him to be reburied in Manawan.

The exhumation proved particularly complex.

Cemetery records indicate Maxime was buried in a plot containing five people, while the two neighbouring plots contained four and five people, respectively, all of them Indigenous.

One body was eventually exhumed and transferred to Quebec’s forensic laboratory for identification testing.

Nearly a year later, on Sept. 30, Canada’s National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, the family received confirmation that the remains belonged to Maxime Ottawa.

“Receiving this confirmation precisely on the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation gave it an even deeper meaning in our story,” Manon Ottawa said.

She added that reconciliation goes beyond words and requires seeking truth and respecting the dignity of families.

Maxime’s story is one of several involving Indigenous children who disappeared or died after being sent to Quebec hospitals decades ago, leaving families searching for answers.

In 2020, Indigenous leaders called for separate legislation to help families access medical records and religious archives to learn what happened to their children. The province passed a law the following year allowing families to access certain records held by health institutions, government bodies and religious organizations.

Maxime’s remains are expected to return to Manawan on Monday, ahead of a reburial ceremony on Wednesday that will honour his memory and the traditions of his community.

In a statement Thursday, the family thanked those who helped bring Maxime home after decades of uncertainty.

“While their search for truth is coming to an end, the journey toward possible reconciliation can now begin,” the family said in a statement issued through their lawyer, Olivia Malenfant.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.
