stories.title: ‘It’s like home for us’: Trailer park users seek answers as their summer home set to close next October
stories.summary: The 42 trailers that make up the Bluewater Trailer Park in Kincardine are all tucked away for winter. Amongst them, Lyle Cowan’s summer trailer.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The 42 trailers that make up the Bluewater Trailer Park in Kincardine are all tucked away for winter. Amongst them, Lyle Cowan’s summer trailer.

“We have people there that we’ve known for 50 years. It’s like home for us,” said the Milton resident, who spends part of his summer’s in Kincardine.

Next year at this time, the Bluewater Trailer Park will likely be empty. The Municipality is closing the trailer park, because a 2023 legal analysis says the park is out of compliance.

The Municipality says part of the park lands were donated to the municipality in the 1880’s, strictly to be used as a public park, walkway, or garden.

“As a result of that, municipal council decided to move forward with a plan to bring the park back in compliance, more clearly stated as that of public use. The seasonal long term rentals of those sites did not comply with the intent of the bequeathed,” said Municipality of Kincardine Mayor Ken Craig.

The prime piece of real estate the trailer park lies on, mere metres away from Lake Huron, has been a tourist camp or trailer park for more than 100 years. In 2024, Cowan and his fellow trailer park summer tenants were given three years to vacate, which comes to a close next October.

“They have no plan. They have no estimates, and they have no schedule. So, basically they’ve got the cart before the horse. They’ve closed the park, and they’re not telling the towns people how much they’re going to spend to do this. If you can reimagine this space into something else, then go ahead and do it. But, get that plan in place, and tell people in the city how much it’s going to cost. We have enough parks already that need work,” said Cowan.

Kincardine was receiving approximately $33,000 in rent from Bluewater Trailer Park summer tenants each year considered well below market value by a 2023 staff report.

Craig says the municipality plans to turn the Bluewater Trailer Park, into a public park, walkway, or garden in 2028 following some community consultation in 2027.

“Might be a phased project, might be all at once, but it will be more in compliance with the original intent of that land. The intent of the bequeath was to have it widely available to all the residents of Kincardine,” said Craig.

Cowan and his fellow Bluewater Trailer Park users are holding out that a possibly new collection of councillors, coming out of Monday’s municipal election, will determine a different future for the Bluewater Trailer Park, and it’s 42 summer tenants.

“It was a surprise, but, there’s still hope. Hope to come yet,” he said.

stories.title: Quebec Conservative leader says his newly elected members will make mistakes
stories.summary: QUÉBEC - Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime says Quebecers should expect the newly elected members of his caucus to make some mistakes.
stories.author: Patrice Bergeron The Canadian Press
stories.content:
QUÉBEC - Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime says Quebecers should expect the newly elected members of his caucus to make some mistakes.

Duhaime made the comments as members of his team were sworn in at Quebec’s national assembly.

His party had no seats before the Oct. 5 election, but now have the second-largest opposition caucus in the legislature.

The vast majority of the elected Quebec Conservatives are newcomers and several have already caused confusion and controversy.

The party’s new whip, Renaud Labrecque, has called on his colleagues to exercise greater discipline.

This is the first time the Quebec Conservatives have had members elected to the Quebec legislature since a previous iteration of the party had members in the legislature in 1935.

Duhaime’s Conservatives made a breakthrough by securing close to 21 per cent of the votes and winning 19 seats.

The leader called on English-speaking Quebecers during the swearing-in ceremony, placing himself as an alternative to the Quebec Liberal party.

“They’ve been taking you for granted for ages. You don’t need to be hostages of those Liberals anymore,” he said.

“They don’t deserve your support. Our doors are open at the Conservative Party of Quebec, and we’re welcoming you for the next blue wave.”

Duhaime faces many challenges ahead, notably managing a largely inexperienced team.

Only former Coalition Avenir Québec member Maïté Blanchette Vézina, who joined the Conservatives in 2025, and Caroline Simard, a Liberal member of the national assembly from 2014 to 2018, have prior legislative experience.

But the Conservatives hold part of the balance of power in this new legislature, where the Parti Québécois government is in a minority with 60 of 127 seats.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Ottawa tells its diplomats not to meet with U.S. midterm candidates
stories.summary: A memo says meetings with other elected officials who aren't candidates in the midterms can happen if necessary, but they should be discussed in advance with senior officials.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Canadian diplomats were directed this week not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections.

Glen Linder, assistant deputy minister for the Americas at Global Affairs Canada, sent a memo midday Tuesday to members of the foreign service in the United States.

The memo, which was obtained by The Canadian Press, says if diplomats find themselves “in the same physical space” as a candidate or elected official, they should avoid being photographed or having their name or position appear in any public communications materials.

It says meetings or events with other elected officials who aren’t candidates in the midterms can happen if necessary, but they should be discussed in advance with senior officials.

The memo says these instructions are similar to those in place during election periods in Canada, when public servants are expected to avoid contact with elected officials except in exceptional circumstances.

“Especially in view of heightened sensitivity, we need to take our obligation of non-partisanship extremely seriously and take a very risk-averse approach,” says the memo.

The memo comes as the Trump administration accuses Canadian politicians of interfering in American elections.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both disputed claims of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterms on Wednesday, after the U.S. embassy in Canada released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claimed indicate “plans to influence American politics.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is quoted five times in the list the embassy released Wednesday.

The list includes quotes from Joly offered without context about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states through counter-tariffs. Joly made the comments while addressing Canada’s response to U.S.-imposed tariffs.

In a news conference on Parliament Hill on Wednesday, Carney — flanked by Joly — responded to a question about the America accusations by pointing out it was the United States which initiated trade actions against Canada.

“All of our actions are in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy,” Carney told reporters after announcing a $9 billion aid package in response to U.S. tariffs.

Ford, who is also quoted in the U.S. embassy release, said he has “no interest at all” in interfering in American elections.

“I’ll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability,” Ford said, adding he spent 20 years in the United States and “loves the American people.”

Janice Charette, Canada’s chief trade negotiator to the United States, said during a discussion at the Toronto Global Forum on Thursday that Donald Trump will continue to be president after the midterm elections and his administration will still drive trade policy.

“The role of Congress and the role of the Senate May or May not change through all of that,” she said. “We will remain absolutely focused on what Canada’s objectives are here and pursue them whenever the moment arrives.

“Canada will continue to work to try to put our best foot forward and make the best case for Canada.” As that discussion began, vice chair of BMO Financial Group Brian Tobin said he wanted assurance, “mostly for the peace and tranquility of the ambassador to Canada from the United States,” that she was not engaged in any kind of electoral activity at the event.

“I think we’re good,” Charette said as the audience laughed.

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that could end Republican control of Congress.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said earlier this month American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.” Joly pushed back last week, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

Wednesday’s post from the embassy ended by saying “Americans decide America’s elections.”

— With files from Nick Murray and Catherine Morrison

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”
Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.
Wednesday’s post from the embassy ended by saying “Americans decide America’s elections.”

stories.title: Terry Fox Foundation receives record-breaking $25M donation from Tanenbaum family
stories.summary: The Terry Fox Foundation received a huge boost Thursday, with the largest single donation in the organization’s history: $25 million from the Larry and Judy Tanenbaum Family Foundation.
stories.author: Heather Wright
stories.content:
Toronto – The Terry Fox Foundation received a huge boost Thursday, with the largest single donation in the organization’s history: $25 million from the Larry and Judy Tanenbaum Family Foundation.

The commitment unlocks matching funds provided by the federal government, creating $50 million in funding for cancer research.

“The determination to actually go out there and run across Canada … not for his own ego, but for the fact of wanting to raise money to help conquer cancer … it gave us that motivation,” said Larry Tanenbaum, former chairman of Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment (Mlse). “And although he didn’t make it across Canada…it gave us that motivation to say, ‘let’s finish it.’”

Larry Tanenbaum said the funding will support a national network of researchers across the country.

“Sixty-some-odd institutions across Canada, 1,300 researchers across Canada, all working for the same thing: sharing information on an open science basis,” he said.

When Terry Fox began his run in 1980, his goal was to raise $1 from every Canadian, or about $24 million at the time. His brother, Fred Fox, said Terry’s mission was simple: to fund more research into the disease that took his leg, and later, his life.

“When Terry was diagnosed in 1977, almost 50 years ago, as an 18-year-old, he did some research of his own and found out that not a lot of money was being directed towards cancer research,” said Fred Fox. “Today, survival rates are so much better in a whole bunch of different cancers and that’s why bringing researchers together … people collaborating and sharing ideas. What they’re doing is amazing.”

Dan Murphy is an example of the advances being made in cancer care. In 2023, the Toronto father was diagnosed with stage four pancreatic cancer, one of the deadliest forms of the disease. Today, he lives a full life with the disease thanks to precision oncology, a personalized approach to care made possible by major strides in cancer research.

“Precision oncology is an advanced cancer care that’s treating patients at a biological and molecular level,” Murphy said. “Because my doctor was able to have my tumor sequenced in those early days, she was able to give me a treatment plan tailored for me. And because I responded well to that treatment plan, here I am today.”

Murphy has been receiving treatment at the Princess Margaret Cancer Care Centre in Toronto, one of the largest in the world. He hopes the funding announced today will ensure people across Canada have access to state-of-the-art treatment regardless of where they live.

“It shouldn’t matter that I’m living in Toronto,” he said. “Everybody should be able to have access to the treatments and the technology and the innovations in science that I’m benefiting from.”

Doctors say this donation will ensure new research, knowledge and treatment options are shared across the country.

“When it comes to research, the data we make available in B.C. ought to be available to the people in Montreal and the people in the Atlantic,” said Dr. Marco Marra, the Terry Fox Leader in Cancer Genome Science. “It needs to be available for everyone. You need to mine that data as aggressively as possible in search of solutions. That’s how we’re going to get the job done.”

The Terry Fox Foundation also unveiled a new campaign slogan and video Thursday called “Powered by Terry,” the second chapter in the “Finish It” campaign.

The launch included a new handcrafted claymation film that begins when Terry’s marathon ended, and features the many people across the country who have carried his legacy ever since.

“I think every Canadian either has had cancer, knows a loved one with cancer, has lost loved ones from cancer, or is scared to death that they will fall into one of those three categories,” said Nadine Caron, a surgical oncologist.

“I think it’s just something that unfortunately just binds us as human beings in Canada. And I think we need to really jump into that space and finish it.”

stories.title: Non-profit asks Nova Scotians to ‘adopt’ a bat as part of conservation efforts
stories.summary: A Nova Scotia non-profit is asking people to "adopt" a bat in a bid to educate Maritimers about a rare species, while supporting bat conservation.
stories.author: Ella Macdonald, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
A Nova Scotia non-profit is asking people to “adopt” a bat in a bid to educate Maritimers about a rare species, while supporting bat conservation.

The Nature Trust of Nova Scotia has launched the Adopt a Tri-coloured Bat initiative, in support of one of the smallest bat species in North America.

The winged mammals only weigh about the weight of a Toonie but play a big role in the region’s ecosystems.

“They’re a keystone species,” said Lucas Greville, a Mount Allison University professor and bat researcher.

“They’re going to be eating and taking care of a lot of moths, beetles, general pests. So they’re something we really want to have around.”

Maritime bat populations were devastated by white-nose syndrome in the early 2010s. The white fungus grows on the bats’ muzzles, wings, and ears during hibernation. The syndrome constantly wakes bats up during hibernation and depletes their resources.

It’s estimated that the populations of all six native species declined by upwards of 95 per cent.

“We’re talking thousands of bats just lying dead in their hibernation sites. Since then, we’ve started to see a slow incline over the last handful of years, specifically of the little brown bats,” said Greville.

“There’s likely some genetic resilience that the individuals who are surviving white-nose now display, as all bats that are surviving today have experienced this fungus and disease in some capacity.”

On average, the bats give birth to two pups per litter, making repopulation a slow process.

“They’re a beautiful part of nature and as bat biologists, we often say the scariest part about a bat is a world without them,” said Greville.

Jaimee Morozoff, the Nova Scotia Nature Trust’s director of conservation, says money raised in their Adopt a Tri-coloured Bat initiative will go directly toward land stewardship and habitat protection.

“They are unique to Nova Scotia in the way that they are roosting with the Old Man’s Beard (lichen), which is, you know, a really charismatic, typical Nova Scotia forest indicator,” said Morozoff.

“It’s really critical that we’re able to protect the places where those remaining bats are still roosting and surviving.”

The initiative is part of the trust’s annual Gifts of Nature program. Donors will receive exclusive artwork and a personalized “adoption certificate.”

“Last year, we redesigned the full program with the Nova Scotia lettering and mural artist named Kristen DePalma. This is a really nice way to support that collaboration, support a local artist, and also help conservation at the same time,” said the trust’s communications manager, Anna Weinstein.

As part of conservation efforts, bat sightings can be reported online at batconservation.CA or by calling the Atlantic Bat Hotline at 1-833-434-2287 (Bats).

stories.title: Crown drops sex offender registry charge against former Nova Scotia police chief
stories.summary: On March 4, 2020, John Collyer was sentenced to 15 months in jail for sexually exploiting a 17-year-old girl when he was deputy chief of the Bridgewater Police Service.
stories.author: Michael MacDonald
stories.content:
A former Nova Scotia police chief convicted in 2020 of sexually exploiting a 17-year-old girl is no longer facing a charge of failing to comply with an order under the Sex Offender Information Registration Act.

John Collyer was charged with violating the act in September 2025 and he was supposed to stand trial this week in a provincial court in Bridgewater, N.S., where he used to be police chief.

But on Monday, Crown prosecutor Hannah Cameron told Judge James Burrill that the Crown was withdrawing the charge, saying there was no public interest in proceeding with the case. She did not elaborate.

Burrill dismissed the charge, but it remains unclear what Collyer was accused of in 2025. The section of the Criminal Code cited in court documents does not offer much guidance.

On March 4, 2020, Collyer was sentenced to 15 months in jail for sexually exploiting a 17-year-old girl when he was deputy chief of the Bridgewater Police Service.

He was also sentenced to one year of probation and his DNA profile was to be added to the national sex offender registry for 20 years.

At the conclusion of Collyer’s trial, the victim told the court that the senior police officer was like a father to her when she and her mother moved to Nova Scotia and were in need support. She was 12 years old at the time.

But by the time she turned 15, the senior police officer admitted he couldn’t trust himself around her, she said.

During Collyer’s trial, a psychiatrist testified that at the time of the offence, the girl had an intellectual and emotional age between 10 and 12 years old.

The court also heard that the girl’s mother gave investigators screen shots of sexually suggestive online messages that Collyer had sent to the girl.

At the conclusion of the trial, Nova Scotia Supreme Court Justice Mona Lynch said the intent of those messages was to groom the girl for sexual contact.

The victim, whose identity is protected by a standard publication ban, told investigators that sometime in the spring of 2016, she and Collyer were driving in his car when he reached between her legs, pushed aside her skirt and sexually assaulted her.

The girl said she did not give her consent.

The 26-year veteran of the police force was originally charged in May 2017 with sexual assault and two counts of sexual exploitation, but one of the exploitation charges was withdrawn.

Sexual exploitation involves the sexual touching of a minor by a person in a position of trust or authority.

Collyer was tried on one count of sexual assault and one of sexual exploitation. Lynch found him guilty of both crimes, but she ordered a conditional stay on the sexual assault conviction based on the principle that an accused cannot be convicted of two offences arising from the same actions.

The former senior officer was granted full parole in August 2020,

stories.title: Lcbo picks 'young, innovative' veteran exec as new CEO
stories.summary: Aaron Campbell, a former prime ministerial aide and a Toronto International Film Festival organizer, is its youngest-ever president and CEO.
stories.author: National Post
stories.content:
The Liquor Control Board of Ontario has named 43-year-old Aaron Campbell, who is both a former prime ministerial aide and a Toronto International Film Festival organizer, as its youngest-ever president and CEO.

“He’s young. He’s creative. He’s innovative. And I think very widely respected through his whole organization, and certainly within the domestic industry,” said Norm Beal, chair of Ontario Craft Wineries and CEO of Peninsula Ridge Estates.

Campbell has led the Lcbo on an interim basis since February.

In his interim role, Campbell publicly championed Ontario wineries and brewers. The “We’re All In On Ontario” campaign, launched in September and running through mid-October, promoted the Lcbo’s catalogue of more than 4,600 Ontario-made beverages, which Campbell said in a promotional video “took centre stage in store and online.”

The Lcbo reported that Ontario-product sales grew by more than half a billion dollars, or 20%, in the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026. In its June 30 statement, the retailer also reported sales growth of 44 per cent for Ontario VQA wines and 25 per cent for Ontario-made beer.

Beal said he learned about the qualities Campbell brings to the job came in a personal phone call. In August, when it looked like a trade deal would bring American alcohol back to Lcbo shelves, Campbell called to ask how the retailer could help Ontario producers mitigate the impact.

“Aaron called me up and said, ‘Look, we know that this is going to have effect on your business, so I want you to really give it a thought as to what you think we can do to help you,’” Beal recalled. “I thought it was very perceptive and quite generous of Aaron to say: ‘What else can we do to kind of soften the blow?’”

Campbell’s Lcbo career began in 2017. Before taking the interim leadership role, he was chief of staff and vice-president of corporate affairs, strategy and sustainability, with responsibilities spanning organizational priorities, long-term planning, stakeholder relations, public policy, government affairs and social impact.

He previously held senior federal positions, in Prime Minister Stephen Harper’s office, and the office of the minister of Canadian heritage.

Campbell’s résumé also includes six years working at the Toronto International Film Festival. A 2013 HuffPost article introduced Tiff’s then-director of programme and event services as “Mr. Protocol himself” – which the article attributed to his wide-ranging work including “processing film submissions to producing all the official Tiff parties.”

Campbell’s arts involvement also included a directorship with DanceWorks Toronto, whose board he was serving on in 2019.

“It is a privilege to lead the Lcbo and the dedicated people who bring our public mandate to life every day,” Campbell said in a statement regarding the new appointment. “Having worked alongside teams across the organization, I have seen first-hand the knowledge, care, and commitment they bring to serving our customers, partners, and communities. I look forward to building on that strength as we continue to evolve and deliver for the people of Ontario.”

stories.title: ‘Take that chance!’: Young entrepreneurs encouraged by established leaders at London summit
stories.summary: Some long-standing southwestern Ontario business owners shared their struggles to reach the top and stay there today.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Some long-standing southwestern Ontario business owners shared their struggles to reach the top and stay there today.

Their stories were part of a London Chamber of Commerce summit designed to engage the next generation of entrepreneurs and business students amidst trade wars and a tough global economy.

Yet, even in challenging times, a panel of established leaders expressed the ongoing need to take risks.

“I invite everybody to, you know, take that chance!”, expressed Brett Lucier, the owner of Provincial Glass and Mirror.

Lucier and other leaders shared the stories of their legacy companies. Many have weathered past recessions and trade crises.

Andrew Tepperman, the executive chairman of his family’s namesake home furnishings chain, argued that long-term business goals remain achievable.

“Is the current trade dispute hurting us? Yes, definitely. It is very difficult moving your supply chain around,” he conceded.

But Michael Abela, a manager at the Business Development Bank of Canada, contended opportunities remain.

“Perhaps the biggest takeaway this year is this: Canadian entrepreneurs have stopped waiting for certainty, which is a huge theme change. They’re focusing on what they can control and taking definitive action.”

Still, for those still in school, uncertainty is unnerving.

“I think it’s overwhelming, to be quite frank with you, especially if you keep up with politics,” remarked Western University business student Ann Ta, who is set to graduate next spring.

Still, Ta remains optimistic her chance will come.

“When you really find that one internship, or that one extra-curricular that motivates you, it could open so many doors to the people and the kind of work you want to do.”

And a little inspiration from those who’ve already done it is helpful, said Sanad Bizanti, a first-year university student.

“Just learning from people who started in their basement, and people who started from one call the whole year, I mean, now look, they are multi-million-dollar corporations, internationally! And so, we just have to recognize that the goal is achievable… if you put in the work.”

stories.title: Canadian diplomats told not to meet with U.S. midterm candidates
stories.summary: Memo sent to members of the foreign service comes as the Trump administration accuses Canadian politicians of interfering in American elections
stories.author: Nick Murray and Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Canadian diplomats were directed this week not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections.

Glen Linder, assistant deputy minister for the Americas at Global Affairs Canada, sent a memo midday Tuesday to members of the foreign service in the United States.

The memo, which was obtained by The Canadian Press, says if diplomats find themselves “in the same physical space” as a candidate or elected official, they should avoid being photographed or having their name or position appear in any public communications materials.

It says meetings or events with other elected officials who aren’t candidates in the midterms can happen if necessary, but they should be discussed in advance with senior officials.

The memo says these instructions are similar to those in place during election periods in Canada, when public servants are expected to avoid contact with elected officials except in exceptional circumstances.

“Especially in view of heightened sensitivity, we need to take our obligation of nonpartisanship extremely seriously and take a very risk-averse approach,” says the memo.

The memo comes as the Trump administration accuses Canadian politicians of interfering in American elections.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both disputed claims of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterms on Wednesday, after the U.S. embassy in Canada released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claims indicate “plans to influence American politics.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is quoted five times in the list the embassy released Wednesday.

It includes quotes offered without context about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states through counter-tariffs. Joly made the comments while addressing Canada’s response to U.S.-imposed tariffs.

In a news conference on Parliament Hill on Wednesday, Carney – flanked by Joly – responded to a question about the America accusations by pointing out it was the United States which initiated trade actions against Canada.

“All of our actions are in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy,” Carney told reporters after announcing a $9 billion aid package in response to U.S. tariffs.

Ford, who is also quoted in the U.S. embassy release, said he has “no interest at all” in interfering in American elections.

“I’ll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability,” Ford said, adding he spent 20 years in the United States and “loves the American people.”

Janice Charette, Canada’s chief trade negotiator to the United States, said during a discussion at the Toronto Global Forum on Thursday that Donald Trump will continue to be president after the midterm elections and his administration will still drive trade policy.

“The role of Congress and the role of the Senate May or May not change through all of that,” she said. “We will remain absolutely focused on what Canada’s objectives are here and pursue them whenever the moment arrives.

“Canada will continue to work to try to put our best foot forward and make the best case for Canada.”

As that discussion began, vice chair of BMO Financial Group Brian Tobin said he wanted assurance, “mostly for the peace and tranquillity of the ambassador to Canada from the United States,” that she was not engaged in any kind of electoral activity at the event.

“I think we’re good,” Charette said as the audience laughed.

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that could end Republican control of Congress.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said earlier this month American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back last week, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

Wednesday’s post from the embassy ended by saying “Americans decide America’s elections.”

stories.title: Officials provide update on fatal fire at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: Fire initially sent 39 wounded to various hospitals, and officials say that number is down to 27, with 13 in critical condition
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A wildfire that killed four Canadian Forces soldiers and injured dozens more at a military base in Wainwright, Alta., ON Saturday started on the base’s automatic grenade launcher range, Brigadier-General Vanessa Hanrahan told reporters on Thursday.

Brig.-Gen. Hanrahan is the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal, the top soldier in charge of Canada’s military police, which are conducting one of several concurrent investigations into the fire. The military is conducting its own board of inquiry, and Alberta’s Chief Medical Examiner is also investigating.

At a news conference Thursday afternoon, Brig.-Gen. Hanrahan said her investigation shows the fire started at what’s called the AGL range, as part of routine training in that area. She did not say whether live firing of explosive rounds ignited the fire.

Initially, the fire stayed within what is known as a “permanent danger area” of the range, which prevented firefighters from attacking it directly. According to Canadian Forces Base Wainwright’s range standing orders , permanent danger areas can be contaminated with unexploded munitions.

“It was therefore monitored throughout the day by both range control and the base firehall,” Brig.-Gen. Hanrahan said.

High winds from a forecast cold front later caused the fire to suddenly change direction and accelerate rapidly, Brig.-Gen. Hanrahan said. It spread to a different range in another part of the base and overran soldiers’ positions. Understanding exactly when, how and why that happened will be a key focus of the three investigations, she said.

The four soldiers killed were identified as Private Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sergeant Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

Initially, 39 injured soldiers were sent to various hospitals. As of Thursday, 27 remained in hospital, according to Major-General Wade Rutland, Commander of the Army’s 1st Canadian Division.

“We are heartened that 12 soldiers are no longer hospitalized, although they will still continue to receive follow-up care,” he said. “The soldiers remaining in hospital are in serious condition.”

Maj.-Gen. Rutland said the military’s board of inquiry will work “as long as it takes” in order to be thorough and uncover what happened.

“We will not shy away from answers, and whatever hard truths they May reveal,” he said.

General Jennie Carignan, Chief of the Defence Staff, reiterated her commitment Thursday that the board of inquiry results will be made public once it has finished.

The Department of National Defence has so far remained tight-lipped about the fire itself, citing the investigation. Maj.-Gen. Rutland told reporters earlier this week that troops had been aware of the fire burning roughly one kilometre away for several hours.

On Thursday, he said the fire was “not originally assessed as a threat.”

“Canadians and families are rightly asking how that assessment was reached, what information it was based on, and whether different decisions should have been made. Those are amongst the central questions the investigation must answer,” Maj.-Gen. Rutland said.

He said eight firefighters from the base’s fire platoon responded to the blaze, but did not say when. They were later joined by a second platoon, and by firefighters from the town and municipal district.

The wildfire risk in Wainwright on Oct. 17 was high. Data from the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System showed a measure called the Fire Weather Index, which gauges the expected intensity of a potential fire, was rated as “extreme.” Environment Canada issued warnings of high winds for Wainwright that day and data showed forest and grassland vegetation as very dry.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland, citing the investigation, would not comment on whether the scale of those risks was adequately communicated to troops on the ground.

However, internal communications obtained by The Globe and Mail told the military the “fire index,” a measure of risk, “was low” for CFB Wainwright on Saturday. The DND has not responded to The Globe’s questions about this apparent disparity, or whether the “fire index” referenced in the memo is the same as the Cwfis Fire Weather Index.

According to the base’s range standing orders, during periods when the fire hazard is rated as extreme, pyrotechnics, tracer rounds and incendiary rounds called white phosphorus are not to be used at any time unless authorized by the base commander. The document also says that between the “high-risk months” of August to October, live firing should be conducted during “early morning shoots” when “the fire hazard is normally low enough to permit the firing of most ammunition natures,” before approximately 10 a.m.

On Thursday, Maj.-Gen. Rutland characterized that as a guideline, not an order, and said officers conducting training must weigh a series of factors including weather, the type of munitions and the number of trainees before deciding whether it is safe to shoot live ammunition.

Wildfire experts told The Globe that conditions on the base, including the extreme fire weather index and forecast high winds, were unambiguously dangerous .

A similar situation in 2023 forced the chaotic evacuation of a BC Wildfire Service fire camp in the province’s Shuswap valley.

In that case, a cold front generated high winds that drove the Adams Lake wildfire more than 24 kilometres in a matter of hours. It swept down from heavily forested mountains and tore across a grassy airfield where firefighters had set up a base of operations. Some were forced to flee while their tents caught fire .

With reports from Reuters and The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘Potentially irreversible harm’: Scientists sound alarm on PM Carney’s Bill C-39
stories.summary: More than 50 of Canada’s top scientists and scholars warn that Bill C-39 must be amended, or the federal government is risking ‘potentially irreversible harm’ to the environment.
stories.author: Rachel Aiello
stories.content:
Ottawa - More than 50 of Canada’s top scientists and scholars are warning that Prime Minister Mark Carney’s marquee legislation aimed at fast-tracking major projects needs to be amended, or the federal government is risking “costly and potentially irreversible harm,” to the environment.

In an open letter published Thursday, 56 fellows from the Royal Society of Canada outline six specific amendments they say need to be made to Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act.

The scientific experts write that while they support the bill’s central aim of streamlining project assessments, there are several clauses within the legislation that need to be altered or scrapped entirely.

They say the changes are needed for the government to keep its promise to protect species at risk, delicate ecosystems, natural resources and human well-being.

“Bill C-39, as drafted, really puts aside a lot of the environmental regulations and laws that we have in place in Canada to protect nature and protect our waters, protect our air,” said Dr. Sarah Otto in an interview with CTV News.

Otto, one of the signatories and a zoology professor at the University of British Columbia, said the speed at which the bill is moving was a key motivator for the coalition to come together over the past week and produce the letter. It has since been submitted as a brief to key parliamentarians.

“These harms, oftentimes can’t be fixed, and so we’re really borrowing from the natural resources of future generations to pay for our economic growth right now,” she said.

While the open letter was signed by Royal Society fellows, the organization was not involved in organizing or mobilizing it, a spokesperson told CTV News.

“We are proud to be an organization that brings together many of Canada’s leading scholars, and we support our members in drawing on their expertise to contribute to important public discussions and work toward better outcomes for Canada,” said Royal Society of Canada President Françoise Baylis in an emailed statement.

Alarms sounded, but bill speeding ahead

The omnibus legislation proposing to accelerate the regulatory approval process for nation-building energy and infrastructure projects while addressing labour uncertainty, was tabled on the first day of the fall sitting. Three weeks later it cleared its first parliamentary hurdle.

When it was presented, in a press release, the government touted the bill as “the most comprehensive and ambitious reform to Canada’s ability to get big things built in a generation.”

Despite assertions from senior government officials and federal ministers that the bill upholds environmental standards and Indigenous rights, there’s been considerable pushback.

“That’s not what this bill does,” Otto said. “It does not maintain our environmental standards. It lowers them, sidesteps them, or allows ministers to dismiss the conditions that are imposed on projects to make sure that they don’t damage and harm our environment.”

In the days following Bill C-39 being introduced, c limate activists brought their discontent right to Parliament Hill, resulting in several people including seniors being arrested for trespassing.

“The prime minister is rightly considering how do we balance our books, how do we make sure people are employed and that is really important across this country. But there’s also environmental books, our natural heritage, what sustains us and the species that we share this country with,” said Otto.

“Those are the environmental books, and I don’t think those are being balanced.”

Labour groups have sounded alarms over changes to the Canada Labour Code rules around collective bargaining included in the bill, which they say will have adverse consequences for workers and strip them of their right to strike.

However, business and industry stakeholders have welcomed the legislative package, which also proposes to create zones of “national interest,” and ensure federal assessments of new projects take no longer than one year and are co-ordinated under a new streamlined process.

So far, it’s largely been these pro-commerce and manufacturing voices that have been given a platform to speak to the bill, in front of the special committee struck to study it on an accelerated timeline. Otto said the experts behind the letter have requested to appear as witnesses, but they haven’t been invited, yet.

MP panel studying C-39 lacks opposition

The bill has been sent to a specially-constructed House Committee, where MPs will focus exclusively on the legislation and no other issue, unlike standing committees, which must juggle multiple bills and studies at the same time.

Given the legislation’s split focus, creating a dedicated committee rather than sending it to the labour, environment, finance or energy-focused committees appears to be an effort by the government to take the path of least resistance.

Of the 12 members tasked with studying the legislation , 11 of them have already voted in favour of it. The sole member of Parliament that voted against the legislation at second reading is Bloc Quebecois MP Gabriel Ste-Marie. Both the Liberals and Conservatives are fully backing it.

Neither Green Party MP Elizabeth May nor any NDP MPs were invited to join the committee, despite seeking an exception that would allow them to participate without official party status.

“The only vehicle open to us as parliamentarians is to amend the bill, but that process is severely limited,” said NDP Parliamentary Leader Don Davies in an interview with CTV News.

“The committee stage is the only stage of the process where Canadians get to weigh in… and it’s a very vital part because very often, through listening to Canadians, you understand the flaws of the bill, and that can often form the basis for amending it to improving it.”

However, in this case the Liberals have limited the amount of time to hear from witnesses they haven’t hand-selected, to eight hours. Davies said the “inescapable” conclusion from the decision is that Carney isn’t interested in hearing opposition.

“Carney has called this legislation the most consequential legislation of this Parliament… then Parliament should take its time,” he said. “We should open the doors to hear from the full range of Canadians, from environmentalists to Indigenous people to labor groups to business groups to everybody who’s affected to make sure we get it right.”

Failing to do so opens a huge risk for the government that the stated aim of the bill – building big things faster – won’t be possible due to a lacking societal buy-in, potential court challenges, or protests, he said.

“That’s no way to govern, and I think it’ll backfire on the government,” Davies said.

Per the workplan MPs agreed to, any proposed amendments to Bill C-39 are due to the committee clerk by 5 p.m. ET on Nov. 4, with clause-by-clause consideration taking place mid-month.

CTV News asked Minister of the Environment, Climate Change and Nature Julie Dabrusin’s office for comment on both the specific scientific concerns and the reservations about the committee process.

In an emailed response, Dabrusin’s office reasserted that Bill C-39 will not compromise on environmental standards.

“The scope of environmental assessments remains the same and will continue to consider a broad set of factors, including environmental, health and social effects, as well as Indigenous and traditional knowledge. Any project will continue to be subject to legally-binding conditions and mitigation measures,” said her press secretary Amy Falkner.

Falkner also said that the government has been open to receiving public feedback about the legislation “and are committed to doing so as bill C-39 moves through Parliament.”

In an open letter published Thursday, 56 fellows from the Royal Society of Canada outline six specific amendments they say need to be made to Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act.

The scientific experts write that while they support the bill’s central aim of streamlining project assessments, there are several clauses within the legislation that need to be altered or scrapped entirely.
They say the changes are needed for the government to keep its promise to protect species at risk, delicate ecosystems, natural resources and human well-being.

“Bill C-39, as drafted, really puts aside a lot of the environmental regulations and laws that we have in place in Canada to protect nature and protect our waters, protect our air,” said Dr. Sarah Otto in an interview with CTV News.

Otto, one of the signatories and a zoology professor at the University of British Columbia, said the speed at which the bill is moving was a key motivator for the coalition to come together over the past week and produce the letter. It has since been submitted as a brief to key parliamentarians.
“These harms, oftentimes can’t be fixed, and so we’re really borrowing from the natural resources of future generations to pay for our economic growth right now,” she said.
While the open letter was signed by Royal Society fellows, the organization was not involved in organizing or mobilizing it, a spokesperson told CTV News.

“We are proud to be an organization that brings together many of Canada’s leading scholars, and we support our members in drawing on their expertise to contribute to important public discussions and work toward better outcomes for Canada,” said Royal Society of Canada President Françoise Baylis in an emailed statement.
Alarms sounded, but bill speeding ahead

The omnibus legislation proposing to accelerate the regulatory approval process for nation-building energy and infrastructure projects while addressing labour uncertainty, was tabled on the first day of the fall sitting. Three weeks later it cleared its first parliamentary hurdle.
When it was presented, in a press release, the government touted the bill as “the most comprehensive and ambitious reform to Canada’s ability to get big things built in a generation.”
Despite assertions from senior government officials and federal ministers that the bill upholds environmental standards and Indigenous rights, there’s been considerable pushback.

“That’s not what this bill does,” Otto said. “It does not maintain our environmental standards. It lowers them, sidesteps them, or allows ministers to dismiss the conditions that are imposed on projects to make sure that they don’t damage and harm our environment.”
In the days following Bill C-39 being introduced, c limate activists brought their discontent right to Parliament Hill, resulting in several people including seniors being arrested for trespassing.

“The prime minister is rightly considering how do we balance our books, how do we make sure people are employed and that is really important across this country. But there’s also environmental books, our natural heritage, what sustains us and the species that we share this country with,” said Otto.
“Those are the environmental books, and I don’t think those are being balanced.”

Labour groups have sounded alarms over changes to the Canada Labour Code rules around collective bargaining included in the bill, which they say will have adverse consequences for workers and strip them of their right to strike.

However, business and industry stakeholders have welcomed the legislative package, which also proposes to create zones of “national interest,” and ensure federal assessments of new projects take no longer than one year and are co-ordinated under a new streamlined process.

So far, it’s largely been these pro-commerce and manufacturing voices that have been given a platform to speak to the bill, in front of the special committee struck to study it on an accelerated timeline. Otto said the experts behind the letter have requested to appear as witnesses, but they haven’t been invited, yet.
MP panel studying C-39 lacks opposition

The bill has been sent to a specially-constructed House Committee, where MPs will focus exclusively on the legislation and no other issue, unlike standing committees, which must juggle multiple bills and studies at the same time.

Given the legislation’s split focus, creating a dedicated committee rather than sending it to the labour, environment, finance or energy-focused committees appears to be an effort by the government to take the path of least resistance.

Of the 12 members tasked with studying the legislation , 11 of them have already voted in favour of it. The sole member of Parliament that voted against the legislation at second reading is Bloc Quebecois MP Gabriel Ste-Marie. Both the Liberals and Conservatives are fully backing it.
Neither Green Party MP Elizabeth May nor any NDP MPs were invited to join the committee, despite seeking an exception that would allow them to participate without official party status.
“The only vehicle open to us as parliamentarians is to amend the bill, but that process is severely limited,” said NDP Parliamentary Leader Don Davies in an interview with CTV News.

“The committee stage is the only stage of the process where Canadians get to weigh in… and it’s a very vital part because very often, through listening to Canadians, you understand the flaws of the bill, and that can often form the basis for amending it to improving it.”

However, in this case the Liberals have limited the amount of time to hear from witnesses they haven’t hand-selected, to eight hours. Davies said the “inescapable” conclusion from the decision is that Carney isn’t interested in hearing opposition.

“Carney has called this legislation the most consequential legislation of this Parliament… then Parliament should take its time,” he said. “We should open the doors to hear from the full range of Canadians, from environmentalists to Indigenous people to labor groups to business groups to everybody who’s affected to make sure we get it right.”

Failing to do so opens a huge risk for the government that the stated aim of the bill – building big things faster – won’t be possible due to a lacking societal buy-in, potential court challenges, or protests, he said.
“That’s no way to govern, and I think it’ll backfire on the government,” Davies said.
Per the workplan MPs agreed to, any proposed amendments to Bill C-39 are due to the committee clerk by 5 p.m. ET on Nov. 4, with clause-by-clause consideration taking place mid-month.
CTV News asked Minister of the Environment, Climate Change and Nature Julie Dabrusin’s office for comment on both the specific scientific concerns and the reservations about the committee process.
In an emailed response, Dabrusin’s office reasserted that Bill C-39 will not compromise on environmental standards.

“The scope of environmental assessments remains the same and will continue to consider a broad set of factors, including environmental, health and social effects, as well as Indigenous and traditional knowledge. Any project will continue to be subject to legally-binding conditions and mitigation measures,” said her press secretary Amy Falkner.
Falkner also said that the government has been open to receiving public feedback about the legislation “and are committed to doing so as bill C-39 moves through Parliament.”

stories.title: Joly, Ford, Housefather among Canadians named in U.S. embassy 'fact sheet' alleging election interference
stories.summary: The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa published a list of quotes from Canadian leaders that it says "describe plans to influence American politics."
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
The “fact sheet” published by U.S. Embassy in Ottawa listing quotes from Canadian politicians that it claims “openly describe plans to influence American politics” has been labelled “not credible at all” by a professor of political science at University of Toronto.

“The Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances,” the document, published Wednesday, reads.

It comes after U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said America is “closely watching Canadian activities” for election interference in a podcast appearance on Oct. 13, referencing comments from Canada’s Industry Minister, ⁠Mélanie Joly, about retaliatory tariffs.

On Thursday, Bloomberg reported that Canadian diplomats working in the U.S. have been directed to stay away from candidates running in the midterm elections to avoid allegations by the Trump administration of political interference.

People familiar with the matter, who spoke to Bloomberg on the condition of anonymity, said that an internal memo distributed Tuesday barred Canadian officials from meeting with or even being in the same room as midterm candidates unless given special permission.

Among the “facts” set out in the U.S. embassy document are four previous comments made by Joly as well as actions taken by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Liberal MP Anthony Housefather and Canadian Consul General in Boston Bernadette Jordan.

These include Joly saying that Canada’s counter-tariffs are “targeting products that will target states in the U.S.” in order to “put political pressure” at a news conference in August , as well as Ford’s August letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney calling for additional retaliatory tariffs on imports from “politically significant states to the current administration’s base of support.”

Some of the instances listed date back to early 2025, including anti-tariff campaigns launched by both Ford and the federal government, and two comments from Joly when she was Foreign Affairs Minister.

Joly hit back at the embassy’s claims while speaking to CBC on Thursday . “Indeed I met with Democrats in the U.S., but I met with Republicans (too), which the American embassy failed to present,” she said.

“I went to Boston and I met with Democrats, and in the same meeting, there was a Republican state senator. At the same time, I went to Florida (and) I met with Republican state senators…That is diplomacy. That’s what we do.”

The document also lists 11 Canadians who it says have been charged or sentenced for illegal voting in general elections and primaries in the U.S. held between 2012 and 2024.

“Canada has the second highest total of prosecutions (in the U.S.) for fraudulent or illegal voting of any country,” it claims.

National Post contacted the Office of the Prime Minister for comment, and was directed to a news conference Carney held with Ford on Parliament Hill on Wednesday .

“The United States initiated a series of trade actions. We’ve responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy,” Carney said when asked by reporters if the government’s previous actions were an attempt to influence American voters.

He added: “All of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy.”

Meanwhile, Ford said he has “no interest at all interfering in American elections.”

“We’re going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario and in Canada to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities,” he said.

Joly was also at the news conference but did not comment on the U.S. embassy document.

Global Affairs Canada did not didn’t immediately provide a comment in response to a request from National Post.

Randy Besco, professor of political science at University of Toronto, told National Post that the U.S. embassy’s claims of election interference are “not credible at all.”

“The things that the statement cited are lists of the Canadian government trying to influence American government policy. They’re trying to convince them to remove the tariffs, mostly. That’s not what most people mean by election interference.”

Besco explained that election interference involves trying to get a particular person elected, or to have someone lose an election. The laws around foreign interference mostly involve spending money on influencing the outcome, he said.

The only possible exception on the embassy list, Besco adds, is the mention of Liberal MP Anthony Housefather campaigning for U.S. Democratic Congresswoman Debbie Wasserman Schultz in Florida in August, during her primary campaign.

“It’s not against the law,” he clarified, “but it was probably ill-advised.”

Americans will head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that are expected to give Democrats a House majority. They also need to gain four more seats to win back the Senate.

National Post previously spoke to analysts about the possibility of U.S. President Donald Trump blaming Canada for potential GOP midterm losses .

“It’s certainly the case that the administration will probably latch onto any sort of external cause to blame bad election results,” said Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute in Washington. “But I just don’t see (Canada) becoming the primary explanation or the primary narrative coming out of the White House.”

Meanwhile, Christopher Hernandez-Roy, acting director and senior fellow at the Americas Program of Csis in Washington, said: “I think President Trump lashing out in the face of a loss is…almost a certainty. They can…try to blame Canada, but…I don’t see how that’s really gonna get much traction.”

Nevertheless, he argued that even if Trump and other Maga Republicans can’t make Canada their scapegoat, the country May still need to brace itself.

“I would expect the next four, five, six months to be rather difficult for Canada,” he said.

“The things that the statement cited are lists of the Canadian government trying to influence American government policy. They’re trying to convince them to remove the tariffs, mostly. That’s not what most people mean by election interference.”

Besco explained that election interference involves trying to get a particular person elected, or to have someone lose an election. The laws around foreign interference mostly involve spending money on influencing the outcome, he said.

The only possible exception on the embassy list, Besco adds, is the mention of Liberal MP Anthony Housefather campaigning for U.S. Democratic Congresswoman Debbie Wasserman Schultz in Florida in August, during her primary campaign.
“It’s not against the law,” he clarified, “but it was probably ill-advised.”
Americans will head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that are expected to give Democrats a House majority. They also need to gain four more seats to win back the Senate.
National Post previously spoke to analysts about the possibility of U.S. President Donald Trump blaming Canada for potential GOP midterm losses .

content_blocks.text: “It’s certainly the case that the administration will probably latch onto any sort of external cause to blame bad election results,” said Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute in Washington. “But I just don’t see (Canada) becoming the primary explanation or the primary narrative coming out of the White House.”

Meanwhile, Christopher Hernandez-Roy, acting director and senior fellow at the Americas Program of Csis in Washington, said: “I think President Trump lashing out in the face of a loss is…almost a certainty. They can…try to blame Canada, but…I don’t see how that’s really gonna get much traction.”
Nevertheless, he argued that even if Trump and other Maga Republicans can’t make Canada their scapegoat, the country May still need to brace itself.
“I would expect the next four, five, six months to be rather difficult for Canada,” he said.

stories.title: London man charged in fatal Upper Queen Street collision
stories.summary: A 22-year-old London man is facing charges following a fatal collision in the Old South area Tuesday.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A 22-year-old London man is facing charges following a fatal collision in the Old South area Tuesday.

London police say Tristen Daniel Legault has been charged with impaired operation causing death and dangerous operation causing death.

The charges were laid after a single-vehicle collision in the 600-block of Upper Queen Street at about 1:20 a.m. on Oct. 20.

A female passenger was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries and later died.

Police say the driver was arrested at the scene and remained in custody.

Legault is scheduled to appear in London court Thursday.

stories.title: Fraudulent fundraisers, disinformation spread following CFB Wainwright tragedy
stories.summary: While support continues to pour in for the military members and families affected by the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, Canada’s latest tragedy is also the target of fraudulent fundraisers.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
stories.content:
While support continues to pour in for the military members and families affected by the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, the tragedy has become the target of fraudulent fundraisers.

Patricia Farrell, the mother of fallen serviceman Pte. Shaun Farrell, says her son’s name and photo are being used in an illegitimate donation page posted to spotfund.com.

She is warning the public not to donate to any fundraising campaigns unless they are verified by the family.

“It is heartbreaking that anyone would take advantage of a tragedy and the generosity of people who simply want to help,” Farrell said in a post on Facebook .

“Please do not let anyone exploit your kindness during this difficult time.”

Shaun Farrell, a 23-year-old from Prince Albert, Sask., was one of four men killed in the fast-moving fire during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright, Alta., over the weekend.

Brian McQuinn, an associate professor and co-director of the Centre for Artificial Intelligence, Data and Conflict at the University of Regina, called the fraudulent fundraiser “particularly reprehensible.”

“I think any normal human being would say this is beyond the pale for something as a society that we would want,” he said.

While the scam is shocking, he said, it is not surprising. This type of fraud is common in the wake of tragedies.

“(Scammers) are actually hacking you,” he said.

“They are hacking your emotions, because when you are emotional you are not being rational. You just sort of react.”

A GoFundMe campaign organized by Heloise Vermeulen is the only legitimate fundraiser for the family, according to the Farrells.

Vermeulen set up the donation page to help her close family friends.

The families met in Canada after they both immigrated from South Africa.

“Our friendship just blossomed and we became very close,” Vermeulen told CTV News.

Vermeulen runs Out of Africa Deli and Sweets in Saskatoon, a South African goods store. She is accepting donations, cards and flowers at the shop this week to send to the Farrell family.

She said complete strangers have shown their love and support for the grieving family – one positive to come from the tragic situation.

“Everybody is trying to contribute in the smallest of ways, in their own way, and it is just helping tremendously,” she said.

Disinformation garners hundreds of thousands of views

Scams along with disinformation can spread rapidly during times of tragedy.

When tragedy strikes and few facts are available immediately, conspiracy theorists try to fill in those blanks, according to McQuinn.

It is important to distinguish between the people who are trying to figure out what happened and the people who are posting disinformation to advance certain narratives, he added.

“They are often very nefarious forces or individuals who are just trying to get attention,” he told CTV News.

McQuinn is also CEO of Cipher AI, an AI-driven disinformation detection and debunking platform.

The group, along with Disinfo Watch, helped compile a report that tracked early rumours, conspiracy theories and disinformation in the wake of the Wainwright fire.

They flagged social media posts riddled with conspiracy theories and disinformation including rumours of explosions and a government cover-up.

Many of the posts garnered hundreds of thousands of views, McQuinn said.

While conspiracy theories and misleading claims did not appear to dominate the overall conversation about the tragedy, they attracted considerable attention on X, according to the report.

“Even though (the posts) May not seem legitimate or valid, by having them repeated and reinforced by hundreds of thousands of views, they can start to seem as if they are legitimate in what they are saying,” McQuinn said.

Capitalizing on tragedy is not a crime of opportunity, but rather a business model for some criminal networks, according to McQuinn.

Things have only gotten worse with generative AI, the expansion of social media and lack of moderation on certain platforms, he added.

“Which means that people get to work illegally, immorally and repugnantly without any real consequences to what they are doing,” he said.

McQuinn believes awareness is the best line of defence against disinformation.

Canadians should double check the sources behind what they are reading, sharing and funding, especially in times of tragedy.

“Become aware that in these moments this is always what is going to happen. It is not a matter of if, it is just a matter of how fast it is going to happen and how dramatic it is going to be,” he said.

stories.title: White Oaks Mall announces hotel, new tenants as transformation builds momentum along upcoming BRT route
stories.summary: The ambitious vision for White Oaks Mall continues to take shape with newly announced plans to build a hotel, add a popular entertainment centre, and open more dining options.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
The ambitious vision for White Oaks Mall continues to take shape with newly announced plans to build a hotel, add a popular entertainment centre, and open more dining options.

On Thursday, President of Westdell Development Corporation Iyman Meddoui revealed several exciting additions coming to the mall in south London.

“We saw an opportunity here that the mall could thrive with our vision, knowing that it’s in a transit village,” Meddoui explained.

He offered a sneak peek at renovations to accommodate Canada’s first Footlab, a state-of-the-art soccer training and entertainment facility backed by superstar Cristiano Ronaldo.

Westdell Developments, which purchased the mall three years ago, will also build a Marriott hotel behind the H&M store on the southside of the property.

A Splitsville entertainment centre will open on the second floor, and a new Swiss Chalet and Wingstop are coming as well.

It’s all in addition to recently opening Canada’s first compact Ikea store.

London Mayor Josh Morgan credits cooperation between the developer and the city, along with the mall’s proximity to the Wellington Gateway Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) route that’s currently under construction.

“The BRT project isn’t just about the underground water and wastewater (improvements), or the flood control measures, it’s about the economic development driver that it can be for both residential and commercial development,” Morgan said after the announcement.

Coun. Elizabeth Peloza, whose ward includes the mall, says the BRT is attracting investment, “As we’re seeing shovels in the ground for new housing, as we see stores coming for retail opportunities and commerce, that is the proof.”

Under a new agreement between Westdell and the London Transit Commission (LTC), bus stops will move from near the Beertown patio to an area outside Entrance 5.

BRT buses will be permitted to turn around on the mall’s property for their return trip north along Wellington to Downtown London until a park-and-ride facility is constructed near Holiday Drive.

The shorter route for buses to turn around will cumulatively save the LTC about a million dollars each year.

Coun. Corrine Rahman, Vice-Chair of the LTC tells CTV News, “We know ridership is going to increase as new jobs and opportunities come here. Customers will have more reasons to come to White Oaks Mall, so we want to make sure that experience is good from the moment they get on transit to when they’re riding on it.”

Meddoui says White Oaks Mall is becoming a place where Londoners can live, shop, work, and play.

“We would see the hotel possibly break ground over the next 12 months, and the residential, depending on the timing of other projects that we have going on, could be within the next 12 to 18 months,” he added.

stories.title: Library and Archives Canada cracking down on AI books amid copyright threats
stories.summary: recently updated its Isbn (International Standard Book Numbers) policy to limit books and other literary content created using artificial intelligence.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Canadian author and publisher groups say they are pleased to hear that Library and Archives Canada (LAC) recently updated its Isbn (International Standard Book Numbers) policy to limit registrations for AI -generated books and other content.

“This change not only protects Canadian authors and our valuable creative sector, it also allows Canada‘s cultural and heritage identity to continue to be developed and shaped by human authors, and not by artificial intelligence or machines,” said the Canadian Authors Association in a statement on Thursday.

ISBNs are used to identify a specific edition of a book or monograph, including internationally, and can help ensure a book is widely distributed to maximize its sales potential. LAC says eligible Canadian publishers can request a free Isbn for printed books, ebooks, audio books and educational or instructional DVDs.

This comes as AI’s impact on intellectual property becomes a growing concern, with a consortium of Canadian news publishers moving this month to sue AI company Anthropic , the makers of Claude, for allegedly using their copyrighted content to train their large language models without paying to license it. Meanwhile, Ottawa is still without modernized copyright protections to protect against unlicensed AI training and replication, which were not addressed in its new federal AI Strategy earlier this year.

“By registering with Isbn Canada, you declare that your publication was written by a human author,” says Library and Archives Canada on its website, which was updated on Oct. 9.

“You May use AI tools only for limited support tasks, such as brainstorming ideas, checking grammar, or formatting your book. Isbn Canada limits the quantity of ISBNs for works whose content is primarily generated by AI (text, illustration, translation).”

It adds: “LAC is currently reviewing its policy regarding the use of AI content creation and our guidance is subject to change.”

LAC also says the Isbn registration itself does not provide copyright protection.

The Canadian Authors Association said they “applaud” the changes.

“Canadian Authors Association is proud to have played a role through their advocacy in this change in the rules with Isbn numbers, governed by Library and Archives Canada. While we applaud this change, we recognize that this is only a first step,” said the Canadian Authors Association.

“We await further information to see how the self declaration of human authorship is monitored and verified by Library and Archives Canada, as well as which penalties May be delivered should the self declaration be proven to be false and the book written by AI.”

The Association of Canadian Publishers said the federal government’s changes are “aligned” with their values, and hopes it will lead to more stringent policy that helps protect human-authored creative work.

“The Isbn policy requiring a declaration of human authorship is aligned with our values. Our members publish works that are the products of human creativity, scholarship, artistry, and craft. We do not support the use of AI to replace or substitute for human creative work,” said the Association of Canadian Publishers in a statement on Thursday.

“Over the last few years, publishers and authors have faced a flood of low-quality, unverifiable, copycat products that are AI-generated and uploaded for sale online. AI-slop books crowd out legitimate titles and create consumer confusion, with real risks to the public from disinformation.”

“We hope that by limiting ISBNs to human-authored books, this new policy will lead to less fraud in the market.”

The federal government unveiled its first official AI strategy in June, but it did not include a focus on copyright protections , including for authors.

In an interview at the time, Artificial Intelligence Minister Solomon ’s parliamentary secretary Taleeb Noormohamed said that work is still underway, and that Canadians should “stay tuned.”

“There’s a lot of comprehensive work that’s being done,” he said, including “ongoing conversations” between Solomon and Culture Minister Marc Miller as well as consultations with the artistic and creative sectors who have made the importance of copyright protection “very, very clear to us.”

In 2025, Solomon’s office said it planned to address the issue of copyright in the strategy , including by emphasizing the role of creators in developing cultural sovereignty protections.

Global News sent a request for comment to Minister Solomon’s office Wednesday asking if this update to Isbn Canada’s policy on AI relates to Ottawa’s updated AI Strategy for intellectual property and copyright policy.

A spokesperson acknowledged the request Wednesday, but a response was not received by publication.

– With a file from Global News’ Sean Boynton

Meanwhile, Ottawa is still without modernized copyright protections to protect against unlicensed AI training and replication, which were not addressed in its new federal AI Strategy earlier this year.
“By registering with Isbn Canada, you declare that your publication was written by a human author,” says Library and Archives Canada on its website, which was updated on Oct. 9.

“You May use AI tools only for limited support tasks, such as brainstorming ideas, checking grammar, or formatting your book. Isbn Canada limits the quantity of ISBNs for works whose content is primarily generated by AI (text, illustration, translation).”
It adds: “LAC is currently reviewing its policy regarding the use of AI content creation and our guidance is subject to change.”
LAC also says the Isbn registration itself does not provide copyright protection.
The Canadian Authors Association said they “applaud” the changes.

“Canadian Authors Association is proud to have played a role through their advocacy in this change in the rules with Isbn numbers, governed by Library and Archives Canada. While we applaud this change, we recognize that this is only a first step,” said the Canadian Authors Association.

“We await further information to see how the self declaration of human authorship is monitored and verified by Library and Archives Canada, as well as which penalties May be delivered should the self declaration be proven to be false and the book written by AI.”

The Association of Canadian Publishers said the federal government’s changes are “aligned” with their values, and hopes it will lead to more stringent policy that helps protect human-authored creative work.

“The Isbn policy requiring a declaration of human authorship is aligned with our values. Our members publish works that are the products of human creativity, scholarship, artistry, and craft. We do not support the use of AI to replace or substitute for human creative work,” said the Association of Canadian Publishers in a statement on Thursday.

“Over the last few years, publishers and authors have faced a flood of low-quality, unverifiable, copycat products that are AI-generated and uploaded for sale online. AI-slop books crowd out legitimate titles and create consumer confusion, with real risks to the public from disinformation.”
“We hope that by limiting ISBNs to human-authored books, this new policy will lead to less fraud in the market.”
The federal government unveiled its first official AI strategy in June, but it did not include a focus on copyright protections , including for authors.
In an interview at the time, Artificial Intelligence Minister Solomon ’s parliamentary secretary Taleeb Noormohamed said that work is still underway, and that Canadians should “stay tuned.”

“There’s a lot of comprehensive work that’s being done,” he said, including “ongoing conversations” between Solomon and Culture Minister Marc Miller as well as consultations with the artistic and creative sectors who have made the importance of copyright protection “very, very clear to us.”
In 2025, Solomon’s office said it planned to address the issue of copyright in the strategy , including by emphasizing the role of creators in developing cultural sovereignty protections.

Global News sent a request for comment to Minister Solomon’s office Wednesday asking if this update to Isbn Canada’s policy on AI relates to Ottawa’s updated AI Strategy for intellectual property and copyright policy.
A spokesperson acknowledged the request Wednesday, but a response was not received by publication.
– With a file from Global News’ Sean Boynton
