stories.title: Fashion runways are featuring older models, including Toronto’s Shani Feldman
stories.summary: At 47, the model’s recent resume included buzzy Paris shows Chanel and Matières Fécales
stories.author: Elio Iannacci
stories.content:
A refreshing shift took over the Spring/Summer 2027 catwalks in Milan, Paris, New York and London as mature models were brought back into focus after years of taking a casting backseat. Models aged 45 and older made for a strong showing, representing a demographic that drives more than half of global luxury spending, according to a recent article by Fortune.

Among the standout faces were Karen Elson, 47, walking at Alexander McQueen; Evelyn Effrim-Botchey, 59, at Moschino; 72-year-old Christie Brinkley who closed Dennis Basso; and 83-year-old Naty Abascal at Gucci. This was in addition to actor Olivia Colman, 52, at Miu Miu.

Chanel booked more than a half-dozen mature models. In that lineup was 46-year-old Canadian Shani Feldman, who, while enroute to a family road trip, got the call to fly to Paris. This big break was three decades in the making: Feldman started modelling in 1996, consistently working in editorials and catalogues, until a career pause in 2010 when she had her daughter.

Her decision to turn her car around after that call led to a tour de force return to fashion, as she ended up walking the runway for two pivotal fashion shows – Chanel and Matières Fécales. Back in Toronto, the model sat down to reflect about her sudden rise, her mentors and her thoughts about fashion’s future.

What kind of response have you gotten from women over 30 seeing you on the runway?

We come from a generation that told us that at a certain age, we would become disposable or invisible. Having friends, peers and strangers tell me that seeing me in campaigns makes them feel seen is incredible. To see mature models on the runway finally connects fantasy with reality. Not only are these the women who actually attend events and purchase these clothes but when you’re young, you haven’t laughed enough to create laugh lines and you haven’t cried enough to create crow’s feet – which, to me, is true beauty.

When walking the runway at Chanel, were you able to have a direct connection with the house’s creative director Matthieu Blazy?

Matthieu is calm. You’d expect someone under that kind of pressure to be stressed but I didn’t feel like I was with someone superior. When I tried on my outfit and walked for Matthieu and his team, the room broke out in applause. He is transforming Chanel into something modern and approachable and that warmth clearly comes from him.

What do you consider the biggest challenge you’ve faced, and what is the greatest feather in your cap?

The only real challenge I face right now is being a mom and being away from my family. The Chanel runways were a milestone. I cried when I booked my first Paris Fashion Week show on the official schedule last year for Vautrait – that felt like winning the lottery. After a 20-year gap, never having walked the runway in Europe and walking for amazing houses like Miu Miu, Agnès b. and now Chanel has been spectacular. I’m glad it happened to me at 47 because I can deal with it in ways I couldn’t when I was younger.

You walked for French-Canadian house Matières Fécales, what did you think about the politically charged message behind their collection – titled the Ninety-Nine Percent?

I didn’t realize the full magnitude until the end, when I was surrounded by people weeping because the show spoke so deeply to them. During fittings, you’re just wearing clothes as pieces of art that represent the designers’ stories, triumphs and hardships. Seeing the final public reaction makes you realize how important it is to have fashion like this makes people talk, think and feel.

How has your relationship with luxury and style evolved over the years?

In the era of celebrity-dominated fashion, I felt a bit disconnected from the whimsy. Now that we are back to celebrating models of all eras, that magic is back. In my everyday life, I live in jogging pants because I dress up for work. However, putting on fabulous pieces that contour your silhouette acts like a performance-enhancing drug. It connects me to a part of myself that gets lost in carpools and cleaning.

Who were the mentors and women who helped shape you?

Definitely my mom – she is a no-nonsense person with a compassionate heart. She taught me strength, humility and to always maintain a strong sense of self regardless of what room you walk into. That came in handy because in modelling, you encounter so much rejection. I also grew up watching Fashion Television with Jeanne Becker. My mom and Jeanne went to middle school together. I never imagining our paths would cross. Watching Jeanne – who is a trailblazer and an icon – cover the shows made fashion feel alive. She also did it with grace.

Looking ahead, how do you feel about the direction fashion is heading right now?

Fashion is best when it reflects the full spectrum of humanity – different ages, backgrounds, shapes and stories. Seeing mature models on the world’s biggest stages isn’t a trend; it’s a necessary evolution. It allows women to see themselves represented with dignity at every single phase of life.

Looking at the fashion industry today, how do you view the future amidst the rise of AI?

I hope we continue to celebrate art and artists rather than replacing them with Vogue World robots, holograms and AI-generated models. We need connection in our lives, not more tech. I’m hopeful that we don’t replace human designers and models – we need to marry creators with clothes in order to preserve what fashion is about: human expression.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

Editor’s note: This article has been updated to correct Shani Feldman’s age.

stories.title: Raccoon rabies continues to spread in Quebec as government reports third infected cat
stories.summary: Montreal - Another cat has been infected with raccoon rabies in Quebec, marking the third confirmed case in a cat this year.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Another cat has been infected with raccoon rabies in Quebec, marking the third confirmed case in a cat this year.

The infection was detected on Sept. 25 in the town of Saint-Denis-sur-Richelieu, in the Montérégie region. The province says the owner and a veterinarian were exposed to the cat’s rabies and treated.

The government’s latest numbers show 313 confirmed cases of raccoon rabies in Quebec this year.

Officials previously reported two cases in cats in late June.

“It is weird to see all these cats (get infected). Just three cats, but still — it’s just unusual, we haven’t seen that,” said Michael Libman, professor in the division of infectious diseases at McGill University.

Most people in Quebec vaccinate their cats against rabies, said Libman.

“It makes you wonder whether we’re slipping a little bit on people’s awareness that their pets should be vaccinated,” he said.

Libman sees this third infected cat as a reminder that rabies is not limited to raccoons.

“You can have a rabid dog, you could have a rabid sheep, you can have a rabid cow. All the mammals are susceptible,” he said.

He urged cat owners to make sure their pets are vaccinated and advised people to be careful when petting animals, as rabies can make them more aggressive and more likely to bite.

Children are overrepresented in those who get rabies treatment, said Libman.

“They’re often more curious, and if the animal is cute, no matter what it is, they May approach it in a way that an adult doesn’t,” he said.

Rabies is usually transmitted through saliva, often from an animal bite, explained Libman. He said any person bitten by an animal who might not be vaccinated for rabies should get treatment right away, as the disease is fatal once symptoms appear.

“The thing about rabies is if you get prompt treatment, the illness is almost 100 per cent preventable. On the other hand, if you don’t get treatment and you start to get sick, rabies is pretty much 100 per cent fatal,” he said.

Raccoon rabies was under control in Quebec until it returned to the province in 2024, according to the provincial government’s website. Their data shows one case of raccoon rabies in 2024 and 93 cases in 2025.

The government has run multiple vaccination programs to slow the spread of the disease, including vaccine bait distribution and “trap-vaccinate-release” operations.

In an email to The Canadian Press, the Quebec department of agriculture, fisheries and food said it had mandated the Université de Montréal’s faculty of veterinary medicine to run vaccination clinics for pets in several regions.

Cat and dog owners can get their pets vaccinated for $15 in these clinics, which are set to run until late November.

The department also advised people to supervise their pets when they are outdoors and said pet owners should consult a veterinarian if their animal has an unknown wound, even if their rabies vaccination is up to date.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Diplomacy or ‘interference’? U.S. warns Canadian officials as midterms near
stories.summary: U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra’s list of perceived Canadian “foreign interference” looks more like pointed public diplomacy to experts.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
America’s top diplomat in Ottawa appears to be conflating public diplomacy with “foreign interference” as the Republicans brace for what polls suggest could be a bruising in the U.S. midterms .

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa issued a list of nine “facts” Wednesday that it claims demonstrate that Canadian politicians — mostly Industry Minister Melanie Joly and Ontario Premier Doug Ford — have been attempting to “influence” American politics.

However, experts were quick to note there are key differences between influence, who is a standard part of diplomatic relations, and interference, which is typically done covertly and with hostile intent.

All nine of the facts were drawn from public statements, media coverage, official government documents, even Ontario’s anti-tariff advertising campaign. Most had to do with Canada’s opposition to U.S. President Donald Trump’s unilateral trade war and tariffs.

The embassy conflated those public activities with “potential interference in U.S. elections” on the eve of next month’s midterm elections. An Ipsos poll for Reuters released Tuesday suggested Trump’s approval rating was down to 31 per cent — a historic low — and that 47 per cent of registered voters wanted the Democrats to control Congress, to just 35 per cent who preferred Republican control.

“The Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances,” the embassy wrote in admonishment.

“All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way. Americans decide America’s elections.”

Public officials publicly commenting on another country’s policies or decisions is not typically considered “foreign interference” under Canadian or American law. Trump’s social media account — or U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra’s retweets of his boss — demonstrate that it happens all the time.

There’s a difference between trying to influence a policy or politician in Canada and foreign interference, according to Carleton University national security law professor Leah West.

“In Canadian law, foreign influence that is a threat to the security of Canada … has to be covert or clandestine or involve a threat to a person,” West said in an interview.

“None of those activities (listed by the U.S. Embassy) would meet that definition … Is it attempting to influence elected officials? Certainly. But that’s not what we call foreign influenced activities that would be a threat or a crime in Canada. It does not meet the threshold.”

The activities detailed by the U.S. Embassy also don’t appear to fit the definition of foreign interference in American law.

The U.S.-based legal think tank Brennan Centre noted the federal government distinguishes between election interference — “degrading or disrupting the ability of election administrators and election workers to conduct free and fair elections” — and the murkier idea of foreign influence.

“Foreign influence (can refer to) a myriad of activities by foreign governments or their agents to sway the participants in elections, including candidates and voters,” wrote Lawrence Nordon and Kate Lurie.

“Under the First Amendment, the government cannot limit Americans’ free speech or access to information, regardless of the source. However, it can expose the foreign source of the information when the intelligence is available and, in some cases, indict foreign actors for otherwise breaking U.S. law, such as hiding their role in sowing false election narratives and laundering money to sidestep U.S. sanctions.”

In other words, an Ontario government-branded advertising campaign encouraging Trump to abandon his tariff crusade is unlikely to qualify as covert foreign interference since its funding and the person or government that commissioned it is clearly identified.

Speaking to reporters Thursday, Joly said the U.S. Embassy neglected to point out that she met with Republicans as well as Democrats on various trips to the country.

“That is diplomacy, that’s what we do,” Joly said.

“Now, the American administration decided to put tariffs on the world, including on Canada. And that is hurting people on both sides of the border. And that’s a problem that they need to address. Meanwhile, we’ll do our work.”

West wondered who the target audience for the U.S. Embassy’s warning was — given both the Canadian and U.S. governments are likely to know that public advocacy isn’t the same thing as covert interference, and that it’s unlikely to change Canadian politicians’ behaviour.

John Manley, the former deputy prime minister and foreign affairs minister, had an even more pointed question.

“Why is the ambassador wasting his time on this? Doesn’t he have anything constructive to do?,” Manley said in in interview with Global News.

With a file from Global News’ Touria Izri

stories.title: N.S. woman says duct-cleaning company used AI-generated photos to fake work
stories.summary: A Dartmouth, N.S. woman says her recent experience with a duct-cleaning company has left her feeling scammed and alleges she was shown AI-generated photos of supposed work.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Mitchell Bailey
stories.content:
A Dartmouth, N.S. woman says her recent experience with a duct-cleaning company has left her feeling scammed, alleging that AI-generated images were used to make it appear work had been completed when it hadn’t.

Shernette Smith says she saw an ad on Facebook Marketplace promoting home duct-cleaning services for $150, which she thought was a good price.

“I’d never had it really professionally done, and I do have asthma. My son has asthma, so, I thought, it’s a good idea. Let me try these people,” she said.

Smith says she began communicating with the company on WhatsApp to set up an appointment and two men showed up at her home on Oct. 9.

During the appointment, which she estimates took about 45 minutes, Smith says a worker told her that the blower motor of her furnace was “filthy.”

“He opened the main furnace door, took a photo, and comes back out and shows me a very dirty motor and said, ‘You’ve got mould, ma’am.’ And I’ve never really looked at (the duct), so I believed him,” she said.

Smith says the workers offered to clean it for an extra $250, which would have brought the total to $400. They eventually agreed on $300 for the entire job.

She said the workers told her the work was finished and she paid them.

“He said, ‘I’m all done, ma’am.’ And he shows (me a picture on his phone of) this motor that looks almost new. I was impressed. I was like, ‘Wow, that is so clean,” she said.

But when Smith went downstairs to check for herself after the crew had left, she was shocked to see a completely different result from the one she was shown in the photo.

“It was still filthy. All the dirt was still in that section where the filter goes. So that’s when I knew he had scammed me,” she said.

Smith received the photos the company had shown her, which she shared with Global News.

She says she spent hours messaging back and forth with the company, which denied any wrongdoing. After repeatedly complaining, she was refunded the $300 she had paid.

The company Smith contacted was called Fresh Air Quality, which has a website that boasts of offering air-duct cleaning services across Canada. The website includes videos the company describes as testimonials from satisfied customers, who are all speaking to the camera and giving glowing reviews.

Global News sent an email and called three phone numbers associated with the business, but received no response. At one point, it seemed someone had picked up the phone but promptly hung up.

Cybersecurity expert Chester Wisneki reviewed the website for Global News and traced phone numbers affiliated with the company to other pages offering the same service under different names. Some shared the identical customer reaction videos.

There have been examples where illegitimate firms have used 20 different brands for the same group of people, said Wisneki, director of global field Ciso at the security firm, Sophos.

“You know they’ll all be the same group and they rotate through the names because as soon as the word gets out that they’re a scam, they need a new brand,” he said.

Siwei Lyu, an AI researcher based at the University at Buffalo, also analyzed the photos provided to Smith.

He and two of his students created an AI report for Global News, which found a Google synth ID watermark on the photo of the clean blower motor, which is a way of identifying AI-generated images.

Lyu says AI-detector Sightengine also gave the photo a 99 per cent AI score.

“It showed a high response that comes from a generative model. So that’s our strongest evidence this image May come from AI,” he said.

Lyu adds that the photos on the company’s website also appear to be AI-generated, however, their customer review videos showed no signs of AI use.

Lyu says Smith did the right thing by collecting and keeping the images, which could be analyzed. Anyone who believes they are being deceived can check for AI use using similar tools.

“All the tools we use are either open source, free, or you pay a small fee for using them. But I think the procedure is very much repeatable,” he said.

The National Air Duct Cleaners Association, a global trade association, says consumers need to take precautions when hiring a company.

Association board member Matt Mountain says training for employees can be lacking “because there’s no licensing requirements like plumbing or electrical.”

As well, prices can vary because the industry isn’t highly regulated.

“If you’re planning on somebody coming to your house and expecting them to spend two to four hours or more, (which is) what you want (for) a high quality cleaning, then if you’ve seen a price that seems way too cheap, if it’s too good to be true, it probably is,” he said.

He adds some companies will use “scare tactics” to get people to spend more money — like saying there’s mould.

“(They’ll) tell you that they’re going to remove mould and they’re going to sanitize your system and they are going to make all these health promises. High quality companies in general aren’t going to resort to those types of (marketing) systems,” he said.

“We certainly do mould remediation as part of Hvac cleaning work but they’re just using those trigger words to try and get people kind of scared.”

He says people should get personal recommendations for contractors “from somebody they know and trust.”

Meanwhile, Smith says she spoke with Halifax Regional Police about her experience. However, she was told by police that her case was considered a civil matter and not fraud.

She was advised that it was not a police matter but that she could approach the media or write a negative review.

A police spokesperson confirmed to Global News the case is not considered fraud.

Moving forward, Smith says she will be extra diligent before using a company’s services.

“Just make sure they’re not showing you just images on their phones, because those can be manipulated,” she said.

stories.title: More than a million Canadian homes need ‘major repairs,’ Cmhc says
stories.summary: Around 6.1 per cent of all homes in Canada are in need of 'major repairs,' a report by Cmhc chief economist Mathieu Laberge said on Thursday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
More than a million Canadian homes were in need of serious repairs as of 2021, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation estimated in a new report.

This figure amounts to 6.1 per cent of all homes in Canada, a report by CMHC chief economist Mathieu Laberge said on Thursday.

“As of 2021, nearly 1 million homes across the country already required major repairs, putting existing housing supply at risk at a time when Canada needs it most,” Laberge said in his analysis.

But the poor housing conditions are concentrated among those who already live in precarious conditions. Indigenous people and those living in subsidized housing are more likely to live in homes requiring major repairs, he added.

More than one-third (36.8 per cent) of all dwellings provided by local governments or First Nations were in need of repair, compared to 6.1 per cent of the overall figure.

Buildings occupied by renters (7.3 per cent) were more likely than those owner-occupied homes (5.3 per cent) to be in need of repair.

Homes in need of repair are 13 times more likely to mould or mildew than homes in good condition, and four times more likely to contain a pest infestation.

“This can reduce housing supply and contribute to poorer housing conditions that can affect their health,” the report said.

Canada’s territories have major repair need rates much higher than the rest of the country, with more than a quarter (26.6 per cent) of the homes in Nunavut, 18.4 per cent of the homes in the Northwest Territories and 12.3 per cent of the homes in Yukon were in need of major repairs.

While all provinces saw major repair need rates improve from 1996 to 2021, the rate got worse in the Northwest Territories.

New Brunswick saw the sharpest improvement, with a 4.44 per cent improvement, followed by Manitoba at 3.05 per cent.

Repairing older homes can be a “critical strategy” in making housing more affordable in Canada, Laberge said.

“Canada’s housing challenge is often framed as a race to build enough homes for a growing population,” he said.

“New construction remains essential. But maintaining the homes we already have is also important, especially in the context of an aging stock when housing supply is needed to support affordability across the country,” Laberge added.

stories.title: Nordspace signs $20-million deal with National Defence for rocket launch pad in N.L.
stories.summary: ST. John's - A company hoping to launch rockets from southern Newfoundland says it has signed a $20-million contract with the Department of National Defence.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - A company hoping to launch rockets from southern Newfoundland says it has signed a $20-million contract with the Department of National Defence.

In a news release, Nordspace says the 10-year agreement gives the federal department priority access to a dedicated launch pad at the company’s Atlantic Spaceport Complex, which is under construction on Newfoundland’s Burin Peninsula.

stories.title: Former Alberta cabinet minister says Smith can’t survive UCP crisis after referendum
stories.summary: A former Alberta cabinet minister says Premier Danielle Smith won't survive the crisis in her United Conservative Party amid fallout from the separation referendum.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson
stories.content:
A former Alberta cabinet minister says Premier Danielle Smith won’t survive the crisis in her United Conservative Party amid fallout from the separation referendum.

Peter Guthrie, who was removed from the UCP caucus after criticizing the government over a health-care procurement scandal, now leads the upstart Progressive Tory Party of Alberta.

He says Monday’s referendum angered both federalists and separatists and leaves Smith with more enemies than supporters.

About 75 per cent of voters cast ballots to keep Alberta in Canada and not to have a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Smith’s office says Guthrie is out of touch with Albertans and peddling misinformation.

On Wednesday, the premier said anyone running for or speaking for her UCP must accept its pro-Canada stance.

She said separatists intent on turning the party into a vehicle for independence should join a different party, warning internal division could cost the UCP next year’s election.

stories.title: How AI allegations led Quebec author from prestigious awards to losing his publisher
stories.summary: Montreal - A few weeks ago, Haitian-born Quebec author Thélyson Orélien was collecting award nominations as his book topped bestseller lists. Then, allegations that he used artificial intelligence to write his debut novel, “C’était ça ou mourir” (“It was either that or dying”), started cropping up.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A few weeks ago, Haitian-born Quebec author Thélyson Orélien was collecting award nominations as his book topped bestseller lists. Then, allegations that he used artificial intelligence to write his debut novel, “C’était ça ou mourir” (“It was either that or dying”), started cropping up.

On Wednesday, his Quebec publisher announced it was cutting ties with the author after it found evidence it says indicates he used artificial intelligence to write his book.

Here is a timeline of the rise of Orélien’s book and the mounting accusations that followed.

2017: Orélien said he began writing his book in 2017 in Laval, north of Montreal.

The book follows a Haitian man forced to flee his country and make a perilous journey through the Americas to Quebec. The story is based on Orélien’s own experience leaving Haiti after the 2010 earthquake, the author has said.

2019: Orélien said he finished the first draft of more than 300 pages, two years later.

Sept. 12, 2025: Les Éditions du Boréal said it received the manuscript of “C’était ça ou mourir.” The publisher later said it couldn’t verify the allegations about the book’s writing process before that date.

March 9, 2026: “C’était ça ou mourir” is published in Quebec. It was published in France a few weeks later and set to be translated into over 20 languages, according to French publisher Éditions Grasset.

Sept. 2: “C’était ça ou mourir” is among 16 nominees for the Prix Goncourt, one of France’s most prestigious literary awards.

Sept. 21: Grasset announces the author has won France’s Prix du Roman Fnac, a literary award chosen by a jury of 400 booksellers and 400 readers.

That same day, the X account “Balance ton Claude” alleges that, according to Pangram software, excerpts of Orélien’s novel had been written “almost entirely by artificial intelligence.”

Sept. 22: Orélien denies AI use in a joint press release with his Quebec publisher. The author says his writing style comes from Haiti’s literary tradition, “where poetry, images, repetitions and rhythm carry a living speech.”

The publisher defends Orélien and denounces statements that “directly damage the author’s reputation.”

Sept. 23: Separate plagiarism allegations emerge as media outlet La Presse publishes an article outlining passages in articles attributed to Orélien and published in Quebec and French media between 2012 and 2014 that were near-identical to previously-published work by other authors.

Sept. 24: Boréal says it is concerned about the plagiarism allegations and suspends promotional activities surrounding Orélien’s novel, citing the author’s well-being. The publisher says it is working with the author to compile a detailed record of his writing process.

The Salon du livre de l’Estrie, a book fair in Sherbrooke, Que., announces it is removing Orélien as a guest of honour after learning of the plagiarism allegations.

That same day, French literary online magazine ActuaLitté publishes an article about a 2023 text on Orélien’s blog which included a sentence that looks like an AI prompt.

Sept. 25: The Académie Goncourt removes “C’était ça ou mourir” from consideration for the Prix Goncourt. The academy cites analyses it considered credible and the separate plagiarism allegations involving Orélien’s previous work.

Orélien declines to respond to the new allegations or provide further comment. “I can’t talk about it. I want to focus on my physical and mental health,” he says in a WhatsApp message to The Canadian Press.

Oct. 13: In a statement, Orélien admits that he plagiarized some of his earlier work and apologizes for making what he described as unacceptable mistakes in his youth. “Admiration does not give you the right to take, to claim as your own texts that are not yours,” he writes.

However, he denies using AI to write his debut novel, saying no sentence was generated by a machine. He adds that he used AI tools for research, for instance to look up foreign-language expressions.

“What I am going through is cruel,” he writes. “By attributing a text, one that is mine...to a machine, they have not only called into question my status as a writer but also my humanity.”

Oct. 14: Boréal condemned Orélien’s plagiarism but said it stood by the author amid the AI allegations and would keep the book on shelves. It said it had no evidence beyond the author’s word to determine how the novel was written.

“The publisher’s role is not to demand proof from authors, but to stand by them, and that is what we are doing,” the publishing house said.

Oct. 17: Boréal confirms Orélien has dropped his efforts to compile evidence he did not use AI to write his novel. “That decision is his to make, and we accept it, although we certainly would have preferred to be able to provide definitive answers to the allegations of AI use against him,” co-director Renaud Roussel wrote in an email to The Canadian Press.

At the time, Roussel said the publisher’s position on the affair had not changed. A new printing was expected the following week.

Oct. 21: Boréal announces it cut ties with Orélien. The publishing house says it found evidence, through an analysis of some documents’ metadata, that Orélien used AI to write his book.

The publisher said it will not reprint the book or publish more books by Orélien.

“We still do not know to what extent AI was used in the creation of ‘C’était ça ou mourir,’ and we will likely never have a definitive answer,” it wrote.

— With files from Charlotte Glorieux

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Singapore firm set to buy Yukon’s Eagle Gold mine for $140M
stories.summary: The company says it would also spend more than $600 million over the initial life of the mine "to support and extend mining operations."
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A Singapore-based mining company has entered an agreement to acquire the beleaguered Eagle Gold mine in the Yukon for $140 million, more than two years after it was shut down following a massive collapse, with plans to invest a further $1.4 billion in operations and other costs.

A statement from Boroo Pte. says that if the deal is approved by the court, it would come with planned capital investment of about $800 million between 2027 and 2029 for environmental rehabilitation, water treatment infrastructure, geotechnical stabilization, and “phased restart activities.”

The company says it would also spend more than $600 million over the initial life of the mine “to support and extend mining operations.”

The 2024 failure at Eagle Gold’s heap-leach facility released about two-million tonnes of cyanide-laced ore and water into the environment, leading to control of the mine being taken over by a court-appointed receiver.

Boroo says that since it entered an exclusivity agreement in April to potentially buy the site it has deployed “substantial technical, environmental, and financial resources” and come up with its own plan aimed at “stabilizing the site, completing environmental remediation activities and restarting the mine.”

The Yukon government is expected to hold a news conference, and Boroo’s statement says the plan is to ask a judge to approve the proposed transaction this December.

stories.title: Global Affairs did not Google staff during vetting when Nato spy suspect was given clearance
stories.summary: Global Affairs Canada would not have Googled or done an open-source search before granting security clearance.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Global Affairs Canada would not have Googled or done an open-source search before granting security clearance to someone like the Canadian woman charged with spying at Nato headquarters.

That’s according to David Morrison, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s senior diplomatic and international affairs advisor and the former top bureaucrat at Global Affairs Canada (GAC).

“I agree… that the use of open-source, Google, however you want to characterize it, I think that should be a standard part of our vetting process. I also agree… that personnel information that speaks to someone’s integrity should be part of the system,” Morrison told MPs on the Public Safety committee Wednesday.

“It was not part of the system at the time, and that has now been rectified, according to my colleagues at GAC,” he added.

Morrison was testifying as part of the committee’s study into the the federal government’s security clearance process after Belgian authorities charged a Canadian intern at Nato with espionage in late July.

The Canadian woman of Chinese descent is suspected of “spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization.” She was denied bail in August and remains imprisoned in Belgium.

The suspect was later identified by media as 33-year-old Biwei Zhang, who also went by Claire Zhang. Belgian and Canadian officials have neither confirmed nor denied her identity.

Government officials have since acknowledged that Global Affairs Canada (GAC) issued the security clearance necessary for her to intern at Nato’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (Shape) headquarters in Mons, Belgium.

At the time Zhang was granted her clearance by GAC, Morrison was the head of the department.

MPs on the committee have spent much of their time trying to understand how Zhang received “at least” a “secret” level clearance to go work at Nato when there was a trail of public red flags in her career.

A public Federal Court decision in early 2024 revealed that Zhang had been denied employment at the Canadian Border Services Agency after it was discovered she committed fraud in her job application.

Morrison’s testimony confirmed that GAC would not have looked for such a document, or even searched public sources for information about Zhang. But the senior public servant also noted that the RCMP and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis) have a role in the background check as well.

“If Global Affairs had been aware of anyone that has derogatory information that would speak to that person’s suitability and reliability to protect Canada’s secrets or Nato’s secrets, I have every confidence that they would have acted on that information,” Morrison said.

Morrison’s blunt admission that there were no open-source searches for a secret-level clearance at GAC at the time stunned Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs.

Conservative MP Rhonda Kirkland described it as a “system failure”, while her colleague Frank Caputo highlighted that even a two-week intern in his office found the Zhang decision after media reported on her identity.

“As she pointed out to me, people research people for a first date, and they would Google this type of information, and I think find it. So I will say it again: when the information is publicly available, and we nonetheless give a security clearance — and a high one at that — that is a failure in intelligence,” Caputo said.

In his opening statement, Morrison told the committee that the government needed to tighten up its security vetting process in the wake of the affair.

He issued four recommendations, including a “government-wide repository” of information on employees’ security clearance and more consistent use of open-source verifications for all levels of security clearances in governments.

He also emphasized that government should be better and continuously assessing employees’ security clearances after they receive them.

“A robust personnel security program should extend throughout employment, through insider risk programs, continuous personnel security assurance, recurring screening, reporting obligations, and security awareness,” he said.

“These would help identify emerging risks, ensure clearance holders remain reliable and loyal, and ensure clearances reflect current information.”

In response, Bloc MP Claude DeBellefeuille wondered why all his recommendations weren’t already in place before the Zhang affair.

“I am pretty floored by your responses,” she said.

paragraphs: Ottawa — Global Affairs Canada would not have Googled or done an open-source search before granting security clearance to someone like the Canadian woman charged with spying at Nato headquarters.
That’s according to David Morrison, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s senior diplomatic and international affairs advisor and the former top bureaucrat at Global Affairs Canada (GAC).

“I agree… that the use of open-source, Google, however you want to characterize it, I think that should be a standard part of our vetting process. I also agree… that personnel information that speaks to someone’s integrity should be part of the system,” Morrison told MPs on the Public Safety committee Wednesday.
“It was not part of the system at the time, and that has now been rectified, according to my colleagues at GAC,” he added.

Morrison was testifying as part of the committee’s study into the the federal government’s security clearance process after Belgian authorities charged a Canadian intern at Nato with espionage in late July.

The Canadian woman of Chinese descent is suspected of “spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization.” She was denied bail in August and remains imprisoned in Belgium.
The suspect was later identified by media as 33-year-old Biwei Zhang, who also went by Claire Zhang. Belgian and Canadian officials have neither confirmed nor denied her identity.

Government officials have since acknowledged that Global Affairs Canada (GAC) issued the security clearance necessary for her to intern at Nato’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (Shape) headquarters in Mons, Belgium.
At the time Zhang was granted her clearance by GAC, Morrison was the head of the department.

MPs on the committee have spent much of their time trying to understand how Zhang received “at least” a “secret” level clearance to go work at Nato when there was a trail of public red flags in her career.
A public Federal Court decision in early 2024 revealed that Zhang had been denied employment at the Canadian Border Services Agency after it was discovered she committed fraud in her job application.

Morrison’s testimony confirmed that GAC would not have looked for such a document, or even searched public sources for information about Zhang. But the senior public servant also noted that the RCMP and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis) have a role in the background check as well.

“If Global Affairs had been aware of anyone that has derogatory information that would speak to that person’s suitability and reliability to protect Canada’s secrets or Nato’s secrets, I have every confidence that they would have acted on that information,” Morrison said.
Morrison’s blunt admission that there were no open-source searches for a secret-level clearance at GAC at the time stunned Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs.

Conservative MP Rhonda Kirkland described it as a “system failure”, while her colleague Frank Caputo highlighted that even a two-week intern in his office found the Zhang decision after media reported on her identity.

“As she pointed out to me, people research people for a first date, and they would Google this type of information, and I think find it. So I will say it again: when the information is publicly available, and we nonetheless give a security clearance — and a high one at that — that is a failure in intelligence,” Caputo said.
In his opening statement, Morrison told the committee that the government needed to tighten up its security vetting process in the wake of the affair.

He issued four recommendations, including a “government-wide repository” of information on employees’ security clearance and more consistent use of open-source verifications for all levels of security clearances in governments.
He also emphasized that government should be better and continuously assessing employees’ security clearances after they receive them.

“A robust personnel security program should extend throughout employment, through insider risk programs, continuous personnel security assurance, recurring screening, reporting obligations, and security awareness,” he said.
“These would help identify emerging risks, ensure clearance holders remain reliable and loyal, and ensure clearances reflect current information.”
In response, Bloc MP Claude DeBellefeuille wondered why all his recommendations weren’t already in place before the Zhang affair.
“I am pretty floored by your responses,” she said.
Last month, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree admitted there were gaps in the government’s security clearance process that were being addressed in the wake of the Nato intern’s arrest.

stories.title: Credibility challenged in retired teacher’s sexual assault trial
stories.summary: Only two witnesses were called during the sexual assault trial of Murray MacDonald: the female complainant and the accused.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Only two witnesses were called during the sexual assault trial of Murray MacDonald: the female complainant and the accused.

During the trial, which got underway Monday, the court heard that MacDonald, 69, was a teacher at Central Secondary School in downtown London in 1985-86. He came across the Grade 11 student one night at The Bavarian, a former bar located in Cherryhill Village Mall on Oxford Street West.

Both testified they had drinks together and, when the bar was closing, he drove her home. The two then began hugging and kissing in his car.

The complainant, now in her 50s, testified that MacDonald initiated a sex act, while the accused said it was the female who started it.

In his closing submissions, defence lawyer Lakin Afolabi told Justice Kelly Gorman that his client’s testimony was more reliable, saying, “His evidence can raise reasonable doubt therefore you should acquit.”

Afolabi said, “He knew he shouldn’t be making out with a student...he got scared and he backed out.”

He went on to say, “It was a situation he didn’t plan or thought was going to happen.”

Afolabi added that even though it was 40 years ago, “He (MacDonald) testified in an honest and consistent way...I submit she’s playing games... I think she’s just making this stuff up.”

At the start of the trial, MacDonald pleaded not guilty to a single count of sexual assault.

Later in the day, Crown attorney Jeremy Carnegie gave his closing submissions and attacked the credibility of the accused, saying he had a selective memory.

Carnegie said, “When you assess the credibility of Mr. MacDonald there are issues.”

The Crown said the accused was wrong about the female being 19 years old at the time, saying, “He made that up, he didn’t want to paint himself as recklessly engaging in sexual activity with a child.”

Speaking about the complainant, Carnegie argued, “This was a sexual assault...she says she was forced to do something.”

He said that despite the 40 years that have passed, “The things she remembered, she was very clear.”

Carnegie wrapped up by saying, “You shouldn’t accept his version of events and you should find him guilty.”

Justice Gorman is expected to hand down her decision in the case on Dec. 14.

stories.title: Recently-released repeat Ontario sex offender back in custody: police
stories.summary: For the fourth year in a row, repeat Ontario sexual offender Keith Constantin has been re-arrested shortly after his release.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Barely a week after his release, an Ontario man with a history of sexual violence against women and children and a track record of aggresive behaviour behind bars is back in custody after allegedly breaching court-ordered conditions of his release.

Keith Theodore Constantin, a high-risk repeat-offender whose rap sheet is peppered with convictions for sexual assault, assault with a weapon, robbery and possession of explosives, among others, was re-arrested after he allegedly breached his curfew on Oct. 19th, the Durham Regional Police Service (Drps) said Wednesday.

The Hamilton native is now being held in custody pending a bail hearing.

His re-incarceration comes nine days after a public safety alert about the 48-year-old’s statutory release to the region was issued on Oct. 11.

Constantin is not currently serving a federal sentence, the Parole Board of Canada (PBC) told National Post in a statement and, as such, is “no longer under” its authority, as the warrant for his last federal sentence expired in August 2023.

While details about the precise nature of his most recent federal sentence of two years, four months and two days are unclear, a July 2023 PBC decision to revoke his statutory release obtained by National Post shows he was serving time for four counts of uttering threats to cause death or harm, threatening to burn a property, assaulting a police officer, a mischief charge and failing to comply with probation orders.

During that stint of freedom in an undisclosed location (May wish to explain what this means?), the PBC noted Constantin showed up at a local hospital talking about self-harm and “thinking about children again.”

The board also said he “misused a media device… to take over 40 pictures of a young male who appeared to be a young female” and that he made statements “about having deviant fantasies of children.”

A subsequent “medication audit” showed he’d reverted to a “concerning pattern” of overusing mental health drugs to “calm” himself.

Constantin’s most current psychological risk assessment at the time placed him in the very high range for sexual recidivism and the high-moderate range for general and violent recidivism.

“You have no insight into your risk,” the PBC wrote. “While in custody and in the community you required close supervision because of your use of aggression, threats, self-injurious behaviour, and suicidal thoughts.”

Constantin was re-imprisoned that summer, but was released again in 2024 under Canada’s statutory release laws, as reported by the Toronto Sun at the time. He was re-arrested at some point thereafter because another warning came from Durham police in March 2025 that he was being released to live in the area. Two days later, they issued a press release noting Constantin had been arrested for breaching conditions of his release.

His most recent release, his fourth in as many years, follows that incarceration.

National Post has asked PBC for additional clarity on all of Constantin’s three federal sentences and his statutory release.

His first sentence came in 2000 when he was sentenced for two armed robberies and two sexual assaults — one against a seven-year-old boy he’d lured to a park and another on a 45-year-old blind woman who lived in the same building as him.

Again, it’s not clear how much time he served, but he was free in fall 2007, as he was later convicted of sexually assaulting an epileptic woman in the basement apartment of his parents’ home as she was recovering from a seizure that September, according to a 2014 story in The Hamilton Spectator .

Because of stress-induced seizures and fears of suicide in his 27-year-old victim, that case never went to trial. Instead, Constantin made a plea deal in 2009, was sentenced to eight years and received four years’ credit for time served. It also earned him a spot on the national sex-offender registry for life.

His 2014 release was met with considerable pushback in the Hamilton neighbourhoods where he was set to reside when York Regional Police (YRP) warned of it, National Post reported at the time. It led him to break curfew and ask to be imprisoned again.

YRP issued another warning in December 2015 when he was released again after serving 18 months for the breach.

The Pbc’s 2023 release revocation decision also shows that Constantin has been anything but an ideal inmate while incarcerated.

“While in provincial custody serving a sentence, you flooded your cell and wiped feces on the cell window. You threatened to throw feces at a correctional officer and also threatened to kill him. You later threatened to sexually assault another female officer’s children,” they wrote.

He was equally problematic while living in a “group home environment” between June 2020 and January 2021 where he “threatened staff and damaged property.”

“In February 2021, while at a hospital for treatment for banging your head on the walls, you threatened to kill two police officers and throw feces at them,” the Board wrote.

Meanwhile, previous PBC documents obtained by the Spectator indicate Constantin’s behaviour earned him a great deal of time in segregation. He was also diagnosed with alcohol and drug addiction, paranoid schizophrenia, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, depression, an “extremely low range of intellectual ability,” and “character features associated with psychopathy.”

His first sentence came in 2000 when he was sentenced for two armed robberies and two sexual assaults — one against a seven-year-old boy he’d lured to a park and another on a 45-year-old blind woman who lived in the same building as him.

Again, it’s not clear how much time he served, but he was free in fall 2007, as he was later convicted of sexually assaulting an epileptic woman in the basement apartment of his parents’ home as she was recovering from a seizure that September, according to a 2014 story in The Hamilton Spectator .

stories.title: Deadly CFB Wainwright brush fire was caused by training on grenade launcher range, officials say
stories.summary: The Canadian Armed Forces will provide an update on the Wainwright fire that resulted in the deaths of four soldiers and injured 39 others.
stories.author: Liam Newbigging
stories.content:
Officials provided an update Thursday afternoon about the incident that resulted in the deaths of four soldiers and injured 39 others.

Brig.-Gen. Vanessa Hanrahan, deputy Canadian Forces provost marshal, revealed new information about the fire, telling reporters that it was caused by regular training exercises on the automatic grenade range that day.

From there, the blaze initially remained in Permanent Dangerous Area 2, which restricted firefighters’ ability to suppress it. Then a sudden change in wind velocity and direction grew the fire and pushed it towards an area where soldiers were training and overtook their position.

Hanrahan said there is no indication natural gas was a factor or damaged as a result of the fire.

“The investigative team is still out there determining all of the decision-making that happened once the fire started, up to and including when they responded to the incident involving the tragedies of today,” Hanrahan said.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, also corrected the record on two points from the weekend. He initially said that an investigation into the incident would take around a month, but clarified Thursday that the formal board of inquiry investigation “will take as long as it takes.”

He also clarified that the injured soldiers weren’t conducting a section attack range — they were setting up for a pairs range.

“This is where two soldiers attack a target, taking turns covering and firing for one another,” Rutland said.

Officials clarified on Thursday that there are now three parallel investigations underway.

Twenty-seven soldiers injured in CFB Wainwright fire remain in hospital: Premier Smith

'Bright light': Friends and family remember Edmonton soldier killed at CFB Wainwright

The military police are investigating whether or not a possible criminal offence took place, while the chief medical examiner’s office is investigating the cause and nature of the fatalities. At the same time, there is a board of inquiry investigation being done by the army.

“The involvement of the military police should not be interpreted as an indication that an offence has taken place,” Hanrahan said Thursday.

Those killed in the incident were Pte. Aidan Goulding, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark with the Third Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Infantry and Sgt. Morgan Wong with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment.

General Jennie Carignan, chief of defence staff, said Thursday she was heartbroken by the loss, and thanked first responders and those who helped care for those caught in the fire.

“Last weekend’s tragedy in Wainwright has had devastating impacts for our members and their families, and they are being felt across our military community.”

The press conference marks the second formal news conference from CAF officials in the five days since a deadly fire broke out at the military base around 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

The training was prepping soldiers for two roles — the Global Response Task Force and for a deployment to Latvia in the spring. It was the Charlie Company, comprised of around 84 soldiers, that was impacted.

stories.title: Why do daycare costs vary so much between Vancouver, Toronto and Calgary?
stories.summary: One reason is provincial governments employ different methods to structure their child care subsidies
stories.author: Kristy Shen
stories.content:
When we moved to Vancouver from Toronto, we expected to pay more for housing, transportation and food. According to Numbeo, grocery prices are 17.9 per cent higher , gas is 13.2 per cent higher and transit tickets are 4.5 per cent higher in Vancouver than Toronto. But one higher expense caught us off guard: daycare.

Wasn’t the Canada-wide Early Learning and Child Care system designed to cut the cost of daycare to an average of $10 a day across the country?

My first instinct was to blame Vancouver’s notoriously unaffordable real estate, but Toronto’s wasn’t exactly cheap either. So why do subsidized daycare costs vary so much?

I decided to look at three big cities: Vancouver, Toronto and Calgary.

According to the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives , in Vancouver the median cost of daycare for an infant is $40 a day. In Toronto, it’s $22 a day, and in Calgary, it’s $15 a day.

In Vancouver, the range of daycare costs is especially jarring because according to the Ccpa, 45 per cent of preschool spaces only cost $10 a day while 25 per cent of them cost nearly five times as much, at more than $46 a day.

This means that one family could be paying $11,960 a year per child, while another pays just $2,600, despite living in the same city.

It’s tempting to blame the price difference on the cost of real estate. After all, renting or buying a space as a daycare operator in Vancouver won’t cost the same as in Calgary, and wages and other expenses also play a role. But that’s only part of the reason and it doesn’t explain why two Vancouver families can face such different bills.

A main reason for these price discrepancies is the method in which provincial governments have chosen to structure their child care subsidies.

B.C., for example, provides a subsidy toward the daycare provider’s market price. This means unless that daycare is one of the ones that participate in the $10 a day option, the cost could vary widely, since it’s a discount from its market value. But if you’re one of the lucky ones who manages to find $10 a day, you’re sitting pretty.

Ontario, ON the other hand, sets capped fees at subsidized centres at $22 a day. If the centre doesn’t apply or isn’t eligible, they charge market rates. So unless you live or work near one of the subsidized centres, you’re paying higher market rates.

Alberta sets a flat rate of $326.25 a month, the equivalent of $15 a day, at participating centres, and there are no separate $10-a-day daycares.

Eligibility differs across provinces. Not all daycares apply and daycares must be approved to participate in the government-subsidized programs. Not all do.

For parents, it’s not as straightforward as just putting yourself on the waiting list of a subsidized daycare and getting a spot.

Unlike choosing a data plan or clothing store, there are special restrictions, such as distance to home and work, or hours that fit your work schedule, among many other factors.

Even if you are lucky enough to snag a coveted $10-a-day daycare spot, you May have to weigh that against the extra cost and time, if the daycare is far from work and home, or you need to supplement with additional child care arrangements if the hours don’t fit your work hours.

The national daycare program has provided significant savings to parents all over the country, and it’s a vast improvement over the fees parents had to shoulder before. But the massive difference in daycare costs means that depending on where you live, some parents May have to work longer to afford daycare.

Assuming full-time daycare of five days a week for 52 weeks a year, it would cost parents $10,400 a year in Vancouver, $5,720 a year in Toronto and $3,900 a year in Calgary, based on the reported median daily fee.

Let’s translate that into hours worked. According to StatsCan, the median hourly wage for Canadian employees in 2025 was $30.77 , before tax. For simplicity, using before-tax wages across cities, this means the Vancouver parent would need to work 211 extra hours a year, compared to the Calgary parent. That’s the equivalent of five extra weeks of work.

I’m not saying parents should pack up and move to Calgary to cut daycare costs. There are many reasons a family might pick a city, outside of daycare. Nor am I saying that national daycare isn’t helpful.

Still, it’s ironic that the Canada-wide Early Learning and Child Care system, which was designed to help parents across the country afford daycare, has inadvertently resulted in costs varying wildly depending on your postal code, because of how provincial governments have chosen to structure the subsidies.

If you’re curious about how daycare costs in your city stack up against other cities, this daycare explorer lets you find out.

Kristy Shen and Bryce Leung are early retirees and co-authors of Parent Like a Millionaire (Without Being One) .”

stories.title: Ontario sending 28 burn-care workers to help with soldiers critically injured in CFB Wainwright fire
stories.summary: Toronto burn surgeon says the soldier-patients are going through “one of the most painful experiences one can endure."
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Ontario is sending 28 health-care professionals to help care for the soldiers severely injured in a deadly fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta last Saturday.

Thirty-nine soldiers were injured in the fire, 19 critically.

Premier Doug Ford announced that the assistance will include surgeons and nurses with burn care expertise.

“As Alberta hospitals continue to respond to the devastating fire that took place at CFB Wainwright last week, Ontario’s heroic health-care workers are stepping up to help,” Ford said in an X post on Wednesday.

“We’re also providing additional equipment to support their work as they care for those who were injured in last week’s fire,” added Ford, commenting that times of crisis are when Canadians come together, “(we) have each others’ backs. That’s exactly what we’re doing.”

“Some of the burns are 30 per cent to 80 per cent of their entire body — and sometimes changing those dressings can take up to two hours per patient,” Smith said.

Smith, noting three of the soldiers in “very dire health” are Ontarians, thanked Ford and welcomed the 19 burn-unit and five operating room nurses, additional resources she said will help ease pressures on Alberta health-care staff.

Toronto surgeon Dr. Alan Rogers is one of two surgeons on standby to go out to Alberta. He is a surgeon with the Ross Tilley Burn Centre at Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, as well as an associate professor of plastic, reconstructive and aesthetic surgery at the University of Toronto.

He told the CBC that the soldier-patients are going through “one of the most painful experiences one can endure.” He said the number of patients would put an “incredible strain” on existing resources in any province.

The complex care for extensive burns can involve weeks, even months, in hospital, while going through multiple surgeries. Rehab is also a “long and arduous” process, he said.

Sunnybrook has been in contact with the burn teams in Edmonton and Calgary, Rogers said.

“When something like this happens (in large) numbers, it overwhelms the system and it does make it very challenging to manage because ordinarily we’re actually close to or near or even often over capacity in our burn centres.”

As previously reported by National Post , the Canadian Armed Forces said four people were killed in the CFB Wainwright fire. The soldiers killed were later identified as Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.

Premier Smith confirmed the four deaths in an X post earlier this week.

“Many more are injured and in recovery across our hospitals,” she wrote. “Every part of the response is being coordinated, from first responders through to the hospitals treating the injured and the critical care teams working right now. Alberta stands with our Canadian Armed Forces and will provide whatever support is requested.”

Speaking on Sunday, Maj. Gen. L.W. Rutland explained that the soldiers were involved in “high intensity combat training with live munitions.” The purpose of the exercises was to prepare them to be a global response task force that could be quickly deployed anywhere in the world. Soldiers were also getting ready to serve in Latvia in April and May in support of a brigade already in the Baltic country.

Some soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range, said Rutland. A group of 10 soldiers were also conducting an attack exercise on a simulated enemy. The deadly “grass fire ignited in the training area,” said Rutland.

“Uncommonly strong winds cause the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range,” he said.

stories.title: Ottawa ‘not responsible’ for regulating AI data centre power use: minister
stories.summary: AI Minister Evan Solomon spoke to the Senate Committee on Social Affairs, Science and Technology on Thursday, where he was asked about power usage by data centres Canada.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
The federal government is “not responsible” for power regulation and cannot regulate power usage by AI data centres, Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon told a Senate committee on Thursday.

Solomon spoke to the Senate Committee on Social Affairs, Science and Technology on Thursday, where he was asked about power usage by data centres in Canada.

“The federal government is not responsible for power. That is the purvey of provincial regulators. So, we can’t put federal obligations on the power regulation,” he said, adding that provinces like Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia are in the process of creating their own data centre laws.

At the same time, however, both information technology and electricity grids are considered critical infrastructure by the federal government, giving Public Safety Canada the ability to “manage risks and reduce vulnerabilities,” according to the National Strategy for Critical Infrastructure.

Doubling the capacity of Canada’s energy grid was “absolutely critical” to rolling out Canada’s AI strategy, Solomon said.

“We work very closely with best practices around the world to develop very high standards on water use, energy use, investment in the community, strategic importance, consultation, and most importantly, transparency on the promises so you can actually hold them to account,” he said.

The federal government’s recently released ‘Responsible Data Centre Development Principles’ require that companies building new data centre projects “do not shift electricity costs onto Canadians” and “minimize water use and environmental impacts.”

Solomon was also asked how many data centres Canada was looking to build.

“We received proposals for… over 160,” he said.

While large data centre projects will require around 100 megawatts of power per building, there “May be some smaller ones” as well, he added.

“We have MOUs with about four (data center companies) so far,” he said.

Ottawa is “supporting the building of Canadian data that are Canadian-owned,” Solomon said, however, some major projects in Canada are being helmed by U.S. tech giants.

A company pursuing a wind and hydrogen development in Nova Scotia says it has plans for a $10-billion AI data centre in Cape Breton that it describes as the largest private investment in provincial history.

EverWind Fuels announced last week that U.S. AI company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for a 18,600-square metre data centre in Point Tupper, N.S., that would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase.

The data centre is scheduled to come online late next year. A 325-megawatt expansion is expected in mid-2028, which would bring the development’s total energy demand to 420 megawatts, the company said.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said the data centre project was a major vote of confidence in the rural area about 200 kilometres east of Halifax. He said Canada does not have enough secure data infrastructure to meet the requirements of its businesses, governments and health-care institutions.

Data centres are typically massive operations that require immense amounts of electricity to run and cool off computer servers.

Water from nearby Landrie Lake will be used to cool the Point Tupper data centre’s servers, and the company stressed it will safeguard the water supply.

EverWind said the cooling system will be closed-loop, similar to a car’s radiator, with cooling fluid recycled or disposed of off site, not in local waterways. The system will use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in the first phase, which EverWind said is about the same as a large shopping mall.

That will expand to an average draw of 500,000 litre per day when the expansion is complete, about one per cent of the lake’s safe daily yield of 34 million litres.

–with files from Canadian Press

A company pursuing a wind and hydrogen development in Nova Scotia says it has plans for a $10-billion AI data centre in Cape Breton that it describes as the largest private investment in provincial history.

EverWind Fuels announced last week that U.S. AI company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for a 18,600-square metre data centre in Point Tupper, N.S., that would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase.

The data centre is scheduled to come online late next year. A 325-megawatt expansion is expected in mid-2028, which would bring the development’s total energy demand to 420 megawatts, the company said.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said the data centre project was a major vote of confidence in the rural area about 200 kilometres east of Halifax. He said Canada does not have enough secure data infrastructure to meet the requirements of its businesses, governments and health-care institutions.
Data centres are typically massive operations that require immense amounts of electricity to run and cool off computer servers.
Water from nearby Landrie Lake will be used to cool the Point Tupper data centre’s servers, and the company stressed it will safeguard the water supply.

EverWind said the cooling system will be closed-loop, similar to a car’s radiator, with cooling fluid recycled or disposed of off site, not in local waterways. The system will use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in the first phase, which EverWind said is about the same as a large shopping mall.
That will expand to an average draw of 500,000 litre per day when the expansion is complete, about one per cent of the lake’s safe daily yield of 34 million litres.

stories.title: Canada welcomes EU leaders to Montreal for talks on next steps in relationship
stories.summary: Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to welcome European Commissioner Ursula von der Leyen to Montreal today after months of pursuing closer ties with the EU.
stories.author: David Baxter The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Thursday this week’s Canada-EU Summit opens up discussions on making Canada the bloc’s first “associate member.”

Ahead of meetings hosted Thursday and Friday in Montreal by Prime Minister Mark Carney, von der Leyen said in a speech that the term is helpful for deepening policy alignment.

“Canada cannot become a fully fledged member of the European Union because of geography. But we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible, and this is why we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union,” she said Thursday morning in Montreal.

After von der Leyen proposed associate member status in a September speech, Canadian and European officials immediately downplayed the language and instead spoke of an “alliance for the future.”

Several EU member nations, including Germany, rejected the term this week when proposed language was floated in documents ahead of the summit. Several European news agencies reported this week that the idea was off the table.

Prime Minister Carney has said the substance of the agreement is more important than the language used to describe the evolving relationship.

Von der Leyen’s visit comes after months of Carney pursuing closer ties with the EU. He has argued Europe complements Canada’s economic strengths and shares its values.

Thursday’s agenda includes a welcome dinner with elected and business leaders before Canadian and European leaders get down to talks on Friday.

In her Thursday speech, von der Leyen said the EU wants to work first with Canada and then with other nations to reinforce their sovereignty and interests.

“We can no longer let ourselves be shackled by the limits of the old world order,” she said.

“We are witnessing a deeper decay in international order. Alliances and assumptions that have enabled our prosperity and security are changing rapidly.”

She cited “choke points” in trade, where one country coerces another by manipulating supply chains. She did not name specific countries, though her comments come in the context of U.S. tariffs and Chinese leverage over critical minerals.

She said countries can work strategically with close partners or try to face down threats on their own.

“We are seeing in real time our sovereignty being attacked,” she said.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly told reporters Thursday that Canada’s work with the EU seeks to reduce reliance on the U.S. as Washington pursues its trade war.

“The challenge of the era is really to be capable of saving companies that otherwise will fail and will have job losses. So we’re in a hurry,” she said in French.

Von der Leyen said in her speech that a new partnership could see Canada use its mining expertise to do more to exploit mineral resources at home, such as those required for electric vehicles. Those efforts would be boosted by European “industrial demand, technology and investment.”

She said Canadian startups and researchers will soon be able to train their models on the EU’s supercomputers.

“Tomorrow we will finalize our agreement to bring Canada into Europe’s infrastructure for supercomputing,” she said Thursday.

Both sides are also working on joint projects in the Arctic on ocean monitoring, “critical raw materials” and connectivity as Russia rebuilds its Arctic military footprint.

The EU “will deepen Canada’s engagement” in university student exchanges through the Erasmus+ program, von der Leyen said. Both sides are also “working to strengthen Canada’s participation” in the next phase of a scientific research program called Horizon, she added.

She said there also could be cross-Atlantic collaboration between elected officials and judiciaries. The European Parliament recently announced it is opening a satellite office in Ottawa to facilitate more exchanges with Canadian MPs and senators.

“The co-operation could also entail parliament to parliament — between our two parliaments — and court to court,” she said.

As von der Leyen spoke, the Conservatives dismissed Carney’s work with Europe as an attempt to distract from deteriorating living standards and the trade war.

“Canadians are faced with another distraction for the next two days, of more meaningless agreements. Meanwhile, they go to food banks and struggle to pay their mortgages,” Conservative trade critic Stephanie Kusie said on Parliament Hill.

Her party colleagues argued Canada should avoid deepening ties with Europe until 10 holdout EU member states ratify a decade-old trade deal with Canada and Brussels stops charging carbon tariffs on Canadian imports.

The Tories have claimed that any new deal with the EU would see Canada lose control over immigration. Federal officials have repeatedly insisted that any labour mobility agreements would be limited to specific professions or student exchanges.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is not participating in the summit and instead sent his newly appointed chief diplomat Pascal Paradis.

St-Pierre Plamondon made the announcement Wednesday after Carney refused his request to speak at the summit.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

— With files from Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman and Dylan Robertson in Ottawa

stories.title: $40M Lotto Max ticket validated hours before expiry in Ontario
stories.summary: The identity of the winner who purchased the ticket in Grey County, Ont., remains unknown.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
A $40 million Lotto Max ticket sold in Ontario has been validated just hours before it was set to expire.

The Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG) said Wednesday the ticket was validated just before its midnight deadline, and the ticket registered as the $40 million winner from the Oct. 28, 2025, Lotto Max draw.

But the identity of the winner who purchased the ticket in Grey County, Ont., remains unknown, and OLG says the prize cannot yet be awarded.

Tony Bitonti, Olg’s director of media relations, said the lottery corporation has contacted the person or people who validated the ticket and will now meet with them to determine whether they are the rightful owner or owners.

Bitonti said the corporation has detailed information about the winning ticket, but because it was purchased at a retailer, it does not know the identity of the person or group who originally bought it.

As with all OLG prize claims of more than $1,000, a review will be conducted to determine rightful ownership. Details about the ticket are being kept confidential because the information will be used to determine whether the person or people who validated it are the owners.

The ticket was purchased at an authorized lottery retailer somewhere in Grey County for the Oct. 28, 2025, draw.

Grey County includes communities such as Owen Sound, Meaford, The Blue Mountains, Flesherton, Markdale, Durham and Hanover.

Ahead of Wednesday’s deadline, OLG urged anyone who bought a Lotto Max ticket in Grey County, or who visited the area around the time of the draw, to check their tickets.

The winning numbers were 06, 14, 17, 19, 26, 43 and 45, with bonus number 27. OLG had said approximately 50 claims related to the ticket were being processed before Wednesday’s deadline.

If OLG determines the rightful ownership of the ticket, it said it will hold a winner celebration and disclose the winner’s story to the media and public.

The ticket was purchased at an authorized lottery retailer somewhere in Grey County for the Oct. 28, 2025, draw.
Grey County includes communities such as Owen Sound, Meaford, The Blue Mountains, Flesherton, Markdale, Durham and Hanover.
Ahead of Wednesday’s deadline, OLG urged anyone who bought a Lotto Max ticket in Grey County, or who visited the area around the time of the draw, to check their tickets.
The winning numbers were 06, 14, 17, 19, 26, 43 and 45, with bonus number 27. OLG had said approximately 50 claims related to the ticket were being processed before Wednesday’s deadline.
If OLG determines the rightful ownership of the ticket, it said it will hold a winner celebration and disclose the winner’s story to the media and public.

stories.title: Stelco owner hopes to recall laid-off steelworkers before Christmas
stories.summary: Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CEO Lourenco Goncalves says he hopes to bring back laid-off Stelco workers before Christmas if a plan to increase Canadian sales succeeds.
stories.author: Brett Bundale
stories.content:
Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CEO Lourenco Goncalves says he hopes to bring back laid-off Stelco workers before Christmas if a plan to increase Canadian sales succeeds.

In a written statement to The Canadian Press, Goncalves says the company is now counting on increased purchases of Canadian-made steel rather than tighter import restrictions to restore jobs at its Ontario operations.

Goncalves says the number of layoffs “was never 500” but is rather 175, despite an internal Stelco letter to employees on Sept. 28 warning that up to 500 workers at Hamilton Works and Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont., could be affected.

He also says Stelco is not for sale for at least the next calendar year, and criticizes Industry Minister Mélanie Joly for publicly discussing the possibility of a sale.

Goncalves says Joly is discouraging foreign investment in Canada by publicly discussing potential buyers for Stelco and criticizing the company’s business decisions.

He says Cleveland-Cliffs had expected to sell more cold-rolled and galvanized steel in Canada when it acquired Stelco in 2024, but that demand has not materialized.
