Friday, 23 October 2026 at 09:46

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

The Braves, Trojans and Merchants all have home games tonight.

PJHL - It's a two-game weekend for the Tavistock Braves, the Thamesford Trojans, and the Norwich Merchants.

The Braves will battle the Paris Mounties at the Tavistock and District Rec Centre tonight, while the Trojans take on the Petrolia Flyers at the Thamesford Rec Centre, and the Norwich Merchants face the Dorchester Dolphins to Nor-Del Arena. The Tavistock and Thamesford games will get underway at 7:30 p.m. and the Norwich game has an 8:00 p.m. start time.

The Trojans will also visit the North Middlesex Stars at 8:00 p.m. tomorrow. Both Norwich and Tavistock will have the day off on Saturday, but the Merchants will welcome the Braves to Nor-Del Arena for a matinee matchup at 2:30 p.m. on Sunday.

The Braves are on top of the Doherty Division standings with 21 points, ahead of the Wellesley Applejacks with 18 points and the New Hamburg Firebirds with 15 points.

The Merchants are in fourth place with 10 points, and the Mounties and Dolphins are tied for fifth place with eight points each. The Hespeler Shamrocks sit at the bottom of the standings with six points.

The Trojans are in fifth place in the Yeck Division standings with nine points, one point ahead of the sixth place Lucan Irish with eight points and two points ahead of the last place Port Stanley Sailors with seven points.

The Mount Brydges Bulldogs are on top of the standigs with 16 points, followed by the Exeter Hawks and the Stars with 14 points each. The Flyers are in third place with 13 points, and the Aylmer Spitfires are in fourth place with 12 points.

Navy Vets Preview - Oct 23rd to Oct 25th Tonight's pre-game ceremony will celebrate the 60th anniversary of the Woodstock Navy Vets.

Norfolk OPP Briefs - October 23rd, 2026 Briefs include two incidents in Waterford; a break and enter on Green Street and a stolen vehicle on Concession 8 Townsend.

Wolverines to Face WPS in Friday Night Lights Charity Classic The Woodstock Wolverines will face off against members of the Woodstock Police Service in the first annual Friday Night Lights Charity Classic on October 30th.

Blandford-Blenheim Candidate Profile - Nancy Demarest When the ballots are cast, a current councillor in Blandford-Blenheim is seeking re-election. Nancy Demarest is seeking a third term on council.

OPP Respond to Weapons Call in Tillsonburg The Oxford OPP responded to a weapons call, which turned into a teaching moment for 5 people.

Navy Vets Celebrating 60 Years It is the 60th anniversary of the Woodstock Navy Vets, and the Woodstock Museum has an exhibit to help celebrate.

Woodstock Receives Gaming Revenue Payment from OLG The cheque is worth $416,310 and its for hosting Gateway Casinos.

Schedule Released for CPKC Holiday Train The CPKC Holiday Train will be stopping in Woodstock on Saturday, November 21st.

Local History Speaker Series Returns Two events will be held in November that are part of the Local History Speaker Series.

Woodstock Police Briefs - Oct. 21st, 2026 An impaired driver has been taken off the road, and a suspect in a theft was arrested by the Woodstock Police Service.

Advance Voting Numbers High in Woodstock As election day comes closer, the City of Woodstock has released the number of ballots cast between online and advance polling stations.

Winning Lotto Max Ticket Sold in Oxford A Lotto Max ticket worth $100,000 was sold in Oxford County. The $90 million jackpot was awarded in Alberta.

Voting Opens and Tickets Available for Chamber Awards The Woodstock District Chamber of Commerce will host the 29th annual Business Awards of Excellence on November 4th.

Oxford Honours CFB Wainwright Victims Several local municipalities have decided to fly their flags at half mast in response to the tragedy.

SWOX Collision Sends 7 to Hospital The Oxford OPP laid a charge after a two-vehicle collision in South-West Oxford sent 7 people to the hospital.

Brantford Man Charged with Impaired The 42-year-old has a November court date in his hometown.

News Poll: World Series 2026 Who do you think will win the 2026 World Series?

Woodstock Hockey Day Returns this Saturday It's a day of fun hosted by the local hockey community in Woodstock.

GoFundMe Page Supporting Waterford Crash Victim Josh Lenze has been in the ICU with a serious spinal cord injury for two weeks now.

OPP Investigating Collision Involving Tillsonburg Resident A two-vehicle collision is under investigation and involves a person from Tillsonburg.

stories.title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet set to continue
stories.summary: Toronto - A coroner's inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony in the presence of police is set to resume this morning after adjourning early on Thursday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s mother was shown snippets of security footage from the day her daughter died as she resumed her testimony at a coroner’s inquest on Friday after making a new allegation against police involved in the case.

Claudette Beals watched several short clips from a nearly 50-minute video combining silent CCTV footage from the hallway outside their west-end Toronto home with audio from 911 calls and a police microphone. The video was previously played in its entirety at the inquest.

In one clip, Beals and her son are seen going into the apartment, minutes after Korchinski-Paquet went in to use the bathroom.

“What is she doing?” Beals says in the recording. She agreed Friday that she was referring to her daughter.

Another clip shows Beals and two officers leave the apartment, and another soon after shows her knocking on the neighbour’s door, saying her daughter “jumped.”

Inquest counsel Roger Shallow asked her about it on Friday afternoon.

“The police told me that Regis committed suicide, so you know what, why are you asking me this question?” she responded.

“Is that what we heard you say at this point in time on the video?” Shallow asked again.

“That’s exactly what you heard me say,” Beals said.

At various points Friday, Beals was asked if she needed a break from watching the video, but she said she was OK to continue.

Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman, fell from a highrise balcony in the presence of police on May 27, 2020.

Beals testified Thursday that she saw officers push her daughter toward the balcony, prompting the inquest to take a prolonged break as counsel for the parties figured out a way forward.

The presiding coroner, Dr. David Cameron, told jurors Thursday counsel were strategizing on how to best have them hear evidence related to the circumstances of Korchinski-Paquet’s death “in a clear and fair manner.”

As the inquest reconvened Friday morning, Cameron said counsel had worked “very late into the evening to reach a consensus on how to proceed forward” but weren’t “quite there yet.”

He encouraged jurors to review and discuss the evidence until mid-afternoon, which is when Beals continued her testimony.

Right before the proceedings wrapped for the day, Shallow asked Beals if she blamed herself for what happened to her daughter, while stressing it was not her fault.

“Do you feel, even though you shouldn’t — because of course we’ve heard of your challenges and your frustration, and you called the police to have your children removed, and this fateful tragedy unfolded — do you feel a sense, even though you shouldn’t, of guilt because of that?” he said.

“I feel very responsible for my daughter’s death, very responsible,” she replied.

Beals is set to face questions from lawyers representing roughly a dozen parties next week.

On Thursday, she said that the family struggled at times to deal with Korchinski-Paquet’s seizures and would have benefited from support and education regarding epilepsy.

The inquest has heard Korchinski-Paquet experienced seizures from epilepsy and had two on the day she died.

Her seizures were often followed by periods of erratic and aggressive behaviour, the inquest has heard. A neurologist who reviewed her records said she had previously shown symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium, an altered state of mind that can follow seizures.

Beals, her son and Korchinski-Paquet each called 911 in the afternoon of May 27, 2020, to report a fight involving knives. Six officers and two paramedics arrived at the building soon after.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Boon or boondoggle? N.S. weighs $10B data centre's promised economic benefits
stories.summary: Halifax - Living more than 200 kilometres from the site of a major artificial intelligence data centre proposal isn't stopping Michael McCluskey from voicing his opposition to the project.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
HALIFAX - Living more than 200 kilometres from the site of a major artificial intelligence data centre proposal isn’t stopping Michael McCluskey from voicing his opposition to the project.

The retired military veteran and training professional from Dartmouth, N.S., has added his name to a Change.org petition that has already collected more than 18,000 signatures since the project was announced last Friday.

Anthropic, an American AI company, plans to lease the Point Tupper, N.S., site for its first Canadian data centre, the first major AI facility to be publicly proposed in Nova Scotia.

However, McCluskey said he just views it as the latest in a long history of Nova Scotia chasing grand economic development projects that never seem to deliver.

He said the site won’t be able to serve any other purpose if Anthropic walks away, and he’s worried the province will be left holding the bag when economic benefits don’t appear.

“They don’t put (data centres) anywhere that’s prospering,” McCluskey said in an interview.

“They don’t put them in San Francisco. They don’t put them in Los Angeles …. What they’re looking for are disadvantaged, economically desperate areas?”

EverWind plans to build the 18,600-square-metre data centre by late 2027 and lease it for 20 years to Anthropic under undisclosed financial terms. San Francisco-based Anthropic says Canada is the sixth-largest worldwide user of its Claude AI model, which is driving the project.

EverWind calls the data centre the biggest private investment in provincial history. It originally planned to build a wind-powered hydrogen plant exporting energy from its Cape Breton marine terminal. The company said it’s still pursuing this hydrogen project.

The proposal has thrust Nova Scotia into a debate that has exploded across Canada in recent months as massive AI corporations race to build computing capacity in areas with enough electricity and water to feed the resource-gobbling sector.

The facilities can range in size from a micro data centre about the size of a refrigerator to a hyperscale campus that consumes a level of power comparable to a small city.

A recent York University report found that Canada’s existing 194 data centres have a combined capacity to draw 1.6 gigawatts of electricity. More than 14-times that amount — about 22.7 gigawatts — are either under construction or in the announcement stage across 213 sites.

The proposals are supersized. Existing data centres have an average capacity of about 11 megawatts and cover an average of 0.05 square-kilometres, about the size of six Canadian football fields. New proposals average about 122 megawatts spread over more than eight square kilometres, almost 1,000 football fields.

York researchers say a 122-megawatt operation will use the same amount of power annually as 49,000 to 78,000 Canadian homes.

EverWind’s data centre will be 95 megawatts in the first phase, and the company has plans for a 325-megawatt expansion by mid-2028.

Paris Marx, a Newfoundland and Labrador-based tech critic and author of “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” said data centre opposition is forming quickly in Canada because communities have seen U.S. headlines about skyrocketing power rates and water consumption over the last 18 to 24 months.

He said if the EverWind project moves ahead, he expects it will follow a global trend where the costs to communities are higher than first projected.

“The benefits just aren’t there to the degree that we expect,” he said in an interview.

“There are not a lot of jobs that are associated with data centres beyond the construction phase. Obviously, we need to employ people to build them. They don’t employ a ton of people to actually run them.”

EverWind expects to create 2,000 jobs during construction and 215 permanent jobs between the data centre and the four wind farms that will eventually power it.

The salaries for the permanent jobs would range between $135,000 and $185,000 per year, the company said, with about half of those jobs in the data centre and half in the wind farms.

Sean Mullin, with the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, said data centres may not create the same amount of jobs as something like an auto factory, but even a couple hundred positions can make a big difference in a small community.

“We’d rather have that economic activity here than somewhere else. And then that also benefits the country in the sense that we have more compute capacity to serve the rest of the country,” he said in an interview.

Kody Blois, a Nova Scotia MP and parliamentary secretary to the prime minister, said at EverWind’s announcement last week that AI is transforming the global economy and Ottawa wants to seize the opportunity.

“These are really important jobs right here in the region. They matter to families, they matter to communities,” he said.

EverWind CEO Trent Vichie said there were already more than 20 Nova Scotian contractors working on the site and economic spinoffs will multiply the direct benefits.

“More people in restaurants, more people buying from local businesses,” he said last Friday. “It’s really providing an anchor to strengthening the community that’s already here today.”

Marx said he doubts the project will actually proceed, saying data centres are seen as a backup at the moment when other projects, such as hydrogen, fail to gain traction. He noted EverWind has already hit roadblocks a planned hydrogen project in Newfoundland.

EverWind said in an email that it’s participating in an auction to sell hydrogen to Europe and that the data centre adds a major industrial use for its renewable energy portfolio and infrastructure while the international hydrogen market develops.

“The data centre helps maintain investment momentum in wind, transmission and shared infrastructure that can also support hydrogen and ammonia over time,” the company said.

“While these investments complement each other, they are not dependent on one another.”

Anthropic lost more than US$80 billion during the first half of 2026, according to Reuters. That’s up from a US$13-billion loss in the first half of 2025. The company is planning an initial public offering of shares as early as November that could value the company at US$1.5 trillion.

The firm declined an interview request this week but has told investors that its plan to spend $518 billion on AI infrastructure over the next decade is needed because computing power is the key constraint on AI development. It has said future demand for AI systems is expected to exceed available supply, according to Reuters.

CEO Dario Amodei and the company’s five other co-founders established Anthropic as a public benefit corporation, a designation that for-profit companies select to balance financial goals and social impact.

The company has also committed to setting aside five per cent of its shares to a public benefit fund which will grow along with Anthropic’s valuation.

The fund will explore large donations to non-profits or direct distributions to specific populations. The company says it has already committed US$200 million to studying and addressing potential impacts of AI technology on the labour market.

But Marx remains skeptical about whether AI companies have a good business model.

“I think that there are also a lot of market questions as to whether something like this will even be necessary, or if a client like Anthropic will actually show up,” he said.

paragraphs: HALIFAX - Living more than 200 kilometres from the site of a major artificial intelligence data centre proposal isn’t stopping Michael McCluskey from voicing his opposition to the project.

The retired military veteran and training professional from Dartmouth, N.S., has added his name to a Change.org petition that has already collected more than 18,000 signatures since the project was announced last Friday.
Anthropic, an American AI company, plans to lease the Point Tupper, N.S., site for its first Canadian data centre, the first major AI facility to be publicly proposed in Nova Scotia.
However, McCluskey said he just views it as the latest in a long history of Nova Scotia chasing grand economic development projects that never seem to deliver.
He said the site won’t be able to serve any other purpose if Anthropic walks away, and he’s worried the province will be left holding the bag when economic benefits don’t appear.
“They don’t put (data centres) anywhere that’s prospering,” McCluskey said in an interview.
“They don’t put them in San Francisco. They don’t put them in Los Angeles …. What they’re looking for are disadvantaged, economically desperate areas?”

EverWind plans to build the 18,600-square-metre data centre by late 2027 and lease it for 20 years to Anthropic under undisclosed financial terms. San Francisco-based Anthropic says Canada is the sixth-largest worldwide user of its Claude AI model, which is driving the project.

EverWind calls the data centre the biggest private investment in provincial history. It originally planned to build a wind-powered hydrogen plant exporting energy from its Cape Breton marine terminal. The company said it’s still pursuing this hydrogen project.

The proposal has thrust Nova Scotia into a debate that has exploded across Canada in recent months as massive AI corporations race to build computing capacity in areas with enough electricity and water to feed the resource-gobbling sector.
The facilities can range in size from a micro data centre about the size of a refrigerator to a hyperscale campus that consumes a level of power comparable to a small city.

A recent York University report found that Canada’s existing 194 data centres have a combined capacity to draw 1.6 gigawatts of electricity. More than 14-times that amount — about 22.7 gigawatts — are either under construction or in the announcement stage across 213 sites.

The proposals are supersized. Existing data centres have an average capacity of about 11 megawatts and cover an average of 0.05 square-kilometres, about the size of six Canadian football fields. New proposals average about 122 megawatts spread over more than eight square kilometres, almost 1,000 football fields.
York researchers say a 122-megawatt operation will use the same amount of power annually as 49,000 to 78,000 Canadian homes.
EverWind’s data centre will be 95 megawatts in the first phase, and the company has plans for a 325-megawatt expansion by mid-2028.

Paris Marx, a Newfoundland and Labrador-based tech critic and author of “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” said data centre opposition is forming quickly in Canada because communities have seen U.S. headlines about skyrocketing power rates and water consumption over the last 18 to 24 months.
He said if the EverWind project moves ahead, he expects it will follow a global trend where the costs to communities are higher than first projected.
“The benefits just aren’t there to the degree that we expect,” he said in an interview.

“There are not a lot of jobs that are associated with data centres beyond the construction phase. Obviously, we need to employ people to build them. They don’t employ a ton of people to actually run them.”
EverWind expects to create 2,000 jobs during construction and 215 permanent jobs between the data centre and the four wind farms that will eventually power it.
The salaries for the permanent jobs would range between $135,000 and $185,000 per year, the company said, with about half of those jobs in the data centre and half in the wind farms.

Sean Mullin, with the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, said data centres may not create the same amount of jobs as something like an auto factory, but even a couple hundred positions can make a big difference in a small community.

“We’d rather have that economic activity here than somewhere else. And then that also benefits the country in the sense that we have more compute capacity to serve the rest of the country,” he said in an interview.

Kody Blois, a Nova Scotia MP and parliamentary secretary to the prime minister, said at EverWind’s announcement last week that AI is transforming the global economy and Ottawa wants to seize the opportunity.
“These are really important jobs right here in the region. They matter to families, they matter to communities,” he said.
EverWind CEO Trent Vichie said there were already more than 20 Nova Scotian contractors working on the site and economic spinoffs will multiply the direct benefits.
“More people in restaurants, more people buying from local businesses,” he said last Friday. “It’s really providing an anchor to strengthening the community that’s already here today.”

Marx said he doubts the project will actually proceed, saying data centres are seen as a backup at the moment when other projects, such as hydrogen, fail to gain traction. He noted EverWind has already hit roadblocks a planned hydrogen project in Newfoundland.

EverWind said in an email that it’s participating in an auction to sell hydrogen to Europe and that the data centre adds a major industrial use for its renewable energy portfolio and infrastructure while the international hydrogen market develops.
“The data centre helps maintain investment momentum in wind, transmission and shared infrastructure that can also support hydrogen and ammonia over time,” the company said.
“While these investments complement each other, they are not dependent on one another.”

Anthropic lost more than US$80 billion during the first half of 2026, according to Reuters. That’s up from a US$13-billion loss in the first half of 2025. The company is planning an initial public offering of shares as early as November that could value the company at US$1.5 trillion.

The firm declined an interview request this week but has told investors that its plan to spend $518 billion on AI infrastructure over the next decade is needed because computing power is the key constraint on AI development. It has said future demand for AI systems is expected to exceed available supply, according to Reuters.

CEO Dario Amodei and the company’s five other co-founders established Anthropic as a public benefit corporation, a designation that for-profit companies select to balance financial goals and social impact.
The company has also committed to setting aside five per cent of its shares to a public benefit fund which will grow along with Anthropic’s valuation.

The fund will explore large donations to non-profits or direct distributions to specific populations. The company says it has already committed US$200 million to studying and addressing potential impacts of AI technology on the labour market.
But Marx remains skeptical about whether AI companies have a good business model.
“I think that there are also a lot of market questions as to whether something like this will even be necessary, or if a client like Anthropic will actually show up,” he said.

— With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Ottawa tells its diplomats not to meet with U.S. midterm candidates
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canadian diplomats were directed this week not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Canadian diplomats were directed this week not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections.

Glen Linder, assistant deputy minister for the Americas at Global Affairs Canada, sent a memo midday Tuesday to members of the foreign service in the United States.

The memo, which was obtained by The Canadian Press, says if diplomats find themselves “in the same physical space” as a candidate or elected official, they should avoid being photographed or having their name or position appear in any public communications materials.

It says meetings or events with other elected officials who aren’t candidates in the midterms can happen if necessary, but they should be discussed in advance with senior officials.

The memo says these instructions are similar to those in place during election periods in Canada, when public servants are expected to avoid contact with elected officials except in exceptional circumstances.

“Especially in view of heightened sensitivity, we need to take our obligation of non-partisanship extremely seriously and take a very risk-averse approach,” says the memo.

The memo comes as the Trump administration accuses Canadian politicians of interfering in American elections.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both disputed claims of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterms on Wednesday, after the U.S. embassy in Canada released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claimed indicate “plans to influence American politics.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is quoted five times in the list the embassy released Wednesday.

The list includes quotes from Joly offered without context about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states through counter-tariffs. Joly made the comments while addressing Canada’s response to U.S.-imposed tariffs.

In a news conference on Parliament Hill on Wednesday, Carney — flanked by Joly — responded to a question about the America accusations by pointing out it was the United States which initiated trade actions against Canada.

“All of our actions are in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy,” Carney told reporters after announcing a $9 billion aid package in response to U.S. tariffs.

Ford, who is also quoted in the U.S. embassy release, said he has “no interest at all” in interfering in American elections.

“I’ll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability,” Ford said, adding he spent 20 years in the United States and “loves the American people.”

Janice Charette, Canada’s chief trade negotiator to the United States, said during a discussion at the Toronto Global Forum on Thursday that Donald Trump will continue to be president after the midterm elections and his administration will still drive trade policy.

“The role of Congress and the role of the Senate may or may not change through all of that,” she said. “We will remain absolutely focused on what Canada’s objectives are here and pursue them whenever the moment arrives.

“Canada will continue to work to try to put our best foot forward and make the best case for Canada.”

Charette said during the discussion that she doesn’t see Canada going back to a “tariff-free existence.”

“We had tariff-free trade, that was the best,” he said. “I don’t think we’re going back. We are in a transition to a new trading relationship with the United States.”

As that discussion began, vice chair of BMO Financial Group Brian Tobin said he wanted assurance, “mostly for the peace and tranquillity of the ambassador to Canada from the United States,” that she was not engaged in any kind of electoral activity at the event.

“I think we’re good,” Charette said as the audience laughed.

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that could end Republican control of Congress.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said earlier this month American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back last week, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

Wednesday’s post from the embassy ended by saying “Americans decide America’s elections.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray and Catherine Morrison

stories.title: Ottawa tells its diplomats not to meet with U.S. midterm candidates
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canadian diplomats were directed this week not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Canadian diplomats were directed this week not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections.

Glen Linder, assistant deputy minister for the Americas at Global Affairs Canada, sent a memo midday Tuesday to members of the foreign service in the United States.

The memo, which was obtained by The Canadian Press, says if diplomats find themselves “in the same physical space” as a candidate or elected official, they should avoid being photographed or having their name or position appear in any public communications materials.

It says meetings or events with other elected officials who aren’t candidates in the midterms can happen if necessary, but they should be discussed in advance with senior officials.

The memo says these instructions are similar to those in place during election periods in Canada, when public servants are expected to avoid contact with elected officials except in exceptional circumstances.

“Especially in view of heightened sensitivity, we need to take our obligation of non-partisanship extremely seriously and take a very risk-averse approach,” says the memo.

The memo comes as the Trump administration accuses Canadian politicians of interfering in American elections.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both disputed claims of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterms on Wednesday, after the U.S. embassy in Canada released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claimed indicate “plans to influence American politics.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is quoted five times in the list the embassy released Wednesday.

The list includes quotes from Joly offered without context about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states through counter-tariffs. Joly made the comments while addressing Canada’s response to U.S.-imposed tariffs.

In a news conference on Parliament Hill on Wednesday, Carney — flanked by Joly — responded to a question about the America accusations by pointing out it was the United States which initiated trade actions against Canada.

“All of our actions are in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy,” Carney told reporters after announcing a $9 billion aid package in response to U.S. tariffs.

Ford, who is also quoted in the U.S. embassy release, said he has “no interest at all” in interfering in American elections.

“I’ll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability,” Ford said, adding he spent 20 years in the United States and “loves the American people.”

Janice Charette, Canada’s chief trade negotiator to the United States, said during a discussion at the Toronto Global Forum on Thursday that Donald Trump will continue to be president after the midterm elections and his administration will still drive trade policy.

“The role of Congress and the role of the Senate may or may not change through all of that,” she said. “We will remain absolutely focused on what Canada’s objectives are here and pursue them whenever the moment arrives.

“Canada will continue to work to try to put our best foot forward and make the best case for Canada.”

Charette said during the discussion that she doesn’t see Canada going back to a “tariff-free existence.”

“We had tariff-free trade, that was the best,” he said. “I don’t think we’re going back. We are in a transition to a new trading relationship with the United States.”

As that discussion began, vice chair of BMO Financial Group Brian Tobin said he wanted assurance, “mostly for the peace and tranquillity of the ambassador to Canada from the United States,” that she was not engaged in any kind of electoral activity at the event.

“I think we’re good,” Charette said as the audience laughed.

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that could end Republican control of Congress.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said earlier this month American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back last week, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

Wednesday’s post from the embassy ended by saying “Americans decide America’s elections.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray and Catherine Morrison
